Amy Costa: Thank you, good morning Madam Chair and members. My name is Amy Costa. I'm Chief Deputy Director at The Department of Finance. I want to thank you for inviting me and allowing me to provide an overview of the governor's proposed 2017/18 budget. I have provided a number of slides which will helpfully hope guide my presentation. As you can see on the second slide and the slide that Senator Nelson referenced in his opening comments. The tide of revenues is beginning to turn. Even in the best of times we often note that the states budget is rather precariously balanced. And you can see that we have what we would consider a modest adjustment compared to the 2016 budget act, when we passed it. It's revenues are coming in lower than we had originally projected across the board. So that's corporation, personal income tax, and sales in use tax. So we're still growing, we're just not growing as quickly as we had estimated in the 2106 budget act. The slower revenue growth is totaling $5.8 billion over three years. And we also have a current year shortfall in the Med-ical program of $1.8 billion. That shortfall is attributable to two main factors, one of which is a drug rebate. And the other of which is a calculation error related to say things for the coordinated care initiative. And that is contributing to a projected budget deficit of $1.6 billion. On the third slide, you can see a chart that we've shown many times before which shows capital gains revenues over time. We've shown this graph in the past to just illustrate the high volatility of this particular revenue source. Through 2017, I note we are still forecasting above historical levels of capital gains. But we are adjusting the forecast we provided at the 2016 Budget Act. Our budget has been helped actually by the recent enactment of several voter approved initiatives. Prop 52, the hospital fee provided 211 million. Prop 56 at tobacco tax provided 1.2 billion, and Prop 57 precinct reformed provided $22 million savings in solution. We've also mitigated our projected deficit by a statue requires determining that the Coordinated Care Initiative is not providing savings. The elimination of what we call CCI provides the state a net benefit of $628 million. We do propose saving one portion of the program CCI which is the Cal MediConnect pilot project which is authorized by the Federal Government. And which we estimated to provided around $22 million in savings through that pilot. If you'll turn to the fourth slide, you'll see that even in light of revenues coming in a little bit slower than we projected, and with our projected budget deficit. We have tried to preserve and maintain several of the core achievements that we've achieved together in recent budgets. And those include the Earned Income Tax Credit, the increased minimum wage, the elimination of the maximum family grant, the continued investment in the Affordable Care Act, the SSI/SSP COLA. As well as continuing funding in education for both K-12 as well as higher education. We also continue our work on infrastructure and the Governor's proposed budget and climate change. Additionally, we grow the Budget Stabilization Act by 1.2 billion in our proposal. For a cumulative total of $7.9 billion which would be 63% of the constitutional target. In light of that, the proposed budget offers $3.2 billion in major solutions. And again, still preserving some of those core achievements. We propose several solutions to bring the budget back into balance while also building up a robust Reserve fund for some of the unpredictability that we're experiencing. We did pull back on a variety of one time spending proposals, and we have tempered some anticipated spending increases. If you look on the next slide, slide number five, I've you'll see the Proposition 98 funding including our proposals. Based on the revenue projection that we've updated and the proposed budget. Air quality is important, and has an important history in California, as our background paper indicates. It's Los Angeles has had dubious honor of not having two professional football teams no, not that dubious honor, but the first place in California to experience severe air quality pollution. As early as 1905, before the great earthquake in San Francisco, Los Angeles was adopting measures to try to control smoke emissions from a severely smoggy day in 1903, caused the city to experience something many described as a solar eclipse. In the summer of 1945, Los Angeles experienced smoke and fumes in the downtown that caused people to experience stinging in their eyes, and a sensation that their throats were being scraped. As a result, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors appointed a smoke and fumes Commission to study the county's air quality. This is in 1943. At Los Angeles' urging, a bill flew through the California Legislature and was signed by Governor Earl Warren, giving counties the authority to regulate air pollution. Then in 1947, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors then established the Los Angeles County. Air Pollution Control District, this was the first air pollution control program in the United States of America. Now, as a group, the chemicals that caused these earliest problems in Los Angeles are the same eight same types of pollutants that we're still dealing with today in California. They're poisonous, they're toxic, they're carcinogenic, and they cause a variety of negative health conditions. Smoke particles, and other organic compounds lead to cardiovascular, and respiratory illnesses, and also premature deaths. Some of the halogenate compounds are known endocrine disruptors, and neurotoxins, which can cause cancerous tumors, birth defects, developmental disorders, central nervous system damage, intellectual disability, persistent memory impairment, epilepsy, and dementia. Now, over the last 65 years, California has instituted programs and measures to protect California air and to reduce the air pollutants. Today, California's air quality has improved, but criteria air pollutants from vehicles and from refineries continue to present real health risks, and environmental concerns to our citizens. So what our goal is, in identifying this scenario for best management practices, is to say, what's the amount of funding that we would need so that the average road will only need a really cheap preservation treatment, rather than a full on reconstruction. So that's the difference between a treatment that costs a few dollars per square yard and totally rebuilding a road for a much greater price. So the problem with the 65 PCI is that we're at the precipice where the deterioration starts to happen faster, and we go much more quickly from those cheap treatments to needing to do very expensive rehab and rehabilitation work. So, we're sort of at this point where we really need to invest more, or we're going to see just a rapid increase in the cost to maintain the system. So in terms of giving taxpayers the best bang for their buck, it's a message you've all heard before, but fix it first is a much cheaper strategy than getting the roads to a failed condition and having to rebuild them completely. So, given that, our needs assessment isn't just about pavements. We also include an analysis of essential components and bridges. So, I'm going to talk a little bit about the essential components that we analyze. So, the things that we collected data on that are included in the analysis are things like your storm drains and gutters, your curbs and sidewalks, your curb ramps, traffic signals, street lights, sound walls and retaining walls, and then, all the signs and safety devices like that that you need to operate your system. So, we were able to get very good data on those eight key components. And we've used that to identify a needs analysis for those elements of the system as well. We have less data available on some of the other requirements. So beyond, ADA compliance needs in excess of just the curb ramps and sidewalks and then other needs related to storm water. But for those eight components, we had good data. And when you aggregate that all together, approximately 30% of our total funding needs are included in those sort of components. These items are funded a little bit differently than some of the pavement, which is largely reliant on gas tax revenue. And local revenues make up over two-thirds of the expenditures on your sidewalks, curbs, streetlights, and things of that nature. [{'start': 0, 'end': 11, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Seth Kerstein: Thank you, Mr. Chair. Seth Kerstein with the Legislative Analyst's office. We've got a handout to a company, my testimony available both on paper and on our website under publications. I'll start on page 1 of the handout, with a very brief overview of California sales tax, and then talk a little bit about the law that applies to technology transfer agreements. The tax that most people know as simply sales tax is actually a tax that has two complementary pieces called the sales and use tax. The first part is a sales tax on goods sold by California retailers, and the second part is a use tax on goods sold by other retailers. In the 2014-15 fiscal year tax payers paid an estimated $51 billion in California sales and use tax. And out of that $51 billion total, about $24 billion went to the state's general fund which makes the sales and use tax the second biggest general fund revenue source after the personal income tax. The remaining sales and use tax revenue, that other 27 million, or 27 billion rather, goes to a variety of funds that support local government programs. The state agency responsible for the sales and use tax is the state Board of Equalization, otherwise known as BOE. BOE is headed by a five-member elected board, and they perform both executive and quasi-judicial functions for the sales and use tax, and many other taxes and fees. So moving to page 2 of the handout, I'll elaborate on what I meant when I described the sales and use tax as a tax on goods. More precisely, the tax applies to retail sales of tangible, personal property. And this word tangible is at the center of some of the issues you'll be considering in this hearing. In California's tax code, something is tangible if it can be seen, weighed, measured, Felt or touched or is in any other manner perceptible to the senses. As you can imagine, there are many instances where it's not entirely clear whether that definition applies to a particular transaction. So over time, different entities have tried to clarify this issue. BOE has issued regulations and ruled on tax appeals, the Legislature has made statutory changes, and the courts have ruled on a variety of disputes over the interpretation of those laws. So moving on to page three of the handout, the history of California's law on technology transfer agreements has all of those elements. The first step was in 1992 BOE ruling on a tax appeal. What happened was, Intel had made some sales to a couple other businesses and included both tangible goods and licenses to use Intel's intellectual property. BOE staff initially determined that Intel owed sales tax on the full amount of those sales, but then Intel appealed, and the board ruled in Intel's favor. What the board concluded was that Intel only owed sales tax on a specific piece of those transactions, which was the value of the tangible goods, not the combined value of the tangible goods and the licenses. Then, the following year, the Legislature passed a law addressing the sales tax treatment of a certain category of transactions similar to the sales in the Intel appeal. The new law called these transactions technology transfer agreements, or TTA for short. And over the last couple decades, courts have considered how to apply this law, most recently in the Lucent case. So then moving to the last page of the handout, this 1993 law did two things, essentially. It first defined what a TTA is, and second, it specified how sales tax applies to TTAs. So to be a TTA, a transaction has to meet three conditions. First, the seller has to hold a patent or copyright interest. Second, the seller has to assign or license a particular kind of right to the buyer, the right to make and sell a product, or use a process. And then third, that right that the seller assigns to the buyer, has to be subject to the patent or copyright interest held by the seller. So then, once you've determined that a transaction is a TTA, sales tax is due only on the tangible component of the sale, rather than the entire sale. So then you have to determine the value of the tangible property, and the law gives taxpayers a few different options for doing that. One last thing to keep in mind is although these transfers are called technology transfer agreements, and many of the businesses that make these kinds of sales include tech companies like Lucent and Intel. They aren't limited necessarily to technology in a narrow sense. They're really based on the use of intellectual properties. So for example, a sale that includes the right to reproduce copyrighted artwork could potentially be a TTA. So that concludes my presentation, and at this time I would be happy to take questions, if you have any.

The good news is that California knows how to create and regulate all three of those things very well. So I think if we can kind of start from that framework, this starts to get a little bit easier. In terms of how do we get there? I think you have to focus on the fundamentals of good policy making. Think about the defaults of the actors involved here, right? For both producers and consumers, there's a way to both produce and consume cannabis that exists regardless of how you're getting it, right? So for you all as policy makers, you have to think about the cost benefit analysis that's going to be done by all of these people to transition into the regulated market. Secondly, as you're thinking about that, think about the trade-offs that each of those actors is facing. I think it has been acknowledged and I think Mr. Houston did an excellent job of articulating it, but basically the more friction points there are for producers and consumers to move into the regulated market, the less likely they're going to do it. And then thirdly, I think for you all, again, is you're trying to think about what can we do now to make this industry a reality. Focus on what every industry needs to succeed, you need a supply chain. Right now there's not a supply chain in the license market, and while there's a lot to talk about what that supply chain could look like, it doesn't exist, it's hypothetical right now. Secondly, every industry needs access to capital. As I said, whether this was technology, whether this was food and ag, whether this was real estate, access to capital would be a given, in this industry it's not. And so I think we need to think very proactively about what we can do. Thirdly, we need a clear set of rules. We need a clear set of rules for us to play by, for you to enforce. And so for many of you have expressed an interest in small businesses succeeding, minority groups being able to have an opportunity in this space, already we're off to a difficult start. So, then, my last point or the last question to be asking is what can we do now? I think right now, you guys should kind of embrace beta. Embrace the concept of beta testing, right? So like when a software company rolls out a new app or whatever, they say hey, this is the beta version. We haven't worked out all the bugs, be patient and work with us, right? I think everyone in here should be thinking in terms of, this is beta and we're going to be in the beta mode for the next five to 10 years, probably. The second thing you guys should be looking for right now are signals that things aren't working. Again, even if we don't know what things will ultimately look like in the space, I think there's still symptoms already that you can see of some problems. The best example is Blue Diamond, which is down the street here. Corporate headquarters, manufacturing, all this stuff, not a single almond tree. It's already gridlocked, it's already a patchwork. Having worked in other industries, that's already a red flag, in terms of how to regulate, and comply, and grow businesses. So I think we need to look for ways to really coordinate at the local level, and give people a place to participate. Lastly, as I've already said, this industry's already getting too expensive to participate in. When we look at projects and investments, we assume it's going to be $3 to 5 million minimum by the time you get real estate, build it out, get licensed, get your business up and going, millions of dollars. And so not a lot of people in the space, believe it or not, have millions of dollars lying around to grow their businesses. So I think for all of you here, again, You need to be looking at those signals to know that there's a course correction needed. My last point, and again thank you for the time this evening, is to keep it simple. Again, you shouldn't need a team of lawyers and lobbyists to tell you how to do your business. If we want people to do the right thing and we want them to have on-ramps to do this. It should be something that they can explain to their family at the Thanksgiving table. So anyway, thank you all for your time and look forward to working with you all.

So I'm very encouraged by the way things have been developing so far. That much said, let me say, unlike other participants at this table, we're a consumer group as opposed to an industry group. And I wanted to raise a few different issues that haven't been brought up that are of particular relevance to consumers. Which may involve some new kinds of, new licensing categories, that should be considered. One of the first of these has to do with special events. There are now all sorts of cannabis expos, and conferences, and fairs, around California. Where cannabis and cannabis products are displayed, and used, and distributed. And a lot of these events are really an economic boon from a tourist standpoint. I think every hotel room in Sonoma was sold out for the Emerald Cup this December. So we need a category, a licensing category, so that events like this can proceed. Because they're a little bit outside the framework that was originally thought of when MRCSA was put together. That dovetails with another issue, on-site consumption. Prop 64 authorizes some on-site consumption. It would be good to have some sort of regulations out there that allow on-site consumption. Not just necessarily in dispensaries, but in places like cafes, or motels, or resorts, that don't necessarily sell the marijuana but want to have on-site consumption. So some sort of license like that, like we sometimes have for alcohol, could be useful. Third concern, a very important one actually, has to do with delivery of medical cannabis. Amma forbids local governments from interfering with any transport of licensed cannabis. However, we have this relic leftover in MRCSA that says local governments can somehow ban the delivery of medical marijuana from licensed providers to residents in their very districts. And this is really not tolerable. We can't have districts, where there is no legal access. So we hope that the distribution, that in particular delivery, is construed to allow medical access via delivery to every patient in need in the state. Fourth point has to do with non-profits. Prop 64 calls for the bureau, I think, to investigate one or more classifications of non-profit licenses and possibly exempting them from taxes. We hope they will do so. There remain a lot of small, sort of informal, patient collectives that In fact, distribute marijuana free or at-cost to truly needy patients. I think with the advent of new taxes, the economic squeeze on patients and especially the poorest ones is going to be Particularly severe so we hope that there remains some sort of system available to them where free or at cost medicine can be made available. And let me say in regard to the taxes we are scared about this 15% retail excise tax especially on medical patients. When you throw in all the other taxes I'm really concerned that this is going to sort of spur the black market. So anything that could cushion the tax burden especially on needy medical patients would be useful. And finally, just a word about scientific research, medical research, educational institutions, museums like that. Often such institutions have a need for marijuana in excess of just one ounce and six plants. So, it seems to be some sort of a licensing provision for this. We ran into this at the Oakland Museum when we were doing the cannabis exhibit there earlier this year. How can the museum do this? And not be outside, and still be within the law. So that's another licensing category that should be considered.

Barry Broad: Good evening Mr. Chairman, members. Barry Broad on behalf of the California Teamsters Public Affairs Council. I actually think that the harmonization of these two statutory schemes is probably not as difficult as it would be in other circumstances, because Prop 64, in our view, contains an unusually large amount of discretion for the Legislature and regulatory agencies to make changes consistent with the drafters of Prop 64. Therefore, a lot of issues, I think, will be resolved relatively easily. And they're not all that far apart, even though there are disagreements. For example, both statutory schemes require a mandatory distributor. The only difference is whether the distributor can hold other licenses, or is independent. That entity, and we support that independent distribution model, and we supported it in the medical marijuana model precisely because it is antithetical to the concentration of market power and monopoly. That's the point of it. And we sat down with the proponents of Prop 64 during the campaign, and worked out language to implement, consistent with the drafters of Prop 64, language to that effect, which you all undoubtedly be seeing, and will be weighing, and determine whether you want to support it or not. Prop 64, as Mr. Rodriguez points out, contains very significant language, in fact, unusual language, preventing the concentration of market power, and licensing decisions that would result in the concentration of market power. Therefore, something along the lines of a rebuttable presumption, that holding licenses in all categories to create vertical integration, might create unlawful competition, unlawful restraint on competition is something that, in our view, is fully consistent with Prop 64, and I think the drafters understood that. It's been raised, I think, somewhat wildly, that having an independent distribution model, it is in itself a monopoly. However, the only licensed category in this entire system where there can be an unlimited number of licensees is distributors. There could be as many distributors who want to enter the market as they feel like. That's not the case with growers, that's not the case with dispensaries, that's not the case with manufacturers. It's not the case with anyone, except distributors. Therefore, to suggest that it is a restraint on trade itself is actually hard to accept. We feel that this proposal has the support of law enforcement, it has the support of local government, it has support of large part of the marijuana industry. And it has the support, at least it had the support, in the medical model for marijuana. So, we support that model. Secondly, I just want to point out that this is an industry that has been amply talked about today, that has existed in the shadows. It's existed in the underground economy, and therefore, it has to come out of the underground economy. And labor practices are an area that are common to every other business are not necessarily common in this business. For example, there are families that trim marijuana in agriculture areas, including children. We can't have child labor. That simply cannot happen, and it's bad for all the reasons that child labor are bad. It may have evolved that way, but that doesn't mean it's something that can stay. And finally, the third point is that we have to protect the people who want to operate legally from the people who will continue to operate Illegally, including cartels and everybody else. And a lot of what law enforcement will switch to is commerce enforcement, that's what it will become, looking for the people that are cheating. If you cheat on your taxes, you've got a competitive advantage over everyone else. If you make it difficult to pay your taxes, that may have the same result. And therefore, we think that the Legislature needs to look very closely at a model that will ensure that the taxes are paid, and it's easy to pay the taxes. For example, the State Board of Equalization is proposing that all three taxes be collected at the distribution level, remitted at the distribution level, as is done with diesel fuel, so that it happens in one part of commerce. It doesn't burden the farmers who, in this case, would have to pay, under Prop 64, a harvest tax upon harvest, which they can't afford to pay in anticipation of selling their crop. It would put them in a position, or many of them, in a position of being forced to go to the underground economy, in order to try to pay their taxes. So, the Legislature, as it crafts this model, needs to make it work and work, so that the players that are playing by the rules are not punished. That they can make a profit, that they can survive, and that the incentives are for them to operate within the above ground regulated economy. Thank you.

Secondly, as you're thinking about that, think about the trade-offs that each of those actors is facing. Barry Broad: Good evening Mr. Chairman, members. Barry Broad on behalf of the California Teamsters Public Affairs Council. I actually think that the harmonization of these two statutory schemes is probably not as difficult as it would be in other circumstances, because Prop 64, in our view, contains an unusually large amount of discretion for the Legislature and regulatory agencies to make changes consistent with the drafters of Prop 64. Therefore, a lot of issues, I think, will be resolved relatively easily. And they're not all that far apart, even though there are disagreements. For example, both statutory schemes require a mandatory distributor. The only difference is whether the distributor can hold other licenses, or is independent. That entity, and we support that independent distribution model, and we supported it in the medical marijuana model precisely because it is antithetical to the concentration of market power and monopoly. That's the point of it. And we sat down with the proponents of Prop 64 during the campaign, and worked out language to implement, consistent with the drafters of Prop 64, language to that effect, which you all undoubtedly be seeing, and will be weighing, and determine whether you want to support it or not. Prop 64, as Mr. Rodriguez points out, contains very significant language, in fact, unusual language, preventing the concentration of market power, and licensing decisions that would result in the concentration of market power. Therefore, something along the lines of a rebuttable presumption, that holding licenses in all categories to create vertical integration, might create unlawful competition, unlawful restraint on competition is something that, in our view, is fully consistent with Prop 64, and I think the drafters understood that. It's been raised, I think, somewhat wildly, that having an independent distribution model, it is in itself a monopoly. However, the only licensed category in this entire system where there can be an unlimited number of licensees is distributors. There could be as many distributors who want to enter the market as they feel like. That's not the case with growers, that's not the case with dispensaries, that's not the case with manufacturers. It's not the case with anyone, except distributors. Therefore, to suggest that it is a restraint on trade itself is actually hard to accept. We feel that this proposal has the support of law enforcement, it has the support of local government, it has support of large part of the marijuana industry. And it has the support, at least it had the support, in the medical model for marijuana. So, we support that model. Secondly, I just want to point out that this is an industry that has been amply talked about today, that has existed in the shadows. It's existed in the underground economy, and therefore, it has to come out of the underground economy. And labor practices are an area that are common to every other business are not necessarily common in this business. For example, there are families that trim marijuana in agriculture areas, including children. We can't have child labor. That simply cannot happen, and it's bad for all the reasons that child labor are bad. It may have evolved that way, but that doesn't mean it's something that can stay. And finally, the third point is that we have to protect the people who want to operate legally from the people who will continue to operate Illegally, including cartels and everybody else. And a lot of what law enforcement will switch to is commerce enforcement, that's what it will become, looking for the people that are cheating. If you cheat on your taxes, you've got a competitive advantage over everyone else. If you make it difficult to pay your taxes, that may have the same result. And therefore, we think that the Legislature needs to look very closely at a model that will ensure that the taxes are paid, and it's easy to pay the taxes. For example, the State Board of Equalization is proposing that all three taxes be collected at the distribution level, remitted at the distribution level, as is done with diesel fuel, so that it happens in one part of commerce. It doesn't burden the farmers who, in this case, would have to pay, under Prop 64, a harvest tax upon harvest, which they can't afford to pay in anticipation of selling their crop. It would put them in a position, or many of them, in a position of being forced to go to the underground economy, in order to try to pay their taxes. So, the Legislature, as it crafts this model, needs to make it work and work, so that the players that are playing by the rules are not punished. That they can make a profit, that they can survive, and that the incentives are for them to operate within the above ground regulated economy. Thank you.

And then a big item that has been consistently discussed is, there is a third party independent to distribution mandate in the medical framework and that does not exist in the recreational framework. CCIS preference is that, the Prop 64 initiative was a mandate by the voters. We would like to see many of those distinctions reconciled so that we are adopting the Prop 64 model. So that is something that we're going to be consistently advocating on throughout the year. But in the meantime, again, going back to the comments made about the licensing entities, we do think they are doing an exceptional job, and we will look forward to continuing to work with them and you as you contemplate, how to reconcile the two frameworks into one system. Thank you.

Barry Broad: Good evening Mr. Chairman, members. Barry Broad on behalf of the California Teamsters Public Affairs Council. I actually think that the harmonization of these two statutory schemes is probably not as difficult as it would be in other circumstances, because Prop 64, in our view, contains an unusually large amount of discretion for the Legislature and regulatory agencies to make changes consistent with the drafters of Prop 64. Therefore, a lot of issues, I think, will be resolved relatively easily. And they're not all that far apart, even though there are disagreements. For example, both statutory schemes require a mandatory distributor. The only difference is whether the distributor can hold other licenses, or is independent. That entity, and we support that independent distribution model, and we supported it in the medical marijuana model precisely because it is antithetical to the concentration of market power and monopoly. That's the point of it. And we sat down with the proponents of Prop 64 during the campaign, and worked out language to implement, consistent with the drafters of Prop 64, language to that effect, which you all undoubtedly be seeing, and will be weighing, and determine whether you want to support it or not. Prop 64, as Mr. Rodriguez points out, contains very significant language, in fact, unusual language, preventing the concentration of market power, and licensing decisions that would result in the concentration of market power. Therefore, something along the lines of a rebuttable presumption, that holding licenses in all categories to create vertical integration, might create unlawful competition, unlawful restraint on competition is something that, in our view, is fully consistent with Prop 64, and I think the drafters understood that. It's been raised, I think, somewhat wildly, that having an independent distribution model, it is in itself a monopoly. However, the only licensed category in this entire system where there can be an unlimited number of licensees is distributors. There could be as many distributors who want to enter the market as they feel like. That's not the case with growers, that's not the case with dispensaries, that's not the case with manufacturers. It's not the case with anyone, except distributors. Therefore, to suggest that it is a restraint on trade itself is actually hard to accept. We feel that this proposal has the support of law enforcement, it has the support of local government, it has support of large part of the marijuana industry. And it has the support, at least it had the support, in the medical model for marijuana. So, we support that model. Secondly, I just want to point out that this is an industry that has been amply talked about today, that has existed in the shadows. It's existed in the underground economy, and therefore, it has to come out of the underground economy. And labor practices are an area that are common to every other business are not necessarily common in this business. For example, there are families that trim marijuana in agriculture areas, including children. We can't have child labor. That simply cannot happen, and it's bad for all the reasons that child labor are bad. It may have evolved that way, but that doesn't mean it's something that can stay. And finally, the third point is that we have to protect the people who want to operate legally from the people who will continue to operate Illegally, including cartels and everybody else. And a lot of what law enforcement will switch to is commerce enforcement, that's what it will become, looking for the people that are cheating. If you cheat on your taxes, you've got a competitive advantage over everyone else. If you make it difficult to pay your taxes, that may have the same result. And therefore, we think that the Legislature needs to look very closely at a model that will ensure that the taxes are paid, and it's easy to pay the taxes. For example, the State Board of Equalization is proposing that all three taxes be collected at the distribution level, remitted at the distribution level, as is done with diesel fuel, so that it happens in one part of commerce. It doesn't burden the farmers who, in this case, would have to pay, under Prop 64, a harvest tax upon harvest, which they can't afford to pay in anticipation of selling their crop. It would put them in a position, or many of them, in a position of being forced to go to the underground economy, in order to try to pay their taxes. So, the Legislature, as it crafts this model, needs to make it work and work, so that the players that are playing by the rules are not punished. That they can make a profit, that they can survive, and that the incentives are for them to operate within the above ground regulated economy. Thank you.

So let me start off by saying Mark Ghilarducci, Director of the governor's Office of Emergency Services and homeland security advisor to Governor Brown. I think everybody knows there's no shortage of crisis in the world and certainly California, the nation's State of California. There is a lot going on here with regards to our population, density, urban centers, our rural communities. We have an international port of entry and 11 very active commodity ports as well as very significant infrastructure and heavy academia and there's just a lot going on here, innovation hub of the country, roughly about 13% of the GDP of the United States, and so protecting California and being in a position to be proactive and try to continue to remain out, in front of, not just threats, but actually events that are unfolding, is a never ending, 24/7, 365 effort. As a part of that, OES is not just the agency responsible with prevention, preparedness, responsive recovery to natural disasters. Things like earthquakes and fires and floods. Notwithstanding that we have plenty of all of those, but we are also the Homeland Security agency for California and responsible working with our parties of the Department of Homeland Security US government to ensure for the security of California through a series of threat assessment centers and intelligence gathering centers that we work very closely in partnerships with Local law enforcement and our federal counterparts, the FBI and DHS, etc and as a part of that, we look at everything from critical infrastructure protection, waterways and lifelines and other kinds of critical infrastructure, power, water, etc. As well as things like port and rail security, transportation security, maritime security, special event large venue, kind of, security that happens throughout the state. As a part of that, we have a granting program where we move quite a bit of money through grant programs to local government, local entities to ensure that they are also working in a combined effort with us to meet a set of matrix that are outlined in a state home and security strategy. Of course that Homeland Security strategy is a part of the overall state emergency part which i will let you in just a second, and Tina will delve into a little bit more in detail for you, but beyond the homeland security and the natural disaster involvement we also oversee all the public safety communications for California, all the 911 centers and the state microwave and communication, which is not only critical for interoperable communications at all levels of government, but also is an integral part of continuity of government and continuity of operations throughout the state. So those physical assets and infrastructure of that capability as well as the technology piece is very, very critical that we work to maintain, and again we do that in partnership with our local government partners, and then of course we've got a very robust training arm through the California specialized training Institute. California Specialized Training Institute, or CSTI as we call it. It's physically located at a campus in San Luis Obispo, but is really an enterprise that reaches out throughout the State of California to provide training and exercises for local and state agencies, but also federal agency, federal counterparts and international organizations and we have been doing more and more private sector training, in recent years, to be able to provide a baseline capability for emergency management and security response recovery and mitigation efforts. Several thousand students go through CSTI ever year, it's modeled after the National Emergency Management Institute, in Emmetsburg, Maryland and is very very close relationship between FEMA and DHS, and other post, organizations where, we have joint effort stay fire marshal we are working together. At the center, it handles the base ball, and then, through the enterprise, throughout the State of California and then lastly is our victim services which really is an area where. We are working on projects. For example, integrating human trafficking task forces, overseeing the rape crisis centers in the state. We have a number of youth programs that we work with through our victim services. We also provide critical incident stress management resources that we go throughout the state. This effort is really a collaborative effort, and if I could just take a second and step back in history to provide context to this discussion that you know, we in California have continued to evolve our emergency management capabilities and I say emergency management as the overarching construct. All these things I talked about, whether it's communications or homeland security or victim's services, the various kinds of disasters and threats fall under this structure of emergency management in California and we have had a number of disasters and events, significant ones over the years that have continued to shape and form us. Have given opportunity to introduction of legislations that help us build our capacity and capability and probably one of the most significant pieces of legislation was done in the 90s. It was the Senator Petris's bill that outlined and developed the standardized emergency management system and SEMS, as we call it, or the Standardized Emergency Management System, is the standard system that we operate at every level of government in California. It is designed so that we can address and adjudicate events at the lowest possible level at the fastest possible way. It's built upon a backbone of relationships between cities and counties and regions, regions and the state and then at the state level we can turn to our federal counterparts or to counterparts at the international level and it's based upon, as a city or local community is dealt with a particular event that grows in complexity beyond the capabilities of that community. That fire chief, or Police Chief, or mayor has the ability through this system and through what we call the Master Mutual Aid Agreement to be able to turn to their neighboring cities or turn to their county and request assistance. Counties throughout the state or what we call operational areas are really the first component of which we at OES have direct tie in relationships with from the form of a coordination standpoint and we have operation area coordinators in fire, law enforcement, emergency management, emergency medical, etc and we at that level, at that county level, a operational area level, that's the first key coordination point. Those operational areas really are having the pulse of what's happening within their cities. They rapidly know whether or not an event is evolving beyond the capability of a particular community, and they, in turn, are sharing and moving information immediately through the system to provide situational awareness up the chain and across the chain. So it's really horizontal and vertical to be able to go to next door operational areas, and the system as designed allows an operational area to go to the next operational area, the next surrounding county, to pull in resources. They know pretty well if an event is again going to be evolving beyond that or if the event of such high profile nature that they're going to need assistance almost immediately. They then can turn to the next level, and that is the region and we have region coordination centers throughout the State of California, region and emergency operation centers. We have fire and law enforcement. We have agreements with, for example, on the law enforcement side, with Sheriffs, which Chief Basil will talk about in a minute. Which they handle the coordination for us for law enforcement mutually as Chief Regels will talk about the coordination for fire and rescue with fire departments and regions can then pull from all the resources within a particular set of counties as far as within the region and then in the event that that is even more complicated they then can turn to the state. Over on the right, you see here, or my right, you see here a map that sort of explains how we break the state up into manageable what we call mutual aid regions. Three administrative regions from the standpoint of administering programs, but six, what we call mutual aid regions, where we actually manage specific tactical resources within those Six mutual aid zones and then we can move resources around the state. It's not uncommon for you to see, particularly during fire season where you see hundreds of fire engines and firefighters and law enforcement personnel being moved from one jurisdiction to another. Sometimes you'll say, wow there's firefighters from San Diego and Eureka or vice versa. That is all done through this mutual aid system. We are the brokers of that. The system is built by the participation of all entities, but it is managed and housed within the Office of Emergency Services and much of the work that these folks do. All of this is outlined in the State Emergency plan which gets updated regularly, but I have to tell you that, look there's always new threats that, and new challenges that are evolving in the state that continues to grow, and evolve like California. We have moved from, maybe what it used to be just natural disasters, to natural disasters and the threat of terrorism and then under terrorism, there's certainly a whole list of different kinds of threats that could be chemical, nuclear, biological or radiological, explosive, a new one we're dealing with today is cyber. And so we are constantly having to pivot to think about what those risks and threats are to our state, to our economy, and to our citizens, and we need to be constantly working to build and stay out in front of those evolving threats. The state emergency plan is critical. It is the basis by which state agencies and local government build their plans, but it's important for me to note that it is not so much, in my view, the issue of the plan. It is the issue of the process, the planning process. We need to continually keep everybody in that evolving kind of steady state where we are constantly updating the plan, so it does not become a stagnant, static you know, door stop. So it's a very complex document with a lot of information and it's updated on a regular basis, but it really is that through a number of committees, working groups. And part of the standardized emergency management system is a maintenance program that is made up of local state and federal, in which we continue to maintain the status and capability of our system in California. We also are an accredited organization nationally. We are accredited by the Emergency Management Performance Accreditation program. This is a national program that state agencies throughout the United States participate in. Emergency management organization and have to meet significant numbers of metrics and capabilities and we have been an accredited agency for some time and just recently went through a reaccreditation again in the last actually few weeks where they looked at all the different aspects. So I mentioned the coordination centers at the regional operation center, we also at Sacramento here have the state operations center. It is the hub where all the state agencies come together with their federal counterparts and it's what we do 24/7, 365 situation awareness through the warning center. It is the place where hazmats get reported and other kinds of incidents reported and that warning center is augmented with six fusion centers. The fusion centers are multi agency intelligence threat assessment centers, they're located throughout California and they're specifically looking at threats to the state, particularly in the context of terrorism and terrorist activity. So we've a lot of feeds coming in, a lot of the analytics which we are working and we work constantly to be able to continue to evolve our process. So with that, I think I'll stop and turn it over to my colleagues and let them sort of brief on some more of the specifics. To put 70,000 acres into perspective, it's about 110 square miles, which is about the geographic footprint size of the City of Sacramento. On a typical day in Lake County, we have anywhere from four to six deputy sheriffs patrolling that large area. Certainly if you had only four or six police officers in the city of Sacramento, it would be inadequate, but that is the reality of the situation in a lot of small rural counties in California. We are often times strapped for resources and when emergencies hit, we rely more than we know on the willingness and the ability of the state to respond. Having had the opportunity to go seventh, I've had the opportunity to listen to everybody speak before me and usually, I'll pick something out and I'll say, I don't necessarily agree with this. I wholeheartedly agree with everything, all the testimony that's been presented to this Committee up to this point. Most notably, the statement by Chief Pazen that the system works and I'll tell you a couple of antidotes from our response during the valley fire of how the situation worked. We had law enforcement come from across the state to help us provide security and patrols in our area. When this fire kicked off, there was a large group of people that were more than willing to go into evacuated areas and commit crimes and burglarize and loot areas where the fire hadn't actually damage the homes, but they knew everybody was out of there. Our small law enforcement response within the county was inadequate to handle that. We were able to reach out through the mutual aid system and request law enforcement assistance. We were able to reach out and request fire mutual aid assistance to come help us battle that fire. At the same time that the valley fire started, a lot of our state fire resources were allocated to the butte fire further south in the state. And I know it was very challenging and taxing on all the resources throughout the state, but I don't think anybody can say, none of our needs went unmet. We had the unique situation of becoming what I believe is the first dispatch mutual aid activation in the state. State dispatch centers throughout the state whether they're county, city run, privately run, I'll have a different records management systems, computerated dispatching systems, some of them use the same systems. We were able to reach out through Cal OES and find which agencies use the same records management system, computerated dispatching system that we did and request help, so that we had dispatchers that were able to arrive on scene. And immediately knew how to operate that system and start providing assistance to our overworked and tax dispatchers after they've been on duty for several days. We're able to reach out for cell connectivity issues with some of our private partners with AT&T and Verizon. This fire burned so quickly that it destroyed several cell towers. It burned down phone lines. We have a mass notification system that we use that use the existing phone lines to alert people that there was a fire coming. For some of those people, the alert didn't come until it was too late. We even had our records indicate that some of the phone lines were burned down. And once the phone lines went back in the calls that where in the queue started to go through and people that have been return to their homes found messages on their machines or actually answer the phone advising them the fire, but the fire burns so quickly that those messages were not able to be delivered in time. The situation in Lake County at that particular time are for various reasons, the Office of Emergency Services had been take away from the sheriff's department and placed under the county administrative office, and what we found that it's important to have somebody in that position as Emergency Service Director that has the authority and the ability to make quick decisions not to have to consult with board members necessarily. Obviously, we'll have to answer for decisions that we make, but there are times where decisions need to be made quickly and decisively and taken to consideration things that are happening right now instead of waiting to build a consensus. That ability was served us very well. As you all know, Lake County is a very agricultural community and the valley fire happened right around when the wine harvest was in process. Several of our wineries were in the evacuated area and to have the ability for a vineyard owner to be able to call up and say, hey, this is my problem. I need to get in there and explain that if we don't get in there and harvest our grapes, we're looking at losing millions and millions and millions of dollars to our local economy. And to be able to have a person in a position where they can make that call right away and say, yeah, we can open it up for those limited purposes in order to minimize the damage to our economy. That's a very important thing. I'd like to close in saying that again, I feel fortunate to go seventh, because the testimony that you've received here as a customer of the system, I like to consider myself, I wholeheartedly agree with everything that I've heard here. The statement that the system works, it did work. It worked for us, it continues to work. We continue to receive assistance and support from our state and local, our state and federal partners both in Cal OES and in the legislature as we continue to recover from the valley fire, as we continue our way through the current existing flood emergency that's plaguing us now. Thank you for the opportunity.

We were finishing the transition of these beneficiaries into this program and that added complexities to the model. And I think that one of the big lessons learned from this going forward is that. The complexity that you add to some of these models for an incremental benefit in accuracy of that model may not always be worth it. Because sometimes that complexity introduces an opportunity to make mistakes. And unfortunately that was what happened in this case and we take full responsibility for that and it was unfortunate. And so going forward, I think one of the lessons learned is that simplicity in some of the estimates, to the extent that it's possible to get an accurate estimate. And that's one of the primary lessons. And we're also trying to extend the time of review for local assistance issues as well.

[{'start': 0, 'end': 11, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Scott Smithline: Thank you very much. Mr. Chairman and members, thank you for the opportunity to come here today. My name is Scott Smithline. I am the Director of the Department of Resources, Recycling and Recovery, also know as CalRecycle. Appreciate the opportunity today to provide an overview of the bottle bill, or the beverage container program, and discuss some of the challenges that the program's currently facing and some of the efforts that the administration is currently working on with respect to reform. This is an old program, it's from 1986. It's initial focus as was just mentioned was on litter reduction and to really introduce the concept of returning of containers really the beginning of idea of recycling, returning beverage containers. The main component that distinguishes these type of program is that it is deposit program in California. We call that the CRV, which is the California Redemption Value. It has successfully achieved it's mandated statutory goal of 80%. There are 10 other bottle bill programs in the United States. California's is the largest. We sell, the beverage manufacturers and grocery dealers sell over 23 billion single use beverage containers in the state every year. The 80% recycling rate puts us over 18 billion containers recycled in this program. On an order of scale, that's in the range of 50 million beverage containers per day are moving through this program. And it's a very complex program, there's a lot of moving parts. I have a pretty ambitious set of notes that I'm going to try and get through, but I think I can do it in a timely fashion. In it's simplest form, this program consists of the consumer paying a deposit on the beverage container, the consumer returning that container, and the program ensuring that there is infrastructure in place for that consumer to go. I mean in its simplest form that is what this program is really trying to achieve. I'm going to walk through some of the main components of the program right now. The program is on single use beverage containers. The program not only is dictated by the beverage but by the container that it's in. So the packaging materials matter. In this case, the program covers aluminum bi-metal plastic in glass containers, exclusively. It also is specific with respect to which the beverages are in the program. So the beverages that are in are water, soft drinks, beer, small juices, and wine coolers. Examples of beverages that are not included are milk, medical food, infant formula, wine, large containers of juices. As we mentioned it is a deposit based system. Under 24 ounces is nickel, 24 or over is a dime. The consumer has two main responsibilities in this program. They pay the initial CRV upon purchase, and then they bring that container back for redemption. They have to have somewhere to go to redeem it. That is the collection infrastructure that we speak of. That's where the beverage container comes back into the stream of commerce essentially, that's where we regain access to that container. There's two main recycling mechanisms in this program. The first and the largest is what we call recycling centers and the second is the curbside program that is available to consumers in the State of California, and I'll discuss those in more detail in a moment. That infrastructure is supported by the program with two main payments. I'm going to describe those payments briefly to you. The first one is called the processing payment, this is a corner stone of this program. The processing payment is designed to cover the fact that when these containers are returned, sometimes the cost of collecting them is exceeds the value of that container. And when that happens, when the scrap value of the material is less than the cost of collecting the processing payment, there's a formula for us to determine what that difference is, so we can assure that those recycling centers are still viable in taking these containers that are already in the program. So that's what the processing payment is designed to do. The second main payment in the program is called the handling fee. The handling fee is made to a subset of recyclers. The processing payment goes to all recyclers. The handling fee goes to a subset of recyclers who are in special zones called convenient zones. A convenient zone is a zone that's within a half mile of a grocery store. Recycling centers in the convenient zones get a handling payment, which is designed to ensure that there are recycling centers in an area that are convenient for consumers to take their beverage containers back. So they get not only the processing payment but they get the handling fee payment as well. There is one further mechanism in the convenience zone program to ensure that there are sufficient opportunities to redeem for the consumer. In the instance where there's no recycling center in the convenient zone, there is an obligation on the grosser in that instance. There are two options that the grosser can comply with the statue in that instance. The first is, they can choose to take the containers back in the store themselves. So sort of what we've colloquially been calling the recycler of last resort in that instance. About 2500 stores have chosen to do that in California. The other option is for them to pay an in lieu fee of a $100 a day to the state, through the department which we use then to support program payments including other payments to recyclers. About 140 stores are availing themselves at that option at this time. So I've talked a lot about payments. I want to talk now, just to shift briefly to how the program is funded. By far and away the largest primary source of funding in this program is the CRV. We call it the unredeemed CRV. And what that means is, every time a beverage is purchased a nickel or dime is paid on that beverage, that comes to the state. But not 100% of those beverages are redeemed. We're at about 80%. So that difference is what we call the unredeemed CRV. And that unredeemed CRV, which is approximately 180 to $200 million, depending on the year, is how we fund the program. There's a secondary source, a couple other secondary sources of funding which are smaller. I'll mention just one more that I haven't mentioned which is the processing fee. A processing fee is paid to the department by the manufacturer. And the idea of the processing fee is that it's designed to cover a portion of the cost of recycling the container that they sell into the state. So that processing fee is then turned around and used to cover part of that processing payment that's used to cover the cost of recycling. With respect to expenditures, by far an away the biggest expense is the returning of the CRV. So that's $1.1 billion going right back out to consumers in terms of CRV redeemed. The processing payments that I've been referring to now is about $100 million a year. The handling fees annually are about $50 million per year. We, of course, administer this program, there's a cost associated to that, it's under 4% of the overall program. And it runs between, I think around mid-40s, depending on the year, $40 million, mid-40s. And then there's a number of other smaller payments I'm not going to go through, that are important. But just for purposes of time, that round out to about $50 million. The last major component of the program that I just want to discuss, is that in the last 10 or 15 years, there have been a couple of efforts to include market development mechanisms in the program. So move from just to focus on collection, to what happens after we have the materials. There's one that's for plastic, and that's called the plastic market development payment. And that's designed to incentivize the in-state re-manufacturing, with the plastic that we have in California. That's a $10 million program. It's been a very important program, but I want to note that it is slated to sunset at the end of this year. The other is a program on glass, it's called the Quality Incentive Payment, and that program is designed to support the cleaning of glass, so it can be kiln ready for manufacturing in the state, and that's also a $10 million program. I'm going to shift now and talk about, sort of some of the trends and changes we've seen over the last few decades, and how that has maybe created some challenges that we're working with in the program right now. Maybe first and foremost beverage packaging has changed very significantly, since the inception of this program. In 1988, 95% of beverages sold were in glass or aluminum containers. Today, that's less than half. So there's been obviously a huge influx of plastic into the container market. We're very familiar with this type of plastic. This is PET water bottles and soda bottles. But there is a number of other container types that have come into the market. Flexible foil pouches, which are like juice pouches. Shelf-stable aseptic cartoning for shelf-stable milks and juice boxes, that type of thing. Those latter products, container types I just mentioned are not covered by this program. So there's an expanding number of container types that are not covered by the program at all, due to these changes. Another significant change in the program in the last few decades has been the curbside collection. Well, a number of changes in collection mechanisms but in particular curbside collection. Just a couple of years after this program was adopted, the state adopted AB 939 which was the local mandate for cities to divert 50% of the waste that they generate. That really was the advent of curbside in the State of California. So that came just after this bottle bill. 99% of cities offer some form of curbside collection to their residents. So there's vast coverage of curbside in the State of California. And there's a number of benefits to curbside recycling for the State of California. Curbside captures all material that's recyclable. It doesn't just capture beverage containers. So it's serving a very significant purpose for the state's environmental goals. And it's obviously very convenient from the respect that, you can just put something at your front door. We are experiencing some challenges with curbside recycling with respect to this program, however, one important point to note is that, it does not provide a direct opportunity to redeem. So if the consumer takes their water bottle or beer bottle and sticks it in the curbside bin, they're choosing to donate that refund value to their curbside operator, in that case. So it's convenient, but it's not convenient opportunity to redeem for the consumer. In like ways, we are experiencing some challenges with the consequence of co-mingling all the materials in the curbside bin. Particularly, this is true with glass. When a glass container goes to a buy-back center, it's much easier to keep that clean and make it kiln ready. When glass is put into the curbside program by virtue of how it is all processed, it's a more expensive and complicated process to get the glass back out that, in some instances, has been adding to the cost of recycling, or affecting the amount of contamination in the glass product. And so those are some challenges that we will need to address with the curbside community. There have been significant fluctuations in the global marketplace, obviously that's a constant, these are all global commodities that we're talking about here. Most significantly virgin prices of plastic, I mean I don't want to just focus on plastic, aluminum and other commodities have had significant drops in price, but in particular plastic has been very bad. With plastic, prices tend to follow the trend of oil. So when we've seen the precipitous drop-off of the price of oil, plastic has gone with it. That directly impacts the value of recycled plastic, which competes with virgin plastic. From 2011 to now, we've seen some of the prices of recycled plastics drop off by half. So these are not insignificant drops. When that happens, we have to try and make up for that difference if we want these recycling centers to still be viable and be able take these materials. The statute, the way it's written now, does not provide the flexibility to the Department to be nimble, to respond to those changes in the marketplace. So that's a significant challenge that we're facing. And I imagine you've already heard or will hear more about that from stakeholders. The results are that there has been a significant decrease in the amount of recycling centers in the State of California. We have 800 fewer recycling centers than we did in 2011. In the year 2015, we lost approximately 500 of recycling centers and again the same number in 2016. Now, some of those have re-opened, those aren't net losses. But that level of turn illustrates how these centers have lost viability to a certain extent. And it's not only a challenge to the recyclers but to the department to keep up with that pace of recycling, opening and closing of recycling centers, so. And finally, I want to talk about sort of the trend in the fund condition over the last couple decades. There's been wild fluctuations. There have been periods where the Beverage Container Recycling Fund has been experiencing surpluses, in the hundreds of millions of dollars. But in the last, more than five years, we've seen ourselves in a sustained condition of structural deficit. The major dynamic that drives that fiscal solvency, that structural deficit really is, CRV-in versus CRV-out. When the recycling rate increases, the amount as I mentioned, the amount of unredeemed CRV shrinks. The payments that the department makes are mandatory payments. So we don't have the flexibility to cut back on some of those payments, we're required to make those payments. And that drives us into position of insolvency We've been there for a number of years. We've had sufficient cash on hand to continue operating, but there's a point at which that will no longer be the case. The only other significant source of funding that would help alleviate that is the processing fee that I discussed, sorry, the processing yeah, fee paid by the manufacturers as I discussed earlier. Originally when this in the original bill the manufacturers were tasked with paying a larger portion of that cost of recycling of the container in 2002 that was curtailed with something called offsets. So what happened was, the amount that the beverage manufacturer had to pay was reduced, and that additional payment present of that payment was made by the unredeemed CRV so that put additional pressure on the unredeemed CRV. However, this is important to understand our most recent projections suggest the significant decrease and the condition of the size of the structural deficit. From fiscal year 15-16, we were projecting a 49 million. We are projecting a $6.2 million deficit in fiscal year 18-19. So why is the deficit shrinking? The projected deficit, I should say. There is number of reasons that are important to understand. The first is, in the last couple of years, the department has had some new tools to address fraud in particular we have a new program that is instituted at the California border with the CDFA. It is now a requirement if you are importing beverage containers into the State of California that you fill out a form, we called it Imported Materials Report Form. You sign under penalty of perjury that you will not redeem those containers in the State of California. It is a crime to bring containers in around a border station in California. So this program has had a significant impact on the viability on those criminal organizations bringing containers into the state. The second sort of anti-fraud or leakage program we've instituted in the last couple years is that we have a new level of oversight at all processors in the State of California. The processors are where the financial transactional occurs with the state. So in the last two years, we have had over $6.8 million in court order restitution, 37 individuals have been arrested. We've seized over 400,000 pounds of material and seize over almost $400,000 in cash. Now, these numbers in and of themselves don't change the structural deficit that much. What's impossible to know is what is the deterrent effect that this new level of enforcement is having on, yes, exactly. Another very specific item that's affecting the structural deficit is, I mentioned the plastic market development payment. That's an annual payment of $10 million to support in-state remanufacturing with the plastic from the program. That is, as I mentioned, set to sunset at the end of this year, so that takes $10 million off the books right there on the expenditure side. Now, I'm not suggesting that's a good thing. I think that's an important program but with respect to the structural deficit, that's $10 million. But to round it back, I think the primary reason that we're seeing a decline in the structural deficit is that the recycling grade is trending down. The 15-16 recycling rate was at 84.5%. We're projecting a recycling rate for fiscal year 18-19 of 80.6%. That's a drop in 4% in the recycling rate. So while we may have a shrinking deficit, these current challenges that I've addressed, including the recycling center closures, increased responsibility on grocers, loss of redemption opportunities for consumers, very significantly declining recycling rate, one that puts us almost right back to the precipice of the statutory goal. And the loss of these market development programs that contribute to the shrinking deficit, these conditions continue to persist and need to be addressed. So while program has had significant success, we're concerned about some of the trends we see in overall performance. As we address these challenges, we very much agree that we need to look at this in comprehensive sense. The administration would like to see a folding in of more modern environmental principles into this program. This program was well before we were talking seriously about green house gas emission reduction and other environmental principles. Also an additional focus on the economic benefits of this program with respect to jobs and in state manufacturing. We outlined a number of those ideas and the policy framework that was published on January 10th. Historically, as Mr. Chairman you already mentioned, a lot of reform efforts have been on one or two components of the program, are focused explicitly on fiscal solvency. We think that there could be unintended consequences of following that particular approach. In the interest of time I'm not going to go through the policy framework in any detailed fashion. If I may just take a minute just to conclude and highlight the three policy goals that were outlined in there. The first is improving recycling and remanufacturing. We've stressed the importance of supporting the recycling infrastructure, so individuals have the opportunity to redeem their container, but we believe that that infrastructure may not need to look like it does today. There might be other efficiencies that we can gain. A lot has changed in 30 years, so we're very open sort of reassessing what convenience looks like? How we create an opportunity to redeem that doesn't necessarily focus around the grocers, so that's something that we've been talking about. And again, this shift towards looking at post-collection. So the policy paper looks at additional mechanisms to support in-state manufacturing. We are not gaining manufacturing capacity in the State of California, we're losing manufacturing capacity. We're losing glass manufacturing capacity. We're losing, as we speak, we're losing plastic manufacturing capacity. We just recently lost glass manufacturing capacity. We want to stop those trends and make sure that we support the infrastructure that we have for manufacturing in the State of California. And then thirdly on that bullet is a reevaluation of the containers and the beverage types that are in the program. As I mentioned there's some beverages that are already packaged in container types that are in the program. We think maybe those beverages should come in. There's also a new packaging types that probably make sense to bring in to the program. There's not actually a reason to keep them out. The second main policy goal of the framework document was shared responsibility and that really just recognizes that a flourishing program will continue to require investment in both the recycling infrastructure and the manufacturing infrastructure. We are proposing to restore the beverage manufacturer's share of responsibility to previous to what it is today. Either through an increased cost share of the cost of recycling or through other mechanisms that were outlined in the document. And then finally and very briefly just enhancing adaptability, and sustainability is a bit of a catch-all, but there's some very important components to that. Some are somewhat less interesting, like cleaning up antiquated provisions and things like that in a program, but others are very significant, like providing us the flexibility to respond to market conditions or changes in the infrastructure in a timely fashion, so we don't see a loss of that infrastructure. So in conclusion, the administration is committed to a comprehensive reform and a collaborative process. We look forward to working with stakeholders, certainly, this Committee and the Legislature. Thank you very much.

OTS is also an active participant on the state's strategic highway safety plan. Many of its outcomes often results in future funding, which include efforts to create a traffic safety culture that does not accept traffic collisions as the price we pay for mobility. As well as data improvements and efforts to increase partnerships. Most recently, OTS gathered together a group of experts including the Department of Motor Vehicles, California Highway Patrol, Department of Justice, Alcoholic Beverage Control, as well as local law enforcement, prosecutors, toxicology, Department of Education, to develop a DUID blueprint for California. The blueprint is expected to address long standing issues through proven counter measures and enhancement of existing programs, such as increasing law enforcement training, addressing equipment deficiencies in laboratories and enhancing data collection. In closing, OTS will be celebrating 50 years of progress in saving lives. Including a decline of more than 20% in highway deaths dating back to 2000, but although recent numbers are increasing we're optimistic about how our continued efforts combined with the advances in technology will help bring this state closer to its goal of zero. On the day after the election, California's legislative leaders declared that the state would not be dragged into the past by a federal government that stands against the principle that have made California a hub of innovation, an economic powerhouse, and a great place to live and raise a family. With well established science being rejected out of hand, critical clean air and clean water protections being discarded with no consideration of the impact on the people who breathe that air or drink that water. And numerous proposals to sacrifice our most fundamental shared resources. This bill is about California protecting itself against those assaults. It would incorporate into state law existing federal standards under the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Safe Drinking Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and workers' safety laws. Those standards currently apply to any affected industry or polluter. This bill doesn't change that. It simply insures that if the Trump administration and a hostile Congress try to undermine those existing protections, the state will take up the slack. California has long treated the federal government as a partner in protecting its natural resources. So even though the state already has several laws on the books to protect many of these resources, California hasn't incorporated all of the existing federal protections into state law but it's built on top of those existing federal standards. That partnership is now collapsing and the federal foundation being pulled out from under us. We need to keep that foundation intact by making sure that state law requires those baseline standards to remain in place. That's the goal of this bill. The political situation in Washington has never been more dangerous for public health and the environment. California can and must protect itself against these threats, and we urge you to do so by passing SB 49. Thank you.
