Effective communication and consultation with California's native tribes is not only what we should do as a state agency, but is now mandated by executive order and by state law. Under Governor Brown's leadership, executive order B10-11 requires every state agency to encourage communication and consultation with California's tribes. And allow for meaningful input in the develop of legislation, regulations, rules, and policies on matters that affect tribal communities. Second, the passage of AB 52, as Senator Mcguire mentioned, the Sequa update. Requires the Commission consult with tribes that are traditionally and culturally affiliated with the geographic area of any proposed projects. These two laws impact the Commission in significant ways, as many of our regulations have a direct impact on the tribal communities. In addition, Commission staff must also acknowledge tribal sovereignty and confidentiality with respect to projects. Having a tribal Committee at the Commission addresses many of these issues. The very nature of the work at the Commission necessitates close and frequent interaction with Native American tribes in order to advance solutions to complex natural resource challenges. Additional consultation and early engagement with the tribes on proposed projects and regulations is something which needs to be structurally implemented within the commissions future proceedings. Serving both as the President of the Commission and chair of the marine resources Committee, I see the clear growth and important role for the tribal Committee. As the tribes and the state become more familiar with how we can all work together. For example, at a recent tribal Committee meeting, we recently discussed co-management concerns, health management, kelp harvest, tribal take, marine protected areas, and climate change. All of these discussions inform Commissioners so that they are well apprised of tribal concerns before the full Commission hears these issues and votes on them. Ensuring that the tribal Committee exists in perpetuity guarantees that the tribal matters with respect to Fish and Wildlife issues will continue to be heard and discussed. And can endure the political and tribal leadership changes that will occur over time. This adds clarity and confirms the state's commitment to ongoing work with the tribal community. And on a philosophical note, it's about respect as well. An ad hoc Committee is as the Senator said, is a short term effort, whereas making the Committee a permanent Committee. Jacque Hostler-Carmesin: My name is Jacque Hostler-Carmesin. I'm the Vice President of the California Fish and Game Commission. Thank you for having me here this morning to testify on Senate Bill 161, formally creating the Tribal Committee within the California Fish and Game Commission. My work on the Marine Life Protection Act for the North Coast, as a regional stakeholder representing Native American tribes, was the catalyst for my interest on the California Fish and Game Commission. I was nominated and confirmed due to my strong interest in representing Northern California tribes and all North Coast constituents. The vision was based on the need for tribes to have a voice and a forum for discussion, collaboration, and communication to work towards true government to government consultation. The California Fish and Game Commission Tribal Committee is an essential platform for California tribes to facilitate, coordinate, and communicate with the state. Before the tribal Committee began at the Commission, communication between the Commission and California Native American tribes was ad hoc and often took place after a conflict occurred. Facilitating better communication between the Commission and California Native American tribes has been a long standing challenge. We have seen benefits and positive resolution of many issues due to the creation of the informal tribal Committee. Formalizing the tribal Committee within the Fish and Game Commission not only ensures regular and frequent meetings. But leads to better, more informed decisions by the Commission regarding our precious natural resources. The format of the Committee is intentionally less formal than a full Commission meeting and allows for issues to be discussed at length. The Committee provides a space for tribes to have lengthy and thoughtful discussion, and time for tribal caucusing on matters before the Commission. For the state, the Tribal Committee, is a very effective use of staff time for both department and Commission staff to gather input on potential policies and regulations. So that the Commission is more informed of tribal concerns and possible impacts to Native American tribes. The overarching goal of the Tribal Committee is to engage in a timely and interactive process to respectfully seek, discuss. And considered tribes views on natural resource issues in an effort to resolve concerns at the earliest opportunity. And in a manner that respects and furthers the interest of tribes and the Commission. Institutionalizing the tribal Committee creates a permanent relationship and provides certainty for both governments regarding the form of intergovernmental relations. And the process through which Fish and Wildlife issues will be addressed. Statutorily mandating the tribal Committee also provides the Committee the ability to weather and withstand political changes in state leadership and tribal leadership to ensure the tribal Committee continues on through such changes. It is for these reasons and many more, that I believe formalizing the tribal community within the Commission is important now and will be for years to come. Ensuring the tribes have built end procedures for communication with the Commission. Commission staffs and Department of fishing and wildlife staff and natural resource issues will pave the road for better and more frequent interactions and hopefully better results at the end of the day. I would like to recognize the tribal leaders who have supported the tribal Committee and contributed to the development and success Committee. And specifically, I'd like to thank Mr. Reg Aljon, he has been the unofficial Co-Chair of the tribal Committee. He is the cultural from the Dry Creek Band of Pomo Indians. He is in the audience today, and I'd just really like to call him out because he's definitely helped build the Committee. I'd also like to recognize Sonke Mastrup, the previous Executive Director of Fish and Game. As well as Valerie Termini, current Executive Director for their dedication in working with California tribal nations and bringing the tribal Committee before you today. Special thanks to Senator Maguire and his staff for the opportunity to speak and for moving this important legislation forward. I welcome any questions.

Robert Sumner: Yes, good morning, Robert Sumner with the California Department of Justice. I'm happy to be here this morning in front of these three committees, I think it will be a really great panel throughout the morning. I'll keep my portion brief and largely submit to the role of the Attorney General as the Constitutional Chief Law Officer for the state. Both the medical marijuana legislation that was passed and Prop 64 actually largely omits a direct role for the Department of Justice, aside from our administrative duty and then disseminating criminal history information. That said, as I go through a basic overview of the bill, you'll see that as the lawyer for virtually every government entity in the state, the Attorney General will be continuing to assess the impact that Prop 64 and the legislation proceeding is going to have on our day-to-day responsibilities through our various legal divisions and sections. We've actually appointed a coordinator within our government law section, an attorney whose sole purpose on this project is going to be to assess the cumulative impact of these new policies for marijuana on the department to understand whether or not we have the appropriate resources to handle all of the complex legal issues and regulatory frameworks that are going to be implemented as a result of the law. In addition to that, we're also going to be actively using our case management system to track any litigation that comes to the various sections that have a core nucleus subject of cannabis or marijuana legalization in order to track the progression of those issues. As a quick overview, I believe the background paper does a fairly good summary of the Prop 64 language, but I can just give a refresher. It's that it makes cannabis under state and local law for adults 21 and older. They can possess up to one ounce of marijuana for personal use and cultivate up to six plants for personal use in a private, locked residence. It can only be smoked and vaped in places where tobacco is allowed and it can't be ingested in a public place. From there, Prop 64 is largely based on the previous medical legislation that was championed by members of this Committee and the Legislature in that it divides up a number of very complicated and necessary regulatory framework pieces across different areas of agency expertise. Of course, the one newly created entity within the past few years is the Bureau of Medical Cannabis Regulation, which is going to be handling the licensure for the transport distribution sale, and, I believe, we'll be testing. That is a new bureau, that, as an entity of the Department of Consumer Affairs, will be a client agency of our licensing section, and then, meanwhile, the Food and Agriculture Department is going to be licensing the cultivation, which is a client of our Natural Resources section. Department of Public Health will be licensing manufacturing, and that is a client of our Health, Education and Welfare section. From there, those kind of key implementors that are obviously working on a tight timeline to implement regulation, there will be a number of other impacted agencies or legal issues that may come to light within the Attorney General's Office. The State Board of Equalization will obviously be in charge of collecting the special taxes implemented by Prop 64, which is a client of our Business and Tax section. Another client of that section is the treasurer, who is, of course, working on a number of issues related to dealing with the profits related to marijuana sales. The various environmental regulations that are going to be set by Food and Agriculture, as well as the State Water Resources Control Board, and the Department of Pesticides. So, kind of our natural resources section, and then on top of that, we expect that there will be a number of reduced penalties as a result of Prop 64, which allows for marijuana felonies to be reduced to misdemeanors with petitions for reduced charges. And so our Appeals, Rights and Trials section, which handles many of those cases, will likely be dealing with those issues, as well as our Correctional Law section. From there, and as our employment administrative mandate section, Prop 64 continues to allow employers discriminate against users of marijuana and that may come up as well as in setting some professional licensure, which is one of the primary BNP Committee issues. Both our Health, Quality and Enforcement section, which deals with the Healing Arts Boards, and our licensing section, which deals with many of the other boards may end up seeing litigation involving disciplinary or license or revocation cases where one of the factors behind the investigation was use of marijuana. To the extent that local ordinances restrict cultivation or use of marijuana in a zoning context. We have a land law section that would deal with that. Prop 64 also envisions the possibility of non-profit licensees, and that would fall under our charitable trust section. It got to a point when we were assessing this, that as we go thru all of those issues which unfold thru the language of Prop 64. Nearly every legal section within the Department of Justice is likely going to have some case or some matter that involves a new issue that has been brought to light by the signing of the initiative. As I mentioned earlier, we do also have a direct role in that we are the state's criminal history depository. So, to the extent that Prop 64 and previous legislation continues to lay out fitness criteria for licensees with the idea they cannot have been convicted of a substantially related crime or a serious or violent felony, felonies involving fraud and deceit, or employment of a minor in a drug business. All of that background check workload will be coming to our CJIS Division, or California Justice Information Services Division, and then, finally, I would also point out that as far as the driving impaired issue, there is obviously going to be a lot of discussion about what constitutes driving impaired following the ingestion of marijuana. We're looking at all the new scientific ways to be able to do roadside testing, and other types of testing by law enforcement and that's something that the various folks that work in toxicology in our Bureau of Forensic Services is likely to have to handle from IT workload issue. Finally, to the extent that law enforcement training and standards impact as chief law enforcement officer. I'm sure we'll be working closely with the various associations, and with post and CHP, to make sure that we are adequately preparing folks that are doing local enforcement and statewide law enforcement for the new laws that will be large change in life for many of them, and then, just to book in with this, if there's any case just generally challenging the constitutionality of either Proposition 64, any of its provisions, any of the regulations, or any local ordinance that will obviously fall upon the Attorney General to defend as the chief law officer for the state. So, while we don't have a direct impact result of Prop 64, you almost get a little annotation next to every provision in the law where the Attorney General will likely have to be present to lend some legal guidance. So, in that serving as kind of a basic and hopefully, brief summary of the provisions of the bill and how we see them from our role at the AG's office. I'm happy to answer any questions.

Karen Smith: Thank you. So good afternoon, Chairs, or good morning, Committee Members. I am Dr. Karen Smith. I'm the State Public Health Officer and the Director of the California Department of Public Health. Today I'm going to talk briefly about the Department of Public Health and its implementation of the Medical Cannabis Regulation Safety Act and Prop 64. As you all know, the Medical Cannabis Regulation Safety Act and 64 both mandate the Department of Public Health to license and oversee medical and adult use cannabis product manufacturers. The department's approached these regulations with the intent of creating a strong foundation for the protection of public health and safety without making the regulatory compliance so onerous that manufacturers of the cannabis products would choose to remain in the underground market. We're drafting regulations that are substantially similar to the manufacturing practices currently in place for food manufacturers. And the regs will include things along the lines of licensing requirements, process control, security, safety, sanitation, destruction, labelling, packaging, product standards and compliance enforcement. We developed the regulations to include those substantively similar both to food, but also to dietary supplements, because there are things about cannabis being added to food products that are very similar to that. From microbial contamination by employees or the environment to incorporation of foreign elements like glass, hair or insects to contamination of a product with unintended allergens, the manufacturing processes provide numerous opportunities for hazards to be introduced. The minimum facility requirements and standard operating procedures for sanitary manufacturing established by the department's proposed regulations are intended to reduce or eliminate potential contamination. The regulations also limit the products that are allowed to be infused with cannabis. Because certain types of manufactured products are more susceptible to microbial contamination. The department's highest priority in implementing the act and Proposition 64 is the protection of the public's health. Based on feedback that we received from stakeholders, the department is contemplating additional license types beyond those allowed for in the current regulation. One of which is an additional license type for businesses that only manufacture products such as edibles, but don't conduct the extractions from the plant. And then a second license type for businesses that do not manufacture the actual product, but package and label them. We have extensive experience in the food manufacturing, processing and safety, but the cannabis industry is new to us as well as others. We estimate that there will be approximately 1,000 applications for medical cannabis manufacturing and potentially as much as twice that for the adult use manufacturing. This required us to really quickly develop an understanding of this entirely new industry which is evolving very rapidly as I think you're all aware. And because of the nature of the industry there isn't a great deal of data actually available. So it becomes difficult to verify. To educate ourselves we met with numerous industry representatives and associations and the department staff visited manufacturing sites of various types throughout the state to learn more about extraction and manufacturing processes. The staff also had numerous calls with other states who have implemented similar programs during the pre-regulatory stakeholder meetings. We also heard from local health jurisdictions and others within the local jurisdictions who represent, they are very clear about their desire to both maintain some level of local control, and that they are important partners in the regulatory process. This is consistent with the way that we practice in food manufacturing, and other activities, in the department. Timely completion of the regulatory packages is also a top priority for us and we've been coordinating, as has been said before, we also are on the same timeline. We anticipate releasing the medical cannabis regulations for public comment in the early spring, and full adoption by January 1st. Because of the compressed timeline, we also anticipate using the emergency regulatory process for the adult use regulations, which will substantially be the same as Proposition 64, although there are some differences that will need to be addressed. Do thank you for the opportunity to share our progress and plans, and implementation and I'm happy to answer any questions that you may have.

I'm happy to be here this morning in front of these three committees, I think it will be a really great panel throughout the morning. I'll keep my portion brief and largely submit to the role of the Attorney General as the Constitutional Chief Law Officer for the state. Both the medical marijuana legislation that was passed and Prop 64 actually largely omits a direct role for the Department of Justice, aside from our administrative duty and then disseminating criminal history information. That said, as I go through a basic overview of the bill, you'll see that as the lawyer for virtually every government entity in the state, the Attorney General will be continuing to assess the impact that Prop 64 and the legislation proceeding is going to have on our day-to-day responsibilities through our various legal divisions and sections. We've actually appointed a coordinator within our government law section, an attorney whose sole purpose on this project is going to be to assess the cumulative impact of these new policies for marijuana on the department to understand whether or not we have the appropriate resources to handle all of the complex legal issues and regulatory frameworks that are going to be implemented as a result of the law. In addition to that, we're also going to be actively using our case management system to track any litigation that comes to the various sections that have a core nucleus subject of cannabis or marijuana legalization in order to track the progression of those issues. As a quick overview, I believe the background paper does a fairly good summary of the Prop 64 language, but I can just give a refresher. It's that it makes cannabis under state and local law for adults 21 and older. They can possess up to one ounce of marijuana for personal use and cultivate up to six plants for personal use in a private, locked residence. It can only be smoked and vaped in places where tobacco is allowed and it can't be ingested in a public place. From there, Prop 64 is largely based on the previous medical legislation that was championed by members of this Committee and the Legislature in that it divides up a number of very complicated and necessary regulatory framework pieces across different areas of agency expertise. Of course, the one newly created entity within the past few years is the Bureau of Medical Cannabis Regulation, which is going to be handling the licensure for the transport distribution sale, and, I believe, we'll be testing. That is a new bureau, that, as an entity of the Department of Consumer Affairs, will be a client agency of our licensing section, and then, meanwhile, the Food and Agriculture Department is going to be licensing the cultivation, which is a client of our Natural Resources section. Department of Public Health will be licensing manufacturing, and that is a client of our Health, Education and Welfare section. From there, those kind of key implementors that are obviously working on a tight timeline to implement regulation, there will be a number of other impacted agencies or legal issues that may come to light within the Attorney General's Office. The State Board of Equalization will obviously be in charge of collecting the special taxes implemented by Prop 64, which is a client of our Business and Tax section. Another client of that section is the treasurer, who is, of course, working on a number of issues related to dealing with the profits related to marijuana sales. The various environmental regulations that are going to be set by Food and Agriculture, as well as the State Water Resources Control Board, and the Department of Pesticides. So, kind of our natural resources section, and then on top of that, we expect that there will be a number of reduced penalties as a result of Prop 64, which allows for marijuana felonies to be reduced to misdemeanors with petitions for reduced charges. And so our Appeals, Rights and Trials section, which handles many of those cases, will likely be dealing with those issues, as well as our Correctional Law section. From there, and as our employment administrative mandate section, Prop 64 continues to allow employers discriminate against users of marijuana and that may come up as well as in setting some professional licensure, which is one of the primary BNP Committee issues. Both our Health, Quality and Enforcement section, which deals with the Healing Arts Boards, and our licensing section, which deals with many of the other boards may end up seeing litigation involving disciplinary or license or revocation cases where one of the factors behind the investigation was use of marijuana. To the extent that local ordinances restrict cultivation or use of marijuana in a zoning context. We have a land law section that would deal with that. Prop 64 also envisions the possibility of non-profit licensees, and that would fall under our charitable trust section. It got to a point when we were assessing this, that as we go thru all of those issues which unfold thru the language of Prop 64. Nearly every legal section within the Department of Justice is likely going to have some case or some matter that involves a new issue that has been brought to light by the signing of the initiative. Karen Smith: Thank you. So good afternoon, Chairs, or good morning, Committee Members. I am Dr. Karen Smith. I'm the State Public Health Officer and the Director of the California Department of Public Health. Today I'm going to talk briefly about the Department of Public Health and its implementation of the Medical Cannabis Regulation Safety Act and Prop 64. As you all know, the Medical Cannabis Regulation Safety Act and 64 both mandate the Department of Public Health to license and oversee medical and adult use cannabis product manufacturers. The department's approached these regulations with the intent of creating a strong foundation for the protection of public health and safety without making the regulatory compliance so onerous that manufacturers of the cannabis products would choose to remain in the underground market. We're drafting regulations that are substantially similar to the manufacturing practices currently in place for food manufacturers. And the regs will include things along the lines of licensing requirements, process control, security, safety, sanitation, destruction, labelling, packaging, product standards and compliance enforcement. We developed the regulations to include those substantively similar both to food, but also to dietary supplements, because there are things about cannabis being added to food products that are very similar to that. From microbial contamination by employees or the environment to incorporation of foreign elements like glass, hair or insects to contamination of a product with unintended allergens, the manufacturing processes provide numerous opportunities for hazards to be introduced. The minimum facility requirements and standard operating procedures for sanitary manufacturing established by the department's proposed regulations are intended to reduce or eliminate potential contamination. The regulations also limit the products that are allowed to be infused with cannabis. Because certain types of manufactured products are more susceptible to microbial contamination. The department's highest priority in implementing the act and Proposition 64 is the protection of the public's health. Based on feedback that we received from stakeholders, the department is contemplating additional license types beyond those allowed for in the current regulation. One of which is an additional license type for businesses that only manufacture products such as edibles, but don't conduct the extractions from the plant. And then a second license type for businesses that do not manufacture the actual product, but package and label them. We have extensive experience in the food manufacturing, processing and safety, but the cannabis industry is new to us as well as others. We estimate that there will be approximately 1,000 applications for medical cannabis manufacturing and potentially as much as twice that for the adult use manufacturing. This required us to really quickly develop an understanding of this entirely new industry which is evolving very rapidly as I think you're all aware. And because of the nature of the industry there isn't a great deal of data actually available. So it becomes difficult to verify. To educate ourselves we met with numerous industry representatives and associations and the department staff visited manufacturing sites of various types throughout the state to learn more about extraction and manufacturing processes. The staff also had numerous calls with other states who have implemented similar programs during the pre-regulatory stakeholder meetings. We also heard from local health jurisdictions and others within the local jurisdictions who represent, they are very clear about their desire to both maintain some level of local control, and that they are important partners in the regulatory process. This is consistent with the way that we practice in food manufacturing, and other activities, in the department. Timely completion of the regulatory packages is also a top priority for us and we've been coordinating, as has been said before, we also are on the same timeline. We anticipate releasing the medical cannabis regulations for public comment in the early spring, and full adoption by January 1st. Because of the compressed timeline, we also anticipate using the emergency regulatory process for the adult use regulations, which will substantially be the same as Proposition 64, although there are some differences that will need to be addressed. Do thank you for the opportunity to share our progress and plans, and implementation and I'm happy to answer any questions that you may have.

They can possess up to one ounce of marijuana for personal use and cultivate up to six plants for personal use in a private, locked residence. It can only be smoked and vaped in places where tobacco is allowed and it can't be ingested in a public place. The State Board of Equalization will obviously be in charge of collecting the special taxes implemented by Prop 64, which is a client of our Business and Tax section. And so our Appeals, Rights and Trials section, which handles many of those cases, will likely be dealing with those issues, as well as our Correctional Law section. From there, and as our employment administrative mandate section, Prop 64 continues to allow employers discriminate against users of marijuana and that may come up as well as in setting some professional licensure, which is one of the primary BNP Committee issues. Karen Smith: Thank you. So good afternoon, Chairs, or good morning, Committee Members. I am Dr. Karen Smith. I'm the State Public Health Officer and the Director of the California Department of Public Health. Today I'm going to talk briefly about the Department of Public Health and its implementation of the Medical Cannabis Regulation Safety Act and Prop 64. As you all know, the Medical Cannabis Regulation Safety Act and 64 both mandate the Department of Public Health to license and oversee medical and adult use cannabis product manufacturers. The department's approached these regulations with the intent of creating a strong foundation for the protection of public health and safety without making the regulatory compliance so onerous that manufacturers of the cannabis products would choose to remain in the underground market. We're drafting regulations that are substantially similar to the manufacturing practices currently in place for food manufacturers. And the regs will include things along the lines of licensing requirements, process control, security, safety, sanitation, destruction, labelling, packaging, product standards and compliance enforcement. We developed the regulations to include those substantively similar both to food, but also to dietary supplements, because there are things about cannabis being added to food products that are very similar to that. From microbial contamination by employees or the environment to incorporation of foreign elements like glass, hair or insects to contamination of a product with unintended allergens, the manufacturing processes provide numerous opportunities for hazards to be introduced. The minimum facility requirements and standard operating procedures for sanitary manufacturing established by the department's proposed regulations are intended to reduce or eliminate potential contamination. The regulations also limit the products that are allowed to be infused with cannabis. Because certain types of manufactured products are more susceptible to microbial contamination. The department's highest priority in implementing the act and Proposition 64 is the protection of the public's health. Based on feedback that we received from stakeholders, the department is contemplating additional license types beyond those allowed for in the current regulation. One of which is an additional license type for businesses that only manufacture products such as edibles, but don't conduct the extractions from the plant. And then a second license type for businesses that do not manufacture the actual product, but package and label them. We have extensive experience in the food manufacturing, processing and safety, but the cannabis industry is new to us as well as others. We estimate that there will be approximately 1,000 applications for medical cannabis manufacturing and potentially as much as twice that for the adult use manufacturing. This required us to really quickly develop an understanding of this entirely new industry which is evolving very rapidly as I think you're all aware. And because of the nature of the industry there isn't a great deal of data actually available. So it becomes difficult to verify. To educate ourselves we met with numerous industry representatives and associations and the department staff visited manufacturing sites of various types throughout the state to learn more about extraction and manufacturing processes. The staff also had numerous calls with other states who have implemented similar programs during the pre-regulatory stakeholder meetings. We also heard from local health jurisdictions and others within the local jurisdictions who represent, they are very clear about their desire to both maintain some level of local control, and that they are important partners in the regulatory process. This is consistent with the way that we practice in food manufacturing, and other activities, in the department. Timely completion of the regulatory packages is also a top priority for us and we've been coordinating, as has been said before, we also are on the same timeline. We anticipate releasing the medical cannabis regulations for public comment in the early spring, and full adoption by January 1st. Because of the compressed timeline, we also anticipate using the emergency regulatory process for the adult use regulations, which will substantially be the same as Proposition 64, although there are some differences that will need to be addressed. Do thank you for the opportunity to share our progress and plans, and implementation and I'm happy to answer any questions that you may have.

Bruce Whitcher: Thank you, Senator Hill, distinguished Committee Members, and members of the public. I'm Doctor Bruce Whitcher, President of the Dental Board of California. I'm currently serving in my eighth year as a member of the board. And I practice oral surgery in Paso Robles, California. And with me, you've already introduced, Karen Fischer, our Executive Officer. And we're here today to present the board's report on pediatric sedation and anesthesia, as well as the recommendations that came out of that study. I provided you with a handout. This is information that we've shared at prior meetings and I'll go into the relevant material there as we go through today's presentation. Most of you will probably have had little experience with sedation or general anesthesia given by dentists. Perhaps you or a family member had their wisdom teeth removed under anesthesia provided by an oral surgeon. But most of you, when you go to the dentist, you might have some local anesthesia to numb a tooth for a filling or a crown or perhaps to have your teeth cleaned. But it's important to understand that many patients are unable to receive dental treatment without sedation or even general anesthesia. Whether this is due to fear, the extensive nature of the treatment, the ineffectiveness of local anesthesia for their condition. Very young and developmentally disabled patients may require general anesthesia because they are unable to cooperate with treatment. As a point of reference, dentists are among the pioneers who developed anesthesia in the early 19th century to make it possible to provide dental care to these patients. Dentists have utilized various forms of anesthesia ever since. And a group of dentists have even limited their practice to anesthesia after becoming trained as anesthesiologists themselves. Now, Senator Hill has indicated in his opening remarks why we are here today. And this is in follow up to tragic events that recently occurred. And we are here to make certain that we do what we can to assure that the treatment, whether it's sedation, anesthesia, or all dental treatment, is safe for our young patients. For the purposes of our discussion, sedation and anesthesia are generally thought to represent a continuum, ranging from minimal sedation, through moderate sedation, to deep sedation, general anesthesia. And I provided you with these definitions on the first page of that handout. And it's important to know that although there are separate definitions for deep sedation and general anesthesia, according to California law those states are considered one in the same and they're regulated as general anesthesia. A report on dental anesthesia and sedation is divided into three parts. The first part compares California laws, regulations, and policies to those of other states and dental associations. The second part provides a review of relevant medical and dental literature. And the third part provides a summary of all incident reports related to dental sedation received by the board for patients under age 21 for the six years from 2010 through 2015. Over the course of four public meetings held during 2016, the board received substantial public input On this issue and I believe you have as well. From stakeholders, professional organizations on this subject. Based on the findings of our study, which you've been provided a copy, the board has concluded that California's present laws, regulations and policies are sufficient to provide protection of pediatric patients during sedation and anesthesia for dental treatment. However, because the board's mission is protection of the public above all other considerations, we have recommended enhancements to the current statute and regulations to provide a greater level of public protection. With less than a year to complete the study, the board's Subcommittee determined that it was not possible to develop detailed recommendations to address all aspects of California sedation laws. The Subcommittee therefore chose to concentrate on what it determined to be the major issues. And most of these were identified with the help of our stakeholders. And basically, the work product here was to make five recommendations. And I will summarize them for you here. First, the board should continue to research the collection of high quality pediatric dental sedation and anesthesia related data to inform our decision making. Second, the definitions of sedation now in our laws should be updated for consistency with current terminology. Third, the board recommends adding pediatric permits for minimal sedation, moderate sedation and deep sedation anesthesia to the current permit system. At present, we have a pediatric sedation permit for oral moderate sedation. The requirements for record electronic monitoring and ancillary equipment should be updated. And finally, the board should be provided with additional authority to strengthen our on-site inspection and evaluation program that we use in conjunction with our permit system for sedation and anesthesia. Now with respect to patient monitors, I referred to them earlier in my description of the recommendations. There's a handout for you that'll be a visual aid that might be helpful. California law has required the use of electronic patient monitors that measure and display the patient's vital signs, for patients who receive sedation since the early 1990s. The use of capnography, a monitoring method that measures exhaled carbon dioxide, has long been used for general anesthesia. The use of capnography is now also being recommended for moderate sedation by a number of professional associations. And I've provided you with a summary of our recommendations. And although we received comment on all of them, recommendation number three, the proposed addition of pediatric sedation permits, received by far the most comment. I will therefore describe those recommendations in greater detail. The board recommends that these permits be issued to dentists who administer sedation or anesthesia to any patient under the age of 13. Why the age of 13? Well, this corresponds to the physiologic changes that occur around the time of puberty. And this has historically been recognized as defining the pediatric age group for dental sedation in California law, by the American Dental Association. And most other dental specialty organizations. As I mentioned, the board recommends pediatric sedation permits for each of the three levels of sedation. Minimal sedation, moderate sedation, and deep sedation general anesthesia. And I'll go through these in sequence here. First, we recommend replacing the current oral moderate conscious sedation for minors permit with a pediatric minimal sedation permit. This would permit dentists to provide oral sedation with the same amount of training as they now undergo for the Oral Conscious Sedation for Minors permit, which is 24 hours in a supervised case. It would be limited to a single dose of a single sedative medication per appointment. The dose of medication given, plus nitrous oxide and oxygen should be unlikely to produce a State of moderate sedation. The medical and dental literature recognizes that this approach provides a greater margin of safety, compared to multiple doses of a single drug, or the use of multiple drugs. Approximately 19 states have established a minimal sedation permit to provide this option. Next, the board recommends adding a pediatric moderate sedation permit, again for patients under 13, to obtain this permit. And this would need to complete pediatric sedation training to a level comparable to that provided in a pediatric dental residency. By purpose of comparison, the Ada guidelines for moderate sedation now recommends 60 hours and completion of 20 supervised cases. Sedation could be administered via any route, but the dosages and drugs given should be unlikely to produce a State of deep sedation. In addition, both dentists and their staff are required to complete training in pediatric advanced life support and airway management. And that brings me to a discussion of the pediatric advanced life support, currently known as PALS, offered by the Heart Association, that does offer this type of training. And has the advantage of being widely available. 17 states currently require dentists who sedate children to complete PALS. But the courts may not include sufficient emphasis on airway management and other aspects of sedation related emergencies. Therefore, a board approved course for sedation permits may require some additional development. That one is currently available. The board recommends that dentists be required to complete a specified number of cases each year, to maintain their moderate pediatric sedation permit. This competency requirement would ensure that dentists treat a sufficient number of patients to maintain their skills. This recommendation is based on principles described in the medical and dental literature, as well as stakeholder input. The specific number of cases necessary to establish competency requires further discussion. In addition, the board recommends that there be a staff member dedicated to monitoring for patients under seven who receive moderate sedation. Some stakeholders have stated that pediatric moderate sedation should only be given by a provider qualified to administer deep sedation or general anesthesia. who can manage patients who enter an unintended State of deep sedation. The board's Subcommittee was unable to identify evidence based guidelines that would support such a recommendation. According to the American Dental Association educational guidelines, a dentist trained in moderate sedation must be able to rescue a patient from an unintended State of deep sedation. And the board is recommending additional training to help ensure that dentists who administer moderate sedation are competent to manage the situation. Other stakeholders comment that additional training is unnecessary and would limit the availability of dental care. The board agrees that the effects of our recommendations on access to care are an important consideration and should be analyzed. Finally, the board recommends that adding a pediatric general anesthesia permit for patients under the age of 13. This permit would require completion of an approved residency training program, as does our current permit. This provides training in general anesthesia. In addition, the dentists and their staff would be required to have training in pediatric advanced life support, as with the moderate permit. The permit would have a competency requirement similar to the moderate sedation permit. And a staff member dedicated to monitoring the patient would be required. For children under age seven, the board recommends the use of a dedicated anesthesia provider in addition to the dentist. Based on the review of the literature, children under seven might be at a higher risk of sedation related complications than older children. And the board felt that addition of the separate provider, in that circumstance, was warranted. At our December 2016 meeting, the board discussed whether or not a dedicated anesthesia provider should be required for children of all ages. Who undergo deep sedation or general anesthesia. But our discussion indicated that this requirement should be reserved for patients under seven. Who may be at greater risk of complications than older patients. This recommendation is supported by literature reviewed as well as board data from our incident reports received by the board for the last six years. And the board received no reports of an office or anesthesia sedation or anesthesia related death, or serious injury if a patient age seven through 21 during the six year study period. And I mentioned capnography earlier, and the board does recommend capnography for pediatric patients who receive moderate sedation, deep sedation, or general anesthesia. This is recommended by the current Ada sedation guidelines, stakeholder input, and we feel that capnography has the potential to provide early warning and airway problems that may be difficult to detect by other means. In conclusion, board members express deep concern about the availability of sedation and anesthesia services for young patients, and heard much testimony about the effects that new regulations might have on access to care. The board recognizes that few topics generate more controversy than the use of anesthesia, especially for children. The challenge of reaching a consensus among interested parties is quite difficult. Although patient safety is always the foremost concern, the effects of regulatory change on healthcare can be fraught with unintended consequences. Any healthcare proposal should therefore strike a balance between established practice and evidence based changes that we can be sure provide greater patient safety. To achieve this balance, the board recommends that there be an analysis of the effect of any proposed new regulation on access to care for pediatric patients. That concludes my presentation. Thank you.>>Thank you Doctor.

Consideration of legislation to require health plans to cover all medically necessary adjunctive services associated with dental care for children, regardless of the setting, should be on the table. Pediatric anesthesia in the dental setting is safe and the record on that is clear. This conversation is about finding out what we can do to make it even safer. The members of the California society of pediatric dentistry stand ready to implement those changes to existing law and regulation that support this end.

First, a little about CRNAs in California. Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetists are advanced practice registered nurses who are required to have a minimum of eight years of combined education, training, and critical care nursing experience. Before passing a national certifying examination, and entering the anesthesia workforce with a master's or doctoral degree. By the year 2021, all nurse anesthesia programs in the United States will award a doctoral degree upon a completion. CRNAs do not require physician supervision in California. And practice independently in every health care setting where anesthesia's delivered from traditional acute care hospitals to ambulatory surgery centers, and physician offices. CRNAs are the primary providers of anesthesia in rural and medically underserved communities, and provide 65% of anesthesia services to these populations. Currently in California, there are nine counties that depend solely on CRNAs for anesthesia services. However, CRNA's also practice in team care settings through out the state, collaborating with surgeons, obstetrician's, anesthesiologist's, dentists and other healthcare providers to deliver safe, high quality, cost effective care. In regard to the Dental Board's report on pediatric anesthesia, and in light of time, Candice supports, in general, all the recommendations to improve collection of data, updating definitions, educational requirements, personnel, requiring capnography usage and increasing authority for the dental board to conduct on site inspections and evaluations and also supports the dental boards assertion that any change needs to strike the balance between established procedures and evidence based changes that provide greater patient safety. As well as the need to examine the effect of any proposed new legislation on access to care and cost effectiveness for pediatric dental patients and a resource-constrained health care system. Sara and I see every day on a first-hand basis the continued need of vulnerable communities for access to safe, effective anesthesia care. One current California statutory requirement impedes CRNA's ability to offer anesthesia services in dental office settings. Even though CRNAs have independent scope of practice, we currently are not able to obtain an anesthesia permit given by the dental board individually, like other anesthesia provider colleagues. Instead, dentists, many of whom practice in rural or underserved communities that may not have other anesthesia providers available, must obtain their own anesthesia permit, which requires additional educational requirements and fees. This creates an undue burden on dentists for using CRNAs in dental offices, which does not exist in any other setting. This includes hospitals and dental ambulatory surgery centers where CRNAs currently provide pediatric dental anesthesia on a regular basis, as well as office settings for a multitude of other specialty services. We do not see this as a scope battle at all between anesthesia providers. We work collaboratively in our daily lives. And there's a need in our communities that provides opportunities for all anesthesia providers. Hannah asks that this inequity in the dental permitting process be addressed in any legislation implementing the reports recommendations so that CRNAs can be utilized more easily in office settings and to provide services to communities in need. Thank you for the opportunity to speak.

Checklist protocols and best practice guidelines. Comparisons are made between us and the airline industry's focus on safety. The mortality of anesthesia has been dramatically reduced by our approach, a more than 10 fold decrease in the decades of my professional life. As a pediatric anesthesiologist, I am heartened to see the California Board of Dentistry embrace safer policy. I fully support them. However, it isn't quite enough in my opinion. I agree with Dr. Seibert's testimony in the CSA, recommendations regarding these issues. A few sedation points repeated here for emphasis. Morally, we are obligated to one standard of care regardless of income. Morally, we are obligated to one standard of care for high-risk procedures no matter office, surgery center, hospital, dentist or MD. Young children are particularly vulnerable. Conscious sedation, or moderate sedation, we use now is an oxymoron in the young pediatric patient. They are typically awake or deeply sedated. Sedation is a continuum and despite anyone's intention a deeper level of sedation is very possible. Practitioners that aim for moderate sedation, must be prepared to rescue a child from deep sedation immediately. This means that moderate sedation should have the same staffing and monitoring requirements as deep sedation. Propofal is a general anesthetic and it's use as a sedative equals general anesthesia without a protected airway. Any sedation medication in a high enough dose or in combination with other medications can result in general anesthesia and the loss of the ability to breathe. Dental assistants who become sedation assistants are required to have a highschool degree, a certificate and dental assistance and a less than two week course in sedation. They are not licensed medical personnel and are not qualified to provide Pals care or anesthesia services, all young children, and all uncooperative special needs children, should have a qualified anesthesia provider, unless the intent is minimal sedation. It has been stated that requiring an additional anesthesia provider may interfere with access to care, implying that the cost would be prohibitive. Oral surgeons and dentists charge for their anesthesia care and their dental care. They are paid for both activities.

Both of these recommendations would add significantly to the cost and overhead for practices offering these services and there is no evidence based data support data for any of these criteria in the interest of patient safety. Barry Currier: Good morning, my name is Barry Currier, I'm the managing Director of Accreditation and Legal Education at the American Bar Association. For a law school to be accredited by the American Bar Association, and actually it's the Council of the Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar of the American Bar Association that's the actual accreditor. The ABA, as a trade Association, can't really control the standards. It's our council that sets them and applies them. To be accredited, a law school must operate in compliance with each of the ABA standards of approval for law schools. These standards are in a variety of areas. They're pretty intuitive. The program of study that a school must require, the teaching resources that a school must assemble, the student services that a school should provide, the admissions program of the law school, facilities, information resources, and the like. One of these standards in the program of study area requires a certain level of performance by a law school's graduates on the bar exam. The reasons for that standard, at least as I understand them, are that the bar examination is a reflection, at least to some extent, of the soundness of a school's program of legal education. There should be and there is, has been, some relationship at least between bar exam outcomes and the quality of the program of education offered to students. And b, most students go to law school to become lawyer and the bar examination is a hurdle that must be jumped to obtain that law license. The council as it should respects the competency determination, cut score, that jurisdictions make. It really has no choice. Whatever the states in which a law school's graduates want to practice is the market that that school's graduates must meet and the program must be designed to do that. The specific causes for declining bar passage outcomes in California are not, at least in my mind known and they no doubt result from a combination of factors. One fact is known, California bar exam takers outperform takers in other states on the MBE portion. That's the closest thing we have to a national measure. Indeed, the California average is higher than the national average by several points. The letter that the California deans sent to the Supreme Court makes that point. The ABA standards require a lot of consumer information to be disclosed, but in the current environment, that disclosure standard is not as effective as it should be. More is needed, a meaningful bar passage standard is part of that requirement. The present standard is complicated and it was adopted in a different era where bar passage rates were a lot higher. The council is proposing to change that standard to make it simpler and to be more responsive to the current environment. The council recognizes that bar admissions is a state by state matter, but the council observes the State's authority and power to regulate admission to practice comes with the responsibility and that responsibility is to design and administer bar exam that's fair and appropriate for the profession, the public, students and law schools. To be accredited, the school must be able to attract people and educate them sufficient to jump that hurdle at a reasonable rate. The standard posits that a law school whose graduates sit for the bar exam should pass in reasonable numbers within a reasonable period of time. If not, then there's some evidence that the law school may not be offering a sound program of legal education, and further, there's a risk of exploitation. If schools cannot meet a reasonable bar passage standard today, given the cost of legal education and the constrained job prospects graduates have if they cannot earn a law license. Schools should not admit people who cannot take their programs and pass the bar in reasonable numbers. If that is so, then it is difficult to understand why the pass rate in California is so low. And the fact that it is, may be unfair to students and very disruptive nationally for law students and law schools. Absent a compelling reason, such as a reason to believe California test takers are less competent or that the standard to be admitted to practice in California must be a lot higher than elsewhere in the country, it seems reasonable to suggest that California should align its passing threshold with other states, particularly other large states. That is, it should exercise the authority that it has to accept the admission standards responsibly. The council has not met since the dean's letter was prepared. It hasn't met since this hearing was called, so I can't speak officially for the council. But the cost can be even higher. Most law students still have outstanding undergraduate loans. Some students have placed their whole life on hold just to do law school. They work hard to get jobs after graduation, but without the ability to pass the bar, they're left back in the place they started, only with a considerable amount of debt. But it's not just that. A low bar passage rate feeds into the predatory bar prep industry. The fact that top bar pass companies charge upward of $3,995 without publishing their bar passage rate is concerning. But add in the $830 bar examination fee, $677, if not using a laptop, each time one takes the test, another $2,000 more for bar prep, a few more thousands for living cost during that time and that's considerably more than the $148,167 average salary a lawyer receive in California. But that's the salary for all lawyers, not entry lawyers. According to the National Association for Law Placement, an average salary for an entry level lawyer in a public interest or a government entity ranges from $44,600 to $51,100. That means, even if a public interest lawyer were to give up their entire salary to pay the loans, they would still not be able to pay off their law school loans for more than three years. And then adding that, delaying a year to retake the bar only exacerbates that. But as it is, legal education also take the hit from a low bar passage rate. Students become more worried about passing the bar than getting a job. Instead of taking clinics or legal work, they stay at school and take more bar courses. One student phrased it well, that the great irony to be a lawyer is that all I have to do is to be more unprepared for the actual job. Even when the bar prep company does, there's no guarantee that one will pass the bar. For example, Themis, one of the three most popular bar prep companies, only had a 66% first-time pass rate in California and 77% pass rate for those who completed 75% of the course. But what are students supposed to do, not take it? They take this financial gamble because A, everyone around them seems to be doing it. B, they are encouraged to do so, and C, they would rather put in money to increase their possibility of passing the bar. But this is parasitic upon law student. Bar passage companies, not law students, not the California public, benefit from a low bar passage rate. Legal education was not made to teach the bar but teach practical skills and experiences to be a lawyer but the bar exam make legal education all about being better test takers than better lawyers. The bar fails to test the competence of law students. One student wrote that quote, the skills of a great lawyer cannot be measured by written exam. It is counterintuitive to choose to pass the bar but not give up the skills to be an attorney. Students have made it clear that despite a diminishing bar passage rate, the last thing law schools should do is throw the baby out with the bath water, and should continue instead to train lawyers, and not just teach the bar.  I've heard that the bar is a bar of confidence. But if it is of confidence, I hope you ponder this point, if US Senator Kamala Harris, former Dean of Stanford Law School, Kathleen Sullivan, and two California governors, Jerry Brown and Pete Wilson cannot pass on their first try but were wildly successful as California's Attorney General, a top law school dean, and governors of our great state, what does that say of the bar? Indeed, a student pointed out that a time test where one is required to memorize rules in and pull them out of one's head in a timed environment is something that no competent attorney would ever do when representing a client. And they agree, stating that the practice of law is not shotgun decision-making or racehorse exams. The white paper makes it clear, a lower threshold on the bar exam means a higher bar pass rate but a lower threshold, as one student puts it, also means less students putting their life on hold for another six months to retake the bar, less students who are unable to pay back their loans, less students who are unable to be lawyers. A lower threshold on the bar exam will also be life challenging. In response to failing the bar, a UC Hastings student committed suicide. So I ask, could this student have been here today if the state bar had lowered its threshold? Possibly. I leave you with this last quote. The UC Hastings Dean wrote letters soon after learning about the suicide of the student, writing, this is not the only story we need to tell, nor to hear. We need to hear that how we score on an exam is not the measure of our potential as a lawyer, much less our worth as a person. So, in recent times, the public has realized the importance of lawyers. There are many good law students in California. There can also just be as good and many good lawyers. And that starts with changing the arbitrary standards of the bar examination. And for that, I urge you to take action. Thank you.

If you turn to page one of the handout, you'll see a summary of the topics that we'll be covering today. There's four different examples of law enforcement oversight processes that we've put together information on. It is important to note that there are other forms out there, but these are a few we wanted to highlight. These include internal investigations, local civilian review boards, external auditors, as well as oversight provided by the California Department of Justice. It's also important to note that, in many in cases, a single agency will use more that one oversight process. So for example, San Francisco uses Multiple of the oversight processes that I just talked about. So if you turn to page two, you'll see a description of the internal investigation that's done by many state and local law enforcement agencies. Agencies that use this oversight process use their own internal staff to investigate allegations of officer misconduct. For example in use of force incidents the officer involved could be reviewed by multiple levels of supervisors. If the investigation revealed that the use of force was unnecessary or excessive, then an Internal Affairs division could perform an investigation. These investigations generally involve interviews of the relevant parties as well as witnesses. Depending on the law enforcement agency, the responsibility for disciplining an officer might rest with a single entity, such as with the agency itself, or a City Council, or it could be spread among multiple agencies, such as the agency itself and its city manager, for example. If the officer is found to have violated agency policy, he or she could be disciplined, to such as being suspended and or terminated. Officers could also be found to simply be in need of additional training to prevent future incidents. So if you turn to page three of the handout, you'll see a description of local civilian review boards. So some local governments use a group of civilians, typically appointed by city councils or county boards of supervisors, to review use of force incidents and other complaints. In some cases these boards review a law enforcement agency's internal investigation to determine whether it was conducted appropriately or if further investigation is necessary. In other cases however, these boards will use professional investigators of their own to investigate cases. Some local civilian boards do not review all use of force incidences or complaints, and instead they only review more high level ones or ones that represent a greater public interest. In cases where civilian review boards investigate specific incidents, these boards can hold an officer accountable by administering the punishment themselves or just by recommending that some form of discipline be administered. In cases where civilian review boards do not investigate specific incidences, these boards can make recommendations for the agency to resolve the problems that are identified by other investigators such as the internal investigators I mentioned before. So, if you turn to page four of the handout, youll see a description of how some agencies use external auditors and the oversight process. When an agency uses external auditors, they will typically use the external Auditor to conduct an actual investigation or to review an investigation already completed to identify any inconsistencies with agency policies. Some external auditors report the results of their investigations to additional entities such as the City Council, county Board of Supervisors or a civilian review board. External auditors who investigate individual cases can review incidents to determine whether the officer's actions followed agency policy and recommend whether disciplinary action is necessary. External auditors who review already completed internal investigations are typically used to confirm the results of the investigation. In either case, however, these external auditors will make recommendations to local law enforcement agencies to change processes that they've identified to be deficient. So if you turn to page five of the handout you'll see discussion of the reviews done by the California Department of Justice. So the California Attorney General has a constitutional authority over all state and local law enforcement agencies. As a result, DOJ can decide to investigate a law enforcement agency regardless of agencies' internal oversight policies. More frequently however, law enforcement agencies ask DOJ to perform investigations on their behalf. This might happen in cases where there are multiple agencies involved in a single incident. At any point DOJ can also launch an investigation to police misconduct or take over such an investigation from a law enforcement agency. If DOJ finds evidence of criminal misconduct the officers involved can face prosecution. So, that concludes my presentation. And as I said to begin with, these are just a handful of examples of the oversight that law enforcement agencies are subject to. And I'd be happy to answer any questions now or after the others have presented.

Song Richardson: Thank you, Madame Weber and members. I'm Song Richardson, I'm Senior Associate Dean for Academic Affairs, and Professor of Law at the University of California, Irvine School of Law. I'm here today to discuss very briefly police community relations and more, specifically racial disparities in policing. Typically, when this issue is discussed, the conversation often focuses either on accusing officers of racism or of saying that community members have acted in objectively suspicious or threatening ways. What I want to suggest and talk about a little bit today is something that most have not heard of, and this is something called racial anxiety. And I want to speak about this psychological process because it's very important to police community relations and it's something that's often ignored in these conversations rather as I mentioned the focus is on officers or community members or unconscious racial biases. So let me talk a little bit about racial anxiety and why it's important. Racial anxiety is meant to have us think about how anxious people feel when they engage in interracial interactions. And what social psychologists have found is that these interactions between white and black community members for instance, can cause great anxiety. And these anxieties work like this. For people who are in dominant groups like police officers, social psychologists have found that those officers who are most afraid of being interpreted or perceived as being racist, so officers who are most concerned with being evaluated as being racist by members of the community, have been found both in the lab and in real life, to have used force more often against young black man than man of other racial groups. I'll just say that one more time because it's counter-intuitive. Officers who are most concerned with being judged to be racist are actually more often the same officers who use force against young black men in the community. This has been shown by social psychologists. There is absolutely no relationship between conscious racial bias, and this concern, this racial anxiety, this worry about being judged to be a racist by a member of the community. So the question is why is it that an officer who may be consciously egalitarian but who worries about being viewed as racist, would use force more often against young black men? So let me talk about why police community relations are so important, and why some form of community policing is important. This is why. Officers are often trained to rely on their authority, their moral authority as officers, to control a potentially threatening situation. However, if an officer is dealing with a member of a community who the officer believes does not give the officer any legitimacy because the community member believes that the officer is a racist That officer views that situation as being more dangerous. And as a result of viewing that situation as being more dangerous, that officer is more likely to rely on his training which tells that officer that in a potentially dangerous situation. You should enact command presence. You should take control of this situation. To deescalate, right? To make sure that it doesn't end in danger, in a shooting. The problem with that is from the community member's perspective, that community member is also suffering from racial anxiety. That community member is concerned that the officer is actually a racist. And so the community member is demonstrating both cognitively and physically the manifestations of anxieties, such as fidgeting, lack of eye contact, being unable to really listen to the orders that the officer is yelling and ordering him or her to do. And so when both the citizen and the officer are suffering from this racial anxiety and the officer is enacting command presence, and the citizen is worried that the officer is about to treat him in a racially, discriminatory way. When those two things, when two people are suffering from this anxiety that situation is much more likely to end in the use of force even when the officer is consciously egalitarian and the citizen is not engaged in criminal activity. So the anxieties on both sides of an interaction can lead to violence. The reason why then community policing the right type of community policing and I can talk more about that in the Q&A. The reason why that is so important, is because building trust and building understanding and building legitimacy between communities and the police is one demonstrated way of reducing anxiety on both sides of this police citizen interaction. So the right type of community policing and police accountability is a second important piece because if members of the community continue to see officers in their communities. Those few officers who are engaged in problematic policing practices that prevents the building of trust between members of the community and members of the police. So that I think I'm out of time. So that's all that I will say for now but I'm happy to take questions. Thank you.

Caitlin O'Neil: Thank you, Caitlin O'Neil, Legislative Analyst's Office. Good afternoon, Madam Chair and members. You should have a handout called overview of felony sentencing in California. I'm going to provide an overview of the different types of felony sentences. Discuss some alternatives to felony sentences and explain how felony cases are typically resolved. On page one, I'll start with an overview of the three categories of felony sentences. The first category includes death and life without the possibility of parole. Reserved for offenders convicted of the most serious offenses. The second category is what this called indeterminate sentences. And individuals who are convicted, who are sentence and determinitently receive a minimum term with no specific maximum term, such as 25 years to life. After they served the minimum term they will appear before Board of Parole hearings, who will consider whether they're ready to be released from prison. The third category of felony sentence is called the determinate sentence. And individuals first sentence determinately receive fixed terms and are released after serving these terms. And based on their offense and their previous offenses, these individuals may serve that term in prison or a county jail. On page two, I'm going to discuss factors that affect the lengths of determinate sentences. And the first thing that's important to know is that for each offense, statute specifies low, medium, and high terms of incarceration. This is known as the triad. And to determine which of these three lengths of time is applied to the sentence, factors surrounding the crime and factors relating to the defendant are considered. Now offenders can often be convicted of multiple crimes at once and in this case they would receive a term for each offense. And they may be required to serve these terms consecutively. Meaning each term would stack up back to back to create the full length of the sentence or they would maybe allowed to serve the terms concurrently. If they're required to serve these terms consecutively, they would serve an amount of time equal to one of the triad terms for the offense that would yield the longest term in addition to one third the middle triad term for each other offense in general. And sentence length can be increased by what are called enhancements. These are specified in statute and in general there are two types of enhancements. Conduct enhancements, which are imposed of certain circumstances occur during the commission of the crime and status enhancements, which are imposed based on offenders criminal history. And on page three, I'll discuss two alternatives to felony sentences. The first alternative is felony probation. And unless prohibited by law, felony offenders may be placed on probation in lieu of serving a felony sentence. The offender may be required to spend up to five years on probation and up to one of those years in county jail. Offenders must agree to certain terms and if they fail to follow these terms of probation, they may be required to serve a felony sentence. The second alternative I'll discuss briefly is called collaborative court. And offenders maybe be referred to collaborative court programs under certain circumstances. Again, they must meet certain requirements. And if they fail to meet these requirements, they may be required to serve a felony sentence. On page four, I'll provide a brief overview of how felony cases are resolved. The first step toward resolution is often plea bargaining. And in a plea bargain the prosecution and defense negotiate over the charges that the prosecutor will bring, and the sentence or alternative to sentence as I mentioned earlier that the prosecutor will seek. And if they come to an agreement, the judge must approve the bargain. If the defense and prosecution do not come to an agreement or can not come to an agreement, the judge may inform the parties of what he or she would give the defendant if the case came to his or her courtroom. This is called an indicated sentence. At this point, the defendant can plead guilty to the charges and receive the indicated sentence offered by the judge, or return to plea bargaining. If the case is not resolved by guilty plea it would proceed to trial, where the prosecution determines what charges are brought against the defendant. A jury typically determines if the defendant is guilty of those charges and the judge determines the sentence. On page five, you'll see a pie chart, which shows how felony cases were resolved in 2014-15. As you can see from the largest slice, the dark gray slice, that about 80% of all felony cases were resolved through the offender pleading guilty prior to trial. While only about 2% of cases were resolved through a trial. And this concludes my prepared comments I'd be happy to take questions at the appropriate time. Thank you.
