Sometimes it really hard to show in a fact where we aim to show the null hypothesis, to show that we can't prove an effect. So it's really, really hard to show that something works. Therefore, it's easy to conclude wrongly that it doesn't work. That may have been true with both policing and rehabilitation. We got rid of the public mental health system in this period, another tool gone. And looking around, we had a relatively small prison population. Our prison population was at a historic low, especially compared to the crime rate. So, the idea that we could actually take a bite out of crime by expanding the prison population and modestly at least increasing prison lengths was not a crazy idea. James Q Wilson advocated it in thinking about crime and a lot of other experts too. I think there's a lot of little evidence that it did work. I mean, crime is much lower today than it was in the 90s, but there's been careful efforts to estimate how much of it is due to long sentences or incarceration generally the high estimate is 25%. The low estimate is like 5% or 6%. We could talk in Q&A about how to think about that, but there's little evidence that it tracks. For instance, a state like New York which started reducing long sentences in the 90s had a much steeper crime decline than California which continued to invest in that strategy throughout the beginning of this century. So, why didn't it work? First of all, it got too big. I mean, at the beginning when you had a relatively tiny prison population and a lot of crime, the next prisoner is a pretty high rate offender probably. By the time you've blown up the prison population by 150% and doubled that again in a few years, you're starting to deal with pretty low rate people who are not going to give you a lot of bang for the buck when you lock them up. Secondly, we got too greedy. It's like everything else. If you think a year of treatment is good, how about five years of treatment? It's gotta be better. Isn't always the case, especially when you take, keep in mind that you're talking about people and people change and that's the big problem with the penal incapacitation theory. It basically assumes that people stay the same, but the person who's doing 10 burglaries a month at 20 is doing 10 burglaries at 30, 40, 50. And of course, they expect Simon to write 10 articles a year now and I don't feel like it and they have incentives to make me do it. That's how it gets done, but people, otherwise, begin to level off over time. So finally, what's the next big idea? I think the most important next big idea really pivots directly off of this which is that we've gotta look beyond the inside of the brain of the person who quote, commits the crime. Not that they're not responsible or unimportant, but criminologists today don't think that it's really the big explanation for crime patterns. We're much more interested in things like hotspots that explain patterns of prime that happened over and over. So it cant just be going on the head of the person, because it Putting on a monthly, weekly basis that we can track statistic with. We're much more interested in the potential to explain crime based on people's social networks that they're involved with, based on their routine activities. Those are all things that we can intervene in without long sentences. So, I think I'll stop there.

Just for context, at the East Bay Community Law Center, I started a traffic clinic where on Wednesdays, people with traffic issues can walk in. Those people include people who have moving violations as well as parking tickets. Which we're not discussing here, but the same population of people impacted by the inability to pay to moving violations also can't pay $500 parking tickets. We then started a in-court clinic at the end of the month in Alameda County where we basically take a public defender approach to traffic citations and represent people there. Just to give a couple of quick client stories, I have currently a client who I've been working with for over six months, who at the time she came to us, had several moving violations and had been having her wages garnished and her taxes intercepted for over five years. Now, this is important because she had applied for amnesty. But because courts were so far behind in processing amnesty applications, her application wasn't processed in a timely manner. And what ended up happening was is, she was being garnished for two tickets Alameda County was reporting as paid, but the private collections company, Alliance One, was still trying to take wages from her. So that resulted in us doing a information practices act request to the Franchise Tax Board. What we found is, is she had been over-garnished by approximately $1000. Now, as a regular person, it's almost virtually impossible to get information from say, Alliance One, because when you ask to speak to a manager, typically, they say that, that person's in a meeting. Similarly with the Franchise Tax Board, it's very hard to get information from them unless you represented by an attorney, because most people can't navigate through their process, but even once you get that information, each one of those entities will take it that you have to follow up with the court. So in this case, I have to send the entirety of the information I got from each one of these to Alameda County to say that my client had been garnished $4,000 more than she owed. And even then, when they did the analysis, they couldn't figure out what it is that she owed. So when you see that chart about the various ways money moves. It's important to understand that when you look at that chart there's real people behind that and in this case, it was only because we are currently engaged in conversations with Alameda County or we're able to have meetings with the Court Executive Officer etc, that I was able to get or start getting resolution for my client. Similarly, when we talk about civil assessment, under the statute, the civil assessment can be up to $300, but in fact, what often times happens is, it's almost always blanket $300, which means that judges aren't using any discretion at all. They're not considering the totality of somebody's circumstances which they're supposed to do. They're not considering somebody's ability to pay which they are supposed to do and so then people end up getting these civil assessments that everybody knows that they can't pay, that the county is not confident that they're going to be able to collect on, and it just adds to more and more debt, and the legislature has the ability to be make decisions about how that kind of thing happens. So with the amnesty program, there was a decision made where if you owed victim restitution, you couldn't apply for the amnesty program. Well the practical effect to that means that people who owe victim restitution can't get their license back which means that may or may not be able to be employed, which means that they may or may not be able to pay the restitution that they owe. So all of this is sort of a hyper-economic issue, but it's also a racial justice issue because we know that the communities that are over-policed are also the communities that have the highest proportion of suspended licenses. That recreates a sort of effect where people would never able to get from underneath that and it has ripple effects has already been discussed that, again, we're not discussing here but some of the things like having a misdemeanor conviction for a drug on a suspended license could make it, so that when somebody tries to apply say, through the Department of Insurance, to be able to sell insurance, they can't, because the Department of Insurance finds that misdemeanor conviction to be something that they see as disqualifying for a person, and that kind of individual, again without legal representation likely will not be able to get a job, because we now live in a sort of era where there's an expansion of professional licensing requirements. And I saw this directly when I worked in the public defender's office, where we had various clients who had driving on a suspended license, were too poor to pay. So every time you get a driver on a suspended license 14601 is about $1100. So if you get multiple of those at makes it harder and harder for you to overcome that. That enforces you deeper and deeper in to the criminal justice system where it results in mandatory jail time. It's almost impossible to get from underneath that and there because I didn't necessarily know better at the time we would say, well let's kick this case for six months for somebody to get their license back because if they got their license back from the DA would offer them a 12500, unlicensed driver, which does not carry mandatory jail time and is less financial burden on people. But the practical impact of that is that most people could not get their license back within six months, which directly impacted what they ultimately were convicted of and had these various ripple effects, which it is that I've been speaking about. So I do think it's important to look at overall over haul of the fines and fees, and why they have expanded in the way that they have when we know that people can't pay. I also think that it's really important to take a real good look at the civil assessments and how they're being allocated. I've requested through Public Records Act, requests and what not to see what it is that I believe, that everybody gets a $300 civil assessment, which doesn't make a whole lot of economic sense. And then, finally, because I know I'm coming close to my time, in the broader construct of the criminal justice system in the fines and fees, I think it's also important to take a look at making sure that the ability to pay exists everywhere, because there are certain fines and fees, even in the misdemeanor context, that when somebody who's indigent, they will need to go through the ability pay process and there's a couple of fines and fees that are not currently subject to that.

That evening no search was conducted and no drug testing was performed after Daniel and his friends returned from their high risk visit to the city. Early the following morning, the manager left the SLE without checking on the residents. Daniel was later found in a bathroom. He had passed away from an opioid overdose from drugs obtained from unknown sources. One day after his birthday. The path to recovery is a long one that can be likened to a chain with many links. Every link has to be strong and every handover between facilities has to be seamless. The certification of sober living residences is but one link in the recovery chain, and must require verifiable adherence to robust policies and procedures designed to protect the resident during recovery. AB-285 is the first step to making this link strong. I support the Bill AB 285.

Based on our hospital data, our program participants were incurring about $63,000 a year in hospital costs, two-thirds of which were born from inpatient hospitalization. They were all on Medi-Cal. These individuals were not going to the emergency room because they wanted a warm place to sleep, they were going because they suffered from very acute healthcare conditions. Our 10th Decile Project is not unique, we see from the last 25 years, study after study. DTSC itself has set a goal of making decisions within two years of receiving an application. Therefore, even under DTSC's own goal, DTSC will allow a facility to operate one and a half years without a permit. Gene Urban: Gene Urban, thank you. This is a matter of some importance. And it's a little bit nuanced, but it's extremely important. There's a big difference between submitting an application and submitting a completed application. And we need to resolve that matter today. I believe that the part A is almost always done while the part B is an iterative process that sometimes involves 2 and 3 NODs, notices of deficiency, which compels the applicant to submit additional information, sometimes extremely complex information, hydrology, toxicology, epidemiology, whatever it may be, engineering and it goes on and on. The department has recently issued a study on its NOD process, notice of deficiency process, and acknowledged the deficiencies in that. But if you compel a completed application two years in advance, you will have to submit it four, 5 and 6 years in advance of the expiration to be guaranteed that it will be deemed complete two years before expiration. And the bill creates the implication that if you have not submitted a completed application two years in advance, you're out of luck. You can no longer operate if your permit expires. It says if it's completed two years in advance, you can continue to operate after expiration. But if you submit it a month late and it's deemed completed 23 months before the expiration date, but you do not yet have final approval on the expiration date, you're out of business, which I don't think is the intended outcome. But the way I read the bill, that's the clear, clear implication, and would be litigated. So we need to distinguish between how soon one submits in good faith a reasonably complete part A and part B, knowing, given the history of the department, that it will be determined to be incomplete. And that's a good thing in a sense you want the iterative process, you want more information submitted. But you can't penalize the applicant fairly. You could penalize them unfairly because my experience is you submit, you wait a prolonged period of time. You're given 30 days to respond. You submit, and then it goes silent for another eight months. So you're penalizing the applicant who in good faith is trying to submit a completed part B. And if they don't make it by the expiration date or in this case two years before the expiration date, they're foreclosed from operating as the expiration date approaches. It's not a good outcome. It's not a fair outcome. But it's a common outcome until we reform the department.

Seth Kerstein: Thank you, Mr. Chair. Seth Kerstein with the Legislative Analysts Office. I'll give a very brief overview of cannabis legalization in California. And then I'll discuss some of the tax related challenges facing the state and the industry. My colleague Shawn Martin will cover the Department of food and agriculture track and trace program and summarize some of the state's key upcoming deadlines related to cannabis legalization. So the path that California has followed to cannabis being illegal under state law to becoming legal has occurred in 4 big steps. The first one was Proposition 215 which voters passed in 1996. Prop 215 legalized the use of marijuana for medical purposes. The second was SB420 of 2003, which legalized nonprofit cooperatives that grow medical marijuana and provided to their members. For many years after this first two laws were passed, the state didn't play much of a role in licensing or regulating medical marijuana. That really just happened at the local level. Then the third major change came along when the Legislature passed some laws in 2015 known collectively as the Medical Cannabis Regulation and Safety Act, or MCRSA. In line with its name, MCRSA required state agencies to regulate several different aspects of the medical marijuana industry. And most recently, we had the fourth major change in state cannabis laws when voters passed Proposition 64 this past November, which legalized adult use of cannabis for non-medical purposes. The next chapter in that story is the state's ongoing implementation of those last two changes, MCRS and Prop 64. And my colleague will touch on that briefly later in our presentation. But now that I've covered some of that general background I'd like to narrow the focus to the main topic of interest today, taxation of the cannabis industry. So Prop 64, which was passed in November, made several changes to the cannabis tax landscape. The first change was a change in the sales taxation of medical marijuana. Shortly after the election, the state implemented a full sales tax exemption for certain medical marijuana sales. The second change was that local governments can now tax both medical and nonmedical marijuana and voters have already approved local taxes in some areas. And the third change was the creation of some new state excise taxes on cannabis effective January 1st, 2018. The excise tax rates on growers are $9.25 per ounce of dried flowers and $2.75 per ounce of dried leaves. The excise tax on retail sales of cannabis products is 15%. The revenue from these taxes will go to a new special fund for purposes specified in Proposition 64. And although cannabis is now legal under state law and the state is developing a system for taxing and regulating it, it is still illegal, as you know, under federal law. And that has some major implications for the states implementation of and the industries compliance with the new excise taxes. In particular it means that the industry has very limited access to financial services. Banks have some very strong incentives not to serve clients who violate federal drug laws. So in most cases, businesses in the cannabis industry can get bank accounts and other financial services only as long as the banks providing those services remain unaware of what their clients are selling. As a result a lot of cannabis businesses are largely cash based, which not only makes it more costly and less secure for them to operate. But also makes it harder for them to pay taxes. And the state agency that administers those taxes, in particular, sales and excised taxes for the state, is the State Board of Equalization. Otherwise known as BOE. BOE is headed by a five member elected board. One of whom is the state controller who's elected on a state wide basis. And for who were elected from four districts, each of which contains about a quarter of the states population. BOEs default policy is not to accept payments in cash, which obviously poses some problems for the cannabis industry. However the no cash policy does allow district administrator in each of the four geographic BOE districts to make exceptions for taxpayers who can demonstrate that the no cash policy would pose a hardship. BOE's capacity to handle cash will need to expand quite a bit under Prop 64. Some components of the administration's 2017-18 budget request for BOE to implement Prop 64 are intended to help them build this capacity. And at a recent meeting, BOE staff presented several alternatives for the board members to consider that potentially further strengthen the agency's ability to take cash payments from tax payers. Of course, enabling cash payments is only one of the steps the state needs to take to implement the tax components of Prop 64. One of the other major challenges is getting the industry to comply with the new taxes. The first basic step in that effort is outreach and education to make sure that the industry is aware of the new excise taxes. There's some complementarity there, potentially with other agency's licensing efforts. Cannabis businesses will need to be registered with BOE, before they can obtain state licenses and both steps are part of the broader process. These businesses will need to go through to move out of the underground economy. Now the second step for those businesses who do not undergo that process and who remain part of the underground economy is to for the state to follow up with enforcement and BOE does have some existing programs in this area. In recent years BOE investigators have participated in several inter-agency task forces that address the underground economy broadly. Two of these task forces have focused specifically on criminal tax evasion. The Revenue Recovery and Collaborative Enforcement Team, which is headed by the Department of Industrial Relations, and the Tax Recovery and Criminal Enforcement Task Force. Thank you. We don't have precise estimates of the number of cannabis businesses in the state that are operating in the underground economy, but it's likely at least in the tens of thousands. Then the biggest piece of that in terms of number of businesses is on the cultivation side. Although growers certainly have income tax liability, they probably don't, in most cases, have much sales tax liability because most of their sales are for resale. The part of the supply chain that typically would owe sales tax on most of their product is the retailers or dispensaries. Right now we're in a short window of time when they'll be paying sales tax only on sort of a narrow piece of their cannabis sales. As I mentioned earlier, BOE has implemented a full sales tax exemption for certain medical marijuana sales. In particular, when the purchaser provides state issued medical marijuana ID cards, along with another form of government issued ID. So, for other medical marijuana sales, dispensaries will still need to remit some sales tax. So Prop 64 contains some language related to tax enforcement, some of which will be helpful for BOE's tax enforcement efforts, and some of which has turned out to be unnecessary. In particular, Prop 64 authorizes BOE to develop Tax Stamps but encoding information on a single physical stamp isn't very practical given the way cannabis changes as it moves through the supply chains. So, for the cannabis excise taxes, the Department of Food and Ag's track and trace system will play a role similar to what Tax Stamps play for cigarettes. My colleague, Shawn Martin, will give you some more information about track and trace.

Michele Pielsticker: Excuse me, thank you very much. Michele Pielsticker, State Board of Equalization. And thank you for providing me with the opportunity to do some background about BOE's current sales and use tax collection and compliance for medical cannabis dispensaries. As well as ongoing challenges resulting from the fact that the cannabis industry largely consists of many cash businesses without adequate access to banking. Under current law, all retailers engaged in business in California must pay sales tax on the tangible personal property they sell, absent an exemption or exclusion. Retail sales of medical cannabis were subject to the tax, to the same extent as any other retail sale of tangible personal property in this state, until November 9th when Prop 64 was enacted. Prop 64 provides an exemption for retail sales of medical cannabis products. When a qualified patient or their primary caregiver provides their medical marijuana ID card and a valid government issued ID card. Now, prior to October 2005, the BOE did not knowingly issue sellers permits to sellers of property that may be considered illegal, including medical cannabis. However, in October 2005, the board directed staff to issue sellers permits irrespective of the potential illegal nature of the product sold and the failure of the retailer to indicate the product sold and registering for a permit. The board's willingness to accept a retailer's registration without specifying the product sold stems from the fact that retailers have feared federal prosecution for selling medical cannabis. Which is considered a schedule one drug as you mentioned. In January 2016, the BOE provided an identification code for medical cannabis businesses when information in the public domain indicates that a business sells cannabis. And the BOE anticipates this will be helpful in more accurately tracking the amount of revenue derived from cannabis retailers. Until now, the BOE has cross-checked industry websites and public advertising with current sales and use tax registrants to identify businesses that don't hold a seller's permit in an effort to register them. Through June 30th, 2016, 1,185 publicly disclosed medical cannabis sellers registered with the BOE, filed returns, and remitted sales and use tax. In fiscal year '15, '16 medical cannabis businesses reported $69 million in sales and use tax. Based on cannabis consumption data, the BOE estimates it would've collected $112 million with 100% compliance rate. Applying those assumptions, the estimated actual compliance rate is approximately 61% on the sales and use tax side. And this percentage is similar to Colorado's stated compliance rate of 60%. Now, I issue the CAVEAT that the estimated $112 million that we might collect with 100% compliance rate is based on assumptions. And we're basing that on consumption data on the national level. So to the extent those assumptions are wrong, that number could be greater or less. This lower rate of compliance reflects an industry that has remained primarily underground due to fear of federal prosecution. To improve compliance, the BOE uses all of the compliance tools it applies to any other business. Audit collection and education. As part of its education program, BOE uses its statewide compliance and outreach teams or scope teams, we call them to find and register dispensaries as they visit various zip codes and that includes actually not just dispensaries, but all businesses. These teams travel to businesses, to make sure they are properly registered in complying with the sales and use tax law and that their feed programs were applicable. The BOE also works with industry groups to educate them about their sales and use tax applications. So, a few things have changed in the last couple of years as prior panels have indicated. In 2015, we had the MCRSA package of legislation that establishes the comprehensive regulatory framework for medical marijuana. And Prop 64, the Adult Use of Marijuana Act establishes a similar framework for adult use marijuana as well as a retail level excise tax and cultivation tax on the product. Prop 64 also expands the medical cannabis track and trace system to monitor all marijuana, and marijuana product movement from cultivation to sale, and this track, and trace system would help the BOE determine the amount of products sold and the amount of cultivation tax due which will be very helpful when taxpayers fail to keep adequate or accurate books, and records. The bureau is prepared to implement the taxes imposed by Proposition 64 when the time comes in January 2018. However, issues remain with respect to cash payments. Due to reduced access to banking, many cannabis businesses pay their taxes in cash as other panels have mentioned. Thank you. In early 2014, the BOE implemented no-cash policy. By statute, when a business has monthly tax liabilities averaging $10,000 or more, they are required to make their payment by EFT and that's for all businesses. Failure to remit the funds by EFT subjects taxpayers to specified penalties, unless the person's failure to pay using electronic funds transfer is due to reasonable cause and circumstances beyond his or her control. To obtain this relief, taxpayers do have to file a request for relief of penalty. Effective January 1, 2017, a new law provides relief from this penalty to medical cannabis dispensaries. However, to reduce costs and ensure employee safety, the BOE's district administrators are empowered to determine whether they will accept cash in their offices. A large cash deposit by one taxpayer alone can take numerous staff hours to count and the potential danger with large sums requires added security. In fiscal year 15, 16, the BOE accepted $22 million in cash from identified dispensaries. In the short-term to address the cash issue, the BOE is looking and working with banks to accept cash payments creating tax service centers at existing secure government buildings and that would include the local sheriff's department. Creating offsite cash acceptance facilities at strategic locations and installing cash acceptance systems at BOE offices. On a broader scale, the treasurer has established a working group to address the cash issue for all state agencies. And as Prop 64 is implemented, the need for this group will be enhanced. The cash issue is bigger than BOE alone and necessitates a longer term statewide approach. We look forward to being a part of those discussions. In conclusion, although the BOE has strived to improve sales and the tax compliance among cannabis businesses, there is more work to be done. The BOE is hopeful the new regulatory framework combined with a track and trace system will improve tax compliance. Additionally, we look forward to working with other state agencies to address the issue of cash, so that all state employees can remain safe and secure as we implement Prop 64. Thank you and I am happy to answer any questions.

I wanted to be and by just talking about is starkly some of the state and federal changes and what's been going on, where we are now and then a few things for you to consider moving forward in terms of some things the Legislature might want to think about. This change in the state accountability system really began in 2013 as part of the adoption of the LCFF, the Local Control Funding Formula. Attached to the legislation that created LCFF was this whole new accountability framework that's been rolled out over the last several years. And some of the things that are part of that framework you may have heard about. We have now been talking for several years about eight state priority areas, that are in statute that specify kind of the key things that the state thinks are most important, and there are other things the state is using to kind of determine whether districts and schools are doing well. And then you have local control and accountability plans which is one of the ways where these priority areas kind of show up. The districts now for three years have been developing these plans that require them to set goals in these priority areas, to use some of the performance measures in statute to measure how they are going to improve in those priority areas, and specify the actions they're going to make that improvement. And we're now in the third year, for the 16/17 year was the third that districts have had to adopt an LCAP and they have to go out and get feedback from their communities, from stakeholders and they have to ultimately get their LCAPs adopted and approved by the County Office of Education. So those are the things I think now, have been around and been going on for a couple years. On page two we talk a little bit more about the detail of what is called the evaluation rubrics. I think ultimately the valuation rubrics will show up for most people in this dashboard that I think the board stuff is sort of expected to be available for the public in the spring of 2017. And the board developed this and adopted the rubrics in September of 2016. What the initial legislation said is that these rubrics are intended to be used to identify districts that might need assistance and to also be a tool for districts to use to identify their own strengths and weaknesses. These rubrics were to be based on these eight priority areas on the things that the state have said are important. And the board, in developing them, they've developed a set of 10 state performance indicators that are used at the district-level and in some cases, can be used for subgroups and individual schools. They kind of split it up into two different kinds of indicators depending on what data we have available. So they are what the board's calling the state performance indicators where we have statewide data that's collected across the state for schools, for school districts, for individual student subgroups. And for that data which I think is a lot about what the conversations have been about in terms of what will be up on the dashboard, that's data that will be, the board has set these performance categories that are color-coded, going from red, which is the lowest performing, to blue, which is the highest performing. And you'll be able to see for all of these, state performance indicators for a school district, how they're doing, for a individual subgroup within the school district. And then for a school and then for subgroups within that school. So the idea there is that this is going to be a tool for districts for the public to be able to use to kind of look at how a district is doing, how schools are doing, how individuals or groups are doing. Those performance categories are based on two things. One is how overall is a district performing in that area and the second thing is what's the improvement or growth over time or potentially change over time. So in general districts who might have be in a red category or districts that have an absolute low performance on that particular indicator and also are not seeing much growth. And then on the other side, the districts with the blue category would be districts with high performance and likely high growth as well. So that's part of what will be when the dashboards are available to the public. You'll be able to see that information and there will be, I know there's been a lot of discussions of the functionality of the tool, but from what we've heard from the State Board of Education, that'd be the ability to drill down and look at, for example, individual student groups', subgroups' scores, scores at the district level or at the school level. It's a little bit different for these other performance indicators, what are called the local performance indicators. And these are areas where the state does not have a uniform consistency state-wide data that I can use to categorize performance based on these different categories. So for example, one example is parent engagement. There is no state-wide measurement for how we're engaging parents. And so what the board is going to be requiring as part of the rubrics is for districts to develop their own local measure of parent engagement, and so they would, at the local level, develop what it is they're going to use to determine that. To measure progress, and to see how they are improving over time and to provide some information in a narrative form that will be uploaded into a dashboard for the public to be able to see. And in this case, as long as districts are developing a local indicator, describing how their performance is changing. And submitting that information will be considered to have, to be meeting that specific standard. So, that's kind of the general framework of what's going on with those rubrics. And we will be available on that dashboard. Then that information then, it can be used and is required to be used by county offices of education to identify which districts need to receive technical assistance. And the state board has specified based on the rubrics how you would define whether a district needs to receive additional assistance, that's tied to some of the language that was in the initial legislation. For districts to receive assistance, generally what we require to receive assistance, if you have any student subgroup that is in that lowest performance category for more than one of the priority areas. So for example, if you have a student sub-group that based on their graduation rates and their student test scores are in that red category, that would reflect that that district needs to receive technical assistance, to get support for improving outcomes for that student sub-group. There's also another more intensive level of intervention. If you have a district where three or more sub-groups are in that lowest performance category for two or more priority areas, in three out of four the consecutive years. So, we're talking about now, multiple students subgroups struggling over multiple years in a number of areas. So, we don't expect that there'll be as many districts who will be in that category. But that is one of the possibilities. So moving on to page 4, that's a very quick summary of what the rubrics or the dashboard is expected to look like. I wanted to highlight a couple of other key things that are now associated with that. First is the California Collaborative for Educational Excellence, which is a state entity that was created in 2013, specifically with the idea that they would be a statewide expert that would help in providing assistance to schools and districts. The idea is that it would be a small entity that would be able to contract out with experts, but also that they might be one of the key entities in helping provide support to some of those school districts, who are persistently under performing for many years. The state has provided two different sources of one-time funding for the collaborative. First, an initial $10 million to get the agency up and running. And then last year in the budget, additional funding for specific activities, one was to conduct statewide professional development or training for anybody actually, anybody in the general public, but also teachers, administrators, parents, to learn about the rubrics and how they can be used. And then also funding to develop a pilot program to work with some school districts who are struggling to improve outcomes with the idea that this pilot program would help inform what the collaborative would do moving forward. As it works to assist some school districts who are struggling to improve outcomes. So those are the key things in the state system. I wanted to briefly talk about the federal changes. So the state has started doing it in 2013, in December 2015 the federal government passed the Every Student Succeeds Act,  which essentially got rid of the No Child Left Behind assistant which was a very prescriptive federal system and it meant that we had a state and federal accountability system. Two systems at the same time that often told districts conflicting things. And now the federal law essentially says, states you can have your own accountability model. It has to meet some very specific requirements. As long as you do those things, we don't need to have a complete federal system. One of the things for California that has been good is that the ESSA, a lot of the components that are required are parts that the State is already developing, through the rubrics and through the multiple measure system that we have now. So the federal government requires a number of key measurements such as academic achievement, graduation rates, academic growth, progress for English learners, and a non-academic measure such as school climate. The State is already doing all that. All of that is already embedded within those state priority areas and those performance indicators. The ESSI also requires two different levels of support for schools. There's this more targeted support if there is a school that's having trouble with a particular sub-group. And there's a more comprehensive level of support for a school that has sort of more persistent systemic problems. It's very similar to the structure that we have in our system for identifying districts that need technical assistance for some specific subgroups that are not performing well versus that more intensive intervention that we set and specific in laws that for more long term ongoing problems in the school districts. The one key difference between the two systems is the ESSA is all about school level performance whereas the state system is mostly district based. But with the dashboard we will be able to look at school level data as well. And so you can imagine very easily being able to combine the state requirements, and the federal requirements together, so that you don't have multiple systems with different ways to identify whether districts are in need of support. When a family goes in and says to a principal, I'm worried about this one data point right here, they have a great principal, the principal acknowledges it. Admits that the school has some challenges and shares the plan for improvement. Unfortunately, many of the low income families that we work with get the run around when they point to a negative data point. They often hear, well, ignore that red, look at this green. Everything here is great. Families have said that without strong summative rating they lack the tool to hold their schools accountable for student performance. And so we are appreciative of all the work to continuously improve the system, appreciative of the move to multiple measures. I really think that the CDE and the state board can build on the current design and provide families an overall rating for all schools. Thank you.

Edgar Cabral: Good morning Mr. Chair and members. Edgar Cabral of the Legislative Analyst's Office. I was asked to provide kind of a very high level overview of the system to just provide you with some context before you hear from the other panelists and some of them are detailed work that's been going on. There's a lot of background, a lot of years of work in developing the system, so I think I'll do my best to just cover at a high level to help you understand some of the things that other panelists will be discussing. And we do have a handout that we developed that I would use on as the basis of this presentation, but I won't go through everything in specific detail. I wanted to be and by just talking about is starkly some of the state and federal changes and what's been going on, where we are now and then a few things for you to consider moving forward in terms of some things the Legislature might want to think about. This change in the state accountability system really began in 2013 as part of the adoption of the LCFF, the Local Control Funding Formula. Attached to the legislation that created LCFF was this whole new accountability framework that's been rolled out over the last several years. And some of the things that are part of that framework you may have heard about. We have now been talking for several years about eight state priority areas, that are in statute that specify kind of the key things that the state thinks are most important, and there are other things the state is using to kind of determine whether districts and schools are doing well. And then you have local control and accountability plans which is one of the ways where these priority areas kind of show up. The districts now for three years have been developing these plans that require them to set goals in these priority areas, to use some of the performance measures in statute to measure how they are going to improve in those priority areas, and specify the actions they're going to make that improvement. And we're now in the third year, for the 16/17 year was the third that districts have had to adopt an LCAP and they have to go out and get feedback from their communities, from stakeholders and they have to ultimately get their LCAPs adopted and approved by the County Office of Education. So those are the things I think now, have been around and been going on for a couple years. On page two we talk a little bit more about the detail of what is called the evaluation rubrics. I think ultimately the valuation rubrics will show up for most people in this dashboard that I think the board stuff is sort of expected to be available for the public in the spring of 2017. And the board developed this and adopted the rubrics in September of 2016. What the initial legislation said is that these rubrics are intended to be used to identify districts that might need assistance and to also be a tool for districts to use to identify their own strengths and weaknesses. These rubrics were to be based on these eight priority areas on the things that the state have said are important. And the board, in developing them, they've developed a set of 10 state performance indicators that are used at the district-level and in some cases, can be used for subgroups and individual schools. They kind of split it up into two different kinds of indicators depending on what data we have available. So they are what the board's calling the state performance indicators where we have statewide data that's collected across the state for schools, for school districts, for individual student subgroups. And for that data which I think is a lot about what the conversations have been about in terms of what will be up on the dashboard, that's data that will be, the board has set these performance categories that are color-coded, going from red, which is the lowest performing, to blue, which is the highest performing. And you'll be able to see for all of these, state performance indicators for a school district, how they're doing, for a individual subgroup within the school district. And then for a school and then for subgroups within that school. So the idea there is that this is going to be a tool for districts for the public to be able to use to kind of look at how a district is doing, how schools are doing, how individuals or groups are doing. Those performance categories are based on two things. One is how overall is a district performing in that area and the second thing is what's the improvement or growth over time or potentially change over time. So in general districts who might have be in a red category or districts that have an absolute low performance on that particular indicator and also are not seeing much growth. And then on the other side, the districts with the blue category would be districts with high performance and likely high growth as well. So that's part of what will be when the dashboards are available to the public. You'll be able to see that information and there will be, I know there's been a lot of discussions of the functionality of the tool, but from what we've heard from the State Board of Education, that'd be the ability to drill down and look at, for example, individual student groups', subgroups' scores, scores at the district level or at the school level. It's a little bit different for these other performance indicators, what are called the local performance indicators. And these are areas where the state does not have a uniform consistency state-wide data that I can use to categorize performance based on these different categories. So for example, one example is parent engagement. There is no state-wide measurement for how we're engaging parents. And so what the board is going to be requiring as part of the rubrics is for districts to develop their own local measure of parent engagement, and so they would, at the local level, develop what it is they're going to use to determine that. To measure progress, and to see how they are improving over time and to provide some information in a narrative form that will be uploaded into a dashboard for the public to be able to see. And in this case, as long as districts are developing a local indicator, describing how their performance is changing. And submitting that information will be considered to have, to be meeting that specific standard. So, that's kind of the general framework of what's going on with those rubrics. And we will be available on that dashboard. Then that information then, it can be used and is required to be used by county offices of education to identify which districts need to receive technical assistance. And the state board has specified based on the rubrics how you would define whether a district needs to receive additional assistance, that's tied to some of the language that was in the initial legislation. For districts to receive assistance, generally what we require to receive assistance, if you have any student subgroup that is in that lowest performance category for more than one of the priority areas. So for example, if you have a student sub-group that based on their graduation rates and their student test scores are in that red category, that would reflect that that district needs to receive technical assistance, to get support for improving outcomes for that student sub-group. There's also another more intensive level of intervention. If you have a district where three or more sub-groups are in that lowest performance category for two or more priority areas, in three out of four the consecutive years. So, we're talking about now, multiple students subgroups struggling over multiple years in a number of areas. So, we don't expect that there'll be as many districts who will be in that category. But that is one of the possibilities. So moving on to page 4, that's a very quick summary of what the rubrics or the dashboard is expected to look like. I wanted to highlight a couple of other key things that are now associated with that. First is the California Collaborative for Educational Excellence, which is a state entity that was created in 2013, specifically with the idea that they would be a statewide expert that would help in providing assistance to schools and districts. The idea is that it would be a small entity that would be able to contract out with experts, but also that they might be one of the key entities in helping provide support to some of those school districts, who are persistently under performing for many years. The state has provided two different sources of one-time funding for the collaborative. First, an initial $10 million to get the agency up and running. And then last year in the budget, additional funding for specific activities, one was to conduct statewide professional development or training for anybody actually, anybody in the general public, but also teachers, administrators, parents, to learn about the rubrics and how they can be used. And then also funding to develop a pilot program to work with some school districts who are struggling to improve outcomes with the idea that this pilot program would help inform what the collaborative would do moving forward. As it works to assist some school districts who are struggling to improve outcomes. So those are the key things in the state system. I wanted to briefly talk about the federal changes. So the state has started doing it in 2013, in December 2015 the federal government passed the Every Student Succeeds Act,  which essentially got rid of the No Child Left Behind assistant which was a very prescriptive federal system and it meant that we had a state and federal accountability system. Two systems at the same time that often told districts conflicting things. And now the federal law essentially says, states you can have your own accountability model. It has to meet some very specific requirements. As long as you do those things, we don't need to have a complete federal system. One of the things for California that has been good is that the ESSA, a lot of the components that are required are parts that the State is already developing, through the rubrics and through the multiple measure system that we have now. So the federal government requires a number of key measurements such as academic achievement, graduation rates, academic growth, progress for English learners, and a non-academic measure such as school climate. The State is already doing all that. All of that is already embedded within those state priority areas and those performance indicators. The ESSI also requires two different levels of support for schools. There's this more targeted support if there is a school that's having trouble with a particular sub-group. And there's a more comprehensive level of support for a school that has sort of more persistent systemic problems. It's very similar to the structure that we have in our system for identifying districts that need technical assistance for some specific subgroups that are not performing well versus that more intensive intervention that we set and specific in laws that for more long term ongoing problems in the school districts. The one key difference between the two systems is the ESSA is all about school level performance whereas the state system is mostly district based. But with the dashboard we will be able to look at school level data as well. I wanted to specify to discuss a little bit of some of the uncertainty about regulations and I think in general, we would say that there are some uncertainty in our regulations but we don't think there's any reason that the State needs to change what it's doing in the current plan or timeline for submitting a plan for ESSA. [{'start': 27, 'end': 40, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 1360, 'end': 1363, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 1368, 'end': 1374, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 1793, 'end': 1801, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Drew Soderborg: Madam Chair and members, Drew Soderborg Legislative Analysts Office. So in front of you you'll find a handout and if you turn to the first page of that handout you'll see where our discussion of the major provisions of Prop 64 begins. So Prop 64 changed state law to legalize the use of cannabis for non-medical purposes by adult age 21 and over. However, there are some restrictions on this use if you look at the first figure on page one of the handout. That figure summarizes both the activities that would be allowed under Prop 64 and the activities that would continue to be restricted. For example, individuals could smoke cannabis in a private home or a business licensed for on-site consumption. However, individuals could not smoke cannabis while driving a car, in any public place other than one of those businesses licensed for on-site consumption. Or anywhere that smoking tobacco is prohibited. In addition, individuals could grow up to six plants in their home and possess the cannabis the plants produced. However, individuals could not grow these plants in an area that's unlocked or visible from a public place. In addition, Proposition 64 creates a system for regulating non-medical cannabis. This system is largely similar to the system the state created for regulating medical cannabis. For example, the state agency's responsibilities under Proposition 64 are largely similar, with some notable differences, as they are for regulating medical cannabis. In addition, under the measure of the system for tracking medical cannabis has to be expanded to track non-medical cannabis. Proposition 64 also allows cities and counties to regulate non-medical cannabis. For example, cities and counties could obtain, could require businesses to obtain local licenses and set rules for these businesses. Cities and counties would also be allowed to completely ban cannabis related businesses. So if you turn to page two of the hand out, you'll see a discussion of the changes and penalties related to cannabis crime under Prop 64. So Prop 64 generally reduces the penalties for cannabis related crimes. For example, prior to Prop 64 selling cannabis for a non-medical purpose was punishable by up to four years in prison and jail. Under the measure, selling cannabis without a license is a crime generally punishable by six months in jail and/or a fine of up to $500. In addition, individuals who are currently serving sentences for cannabis related crimes that have lesser penalties on Prop 64 could petition the courts to seek that their sentence be modified to the lesser penalty. In addition, individuals who have already completed their sentences could petition the courts to have their criminal history modified to reflect a lesser conviction. Proposition 64 also imposes taxes on cannabis. And the figure on page two summarizes the tax structure under Prop 64. To begin with there is going to be a new state tax on the growing of cannabis. This would apply to both medical and non-medical cannabis. And would be $9.25 per ounce of dried cannabis flowers and $2.75 per ounce of dried cannabis leaves. In addition, there will be a new state retail excise tax on both medical and non-medical cannabis at a rate of 15% of the retail price. The measure also indicates that existing state and local sales taxes will continue to apply to cannabis for non-medical purposes. However, individuals who have a medical marijuana card can get the sales tax that's levied on them reduced under the measure. In addition, the measure also allows local governments to levy additional taxes on cannabis. The state excise tax on retail sales and the state tax on growing, as well as certain fines, will be deposited into a new special fund known as the California marijuana tax fund. As we discuss later, Proposition 64 will specify how the monies in the fund would be allocated. So that gives you an overview of the major provisions of Prop 64, I'd be happy to answer any questions that you might have about them.

Today I'm going to just give you a brief overview of the revenue, the revenue estimates that we prepared as part of the '17-'18 Governor's Budget that went into the, for the marijuana tax revenues. So I'm going to start by reiterating some of the concerns that have already been raised. And so some of the caveats and the broad-based assumptions that had to be made for this revenue forecast. So have to assume basically that there's going to be no signficant change in federal action. Obviously, if that changes significantly, that could have some very significant impacts on the revenues. We did adjust the revenue estimates for start-up difficulties. But we do assume a substantially functional market by July 1, 2018. And that's six months following when the regulations are due. So we have assumed no revenues in '17-'18, and we assume $100 million reduction from our baseline forecast in '18-'19. This forecast that I'm going to provide to you today, it's only related to the excise tax revenues for the marijuana. So it includes the tax on the flower and the leaf, and it includes the 15% excise tax. It does not include income taxes, it does not include direct or indirect or secondary impacts on the economy, and it does not include sales taxes. I just would point out, as other people had mentioned, there's large uncertainties with this forecast. So I'll be providing point revenue estimates. However, the actual numbers, given the variety of uncertainties, could be significantly above or below these estimates. And as we do with all of our tax revenue forecasts, we will be looking at this again at the May revision, and we'll be refining assumptions, and looking at new data. And we'll be continuing to revise these estimates going forward. So with that, if you turn to the next page in tax structure. And this has already been covered, so I'll just briefly reiterate. There's a cultivation tax, 925 per ounce, 275 per ounce of leaves. And then the 15% excise tax on the final retail selling price. And those are the estimates that I'll be providing to you today. As we approached this revenue estimate, we divided it basically into three different modules, and so we looked at three things separately. We looked at the recreational market, and the medical market and the tourist market. So we expect some revenue gains from people visiting California and consuming marijuana. To forecast the recreational and medical markets, we start with a look at kind of what the current market looks like today. Obviously, that's a bit difficult given that the recreational is a black market for the most part. What we did, we looked at surveys that were provided by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. And they survey people on their marijuana usage. And we look at what, so roughly they say 14.5% of Californians have consumed marijuana within the last year. And so that kind of gives us a population of users in California. And then we look at when we have to estimate the number of medical users. And so, California does not require you to carry a card, to have a medical marijuana carrying card, it's optional. So unlike other states, like Oregon for example, where they have actual really good data on the medical users, we don't have that here in California yet. So when we looked at Oregon and how many users they have, medical marijuana users, and we adjusted for California's population. So that gives us 750,000 medical users, and out of a population of about 4.8 million total users. So, and then that leaves about 4.1 million recreational users. We then have to estimate rates of usage. And we did this, for the recreational we assumed 3.5 ounces per person on average. This consists of some very heavy users and also some very light users. These were similar estimates that were employed by Colorado and Oregon when they initially did the revenue estimates that they were able to achieve. And we assume a much higher use among medical, as you'd expect. Medical users should be much heavier users, and on average we assume 9 ounces per person, per year, for medical users. So that kind of gives us the State of the current market, which roughly 14 million ounces recreational, almost 7 million ounces medical. So from there, we prepare a forecast for each part of each module. So, we looked at, so recreational. So one of the biggest challenges with recreational is how big, large the black, gray, homegrown market is currently. We expect it to be quite significant in the beginning. And so we're estimating that roughly two-thirds of the market will initially be black or gray, or outside of the taxable market.

[{'start': 4, 'end': 18, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 481, 'end': 488, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Seth Kerstein: Thank you Madam Chair. Seth Kerstein, Legislative Analyst Office. Some of the information I'll be presenting appears on page three of our handout. And to a large extent, will be covering ground that the Department of Finance has covered, so I'll try to make it brief. The way the excised taxes are structured, you have three basic factors that determine how much revenue the state will collect. The amounts of cannabis grown and consumed, the prices consumers pay, and the rate of compliance with the new taxes. We and the administration have tried to ascertain those things as best we can given available data, but as Mr. White mentioned they're tremendously uncertain. Just to briefly illustrate that uncertainty. Consider a comparison between the new cannabis excise taxes under Proposition 64 and the new tobacco taxes under another November ballot measure, Proposition 56. On the tobacco side, we have an established tax program that gives us a precise measure of the existing tax base. We also have the experiences of quite a few other states that have raised tobacco taxes, which helps us gauge how producers and consumers are likely to respond. And so our office in analyzing that ballot measure was able to come up with a relatively concrete quantitative revenue estimate for Prop 56, but it was still even then subject to significant uncertainty. We had a range of several hundred million dollars. With cannabis, we have a tax base that is very difficult to measure because most of it is still part of the underground economy. Experiences from a relatively small number of other states. The potential as Senator Skinner and others have mentioned for major changes in federal enforcement and a concurrent effort at the state level to apply a brand new regulatory framework to the industry. So it's really a whole other level of uncertainty. That said, with revenue potentially materializing before the end of the upcoming 2017-18 fiscal year, the budget will need to incorporate some kind of revenue assumption. In our ballot analysis of Prop 64, our best estimate was that the state and local governments could eventually collect net additional revenues ranging from the high hundreds of millions of dollars to over $1 billion annually. We noted that the revenues likely would be significantly lower in the first several years following the passage of the measure. Our current estimates are based on the same analysis that led us to that conclusion, which actually has a lot in common with the analysis that the administration has done. I'll highlight two things to keep in mind, relative to our summary for the November ballot. First, related to a point that Senator Moorlach has raised, that estimate totaled up the net change in revenue for all state and local taxes, at least the ones that, based on our initial estimates, were significant enough to include in the total. The biggest piece of that is what we're discussing today, revenue from the new state excise taxes on cannabis. That accounted for about three quarters of our total estimated net increase in state and local revenue. The second thing is this distinction between the short run and the long run. Even if the state's implementation were to go relatively smoothly, the transition from the current State of the world to the world that's envisioned in Prop 64 will be drawn out over a number of years, likely the better part of a decade. And to some extent that's by design. The measure for example doesn't allow the state issued licenses for the largest scale cultivators until 2023. So whatever form the industry will take in the long run, we probably won't see it until the mid 2020's at the earliest. So then focusing on that Shorter run revenue, the scenario that we've put together is in many ways similar to what the administration has presented. In the first year of full implementation, so full implementation meaning assuming that everything is up and running as planned, we're looking at annual revenue roughly on the order of half $1 billion initially. Relative to the administration, our scenario has somewhat slower growth in subsequent years. But in light of the uncertainty we've emphasized, we'd say the administration's estimates are reasonable. One last key point to consider is both our revenue projections and the administration's depend quite heavily on a variety of assumptions about government actions at the federal, state, and local levels. On the whole, our estimates are aligned with what you would expect if things play out in a way that's relatively favorable to the formation and growth of a legal cannabis market. For example, if as has been discussed, the federal government takes a more aggressive approach to enforcement. Or, as another example, if local governments throughout the state, take a highly restrictive approach to licensing and regulation then revenues could potentially come in much lower than either our estimate or the administrations. I'll conclude my comments with that and if you have any questions I'd be happy to answer them.

Richard Miadich: Good morning, Madame Chair, Members of the Committee. My name's Richard Miadich, I'm a partner with Olson, Hagel and Fishburn. Our law firm in consultation with the Drug Policy Alliance, Tamar Todd, who I know will be speaking to you later. We were the primary drafters of Prop 64. I just want to take a few minutes and give you sort of a brief overview of what our thinking was in terms of the allocations. And what limitations we faced when we were doing that, the first in terms of a legal restriction, we were mindful of the single subject rule that we have in California. That requires that initiatives, all the provisions within an initiative, are reasonably germane to each other. And so from our purposes as the lawyers, we wanted to make sure that where we allocated the tax revenues had some connection to the main purpose of the initiative which was to decriminalize marijuana. If we violate the single subject rule, the entire initiative is invalidated. So we made a risk assessment there and we wanted to make sure we were careful on how we allocated that money. From a policy perspective, of course the members of the coalition had significant input on how we allocated those monies. We had significant outreach with various groups that includes social justice groups, drug policy alliance and others, environmental groups. A number of environmental groups gave us extensive feedback which we incorporated by and large into the initiative. And then the state and local governments also provided input which was incorporated into the initiative. In addition to that, at the time we were drafting the initiative, the Lieutenant Governor's blue ribbon Commission on marijuana policy was holding stakeholder meetings around the state, receiving input. We looked at other states, and one of the lessons we felt that we Learned was that it would be a mistake to treat the new revenues we generate as sort of a panacea for all of California's financial woes and instead the best approach would be to direct it at specific purposes. That's in the Blue Ribbon Commission report and I think we've seen that experience in other states, so that was part of our thinking as well. Then finally during the drafting process we reached out and received significant feedback on the tax structure and the allocations from the Board of Equalization. So we tried to engage them during the drafting process to make sure that they were able to provide their feedback to us before the initiative went final. The final point I want to make, this dove tails with something Drew just mentioned, we're also mindful that we want to provide some measure of flexibility for the Legislature with respect to the allocation of the tax revenues over time. And so, that is what lead to the provision that does allow the Legislature to reallocate the money after 10 years. And in addition to that, we do provide that the Legislature may, by a two thirds vote, amend the initiative consistent with the purposes and intent. And those are my prepared remarks. I'm happy to answer questions.

It has to be a look beyond that in order to create opportunity for people in the past who have criminal records. All of the licenses are not so enormous, that it doesn't allow an average person, a smaller actor, to come in and not to seek employment in this new industry. Kathleen Howard: Thank you very much, Madam Chair, Members of the Committee, Kathleen Howard, or I go by Katie, the Executive Director of the BSCC, very happy to be here to talk with you about this important subject. I would like to fill in some additional background from the perspective of the board about our activities on this regulation over the last year, and in particular, focusing on the approval that was approved last week and that is a draft regulation which then begins the Administrative Procedures Act, processed through the Office of Administrative Law. So I wanted to say at the outset that there still is the opportunity for additional public comment on this proposed regulation and to bring you up to date about, I think there really actually has been a significant move toward what the legislature attempted to do last year in SB 1157 with this regulation and there was a particular sense of urgency for the Board to move quickly at the meeting last Thursday, so that there could be a date certain on which the regulation changes. With that, the Board is intent on saying that additional facilities should not be permitted to move to an exclusively video option and I realize that reasonable minds can and will differ on this, but the position of the board is that the regulation has to be clear and specific as to date and measurable. The Board of State and Community Corrections has the responsibility to inspect our local facilities for compliance with the regulations. And the issue here is that on a going forward basis, we need to be able to say, as of this date, no additional facilities can do this, and some of the discussion that you were in with the previous panel focused on, well, why is there this issue of grandfathering a number of facilities? And the difficult legal issue, from the Board's perspective, is that until the rule is changed, the elevation of the rule was at such a spot that it required that there be visitation available, but it did not specify whether the video option could be allowed. So I realize that's one significant area of disagreement, but that's where we get into this gray area with some facilities being grandfathered and then everything else going forward would not be able to move to the video only option on sight. So, backing up for just a minute about how we got here, as you know, the Board of State and Community Corrections is responsible for regulations for the local detention facilities, and those are Title 15, Operational Regulations and Title 24, which are the Physical Plant and the Building Regulations and in the operational regulations, generally speaking, the altitude of the regulations is quite high, the Board does not direct the specific details about what policies around operations should be, and I can say that that was part of the thought process last year, this has been an emerging issue and as Lynn outlined, the Executive Steering Committee did look at the regulation on visitation, did consider adding language, which the Board did not act on, as Lynn also pointed out. But nonetheless, this issue of, generally speaking, the regulations set a minimum standards and then the local facilities, the local agencies, are responsible for promulgating the regulations in compliance with those regs. So I think I would say the good news is that as we've moved forward, collected a lot more information, understood the level of concerns, and taken the direction from the Governor in the veto message to talk with the concerned stakeholders and identify options for going forward, we've landed in a compromised space, which addresses, frankly, more detail than the Board typically puts into the regulations for local facilities, and says now there is a requirement for in-person visitation. The very short summary of what the regulation does are a couple of different features, it prohibits additional facilities, as I've emphasized, from moving to a video-only approach. It requires that all new adult detention facilities are required to provide in person visitation and any future must be constructed with sufficient space for in person visitation, and then, as mentioned, because of the significant costs and the fact that the rule was not specific as to the manner of the delivery of visitation, there, the regulation is perspective only, that gets into the grandfathering issue. As noted by the previous panel, we initially had put the draft to the Board with a provision that said the first hour of remote video visitation would be free of charge, there was some significant discussion by the Board about that last Thursday and one of the things I also wanted to mention is that Chair Linda Penner and I visited the Santa Rita Jail in Alameda County just a couple of weeks ago, you'll hear from Sheriff Ahern later, and in that example this was one of the considerations that was clearly on the Board's mind. The video visitation at the Santa Rita Jail will be exclusively supplementary, they will always have space for in-person visitation, and although I understand some of the concerns about the technology for video visitation, it seems the technology is improving. There were issues and concerns when we talked with the sponsors about connections being cut off, sometimes cameras pointing at the top of heads, we saw the setup in the Alameda County Jail and for a supplemental option, it really does look like it's technologically the State of the art, and it's only going to be a supplemental remote type service. There are some other details but for purposes of this conversation, I just want to say that the Board was concerned about the operational aspect of not charging for that first hour free, tracking of how that would work, as well as how the contracts are set up, particularly, I think, in the positive case of Alameda, that it's supplemental only. They also have a less expensive rate, from what I understand, in their contract of $9.00 for 30 minutes, the Board did decide to remove that provision about the first hour being for no charge. Just a couple of other thoughts to add here and then I'm very happy to take your questions. You've heard about the Governor's veto of Senate Bill 1157, I don't need to repeat what the prior panel walked you through. The Governor did direct the BSCC to work with stakeholders and explore ways to address these issues, Chair Linda Penner and I, and some of our colleagues, had meetings throughout November and December with the sponsor organizations, with many advocates, with the State Sheriff's Association, CSAC, Urban County Caucus, and others. And the issue of a requirement coming through a regulation that would have the local facilities responsible for something that has a cost attached to it was just something that the Board did not feel that it could do. I mean, that is certainly within the province of this legislature, but for the regulation, this issue of having a clear date and a perspective regulation seemed like the best landing spot that we could get to, with that, I'm happy to take your questions.
