With that, the Board is intent on saying that additional facilities should not be permitted to move to an exclusively video option and I realize that reasonable minds can and will differ on this, but the position of the board is that the regulation has to be clear and specific as to date and measurable. The Board of State and Community Corrections has the responsibility to inspect our local facilities for compliance with the regulations. And the issue here is that on a going forward basis, we need to be able to say, as of this date, no additional facilities can do this, and some of the discussion that you were in with the previous panel focused on, well, why is there this issue of grandfathering a number of facilities? And the difficult legal issue, from the Board's perspective, is that until the rule is changed, the elevation of the rule was at such a spot that it required that there be visitation available, but it did not specify whether the video option could be allowed. So I realize that's one significant area of disagreement, but that's where we get into this gray area with some facilities being grandfathered and then everything else going forward would not be able to move to the video only option on sight. So, backing up for just a minute about how we got here, as you know, the Board of State and Community Corrections is responsible for regulations for the local detention facilities, and those are Title 15, Operational Regulations and Title 24, which are the Physical Plant and the Building Regulations and in the operational regulations, generally speaking, the altitude of the regulations is quite high, the Board does not direct the specific details about what policies around operations should be, and I can say that that was part of the thought process last year, this has been an emerging issue and as Lynn outlined, the Executive Steering Committee did look at the regulation on visitation, did consider adding language, which the Board did not act on, as Lynn also pointed out. But nonetheless, this issue of, generally speaking, the regulations set a minimum standards and then the local facilities, the local agencies, are responsible for promulgating the regulations in compliance with those regs. So I think I would say the good news is that as we've moved forward, collected a lot more information, understood the level of concerns, and taken the direction from the Governor in the veto message to talk with the concerned stakeholders and identify options for going forward, we've landed in a compromised space, which addresses, frankly, more detail than the Board typically puts into the regulations for local facilities, and says now there is a requirement for in-person visitation. The very short summary of what the regulation does are a couple of different features, it prohibits additional facilities, as I've emphasized, from moving to a video-only approach. It requires that all new adult detention facilities are required to provide in person visitation and any future must be constructed with sufficient space for in person visitation, and then, as mentioned, because of the significant costs and the fact that the rule was not specific as to the manner of the delivery of visitation, there, the regulation is perspective only, that gets into the grandfathering issue. As noted by the previous panel, we initially had put the draft to the Board with a provision that said the first hour of remote video visitation would be free of charge, there was some significant discussion by the Board about that last Thursday and one of the things I also wanted to mention is that Chair Linda Penner and I visited the Santa Rita Jail in Alameda County just a couple of weeks ago, you'll hear from Sheriff Ahern later, and in that example this was one of the considerations that was clearly on the Board's mind. The video visitation at the Santa Rita Jail will be exclusively supplementary, they will always have space for in-person visitation, and although I understand some of the concerns about the technology for video visitation, it seems the technology is improving. There were issues and concerns when we talked with the sponsors about connections being cut off, sometimes cameras pointing at the top of heads, we saw the setup in the Alameda County Jail and for a supplemental option, it really does look like it's technologically the State of the art, and it's only going to be a supplemental remote type service. There are some other details but for purposes of this conversation, I just want to say that the Board was concerned about the operational aspect of not charging for that first hour free, tracking of how that would work, as well as how the contracts are set up, particularly, I think, in the positive case of Alameda, that it's supplemental only. They also have a less expensive rate, from what I understand, in their contract of $9.00 for 30 minutes, the Board did decide to remove that provision about the first hour being for no charge. So I wanted to say at the outset that there still is the opportunity for additional public comment on this proposed regulation and to bring you up to date about, I think there really actually has been a significant move toward what the legislature attempted to do last year in SB 1157 with this regulation and there was a particular sense of urgency for the Board to move quickly at the meeting last Thursday, so that there could be a date certain on which the regulation changes. With that, the Board is intent on saying that additional facilities should not be permitted to move to an exclusively video option and I realize that reasonable minds can and will differ on this, but the position of the board is that the regulation has to be clear and specific as to date and measurable. The Board of State and Community Corrections has the responsibility to inspect our local facilities for compliance with the regulations. And the issue here is that on a going forward basis, we need to be able to say, as of this date, no additional facilities can do this, and some of the discussion that you were in with the previous panel focused on, well, why is there this issue of grandfathering a number of facilities? And the difficult legal issue, from the Board's perspective, is that until the rule is changed, the elevation of the rule was at such a spot that it required that there be visitation available, but it did not specify whether the video option could be allowed. So I realize that's one significant area of disagreement, but that's where we get into this gray area with some facilities being grandfathered and then everything else going forward would not be able to move to the video only option on sight. So, backing up for just a minute about how we got here, as you know, the Board of State and Community Corrections is responsible for regulations for the local detention facilities, and those are Title 15, Operational Regulations and Title 24, which are the Physical Plant and the Building Regulations and in the operational regulations, generally speaking, the altitude of the regulations is quite high, the Board does not direct the specific details about what policies around operations should be, and I can say that that was part of the thought process last year, this has been an emerging issue and as Lynn outlined, the Executive Steering Committee did look at the regulation on visitation, did consider adding language, which the Board did not act on, as Lynn also pointed out. But nonetheless, this issue of, generally speaking, the regulations set a minimum standards and then the local facilities, the local agencies, are responsible for promulgating the regulations in compliance with those regs. So I think I would say the good news is that as we've moved forward, collected a lot more information, understood the level of concerns, and taken the direction from the Governor in the veto message to talk with the concerned stakeholders and identify options for going forward, we've landed in a compromised space, which addresses, frankly, more detail than the Board typically puts into the regulations for local facilities, and says now there is a requirement for in-person visitation. The very short summary of what the regulation does are a couple of different features, it prohibits additional facilities, as I've emphasized, from moving to a video-only approach. It requires that all new adult detention facilities are required to provide in person visitation and any future must be constructed with sufficient space for in person visitation, and then, as mentioned, because of the significant costs and the fact that the rule was not specific as to the manner of the delivery of visitation, there, the regulation is perspective only, that gets into the grandfathering issue. As noted by the previous panel, we initially had put the draft to the Board with a provision that said the first hour of remote video visitation would be free of charge, there was some significant discussion by the Board about that last Thursday and one of the things I also wanted to mention is that Chair Linda Penner and I visited the Santa Rita Jail in Alameda County just a couple of weeks ago, you'll hear from Sheriff Ahern later, and in that example this was one of the considerations that was clearly on the Board's mind. The video visitation at the Santa Rita Jail will be exclusively supplementary, they will always have space for in-person visitation, and although I understand some of the concerns about the technology for video visitation, it seems the technology is improving. There were issues and concerns when we talked with the sponsors about connections being cut off, sometimes cameras pointing at the top of heads, we saw the setup in the Alameda County Jail and for a supplemental option, it really does look like it's technologically the State of the art, and it's only going to be a supplemental remote type service. There are some other details but for purposes of this conversation, I just want to say that the Board was concerned about the operational aspect of not charging for that first hour free, tracking of how that would work, as well as how the contracts are set up, particularly, I think, in the positive case of Alameda, that it's supplemental only. They also have a less expensive rate, from what I understand, in their contract of $9.00 for 30 minutes, the Board did decide to remove that provision about the first hour being for no charge. Lauri Damrell: Great. Well, good morning. Committee chairs and Assembly members, my name is Lauri Damrell. And I am the second Vice Chair of the California Commission on The Status of Women and Girls. I'm also the Co-Chair of the California Pay Equity Task Force with California Labor Commissioner and Statutory Member of the Women's Commission Julie Su. The California Labor Commissioner's Office is the administrative agency that enforces the Equal Pay Act. I should also mention that I'm a partner at Orrick, Herrington, and Sutcliffe in their Employment Law Group, and regularly litigate these issues and advise employers on these issues as well. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today regarding the gender wage gap in the US and California. And specifically to provide you with an overview of the California Pay Equity Task Force's goals and objectives supporting meaningful compliance with the California Fair Pay Act, or SB 358. Authored by Senator Hannah Beth Jackson and signed into law by Governor Brown on October 7th of 2015. It's good to see Commission First Chair, First Vice Chair in Legislators' Women's Caucus Christina Garcia here. The Commission benefits every day from her leadership and passionate commitment to creating opportunities for California's women and girls. I also want to say how honored I am to be here today with the team from Secretary of Government Operations Marybel Batjer's office. I know she's spent much of her career in senior government positions while simultaneously striving for gender equity. And I know she's passionately committed to leading our state government forward on this issue as well. Despite Congress not yet passing the Paycheck Fairness Act, equal pay has emerged as an issue front and center in our national consciousness, and is gaining in momentum at the state and local levels. California, as you may know, has been a big player in this movement; enacting SB 358, the Fair Pay Act. Which is widely recognized as perhaps the most aggressive equal pay legislation in the country. Even now, as Massachusetts, New York, and Maryland follow suit with their own legislation aimed at eliminating the gender pay gap. And more recently as big city mayors are proactively working to close the gender pay gap in their communities. California continues its leadership by bringing together a multi-stakeholder Task Force that includes representatives from the public and private sectors as well as from employee and employer groups. In California the Task Force is looking for the best ways to address a pay gap that not only varies by gender, but also by ethnic and race categories. According to the Institute for Women's Policy Research, $41,486, that is the median annual pay for women of any color who hold a full-time job year round. This is 84 cents to every dollar earned by a man. For Asian women, the median is 72 cents for every dollar. For African-American women, the median is 63 cents for every dollar. And for Latinos, it's 43 cents. In addition, there are 1.75 million women heads of households in California, to your point, Ms. Eggman. Close to 500,000, or almost 30%, who have incomes that fall below the federal poverty line. The factors that contribute to the pay gap are complex and nuanced and require close attention. With the strongest pay equity legislation in the country enacted by our state, and a pay gap that has remained relatively stable. The Commission decided in January 2016 to make supporting the sound implementation of that law a priority. It was with an eye toward continuing the bipartisan work that went into the Fair Pay Act. And including employee and employer advocates, as well as government agency representatives, that we conducted an open application process. And then selected Task Force members from a distinguished group of applicants. A few short months later, the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls convened the first meeting of the California Pay Equity Task Force in late July. Since that time we've held four full Task Force meetings, and at least six publicly noticed Subcommittee meetings. Commissioner Su and I view the Task Force as a forum for bringing together diverse interests with a common goal of proactive compliance. And we believe that to move the needle forward, it's crucial for those impacted to collaborate. Our work challenges the assumption that employees and employers are on the opposite sides of this issue. Whether you're a business looking to reach the top of the Fortune 500, a Silicon Valley tech leader, or an employee working or looking for a job. We all want to see the gender pay gap close once and for all. Collaboration is already fostering deeper understanding of the challenges faced by all stakeholders. By convening enforcement agencies, employers, and employees, as well as their advocates. Research experts, labor economists, and human resource practitioners. The Task Force is creating practical, thorough, and widely applicable guidelines for proactive compliance. We find that employees need guidance to make informed choices about their careers. And employers need guidance to create workplace policies and procedures that promote gender pay equity and compliance with the Fair Pay Act. We are developing tools to assist all stakeholders in this effort. We brought for you today a draft of our interim report which will be released on April 4th, 2017, which is Equal Pay Day. It provides a summary of our work so far and what we aim to accomplish in 2017. We are creating tool kits for employers, employees, and employer organizations. Some highlights include our work to define legal concepts in the Fair Pay Act. Such as the term substantially similar work which is different than the previous term equal pay for equal work. Which data employers should maintain about employee wages, how to analyze that data and how to remedy pay gaps that they find. The toolkits for employers will be tailored for small and large employers to accommodate differences in budgets, staff sizes, and available resources, such as Human Resource Departments. For employees, we will offer guidance about how to file a claim, where to go, and what to consider when looking for a job. And for employee organizations, we will provide sample contract language and information requests. Finally, our primary goals in 2017 are to bring all of the pieces together in one place on the web, to convene business leaders, to discuss guidelines, inform employees about equal pay protections and their rights under the law through outreach, and prepare a plan for ongoing future guidance. Our task force is confident that the results of our collaborative efforts will provide well drawn roadmaps for effective implementation of the Fair Pay Act, while simultaneously demonstrating successful approaches for government enforcement, transparency, and collaboration. Thank you, and I'm happy to answer any questions you have.

Lauri Damrell: Great. Well, good morning. Committee chairs and Assembly members, my name is Lauri Damrell. And I am the second Vice Chair of the California Commission on The Status of Women and Girls. I'm also the Co-Chair of the California Pay Equity Task Force with California Labor Commissioner and Statutory Member of the Women's Commission Julie Su. The California Labor Commissioner's Office is the administrative agency that enforces the Equal Pay Act. I should also mention that I'm a partner at Orrick, Herrington, and Sutcliffe in their Employment Law Group, and regularly litigate these issues and advise employers on these issues as well. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today regarding the gender wage gap in the US and California. And specifically to provide you with an overview of the California Pay Equity Task Force's goals and objectives supporting meaningful compliance with the California Fair Pay Act, or SB 358. Authored by Senator Hannah Beth Jackson and signed into law by Governor Brown on October 7th of 2015. It's good to see Commission First Chair, First Vice Chair in Legislators' Women's Caucus Christina Garcia here. The Commission benefits every day from her leadership and passionate commitment to creating opportunities for California's women and girls. I also want to say how honored I am to be here today with the team from Secretary of Government Operations Marybel Batjer's office. I know she's spent much of her career in senior government positions while simultaneously striving for gender equity. And I know she's passionately committed to leading our state government forward on this issue as well. Despite Congress not yet passing the Paycheck Fairness Act, equal pay has emerged as an issue front and center in our national consciousness, and is gaining in momentum at the state and local levels. California, as you may know, has been a big player in this movement; enacting SB 358, the Fair Pay Act. Which is widely recognized as perhaps the most aggressive equal pay legislation in the country. Even now, as Massachusetts, New York, and Maryland follow suit with their own legislation aimed at eliminating the gender pay gap. And more recently as big city mayors are proactively working to close the gender pay gap in their communities. California continues its leadership by bringing together a multi-stakeholder Task Force that includes representatives from the public and private sectors as well as from employee and employer groups. In California the Task Force is looking for the best ways to address a pay gap that not only varies by gender, but also by ethnic and race categories. According to the Institute for Women's Policy Research, $41,486, that is the median annual pay for women of any color who hold a full-time job year round. This is 84 cents to every dollar earned by a man. For Asian women, the median is 72 cents for every dollar. For African-American women, the median is 63 cents for every dollar. And for Latinos, it's 43 cents. In addition, there are 1.75 million women heads of households in California, to your point, Ms. Eggman. Close to 500,000, or almost 30%, who have incomes that fall below the federal poverty line. The factors that contribute to the pay gap are complex and nuanced and require close attention. With the strongest pay equity legislation in the country enacted by our state, and a pay gap that has remained relatively stable. The Commission decided in January 2016 to make supporting the sound implementation of that law a priority. It was with an eye toward continuing the bipartisan work that went into the Fair Pay Act. And including employee and employer advocates, as well as government agency representatives, that we conducted an open application process. And then selected Task Force members from a distinguished group of applicants. A few short months later, the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls convened the first meeting of the California Pay Equity Task Force in late July. Since that time we've held four full Task Force meetings, and at least six publicly noticed Subcommittee meetings. Commissioner Su and I view the Task Force as a forum for bringing together diverse interests with a common goal of proactive compliance. And we believe that to move the needle forward, it's crucial for those impacted to collaborate. Our work challenges the assumption that employees and employers are on the opposite sides of this issue. Whether you're a business looking to reach the top of the Fortune 500, a Silicon Valley tech leader, or an employee working or looking for a job. We all want to see the gender pay gap close once and for all. Collaboration is already fostering deeper understanding of the challenges faced by all stakeholders. By convening enforcement agencies, employers, and employees, as well as their advocates. Research experts, labor economists, and human resource practitioners. The Task Force is creating practical, thorough, and widely applicable guidelines for proactive compliance. We find that employees need guidance to make informed choices about their careers. And employers need guidance to create workplace policies and procedures that promote gender pay equity and compliance with the Fair Pay Act. We are developing tools to assist all stakeholders in this effort. We brought for you today a draft of our interim report which will be released on April 4th, 2017, which is Equal Pay Day. It provides a summary of our work so far and what we aim to accomplish in 2017. We are creating tool kits for employers, employees, and employer organizations. Some highlights include our work to define legal concepts in the Fair Pay Act. Such as the term substantially similar work which is different than the previous term equal pay for equal work. Which data employers should maintain about employee wages, how to analyze that data and how to remedy pay gaps that they find. The toolkits for employers will be tailored for small and large employers to accommodate differences in budgets, staff sizes, and available resources, such as Human Resource Departments. For employees, we will offer guidance about how to file a claim, where to go, and what to consider when looking for a job. And for employee organizations, we will provide sample contract language and information requests. Finally, our primary goals in 2017 are to bring all of the pieces together in one place on the web, to convene business leaders, to discuss guidelines, inform employees about equal pay protections and their rights under the law through outreach, and prepare a plan for ongoing future guidance. Our task force is confident that the results of our collaborative efforts will provide well drawn roadmaps for effective implementation of the Fair Pay Act, while simultaneously demonstrating successful approaches for government enforcement, transparency, and collaboration. Thank you, and I'm happy to answer any questions you have.

Secretary Batjer her deepest regrets that she couldn't be here today and I know she's looking forward to meeting with all of you soon. Thank you so much for the opportunity to testify before you today on a very important subject of gender pay equity in state civil service. As you've noted, California State government, while having made significant improvements, still has a gender pay gap of 20.5%. GovOps shares your concerns that this is too high and we are working on a variety of fronts to lower this number. One of the first initiatives we tackled when the Governor operations agency was created several years ago was civil service improvement. Our state civil service is complicated, inflexible and highly bureaucratic set of rules, regulations, and policies, that had been slow to adapt to generational, and demographic changes in the work force, and to the emerging trends in the work place. We're working in concert with our partners CalHR, the State Personnel Board, the Department of Finance and the governor's office and of course our union partners, to make changes to our system that will allow California to become an employer of choice. Through the process we're also making changes that will hopefully continue to make improvements in our pay equity numbers. I want to talk about those numbers a little bit more. And then I will share in more detail about our efforts to date. First, I want to note good news in one area of state service. And that is in our career executive assignment, or CEA class. Because there are three different levels of CEAs each with a different pay range. And at the top pay scale, in the CEA level C, there are 36 more men than women. So while the gender composition of the executive workforce has gender parity. There is still work to be done to reach parity at the most senior level. To this end we have been working on the issues of unconscious bias and hiring and promoting in our supervisory training with a focus on talent management. We don't want to just train people when they start their job, but develop them throughout their career. Their perspective, duties and issues may all change and our training should speak to that. In response, we've created the California Statewide Leadership Training and Developement Program which serves as the cornerstone for developing leaders across the state. With the skills and competencies they need to succeed in a leadership position. The talent management skills to recruit, hire, train, develop, and retain a diverse and dynamic workforce. And the organizational capabilities and tools to achieve those results. At the heart of this effort, is a full order stating that our people are our greatest resource. That our workforce must be represented of Californians, and we must welcome our best and our brightest to achieve great results for the people of our state. Our leaders set the tone for creating a diverse and dynamic workforce. And our training program will provide them with the knowledge, skills, tools, to cultivate a diverse workforce and mitigate biases, conscious and unconscious. [{'start': 135, 'end': 146, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Kurt Karperos: Good morning Chairman Weickowski, Senators. I'm Kurt Karperos. I'm Deputy Executive Officer of the California Air Resources Board. To follow Professor Frank's comprehensive background in history of the Clean Air Act and its waiver and authorization provisions. I'll provide a brief overview of CARB's mandates, the state's air quality policy portfolio and a path forward. The Legislature established CARB in 1967 as the first air agency of its kind predating the EPA. Over our 50 year history, California has been at the forefront of air pollution control in the nation. Today the Legislature has tasked CARB with three key mandates. Achieving health based air quality standards for ozone particulate matter and other air pollutants under the state and federal clean air acts. Reducing public exposure to toxic air contaminants such as diesel particulate matter and reducing greenhouse gas emissions to 1990 levels by 2020. And further reductions to 40% below 1990 levels by 2020 and then 40% below 1990 levels by 2030. In my testimony today I'll focus on the work to meet federal quality standards. However it's important to note that CARB is working to develop programs simultaneously, reduce smog forming, diesel particulate and greenhouse gas emissions. The Clean Air Act directs EPA to set health based standards and review them regularly to ensure they're based on the latest science and remain health protective. This has lead EPA to set a series of increasingly stringent health protective standards over time. CARB's current plan in focus is on meeting the federal ozone standard and the annual fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 standard. California has a long and successful history of meeting these health based standards. Of the state's 19 areas, the 160 to the one hour and original eight hours on standards. Only four exceed those standards today. Still, the South Coast and the San Joaquin Valley are the two areas of the state that face the nation's most critical air quality challenges. These regions are the only two areas in the nation within extreme non attainment classification for ozone, and they also record some of the nation's highest PM 2.5 levels. However even these areas have made notable progress. The valley now meets the one hour ozone standard and is making significant progress towards attaining the eight hour ozone standard. Fine particulate pollution levels in the valley have dropped 20% since 2001. The South Cost one's majored one hour ozone values above the standard on over 200 days per year. Today it is dropped to less than 20. Similarly the number of days over the eight hour standards has been cut in half since 1990. This progress is occurred at the same time the California's population has increased by 25% and the States' economy has continued to grow and prosper. Our economy is now the world's sixth largest and job growth in the States has out paced the national rate. This while pursuing the nation's most aggressive air quality and climate policies. Looking forward, EPA estimates the new 70 parts per billion ozone standard would save Californians an estimated $0.4 to $1.4 billion per year when accounting for both the costs of reducing emissions, and the avoided costs of health care, lost work days, and low productivity, and other impacts of pollution. EPA's estimates for attaining the annual PM 2.5 standard are even more compelling, showing a net benefit in 2020 of at least $3.3 billion in California, with over 90% of the benefit coming from fewer premature deaths. With its health based standards, meaningful deadlines and requirements for comprehensive plans, the Clean Air Act, the cooperative federalism that Professor Frank described has been the key tool for achieving this combined air quality and economic success. Going forward, collective efforts involving the Legislature, air districts, environmental groups, and regulated industries will be critical to building on this success. Achieving California's multiple environmental goals will require comprehensive actions to transform the technologies and fuels we use, the design of our communities, and the way we move people and freight throughout the state. In partnership with the Legislature, these efforts will continue California's leadership role both nationally and internationally. As Professor Frank outlined, while EPA has primary authority over new engines for cars, trucks, locomotives, and some farm and construction equipment, the Clean Air Act allows California to seek a waiver from the EPA to enact more stringent standards from these large pollution sources. Many, though not all, of CARB's activities rely on existing waivers. And the future application of this authority will continue to be critical to California's continued progress towards clean air. Next month CARB will consider adoption of a mobile source strategy that outlines the coordinated suit of actions to meet federal quality standards. And at the same time achieve greenhouse emission targets, reduce petroleum consumption, decrease toxic health risks from transportation emissions. This strategy maps out a mobile source regulatory agenda to support the multiple planning efforts currently under way in response to state and federal directives. These efforts include the state implementation plan, which includes elements in the mobile source strategy necessary to meet Clean Air Act requirements and to achieve an 80% reduction in smog form in particulate emissions. The 2030 target scoping plan update charts the state's pathway to achieve the 2030 greenhouse gas reduction target in SP32. These actions will also establish a trajectory for meeting the longer term 2050 targets. The short-lived climate pollutant reduction strategy establishes the plan to reach the goals for reduction of black carbon, methane, and fluorinated gases as directed in SB604 and SB1383. And finally, the California Sustainable Freight Action Plan is a multi agency effort to improve freight efficiency, transition to zero emission technologies, and increase the competitiveness of the California's freight system. The work ahead is to implement these plans over the coming years. Since while we've accomplished a great deal already. Approximately one-third of California's 38 million residents still live in communities that exceed the Federal ozone and PM 2.5 standards. And the public's exposure to toxic diesel particular matter is too high, especially in disadvantaged communities near freight facilities such as ports, rail yards, and distribution centers. So what are the elements of a path forward? It's critical that California ensures that regulated vehicles and non-road engines and equipment are fully compliant with applicable standards from the time they are first sold and throughout their life as they are driven and operated in the state. The Volkswagen incident has highlighted the need for us to remain alert and to vigorously administer and, as needed, modify our certification and compliance programs to discover and remedy, quickly, situations that can have significant adverse air quality impacts. And while the state may not receive the same degree of collaboration in the near term, as Professor Frank explained, we anticipate that our existing waivers, those are already granted for us to enforce existing California emission standards, will not be significantly compromised. Consequently, California's current on and off-road vehicle emission regulations, which set standards many years into the future, should remain into effect. The regulatory actions and the plans I spoke of previously, namely the mobile source strategy, the state implementation plan, the scoping plan. The short lived Climate Pollutant Plan and The Sustainable Freight Action Plan will keep California on the path toward healthful air and continue to provide national and international climate leadership. The scientific, technical, and regulatory capacity of CARB and the air districts developed through decades of implementing the Clean Air Act will provide the foundation for moving forward and the clear arguments for future waivers. And partnerships with states that it can opt in to California's vehicle standards will continue to provide national support for California's actions. California's own Clean Air Act, adopted by the Legislature in 1988, became a model for amendments to the federal act in 1990. Today, the California's legislatures leadership in integrating the state's climate and air quality efforts is a path towards the future that can be copied elsewhere. Starting with a waiver authority first given in the 1967 under quality act to today's zero emission program with its growing number of ZEV's nationally and internationally, California has led the way. And we are fully committed to continuing to work with you to provide the same ongoing leadership and address our state's air quality challenges. Thank you and I'd be happy to answer any questions

Philip Fine: Thank you Chairman, Members of the Committee. My name is Philip Fine. And the importance of the federal approval of the California's Clean Air Act waivers needs to be viewed In terms of the significant air quality challenges and health challenges facing Californians and specifically the South Coast Air Basin's residents, which make up over 40% of the state's population. It would be the fifth largest state in the US if you just look within the South Coast Air Basin. And as you heard earlier, between 3 and 4000 premature deaths are caused every year by poor air quality in our basin, plus hundreds of thousands of hospital visits and lost work days and lost school days. As a local air district, we continue to do everything within our primary authority to reduce emissions from the stationary sources. But between 80 to 90% of our air quality problems come from emissions outside of our direct authority which are mobile sources. Thus, it is impossible to achieve these federal ambient clean air standards and provide healthful air to our residents without significant emissions reductions from those mobile sources. The Federal Clean Air Act gives primary jurisdiction over most of those sources to the federal government. But the waiver process has allowed California to be more aggressive to address the most significant of these mobile sources and right now the most significant of those are heavy duty trucks. California's actions under the waivers have not only achieved accelerated and necessary emission reductions in California and in South Coast, they have driven technological development for low emitting vehicles that, in turn, drive national standards that further reduce emissions within California from such sources as trucks coming in from out of state that would be subject to federal regulation. But without approval of the California waiver, the most important tool, the Clean Air Act waiver, the most important tool California has in our fight for clean air will be taken away. Our air quality management plans continue to include measures with significant emissions reductions that will require existing approval of waivers, as well as potential new federal approvals of waivers for California regulations. I do want to note though, that even with these approved waivers and state regulations, the air quality challenge is still daunting and state regulations will not be enough. We will still need actions from the federal government to reduce emissions that are solely under their control. That are not even subject to these waivers, such as trains, and planes, and ships. We recently petitioned along with many other states. We petitioned EPA to initiate rule making for a national Ultra Clean Low-Nox standard for heavy duty trucks. And they responded affirmatively, committing to begin the rule making process in the near future. We sincerely hope the EPA fulfills this commitment. As our current AQNP demonstrates, we will also need significant funding to accelerate the deployment of clean technologies in a way that cannot be be achieved quickly enough through regulatory actions alone, both for the California waiver sources as well as the federal sources. So we look forward to working with the Legislature to identify sources of funding that are not born disproportionately by Californians, especially those that can at least afford it within California. For example, our entire country benefits greatly from the goods movement through our region, but we suffer in Southern California and around our ports, the impacts to our health. Concepts such as a container fee on imports can help internalize these external costs that are not currently being properly accounted for in the price of goods in other areas of the country. I want to emphasize the air quality in the most populated areas of California is still the worst in the nation. And it is clearly unfair to expect California to achieve federal standards while further limiting the authority we have to do so. And if we don't meet those federal standards by the deadlines that are set up under the federal Clean Air Act. We are subject to federal sanctions, including the loss of billions of dollars in transportation funding. So in closing, our local and state tools for achieving federal standards are already reaching their limitations. We need to be adding tools to the toolbox, not taking them away.

Blade Oestreich: Good afternoon and thank you for holding today's hearing and listening to my testimony. My name is Blade Oestreich, I'm 24 years old. Currently I hold position as a policy assistant at California Youth Connection and also run my own business and a father of two and I'm married already. My future goals are to move up in my organization that I'm working in right now. And yeah, that's it on my intro. Today is the first time I have ever shared my experience of being placed in the juvenile justice system from kinship care. I think there are things that are different about my experience from many other foster youth but also some things in common that you have the future, the power to change. And that I hope you will take action on. I know my life has turned out well but a lot of that is because of my own advocacy and focus, and it doesn't turn out that way for most youth. I grew up in kinship care living with different relatives. I did not have a lot of support. I never really received parenting. I only saw a social worker twice over all the years that I was in kinship. My relatives only worried that I would come home by curfew, but often I didn't get support or guidance I needed. I didn't have anyone to teach me self sacrifice or self discipline. And so I started trying to fill the void with making people like me. I was eager and hungry to be liked and to prove myself as being the strongest and the best. I didn't have anyone who I felt saw me as the best. Like I do for my son today, I always support and try to get him to the place that I wasn't as a youth. I didn't have anyone who I've felt supported all my decisions. I tried to fill my emptiness with people. This resulted in behaviors that weren't normal for me and hanging out with the wrong people. Eventually, I ended up getting a year for someone else's crime. I didn't want to talk to anyone about it. And I didn't want to share the real story, I just decided to take the punishment. I felt that even if I was honest, the result would be the same. I spent six months in juvenile hall while my case was in court, and then I served an extra six months on top of that when it was finished. It was pretty scary being in juvenile hall. I would go to sleep having vivid dreams and being out and having fun with my family and siblings, waking up to the same brick wall every single day. The feeling of having nothing of your own there, not having your own clothes, not your shoes, not your underwear, toothpaste, or your food. You having to turn into a drone having to listen to all the mindless tasks all the time. I tried to make the best of my experience and sought out help. This was different from almost all the youth around me. I sought out what I needed: medic time to deal with health issues, school support so that I got teaching that matched how I learn, and individual time with staff. I was able to get what I needed but the only reason I got help was because I advocated for myself. That's not realistic for most youth. Almost all the youth around me did not have the same experience because they did not seek out anything, so they didn't get anything. Most children, even adults, can't seek this kind of help out. I'm a dad now and I wouldn't expect this from my own child. Finally at 18, I was exited to a program in an ankle bracelet. I graduated high school a month after I got out. I attended a mandatory program that provided me transportation to and from school. So I was never really alone unless I was at my house. My probation officer stereotyped me as being the same as the rest of his cases. He required me to have proof of everything I did. If I went to a job interview, I needed to get a note to prove that I was there. That was so hard because it would have let everyone know that I was on probation. I wouldn't even get that job, completely wasting my time for that interview in the first place. I am lucky because I had plenty of support from my family, they offered me forgiveness and understanding, they helped me get a job and what I needed, many youth do not have this type of support. While my situation turned out well, it could have been, this support could have been offered before I went to juvenile home and would have prevented me from ever going. Here are some ideas I hope you will take action on for other youth. Number one, when it comes to our foster youth and teens in general, the only way to combat the problem is to stop using law enforcement and juvenile hall as the first step. Too often when a problem with a youth happens, that's the only way the system response. But, most of the time when someone is acting out, they want attention, social workers need to take extra steps to make sure the youth are not locked away. Number two, the youth need the support before there is contact with juvenile justice system. I only got support after. Social workers and teachers need to understand youth stories, understand how their different experiences can impact behavior and give support to ones who need it before there's a problem. Number three, programs need to be in place to support extracurricular activities and healthy friendships for youth. Like many youth, I tried to fill my emptiness with the wrong people because I didn't have the activities and healthy friendships. Not everyone gets the support they need from a parent and so they look for it. Funding should be provided to support extra activities at school and policies should support youth participating in social activities and places to find healthy relationships. It is so important to be able to meet youth who have been in the same situation to build and find support with. Experiences like participating in the California Youth Connection can support youth so they don't have to teach the rights and wrongs of the world to themselves. Number four, where youth lives matters. Some group homes and staff are just clocking in and out. They are paid very little and care very little. Those staff are the ones that will place the immediate call to the police and give seven days notice to a youth. They are getting paid minimum wage to sit eight hours, so their care is not there. If they got training, it might not be this way. Families would care and spend more time. There's going to be substantially more care and more thought put into the youth in the family that are not supported by staff. But they have to be families that want to be family, not just getting by. Number five, running away should never be disciplined and result in police being called and youth going to juvenile hall. Running away is really an opportunity to train families and social workers about responding appropriately rather than sending to juvenile hall. The reasons youth run away need to be dealt with. When youth run away they have to survive, survival is going to land them in juvenile hall. Thank you for listening to my ideas today. My experience turned out good, but it is not the case for 90% of other youths who cross over. But if you take action by creating new policy that stops juvenile hall from being used as a first stop, providing new funding for normal activities and programs that support healthy relationships and making sure youth are treated differently by professionals. Then the youth experiences will end differently and more positively too.

Blade Oestreich: Good afternoon and thank you for holding today's hearing and listening to my testimony. My name is Blade Oestreich, I'm 24 years old. Currently I hold position as a policy assistant at California Youth Connection and also run my own business and a father of two and I'm married already. My future goals are to move up in my organization that I'm working in right now. And yeah, that's it on my intro. Today is the first time I have ever shared my experience of being placed in the juvenile justice system from kinship care. I think there are things that are different about my experience from many other foster youth but also some things in common that you have the future, the power to change. And that I hope you will take action on. I know my life has turned out well but a lot of that is because of my own advocacy and focus, and it doesn't turn out that way for most youth. I grew up in kinship care living with different relatives. I did not have a lot of support. I never really received parenting. I only saw a social worker twice over all the years that I was in kinship. My relatives only worried that I would come home by curfew, but often I didn't get support or guidance I needed. I didn't have anyone to teach me self sacrifice or self discipline. And so I started trying to fill the void with making people like me. I was eager and hungry to be liked and to prove myself as being the strongest and the best. I didn't have anyone who I felt saw me as the best. Like I do for my son today, I always support and try to get him to the place that I wasn't as a youth. I didn't have anyone who I've felt supported all my decisions. I tried to fill my emptiness with people. This resulted in behaviors that weren't normal for me and hanging out with the wrong people. Eventually, I ended up getting a year for someone else's crime. I didn't want to talk to anyone about it. And I didn't want to share the real story, I just decided to take the punishment. I felt that even if I was honest, the result would be the same. I spent six months in juvenile hall while my case was in court, and then I served an extra six months on top of that when it was finished. It was pretty scary being in juvenile hall. I would go to sleep having vivid dreams and being out and having fun with my family and siblings, waking up to the same brick wall every single day. The feeling of having nothing of your own there, not having your own clothes, not your shoes, not your underwear, toothpaste, or your food. You having to turn into a drone having to listen to all the mindless tasks all the time. I tried to make the best of my experience and sought out help. This was different from almost all the youth around me. I sought out what I needed: medic time to deal with health issues, school support so that I got teaching that matched how I learn, and individual time with staff. I was able to get what I needed but the only reason I got help was because I advocated for myself. That's not realistic for most youth. Almost all the youth around me did not have the same experience because they did not seek out anything, so they didn't get anything. Most children, even adults, can't seek this kind of help out. I'm a dad now and I wouldn't expect this from my own child. Finally at 18, I was exited to a program in an ankle bracelet. I graduated high school a month after I got out. I attended a mandatory program that provided me transportation to and from school. So I was never really alone unless I was at my house. My probation officer stereotyped me as being the same as the rest of his cases. He required me to have proof of everything I did. If I went to a job interview, I needed to get a note to prove that I was there. That was so hard because it would have let everyone know that I was on probation. I wouldn't even get that job, completely wasting my time for that interview in the first place. I am lucky because I had plenty of support from my family, they offered me forgiveness and understanding, they helped me get a job and what I needed, many youth do not have this type of support. While my situation turned out well, it could have been, this support could have been offered before I went to juvenile home and would have prevented me from ever going. Here are some ideas I hope you will take action on for other youth. Number one, when it comes to our foster youth and teens in general, the only way to combat the problem is to stop using law enforcement and juvenile hall as the first step. Too often when a problem with a youth happens, that's the only way the system response. But, most of the time when someone is acting out, they want attention, social workers need to take extra steps to make sure the youth are not locked away. Number two, the youth need the support before there is contact with juvenile justice system. I only got support after. Social workers and teachers need to understand youth stories, understand how their different experiences can impact behavior and give support to ones who need it before there's a problem. Number three, programs need to be in place to support extracurricular activities and healthy friendships for youth. Like many youth, I tried to fill my emptiness with the wrong people because I didn't have the activities and healthy friendships. Not everyone gets the support they need from a parent and so they look for it. Funding should be provided to support extra activities at school and policies should support youth participating in social activities and places to find healthy relationships. It is so important to be able to meet youth who have been in the same situation to build and find support with. Experiences like participating in the California Youth Connection can support youth so they don't have to teach the rights and wrongs of the world to themselves. Number four, where youth lives matters. Some group homes and staff are just clocking in and out. They are paid very little and care very little. Those staff are the ones that will place the immediate call to the police and give seven days notice to a youth. They are getting paid minimum wage to sit eight hours, so their care is not there. If they got training, it might not be this way. Families would care and spend more time. There's going to be substantially more care and more thought put into the youth in the family that are not supported by staff. But they have to be families that want to be family, not just getting by. Number five, running away should never be disciplined and result in police being called and youth going to juvenile hall. Running away is really an opportunity to train families and social workers about responding appropriately rather than sending to juvenile hall. The reasons youth run away need to be dealt with. When youth run away they have to survive, survival is going to land them in juvenile hall. Thank you for listening to my ideas today. My experience turned out good, but it is not the case for 90% of other youths who cross over. But if you take action by creating new policy that stops juvenile hall from being used as a first stop, providing new funding for normal activities and programs that support healthy relationships and making sure youth are treated differently by professionals. Then the youth experiences will end differently and more positively too.

Daina Lujan: All right, thank you. Thank you for this opportunity. My name is Daina Lujan. To give you a sense of who I am, I am Vice President of the South San Francisco Unified School District, Board of Trustees and currently, principal of Meadows Elementary in Millbrae. I taught for eight years and am currently in my, sixth year of administration. My goal today is to provide a local perspective on the impact of the teacher shortage and strategic responses. As a touch on responses, I'd like to talk about both the district-level response as well as a county-level response. The county-level response I will share today is unique to San Mateo County. Because this is the only place we've really had the opportunity to launch our work, but our work is scalable and replicable. So what does the teacher shortage look like on a school site? I am a principal of a TK through fifth grade elementary school with 435 students. In the 15, 16 school year we were awarded the Gold Ribbon Award. I was lucky and I opened this current school year, 16-17 fully staffed but barely. I have an intern teaching my moderate severe class of students. This class includes non-verbal students who have autism, gross and fine motor delays or traumatic brain injuries. They can not communicate verbally, so they communicate with behaviors. Starting the year with an intern means that she teaches all day, she oversees three aides all day, and then takes classes at night and on weekends. I opened the year with this intern in place and three brand new aides because paraprofessionals are also in great need. And students responded to the change in the only way they could, with big behaviors. They began running a lot. So I spent two months running after students, trying to keep them from getting into the street. And run over by a car or getting lost in a neighborhood and having no way to advocate for themselves. When I am running after students to keep them safe, I do not care about their learning goals, my biggest concern is their safety. And for this group of students, that's tragic. Because they can and should be productive, engaged members of society in the future. But their learning goals are the least of my concerns when I'm trying to keep them safe. To ensure that I open the school year fully staffed, the Millbrae School District employed several strategies to help minimize the impacts of the teacher shortage. We determined hiring needs early. We began recruiting early and we had partnerships with local universities. Beyond this, we also offer pay incentive in the form of an annual stipend to our special education teachers and and we have capped their classes. So my mod-severe teacher can have no more than 10 students. District level responses, such as recruiting early and providing pay incentives, as recommended by Learning Policy Institute are quite effective in ensuring individual district opens the school year fully staffed. But, they do nothing for our neighboring district down the road because the underlying supply and demand problem has not been addressed. In San Mateo county, where I work, this is a serious challenge. There are 23 school districts all competing for the same pool of teachers who serve over 94,000 students. So at this juncture I'd like to shift the perspective just a little bit and talk about some of our county level responses. Under the leadership of county Superintendent Ann Campbell the San Mateo County Office of Education has organized a work group to analyze Data. Identify causes of the shortage and outline strategic plans and has taken actions to assist with attracting, training, retaining and sustaining teachers. Representatives include administration from the county office events, San Francisco State University, Notre Dame De Namur University, local school districts and our community college district. Our work group has looked beyond district level responses that make one district seem more appealing than another and considered one how do we address immediate needs. And two, how can we build a sustainable pipeline to ensure every school opens fully staffed? This second question of how do we build a sustainable pipeline is of critical importance. Because looking beyond times of crisis when there are no shortages, as a county we know that there's always a relative need for teachers. For those who are retiring, who leave the profession because it truly is not a good fit, or who have have a life change. So naturally we have 7% attrition no matter what. So in looking to how do we address immediate needs, members of our work group pursued the classified employee credential program grant and the four year BA plus credential planning grant. The San Mateo County Office of Education was successful in earning a classified employee credential grant for 50 candidates a year. San Francisco State earned two planning BA plus credential grants, and Notre Dame De Namur earned one BA plus credential planning grant. These wins have been instrumental in working to address some of our immediate needs. But there's still a crisis ahead. So, and looking at how do we address longer term needs and another key accomplishment of the county work group over the past several months includes building a pilot pathway project within local high schools to attract students to future careers in teaching. We began looking at high schools because some key data points struck our group. According to data from the Learning Policy Institute, 60% of teachers work within 15 miles of where they went to high school. If we look to San Mateo County, there are 6,000 high school seniors at this moment in time. County education is provided by 4,700 teachers, and if we count for 7% attrition, we need about 300 teachers annually. So, if I look at my 6,000 high school seniors, I need 300 of them, or 5% to become teachers. So, to built a pilot pathway we have partnered with Project Tomorrow, an organization in Southern California that oversees educators rising and Youth Teach to Learn. Youth Teach to Learn provides a high school curriculum for a two part course designed to get students familiar with the basic of learning theory as well as quality lesson design in the areas of math and science. We have supported community colleges and local high school districts with engaging in conversations about articulation agreements. And we have supported the high schools with taking the Youth Teach to Learn program and building a career technical education pathway in the education sector. As I wrap up, I would like to state that yes, we as a state have faced a teacher shortage before. When class size reduction was instituted, we faced massive shortages of multiple subject credential candidates. Some of the solutions of the past are of significant importance once again, but I must also express that today's shortage is slightly different and more critical. Today we face critical needs in specialized areas. Additionally, where I work, few districts, if any, still implement class size reduction. If anything, class sizes has certainly increased. So as we look to the future we want for our students, we must draw upon lessons from the past, such as loan forgiveness. But we must also dream big, and think strategically for our students. Building a sustainable teacher pipeline that attracts, trains, retains, and sustains teachers is a long term and permanent endeavor. Every year, we must start to develop the next cadre of teachers who will replace those retiring or who are leaving the profession for other reasons. This is a necessary step to ensure all children of California have access to dynamic, dedicated, valued and highly trained educators throughout their educational experience, thank you.

Our work group has looked beyond district level responses that make one district seem more appealing than another and considered one how do we address immediate needs. And two, how can we build a sustainable pipeline to ensure every school opens fully staffed? This second question of how do we build a sustainable pipeline is of critical importance. Because looking beyond times of crisis when there are no shortages, as a county we know that there's always a relative need for teachers. For those who are retiring, who leave the profession because it truly is not a good fit, or who have have a life change. So naturally we have 7% attrition no matter what. So in looking to how do we address immediate needs, members of our work group pursued the classified employee credential program grant and the four year BA plus credential planning grant. The San Mateo County Office of Education was successful in earning a classified employee credential grant for 50 candidates a year. Youth Teach to Learn provides a high school curriculum for a two part course designed to get students familiar with the basic of learning theory as well as quality lesson design in the areas of math and science. And I still get to do that. I think one of my favorite experiences recently was when I was working with my high school student doing some math work. My middle schooler came and asked for help, and then my college student calls me on the phone, and three boys in one night all ask for math help, and I love that, that's an experience that I love. So, let me tell you a little bit about how I got to teaching. So, after working in tech and enjoying that after school type of activity, I actually attended a training program where I learned about living life powerfully and living a life I love. And I really started to think about what I was doing every day and as my wife puts it, I didn't have a mid-life crisis about having a new car or another pretty woman, it was about my career, and that's where it started. I actually took some time off from work, was involved with an organization called ProMatch, which is part of Experience Unlimited, to help people who are professionally looking for work after having been out of work, and I also, at this time, heard about something called the Encore Teacher Program, which helps people to consider what education would be like after having worked In high technology. Specifically, in the STEM areas, specifically at high-needs schools. Though I was involved in investigating teaching a little bit, I was, bluntly, very scared. I think as we get older sometimes we, or at least for me personally, the older I got, the more scared I was of changing things, and I saw that in a lot of my colleagues, they kept pining for retirement and they're saying, this is what I want to do in 10 years when I retire and I'm thinking to myself, why are you waiting? Why in the world are you waiting to retire? So, I finished my last tech job in 2010 and when I walked out of the door, I knew I would never work in technology again, and I was going to be a teacher, and there are whole bunch of things you have to consider when you go into teaching because I left a job that was paying me about $110,000 a year to look into a job that was going to pay me maybe a little more than half that, and my wife needed go back to work. Now she's an elementary school teacher, so trust me, I've had teaching around my house for a long time. I got to retain my 401K, but I had to give up the possibility of Social Security. Because the way things work, I pay in to CalSTRS, I don't pay into Social Security anymore. So likely I'll never see anything, and the money that I put into Social Security while I was working in high-tech, but I also kept reflecting back on living life powerfully and living a life that I love, and I was reflecting on my work-life balance, my own personal happiness, as well as happiness of my family, and I wanted to set an example for my sons, an example of the difference between having a capability and being passionate about what you do everyday. So my family laughs at me because I leap out of bed at 5:30 in the morning so excited to go to the classroom, it's not even funny. I went through a program where I substituted, I had a sub permit within three weeks from leaving my last tech job. I told lots of people that I wanted to go into teaching, and they were all very supportive. A superintendent, who happened to be a classmate of mine from high school, says, go in, tell them you want to be a sub and we will get you on the sub list, and I was substituting K to 12, I was substituting in special day classes. I was substituting in Catholic schools, and when they had math lessons to teach, I said, please leave me a math lesson. I want to teach math, and they gave me that opportunity. I took subject matter tests, I was a tutor in a high school tutorial center, and I started investigating credential programs. One thing important to me and it's been mentioned today, is I needed income while I was going to school, and fortunately I was accepted into the San Jose State Intern Credential Program, where I was able to prepare, over a summer, not a lot of preparation, but it was some preparation to at least get ready to enter the classroom. There were no openings though I applied in 2011 to go into the classroom. Until I get a phone call from the Fremont Union High School District in November and they said, we need somebody to come in and teach math and by the way there might be some engineering involved, a-ha. So, at this time I also applied to the EnCorps Teacher Program, where I started to get some professional development in the teaching realm. In addition to getting the professional development in the classroom at San Jose State, I started getting professional development from EnCorps, and then, two 20 minute interviews later, I had a job as a math teacher at Fremont High School in Sunnyvale. After having spent 6 hours going through interviews in high tech, I couldn't believe two 20 minute interviews was all I needed, but that's where we started. The supports I got after that were unbelievable. First and foremost the people I have to always thank are my wife and my sons, I could not do what I do today if it were not for the support that they provide me every single day, but, of course, I got huge supports in my school district. You've heard about professional learning communities today, my peers collaborate. We really collaborate. They share and they share and they share, and they're like, do you need some help with this, how can I help you. That is the culture at our school and there was a question earlier about, how do we get that ingrained? It's culture. It's something that the school has to own. It's something that everybody at that school owns. It's not something that somebody forces down, top-down. It's something that we all agree, we would be a better community if we all contributed, and, I guess one thing that I want to leave with you as well today, is that I was growing up, I thought I was suppose to teach my sons. That's what I thought I was supposed to do as a parent. I had no idea what they were going to teach me, and I experience exactly the same thing in the classroom. So, it's truly a teaching learning environment for me in the school classroom. After teaching for 6 months, 1 semester in Fremont High School, the district spent $2,500 to send me to a training class so I could teach Project Lead Engineering at our school, and since that time when I started teaching one Project Lead The Way class, we now have five courses. Three different types of classes with five different sections so our students can experience what an engineer does. Now in my district, Fremont's a unique school. We are a high needs school, 42% Hispanic, but in the district that you go, wait a minute, this district isn't high needs. We have four other comprehensive high schools that have a very different population. So most of the kids at Fremont don't know what an engineer does. Unless they think it's somebody who drives the train down the tracks. So our kids get an opportunity to see what an engineer does, and they get to see this distinction, either I love engineering, I want to do more of it, or ew, that's engineering, I don't want to have anything to do with it. And both of those things are phenomenal for our students. I've been given a mentor from my district while I was an intern. I taught for a year and a half under an intern credential and then, once I finished that, I got an intern to help me continue on to help me clear my credential. So those supports have been tremendous. I've continued to be part of the EnCorp teacher education program where I get additional professional development. So, there are opportunities out there to grow and develop. And with in my school itself, we continue to do things as teacher led activities, as well as activities that the district say's hey, this would be a neat thing that we need to put into place across the district. So, I just want to thank you very much for your time today. I wanted to just leave you with just a little bit of this story of how I got into teaching, and how I'm just so thankful that I found something that I'm passionate about and I get to do every day. It is a privilege and it is so much more fun to teach than it is to go to work. I can't begin to tell you.

A study by the FBI shows that analyzed 160 active shooter incidents and found only one successful armed civilian intervention, and that civilian was a highly trained US Marine. Researchers at Everytown analyzed 113 shootings at elementary, middle, and high schools since 2013, and of those shootings, one in 10 was unintentional. And more than one in six began as a verbal altercation that escalated because of the presence of a gun. So, introducing guns in schools increases the potential for such tragedies. So in short, arming teachers is unnecessary, ineffective and in fact, dangerous. For those reasons, Everytown urges the Committee to approve AB 424 and keep guns out of California schools.

This is what the author of the bill testified in both houses of this Legislature. So this bill, there is no loophole here. A loophole is something that was unforeseen or inadvertant or something like that. This was totally foreseen with the intention of giving school administrators the responsibility of deciding whether this was proper for them. Now, we're talking about school districts in Los Angeles County, and San Diego County, San Francisco. But we're also talking about school districts in Kern County and Shasta County and Sierra County where the cultures are very different and even police response is vastly different than it is in your greater urban areas. And the administrators were given this option to consider this if it was something that they wanted to do. They had storage requirements where no one, none of the facility, people the teachers, or anybody knew where these firearms were, they were secured. Only the administrator and the person that was selected. We are opposed to the bill. First of all, I want to thank both the authors' office, the sponsor, and others that we've for engaging in conversations with us over the last couple of weeks on this bill. Let me just clarify our position. We are opposed primarily because I think the resolution that's being offered that they're solving some sort of problem is actually a little bit more complicated. And I think it maybe well intentioned, but I think that the Johnson case actually makes this more complicated and it's really unclear what the effect of this amendment will be to current law. And here is why we talk about identifiable in the kind of common understanding what that word means but in the Johnson case it made it very clear that it is not clear what identifiable means. I think in the Johnson case they looked at a number of different things, is it that the individual can be identified by the photo itself, can the individual be identified by other means, the photo, in combination with other evidence? It kind of opened up the door and made it less clear what Identifiable actually means. By removing identifiable we're creating a legislative history that all of those questions are out the door. If you read the case with this change. What happens? We have a situation where the individual doesn't need to be identified by the photo, doesn't need to be identified by other potentially, by any other evidence. We're left in a situation where, is it possible to prosecute someone and I'm not talking about fitting rooms, I'm talking about mainly in someone's house, or someone's bedroom which is covered by this bill. Where photos are found and law enforcement decides to prosecute someone even though the photos don't identify who the person is, they may not have other evidence of who the person is, they may just say, well from the cameras we found and from the photos we found, it appears as if there was no consent. And this may sound like me just being extreme, but the reality is in the Johnson case that's in fact what happened with some of the prosecutions. There were Jane Does that were listed as victims. They were never identified in how we talk about it. I think the bottom line for us is this, if the concern is that there should not be a requirement, that the photo identify the individual, then that's what the bill should state. By simply removing the term, identifiable, it opens up the door for many interpretations. It may cover what the intent is of the bill, but it may cover a lot more. And I think it's going to be, worse for everyone because we want to make sure we want to deal with this. It is a crime now, this is not creating a new crime. It's just simply making clear. Let me just close by raising kind of specific examples, talking to some of the attorneys down the state. There have been cases where someone's home search for a number of for a warrant for other reasons and they find photographs taken in someone's bedroom. This bill will cover bedroom as I understand it. And the photos themselves, there was a dispute of whether those photos were taken with consent, whether those photos what they covered, and the individuals who own the home claim that he and partners would engage in photographs and videos during their intimate time. And there was a dispute as to who was in the photo. He claimed it was someone who consented. Law enforcement thought well, the way that the camera was put and hidden away that they wouldn't be able to consent. And that it might not be that person they identified, it may be be someone else. That's problematic, because we need to be very clear what we're doing with this bill. I'm happy to work with the Committee and the author going forward to really specify what they're trying to accomplish. because we think this may be simple on its face, but it makes the law much more complicated and unclear.
