Cathy Sure: Good morning. Cathy Sure on behalf of the ACLU of California and I want to start out by stating that we are not anti-dog. Our concern with AB 411 is with the standard it sets for the court in deciding whether to allow use of a dog in a particular case. Under AB 411, the court would be mandated to permit use of the dog once the party making the request has shown that the dog and handler are suitably qualified and will reasonably assist the testifying witness. A judge with concerns in a particular case as to potential prejudice to a defendant could not deny the motion for use of the dog for that reason the way we read the bill as it is currently drafted. Or for that matter for other reasons such as somebody in the courtroom who is allergic to dogs or any other concern the judge might have about the dog in that particular case. I want to note that the court of appeals in the Chaneux case, I am not sure how to pronounce it, cited in the analysis did not find the trial court required to allow use of the dog once a showing had been made that the dog would assist the witness in providing truthful and complete testimony but only that the trial court was within its discretion in doing so. The opinion expressly states that in the event the trial court finds that the prejudice to the defendant can not be eliminated or at least reduced to a level that does not infringe on the defendant's constitutional rights to a fair trial and to confront witnesses. The court generally should exercise its discretion by denying the request for presence of a support dog. We believe that, that standard which requires the trial court in each case to consider not only whether the dog is suitably trained, and whether it will be helpful to the witness. But also, the questions of in a particular case, is there a way to minimize any prejudice to the defendant should be part of this bill. We appreciate the willingness that the author and sponsor have shown to work with us on our concerns. But in its current form, because it does not require a consideration of potential prejudice, we must respectfully oppose.

Caliph Assagai: Good morning, Mr. Chair and members. Caliph Assagai on behalf of the California Public Defenders Association. First, I want to thank the witnesses for their testimony. I know it's difficult to come here and tell your story, and so we appreciate that. But I am here in respectful opposition of this measure on behalf of 3000 public defenders and private council who represent indigent defendants and criminal defendants throughout the State of California. It is our belief that this bill is inconsistent with the intent of the voters who overwhelmingly passed the ballot initiative, Prop 47. And that it will add when already disproportion number of racial minorities, whose DNA has been collected and added to the DNA database. As I believe you are aware, a number of studies have shown that despite the fact that people of color, particularly, African-Americans and Latinos, are far from more likely, excuse me, do not commit crime at any higher rate than white individuals, they are far more likely to be arrested and prosecuted for alleged criminal activity. Rates at which African Americans were arrested for violent offences and for drug offenses and for drug offenses were each approximately 3.5 times the rate of whites were arrested for those categories of offenses. Because people of color are arrested and prosecuted at higher rates than whites, people of color are disproportionately included in the DNA database. While some believe that if one is law abiding, there should be no real concern over having one's DNA in the DNA database, this is however patently incorrect. Existing DNA technology permits laboratories to obtain DNA results from samples that contain as few as 10 cells. And more importantly, from DNA that was left on items years before it was collected and analyzed. The type of crime in which DNA evidence is being collected is ever expanding. And now includes property crimes, such as, auto burglaries where a DNA profile emanates from skin cells left on an item of evidence at an unknown point in time. In other words, DNA evidence is no longer collected only from items from which it can be clearly established, that there is an association between the evidence and the crime being investigated. Increasingly, Items of evidence are being collected and analyzed from property found at the crime scene where the relationship between the evidence and the crime is not always entirely clear. Additionally it is no longer the case that only a single source complete DNA profiles are uploaded and searched against the database. Today law enforcement may request a search of inferred DNA profile that may be partial or incomplete. Such a search may result in more than one hit, or candidate, which may potentially result in the identification of an individual who is innocent of a crime being investigated or a crime lab analyst may fill in gaps of evidence and submit it for upload to the database. Consequently, when a DNA profile hits a profile in the DNA database, it is far from certain that the DNA match will identify the perpetrator of a crime. Nevertheless, that person will come under scrutiny by law enforcement, will frequently be considered a suspect, and will often be questioned and subjected to criminal investigation. This can be extremely traumatic for an individual who is innocent of a crime being charged or investigated and particularly for those who was included in the database for a non-violent drug or theft offense years prior and who has subsequently turned their life around, now to be considered a suspect in a serious criminal case. Because this will happen in a disproportionate way to minority populations, and will cause undue hardship and stress to individuals who are innocent of crimes, we urge your no vote when this bill comes up for consideration.

Alissa Anderson: Good afternoon, Mr. Chairman and members of the Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today about the importance of strengthening the CalEITC. My name is Alissa Anderson, and I'm a senior policy analyst with the California Budget and Policy Center. I want to point out from the outset that we're not an advocacy organization. We don't tend to take positions on policies and so we don't have a position on this particular bill. But I'm testifying because generally, we think it's a good idea to expand the CalEITC. And that's because State Earned Income Tax Credits can enhance the well documented benefits of the Federal Earned Income Tax Credit which is a proven tool for building economic security and opportunity. Extensive research shows that this tax credit has benefits for families and children, and I've submitted to the Committee a summary of this research for your reference. I think what's most striking about this research, is that it shows that the benefits of the EITC go well beyond just helping families get by day to day. They may actually extend into the next generation, helping to create a brighter future for children. So for example, several studies have linked the EITC to improved health for mothers and babies, including to higher birth weight for infants which as you may know, is a key predictor of children's future health, as well as their economic well-being as adults. The EITC has also been linked to better school achievement, like higher test scores and to greater educational attainment. So for example, children in families who receive larger earned income tax credits are more likely to graduate from high school and attend college and because of their greater school success, these children may even earn more when they grow up. So for example studies find that because of their greater school success, I'm sorry, because of modest increases in their families incomes. I'm sorry, let me start over. Studies find that modest increases to low income families' incomes, regardless of the source, can lead to increased earnings when they grow up. So one study found that when their families receive $3,000 in additional income, when children were very young, those children went on to earn 17% more as adults. So essentially what this shows is that boosting low income families' incomes today could have a lasting impact on children well into the future. So I think all of this evidence strongly supports expanding our new version of this state EITC, because it would allow more families to reap these well-documented benefits of the federal credit. Thank you very much.

Julie Hall-Panameno: Okay. Hello, I'm Julie Hall-Panameno, LAUSD's Equity and Title IX officer just to keep it short. Thank you for giving us the opportunity to speak here today. Today you're going to hear opposition to AB 23 purporting it is against the law. Authorities authorizes single gender instruction based on differing learning styles or stereotypes of males and females is based on faulty science. And it would result in potential harm to LGBTQ youth and open the doors to segregation. These statements are false for the following reasons. First, California and LAUSD are the model of progressive LGBTQ policies and law. And I'd especially like to share with you today that we published our first all gender restroom policy just this month. AB 23 will not allow programs to skirt nondiscrimination protections or discriminate on the basis of actual, perceived sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression. Further, the bill will not be proposing the single gender instruction be allowed on the basis of different learning styles or stereotypes. Instead it proposes the single gender instruction be allowed in narrow circumstances as espoused by Title IX which has been in effect for 45 years. Committee amendments make clear these programs will need to relate to an important governmental objective of improving educational achievement of its students through an overall established policy to provide diverse educational opportunities or to meet the particular identified educational needs of its students and in either case when the single gender nature of the program is substantially related to achieving that objective. Lastly, the Department of Education previously advised, when it outlined suggested research standards in this area, that meta analysis is contraindicated. Studies often have varying criteria, number of studies, and issues with statistical controls such as ruling out the very voluntary nature of the many programs identified or studied. There are legal, practical, and ethical implications in attempting to create randomized treatment and control groupings to develop quality studies. Thus, research in this field is undebatedly mixed. However, it's unrefuted that females are under-represented in fields such as science, technology, engineering, and math and that programs that are inclusive of females and exposure to like role models are beneficial. Again, AB 23 seeks to align state with federal law, which allows this narrow exception to single sex education, and does not allow for discrimination, thank you.

Melissa Goodman: Sure. Hello. I'm Melissa Goodman on behalf of the ACLU. This is simply a school choice that the California Constitution does not allow. The California Constitution prohibits separating and excluding students from public education programs because of their gender. Creating schools that are tailored to boys or girls based on debunked science and stereotypes about how typical girls and boys learn violates state law and federal law. This bill seeks to align California with Title IX but it ignores that our state constitution is actually far stricter than Title IX, as well as the federal constitution. It's presumptively suspect and unconstitutional to exclude students from educational opportunity because of their gender, just as it is for race. Prop 209, in addition, flatly prohibits treating students differently or giving them any preferential treatment based on gender even if it's meant to help them. The U.S Supreme Court struck down a single gender public college under a less strict constitutional standard than California's. Separating students by gender won't meet constitutional scrutiny. Overwhelming evident shows that single sex education is not more effective than co-education. This form of solution treats boys and girls as undifferentiated groups, as opposed to individuals with different needs and different attributes. Amending out the language about gender based learning styles will not make this bill constitutional, it won't erase stereotyping that's at the root of single sex programs, and it won't make it okay to teach girls and boys differently. Every classroom or school created under this bill will be very easily susceptible to legal challenge. The bill also fails to incorporate important Title IX rules, like how every single gender class must be justified by solid evidence. Public schools should not being telling young people that the most important defining thing about then is their gender or be harming gender non-conforming, transgender or non-binary students. California's 1990 single sex school experiment proved a failure and it happened before we had Prop 209 on the books which has a very bright-lined rule against gender classifications in public education. We do need evidence-based reforms, just not discriminatory ones that open schools up to liability. Thank you.

Jennifer Marrone: Good morning Chairman Allen and Members of the Committee. My name is Jennifer Marrone, the Food Service Business Manager at San Diego Unified School District. It also includes the free and reduced-meal application. In May, 2015, our district started on the USDA Pilot Program for direct certification, this program allowed our districts, and 13 other districts, to directly certify students, not only by SNAP, CalFresh, and TANF CalWORKS, but to start including students that were receiving Medi-Cal and also met the free and reduced income eligibility guidelines. The first download had an immediate impact on our direct certification percentages. From May, 2015 to June, 2015, our direct certification rate went up 7.39%, which is a total of increase of 30%. From April 1st, 2015, which is the state, excuse me, the date that the USDA uses for community eligibility provision, to April first 2016 the direct certification percentage increased 12.87% which is a total increase of 53%. The impact of these great increases in students being directly certified affected our department and the students in many ways. For our department, we were able to process 16% fewer meal applications from 2015 to 2016. Also, the percentage of students chosen for additional verification dropped 30%. These both helped reduce administrative costs and streamline the eligibility process. It was very helpful for the families to not have to fill out an application and it reduced the amount of negative balances. The greatest outcome of the MediCal demonstration project for our students is that now we currently just put 18 new schools on the community eligibility program to eat breakfast and lunch at no cost. Having these 18 schools on CEP has already increased participation and we're planning on implementing breakfast after the bell in the following school year. These 18 schools have about $20,000 in unpaid charges, which will also not be incurred next year. Meal service is now quicker, and there are fewer stigmas to eating school meals. School districts as a whole, benefit from increasing the number of students directly certified for free reduced meals because they receive more concrete data for LCFF, and Title One purposes. I do not have to chase either the school meal application, or the alternate income form. In fact, you have to choose the alternate income form, which would be in a CEP situation. The form is much easier to fill out than the school meal application. The alternate form only requires a box being checked and a signature. In summary, direct certification with Medicaid and increasing universal free school meals are important fiscal strategies for school districts and food service departments, the major benefits for students and families. Thank you for your time and I'd be happy to answer any questions.

Stephanie Haffner: Thank you. Thank you, Chairman Allen and Members of the Committee. My name is Stephanie Haffner, I am an Attorney at Western Center on Law and Poverty. Western Center is a cosponsor of this legislation. And in addition to representing low-income Californians in state Legislature in budget matters, Western Center serves as a support Center for legal services programs and legal services attorneys throughout the state. This legislation would ensure that food is not used to punish children, nor is it used to humiliate children or treat them differently when their parent or legal guardian is not able to pay for a meal. We became alerted to this issue after learning of instances when a child had been denied food as the result of a disciplinary action and we later Learned of cases in which children were denied meals as a result of their parents' unpaid school debt. We Learned that this was happening not because of rogue decisions by school nutrition workers, but because district policies were either silent or they directed staff to deny a meal or provide a less than complete meal to children. In review of policies in your district, Mr. Chair, we found school districts that direct staff to withhold a meal to children who come to school on a single day that they don't have the amount required for complete payment. And we found that these same policies direct school nutrition professionals to provide instead of a regular meal, a cheese sandwich. And in one case, a half of a cheese sandwich. While the premier policy to ensure that children don't miss a meal is community eligibility, that makes all children eligible without payment. This option is not available to every school district, nor is it taken by every school district that can. So existing law includes protections from unfair treatment of a child already certified for a free or reduced price meal, but there's no current law to protect children who are not already certified for free or reduced-price meal. And there's no current law that helps schools insure that children do not suffer, because of the debt of their parents or their caregivers. SB 250 simply requires the Department of Education to ensure that districts make a locally determined appropriate policy for ensuring that children are not treated differently or left to go hungry and to make that policy public. And when families find themselves unable to pay, this legislation also requires districts to exhaust options to help the family get certified for a free or reduced-price meal in case lack of information is the issue. This legislation is timely, it provides direction to CDE for how it should implement USDA guidance and fair treatment of children in school as to their access to meals without shame or humiliation is a value we all share. SB 250 helps insure that this value will be adhered to in the school environment through clear, fair and public policies. For this reason, we're proud to sponsor this legislation and we urge your aye vote. Thank you.

[{'start': 0, 'end': 13, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 104, 'end': 109, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Karen Micalizio: Good morning, my name is Karen Micalizio, I'm Dean of Financial Aid in Special Programs at Butte College. I also serve as the EOPS Director in this role. I am here today to express my strong support of Senate Bill 12, which will make college possible for California's foster youth by improving access to financial aid. I have worked with students for 34 years. For the past nine years, I have worked directly with foster youth. During that time, I have assisted hundreds of foster youth, and have come to understand why just half of foster youth at California community colleges receive the Pell Grant, when 85% are eligible. The first reason is a lack of preparation. Foster youth arrive at Butte College with little knowledge of the financial aid process. Many have not completed the free application for federal student aid, known as the FAFSA, or have completed it incorrectly, and received no financial aid, which quickly leads to disenrollment. Senate Bill 12 will change this by requiring each use case plan to identify an individual to assist the foster youth in the college and financial aid application process starting at age 16. A second reason for low rates of Pell Grant received among foster youth is the financial aid verification process. At View College and the other 112 community colleges in California, we require foster youth to hunt down a piece of paper documenting their foster care status to confirm that they are independent students as required by federal regulations. Many are unable to do so in a timely manner, and the financial aid process comes to a halt. SB 12 will change this by requiring the California Student Aid Commission to automate the verification process, using data provided by the California Department of Social Services. This has worked for the Chafee Education and Training Voucher and it can work to improve access to other forms of financial aid as well, including the Federal Pell Grant. Finally, SB-12 will expand an effective program for foster youth on campuses called the Cooperating Agencies Foster Youth Education Services program, known as CAFYES. CAFYES was created by Senate Bill 1023, authored by former Senate Education Committee Chair Carol Lou. SB 1023 authorized the California Community College Chancellor's Office to award up to 15 million annually to 10 community college districts. These 10 districts were selected in the fall of 2015, and implementation began in 2016. Since then, CAFYES has delivered positive results to 1,157 participating foster youth. 88% of youth reported that CAFYES helped them enroll in the right classes, 83% reported it improved access to priority registration, and 71% report that it has helped them remain enrolled full time. CAFYES has been particularly effective in improving access to financial aid. Foster youth on CAFYES funded campuses are 46% more likely to receive the federal Pell grant than the state average. And fortunately, the vast majority of foster youth, 73%, don't attend a CAFYES -funded campus. This includes the 75 potentially eligible foster youth on my Campus at Butte College. Other community colleges with large numbers of foster youth enrolled that are not funded by CAFYES  include those represented by Members of the Committee. Santa Monica Community College, Antelope Valley, and Victor Valley Colleges, Modesto Jr. College and San Joaquin Delta College, San Bernardino Community College, Cerritos and Rio Jando Colleges and American River Sacramento City College and Cosumnes River College and Westhills College. Like Butte College, these colleges are struggling to meet the complex needs of foster youth on campus. This is in spite of the fact that 6 million of the annual $15 million budget for CAFYES is unspent and could be used to support vulnerable foster youth. SB 12 will change this by authorizing the chancellor's office to fund up to an additional 10 community college districts to this available funding. SB 12 will open the door to college for thousands of Foster youth and do so using currently untapped federal funds, the Pell Grant. With SB 12, Foster youth are guaranteed to get information about financial aid earlier and an estimated 7,000 additional Foster youth will receive the Pell Grant which provides students $5700 annually for college expenses, leading to increased retention in graduation rates. Thank you and I very much urge you to support SB12.

You're going to have, there's a carve out in the bill right now where if it's not related, if it's related to a transfer or sale of a home or commercial property, it's completely exempt which is essentially a logical application of the fee. It's going to make it difficult for title companies and I think many consumers to know, when do we pay the fee, when do we not pay the fee? In transfers they'll know. But maybe a week later there's a reconveyance that's recorded to show that the lien has been paid off on the mortgage in full, is that subject to to the transfer fee, I mean to the affordable housing fee or is it not? It's going to be difficult right now with the carve out for recorded fees associated with transfer tax, those exclusions. We're finding that they're not being recorded or being charged uniformly across the state. In some cases, it's very hard to tell whether it's connected to a real estate sale or transaction. We think it's going to be regressive and hit low income home owners pretty hard. If they go to refinance their house, they're going to have a $225 recording free charged because most of the time it's going to be multiple documents, multiple pages that will easily get the $225 cap in the bill. We think they're going to be facing pretty erroneous cost to just record those documents. I think from CLTA's perspective and we've raised this before with sponsors, we would be also in the position, I think where we'd be better off by eliminating the exclusion on recorded documents for sales under the bill and make it apply to all documents. Bringing that fee down from $75 to a lower fee, put it across the board on all recorded documents. And then it would be easier for us from a software standpoint, consumers would know and then we will be able to have an easy to ascertain, easy to run program rather than what we have in front of us now. For those reasons we oppose the bill currently written. Okay, thank you.

[{'start': 0, 'end': 13, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Caitlin O'Neil: Caitlin O'Neil, Legislative Analyst's Office. Good morning, Madam Chair and Senators. I've been asked to provide you with a brief overview of the recent efforts California has made to reduce its inmate population. You should have a handout called Impact of Recent Criminal Justice Policies on the State Correctional Population. And my presentation has three components. First I'll provide a history of the federal court oversight that has led to the reductions in the inmate population. Second, I'll discuss recent policy changes that have allowed the state to make these reductions. And finally, I'll present a chart to illustrate the size of these reductions. On page one, you'll see an overview of federal court oversight of the state's inmate population. In 1995, a federal court ruled that the states' provision of mental healthcare to inmates was in violation of the 8th Amendment of the US Constitution. This case is now known as Coleman v Brown. Similarly, in 2005 a Federal Court ruled in a case now known as Plata v Brown that the state's provision of medical care to inmates was constitutionally inadequate. In 2006, the plaintiffs in the Coleman and Plata lawsuits filed motions to convene a federal three judge panel, to assess why the state was unable to provide constitutionally adequate care to inmates. In 2009, the panel declared that prison overcrowding was the primary reason why the state was unable to provide adequate care. In 2010, the three judge panel ordered the state to reduce the population of its state owned and operated prisons to 137.5% of their design capacity. And in 2014, the panel ordered the state to develop and implement various population reduction measures, to achieve and maintain compliance with the cap. If you turn to page two, you'll see that the state has used and continues to use various other means in addition to the court-ordered measures, to reach and maintain compliance with the cap. These include housing inmates in contracted facilities, because contracted facilities don't count toward the capped population. And constructing additional capacity in the state-owned and operated prisons to increase their design capacity and therefore, increase the number of inmates that the state is allowed to hold in these facilities under the cap. And finally by enacting several policy changes that have allowed the State to reduce its inmate population. And along with several voter approved measures, I will discuss these policy changes on page three. And specifically, I'm going to talk about five policy changes. The first was the 2011 Realignment, which limited who could be sent to state prison, so instead requiring that certain lower level felons serve their incarceration terms in county jail rather than state prison. It also required that counties rather than the state supervise lower level felons when their released from prison. Second, Proposition 36, which was approved by the voters in 2012, changed California's Three Strikes law to impose a life sentence on a third felony conviction only in cases of serious or violent crimes. It also allowed for re-sentencing of inmates who were serving life sentences under California's Three Strikes law, for a non serious, non violent felony. Third, Proposition 47, which was approved by the voters in 2014, reduced penalties for certain non violent, non serious drug and property crimes and allowed people who were previously convicted of these crimes to apply for re-sentencing. And fourth, as I mentioned, the three judge panel ordered the state in 2014 to implement various population reduction measures. These included expanding inmates' eligibility to reduce their prison terms through credits that inmates earned from good behavior. Creating new parole consideration processes for elderly inmates and non violent second striker inmates, and expanding parole eligibility for medically incapacitated inmates. And the fifth and final population reduction measure I'm going to talk about today is on page 4, and that is Proposition 57 which was passed by the voters in November of 2016. And is expected to allow the state to further reduce its inmate population through expanding inmate eligibility for parole consideration. Increasing the state's authority to reduce inmates' prison terms through credits that inmates earn through good behavior and participating in rehabilitative and educational type programs. And mandating that judges determine whether youth be subject to adult sentences in criminal court. And on page five, you'll see a chart which illustrates how these policy changes have affected the state's correctional population. The shaded portions of the columns show how the inmate and parolee populations have declined since 2011. And the dashed lines show what CDCR estimated these populations would be absent the various population reduction measures. So between 2011 and 2016, the state's inmate population declined by 21%, and the parolee population declined by 52%. Absent the various population reduction measures that took place over this timespan. The inmate and parolee populations were both expected to each be about 34,000 higher than they actually were in 2016. And this concludes my presentation, I'd be happy to take questions at the appropriate time.

[{'start': 11, 'end': 27, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Dan Kaplan: Dan Kaplan with the Legislative Analyst's Office. We've been asked to come here today to provide an overview of the state school facility program, how districts go about applying for funding in that program. And then provide an overview of some of the shortcomings with the current model. And then some issues for considerations as the Legislature begins to think about how to revamp the current school facility program. You should all be receiving a copy of the handout I'll be referring to throughout the presentation, called Overview of School Facilities Program. So to start with, one page one, you'll see a background of the school facility program, which was established by the Green Act of 1998. And what the Green Act really establishes is a cost-sharing arrangement between the state and local districts. Prior to 2016, the state has issued about $36 billion worth of funding for K12 school facility projects. However, it exhausted funding by 2012. As was mentioned earlier, Prop 51 was passed in November which provides an additional $7 billion for K12 facilities funding. Turning to page two of the handout you'll see a flowchart that describes the overview of the state school facility review process. And I want to highlight that this just covers the state's role. There's also a rather extensive role that local districts engage in before they even come to the state seeking funding. We break it up into three broad categories. The first is the process for obtaining approval of the site or the land that they plan to build on. The second is the actual design of the building and then the third is how they actually obtain the funding. To first jump into the site approval process, district's first go to the Department of Toxic Substances Control, which conducts a review of the plot of land to ensure that it's not contaminated. Assuming DTSC gives its approval, districts then move to the California Department of Education, which conducts a review to ensure that the plot of land is appropriate for a school. So this is typically a review to ensure that the plot of land is safe. We are looking to make sure it's a minimum distance from high voltage power lines, from airport runways, and a number of other factors. Assuming the Department of Education gives its approval, we then move into the the design approval process. And it's most efficient for a district to do dual track applications through both the State Architect as well as the Department of Education. The State Architect has the team of engineers which are reviewing the project, ensuring that it's structurally sound. While the Department of Education are reviewing the plans to make sure they comply with minimum standards for school facilities that we have in the state. Such as our classrooms of a minimum size, our science rooms equipped with the basic amount of equipment. Moving forward to the funding model, assuming that both the Division of State Architect, as well as the Department of Education, give their approvals, districts then go to the Office of Public School Construction, which determines both funding eligibility and the size of the grant that districts are eligible for. The OPSC conducts its review and makes a recommendation to the State Allocation Board, which is the body that formally votes on the project and votes to approve funding for the project. At that point, the district actually receives state funding and may proceed with the project. Turning to page three, you'll see a table of the median lengths of time that it takes each of these agencies to review projects. We highlight the three key agencies, being the Division of the State Architect, the Office of Public School Instruction, and the Department of Education. Just to point out a few findings here. We can see that processing times really vary by both project type, being new construction or modernization, as well as the agency conducting the review. What's not shown on the table, but we have seen through data from each of the agencies, is that larger projects tend to take additional time to review than smaller projects. For example, at the Division of State Architect, on average it can take about 100 days longer to approve a project that's over $5 million than a project under $1 million. All agencies we've spoken with have cited concerns with the role that districts play in the approval process. As they're conducting their reviews they might find deficiencies with the applications to which they'll need additional information from districts, which can take additional time. While all agencies have cited these concerns, only the Division of State Architect formally tracks this amount of time. And they find that for projects that are over $5 million, about half of the review time is associated with waiting for districts to respond to requests for additional information. Moving on to page four, we highlight some of the shortcomings with the approval process. And what I've hopefully conveyed is that the Green Act really establishes a fragmented review system, which can be rather confusing for districts to navigate, as they must submit applications to several different agencies. Our review also found that the state does not have any mandated timelines for each of these agencies to complete their reviews. Now there can be a number of different reasons why reviews take as long as they do. But some of the factors that we've found have been potentially insufficient staffing levels of agencies. The fact that the scope of projects that districts submit to the state can change throughout the review process. Basically, we can add classrooms to a site, remove classrooms, all of which might require further review. And there can also be delays with the architectural consultants that districts work for. Basically, these consultants have several different clients, one of which is the district. So the extent to which they need further work, there might be some delays. All these delays, however, can have some real consequences. It can mean that districts have to continue to use outdated buildings or else temporary classrooms or portables. It can also have real cost implications. For instance, in 2016, we found that construction costs statewide have increased four and a half percent. So the extent to which that the applications are tied up in state review process, we see that cost can increase on a daily basis. So taking all these factors into account as the Legislature begins to think about modifications to the current program, we would like to offer a few issues for consideration. Which you see on the final page of our handout. When it comes to streamlining the review process, we ask does it make sense to designate a lead a agency for school districts to work with such that they'll have a primary point of contact? Or does it make sense to have a common application such that they don't need to submit applications to each individual agency. If the state is interested in reducing the length of the actual review process, we ask, are there ways for agencies to operate more efficiently? Are the current staffing levels appropriate at each of the different agencies? Another way we could potentially streamline the review process would be to potentially modify regulations. But we ask, what are the tradeoffs of doing so? The extent to which we potentially reduce the requirements of building code might have some safety implications. When it comes to the district level, we ask, how can the state better prepare districts or better work with districts up front to submit more complete applications, so there's less delays? As agencies have to go back to districts for follow-up information. We also have found that while some agencies collect robust data on how long it takes to complete each phase of their internal review process, many do not. So it is possible for the state to collect better data so we can see where within each of these agencies are the delays occurring. Finally, the question that we want to pose to the Legislature is should the state potentially set some sort of formalized expectations as far as how long each of these reviews should take? And with that I conclude my presentation, and I'm happy to answer any questions.

Juan Morales: Good afternoon, Mister chair, Mister Vice Chair, Members of the Committee. Again, my name is Juan Morales, I'm the Director of the school facilities and transportation services division at the California Department of Education. It's a privilege to be here today to provide you a brief overview of our role in the School Facilities Program. I wanted to start off by sharing our vision for public schools facilities. We, the Department of Education, envision school facilities that enhance the achievement of all students. That they are safe, learner-centered, sustainable, and centers for the community. And this is what we keep in mind when we fulfill our role in this process. Now the law requires us to review school sites and to provide the school district's governing board a list of recommendations in order of merit as they relate to education, safety, traffic and conformance to the general plan. We are also charged with the responsibility to develop school sites election standards that are used by school districts in order to meet the objectives in statute. Furthermore, the law also requires us to establish standards for school districts to use to ensure that schools are designed to be educationally appropriate and to promote safety. The standards that we developed are part of the Title 5 regulations. And I'll be speaking more about that during my presentation. Now, the school sites election and acquisition process is a combined local and state process. In fact, the state's role is quite limited as most of the time during the process is spent at the local level. There are other statutes that outline the process that school districts have to go through. For example, education code section 17211 requires school districts to hold a public hearing and approve sites that are consistent with our Title 5 standards. Education code section 17212 specifies that school districts will select sites by validating all factors that affect public safety and not just based on cost. It's important to note that all school districts must select sites that are consistent with Title 5 standards. They must also meet California Environmental Quality Act requirements. School districts are the lead agency when it comes to this process. And they must meet other applicable laws. And there are many other local laws that they have to meet. I'm not going to go through the list in the interest of time. But there's also required communication between the school districts and other city and county agencies, such as the county planners. All of these requirements are outside of jurisdiction. However, if the school districts are requesting state funding, then the law requires them to receive our approval for site and plans. And they must also receive the site approval from the Department of Toxic Substances Control. Some of the requirements currently a part of the Title 5 regulations that we use for these sites include things like Mr. Caplan mentioned earlier in terms of requiring additional analysis if school sites are within a certain proximity of pipelines, railroads, power lines. And the idea here is that Title 5 regulations steer districts away from school sites that may pose a risk to the students, to the staff, and to the campus users. We also review the site size and shapes, and the compatibility of surrounding land uses. And just to give you an idea, as a general rule of thumb site sizes are 10 acres for a 600 student elementary. 20 acres for a 900 student middle school and 40 acres for a 2,000 student high school. Now, by no means are these requirements or are they minimums. This is just to give you an idea of the general site sizes. On slide nine and part of your packet we have a very high level flowchart of site of approval process for the state funded projects. The first step is evaluating the need to build a school. Many school districts use a Facilities Master Plan. The Facilities Master Plan often includes enrollment projections. They include an inventory of existing classrooms. They assess the condition of the existing classrooms. And sometimes they include prioritization of projects. Unfortunately, a lot of school districts don't use Facilities Master Plan. And this is something that we're taking a close look at to see if we can provide additional technical assistance for the school districts. As we believe that it's a necessary tool in planning in order to be able to make wise, multi-million dollar capital investments. There are many other factors that districts consider such as community growth, land availability. But once the district determines that they do need a new school, then they identify potential sites for my staff to review. We then review all school sites using our standards. And we rate them in order of merit. The school district then identifies the preferred site and they complete any other required studies. Such as proximity to railroads, that we mentioned earlier. And they also need to get the approval from the Department of Toxic Substances Control. School districts then obtain a governing board approval and they forward a packet to our offices for final approval. Once our approval is granted, then they use a letter to go along with the other funding requirements, to submit a funding request to the office of public school construction. Again, I want to highlight that the Department of Education does not identify or select sites. We review and rank sites for compliance with law and regulations. The new school plan approval process is somewhat similar. School districts may still be required to obtain other agency approvals such as DTSC and CEQA approvals unless it's a minor addition, eligible for certain exemptions. However, if districts are pursuing state funding, then they do have to submit their plans to us for approval. And when we do review plans, there are several areas that we review such as classroom size. This is an area that we're looking at very closely to take a look at to see if we need to update this definition since today's educational space differs from the traditional classroom design of yesterday. And I'll speak more about this a little later in my presentation. But we also make sure that the adequate support facilities are included in the plans, such as libraries, fields, and multi-purpose rooms. On slide 12 there's another flow chart that outlines a new school plan approval process. In this case, school districts usually begin by developing their educational specifications. The process for additions to an existing school or a monitorization project they typically don't require an educational specification. Then they submit the preliminary plans to my division for review to ensure that they're consistent with Title 5 standards. Oftentimes we'll provide comments and the districts respond to those comments. And then they submit the plans for our final approval. And again just like site approvals, school districts must obtain our approvals before they can submit a fund request to the office of public school construction. Finally I wanted to highlight a couple of initiatives that we're currently executing. The first one is in the area of sustainability. The department administers the state's green ribbon schools program that recognizes school districts that excel in three main areas or pillars as they're called. The first is that they reduce the environmental impact and cost, the second is that they promote the student health and wellness, and the third is that they provide environmental education. Each year school districts submit applications to us and we review and score them. The top five schools or districts are then nominated for federal recognition at the US Department of Education. And the remaining schools or districts that score above 55% receive either a gold, silver or bronze recognition from the State. Another initiative is our review of Title 5 regulations that we talked a little about earlier. The regulations, as the state Superintendent mentioned, they have not been updated since 2000. And we all know that there's been a lot of changes since then to our education. We started accepting input in October from all stakeholders. We're going to continue to receive inputs till the end of this month. And then we're going to take that input and analyze and develop a proposal for the state board of education consideration. We invite anybody to provide us input on how we can improve Title 5 regulations. And again, this includes our site selection process and plan review process. And lastly, I just wanted to highlight what the school superintention mentioned earlier, we have started reaching out to the small school districts in an effort to provide them assistance with their facility needs. And again, we recognize that a lot of the small school districts, they don't have the same resources that the larger school districts have, so we want to be able to try and provide them any assistance that will allow them to access the state bond funds. Both the Division of State Architect and the Office of Public School Construction will be joining us in this effort. We look forward to working with them to help the small school district community. That concludes my presentation, I'll be happy to answer any questions.

Paul Golaszewski: Thanks, Paul Golaszewski with the Legislative Analyst's Office. As the Chair described, the 2016-17 budget directed our office to prepare a report on options for what's being called a Debt-Free College Program that would reduce and eliminate student loan debt and we published a report last month and delivered copies to your office and the sergeant just distributed copies, as well. The reporting language as the chair described set the parameters for the program as additional state aid to pay for all college costs, so this would be tuition, living expenses, and books. After factoring in three things. First, apparent contribution. Second, a string contribution and third, all of the existing state and federal gift aid. You've heard a bit on the previous panel about a lot of the existing state grant-hood programs. Though it wasn't specified in the reporting language our understanding was for the intent for the program to focus on students at UC, CSU and community colleges so that's what we based our analysis on for the most part. Although we did, at the end of the report, consider students attending private colleges, as well. The reporting language did not necessarily direct us to assess the manageability of current student loan debt levels or to explore other ways to reduce student borrowing such as reducing college costs. But we think that those are important issues for you to consider. For example, the federal government currently, and making efforts to make student loan repayments more manageable by basing repayments on income and also you might want to think of ways to explore reducing college costs, in addition to increasing aid, but those were outside the scope of the report that we did. So with that said, I'll provide an overview of the findings from our report. First, I'll briefly describe the assumption that we used. Second, I'll walk you through the result that we found, and lastly I will leave you with two overarching thoughts to consider as you think about this proposal. First, on the assumptions, as I mentioned, we were starting with total college costs of both tuition, living expenses, and books, and as you heard previously, this is little bit of a departure. Today, most state aid programs are focused primarily on tuition and this new program will be all encompassing all college costs. We use the, for tuition it's pretty straight forward with costs array we know from ECSU and community colleges what it is, for living expenses we used the estimates as prepared by the segments themselves so they survey students and ask how much their living expenses are, rent and food, etc, and that's how they come up with their student budgets. And then they do this for base periodically and some are older than others, but if they are older they update them for inflation. So that was our starting point. For the parent contribution portion, we used, we based on the federal needs methodology, so the federal government actually has a formula that drives off of the FAFSA, which you heard about earlier. It's based on a family's income, their assets, their household size, how many students they have in college. It's a bit complicated, but essentially what it does is it provides a number that they think that parents could contribute based on these various factors. So we stuck with the federal methodology, which is used for most existing programs today. Next, for the student contribution, we assumed that students work 15 hours per week during the academic year and we based that on a review of the academic research looking at how children employment during the academic year affected outcomes such as GPAs and persistence and a lot of studies seem to indicate that working 10 to 20 hours per week during the year did not adversely effect students outcomes, which is 15 hours per week and during the summer, we assume students work 40 hours per week. After factoring in expected taxes and some summer living costs, we estimated that students could contribute $7,300 per year towards their education and the last part of the equation is the existing state and federal grant aid. So we factored in all of the Cal Grants that you just heard about. We also factored in all of the institutional aid that UC, CSU, and the community colleges provide. They have their own aid programs, we factored that in. We also factored all of the federal grant aids students are receiving, which primarily is the Pilgram. We do not factor in federal tax credits to do some methodological challenges, but that's another source of aid that might want to consider building into the program. And we had two additional assumptions beyond this, first we assumed that only students taking six or more units will participate and that's consistent with the aid programmer such as Cal Grants and it's intended to focus on students who with regard pursuing degrees and certificates and are not more casual students and finally, we didn't assume any changes in enrollment although if the state were to significantly increase financial aid in the form of grants, we would expect it might attract more students to enroll and we think it could also change their decision on segments they attend, and as well as their living arrangements, but we weren't able to quantify those. So based on these assumptions, we estimated the new program would cost $3.3 billion annually. So this would be on stop of all existing gift dates. On top of what we're spending on Cal grants, which you heard about, on top of what the universities are spending, on top of what the Federal government is spending, this would be additional dollars, and that amount consists of $2.2 billion for community college students, $800 million for CSU students, and $300 million for UC students, and the difference across the segments primarily is due to differences in the number of students. There are far more community college students. That's why the number's far higher at community colleges as well as some differences in the amount of aid students receive at each of the segments and you heard on the earlier panel that community college students tend to receive a little less aid currently as compared to students at the other segments. These amounts that we estimated don't necessarily match the amount that students are currently borrowing for a couple of reasons that it's important to note. One is that some financially needy students right now they tend to borrow, they, some of them don't borrow right now they might be working more than the amount that we assume right? They might be working 20 or 25 hours a week. There's probably some students like that. Conversely, some right now might be choosing to borrow more and working less. So if you compare our estimates to the amount is currently being borrowed, they don't exactly map one to one for those. After our initial estimate, we then said, well, what if we limit the program to full-time students, which generally is defined as students taking 12 or more units. And if we did that, we think it would cut the program costs roughly in half, so it would be about 1.6 billion. Primarily, it would exclude a lot of community college students who tend to go part-time more frequently than students at the universities. We also suggested the Legislature consider having a time limit consistent with current programs, as well as some academic achievement, making minimal academic progress, as another requirement. Which would reduce the cost somewhat, but we weren't able to factor that into our estimate. And then finally, we laid out a couple of options for the Legislature to phase in the program if it wasn't going to fund it fully. You could target awards to the neediest students first, as defined by the federal formula I eluded to earlier. You could target the program at a particular institution first. So you could start, for example, maybe at the community colleges. You could also take an approach like the state did with middle class scholarships where it set a fixed budget in state law, and then just rationed awards if the program couldn't be fully funded. That hasn't happened yet to that program. So those were some of the phase and options we considered. In closing, two points in particular that we wanted to highlight as you think about this proposal. The first is that we concluded that the program probably would significantly reduce student loan debt. We don't think it would necessarily eliminate student loan debt for a couple of reasons, and that's because of the way the program is structured. So for example, it relies on the expected parent contribution. But you can't necessarily force all parents to contribute. There might be some parents who don't, so a student might have to borrow in that situation. In addition, we did have our assumption on how many hours students work. And students wouldn't be required to work. Some students might choose to borrow instead of working the number of hours that we assume. There could also be circumstances where some students can't find jobs, particularly maybe in a recession where jobs are scarcer and students can't find them, so they might still have to borrow. The second closing point that we wanted to highlight is that the program is a big change, as you've heard from focusing financial aid on tuition coverage as the state has done historically to also include in living costs, which we haven't done of as much in the past. And this does raise some questions about cost control, the state has more control over tuition. The Legislature actually sets tuition in state law for the community colleges for using CSU, the governing boards set tuition. But the state has a lot of influence over tuition level student budget. With living expenses, the state has less structure control over those costs, obviously. It also could create some, perhaps, unintended, consequences. Some students who maybe right now are living at home to save on cost, if there's a new state program that's going to fully fund them, maybe they would choose to move off-campus because the state would pay for it. So we think those are important considerations to keep in mind as you think about expanding aid to cover living cost in addition to tuition. And with that, I'll take any questions.

Paul Golaszewski: Thanks, Paul Golaszewski with the Legislative Analyst's Office. As the Chair described, the 2016-17 budget directed our office to prepare a report on options for what's being called a Debt-Free College Program that would reduce and eliminate student loan debt and we published a report last month and delivered copies to your office and the sergeant just distributed copies, as well. The reporting language as the chair described set the parameters for the program as additional state aid to pay for all college costs, so this would be tuition, living expenses, and books. After factoring in three things. First, apparent contribution. Second, a string contribution and third, all of the existing state and federal gift aid. You've heard a bit on the previous panel about a lot of the existing state grant-hood programs. Though it wasn't specified in the reporting language our understanding was for the intent for the program to focus on students at UC, CSU and community colleges so that's what we based our analysis on for the most part. Although we did, at the end of the report, consider students attending private colleges, as well. The reporting language did not necessarily direct us to assess the manageability of current student loan debt levels or to explore other ways to reduce student borrowing such as reducing college costs. But we think that those are important issues for you to consider. For example, the federal government currently, and making efforts to make student loan repayments more manageable by basing repayments on income and also you might want to think of ways to explore reducing college costs, in addition to increasing aid, but those were outside the scope of the report that we did. So with that said, I'll provide an overview of the findings from our report. First, I'll briefly describe the assumption that we used. Second, I'll walk you through the result that we found, and lastly I will leave you with two overarching thoughts to consider as you think about this proposal. First, on the assumptions, as I mentioned, we were starting with total college costs of both tuition, living expenses, and books, and as you heard previously, this is little bit of a departure. Today, most state aid programs are focused primarily on tuition and this new program will be all encompassing all college costs. We use the, for tuition it's pretty straight forward with costs array we know from ECSU and community colleges what it is, for living expenses we used the estimates as prepared by the segments themselves so they survey students and ask how much their living expenses are, rent and food, etc, and that's how they come up with their student budgets. And then they do this for base periodically and some are older than others, but if they are older they update them for inflation. So that was our starting point. For the parent contribution portion, we used, we based on the federal needs methodology, so the federal government actually has a formula that drives off of the FAFSA, which you heard about earlier. It's based on a family's income, their assets, their household size, how many students they have in college. It's a bit complicated, but essentially what it does is it provides a number that they think that parents could contribute based on these various factors. So we stuck with the federal methodology, which is used for most existing programs today. Next, for the student contribution, we assumed that students work 15 hours per week during the academic year and we based that on a review of the academic research looking at how children employment during the academic year affected outcomes such as GPAs and persistence and a lot of studies seem to indicate that working 10 to 20 hours per week during the year did not adversely effect students outcomes, which is 15 hours per week and during the summer, we assume students work 40 hours per week. After factoring in expected taxes and some summer living costs, we estimated that students could contribute $7,300 per year towards their education and the last part of the equation is the existing state and federal grant aid. So we factored in all of the Cal Grants that you just heard about. We also factored in all of the institutional aid that UC, CSU, and the community colleges provide. They have their own aid programs, we factored that in. We also factored all of the federal grant aids students are receiving, which primarily is the Pilgram. We do not factor in federal tax credits to do some methodological challenges, but that's another source of aid that might want to consider building into the program. And we had two additional assumptions beyond this, first we assumed that only students taking six or more units will participate and that's consistent with the aid programmer such as Cal Grants and it's intended to focus on students who with regard pursuing degrees and certificates and are not more casual students and finally, we didn't assume any changes in enrollment although if the state were to significantly increase financial aid in the form of grants, we would expect it might attract more students to enroll and we think it could also change their decision on segments they attend, and as well as their living arrangements, but we weren't able to quantify those. So based on these assumptions, we estimated the new program would cost $3.3 billion annually. So this would be on stop of all existing gift dates. On top of what we're spending on Cal grants, which you heard about, on top of what the universities are spending, on top of what the Federal government is spending, this would be additional dollars, and that amount consists of $2.2 billion for community college students, $800 million for CSU students, and $300 million for UC students, and the difference across the segments primarily is due to differences in the number of students. There are far more community college students. That's why the number's far higher at community colleges as well as some differences in the amount of aid students receive at each of the segments and you heard on the earlier panel that community college students tend to receive a little less aid currently as compared to students at the other segments. These amounts that we estimated don't necessarily match the amount that students are currently borrowing for a couple of reasons that it's important to note. One is that some financially needy students right now they tend to borrow, they, some of them don't borrow right now they might be working more than the amount that we assume right? They might be working 20 or 25 hours a week. There's probably some students like that. Conversely, some right now might be choosing to borrow more and working less. So if you compare our estimates to the amount is currently being borrowed, they don't exactly map one to one for those. After our initial estimate, we then said, well, what if we limit the program to full-time students, which generally is defined as students taking 12 or more units. And if we did that, we think it would cut the program costs roughly in half, so it would be about 1.6 billion. Primarily, it would exclude a lot of community college students who tend to go part-time more frequently than students at the universities. We also suggested the Legislature consider having a time limit consistent with current programs, as well as some academic achievement, making minimal academic progress, as another requirement. Which would reduce the cost somewhat, but we weren't able to factor that into our estimate. And then finally, we laid out a couple of options for the Legislature to phase in the program if it wasn't going to fund it fully. You could target awards to the neediest students first, as defined by the federal formula I eluded to earlier. You could target the program at a particular institution first. So you could start, for example, maybe at the community colleges. You could also take an approach like the state did with middle class scholarships where it set a fixed budget in state law, and then just rationed awards if the program couldn't be fully funded. That hasn't happened yet to that program. So those were some of the phase and options we considered. In closing, two points in particular that we wanted to highlight as you think about this proposal. The first is that we concluded that the program probably would significantly reduce student loan debt. We don't think it would necessarily eliminate student loan debt for a couple of reasons, and that's because of the way the program is structured. So for example, it relies on the expected parent contribution. But you can't necessarily force all parents to contribute. There might be some parents who don't, so a student might have to borrow in that situation. In addition, we did have our assumption on how many hours students work. And students wouldn't be required to work. Some students might choose to borrow instead of working the number of hours that we assume. There could also be circumstances where some students can't find jobs, particularly maybe in a recession where jobs are scarcer and students can't find them, so they might still have to borrow. The second closing point that we wanted to highlight is that the program is a big change, as you've heard from focusing financial aid on tuition coverage as the state has done historically to also include in living costs, which we haven't done of as much in the past. And this does raise some questions about cost control, the state has more control over tuition. The Legislature actually sets tuition in state law for the community colleges for using CSU, the governing boards set tuition. But the state has a lot of influence over tuition level student budget. With living expenses, the state has less structure control over those costs, obviously. It also could create some, perhaps, unintended, consequences. Some students who maybe right now are living at home to save on cost, if there's a new state program that's going to fully fund them, maybe they would choose to move off-campus because the state would pay for it. So we think those are important considerations to keep in mind as you think about expanding aid to cover living cost in addition to tuition. And with that, I'll take any questions.

The recent drought added the final blow to an already stressed system. The system, this is not the first drought that this state has had, nor is it the first drought that these trees have experienced, but what is the difference this go around is the density of the trees. Forest management professionals have known for decades, our forests are overly dense where on average historically, we had 20 to 50 trees an acre, today in some of our forests, we have over 500, even 1000 trees per acre in some areas. We call it dog hair thickets, where you can't even get through it. These densities are not historically natural nor are they stable. With higher density, there's higher competition amongst the trees for water and nutrients. It's a basic function of supply and demand. Without adequate waters, the trees become stressed and are unable to use their natural defense systems against insects because all of their energy is literally being focused on just staying alive. As US Forest Service, specific South West research station demonstrates, that given standard densities measured as the standard density index, forest resource managers can predict which insects are going to attack our forest at certain densities. So it's no surprise for those of us that study this thing, that the bark beetles are here and have grown to epidemic populations, given the high density of trees that exist today. I personally learned that we were on the tip of this iceberg back in 1992 when I started forestry school. We were talking about it then. So, how did we get here. So as others have said, historically our forests have always evolved with disturbance, rather it was in the form of insects, disease, or fire, we always had some kind of agent that was in our forests reducing the number of tress. However around the middle of the last century, we became very professional in suppressing these natural disturbances, primarily fire. And also around the 80s or early 90s, we substantially limited the amount of harvesting that we did on a national forest, which by our practical definitions, is a disturbance you know mechanism. So now fast forward to today where our forests grow many times more volume each and every year than we harvest, and you end up with a density fuel situation, which is the catalyst for the insects that we're experiencing now, and then you add on the drought and it's a perfect storm and our forests literally become a buffet for the insects. So had we been proactive and at least went in and thinned and reduced those densities, our forests would not have been under such stress and competition for resources, and they would have, by all practical measures, in most instances, been able to fight the insects like they had before. So now that we not only have the mortality issue, we also have the impending risk of catastrophic wildfire, which will right the ship and get the system back to historic levels, and with that, our forests are now on their way of being net emitters of carbon, so think about that. Instead of being an incredible sink of carbon, because that's what woody biomass is, it's stored carbon. The recent drought added the final blow to an already stressed system. The system, this is not the first drought that this state has had, nor is it the first drought that these trees have experienced, but what is the difference this go around is the density of the trees. Forest management professionals have known for decades, our forests are overly dense where on average historically, we had 20 to 50 trees an acre, today in some of our forests, we have over 500, even 1000 trees per acre in some areas. We call it dog hair thickets, where you can't even get through it. These densities are not historically natural nor are they stable. With higher density, there's higher competition amongst the trees for water and nutrients. It's a basic function of supply and demand. Without adequate waters, the trees become stressed and are unable to use their natural defense systems against insects because all of their energy is literally being focused on just staying alive. As US Forest Service, specific South West research station demonstrates, that given standard densities measured as the standard density index, forest resource managers can predict which insects are going to attack our forest at certain densities. So it's no surprise for those of us that study this thing, that the bark beetles are here and have grown to epidemic populations, given the high density of trees that exist today. I personally learned that we were on the tip of this iceberg back in 1992 when I started forestry school. We were talking about it then. So, how did we get here. So as others have said, historically our forests have always evolved with disturbance, rather it was in the form of insects, disease, or fire, we always had some kind of agent that was in our forests reducing the number of tress. However around the middle of the last century, we became very professional in suppressing these natural disturbances, primarily fire. And also around the 80s or early 90s, we substantially limited the amount of harvesting that we did on a national forest, which by our practical definitions, is a disturbance you know mechanism. So now fast forward to today where our forests grow many times more volume each and every year than we harvest, and you end up with a density fuel situation, which is the catalyst for the insects that we're experiencing now, and then you add on the drought and it's a perfect storm and our forests literally become a buffet for the insects. So had we been proactive and at least went in and thinned and reduced those densities, our forests would not have been under such stress and competition for resources, and they would have, by all practical measures, in most instances, been able to fight the insects like they had before. So now that we not only have the mortality issue, we also have the impending risk of catastrophic wildfire, which will right the ship and get the system back to historic levels, and with that, our forests are now on their way of being net emitters of carbon, so think about that. Instead of being an incredible sink of carbon, because that's what woody biomass is, it's stored carbon. Katarina Eleby: Morning Chairman Jerry Hill, Chairman Ruiz Salas, Committee Members, we are pleased to be here today for our sunset hearing. My name is Katarina Eleby, board President and public member. Joining me today is Jason Kaiser the executive officer and Alicia Rabena-Amen our Vice President. The mission of the Physical Therapy Board is to protect consumers from incompetent, unprofessional and fraudulent practice through regulation of practitioners. Specifically, the Physical Therapy Board administers the licensing and enforcement programs for physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, and unlicensed physical therapy aides. Regulation of the practice of physical therapy began in 1958, when the Legislature passed the Physical Therapy Practice Act. Initially, the Practice Act established the Physical Therapy Examining Committee as a Committee under the Medical Board of California. Between 1971 and 1996 amendments to the Practice Act shifted regulatory responsibility over physical therapy away from the Medical Board to the Committee and eventually renamed and converted the Committee into its own board. The board is comprised of seven members, four practitioners and three public members. The Governor appoints five members in total, all four professional members and one of the public members. The Senate Rules Committee and the Assembly Speaker each appoint one public member each. Currently, there are no vacancies. As of fiscal year 15-16, the Physical Therapy Board regulates approximately 31,000 physical therapists and 6700 physical therapy assistants. The Board's budget is just over $4 million and it has approximately four months of reserves in its fund. I'll be giving the response to the issue item number one, regarding the statutory fee increase. Currently we are at statutory caps as of December 26, 2016. This is a concern for us for the following reasons. The board may need to develop examinations, our jurisprudence exam needs to be updated and, should a need arise, we may need to develop a national exam. If so, it would be emergent and would need to be addressed immediately. In addition, our reserves are still relatively low, with only four months in our fund. Although projections are positive, there may be unforeseen litigation that would be a strain on resources. Thirdly, the Board is planning to move to a larger office space in the near future, as we are currently at capacity in our current office. We want to be clear that we are not planning on increasing fees. We are simply asking the Legislature to consider increasing our Statutory Caps because we don't know what we don't know. Although there is no immediate need to raise fees, the board is trying to be proactive and prepare for a rainy day. This approach is proactive and will allow us to plan for the future in a fiscally responsible manner. And with that, I'll hand it over to our executive officer, Jason Kaiser, to address the next issue regarding BreEZe.
