Alicia Rabena-Amen: Good morning Chairman Salas, Chairman Hill, and Committee Members. And thank you all for your public service, and for the opportunity to testify before you today. My names is Alicia Rabena-Amen, and I've been a professional member of PTBC board since February 2014. This morning I'm going to discuss issue number 15 under edits to the Practice Act, which asks, should the Practice Act be amended to change the PTBC's ratio of public members to professional members? There's been much thought and discussion about board composition and the potential for anti-competitive decisions, especially since the US Supreme Court's decision in the case of the North Carolina Board of Dental Examiners versus the Federal Trade Commission, the FTC. While attempting to balance the boards with a public member majority may enhance consumer perspective of antitrust protection, the FTC guidance suggested that a board with even just one professional member could still be a controlling majority. As it is not uncommon for public members to defer to professional members on matters even outside of practice issues, such as administration of the board. Given the North Carolina case and decision, we board members of the PTBC understand why the Legislature might be considering such a change to the Practice Act. This board, however, does not feel that this change is necessary and please allow me to explain why. Just as a reminder, our board is made up of three public members and four professional members. During my three years of service on this board, I've not seen one example of a professional member using his or her position to drive a decision. It's my belief that if a professional member tried such a thing, the other professional and public members would be quick to reign that member in. I've witnessed only positive contributions from the professional members who sit on this board. And as a professional board member myself, I've seen first hand the benefits of a board that consists of four professional members who come from diverse work settings. And one of the areas where professional members bring added enhancement is during case deliberation, where we can each apply our various workplace experiences to a licensee's case, in order to contribute to a fair decision all the while, while still honoring our consumer protection mandate. I feel very grateful and blessed for the PTBC board members who came before me, and engrave the culture of consumer protection to be first and foremost the focus of our existence and decisions. Yes, the PTBC has other functions, such as testing and licensing and other things. But it is our mandate to protect consumers that is always at the forefront of our minds of our board members. Because we clearly understand our purpose, we PTBC board members feel that each one of us is a public member. I would even issue a challenge to anyone who is willing to take a look at one of our board meetings and see if you can tell which members are public and which are professional. I think you'd have a hard time trying to figure it out. And since this culture has been in place for years before most of us current board members were appointed, opinions and responsibilities are shared freely and openly among us. I think our Board President, Ms. Eleby, and Board members Mr. TJ Watkins, and Ms. Tonia McMillian, who are all public members, would agree that any notion of a turf war is nonexistent within the PTBC Board. And so it is for these reasons that this board has no concern with changing the board composition. We do, however, think that perhaps all boards should be looked at individually in order to determine each board's history and liability on a board by board basis. Once again, thank you for your service and thank you for your consideration.

Jeffrey Mason: Thank you, Chair Hill, Chair Salas, and members of the committees. I'm Jeffrey Mason, Chief Deputy Director for the Department of Consumer Affairs. This afternoon, we will be presenting as a panel. As the committees may be aware, the department is currently undergoing a leadership transition. Director Alok ...'s last day is tomorrow. And we welcome our newly appointed director, Dean Grafilo. The department's also appreciative of the assistance and the partnership of Secretary Alexis Podesta and the Business Consumer Services and Housing Agency has provided the department through this transition. I'd like to take a moment and introduce the panel, first of all, we have Peter Williams, Deputy Secretary at the Business Consumer Services and Housing Agency, and Adam Quinonez, Deputy Director of Legislation for the Department of Consumer Affairs. To begin, I would like to do a quick overview of the department. The Department of Consumer Affairs oversees 40 boards, bureaus, and commissions, whom, together, licenses and regulates over 3 million licensees in more than 200 professional and 100 business categories. The Department serves and supports these 40 separate entities in the areas of enforcement, budgeting, information technology, legal affairs, communications, legislation, and regulations. Several department highlights from 2016 include the following, DCA responded to approximately 530,000 consumer calls. Working in conjunction with the Bureau of Postsecondary Education, we hosted 76 student outreach events in response to school closures throughout California. This included students impacted by the closure of ITT Tech. The Department's information technology team implemented 1,243 brief system enhancements. And DCA conducted 2,078 investigations on behalf of the boards and bureaus. We've been asked to speak to issue number one, the investigator vacancies currently in the Department's health quality investigation unit. As the committees are aware in July of 2014, the investigative staff of the California Medical Board moved under the management of the Department Consumer Affairs division investigations. Since that date in 2014, 47 individuals have left the Department, but the vast majority transitioned to positions elsewhere in the state that have less complicated case types, lower case loads, and most impactful, higher pay scales. Currently, the unit that investigates Medical Board cases has 31 investigator vacancies, a number which represents 40% of the total investigative positions. The results of the vacancies have been an increased workload on remaining staff and an increase in overall investigation timelines. The Department's addressing these vacancies as follows, first of all, we're hiring, hiring, hiring. Beginning on August 2014, DCA has received and reviewed over 1,600 applications, interviewed over 475 candidates. And we've had 18 individuals successfully complete the required year-long background check process that it takes to become a sworn peace officer in the state. The Department also has an additional 15 candidates currently undergoing that background check process. From an operational standpoint, we reassigned cases based upon type cases, and we provided overtime to existing staff. We're also using what we consider to be an innovative approach to bring on new investigators in a non-sworn capacity. We're taking advantage of that year long background check process, bring in the individuals on board, on staff in a non-sworn capacity, they investigate less egregious, less complex cases. They get used to our processes, our procedures, how we do business, our culture. We get used to them as employees. They complete the year long process. They go to the academy; and they come back to the Department as a sworn investigator. We look at this a little bit like having a AAA baseball team for our Major League team. And while the Department has been very active in recruiting and replacing sworn officers, we also need to be able to retain them. And in light of that, the Department has submitted a retention pay proposal, which is currently at Cal HR. And we anticipate hearing the resolution of that very soon. The issue number two, status of IT upgrades for the release three entities. In October 2013, the Department implemented release one of the BreEZe system. And that release placed 10 boards on the new BreEZe platform. In January of 2016, another eight boards and bureaus were moved to BreEZe in release two. Since that launch of release two last year, the Department's been focused on two primary activities, the first being the upgrade and the stabilization of the BreEZe platform. Today the BreEZe system is stable and performs millions of processes everyday. It's used by 1,200 employees approximately and about 1.4 million registered users. One important capability that's been expressed by the board you've heard today is the ability to have an online presence where the prior business system didn't have. Individuals who are applying for life insurance can now apply online. And current licensees who are seeking renewal of their license can submit their license renewals online. In 2016, the BreEZe system processed $115 million through online submissions. Current licensees submitted approximately 466,000 online renewals last year, 91% of which were processed in the same day. Put that in context, those in the past would have had to be put in an envelope with a check by the licensee, sent to us. We would have to open the mail, cashier the check, and process the paperwork, now that's being accomplished in a day or two. The second initiative related to BreEZe is the transition of release three boards and bureaus to a new IT platform The department has learned a great deal from the first two releases. We've learned how best to maintain the system, we've learned how to better manage and implement the sustained levels of program-related enhancement requests. And we've learned how to mitigate the impacts of legislative and regulatory modifications. As a result, we've adjusted our approach for the remaining 18 Boards and Bureaus. Going forward, DCA will be using the Department of Technology's Project Approval Lifecycle Process to determine what IT solution is most effective and most efficient for each individual Board and Bureau. The overall objective of the Department of Technology's process is to match an entity's organizational readiness and business needs with the most appropriate IT solution. This process also includes a cost-benefit analysis, which occurs in phase two of the Department of Technology's process. And that analysis will play a key factor in determining what is the most appropriate IT solution for an individual board or bureau. DCA's expectation is that in some cases the process will determine that BreEZe is the best solution. In other cases, such as our new Bureau of Medical Cannabis Regulation, a different platform was deemed better able to meet that individual entity's specific business needs. DCA is organizing the remaining 18 Boards and Bureaus into groups based upon their individual operational readiness to move through the Department of Technology's process. Each program will begin by focusing on their business needs. They're currently mapping out processes, documenting, assessing their operational needs, looking at staffing impacts of not just the preparation to launch a new system, but the transition and the workload of a new system. We currently have five programs preparing to enter the Department of Technology's process, and we will have an additional two begin next quarter. We've been asked to speak to issue number three, which is barriers to licensure. The Department has been actively working with the the Business Consumer Services and Housing Agency to identify areas where unnecessary barriers to licensure can be reduced. One key area of this work has been on the examination of possible barriers to licensure for individuals re-entering society after incarceration. We've been working to understand how individual Boards and Bureaus determine if a past conviction is deemed substance-related. And we're also attempting to ascertain how they consider rehabilitation in their assessment. In October of 2016 the Little Hoover Commission issued a report titled Jobs for Californians: Strategies to Ease Occupational Licensing Barriers. The report offered a number of recommendations to minimize barriers to entry into licensed professions and included anecdotal discussions of individuals attempting to re-enter society after incarceration simply not applying for licensure because they assumed they would be denied. The department and DCA, DCA and the agency agree that it can be confusing and it can be intimidating for individuals to understand if a prior conviction would be considered substance-related, as well as how one demonstrates rehabilitation. And we're seeking to clarify criteria through regulation or through FAQs, update the websites, to assist applicants, to potentially encourage more folks to apply. Demographic data. The Little Hoover Commission report also recommended that the department collect demographic data on a mandatory basis. Currently the department has a few examples of boards that do collect demographic information, but this activity is completed post-licensure and the response is voluntary on the part of the licensee. The department is not opposed to the collection of data but we believe it should never be condition for licensure and we believe it's best conducted by a third party. We appreciate your time and we look forward to your conversation. Thank you.

And AB 2024, which was passed last year, which would create a temporary exemption to the corporate bar for critical access hospitals requires a report back to the Legislature on the program's effectiveness. We believe a conversation about the elimination at this point without that additional information is premature. We continue to oppose the idea of mandatory notification of probation, issue 28. We continue to be concerned about the due process issues that we raised on SB 1033. And we disagree, Senator Hill, about the assertion that our proposal AB 505, which we introduced after hearing the concerns about probation being an inappropriate disciplinary action for many of the cases being discussed, does not include due process. Additionally, we believe that the Sunset Review is not the appropriate venue for this clearly controversial issue. We take issue with the assertion in the staff analysis that a stipulated settlement is an admission to violating the charges and that accusations are equivalent to proven charges. This is not an accurate portrayal of the process. It only serves to further confuse the public, and it decreases our confidence that this venue is appropriate to address this concern. The staff analysis raises the issue of cost recovery, issue 14. The current licence fee includes a $15 that's spread across all licensees to pay for the cost of what the medical board previously recovered through cost recovery. Should the Committee seek to reinstate, or committees, seek to reinstate the cost recovery, we would request that the license fee be reduced accordingly. Without that, the physician would be paying twice. We do question, however, the rationale for seeking this reinstated cost recovery, as other boards have shown to have varying degrees of success in actually recovering the costs that have been ordered. The Board of Optometry is reporting that only 21% of the amount ordered is being actively collected. The Acupuncture Board is reporting a return of 3% on unrecovered costs in its 2015 Sunset Review Report. We do support the idea of readdressing vertical enforcement issue 64, though I would note we have in the past opposed what was suggested by Mr. Howard which is moving the investigators to the AG's office. So I'm sure there will be ongoing conversations about that, but I wanted to put out that we do support reviewing and readdressing vertical enforcement. And as to the other issues in the report, our assessment on the language as I noted will be language dependent, but there will be important factors that we'll be considering. What is the impact on due process? Physicians as all other licensees have a constitutional right to due process, and the language must maintain those due process protections. What is the impact on patient privacy? Both federal and state law establish patient privacy protections because of the very sensitive nature of medical information. And when you start to consider making changes to those, they need to be very carefully weighed, the balance between the desire to change it and what the impact would be. And is the issue one that's better addressed consistently across all types of healthcare licensees? For example, the report suggests adding a physician specific requirements to the office notifications that are currently required for all licensees. What about physicians recommends that different requirement from physicians from those other licensee types? We appreciate the opportunity to provide this analysis, and continue to have a dialog with you as the process continues.

Katarina Eleby: Morning Chairman Jerry Hill, Chairman Ruiz Salas, Committee Members, we are pleased to be here today for our sunset hearing. My name is Katarina Eleby, board President and public member. Joining me today is Jason Kaiser the executive officer and Alicia Rabena-Amen our Vice President. The mission of the Physical Therapy Board is to protect consumers from incompetent, unprofessional and fraudulent practice through regulation of practitioners. Specifically, the Physical Therapy Board administers the licensing and enforcement programs for physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, and unlicensed physical therapy aides. Regulation of the practice of physical therapy began in 1958, when the Legislature passed the Physical Therapy Practice Act. Initially, the Practice Act established the Physical Therapy Examining Committee as a Committee under the Medical Board of California. Between 1971 and 1996 amendments to the Practice Act shifted regulatory responsibility over physical therapy away from the Medical Board to the Committee and eventually renamed and converted the Committee into its own board. The board is comprised of seven members, four practitioners and three public members. The Governor appoints five members in total, all four professional members and one of the public members. The Senate Rules Committee and the Assembly Speaker each appoint one public member each. Currently, there are no vacancies. As of fiscal year 15-16, the Physical Therapy Board regulates approximately 31,000 physical therapists and 6700 physical therapy assistants. The Board's budget is just over $4 million and it has approximately four months of reserves in its fund. I'll be giving the response to the issue item number one, regarding the statutory fee increase. Currently we are at statutory caps as of December 26, 2016. This is a concern for us for the following reasons. The board may need to develop examinations, our jurisprudence exam needs to be updated and, should a need arise, we may need to develop a national exam. If so, it would be emergent and would need to be addressed immediately. In addition, our reserves are still relatively low, with only four months in our fund. Although projections are positive, there may be unforeseen litigation that would be a strain on resources. Thirdly, the Board is planning to move to a larger office space in the near future, as we are currently at capacity in our current office. We want to be clear that we are not planning on increasing fees. We are simply asking the Legislature to consider increasing our Statutory Caps because we don't know what we don't know. Although there is no immediate need to raise fees, the board is trying to be proactive and prepare for a rainy day. This approach is proactive and will allow us to plan for the future in a fiscally responsible manner. And with that, I'll hand it over to our executive officer, Jason Kaiser, to address the next issue regarding BreEZe.
[{'start': 17, 'end': 27, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 38, 'end': 48, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 136, 'end': 150, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 207, 'end': 219, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 246, 'end': 264, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 2908, 'end': 2920, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Alicia Rabena-Amen: Good morning Chairman Salas, Chairman Hill, and Committee Members. And thank you all for your public service, and for the opportunity to testify before you today. My names is Alicia Rabena-Amen, and I've been a professional member of PTBC board since February 2014. This morning I'm going to discuss issue number 15 under edits to the Practice Act, which asks, should the Practice Act be amended to change the PTBC's ratio of public members to professional members? There's been much thought and discussion about board composition and the potential for anti-competitive decisions, especially since the US Supreme Court's decision in the case of the North Carolina Board of Dental Examiners versus the Federal Trade Commission, the FTC. While attempting to balance the boards with a public member majority may enhance consumer perspective of antitrust protection, the FTC guidance suggested that a board with even just one professional member could still be a controlling majority. As it is not uncommon for public members to defer to professional members on matters even outside of practice issues, such as administration of the board. Given the North Carolina case and decision, we board members of the PTBC understand why the Legislature might be considering such a change to the Practice Act. This board, however, does not feel that this change is necessary and please allow me to explain why. Just as a reminder, our board is made up of three public members and four professional members. During my three years of service on this board, I've not seen one example of a professional member using his or her position to drive a decision. It's my belief that if a professional member tried such a thing, the other professional and public members would be quick to reign that member in. I've witnessed only positive contributions from the professional members who sit on this board. And as a professional board member myself, I've seen first hand the benefits of a board that consists of four professional members who come from diverse work settings. And one of the areas where professional members bring added enhancement is during case deliberation, where we can each apply our various workplace experiences to a licensee's case, in order to contribute to a fair decision all the while, while still honoring our consumer protection mandate. I feel very grateful and blessed for the PTBC board members who came before me, and engrave the culture of consumer protection to be first and foremost the focus of our existence and decisions. Yes, the PTBC has other functions, such as testing and licensing and other things. But it is our mandate to protect consumers that is always at the forefront of our minds of our board members. Because we clearly understand our purpose, we PTBC board members feel that each one of us is a public member. I would even issue a challenge to anyone who is willing to take a look at one of our board meetings and see if you can tell which members are public and which are professional. I think you'd have a hard time trying to figure it out. And since this culture has been in place for years before most of us current board members were appointed, opinions and responsibilities are shared freely and openly among us. I think our Board President, Ms. Eleby, and Board members Mr. TJ Watkins, and Ms. Tonia McMillian, who are all public members, would agree that any notion of a turf war is nonexistent within the PTBC Board. And so it is for these reasons that this board has no concern with changing the board composition. We do, however, think that perhaps all boards should be looked at individually in order to determine each board's history and liability on a board by board basis. Once again, thank you for your service and thank you for your consideration.

Jeffrey Mason: Thank you, Chair Hill, Chair Salas, and members of the committees. I'm Jeffrey Mason, Chief Deputy Director for the Department of Consumer Affairs. This afternoon, we will be presenting as a panel. As the committees may be aware, the department is currently undergoing a leadership transition. Director Alok ...'s last day is tomorrow. And we welcome our newly appointed director, Dean Grafilo. The department's also appreciative of the assistance and the partnership of Secretary Alexis Podesta and the Business Consumer Services and Housing Agency has provided the department through this transition. I'd like to take a moment and introduce the panel, first of all, we have Peter Williams, Deputy Secretary at the Business Consumer Services and Housing Agency, and Adam Quinonez, Deputy Director of Legislation for the Department of Consumer Affairs. To begin, I would like to do a quick overview of the department. The Department of Consumer Affairs oversees 40 boards, bureaus, and commissions, whom, together, licenses and regulates over 3 million licensees in more than 200 professional and 100 business categories. The Department serves and supports these 40 separate entities in the areas of enforcement, budgeting, information technology, legal affairs, communications, legislation, and regulations. Several department highlights from 2016 include the following, DCA responded to approximately 530,000 consumer calls. Working in conjunction with the Bureau of Postsecondary Education, we hosted 76 student outreach events in response to school closures throughout California. This included students impacted by the closure of ITT Tech. The Department's information technology team implemented 1,243 brief system enhancements. And DCA conducted 2,078 investigations on behalf of the boards and bureaus. We've been asked to speak to issue number one, the investigator vacancies currently in the Department's health quality investigation unit. As the committees are aware in July of 2014, the investigative staff of the California Medical Board moved under the management of the Department Consumer Affairs division investigations. Since that date in 2014, 47 individuals have left the Department, but the vast majority transitioned to positions elsewhere in the state that have less complicated case types, lower case loads, and most impactful, higher pay scales. Currently, the unit that investigates Medical Board cases has 31 investigator vacancies, a number which represents 40% of the total investigative positions. The results of the vacancies have been an increased workload on remaining staff and an increase in overall investigation timelines. The Department's addressing these vacancies as follows, first of all, we're hiring, hiring, hiring. Beginning on August 2014, DCA has received and reviewed over 1,600 applications, interviewed over 475 candidates. And we've had 18 individuals successfully complete the required year-long background check process that it takes to become a sworn peace officer in the state. The Department also has an additional 15 candidates currently undergoing that background check process. From an operational standpoint, we reassigned cases based upon type cases, and we provided overtime to existing staff. We're also using what we consider to be an innovative approach to bring on new investigators in a non-sworn capacity. We're taking advantage of that year long background check process, bring in the individuals on board, on staff in a non-sworn capacity, they investigate less egregious, less complex cases. They get used to our processes, our procedures, how we do business, our culture. We get used to them as employees. They complete the year long process. They go to the academy; and they come back to the Department as a sworn investigator. We look at this a little bit like having a AAA baseball team for our Major League team. And while the Department has been very active in recruiting and replacing sworn officers, we also need to be able to retain them. And in light of that, the Department has submitted a retention pay proposal, which is currently at Cal HR. And we anticipate hearing the resolution of that very soon. The issue number two, status of IT upgrades for the release three entities. In October 2013, the Department implemented release one of the BreEZe system. And that release placed 10 boards on the new BreEZe platform. In January of 2016, another eight boards and bureaus were moved to BreEZe in release two. Since that launch of release two last year, the Department's been focused on two primary activities, the first being the upgrade and the stabilization of the BreEZe platform. Today the BreEZe system is stable and performs millions of processes everyday. It's used by 1,200 employees approximately and about 1.4 million registered users. One important capability that's been expressed by the board you've heard today is the ability to have an online presence where the prior business system didn't have. Individuals who are applying for life insurance can now apply online. And current licensees who are seeking renewal of their license can submit their license renewals online. In 2016, the BreEZe system processed $115 million through online submissions. Current licensees submitted approximately 466,000 online renewals last year, 91% of which were processed in the same day. Put that in context, those in the past would have had to be put in an envelope with a check by the licensee, sent to us. We would have to open the mail, cashier the check, and process the paperwork, now that's being accomplished in a day or two. The second initiative related to BreEZe is the transition of release three boards and bureaus to a new IT platform The department has learned a great deal from the first two releases. We've learned how best to maintain the system, we've learned how to better manage and implement the sustained levels of program-related enhancement requests. And we've learned how to mitigate the impacts of legislative and regulatory modifications. As a result, we've adjusted our approach for the remaining 18 Boards and Bureaus. Going forward, DCA will be using the Department of Technology's Project Approval Lifecycle Process to determine what IT solution is most effective and most efficient for each individual Board and Bureau. The overall objective of the Department of Technology's process is to match an entity's organizational readiness and business needs with the most appropriate IT solution. This process also includes a cost-benefit analysis, which occurs in phase two of the Department of Technology's process. And that analysis will play a key factor in determining what is the most appropriate IT solution for an individual board or bureau. DCA's expectation is that in some cases the process will determine that BreEZe is the best solution. In other cases, such as our new Bureau of Medical Cannabis Regulation, a different platform was deemed better able to meet that individual entity's specific business needs. DCA is organizing the remaining 18 Boards and Bureaus into groups based upon their individual operational readiness to move through the Department of Technology's process. Each program will begin by focusing on their business needs. They're currently mapping out processes, documenting, assessing their operational needs, looking at staffing impacts of not just the preparation to launch a new system, but the transition and the workload of a new system. We currently have five programs preparing to enter the Department of Technology's process, and we will have an additional two begin next quarter. We've been asked to speak to issue number three, which is barriers to licensure. The Department has been actively working with the the Business Consumer Services and Housing Agency to identify areas where unnecessary barriers to licensure can be reduced. One key area of this work has been on the examination of possible barriers to licensure for individuals re-entering society after incarceration. We've been working to understand how individual Boards and Bureaus determine if a past conviction is deemed substance-related. And we're also attempting to ascertain how they consider rehabilitation in their assessment. In October of 2016 the Little Hoover Commission issued a report titled Jobs for Californians: Strategies to Ease Occupational Licensing Barriers. The report offered a number of recommendations to minimize barriers to entry into licensed professions and included anecdotal discussions of individuals attempting to re-enter society after incarceration simply not applying for licensure because they assumed they would be denied. The department and DCA, DCA and the agency agree that it can be confusing and it can be intimidating for individuals to understand if a prior conviction would be considered substance-related, as well as how one demonstrates rehabilitation. And we're seeking to clarify criteria through regulation or through FAQs, update the websites, to assist applicants, to potentially encourage more folks to apply. Demographic data. The Little Hoover Commission report also recommended that the department collect demographic data on a mandatory basis. Currently the department has a few examples of boards that do collect demographic information, but this activity is completed post-licensure and the response is voluntary on the part of the licensee. The department is not opposed to the collection of data but we believe it should never be condition for licensure and we believe it's best conducted by a third party. We appreciate your time and we look forward to your conversation. Thank you.

Mark Stivers: Yes, good afternoon members.Again, Mark Stivers, the Director of the Tax Credit Allocation Committee. And we really do one thing, we fund the development of affordable rental housing. So LHD and college FA, they're both single-family and homeownership. We are focused on apartments for those serving, person's earning 60% of the area median income and below. And we do that with low income housing tax credits. They really come in two forms. There are federal, and state credits. They're predominantly federal but we have a significant but fairly small amount of state credits. And all those credits really are bunched into two programs. We have a competitive program. And those include the 9% federal tax credits or the state credits which are limited in number. So, because they're limited, we hold the competition to figure out sort of which projects are worth of those credits. And we have a non-competitive program which consists of the 4% federal housing tax credits. And that's where really the growth potential is. Because the 9% credits are limited and they're oversubscribed, there's really not much more we can do there. We're producing the maximum number of units possible each year. With these 4% federal credits, we actually have a lot of uncapped capacity. And that's been our goal for the last two years, is how do we bring in more of those federal tax credits? And the real issue there has been that, the tax credits provide a certain amount of funding but not enough. They don't fill enough of that gap that exists between the costs of the project and what a private mortgage can support. And as a result, the projects are infeasible. If we can make more of these projects financially feasible, we can draw down more of those federal credits. And so, we make projects feasible. First of all, you reduce costs. And we've done various things to try and reduce the requirements of our program, reign in some of those costs. Obviously, a lot of costs are beyond our control. And we've done some things to also increase the amount of tax credits so we can put in to individual projects. And the result last year was that we had a record year. Our previous record was in 2001. We financed about 16,000 units with 4% tax credits. Last year, we were over 20,000. So, we had the best year in our history, but we still would like to do more. There are some, still there are 4% credits sitting on the table and if we can provide some additional gap financing, we can make that work. Whether that's in the form of a permanent source, whether it's in the form of a bond, whether it's in the form of additional tax credits. It doesn't really matter what flavor that public subsidy comes in, but the public subsidy is what would fill that gap and allow us to draw down more federal credits. And then the last thing is that, well we did have a record last year, we are a little bit concerned going forward because of the prospect of federal tax reform, there is less demand for our tax credit and the pricing has dropped about 15 percent since November. And as a result, that means that these gaps that I just talked about are going to be bigger on the natural. Which means that, for us to hit our goal of fully utilizing 4% credits, we're going to need, that need for gap financing from some other public sources greater than it was before. So, I will stop there and help answer any questions. Again, but we are sort of the basic building block of all affordable rental housing. Just about every affordable apartment complex that's developed these days has one form of these tax credits or the other. And it's our other partners that then provide the gap financing that really make these projects possible.

Natasha Collins: Good morning Mr. Chair and members. I'm Natasha Collins with the Legislature Analyst's Office. The sergeant has distributed a handout, which we'll be speaking from today. We've been asked to provide a brief overview of federal funding that California receives for K12 and early childhood education. I'm going to start with the K12 portion. And then allow my colleague to describe early childhood education funding.  After our presentation, the Committee will hear from the California Department of Education that will provide recent and possible federal actions that might affect education in California. So on page one of your handout, we provide an overview of the federal role in education which historically was limited but increased significantly with the 1965 passage of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act which provided federal funds to school districts with high proportions of low income students. Over time the federal role has increased and has led to requiring schools to administer some standardized tests and develop school improvements plans if schools do not need certain performance expectations. The 2001 re-authorization of the ESEA was known as the No Child Left Behind Act which you may have heard of and this expanded testing to more grades and required certain corrective actions as schools did not meet certain performance expectations. The most recent authorization of the ESEA is known as the Every Student Succeeds Act or ESSA. It so requires testing but removes many of the repercussions associated with the No Child Left Behind Act.  Today, three major acts governing the federal role on education and they are all administered by the California Department of Education. There are the Healthy and Hunger Free Kids Act which supports child nutrition programs, the Every Student Succeeds Act which supports various secondary and elementary education programs, and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. On page two of your hand out, we provide, we put federal funding and for K-12 education in context. Overall federal funding makes up about 10% of total K-12 funding in California or about $7.5 billion as proposed in 2017-18. Remaining K-12 funding comes from state and local sources. At a school district level, some school districts rely more heavily on federal funding than others. We found that about a third of school districts rely on federal funding for 10% or more of their budget with districts with relatively large numbers of low income and English learner students relying more on this piece of their budget. We begin to provide an overview of the three largest federal programs on page three of your handout. We begin with federal child nutrition programs which provide $2.6 billion in federal funding and are authorized through the Healthy and Hunger Free Kids Act I mentioned earlier. The largest programs are the National School Lunch Program and the School Breakfast Program, which comprise about 80% of this funding. These programs reimburse schools for providing free or reduced meals to low income students. In addition,California supplements these reimbursements annually about $160 million. Another large federal program are those for students with disabilities, and the federal government provides about $1.3 billion annually towards this purpose as authorized through the Individuals of Disabilities Education Act. Most of this funding goes to provide direct services for students with disabilities between ages three through 22. In addition, California provides about $4 billion annually towards special education in addition to this federal funding. Page four wraps up our overview of major federal programs with informations about programs for students from low income families which provides about $2.6 billion in federal funding. The vast majority of this funding goes towards Title 1 programs for low income students which were generally formula based as you can see at the figure at the bottom of your page. In addition, California provides about $9 billion annually for supplemental services to English learners and low income students all through the local funding formula. You can also see in your figure that the Every Student Succeeds Act provides support for various other elementary and secondary programs, including professional development programs, after-school programs, and programs for English learners. Page five provides an overview of other federal funding including funding for the Perkins Career Technical and Education Act and for the McKinney-Vento Homeless Assistance Act. In addition, there are various grants that are provided directly to educational service providers or directly to schools. For example, funding through the e-rate program that provides telecommunication providers with funding to support internet at schools and funding that goes directly to schools to offset losses of certain revenues due to schools location on federal lands. Lastly, the CDE receives federal funding for state operations. The CDE is to receive about $160 million in 2017-18 for these purposes. In a review our office did a few years ago, we estimate that federal funding supports about 70% of CDE's operations budget. That concludes my presentation on K-12, a very high level K-12 federal funding. I'll pass the baton now to my colleague to provide a brief overview of early childhood education federal funding. Thank you.

Marguerite Ries: Good morning. Marguerite Ries on behalf of the State Superintendent Public Instruction. Congress recently confirmed Betsy DeVos as Secretary of Education with only two Republicans crossing party lines to vote against her. With Senators Collins and Murkowski defecting the Senate was tied 50-50 forcing Vice President Mike Pence to cast the deciding vote for her confirmation. The first time in recorded in history. Congress has introduced resolutions under the Congressional Review Act or the CRA, to appeal some Obama era education regulations. The CRA allows Congress to reach back 60 legislative days, and repeal regulations if a resolution is approved by the House and Senate and approved by the President. These resolutions pertain to accountability in state plan regulations under Title 1 of the Every Student Succeeds Act, and the teacher preparation regulations under Title 2 of the Higher Education Act. If the resolutions pass, the agency will be prohibited from enforcing the regulations, and from ever issuing substantially similar regulations on the same legislative language. Bills have been introduced to revoke the every Student Succeeds Act and abolish the U.S. Department of Education. However, these are both message bills introduced to rile up the base and are very unlikely to pass. Last week a proposal was floated for a private school tuition tax credit for working class families totaling up to $20 billion. But at this time, it's not clear where the money would be coming from, and would still require action from Congress. It is extremely unlikely the money would come from an existing federal education source. From a fiscal perspective, the federal government is still running on a temporary budget measure known as a Continuing Resolution through April 28 of this year. Law makers are expected to extend this measure without much fanfare, or significant changes through the end of the year but may not do so until this spring. The real potential for change comes in federal fiscal year 2018. Law makers are discussing making more significant changes in order to cut federal spending including, potentially in across the board cut of up to 10% to discretionary spending, a category that includes education funding. Such across the board cuts, tend to be more or less equally painful to all sectors, and thus are more attractive to appropriators than targeted cuts. Still we expect to see a limited number of programs like Title 1 of ESSA and part B of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act more or less protected, because law makers considered that spending an obligation. Action on other policy legislation will take a backseat until Congress completes its work on nominations and appropriations. Though Perkins Acts reauthorization, the Higher Education Act, and a revamp of child nutrition programs are all in congresses to do list, no substantive policy proposals have been put forth to date. New Secretary of Education Betsy Devos has made clear she knew priorities for her Department of Education. While President Obama's education secretaries focused on access and equity in education, we expect Devos to focus on state autonomy and parental choice. This could mean the review or appeal of regulations or guidance that limit such autonomy, closing or shrinking the U.S. Department of Education like the Office of Civil Rights, or reevaluating policies on charter school flexibilities. The President has issued two executive orders, that will impact the education regulations. One pauses the effective date regulations which were final but not yet going into effect, and other executive order instructs agencies to cut two old regulations for each new rule published. Regardless of how it happens, it is clear that regulations and guidance under the Every Student Succeeds Act, and other federal laws could be drastically changed or repealed wholesale in the coming months. In their absence, California and it's local educational agencies will rely on the language of the statute, and other non-effective guidance and regulations. However, uncertainty will be the constant in coming months. This concludes the CD Federal education update but I'm happy to answer any questions, thank you.

Erin Hamilton: I will. My name is Erin Hamilton. I'm associate Professor of sociology at UC Davis. For the past 15 years, I've studied international migration as a sociologist and demographer. My research has focused on the determinants and demography of Mexico-US migration and on the health and well being of immigrant families and children. And I've written more than 25 scholarly articles and book chapters on this topic. In my view, children of undocumented immigrants are the single most vulnerable population of children in this country. They are vulnerable for many of the reasons that you can imagine, including disadvantages their parents face in the labor force. And the restricted access to social services. But perhaps most importantly, deportation shatters immigrant families and the threat of deportation casts a shadow of terror over immigrant families. Preventing some of these deportations and expanding due process rights of immigrants and detention and deportation proceedings would provide some protection to these most vulnerable families in California. I think it's important to remember that this population at risk of deportation in California is quite large. The best demographic estimates of the undocumented population in California place it at 2.3 and 3 million people in 2014. This means that undocumented immigrants are 22% of all California immigrants, and 6% of the state population. Undocumented immigrants are by and large, long term residents. In California, 87% have been in the United States for more than five years. And a full quarter have been in the United States for at least 20 years. As a result, many undocumented immigrants have US citizen children In California in 2014 it was estimated that there were 1.3 million US citizen children with at least one undocumented parent. So what are the impacts of deportation on these California children and families? In 2013 the US government deported 70,000 parents claiming a US citizen child and in 2015 after the Obama administration implemented its new priority enforcement program, the number fell to 31,000. In the most severe cases deportation results in the termination of parental rights. In 2011 an estimated 5,100 of deported parents were in the child welfare system nationwide. More commonly, one parent is deported and the other remains with their children. Men are vastly over-represented among deportees. As a result, the deportation of father creates quote suddenly single mothers. Who suffer severe economic consequences due to the loss of the primary wage earner in their household. For example, in census data, it is found that the median income of households with at least one undocumented member is $41,300. If that member were removed from the household, the median income would fall to $22,000 which is below the poverty level for a family of four. This would raise poverty rates from about 33% of undocumented immigrants to over 50%. The economic impacts extend well beyond the immigrant households. Economists have used simulation models to estimate what would happen to the size of the US and state economies if all undocumented people were deported. Using a wide range of assumptions about those impacts, one report estimated that 10 year loss to the California economy. Would be in the order of $103 billion, without outsized impacts on agriculture, leisure and hospitality, and wholesale and retail trade. But deportation doesn't just have economic consequences. For families, the consequences are far more profound. Research finds that some families never recover. Deportation is a triggering event that eventually leads to marital dissolution. And a large body of social science research that children are healthier, perform better in school, are less likely to become teen parents or delinquents, and have better adult outcomes when they live in stable family environments. Other families attempt to stay together in the face of deportation. My colleague at the College of Mexico Claudia Masferrer Leon is an expert on the return migration to Mexico. She and I are beginning a study of the well-being of nearly 500,000 US citizen children who have returned to Mexico in the past decade. Some of these are voluntary returnees who have left with their parents after the great recession, but others are returning with their parents who were deported. It's unclear how their return to Mexico will impact the lives of these young, US citizens. But Professor Mesfer's early research suggests that integration into Mexico is fraught with difficulties. Still, other deportees intend to return to the United States in spite of the serious criminal and immigration penalties they face if they're caught. In a research study I wrote on men deported to El Salvador, the single most important factor predicting their intent to return to the United States was having a US citizen child left behind. The majority of fathers in this study intended to return. While these impacts on families who experience deportation are severe, a much broader swath of children and families experience deportation threat, which is risk and fear of oneself or family member being deported. I recently spoke with a Davis community member about this. She and her husband have lived in the United States for 11 years and both are undocumented. They have three kids. The eldest is undocumented and two are US citizens. All are enrolled in elementary and high schools in Davis. Following the Trump administration's announcement about expanded enforcement efforts, she expressed the terror she felt. She says she went to the Walmart in West Sacramento and it was unusually empty. She had heard that ICE frequents Walmart in quote, Mexican stores, to pick up undocumented people. She became paralyzed with fear that ICE was at her Walmart and that she would be picked up. Her vision blurry, heart racing, unable to hear, she grabbed her children and she fled from the store. She told me this story two days later on the verge of tears, she was so traumatized by it. What should we do, Erin? Shall we take the children out of school and go back to Mexico? She's worried about drug violence in her home town in Mexico, she's worried that her children's speaking English better than Spanish and her eldest daughter who's a straight a student wants to go to UC Davis. But she's also terrified of being separated from her children if she is detained this is not an isolated occurence. A similar story appears in today's Sacramento Bee, and research also confirms that this fear is widespread. It has real consequences for families and communities. For example, a study of 132 Latino parents in 2009 found that 45 percent reported that the mere existence of deportation affects how their child performs in school and 53 reported that the existence of deportation affects their ability to financially provide for their children. This study included documented and undocumented immigrants, and it predated the current enforcement climate, so we can imagine that these are lowball estimates of current impacts of deportation. Deportation threat also affects how community members live their lives. My collaborator, Jaqueline Hagan at UNC, has studied this topic extensively. She found that immigrants, like the community member I just mentioned, respond to deportation threat by withdrawing from public spaces like libraries, parks, churches, and school meetings, the very places that create community and support immigrant families. In a county in North Carolina where police were trained to collaborate with ice under the 287G program, immigrants withdrew to such an extent that some immigrant serving businesses reported sales plummeting between 30% and 90%. Research in Arizona found that SB1070, which expanded police power to stop and detain people suspected of being undocumented undermined police community relations, and trust in immigrant communities. A final point that is not just a family members of undocumented immigrants who suffer the consequences of deportation, this issue is constructed in such a way that many children conflate the terms immigrant and illegal, and experience this stigma of undocumented status. Even if they or their family members are not undocumented. This in turn threatens two characteristics that sociologists think are very protective about immigrants. One is immigrant optimism, or the belief that hard work and investments will pay off, and ethnic pride, which is a bulwark against discrimination. And as my colleague Caitlin Patler will now discuss, similar consequences can be seen with immigrant [INAUDIBLE]

So given the level of these family ties, long-term detention really causes increased economic strain at the household level. For example, while 16% of the detainees reported there families had been late paying rent, mortgage, or utility bills in the six months prior to detention, that number shot up to nearly two-thirds during the time in detention. Judy London: Thank you so much for inviting me today and thank you for staying here at this late hour. My name is Judy London and I'm Directing Attorney of Public Counsels Immigrants Rights Project. We provide full scope legal representation in immigration courts, the federal courts. And for affirmative relief, such as U visas before USCIS. The one difference with public counsel is that we also do impact litigation. So we use our experience with our clients to inform our litigation and identify significant impact issues that need to be addressed. We are co-counsel in the Franco litigation, which established a right to counsel for immigrant detainees with severe mental disabilities. And just to paint a picture of this, when a government building is labelled a court house, we imagine that the function of that building, of the court, is to render justice. And we imagine when we have a picture in our head of what a just court looks like, as a judge and two parties on an equal playing field each represented by counsel. So, after spending 20 years in immigration courts I can tell you that this crisis is not new. I've never believed that we should be calling these institutions courts because there cannot be any degree of fairness when you have people from other countries facing life and death decisions who do not have a right to counsel. And it is public counsel's goal to rectify that and to join you in making that happen. That is why we ware very pleased that there is this amendment to SB 6 to essentially recognize that everyone deserves due process, everyone deserves a lawyer. In the case of Mr. Franco, our detention attorney found Mr. Franco at the Santa Ana Jail. He had been detained there for over five years, after a judge had closed his case, determining that he lacked mental competency to represent himself. He was lost in detention at tax payers expense, for five years. And this is what happens when there is not a right to counsel. We are also co-counsel in J.E. F.M. v Lynch and we continue to seek to establish a right to counsel for all children under 18 in immigration court. One of the Senators referenced the fact that our government thinks an eight year old can represent themselves. Well, that government has argued that a one year old can represent themselves. Some of our clients are one years old. We had a one year old who went to court for, that same month, the government had granted permanent protection in this country to the teen mother of that one year old. And yet Ice argued in court that the one year old remained an enforcement priority of the United States government. This is a one year old who would have been deported away from the only parent that one year old had back to Central America, the most violent place in the world for children. So that struggle continues. But I bring up the point of impact work because it has been very important and will be very important in the days ahead. And it's informed when lawyers have access to courtrooms and can be there to observe what is happening and not rely on representations of the government. I'm going to briefly touch on some of the gaps I see in legal services, other than this massive gap of representation. And foremost, the detention, where nearly 70% of detainees go unrepresented. Just to tell you what our program looks like, we have a lawyer assisted by two law fellows who are with us only for a short amount of time to cover the Orange County detention centers. In my 20 years working in Southern California, I have never seen funding for more than one full-time lawyer in Southern California to provide removal defense to immigrant detainees. I don't think people understand that. They think maybe there's a dozen, maybe there's 20. There's 1, perhaps, right now there's 1.5, if we don't include the fellows. There is an organization that is funded to go do Know Your Rights presentations but not provide the actual representation that we provide. Stacy Shargroni: Good afternoon, my name is Stacy Shargroni, I'm with the Vera Institute of Justice, and we have offices here in Los Angeles and also in New York. And the decision there to follow a universal representation model where as long as someone is financially eligible, unrepresented, and wants representation, they get an attorney. So there are no carve-outs for people with criminal convictions or anything of that sort. And what we're finding in having run this program for about three years, and currently working on a comprehensive evaluation of it, is that the universal representation model provides obviously greater access to justice, but also efficiency, both for the court system and for the program itself. I think a lot of the immigration lawyers in the room have long experience with the triage model, where we're trying to quickly screen cases and figure out who might have a quote, unquote winning case. But we all know, and have lots of examples that during a one time screening, it can sometimes be really hard to develop the pertinent facts. That can often take multiple meetings to kind of figure out if someone has a case and even if that criminal charge that is being lodged makes the person deportable, removable. And so what we found is that it takes a huge up front effort to kind of sort who deserves and doesn't deserve an attorney. Lots of legal time that is ultimately not used to represent the person so we've made a decision in New York City to give everyone representation as the panel described too. That doesn't mean, the judges are still deciding on whether the person stays or not, but there's a due process right to that representation. And so just wanted to share that experience from New York for your.

The new federal rule that Ms. Cantwell described was finalized in two parts as she indicated towards the end of her testimony. First, in May of 2016, and then a second set of provisions on January 17th, 2017, three days before the inauguration. The two rules will have a significant impact on how the hospital fee program will be implemented, but the provisions in that second rule are even more damaging for that program. The Medi-Cal program fails to cover the cost of treating Medi-Cal patients in hospitals by more than $8 billion a year. The hospital fee program is used to draw down those unclaimed federal funding, those dollars, to help mitigate less than half of that massive shortfall. Nearly every general acute care hospital or hospital system benefits from the hospital fee program, including public hospitals, rural hospitals, and all safety net hospitals. The funding follows the patient. Therefore, there are several methods for making payments, including fee for service, supplemental payments, and as Mary Cantwell mentioned, managed care supplemental payments. The managed care plans, over the last eight years, have been very good partners in helping get these payments to the hospitals that treat the Medi-Cal patients. The current method of making these supplemental payments through the Medi-Cal managed care plans is not aligned with the requirements in the final rules. They are considered pass through payments, and they must be phased out starting July 1, 2017, just a few short months away. As pass through payments are phased out, they can be replaced with an allowable directed payment. These directed payments can be an add-on to the adjudicated claims by a fixed amount or a flat percent. And quite frankly, it's really not much different than how we are passing through the dollars now. But this nuance creates two significant problems that we want you to be aware of. First, the final rule states that these allowed directed payments can only be made to network providers. This will impact the ability to make a supplemental payment for all Medi-Cal patients. Even non-contracted or out of network patients that receive care in a children's hospital, or a tertiary care hospital that provides some of the highest acuity and specialty care to children or others with extremely complex health issues. These payments on an annual basis are potentially about $2 billion a year, or about 20% of the entire hospital fee program. If we can't find a solution for this problem, it'll be difficult for CHA to support this funding strain continuing. The second issue, the directed payments must be made on current adjudicated claims rather than utilizing, than using utilization trends to calculate a lump sum payment. And while we don't anticipate, there being much of a change about the distribution among the hospitals of the payments. It does raise a number of questions on how we resolve related to ensuring that hospitals are not at risk for excess directive payments made to the health plans, and how health plans are not at risk for making directed payments if they haven't had the funds allocated by the department. Let me give you an example. If funds are allocated to a health plan based on historic utilization of say, 100,000 medical impatient days, and the plan only experiences 75,000 days in that period, the plan will be holding excess funds with no ability to get those funds to the hospitals. Those funds represent hospital dollars matched with federal funds. It is not state money, it is the hospital fee program and the federal dollars. This guessing game could result in hundreds of millions of dollars being at risk to hospitals. Another scenario that CHA can't support. On the flip side of that example, the health plan could actually experience more utilization. Let's say they experienced 125,000 inpatient days, yet they only received funds to cover 100,000 inpatient days. The plan could be at risk for making those payments as directed by the Department of Healthcare Services. And again, CHA does not support putting the plans at financial risk to pass this dollars through. As Mary said, these are really complex issues, probably some of the toughest that we've had to grapple with for a long time. What is at risk if we don't find solutions? I think that is the big question. The hospital fee could be much smaller than any of us want it to be, billions of dollars less. This means less money for hospital care from Medi-Cal beneficiaries and it means that for every dollar we might have to shrink the program, the state loses $0.24. Sarah Brooks: Good afternoon. Sarah Brooks, Deputy Director over Healthcare Delivery Systems at the Department Of Health Care Services. As Ms. Cantwell mentioned, I'll talk today about network adequacy and its applicability to our delivery systems as is set forth in the final role. I want to clarify that the effective dates for these requirements is July 1 of 2018. And so we will be continuing to work on these in the near future. With regards to network adequacy, the final rule sets forth requirements, but provides flexibilities to states to develop standards, as long as certain considerations are made when setting those standards. In developing the standards that we've proposed, our thinking is that it is important to set a floor that plans must meet but at the same time, provide for reasonable, timely access to care for beneficiaries. We've developed these standards with the beneficiaries and plans in mind. Our priority is to promote access to services that beneficiaries will need while balancing the plans ability to meet them as well. We carefully consider the plans existing networks and the reality of providers that actually exist in the state when setting them. We are also aiming to set standards that are not complex and are easy to understand and measure. As Ms. Cantwell noted earlier, these requirements apply to all four areas of the delivery systems as well. For Medical managed care and dental manage care health plans, California already has network adequacy standards in place today. You'll hear a little bit from our partners at DMHC later today about that. Both for time and distance, and timely access. These standards are set forth in both knox keene regulations. But and also, in contracts between managed care and dental managed care health plans and the Department of Health Care Services. For county specialty mental health plans, network standards do not currently exist and thus, it will take a little more work for these systems in the department to implement network adequacy standards for them. For DMCODS health plan that Ms. Cantwell talked about earlier, we will utilize network adequacy standards per the requirements under the waiver as we initially implement them and they roll out in California. The final rule does require network adequacy standards in a number of areas we establish. They'd be established for primary care, specialty care, hospital, OB-GYN, behavioral health, pharmacy, pediatric, dental. And also for LTSS services that are required when beneficiaries are actually travelling to providers, as opposed to when providers are travelling to beneficiaries. The department recently released a final role network adequacy proposal that is out for stakeholder comment right now. Ms. Leirman mentioned it earlier. Comments are due today, however we do continue to welcome feedback. When setting the proposed standards in the department's network adequacy proposal, we first considerd standards that already existed today. So we looked at knox keene standards, we looked at what was included in our contracts with our Medical managed care plans and our dental managed care plans, and we looked at what was included in the 1115 waiver. Whenever possible, we really mirrored those standards. So we kept in place the standards, or we proposed the standards that are already in place today to continue under our proposal. Those standards include for Medical managed care and dental managed care plans, primary care, and hospital time and distance standards. And then primary care specialist mental health and pharmacist timely access for non urgent appointments as applicable. When setting any new standards prescribed in the final rule, when we didn't have standards already in place, we considered a number of different things. Many of them are required by CMS. And examples of those are expected enrollment and utilization of services, characteristics and needs of specific populations. Number and types of network providers, and geographic location of network providers. In addition, we also considered other factors such as Medicare standards, we utilized geo-mapping and looked at state medical board data. We also took a look at what current alternate access standards have been submitted to the department entity and may see for consideration purposes. When developing our core specialist list, we considered the specialists that are most critically used and also the reality of what specialists are available across the state in California. We excluded facility-based specialists such as anesthesiologists because time and distance standards really don't make sense and really are not applicable to them. The final rule requires network adequacy standards for LTSS services, when the beneficiary is traveling to the provider. So in this instance for example, IHSS, MSSP services, we wouldn't set standards, because the provider is going to the beneficiary. We also did not set standards when the beneficiary was residing at a facility such as a skilled nursing facility because the beneficiary, again, was not traveling to the provider. I also wanted to touch on the fact that there is an ability, as Ms. Leirman mentioned, to have alternative access standards requested. So we do work in partnership with the Department of Managed Healthcare to approve this alternative access standards. This would occur in a place such as a rural area, where there just simply aren't providers. Or there aren't certain types of specialists available, and so we are able to approve separate standards than what is set forth in the core standard requirements. This is a new system that we really have just recently implemented and we're really excited about all of the opportunities that it will provide for us. This is a requirement that is set forth in the final rule. Marta Green: Thank you. So as you said, my name is Marta Green. I'm the Chief Deputy Director of the Department of Managed Health Care. I want to thank you all for having us here today. The DMHC license and regulate health plans that provide coverage to more than 25 million Californians. We regulate the vast majority of commercial plans and the majority of the medical managed care plans in California. Our mission is to protect consumers' healthcare rights and ensure a stable healthcare delivery system. We do this by administering the Knox-Keene Act. There are many topics in the Knox-Keene Act, but two of the big ones are network adequacy and financial reporting. And those are the two that the Committee staff has asked me to touch on today. So first, I'll talk about network adequacy. Plans provide to the DMHC, information on their networks in a variety of ways. A critical among those is the plan's annual network submissions. Plans submit their entire network to the DMHC on March 31st of each year. And this report also includes the results of all grievances related to networks throughout the year. All health plan policies and procedures must comply with the geographic standards set forth in the Knox-Keene Act. Specifically, 15 miles and 30 minutes for access to primary care physicians. And there's a list of types of physicians that fall under that category for the DMHC, as well as to hospitals from either their home or their workplace. Some health plans do request alternative access standards for many of the reasons that we've talked about here today. And we analyzed those alternative access standards against permitted justifications in the act. And that can be such as a lack of practicing providers in a specific geographic region. Generally, all our alternative access standards are limited to specific affected zip codes. For all other provider types, so non-primary care, non-hospital, the Knox-Keene Act requires that all health plans provide reasonable access. So to identify reasonable access, we look at access to specialists at a specific plan and compare that to all other plans that operate in that similar geographic region. As well as access standards or benchmarks that are generally accepted in the marketplace, such as the Medicare access standards. So to perform this analysis we used software, as does everybody these days. And we use a Geographical Information System, or GIS system software, to map the distances that enrollees must travel for a large number of provider types. So the primary care providers we look at include family practice, general practice, internal medicine, OBGYN, and pediatrics. We looked at a very wide array of specialty types, I won't name them all, but they do include psychiatry, HIV-AIDS specialists, mental health professionals, and hospital based providers. Our software also maps the location of hospitals, in-patient hospice facilities, ambulatory surgical clinics, and urgent care locations. Another important aspect of our network adequacy review is our timely access standards. These standards require health plans to maintain provider networks sufficient to ensure that people can get a timely access to an appointment. The requirements are based on the individual's specific clinical condition, and they set forth certain standards for types of appointments. So 48 hours for urgent care when no prior authorization was required. All of the way up to 15 days for non-urgent appointments with a specialty physician or other ancillary providers. So to demonstrate compliance, health plans conduct an annual telephone survey of the providers to assess availability of appointments. This information has then compiled together into a report given to the DMHC. We review the report, issue findings regarding the data, and make recommendations for changes. Unfortunately, the DMHC's 2015 report issued earlier this year, stated that the DMHC was unable to determine whether health plans met the timely access standards due to significant inaccuracies in the data. The report also detailed a number of next steps for health plans in the DMHC, to design to improve the accuracy of the data reporting so that we will have a better report next year. These steps do include some data validation steps, vendor requirements, as well as some enforcement investigations. Last week, we held a stakeholder meeting with plans, providers, other interested parties, to discuss these next steps. The next topic I've been asked to address is the DMHC's role in ensuring health plans meet the affordable care act's Medical Loss Ratio, or MLR, for short requirements. So to ensure that consumers receive value for their premium dollar, the Affordable Care Act and California State law require commercial health plans to meet certain MLR requirements. So health plans offering coverage in the individual and small group market must spend at least 80% of premium revenue on clinical services and activities that improve health care quality. And health plans in the large group market must meet an 85% standard. That means that health plans are limited in the percent of premium revenue that they can spend on administrative costs or profit. Health plans that fail to meet these Medical Loss Ratio requirements must provide rebates to consumers. I won't get into the details of what falls into each category, but if you have questions about what's in the clinical and what's in health care quality, versus what's in administration profit, I'm happy to go over that. So since the new requirements were enacted, California consumers have received a total of 206 million in rebates for the five reporting years of 2011 to 2015. This breaks down to a total of 64 million in rebates for the individual market. 139 million in rebates for the small group market, and 3 million in rebates for the large group market. We can audit health plans for compliance with the Medical Loss Ratio requirements for commercial coverage. We review their reporting that comes into the DMHC, and we determine whether or not to conduct an audit based upon that reporting. So, for an example, if a Medical Loss Ratio report came into the DMHC that was very, very close to the threshold, that may trigger an audit. When we conduct a Medical Loss Ratio examination, a health plan must submit a significant amount of data, which the DMHC reviews to verify the plan's representations on the reporting form. We review the validity of the data on expenses and premiums including the appropriateness of plan allocations for expenses, taxes, and revenues. And reviews the allocation and classification of expenditures for quality improvement activities. We can, under state law, require a health plan to pay an additional rebate to consumers if the examination identifies the plan inaccuracies. We have completed three Medical Loss Ratio examinations since reporting began, and we're in the process of completing three more. Now, we post the final reports of all Medical Loss Ratio exams on our website. In addition to our Medical Loss Ratio of commercial plans, we have historically performed some limited Medical Loss Ratio work on behalf of the Department of Health Care Services through an inter-agency agreement. This inter-agency agreement is set to terminate on June 30th of this year. This concludes my prepared remarks. And I'm happy to answer questions.
