We recommend DHCS prohibit plans from requiring members to participate in multiple levels of internal review before seeking a fair hearing. The new rule also gives states the option to require a voluntary external medical review process as part of their appeal. Currently, consumers in Knox-Keene licensed plans have access to an independent panel of medical experts, through an independent medical review IMR. Consumers and county organized health system codes that are not Knox-Keene licensed can not access the IMR process. For these consumers, their only recourse is a state fair hearing before the administrative law judge, a lengthy process that is determined by someone with legal, not medical training. To illustrate the need for an independent medical review, a 28 year-old man in Lane County with a chronic illness, had his medication denied by his cosplan as being ineffective. This was a major dispute between the consumer's doctors, and the plans and the medical director. Both of whom appeared at the state fair hearing. The administrative law judge conducting the hearing had no idea which Doctor to believe. And ultimately asked the consumer to seek a third opinion from another infectious disease specialist. The whole process from hearing requests to seeing a third specialist took several months. And the consumer would have been much better served by going to IMR. Therefore, we urge DHCS to make an IMR available to all Medi-Cal Managed Care members so that beneficiaries' rights aren't dependent on what county they live in. With the shift in the Medi-Cal delivery system tomanaged care due to mandatory enrollment, it is critical that members throughout the state have access to medically necessary services in a fair and consistent manner. Given the uncertainty of federal regulations, and for conformity of Knox-Keene, we recommend codifying these changes in state statute. Thanks.

[{'start': 23, 'end': 36, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 382, 'end': 386, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Anne McLeod: Good afternoon, chairs and members of the committees, Anne McLeod, California Hospital Association, on behalf of all the hospitals in California. The new federal rule that Ms. Cantwell described was finalized in two parts as she indicated towards the end of her testimony. First, in May of 2016, and then a second set of provisions on January 17th, 2017, three days before the inauguration. The two rules will have a significant impact on how the hospital fee program will be implemented, but the provisions in that second rule are even more damaging for that program. The Medi-Cal program fails to cover the cost of treating Medi-Cal patients in hospitals by more than $8 billion a year. The hospital fee program is used to draw down those unclaimed federal funding, those dollars, to help mitigate less than half of that massive shortfall. Nearly every general acute care hospital or hospital system benefits from the hospital fee program, including public hospitals, rural hospitals, and all safety net hospitals. The funding follows the patient. Therefore, there are several methods for making payments, including fee for service, supplemental payments, and as Mary Cantwell mentioned, managed care supplemental payments. The managed care plans, over the last eight years, have been very good partners in helping get these payments to the hospitals that treat the Medi-Cal patients. The current method of making these supplemental payments through the Medi-Cal managed care plans is not aligned with the requirements in the final rules. They are considered pass through payments, and they must be phased out starting July 1, 2017, just a few short months away. As pass through payments are phased out, they can be replaced with an allowable directed payment. These directed payments can be an add-on to the adjudicated claims by a fixed amount or a flat percent. And quite frankly, it's really not much different than how we are passing through the dollars now. But this nuance creates two significant problems that we want you to be aware of. First, the final rule states that these allowed directed payments can only be made to network providers. This will impact the ability to make a supplemental payment for all Medi-Cal patients. Even non-contracted or out of network patients that receive care in a children's hospital, or a tertiary care hospital that provides some of the highest acuity and specialty care to children or others with extremely complex health issues. These payments on an annual basis are potentially about $2 billion a year, or about 20% of the entire hospital fee program. If we can't find a solution for this problem, it'll be difficult for CHA to support this funding strain continuing. The second issue, the directed payments must be made on current adjudicated claims rather than utilizing, than using utilization trends to calculate a lump sum payment. And while we don't anticipate, there being much of a change about the distribution among the hospitals of the payments. It does raise a number of questions on how we resolve related to ensuring that hospitals are not at risk for excess directive payments made to the health plans, and how health plans are not at risk for making directed payments if they haven't had the funds allocated by the department. Let me give you an example. If funds are allocated to a health plan based on historic utilization of say, 100,000 medical impatient days, and the plan only experiences 75,000 days in that period, the plan will be holding excess funds with no ability to get those funds to the hospitals. Those funds represent hospital dollars matched with federal funds. It is not state money, it is the hospital fee program and the federal dollars. This guessing game could result in hundreds of millions of dollars being at risk to hospitals. Another scenario that CHA can't support. On the flip side of that example, the health plan could actually experience more utilization. Let's say they experienced 125,000 inpatient days, yet they only received funds to cover 100,000 inpatient days. The plan could be at risk for making those payments as directed by the Department of Healthcare Services. And again, CHA does not support putting the plans at financial risk to pass this dollars through. Our current contracted requirement for medical loss ratios on dental managed care is 70%. And so certainly we anticipate a shift to 85% potentially having significant impacts. We actually commented on this issue, when CMS released the rule in draft form. Because we were very concerned about the concept of taking a minimum MLR that really was developed for a full scope coverage program. And applying that to a specialized program like dental. In the 20s and 30s and 40s, not in the hundreds of dollars. And so the fixed cost of administration don't go down that much compared to the total cost of the services. So you actually expect an MLR to be lower than what you would expect from a full service plan. So we are concerned about the potential impact on our dental managed care plans and sustainability of that. And what impact it might have on their rates, since again, we're going to have to use the MLR to target an 85% in the rate setting. And so we're going to continue with our dental manage care plans on what that might mean for them and how we will comply with that part of the rule. The second is choice counseling and enrollment assistance to help them understand what are their plan options and to help them select a plan. And finally, the third requirement is to provide assistance for those who access long-term services and support through managed care. They really made these changes that's probably the one example where they were fairly consistent with the Medicare program as well as the private marketplace. So those key changes include beneficiaries being able to file a grievance at any time. Currently for us, we require that to happen within 180 days. One of the most significant changes for both plans and beneficiaries is that the rule actually requires that a beneficiary go through the plan's appeal process before they can go to a state fair hearing. The way that we operate currently in California, they can do that. They can do both simultaneously, or they can just do a state fair hearing. Plans are limited to one level of appeal only, and then there are certain timeframes that were shortened for how quickly plans must resolve appeals. 30 days for resolution of standard appeals and 72 hours for expedited appeals. Sarah Brooks: Good afternoon. Sarah Brooks, Deputy Director over Healthcare Delivery Systems at the Department Of Health Care Services. As Ms. Cantwell mentioned, I'll talk today about network adequacy and its applicability to our delivery systems as is set forth in the final role. I want to clarify that the effective dates for these requirements is July 1 of 2018. And so we will be continuing to work on these in the near future. With regards to network adequacy, the final rule sets forth requirements, but provides flexibilities to states to develop standards, as long as certain considerations are made when setting those standards. In developing the standards that we've proposed, our thinking is that it is important to set a floor that plans must meet but at the same time, provide for reasonable, timely access to care for beneficiaries. We've developed these standards with the beneficiaries and plans in mind. Our priority is to promote access to services that beneficiaries will need while balancing the plans ability to meet them as well. We carefully consider the plans existing networks and the reality of providers that actually exist in the state when setting them. We are also aiming to set standards that are not complex and are easy to understand and measure. As Ms. Cantwell noted earlier, these requirements apply to all four areas of the delivery systems as well. For Medical managed care and dental manage care health plans, California already has network adequacy standards in place today. You'll hear a little bit from our partners at DMHC later today about that. Both for time and distance, and timely access. These standards are set forth in both knox keene regulations. But and also, in contracts between managed care and dental managed care health plans and the Department of Health Care Services. For county specialty mental health plans, network standards do not currently exist and thus, it will take a little more work for these systems in the department to implement network adequacy standards for them. For DMCODS health plan that Ms. Cantwell talked about earlier, we will utilize network adequacy standards per the requirements under the waiver as we initially implement them and they roll out in California. The final rule does require network adequacy standards in a number of areas we establish. They'd be established for primary care, specialty care, hospital, OB-GYN, behavioral health, pharmacy, pediatric, dental. And also for LTSS services that are required when beneficiaries are actually travelling to providers, as opposed to when providers are travelling to beneficiaries. The department recently released a final role network adequacy proposal that is out for stakeholder comment right now. Ms. Leirman mentioned it earlier. Comments are due today, however we do continue to welcome feedback. When setting the proposed standards in the department's network adequacy proposal, we first considerd standards that already existed today. So we looked at knox keene standards, we looked at what was included in our contracts with our Medical managed care plans and our dental managed care plans, and we looked at what was included in the 1115 waiver. Whenever possible, we really mirrored those standards. So we kept in place the standards, or we proposed the standards that are already in place today to continue under our proposal. Those standards include for Medical managed care and dental managed care plans, primary care, and hospital time and distance standards. And then primary care specialist mental health and pharmacist timely access for non urgent appointments as applicable. When setting any new standards prescribed in the final rule, when we didn't have standards already in place, we considered a number of different things. Many of them are required by CMS. And examples of those are expected enrollment and utilization of services, characteristics and needs of specific populations. Number and types of network providers, and geographic location of network providers. In addition, we also considered other factors such as Medicare standards, we utilized geo-mapping and looked at state medical board data. We also took a look at what current alternate access standards have been submitted to the department entity and may see for consideration purposes. When developing our core specialist list, we considered the specialists that are most critically used and also the reality of what specialists are available across the state in California. We excluded facility-based specialists such as anesthesiologists because time and distance standards really don't make sense and really are not applicable to them. The final rule requires network adequacy standards for LTSS services, when the beneficiary is traveling to the provider. So in this instance for example, IHSS, MSSP services, we wouldn't set standards, because the provider is going to the beneficiary. We also did not set standards when the beneficiary was residing at a facility such as a skilled nursing facility because the beneficiary, again, was not traveling to the provider. I also wanted to touch on the fact that there is an ability, as Ms. Leirman mentioned, to have alternative access standards requested. So we do work in partnership with the Department of Managed Healthcare to approve this alternative access standards. This would occur in a place such as a rural area, where there just simply aren't providers. Or there aren't certain types of specialists available, and so we are able to approve separate standards than what is set forth in the core standard requirements. I want to talk a little bit about monitoring today, so how do we make sure that the plans actually meet these requirements, and how will we do so moving forward? We will continue to build on our existing processes to monitor our plans as we implement these additional requirements. Examples of what we do today include plan submission of their provider networks. They submit grievances and appeal reports ombudsman and state for a hearing reports, we work with them on corrective action plans. And more recently, we have started to work with our independent entity, our External Quality Review Organization or EQRO, to do quarterly surveys of timely access for our providers with our health plans. I want to note that DHCS will also have to annually certify our networks to CMS, that's something that Ms. Cantwell will need to sign off on when it is submitted to the federal government. But, and we will collect data annually, so that we can make sure the individual plans continue to meet those network adequacy standards so that she can sign off on them. One way that DHCS does intend to monitor health plan compliances through a new system that we have built, called the managed care provider file. This new system collects data monthly from our health plans through an automated system that will reject data if it is not accurate. It collects full information about health plan networks down to the delegated level, and allows us to collect information about provider panel size and whether or not they are open or closed. It also provides automatic reports about individual and all health plan performance in compliance with network adequacy standards. This is a new system that we really have just recently implemented and we're really excited about all of the opportunities that it will provide for us. Findings from this system and from our monitoring program will be included in the managed care program report that we will submit to CMS annually. This is a requirement that is set forth in the final rule. And this report will be made publicly available on our website along with postings of our network adequacy standard which is also required in the final rule. Our proposal as I mentioned is currently out for public comment and it includes additional detail than what I talked about today. We welcome stakeholder feedback on it. Thank you for the opportunity to talk with you and we're happy to answer any questions.

Marta Green: Thank you. So as you said, my name is Marta Green. I'm the Chief Deputy Director of the Department of Managed Health Care. I want to thank you all for having us here today. The DMHC license and regulate health plans that provide coverage to more than 25 million Californians. We regulate the vast majority of commercial plans and the majority of the medical managed care plans in California. Our mission is to protect consumers' healthcare rights and ensure a stable healthcare delivery system. We do this by administering the Knox-Keene Act. There are many topics in the Knox-Keene Act, but two of the big ones are network adequacy and financial reporting. And those are the two that the Committee staff has asked me to touch on today. So first, I'll talk about network adequacy. Plans provide to the DMHC, information on their networks in a variety of ways. A critical among those is the plan's annual network submissions. Plans submit their entire network to the DMHC on March 31st of each year. And this report also includes the results of all grievances related to networks throughout the year. All health plan policies and procedures must comply with the geographic standards set forth in the Knox-Keene Act. Specifically, 15 miles and 30 minutes for access to primary care physicians. And there's a list of types of physicians that fall under that category for the DMHC, as well as to hospitals from either their home or their workplace. Some health plans do request alternative access standards for many of the reasons that we've talked about here today. And we analyzed those alternative access standards against permitted justifications in the act. And that can be such as a lack of practicing providers in a specific geographic region. Generally, all our alternative access standards are limited to specific affected zip codes. For all other provider types, so non-primary care, non-hospital, the Knox-Keene Act requires that all health plans provide reasonable access. So to identify reasonable access, we look at access to specialists at a specific plan and compare that to all other plans that operate in that similar geographic region. As well as access standards or benchmarks that are generally accepted in the marketplace, such as the Medicare access standards. So to perform this analysis we used software, as does everybody these days. And we use a Geographical Information System, or GIS system software, to map the distances that enrollees must travel for a large number of provider types. So the primary care providers we look at include family practice, general practice, internal medicine, OBGYN, and pediatrics. We looked at a very wide array of specialty types, I won't name them all, but they do include psychiatry, HIV-AIDS specialists, mental health professionals, and hospital based providers. Our software also maps the location of hospitals, in-patient hospice facilities, ambulatory surgical clinics, and urgent care locations. Another important aspect of our network adequacy review is our timely access standards. These standards require health plans to maintain provider networks sufficient to ensure that people can get a timely access to an appointment. The requirements are based on the individual's specific clinical condition, and they set forth certain standards for types of appointments. So 48 hours for urgent care when no prior authorization was required. All of the way up to 15 days for non-urgent appointments with a specialty physician or other ancillary providers. So to demonstrate compliance, health plans conduct an annual telephone survey of the providers to assess availability of appointments. This information has then compiled together into a report given to the DMHC. We review the report, issue findings regarding the data, and make recommendations for changes. Unfortunately, the DMHC's 2015 report issued earlier this year, stated that the DMHC was unable to determine whether health plans met the timely access standards due to significant inaccuracies in the data. The report also detailed a number of next steps for health plans in the DMHC, to design to improve the accuracy of the data reporting so that we will have a better report next year. These steps do include some data validation steps, vendor requirements, as well as some enforcement investigations. Last week, we held a stakeholder meeting with plans, providers, other interested parties, to discuss these next steps. The next topic I've been asked to address is the DMHC's role in ensuring health plans meet the affordable care act's Medical Loss Ratio, or MLR, for short requirements. So to ensure that consumers receive value for their premium dollar, the Affordable Care Act and California State law require commercial health plans to meet certain MLR requirements. So health plans offering coverage in the individual and small group market must spend at least 80% of premium revenue on clinical services and activities that improve health care quality. And health plans in the large group market must meet an 85% standard. That means that health plans are limited in the percent of premium revenue that they can spend on administrative costs or profit. Health plans that fail to meet these Medical Loss Ratio requirements must provide rebates to consumers. I won't get into the details of what falls into each category, but if you have questions about what's in the clinical and what's in health care quality, versus what's in administration profit, I'm happy to go over that. So since the new requirements were enacted, California consumers have received a total of 206 million in rebates for the five reporting years of 2011 to 2015. This breaks down to a total of 64 million in rebates for the individual market. 139 million in rebates for the small group market, and 3 million in rebates for the large group market. We can audit health plans for compliance with the Medical Loss Ratio requirements for commercial coverage. We review their reporting that comes into the DMHC, and we determine whether or not to conduct an audit based upon that reporting. So, for an example, if a Medical Loss Ratio report came into the DMHC that was very, very close to the threshold, that may trigger an audit. When we conduct a Medical Loss Ratio examination, a health plan must submit a significant amount of data, which the DMHC reviews to verify the plan's representations on the reporting form. We review the validity of the data on expenses and premiums including the appropriateness of plan allocations for expenses, taxes, and revenues. And reviews the allocation and classification of expenditures for quality improvement activities. We can, under state law, require a health plan to pay an additional rebate to consumers if the examination identifies the plan inaccuracies. We have completed three Medical Loss Ratio examinations since reporting began, and we're in the process of completing three more. Now, we post the final reports of all Medical Loss Ratio exams on our website. In addition to our Medical Loss Ratio of commercial plans, we have historically performed some limited Medical Loss Ratio work on behalf of the Department of Health Care Services through an inter-agency agreement. This inter-agency agreement is set to terminate on June 30th of this year. This concludes my prepared remarks. And I'm happy to answer questions.

Jessie Ryan: Good morning, Jessie Ryan, Executive Vice President for the Campaign for College Opportunity, a California-based nonprofit dedicated to ensuring that more students have access to college, and succeed in college. I could have easily become a statistic. As the daughter of a struggling single welfare mother, having attended eight schools between kindergarten and high school, I've viewed a college education as my ticket out of poverty. And like the vast majority of students in the state, I saw community college as an affordable way to access my college dreams. When I arrived at Sacramento City College, eager to begin my college journey, I was immediately ushered into a room, where I was told to take an assessment test. I hadn't prepared for the test, I'd skipped breakfast that morning. I was flustered from a missed bus connection, and was totally unaware that this high-stakes test could, effectively, determine my academic future. I passed the English assessment with flying colors, but was told that I placed into elementary algebra. I was dejected. I still remember the sinking feeling as I was handed a list of the several remedial math courses I would need to take before arriving at a college credit-bearing course that would actually count towards my degree. As a non-math major that only needed a single statistics class before transferring, the idea of adding three semesters of non-college credit-bearing math to my pathway left me seriously contemplating, as so many students do, giving up. As Paul Steenhausen shared, the reality is, frustrated by their placement, each year, thousands of students placed into remediation never show up for classes. However, I was lucky. With the support of a counselor, I managed to skip my required remedial math sequence and enroll directly in a statistics class, where I worked hard, earned a B+, and became part of only 4% of community college students that will successfully transfer within 2 years. Unfortunately, of the 80% of California community college students required to take remediation, less than a quarter will persist and, ultimately, successfully complete college-level English or math. This is astonishing, particularly when research shows that students just like me, who skipped their remedial assignments, do just as well in gateway courses as those who took remediation first. As Katie's testimony illuminates, remedial classes are a huge stumbling block on the way to a degree. But there's innovation occurring that bucks these troubling dynamics. Some phenomenal faculty across the state are leading efforts to fix the broken remedial education system. While there's broad awareness of the problem of remediation and its implication for students, colleges, and the cost to the state, the student perspective of this experience is not well understood. Any effort to improve the success of underprepared students must begin with an understanding of their experience. Each year, the campaign for College Opportunity trains a cadre of community college students, known as the Completion Core. For years, these students have identified reforming remedial education as among their top priorities. They've described their remedial education path as a game of chutes and ladders, with multiple slides, turns, and exit points along the way. Completion Core students share that community college students overwhelmingly enter a community college expecting to achieve their academic goal within two years. Lengthy remedial education sequences only add to frustration, and promote a feeling that community college is not, in fact, a college experience, but a high school redo. Many view basic skills math and English classes as, and this is a quote from students, where students go to die, and lament standardized testing that doesn't account for past academic success. Take, for instance, Olivia Light, a first-generation college student, who went directly from high school to a California State University, where she assessed into college level math. After her parents lost their home, due to financial hardships, she returned to her local community college to help her family get back on their feet. Olivia had to take yet another assessment test. But this time she was told that she had failed her math assessment and would need to retake algebra. Olivia was devastated, having completed algebra 2 successfully, with a B, in high school. She asked the community college if they could simply accept the results of her previous assessment, and was told no. She was distraught, explaining that she didn't get the disconnect that Senator Pan was talking about. How could multiple assessments yield different results? Why didn't her successful completion of high school courses and her GPA land her into college-level math? Like many students, Olivia decided this process was not student-centered. But she resigned herself that she would have to take a few years longer before she would achieve her dream of a college degree. Lula Matute on the other hand, the daughter of Hondurian immigrants, having completed all her high school math requirements, was totally demoralized after placing into the lowest level of remedial math. Brian Leahy: Good morning, Senator Wieckowski and Members of the Committee. I am Brian Leahy, Director of the Department of Pesticide Regulation. I am here alongside Teresa Marks, the Chief Deputy Director of DPR, and Randy Segawa, Special Advisor to the Department and lead staff in this regulation. I have to tell you that every single word in this pages I am about to read has been gone over a few times to do it justice. I am simply going to read it, and then we can deal with the questions and what not. So, thank you for this opportunity to discuss the department's proposed regulation that we create a state-wide standard to provide an extra margin of safety around public K-12 schools and licensed childcare facilities, as pesticides are applied by their neighboring farms. We refer to these facilities as school sites. I will give a brief overview of the Department of Pesticide Regulation and how pesticides are regulated in California and the role of science in that process, then address specific questions of how the proposed regulation was developed, which stakeholders were consulted, and why the proposed regulation is health protective. We have recently received additional questions associated with the background material and we will be providing a written response to those questions as soon as possible. Nearly 40 years ago, I converted our family farm to an all-organic operation. Since then, California has made remarkable progress in how agricultural pesticides are applied. The Department of Pesticide Regulation is one of the most comprehensive, is the most comprehensive state pesticide regulatory program in the nation. Within our department are more than 300 scientists who are experts in everything from toxicology through environmental science. Our mission is to protect human health and the environment by assuring proper and safe use of pesticides essential in a modern society to protect public health, food supply and effective resource management. We also foster reduced-risk pest management. Before any pesticide can be sold or used in California, it first has to be registered by US EPA, and then registered by my department after a comprehensive evaluation of studies and a determination that its use, according to labor requirements, will not result in undue harm to human health or the environment. In addition, even after pesticides are registered for use in California, we continuously evaluate them for potential impacts to field workers, pesticide applicators, by-standers, the public, and the environment. We pay particular attention to the most vulnerable groups like children. This includes, assessments of acute exposure, chronic exposure, sub-chronic exposure, and lifetime exposure to monitoring and surveillance. Our scientists also review published peer-review literature. DPR monitors for pesticides in the air, water, and produce. We also track illnesses that may have been related to pesticide exposure, tracking and investigating pesticide illnesses provides important information to the department and assists us in making advances in pesticides safety. Important contributions to the improved application of pesticides have been made through education, licensing, and enforcement. All commercial applicators of agricultural pesticides are required to have a license in California. Education of applicators and farm workers is a critical component in promoting safe and effective pesticide practices. And of course, enforcement is a mainstay of any effective regulatory program. Our partnership with California's County Agricultural Commissioners to enforce pesticides use laws is unique in the nation. When I first became Director of DPR, I spent a lot of time out in the community, visiting farm workers, farmers, applicators, community members. I sat with individuals in their homes and yards, I visited schools and listened to their concerns. I contracted with the University of California to organize a series of workshops in In the summer of 2015, DPR hosted 15 workshops in five communities to discuss regulation concepts related to pesticides in schools. We listened to numerous stakeholders, both informally and formally in developing the proposed regulation, including school administrator organizations, health agencies, NGOs, labor unions, farmers, and pesticide organizations. DPR receive comments on regulation concepts from several thousand people, and those comments were instrumental in forming the basis of the proposed regulation. Some of the takeaways from these meetings were good communications and information between growers and their neighbors can help resolve conflict. Pesticide applicators are generally very responsible and take due care when applying pesticides near school sites. Schools and childcare facilities may not have the necessary information to prepare for and respond to a pesticide drift incident. Although some counties have ordinances governing pesticide use near school sites, there is a great need for a consistent, statewide standard for all agricultural pesticide applications near school sites in California. There were also concerns raised by recent studies about pesticide use AND community health. DPR scientists had already reviewed these studies including the California Department of Public Health's report entitled "Agricultural Pesticide Use Near a Public School in California," which focuses on the amount of pesticides useD near schools. We found these studies be useful, and we will continue to evaluate them in future research efforts. We asked for input from our county agricultural commissioners in order to better assess actual conditions on the ground. We surveyed county agricultural commissioners about the requirements and the conditions and effect when a farmer, adjacent to a public school, applied pesticides in their county. We looked at the effective practices used in reducing drift and the subsequent public concern. We also inquired of them as to what practices and approaches they thought could be effectively enforced. We evaluated our toxicity and exposure data, particularly recent air monitoring data, which indicates that the risk to children from agricultural pesticides applied near schools is low for most pesticides. This conclusion assumes compliance with current requirements in normal situations and does not account for exceptional circumstances or violations. DPR estimates that approximately 137,000 agricultural pesticide applications occur within one quarter mile of a school or daycare facility annually, 137,000. Given the large number of applications that occur around schools, the risk of potential exposure to children at schools, while small, is still present. Therefore, DPR decided to develop a regulation to provide an additional level of protection and address emergency preparedness issues for pesticide use near schools and childcare facilities. In other words, these regulations will provide an extra margin of safety for schools, in case something unexpected were to happen, for example a malfunction with the spray equipment or change in weather. And if an incident were to occur, these regulations would provide schools with information to assist them in appropriately responding to the emergency. The regulation published in September, 2016 included prohibitions on certain pesticide applications made within one quarter mile of a school site, Monday through Friday, during the hours between 6:00 AM and 6:00 PM. Certain other pesticide applications are prohibited within 25 feet or are not subject to restriction. That gets very detailed, we can go into it. The restriction will depend on the application equipment used, and the form of pesticide applied. The proposed regulation also requires the farmer to provide notification to his school site. The notification will provide, sufficient information to the effective school sites by identifying which pesticides will be applied and where, and who will make the application within a quarter mile the school site. To address local conditions, the proposed regulation includes an option for a written agreement between the farmer, school, and commissioner for alternative application requirements to achieve the same or increase levels of protection. DPR held three formal hearings for the regulation during the comment period. The comment period was extended beyond the required 45 days to 70 days to allow for additional pubic participation and ended on December 9th, 2016. DPR received comments from approximately 19,000 people, and is considering revisions to the proposed regulation based on the comments. DPR is in the process of evaluating and responding to the comments. DPR anticipates completing the rule making process and having the regulation adopted in the fall of 2017. Finally, I would like to make some key points about the proposed regulation. The purpose is to build an additional level of safety into existing systems by putting prohibitions on pesticide applications with the potential for drift during the hours when children are normally present and by establishing an additional buffer zone for the other applications. It also forces communications between farmers and their school neighbors. It simply makes it more difficult to create an unacceptable pesticide exposure at a school site. The current regulatory requirements for pesticide applications near schools vary from county-to-county and are primarily designed to prevent unacceptable exposures from normal pesticide use. The purpose of this proposed regulation is to one, provide minimum statewide standards for all agricultural pesticide applications near public K-to-12 schools and licensed childcare facilities. Two, provide an additional margin safety, in case of unintended drift or when other problems with application occurs. Three, increase communications between growers and schools and child care facilities. And four, provide information to assist schools and childcare facilities in preparing for and responding to pesticide emergencies. This regulation will add an additional layer of protection for children, while recognizing the needs of farmers. We believe it will provide Californians with the most robust protection in the nation for school children when agricultural pesticides are applied near their schools. And with that, thank you for this opportunity, and we will entertain questions.

Tony Linegar: Excuse me, thank you, Chair Wieckowski and Members of the Committee. My name is Tony Linegar. I'm the Agricultural Commissioner in Sonoma County. And I'm here today representing the California Agricultural Commissioners and Sealers Association. County Ag Commissioners have been in existence since 1881. We act as an arm of the state enforcing state laws in regulations at the county level. So, we're acting an extension of the California Department of Food and Agriculture, as well as are partners at DPR, the Department of Pesticide Regulation. As such, we are the local authority with the responsibility for enforcing pesticide laws and regulations. We have a responsibility to protect the public health and the environment, as well as agricultural workers from adverse impacts of pesticide use. We take this responsibility very seriously. We work very closely with our state partners at DPR. DPR provides us with technical support, training, and oversight of our local enforcement activities. Together, we administer the most comprehensive pesticide regulatory program in the country, if not in the world. The regulatory program at the county level is a very robust program that includes permitting for restricted materials, training for applicators, inspections, investigations, and enforcement. We rely on DPR's technical expertise to assess the risks that are associated with the use of these materials, and to promulgate science-based regulations designed to protect public health and the environment. We also rely on DPR registration branch to evaluate the pesticides prior to their use in California. So, the Ag Commissioner service to boots on the ground in the 58 counties throughout the State We provide input to DPR on regulatory issues with our knowledge and experience in the field. This is a vital relationship, as any good regulation must consider the farming practices involved, and the practical application of such regulations in the field. In mid 2014, after the release of the California Department of Public Health's report, and with more attention being paid to this issue particularly on the central coast, we began to discuss amongst commissioners what different counties were doing in terms of conditioning restricted materials for pesticide use around schools. Commissioners do have the authority to add site-specific permit conditions for the use of restricted materials. The application of these materials is also time specific, which gives the Commissioner an opportunity to perform an inspection of the application. This ability allows the Commissioner and his or her staff to take into account the site-specific conditions and to tailor the permit for the use of these materials to account for the pesticide that's applied and the particular conditions on the ground. Such considerations include proximity to specific sensitive sites including schools, residences, water courses, the specific formulation of the pesticide, the weather conditions at the proposed time of application, the topography of the surrounding area, the timing, and the type of equipment used to apply the material. Commissioners recognize the value of applying the site-specific conditions that allow them to more appropriately address and mitigate any potential impacts. Through our initial conversations amongst commissioners, we recognized that ideally we would have a minimum standard statewide amongst counties with regard to restricted material permitting conditions. We also understood the importance of having the ability to condition a permit, to address the site-specific conditions on the ground. DPR releases suggested permit conditions for certain restricted materials, however commissioners also have the discretion to tailor those conditions to mitigate risk for the unique site and local situation. In late 2014, DPR put together a small group of Ag commissioners representing the different areas of the state to begin discussing regulatory concepts around this issue. Since commissioners do not have authority to condition the use of nonrestricted materials, we all recognized that the only way to have a statewide standard for pesticide use around schools is that it must come through regulation. We discussed the different approaches in consideration of the feedback that had been received at the public workshops. DPR conducted a survey of ag commissioners to determine just how common were drift or exposure incidents related to schools. The survey looked at a three year period from 2011 to 2014. Of all the pesticide complaints received by the 39 responding counties, only two violations were associated with agricultural pesticide use near schools. Neither of which resulted in an illness. Conversely, there where eight violations associated with applications taking place on the school grounds. Although the survey did not indicate a significant problem, we understood the importance of responding to the public's concern by building in an extra level of safety into the existing regulations. We also understood the benefit of increasing and improving the communication between the school and the farmers adjacent to the school. The result is the draft regulation released by DPR that we are here to discuss today. We believe the proposed regulation provides an additional layer of safety for children from pesticide exposure at schools. DPR not only looked at the toxicity of the materials, but also considered the formulation and the application method, as those all play a role in determining the potential for drift. After careful analysis, DPR proposed to prohibit applications during school hours that pose the greatest potential for drift. Our State Association supports the proposed regulation requirements to the degree that it provides uniformity and an additional layer of regulatory protection for schools. Although the occurrence of drift incidents is extremely low, based upon a recent survey conducted by DPR, we feel that these regulations will further reduce potential for drift related incidents. Most growers have already adopted these practices of not spraying near schools during school hours. So this aspect of the regulation will not have a tremendous impact on those growers. The area of greatest concern from a regulatory perspective is the 48 hour notification, and a few references have been made to that. Administration of this requirement will be logistically challenging, time consuming, and will take valuable resources away from high priority enforcement activities. Since the applications most prone to drift have already been prohibited during school hours, we believe there is limited value to providing notification for applications that are not prone to drift. We believe that public resources should be dedicated to efforts that have demonstrated value for reducing risk to benefit public safety for school children, farm workers, and the environment. Thank you.

The proposed regulations put forth by the Department of Pesticide Regulation are a crucial step in insuring that all students in California are protected from agricultural pesticides while at school. But they do pose a variety of both environmental and public health risks. To that end, California has been, for decades, at the forefront of pesticide controls, safety, and research. But despite these efforts, pesticide incidents do still occur and can pause a risk to the public's health. Pesticides have well documented impacts on human health. Historically, these health concerns have centered largely, as has been mentioned here, on emergency pesticide illnesses and acute effects. In the case of acute pesticide poisonings, individuals can experience anything from mild symptoms to, in more serious cases, even death. These impacts, however, are generally fast acting and visible, so they can be clearly linked to specific pesticide exposures. In response to these kinds of high-profile incidents and increased public concerns, regulatory approaches have been implemented to prevent incidents of acute pesticide illness. Increasingly, however, public health research has also shown that repeated exposures to low level pesticides contribute to chronic negative health effects. Associations have been demonstrated between living in proximity to agricultural pesticide use and cancer Neurological disease, respiratory impacts, birth outcomes, and other adverse conditions in human populations. Ongoing research being carried out in California's Salinas Valley and elsewhere. Important to our understanding of how living in close proximity to pesticide may increase adverse health outcomes. Particularly among children both prenatally and through early life exposures. This research has shown decreases in cognitive functioning in young children living near agricultural or pesticide applications. And in young children who may have been exposed prenatally. Unlike acute illness resulting from pesticide poisoning this chronic health outcomes maybe multi factorial and not occurring until many years after the exposure. Any cause effect, that relationship between the pesticides and these chronic illnesses would not be readily apparent. We also know that living in agricultural communities can place populations at risk for pesticide exposures. Not only farm workers handling pesticides or working in the fields are exposed. Research has shown that agricultural pesticide residues can be detected in nearby homes and rural communities. We also know that the children in general are most susceptible to health effects of pesticides exposure. Relative to their body weight children eat, drink, and breathe more than adults increasing their exposure to environmental hazards on a pound for pound basis. Children often exposed are also exhibit behaviors that increase their risk for pesticide exposures. Playing outside, putting objects into their mouth, and spending time crawling around on the ground. Finally, children are maturing and their physiology, and in particular their brain development undergo rapid precisely choreographed changes. Toxic exposures during this time may interrupt to critical developmental milestones leading to long term damage. In April of 2014, the California Department of Public Health released a report estimating the pounds of pesticide used to Jason public schools. For 15 agricultural counties in California in 2010 which was the most recent year at that time for which data was available for the study. The purpose of the study was to characterize pesticide use near public schools for agricultural counties in California. Incorporating the best publically available geospatial data of the time. The program mapped the boundaries of school properties and with assistance from the Department of Pesticide Regulation and county agricultural commissioners. Agricultural field boundary data were obtained from 13 of the 15 counties. When combined with the records of pesticide applications through the pesticide use reports data collected by DPR. This allowed us to better pinpoint where pesticide applications had occurred. Using the intersection of pesticide use records and field location data, we were able to estimate the pounds of pesticides applied within a one quarter mile buffer around each school. The quarter mile buffer was used for this hazard assessment because it was the most common buffer size cited in county restrictions already in place on pesticide use near schools. And because it is the most common buffer used in published studies. This hazard assessment did not measure pesticide drift nor does it protect or predict pesticide exposure. The assessment was done to provide better data on potential pesticide hazard near schools. The assessment found out of 2500, 64% or about 1600 schools had no pesticide use within a quarter mile in 2010. While 36% of schools around 900 schools, had some pesticide use within that same buffer. Of the top 5% of schools with any use nearby, this was 45 school affecting over approximately 35,000 students. Pesticide use range from 2,600 pounds to 28,000 pounds. Overall Hispanic children are 91% more likely than white children to attend to school in the highest quartile of agricultural pesticide use. Across the 15 counties assessed, three fumigants were the most heavily used pesticides within the quarter mile buffer. Chloropicrin, 1,3 dichloropropene and methyl bromide, all three compounds are classified as classic air contaminants. 1,3 dichloropropene is a potential human carcinogen and methyl bromide is classified as a reproductive and developmental toxicant. Of the top 10 most commonly used pesticides near schools nine have a half life in the range of days to months. Six of the 10 remaining chemicals are active for 50 days or longer. All of these findings were documented in detailed and the report as well as break down of pesticides. Pesticides use new schools for each of those 15 county.

Uniform buffers are problematic, as supported in a recent 9th Circuit Court of Appeals opinion, which affirmed the position of the US EPA. Which stated that uniform buffers are not an appropriate standard for the use of crop protection products. Furthermore, the existing scientific research and review process accounts for potential off target movement of a product. And labels instruct operators to apply products in a manner that avoids drift. The potential for DRIFT is scientifically modeled and appropriate label restrictions are implemented in order to address and mitigate this issue. An arbitrary one size a buffer does not reflect specific items like influencers like wind direction, physical barriers and also a lot of new technology that our growers continue to use and are bringing more more into the field. Things like electrostatic or magnetic spray Machines. We also believe that the annual and application-specific notification have the real potential to cause unnecessary concern and confusion for schools and child daycare centers. When the annual notification and application-specific notifications are received. These notification requirements are also impractical and inflexible when we kind of look at how our operations work on a daily basis. As an example, the 48-hour application specific notification does not recognize the daily challenges growers routinely face when responding to or planning for forecasted weather events. Crop protection products are selected and applied in response to pest pressures, and again weather events, costs, logistics and many other factors in order to safeguard the crop from loss or to impede the spread of disease. It is critically important to be able to respond rapidly to the unique nature of each pest or disease problem in order to reduce the likelihood that additional applications need to be made. The 48-hour notice restriction ties the hands of the grower and puts California farms in a position of not being able to implement their pest and disease management plans. In closing, we believe that the existing federal and DPR registration and regulatory processes that utilize science to determine and address the risk of each pesticide product via the label, are working as intended. The result of this rule is likely to be many acres of land coming out of ag production in California. However, we do advocate that additional training and education about proper detection tools is always beneficial for both growers and schools. And that more substantial conversation really needs to occur regarding school site planning decisions and citing schools in agricultural zones. I want to thank you again for the opportunity this afternoon. And I welcome any questions.

Sonja Petek: Thank you, good afternoon, Mr. Chair and members, Sonja Petek from the Legislative Analyst's Office, you should have a copy of okay, great, the handout. I've been asked to present an LAO overview and perspective on the Developmental Services budget, and to that end my talk will have three parts. I'm going to first highlight some recent state and federal policies that are really moving this system into a consumer independence direction, more focused on consumer choice. I'll also talk about some of the resulting funding pressures from those policies. I'll then, second, talk about some other funding pressures on the system, some of which Nancy already mentioned. And then I will raise four issues for legislative consideration, including one of the items we were just talking about. So, if you'll turn to page one of our handout, I'm going to highlight three, I'm sorry, four policy areas that have had recent changes. The first being the HCBS home and community-based services waivers. As Nancy already mentioned, and as some of our members of the public have already talked about, these, the home and community-based services waivers provide significant funding to the Department. It's about 30% of the total department budget. And the new rules that the federal government passed in 2014, that the state has to be in compliance with by March 2019 exert financial pressures on the state. Not only is there the potential loss of significant federal funding, but there's also the cost associated with getting these service providers into compliance. The next policy area that I would mention is the closure of the developmental centers. While this is an action that will likely result in reduced cost to the state, it was also a move to try to further integrate consumers into the greater community. And again, while this may save the state money in the end, I'm now on page two, there are some funding pressures associated with the transitional phase. Namely, that the developmental center budget now relies much more heavily on the state's General Fund. In addition, there is the cost to develop community resources for people moving out of the developmental centers. A third area that has already been mentioned today is competitive integrated employment, CIE. And basically, CIE means that people have full- or part-time jobs in integrated settings, making the going wage, or the minimum wage, whichever is higher. Both state and federal law have moved in the direction of promoting CIE for people with developmental disabilities, and generally prohibit sub-minimum wage pay going forward. There will be some funding challenges associated with these changes when it comes to training and educating consumers to training them for jobs. And then also, once they have jobs, to provide job coaching and job support. Turning to page three, l'll just mentioned the last policy shift that we wanted to mention and which Nancy already brought up, which is self-determination. She provided degree description of what self-determination means and we just would like to note that while self-determination could in the end, end up saving the state money the transitional roll-out period may end up increasing costs, at least temporarily. If you turn to page 4 for the second part of my talk, I just wanted to mention some other funding pressures on the developmental services system at large. The first has to do with changes in the labor laws. And specifically, the increases to the state's minimum wage has put a pressure on the state. There's precedent for the Legislature to provide increased funding to cover service providers, staffing costs that are associated with paying staff the increased minimum wage. There are also other changes in labor laws. At the federal level, there was a law that limits the amount of unpaid overtime. And the Legislature did provide a rate increase for home care providers to cover those increased overtime costs. At the local level, about 20 cities around the state now have a minimum wage that's higher than the state's minimum wage. However, there is not precedent for the Legislature to systematically cover those increased staffing costs. It's more likely to come out as sort of individual consumer by consumer requests for additional funding by the service providers. And then lastly I just wanted to mention some demographic changes that are causing some funding pressures on the system, and Nancy did a good job describing many of these. Not only is there a rapidly rising overall growth in the consumer population, and it's outpacing overall state population growth. But on page five you'll note that there's the rising share of consumers with autism. And this has been shown on average to be the most expensive developmental disability to serve. There's a significant share of non-English speaking consumers. And consumers are living longer, which is a good thing, but it does come with increased costs. We have a chart at the bottom of page 5 showing the significant increases in consumer caseload growth as well as expenditures. And then, finally, I will bring up four issues for legislative consideration. The first we've already talked about a bit, but the LAO is concerned that the state could miss the compliance deadline for the new HCBS rules, the compliance deadline being 2019. Although the Department has made efforts in this area, we're concerned that service providers have not been given enough guidance about what compliance means or what they will have to do to get into compliance by that deadline. What we would recommend at this time is that the Legislature require the Department to provide more information about the nature of the requests that were made in the fall for the $15 million. And I want to put one thing into context. As Nancy mentioned, 900 service providers made requests for that funding. That is an impressive number but it's also only a fraction of the service providers around the state. And given that they requested $130 million, that's nearly nine times the amount of funding that was appropriated. So, this raises some concerns for us. We're thinking that the information they can provide about those requests could hopefully give a better sense of the extent and severity of non-compliance problems. And perhaps provide more information about what additional resources might be needed to get service providers into compliance. The next issue I want to discuss is the rate study. Last year the Legislature provided DDS with $3 million for a contractor to conduct a study of the rate structure and to provide recommendations for reform. The Department just issued a request for proposal. And within that RFP there is an activity that requires the winning contractor to provide recommendations about a rate maintenance process. We noted, as we read the RFP, that the rate maintenance process, we assume that that means recommendations for how to make adjustments to rates on an ongoing basis, but we note that it did not include consideration of economic conditions or other policy changes. And it's interesting because the current complexity and inflexibility of the rate structure is in large part due to those types of economic conditions and other policy changes. So the changes that were made during the recession. Or the changes that are made to account for increased state minimum wages. What we would recommend, we respect that the RFP has already been issued. The proposals are due in early April. So what we would recommend during this month before the proposals are due is that the Legislature ask the Department to provide more clarity about what rate maintenance means and discuss with prospective bidders that that process could include consideration of some of these economic conditions, regional market conditions or other policy changes, and how those may be included and considered in a rate maintenance process. The third issue that we would like to bring up is last year the Legislature appropriated some funding for the Department to create a fiscal and program research unit. The Department had requested the funding. We really think that this new unit can play a critical and crucial role as the system shifts toward a more consumer- oriented system of service delivery. Without being overly prescriptive, we recommend that the Legislature think about setting some more specific goals for the research unit so that it doesn't become overly focused on just responding to requests for information. And then lastly, to address the implementation of the rate increases from last year for the staff that spend at least 75% of their time providing direct care. We believe that the amount of time and the resources that it takes to implement, report, and enforce this rate increase has involved a significant amount of administrative work on the part of DDS, the service providers, and the community, and the regional centers. We think that the cost of implementing and enforcing this requirement may outweigh the benefit of having targeted the increase to begin with. Especially because a lot of the service providers are already limited in how much they can spend on administrative costs. We would note that requiring service providers to forfeit the increase if they don't meet that October 1st deadline sort of goes against the intent of the Legislature from last year. To increase funding for these service providers. Okay. Thank you.

Nancy Bargman: Good afternoon, I'm Nancy Bargman, the Director of the Department of Developmental Services. Thank you Chair, thank you members for allowing us to provide you an update on many of the issues that are before us today, in the proposed budget. I've been asked to provide you a little bit of an overview of our service delivery system. So, I'll go ahead and do that and then just jump right into issue one if that's okay. So, to give just an overview of our system, and we take a look at our very special system. It's something I think that we're all here to demonstrate, as far a very strong passion for what we do. But in California, we have a unique system. We have every individual who has a developmental disability in California's entitled to necessary services. I mean that's done through a number of different ways. So as far as the Department of Developmental Services, we move forward in providing the services to the individuals that we serve. We have over 300,000 individuals in our service delivery system today. We do so in two different ways. The first is through four state operated facilities, three of which are developmental centers. One is a community center, and then we also provide services through the 21 Regional Centers throughout the State of California. For our proposed budget for 17-18, we're proposing to update our budget to $6.9 billion. In this, it includes a projection that we're going to be serving about 317,000 individuals in California who have a developmental disability. Of which 42,000 are in our early start program. So that's for anybody who is under the age of three that's at risk for developmental disability. Regional Centers in California vary in size. We have our smallest Regional Centers that's serving approximately 3,700 individuals. Our largest Regional Center in this state is serving 32,000 individuals. We continue to see a significant amount of change in our service delivery system. To give you kind of way of background, the Lanterman Act is what we really operate under. The Lanterman Act is celebrated its 50 years of service this past year. Under the Lanterman Act, we're able to provide those services under the entitlement. Regional Centers contract and provide services directly to individuals in the community through their contract relationships with service providers. Currently, we have about 25,000 service providers in the state, well each individual provider may be providing a number difference services. So it doesn't represent the number of actual service delivery but the number of providers that are contracted with Regional Centers. Throughout the years, when we're taking a look at our service delivery system, it's important to look at how the services are changing. Because the trends in the services and the individuals that we're trying to meet their needs are also changing. When we take a look at our growth year-over-year over the last couple of years. We are seeing a growth in our service population, our consumer population, of about 12 to 13 thousand individuals per year. So when we take a look at the 21 Regional Centers, a midsize Regional Center is serving about 13 individuals. So we are growing as a system, almost a Regional Center a year. We're continuing to serve the individuals through the 21 Regional Centers without change. Over the past 10 years we've seen a 43% increase in the number of individuals that we're serving. We're also seeing that individuals are living longer and we're having a growing aging population. 10% of our population is over the age of 55. There's been a shift in the most populous ethnicity representation. 10 years ago, 41% of our consumer population was white. Today, 33% of our total consumer population is white. Where during the same time period, the change as far as our Hispanic consumer population has increased. It's increased from 33% to 38%, and has become our largest population of individuals that we serve through the Regional Center system today. We have also seen a significant increase with individuals who have autism diagnosis. In the last 10 years, we were seeing the change which was 18% 10 years ago. Today we're seeing 34% of our population are individuals with autism. We've also seen many changes but also challenges within our system. We are facing the closure of three developmental centers. Currently, we have Sonoma, Fairview and Porterville that are currently closing concurrently. We also have a requirement to be in compliance with the new federal guidelines that where we are been able to seek federal participation, home and community base services. You're going to here us references it as HCBS. So we have compliance requirements to achieve that by March to 2019. And so, you're going to hear more about that throughout your agenda today. We're also seeing challenges within our service delivery access to our underserved ethnic populations, to include inequity of funding. And we also see challenges in housing and employment. So, again, these are areas that we're going to be able to continue to discuss today and future discussions. Among those challenges we are also having many many opportunities. So we have seen with the approval of special session ABX21 funding, that we began to start addressing some of these challenges. Such as being able to more forward with the HCBS compliance, starting to address and try to move that needle forward to address the disparities in our inequity of funding. For our disparities in different ethnic groups. And also move forward initiatives with competitive integrated employment. We're also excited to continue to move forward within our federal application for Self-Determination Program. Self determination is California's only state that has a state law that we have to submit, which we did a couple years ago, an application for self determination. in which an individual can have management and responsibility of their own budget and make the choices that they choose to make. In the first three years, once we do receive approval of our application from the federal government. We'll be able to provide that opportunity for 2500 individuals in California. We also have seen significant amount of legislative support in our system. Currently, we have projected, in our community services budget. We're seeing that from 15-16 fiscal year to our proposed budget that we are proposing for 17-18, that there is an increase of $1.2 billion, if so approved. Because most of the drive within the growth in that 1.2 billion is really based on case load increases that I just references as far as our growth that we're seeing year over year. But also because of the funding was approved with ABX 21, we had nearly half a billion dollars that was approved to help our system. So if you don't mind, I'll go ahead and go into issue one and walk you through that.

Many years ago, not that you want to know my entire background, but I started in the field many years ago and also working at a Regional Center. During that time, it was back in the 90s, we had what was available to us at the timed program development fund. We used the funds to be able to help with startup with service providers to start new services. Could be residential, it could be day, it could be early intervention, it could be developing training, there's a number of items that was available to us. We also had, in our system, the ability within the Regional Centers, up to 2005, 2006, I may be off by about a year, one way or the other. But it's right around that time in which the Regional Centers had the ability to use part of their purchase of service dollars. They could earmark funds specifically for startup for community resources. Back in 05, 06, that was no longer available to them. During the time when they did have it, there was very specific startup protocols that they had to meet, that they had to submit to the department for review. So we would make sure that Regional Centers were in compliance with their startup protocols. So there's some assurance and accountability to the funds that were used for that purpose. 05, 06 was also about the time when community placement planned dollars were available. This is also in alignment with the closure of Agnew's developmental center. So, as we were moving forward with the change in policies where folks were moving from developmental centers to the community, there's a need to start developing resources that were going to meet the very complex needs of individuals. So, kind of fast forwarding then to 2012, in 2012, we had a change in statute that put a moratorium of placements of anybody going into a developmental center. At that time, when we had the moratorium in place, we had approximately between 100 and 200 individuals that weren't being admitted into the developmental centers at the time. So immediately, we need to provide supports in the community. We needed to develop the supports to make sure that our service delivery system was moving with the change of the needs of the individuals, complex medical needs, complex needs as far as related to behavior needs. So we had to do some things that were very different. The community placement plan at the time was earmarked only for individuals moving from developmental centers. So with the change of statute in 2012, when no longer could people be admitted to the developmental centers, we had to make some modifications to our CPP language that allowed for the development of resources. For individuals not only moving from a developmental center, but also for individuals what's called with challenging services needs. So we had a modification of CPP at that time to also move with changes within our policies. So again, moving forward, as we are now, we had announcement of closure of all of the developmental centers. We will have the closures completed no longer than 2021, but as we have folks that are moving into the community, we still have the need to be able to take a look at how are we developing our resources. So within the community, when you take a look at other than for folks that are moving out of developmental centers, individuals with very challenging services needs, there have not been community resources or funding to be able to start up new services outside of those parameters, really, since prior to 05, 06. So, in order to move forward with the policies, making sure that we're able to be responsive to our ever changing needs, we talked earlier about that we have a population that is aging. So we have a need to be able to support folks that are aging. We are seeing individuals with Down syndrome, with early onset of Alzheimer's and dementia. We also are seeing one of the fastest growing areas that we have in our community is the early start age. Are we developing the resources to meet the needs of the individuals? Within the early start growth and our intakes, we are seeing a very different population. We are seeing definitely a difference in the ethnic mix in making sure that we're responsive to developing new resources that are also changing within the needs of our community. So with that in mind, we're putting forward the trailer bill language to adjust the language and statute to allow the department to move forward with community placement planned funds. So as we are facing the end of closing the developmental centers, as we're meeting the priority of needs to move folks from institutes for mental diseases, that we're also able to attend to some of the other needs within the community. We have doubled, because of the closure, we're doubling the development of the housing. So to that end, we're looking for the positions to provide the oversight to make sure that the housing groups are in compliance with the requirements that we set forth to protect the investment of the state. And to have assurances that the homes will be in perpetuity for the individuals that we serve. And the four positions would be able to help us achieve the support of the growth that we're seeing.

[{'start': 35, 'end': 48, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Sean Hoffman: Morning, Mr. Chair, Sean Hoffman with the California District Attorney's Association. Many of you will recall last year, the committe considered Assembly bill 2477 which is very similar to the bill in front of you today. Although that bill contained no statute of limitations for the court retaining jurisdiction over the restitution. This bill has been narrowed to address the Committee concerns that were raised last year. We believe it strikes an appropriate balance between insuring that victims have preserved their constitutional right to restitution and preserving the defendant's due process rights. Assemblyman Patterson explained how this would work, but let me give you an example of why this is important. Let's say there's a case, a DUI involving injury. The defendant receives a sentence of two years probation. The victim has serious injuries that may require surgeries beyond those two years. Under existing law, the court would not have jurisdiction to modify the restitution in order to reflect the expenses incurred after the expiration of probation. If AB 194 were in place the court would retain jurisdiction for an additional three years for a total of five years post sentencing. To ensure that the victim is appropriately compensated for his or her injuries and the expenses incurred. This ensure three things. One that the victim with a valid claim diligently pursues that claim in a reasonable period time. The defendant does not lose any evidence that they could use to contest a false or stale claim. And that a long dormant claim doesn't do more cruelty than justice. So again, we think that this strikes an appropriate balance between preserving restitution and protecting those due process rights of the defendants. We appreciate the feedback and the work of the Committee staff and we ask for your aye vote. Thank you.
