Kathy Sher: Good morning, Kathy Sher on behalf of the ACLU of California. We oppose AB 194, because it extends the period during which a person convicted of a crime remains under court control. In some cases, far beyond the period of supervision set by the court at sentencing. In many cases, AB 194 would subject a defendant to a period of uncertainty that would many times over the period of probation set by the court. A defendant sentenced to one year of probation, for example, would then have four more years during which he could be called back into court and ordered to pay additional restitution, even after the amount initially determined and ordered had been fully paid off. This undermines the determination of the court as to the appropriate sentence and lessens the incentive for the prosecution and victim to determine in a timely manner, the amount of restitution to be requested where that cannot be determined at the time of sentencing. Existing law offers considerable flexibility. Under Penal Code Section 1203.3, the restitution order can be modified at any time while the defendant remains on probation in those cases where a defendant is sentenced to probation. That is a reasonable and workable limit that appropriately balances the victims interest in receiving full restitution with the interest of both sides in reaching a point of finality in a reasonable period of time. For these reasons, we respectfully ask for your no vote. Thank you.

Sophie Cabrera: Good afternoon, Sophie Cabrera, Department of State Hospitals, Program Director for the Enhanced Treatment Program. Along with the provisions of 1340, there are very specific requirements. Under 1340, there's a distinct referral process. The ETP is going to be at two locations, Atascadero and at Patton, but will accept placements from all five hospitals around the state. The referral is made from the home hospital by the psychiatrist or psychologist and treatment team It's sent to the supervisor within clinical operations for review of the packet. It's assigned to a designated forensic evaluator who would do an initial assessment of that patient and make a recommendation to what is the forensic needs assessment panel which is comprised of a Psychiatrist, a Psychologist, and a Medical Director to determine the patient's appropriateness for the ETP. If what's called the FNAP certifies that patient for the ETP it is for up to one year. That referral is sent to a forensic needs assessment psychologist, who does an in-depth violence risk assessment, and then with the ETP treatment team, developes a treatment program. Those patients that are certified for the ETP are then transferred from their home hospital to either Atascadero or to Patton to receive ETP services. The statute also requires a multidisciplinary team for the ETP which is comprised of a Psychiatrist, a Psychologist, a Clinical Social Worker, a Rehab Therapist, a Registered Nurse and a Psychiatric Technician and hat comprises the ETP treatment team. The statute requires recertification of that patient every 90 days by the FNAP, and then also requires and independent evaluation if the patient is in for a year to determine if they are still appropriate for the ETP. As Stephanie mentioned, that also requires that we analyze the outcomes and report our recommendations to the Policy and Budget Legislative Committees annually, beginning January 10th, the first year after the ETP opens. Our implementation schedule, we have four units. Three in Atascadero, one in Patton. We expect to have the first unit at Atascadero open in April of '18. The second unit would open in August of 2018. The third unit at Atascadero in December of '18.  And the one unit at Patton also in December of '18. So, we expect to have 39 beds at Atascadero and 10 beds at Patton activated by the end of 2018.  Because it is an enhanced treatment program and these are the patients at risk of most dangerous behavior what ETP does that is different from the regular hospital, we have set up, it allows for the management of the patient's violence. We have three units that are comprised, at Atascadero, of 13 individual rooms. They're equipped with a combination sink and toilet. They have the ability to lock the doors for a patient when it's clinically indicated or at such a high risk of violence, they are not safe with other patients or with staff. Each unit will also have a treatment wing, which has group rooms, rehabilitation therapy rooms, a day dining area. Individual contact and non-contact rooms for those patients that are violent will still receive therapy in the non-contact rooms by their psychiatrist or their psychologist. There's a courtyard available in each of the units that allows for outdoor space, and there are treatment programs throughout the entire day. Because these are the most, the patients at risk of most violent behavior, we have asked for enhanced staffing. We did some studies at our current ETU that has treatment unit at Atascadero, and then based on our programming schedule, looked at what the actual nursing duties would be throughout the day. So we're asking for a one, a staffing ratio of 1-1.5 during AM and PM shifts, 1-3 in the night shift. We're also asking for an additional psychologist and rehabilitation therapist, so we can provide treatment throughout the program day, as well as on the weekends and two hospital police on shift every shift for all the units. The enhanced treatment program, that's the staffing. The DSH will bring staffing on board. We're asking for staff to come over two months prior to the activation of each unit. Because this is a new model, it's a new way of thinking about treatment. We want staff to be available two months ahead of time to learn not only hospital operations, but also learn the ETP model and all of the clinical interventions that we will expect them to use with our patient population. We have currently gone through preliminary plans. We are at 50% working drawings that we will be looking at in the beginning of March. We expect to start construction in December of 17 and have all the units open by December of 18. We have met with the Department of Public Health to take a look at what licensing and regulatory changes we may need. We have advised our unions, whoever are interested the project of our status, and we have also met with our patient's rights advocate in-house to go over our program planning. I'm happy to answer any questions.

And I've been asked to provide a brief overview of OSHPD's program and budget, if I may proceed. Thank you, sir. The Office of Statewide Health Planning and Development advances Californians access to state, safe rather quality healthcare environments by focusing in three primary areas. Healthcare workforce Development, Healthcare Data Collection and Reporting and Healthcare Construction and Financing. We have two areas of the department focusing on Health Care Workforce Development, the Healthcare Work Development division and Health Professions Education Foundation. Our Health Care Workforce Development Program seek to increase access to health care for under served communities and populations. By incentivizing a diverse and culturally and linguistically competent health care workforce. We focus on recruiting and retaining various health professionals in areas of unmet need. We increase the geographic distribution of California's healthcare workforce, and we explore a new service delivery models. Since fiscal year 2011-12, OSHPD has provided more than 8,000 awards to individuals. And 650 institutional awards, totalling more than $204 million to support the education of health professionals in a variety of practices throughout the state. One of our primary health care workforce programs is the [UNKNOWN] program. [UNKNOWN] awards funding to healthcare training and residency programs to increase access to healthcare providers in underserved communities. This is done through the recruitment of underrepresented minorities. Clinical training in areas of unmet need and graduate placement of health care professionals in those areas of unmet need. We have a health care information division which serves as a health care data collection and reporting hub. We collect health care data from nearly 6,000 health care facilities licensed by the Department of Public Health. This data includes hospital patient records as well as public utilization, and financial data. We make much of our data available to the public, researchers, policy makers, the media, and others. We also produce measures, analyses, and reports on healthcare outcomes and quality, and other related health topics. Since 2012 OSHPD has release more than 600 data products about California health care quality, cost, utilization and outcomes on topics that included hospital and patient mortality. Access to community based primary care and first time reports about ischemic stroke outcomes and hospital readmissions. We also coordinate and administer the California Health and Human Services Open Data Portal. More than 230 datasets have been published in open format from all 12 CHHS departments since the open data initiative launched in the fall of 2014. OSHPD is the building department for California's hospitals and skilled nursing facilities, and we're probably best known for this function. We administer the Seismic Safety Program, focused on strengthening California's hospital buildings. So they can remain operational in the event of an earthquake or other disaster. In 2001, 40% of California's hospital building inventory over 1,000 buildings was classified as being potentially at risk of collapse in a major earthquake. Today, I'm pleased to report that more than 92% of acute care hospital buildings in the State now comply with the Seismic Safety Act. And we continue to work with the remaining hospitals to meet the 2020 deadline for buildings to withstand a major earthquake or be removed from service. We've also promulgated a new seismic performance category called SPC4D. That will allow older hospital buildings to upgrade to a standard that will keep them seismically compliant past 2030. That's a great option, particularly for hospitals in areas of low seismicity, that would otherwise have to be replaced or removed from service. And this should really be a benefit to rural facilities. Additionally, since 2012, OSHPD has reduced hospital construction plan review time on remodel and renovation projects by more than 26%. In 2016, 98% of our project reviews were completed on schedule. We've increased face to face over the counter services and rapid review services. For smaller construction projects, and we've leveraged technology to provide real time plan review and a one stop electronic services portal. In 2016,90% of all project applications to OSHPD were directly submitted electronically into our eServices Portal. Also last year, we launched a completely electronic and paperless construction project review process for smaller projects roughly under $500,000 in construction cost. These innovations have greatly improved our customers experience with OSHPD. And contribute to improved health and safety for hospital patients, staff, and visitors. Finally, Mr. Chair, our Cal Mortgage Program provides health facility construction loan assistance for California's non-profit and public health facilities, they can gain access to low cost financing for the capital construction needs. And since 2012 Cal Mortgage has insured 45 loans totaling over $1.48 billion for these non-profit and public health facilities throughout the state. A brief overview of our budget. Our 2017-18 proposed budget is a 131.5 million and 479.6 positions. Our department is funded primarily by special funds, many of them are fee supported. Senate Bill 906, which was chaptered in 2014, established the elective PCI program. Prior to the elective PCI program, hospitals that were offering PCI were required to have on-site surgical backup. The elective PCI program was established as a program administered by the California Department of Public Health, that allows hospitals to get certified to provide PCI without the on-site surgical backup. SB 906 also established the requirement for the Office of Statewide Health Planning and Development to annually publish a report on outcomes of the program, specifically on mortality, post-operative stroke, and post-operative coronary artery bypass graft. The analyses will be risk-adjusted in order to ensure that the underlying patient risk is accounted for, to have a equal or like-to-like comparison of the participating facilities. For the risk-adjusted analysis, Senate Bill 906 required that we contract with the American College of Cardiology and receive data from the National Cardiovascular Data Registry for the analyses. Currently, we have two limited term positions to fulfill the analysis and reporting mandates that were established by SB 906. To date, these positions have been meeting with stakeholders and clinicians to develop the evaluation protocol, the framework for the program and the evaluation, and the conceptual models for the analysis. They have developed and have received approval from the Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects to conduct these evaluations. They received approval to receive and link to other data sources. They've developed and executed the contract for the receipt of the data from the National Cardiovascular Data Registry. And they've been working with academic partners to, or actually, have created a prototype data set in advance of the receipt of the actual data so that we can begin our work actually developing the analysis code and the risk adjusted model concepts further. And most importantly, they have been developing and have developed their own subject matter expertise of PCI, of the underlying scientific literature to inform our analyses, and the data itself. For the first formal evaluation of outcomes, the very first hospitals for the program were certified by the California Department of Public Health in the latter part of 2015. As data from these hospitals began to move into the National Cardiovascular Data Registry, we began receiving quarterly files that are non-final from the Data Registry so that we can begin our analyses in the development for the risk adjusted model. And we have been doing so. We've been using these data to make revisions to the analyses as they've been coming in because from one quarter to the next, the underlying patient populations and the characteristics of those participating in the program could change. The final annual data is due to the National Cardiovascular Data Registry on April 15th. They have informed us that it will take a few months for us to receive the final annual data file. At which point, we will rerun our analysis code and move towards the production of the initial results. We do anticipate that there will be some unknowns despite our preparatory work, once we do get the final data. And so factoring in those unknowns and the stakeholder engagement in the process, we plan to release the first report by the close of the calendar year. Our goal is to then maintain that similar cycle, releasing a report each year as required by SB 906. The work is ongoing, and each report essentially requires us to start anew on the methodology because each year, there may be new hospital certified, the underlying patient population and the associated risk may change. And there are certainly evolution in clinical practices and standards, and the clinical decision making, that's occurring. So the BCP requests that the two limited term positions get converted to permanent, and that the authority for contract resources in order for us to receive the data and to have ongoing clinical consultation. And for this program currently, the healthcare data planning fund is being used to support the work that we're doing, and is also proposed as the resources in the BCP. Thank you.

Margot Kushel: Senate Chair Pan and other Members of the Committee, thanks for inviting me to come and speak with you today. My name is Margot Kushel and I'm a physician and a Professor of medicine at UCSF. I'm a practicing general internist at our public safety net hospital, Zuckerberg San Francisco General. And I'm also an IH funded researcher who has spent many years studying homelessness and health. The County Welfare Director's Association asked me to come and present to you today on issues of elder homelessness, to help explain the importance of the home safe budget proposal. I come before you today to share what I've Learned in my 20 years as a researcher and a practicing clinician. About the toll of homelessness in older adults. And also about the urgent need to prevent homelessness among vulnerable elders. We have found that over half of single homeless adults are aged 50 and older. In our work in Oakland, we found that among those who are age 50 and older and homeless, almost half, or 44%, had never been homeless before the age of 50. Many of these individuals left vulnerable by an illness, a job loss, a loss of a family member, became a victim of elder abuse. And it was that abuse, either physical abuse or financial exploitation, that led directly to their becoming homeless. Being victimized this way can precipitate their homelessness. And as you know, homelessness leads to devastating consequences for health and safety. Adult protective services workers interact with vulnerable elders at a moment of crisis. And this crisis, if acted on, presents a really a golden opportunity to prevent homelessness. I want to tell you about one of our study participants who I'll call Jay, who moved in with his daughter in Oakland when his kidneys began to fail. His daughter took his money, but then kicked him out. And so he had no place to stay and became homeless. Three days a week he went to dialysis. Every night, he slept on an AC transit bus. After months of sleeping on the bus, he obtained emergency shelter, eventually moved to transitional housing, but died before he regained housing. His situation unfortunately, it was not unique. We found the story repeated over and over. There are well known and severe consequences to homelessness among older adults. Our older adults 50 and older, look more like adults in their 70s and 80s. So when I say someone is 52, I want you to envision an 80-year old living on the street, and frankly, some of them were in their 80s. Homelessness ages people. When they become homeless, they lose the ability to access regular health care, to get good nutrition, and to stay safe. And as a result, they wind up in the hospital, and emergency departments, and nursing homes. 50% of our participants have been in the ED, Emergency Department, in the past six months, which is an astronomical number. And 11% had been hospitalized in the past six months. Homelessness, as you know, is catastrophic to health and well-being. As a physician, I can say to you that the single most important step I can take for patients, is saving their housing. There is no medicine that I have access to, that is nearly as important or as potent as housing. And there's no threat to health as bad as homelessness. APS workers come into contact with older adults at a time when they're highly vulnerable. A recent study done in the Midwest showed that relatively modest assistance, on the order of $1,000, at a time when people were at a high risk of homelessness, had lasting impacts on reductions in homelessness. 76% reduction six months later, compared to those who are eligible but didn't receive it. APS workers are well-positioned to intervene to prevent the onset of homelessness, and the devastating health consequences that follow.

So that's the first reason that the particular manner in which the unwinding on the CCI was so problematic. The second is that the way the Governor proposes to restructure the relationship or to the return to the state county sharing ratio requires the counties pick up the lion's share of cost caused by actions that were beyond our control, including the lion's share of minimum wage costs, particularly because the interaction with the wage gap that's been discussed earlier. I think that's important to point out that when the state realigned programs to the counties, the legal basis for realignment was that in the aggregate, the amount of costs imposed on the counties would be more or less covered by the revenue source that was provided. The reason case load driven programs were given first priority is because in the absence of covering those costs there would be a mandate. And so it was the counties knew under realignment that in some years maybe the revenues wouldn't be quite enough. And in some years maybe there'd be a little more. But over time this is largely expected to be a fiscally neutral transaction. And so what the action that the Governor took does is take that legal principle, and sends it sort of way out of whack. Because the cost that we would bear under our estimate is about a half $1 billion, growing to over $1 billion of unreimbursed cost, which subverts the original legal basis for realignment. Joe Rodriguez: Thank you. Joe Rodriguez, California State Long-Term Care Ombudsman. The Ombudsman program is charged in both Federal and State law to identify, investigate, and resolve complaints made by or on behalf of residents of long-term care facilities that affect their health, their safety, their welfare and their rights. Also in state law we're mandated to receive reports of suspected elder independent adult abuse and neglect that occurs in long term care facilities. All general fund local assistants funding for the Ombudsman program was eliminated in fiscal year 08/09. The agenda details the state one time only appropriations to partially backfill the lost general funds using a variety of sources. We receive funding from the state citation penalties account. That's managed by the Department of Public Health. We receive funding from the Skilled Nursing Facility Quality and Accountability fund. That is managed by the Department of Health Care Services. The Legislature restored $1 million in general fund support for the program in fiscal year 15/16 which continues this year. The Legislature also appropriated $400,000 from the Department of Public Health's Licensing and Certification fund. So local assistance funding for the Ombudsman program currently totals $8 million. 1 million of that is one time only money that the Legislature gave us last year which will end at the end of this fiscal year. These funds have been used to increase staff, hours and limited term appointments to fill local staff positions in the 35 local programs throughout the state. We've also been able to support our volunteers we have about 740 volunteers and 150 paid staff throughout the state that operates and has a regular presence in about 1,250 skilled nursing facilities and 7,500 residential care facilities for the elderly. With this additional funding, we've seen some increases in our capacity to serve residents. We've seen a 9% increase in information consultation to individuals. We've seen a 24% increase in the number of consultations provided to facility staff on various issues. We've seen and 18% increase in our ability to get out to residential care facilities for the elderly, assisted living warden care homes. We've seen a 10% ability to get out to skilled nursing facilities once a quarter. We'd seen a increase in the number of complains by 3% last year and a 13% increase in paid staff that are able to respond to these reports of abuse and neglect and exploitation and other complaints affecting the health and safety of residents.

They're choosing each month, or each week, or each day, between paying for medications, getting rides to their doctors, paying their rent, or buying food. And food typically is where the hit comes. Costs of providing these services go up every year by about a quarter per meal. That's less than inflation, but it's just the reality of milk costing more, vegetables costing more, of delivery services costing more. And one concern that we have is even if the funds of the federal and state levels stay flat, we're going to lose almost half a million meals this next year and that includes the one time only funds that we received last year which are going to be renewed. So with flat funding alone we're looking at half a million meals being taken away from at risk seniors, so anything we can do to put that in place is really critical. Also, one way or another we know that this state is going to incur costs for the care of seniors. There's kind of two choice in this. One, we can do nothing and hope that everything goes well. When we do that we know that healthcare costs go up. That seniors with poor nutrition are twice as likely to end up in the hospital or end up in institutionalized care, or end up with some chronic or traumatic illnesses, heart attack, etc. So we can do nothing and let that happen and incur really large costs. Or we can invest some dollars in effective programs and I don't think anything is more effective or basic than feeding somebody, keep them healthy, and lower those costs in the future. And I think that's really my message today. In the past, when I've come up here I've really focused on statistics and numbers and the cost benefit of this, but time's limited, you guys are going to be here a long time, but really the bottom line is that, one way or another, you're going to pay for the needs of seniors. You can do it cost effectively by providing food now. And the other this is it's the right thing. No senior should have to go hungry in this community. So not only is it morally the preferred approach. It's also the fiscally sound approach. It's the way that will cost the state money. So our ask is for 12.5 million to augment the nutrition program, that will address the 25 cent rise in meal cost and allow us to serve some of this growing population that currently aren't being served.

And we have got what we sowed, bad results, bad public safety, and more victims. We are changing how we incarcerate people in the state. We're emphasizing positive programming and motivating individuals to want to change. I'm very proud of this organization and what we stand for. And I'd like to give you some very specific examples. In our juvenile justice system, we have got out of a decade-old federal lawsuit, we have created a sustainable, humane system for our most troubled youth. In parole, we changed from a system that, at its height, incarcerated over 100,000 inmates a year, placing them in triple bunks in gyms and day rooms throughout our prisons. And we've created a system that actively seeks to make the parolee successful. In our Division of Rehabilitative Programs, we are building an infrastructure of evidence-based and best practices in rehabilitative programming, academic, vocational, college, substance abuse, cognitive behavior, reentry, innovative grants, the arts, PIA, long-term offender programs, and our community programs. We have over 10,000 volunteers that come into our prisons on a regular basis to help with our self-help programs. Under our gang management, we changed from a system of identification and isolation to a behavior-based system. Over 3,000 inmates have been removed from our security housing units and placed in our general population setting. In medical, we're making significant process. We have 10 prisons delegated to CDCR authority. And we're working better with the receiver to provide a constitutional level of healthcare. In fact, we're making progress in all of our class action lawsuits. Under staff development, with the help of this Legislature, we're implementing programs lost to harder economic times. We're providing first and second-line custody and non-custody training. We're doing executive development programs. We're involved in a partnership with Chico and Sac State to provide higher level leadership programming to our executives. We're doing employee wellness and working with CCPOA and the administration to recognize the significant challenges our staff face in the prisons every day. And we're doing succession planning to try to keep our executives in these positions of leadership for longer periods of time. We've made significant changes to our classification system to expand program opportunities to our offenders, and recognizing the sustained positive behavior of the individual. We're moving inmates to the lowest possible level in our prisons to give them higher access to programming and to better serve their needs. And let me conclude by saying that Prop 57 builds upon the previous reforms of the past. It puts responsibility on the inmate to participate in positive programming and earn time off their sentence or to parole suitability hearing. It delegates to the correctional professionals to determine when an inmate progressed to a point that they no longer pose a threat to public safety. Prop 57 has a number of components, including the expansion of a nonviolent parole process, credits, modest credit changes for our offenders, milestone programs that recognize completion of academic programs, significant educational achievements, the attainment of a high school diploma or an AA degree, and others. And then taking a nontraditional approach, I think, to recognize the hundreds of self-help programs that we have throughout the institutions, and awarding inmates credits for participating in those very positive programs. We expect the regulations to be completed very soon, and anticipate implementing in phases in the coming months. As a result of Prop 57, we will be able to address and bring back our inmates that are currently housed in Mississippi, and reduce that out-of-state facility. And we believe, in fact, we'll be able, excuse me, to get out of the out-of-state program altogether by 2020. So I hope you will agree with me that this is a department that's on the move and making some very positive steps. And I'd like to take any questions that you might have.

Karen Smith: Good afternoon. Okay, Mr. Chair, members, I'm Dr. Karen Smith. I'm the Director of the California Department of Public Health and the state public health officer. It's my pleasure to provide you with an overview of the department and its budget, at which point I'll defer to my colleagues to provide additional detail. Throughout our testimony, we'll endeavor to answer the Committee's questions fully. The Department of Public Health is dedicated to optimizing the health and well-being of the people of California, primarily through population-based programs, strategies, and initiatives. The department's goals are to eliminate health disparities and achieve health equity. Eliminate preventable disease, disability, injury, and premature death. Promote social and physical environments that support good health for all. Prepare for, respond to, and recover from emerging public health threats and emergencies. And improve the quality of the workforce and workplace, as well as promoting and maintaining an effective organization. The governor's proposed budget for 2017-18 includes approximately $3.3 billion for the department overall, representing 289.3 million in total funds, or 8.8%, from the current budget year. This primarily reflects the infusion of Proposition 56, the 2016 tobacco tax funding. General fund dollars of 132.2 million make up approximately 4% of the department's total budget. Federal funds make up approximately 52%, or 1.7 billion, of the total department budget. The remainder of the department's funding comes from approximately 50 special funds. The Committee asked what our higher priorities are this time. And in addition to maintaining our core public health funding, our core public health activities, some of the priorities for us this year are the dramatic rise in opioid use, misuse, and abuse. As well as overdoses in California, which have become a significant public health issue. In response, the CDPH convened a work group in 2014 that includes, by now, over 25 agencies and partners as part of a multifaceted approach to address the epidemic. We're leveraging this unusual multi-agency partnership to apply for and have received grants. Not only CDPH, but also the Department of Justice, who is a key partner with us. With a grant that we received from the CDC, we will be allocating additional funding to eight to 10 local opioid abuse prevention coalitions who work together at the local level to reduce the number of opioid overdose incidents, deaths, and unsafe prescribing, in a way that is specific to their individual communities. Similarly, the Governor's Budget allocated a total of $3 million to us, to be spent by June 30th, 2019, on a one-time basis, to support a new naloxone grant program. Our goal is to distribute naloxone to high-risk communities as quickly and efficiently as possible. A brief RFA process will be used and will be directed to all 61 local health jurisdictions, who will then, in turn, distribute that funding out to organizations throughout their communities that are prepared to and deal with populations or prepared to get it out quickly to the populations that will be able to use it most expeditiously. Another way that we're expanding our impact in an environment with limited funding is in the case of Zika virus. With additional resources provided by the CDC Zika funding, we have successfully met our primary objective of enhancing surveillance in California for cases of microcephaly and other birth defects resulting from Zika virus infections. The annual birth population now being monitored in California is approximately 370,000, which represents 74% of all annual births. Surveillance of all births in 19 counties, including babies whose mothers were not suspected of having Zika infection during their pregnancy, is helping us identify additional cases of Zika-associated birth defects. This information is also helping the department and local health departments with planning and providing follow-up services for affected families. Supplemental federal funding is also being used for mosquito surveillance, providing us with better on-the-ground assessment of areas of the state that may be at risk for transmission of Zika virus in the future. And finally, another example is the partnership that we've developed between CDPH's Women, Infants, and Children Program and the Department of Social Services' CalFresh Program. Where the two departments are sharing data that allow us to identify areas of need and opportunity, where either one of the other program has low penetration into the area where we know there are eligible persons. We're then geomapping those areas and allowing smaller teams of individuals to go in and work proactively with those local jurisdictions, both social services and public health, to expand their outreach into the communities at greatest risk. We think this is increasing our efficiency at getting to increase the number of persons who are enrolled, who qualify for these programs. In the upcoming weeks, the programs will be visiting sites in Sacramento and the Central Valley, both, this month to gather qualitative data, which will then help them to identify strategies to mitigate barriers from individuals. The barriers for both of these programs are different in different areas. And therefore, our responses to those barriers also need to differ. I'm going to ask Brandon Nunes, our Chief Deputy for administration, to respond to some of your additional questions.

And then a third highly overarching area is to promote the use and increased access to national models in diabetes prevention. Then within that lie very specific activities that the Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion do including promoting healthy eating, increased physical activity, tobacco cessation, prevention and control of obesity and overweight, and secondary prevention activities, focused on evidence based strategies to prevent the delay of onset of complications among Californians diagnosed with type 2 diabetes or pre-diabetes as well. As far as what we're recommending on what the state should do to address diabetes, we believe that it is of course important to continue the work that we've embarked on thus far, and it's not just Including the Department of Public Health. As well as focus on some of the broader upstream efforts that Doctor Smith mentioned earlier when she talked about the health equity and some of the social determinants of health aspects. So, overall, I think we just wanted to point out that we feel it's important to recognize that unhealthy behavior and lifestyles alone, do not solely explain poor health outcomes among lower socioeconomic groups, which are exactly the groups at highest risk for diabetes. Social and environmental risk factors play a crucial role in health outcomes, including in diabetes. And factors such as diabetes related health costs, family and other social support, housing, availability of healthy foods and transportation, all effect health outcomes for persons with diabetes. If those social environmental factors aren't addressed, improvements in health outcomes are likely to be short-lived. So it really needs to be a combination of efforts. There was a specific question about the value of the Diabetes Prevention Program, and wanted to share high-level, and then we can certainly answer more specific questions. The Diabetes Prevention Program secures funding to not only those to develop state capacity, but also provides funding for 10 local health departments to conduct their own local efforts. Significant value of the program is a convener role, again, as noted by the California Prevent Diabetes STAT program, or PDSTAT program, as well as in the California Wellness Plan. Another opportunity that presents itself in that area, is the area of electronic health records. In this area of the electronic health records, we see significant opportunity and are exploring ways to work with health care providers to gather electronic health record data to conduct more analyses of diabetes hot spots. And geographic hot spots and geographic distribution as well, and that will then, again, better inform more targeted intervention as well. So the Diabetes Prevention Program will help to reduce the burden of type 2 diabetes in California, and will reduce the financial burden of the disease in California as a result. There was also specific question about the work that's done specifically to prevent diabetes in children, Latino children. And there was a question specific to the Central Valley as well. CDPH has worked to prevent diabetes in children, includes the Nutrition Education and Obesity Prevention Branch, or NEOP, which implements the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program Education,or SNAP-Ed. Developed the Power Play campaign to provide nutrition education in schools, after school, and community youth organizations, including promotion of water over sugary drinks, fruits and vegetables, and physical activity. Those materials are available both in English and Spanish. Additionally, we have the Rethink Your Drink Campaign, which targets youth, provides education about sugary drinks and options for healthy beverages. Again, those materials are also available in both languages. All Central Valley counties participant in SNAP-Ed as well as Power Play. In the Prevention First Grant, two school districts from San Joaquin and Fresno, receive additional support services to promote physical activity and safe routes to school. As well as training and technical assistance to approve nutrition services through school wellness policies, and implementation of smarter lunchroom techniques, for example. That's one of the grants. Another grant, The Lifetime of Wellness Grant, and that one is available to people 18 and up, is for local diabetes prevention efforts as well, where CDPH provides funding to the local health jurisdictions in Fresno, Tulare, Merced, San Joaquin, as well as other counties. And for activities that include implementing systems, partnerships, and evidence-based engagement strategies to support lifestyle changes. Linkages between health systems and community resources, and that one specifically, I believe, targets adults with hypertension and pre diabetes or those that are at high risk for type 2 diabetes, is that correct? So that was fairly high-level, but we have specific examples, if you would like, in any of the areas.

We want to increase their access to and utilization of healthcare services. Their social and emotional support. We really strive to increase their educational attainment, keep them in school. Help them to improve pregnancy planning, reproductive live planning, so that there isn't a second pregnancy while they're a teen. They have month to month, face to face visits with the counselors who are involved in the program. This is funded through Title V funds. Right now we are in the process of similar to BIH to implementing a single standardized model throughout the state that we've been studying. We've been having external federal evaluation dollars and it's called the positive youth development. This is our new RFA that was just released as to not only implement this program throughout California again, so that you can get better measures of outcome, and you have more confidence in them. But we've also used a measure to determine areas of need, so that we're sure that there are counties of greatest need are getting the dollars that we have available for this program. And finally I thought you might be interested in our home visiting program. Title five is our major source of funding. We get about $39 million a year for our home visiting program. Our federal dollars are around $22 million a year. Home visiting was created as a result of the patient protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010. Its goal is to provide comprehensive coordinated, in home services to support positive parenting, and to improve outcomes for families. This is another long term program investment, where people, women are included when they're in pregnancy, high risk women . And then they can be followed with their families and children, sometimes up to age five. And they get in a very structured model program. The Home Visiting Program is strongly evidence based, there's an expectation that if we implement it they way that it was intended to, that we'll get the same positive outcomes and indeed that's what's happening in California. We've reached all of our benchmarks and all of our federal reporting. We are very proud of this program. As of March this year, we've served over 8,600 families and we are currently at 95.6% capacity. Several of our counties have wait lists. So we're on our sixth year of implementation. We consider it to be a mature program of robust infrastructure. That includes fully staffed local implementing agents with very highly trained nurse and home visitors. We do recognize there is a water problem here in the State of California. And we want to make it easier for this legislature and local governments to use storm water as a legitimate water source, as long as it goes back to projects that benefit actual people. Not for environmental purposes where we're pumping it out into the ocean, but for potable water for drinking water, for agriculture, for those things. That is a legitimate use of water and that should not require an additional vote of the people beyond the protest process that's currently in place under Prop 218. We're okay with that, so the issue is not water, and it's not water storage, but it is sewer. Members, it's not the job of the legislature to clarify judicial intent if you happen to amend statute in a way that violates the California constitution, which is precisely what this bill does. The Salinas Court, in it's decision, and it is an appellate court and that is a settled decision made a very clear distinction between sewer and drainage systems. The bill, SB 231, now states in the intent language, that this Salinas Court was fundamentally wrong in refusing to use the statutory definition of the term sewer system, as was located in Section 230.5 of the Public Utilities Code. It further creates legislative intent language to state that this definition should now be used within the Prop 218, Omnibus Implementation Act, the legislative language that implemented Prop 218, but the definition of public utility used in the PC code 230.5 does not include public agencies, only PC regulated private companies, and it's very important because both the Omnibus Act and the Salinas Case only apply to public agencies and not private companies. So the whole justification for the bill, at least using that statute, just falls completely flat on its face right there. Senator Hertzberg brought up litigation, and there would be a mess of litigation, Members, if this bill moved forward because, again, we are dealing with settled appellate court law here. So should SB 231 be signed into law and be adopted by local agencies if there is a precedent setting victory in validating this bill, should it become law, and numerous cities have signed onto this, and started collecting fees and assessments. It's going to be very, very bad I think for local governments up and down the state. We certainly want local governments to avoid that, as should the legislature. Members, listen, Prop 218, when it was passed in 1996, was the right to vote on taxes, and that said, for every single property related fee and assessment other than water, sewer, and garbage that does need a vote of the people. The Salinas Court did provide a clear distinction between water and storm water and said storm water and urban runoff management does, in fact, need a vote of the people per a mail ballot election. We see no need to undermine the vote of the people and undermine the Salnas decision and cities are concerned with regards to this bill. Erin Palacios: My name is Erin Palacios, and I am from Bay Area Legal Aid. We are, just by a way of brief background, the largest provider of civil legal services for the poor in the San Francisco Bay Area and we have offices in six counties. I am the coordinator of our youth justice program, and we specialize in that program in providing civil legal services to youth directly, particularly homeless, foster, and trafficked youth, so very vulnerable populations. I had come prepared to describe a little bit about the services related to AB 12, but it sounds from my listening in the Cali that you guys are pretty well familiar with what those services entail. So I will just point out that what this bill does is work to close a revolving door between our homeless youth system and our foster youth system. We have, in California, over 11,000 unaccompanied homeless youth, which represents 31% of our nation's total. We have over 800 minor unaccompanied homeless youth. When that point in time count was done in January, there were over 600 of those youth who were minors were unsheltered on that night. Those youth have a large number of life experiences that are the same as youth who are in foster care. Abuse, abandonment, and neglect at very high rates. One of the things that AB 12, obviously, was aiming to prevent was homelessness, and aiming to prevent the poor outcomes that those youth face. This would allow a subset of those youth who do not come to the attention of the Child Welfare System until they are slightly older, perhaps in their 17th year, to become eligible for those services despite the fact that they didn't leap certain procedural hurdles before. Specifically, it would allow youth who did not have a dispositional hearing yet to be eligible for AB 12. They were in foster care, they simply did not have that dispositional hearing. I just want to share two stories that I think illustrate the point of a couple of our clients. We represented a 17-year-old boy who was living alone in a youth shelter. His father died when he was in elementary school, his mother, a few years later, took her own life. For some time, he bounced between family members and tried to make ends meet. Ultimately, his family was a combination of unwilling and unable to provide support for him, and he leaned on community partners and providers. That worked for a little while, and he tried to make ends meet. They reached out to the child welfare system several times, but he was not the classic candidate. He was not literally abused, he just had deceased parents, so it took some time to get that case into court and some advocacy. In the meantime, he left high school even though he was just a few credits shy and entered a GED program. He had decided he could not finish high school without that kind of support, and he then was ready to find his own apartment, and he applied for federal and state benefits. We were able to get him qualified just shy of his 18th birthday, and that young man, with that support, which was critical, which he almost did not receive, was able then to re-enroll in high school, which he graduated from, and he attended college starting that fall. Another young man we represented is the opposite and less fortunate scenario who also came to the attention of Child Welfare Services just before he turned 18. For reasons that I won't get into here, the Child Welfare Agency delayed the hearings in his case, not for any fault of the youth, but it took till just after his 18th birthday for the dispositional hearing to come up. He was thus declared ineligible for extended foster care services and is now, based on the decision of the juvenile court and an appellate court, not eligible because he did not get formally declared a dependent and he remains unable to meet basic needs and living in a homeless shelter at this time. So I just would give my support for this bill and say that it makes a large difference in the lives of those youth who come to the attention of the services very late, thank you.

Dennis Mathisen: Very good. Thank you, Chair Maguire, Senators. Thank you for inviting me. First, I'd like to introduce myself, I am Dennis Mathisen, California State Fire Marshal as appointed by Governor Brown about two months ago. So relatively new in the position. But with that said I have over 30 years of experience in the California Fire Service, 26 of those at the local government level and most of that as a local Fire Marshal. So I can kind of look at things from both perspectives. Our offices is responsible for management oversight of a variety of programs including fire and life safety inspections, new construction plan review for state buildings, code development and analysis relative to fire and life safety standards, fire protection equipment listing and licensing fire and fraud investigations, fire work safety hazardous pipeline, safety wild land fire prevention and stay fire training. So we have a lot of variety. First I'd like to compliment your staff who provided the background information to you, the information relative to the state's role in code development is spot on. And so I'll just kind of touch on that and emphasize it and be available to answer any questions that you might have. So in terms of the California safety standards, fire and life safety related regulations go, our regulatory process involving building standards is run through the state Building Standards Commission. And how that works is various state agencies, state Fire Marshalls specifically addressing fire and life safety issues. Looks at the national model code in the case of California we utilize the International Code Council published documents, international building code, international fire code, and so on. Those documents are updated every three years with intervening updates in the interim years. Our office looks at fire and life safety issues, we address statutory requirements that are unique to California, we propose those amendments utilizing a process that involves a lot of stakeholders. And ultimately goes to the State Building Standards Commission for adoption. Once that's adopted, it becomes the code for California. At that time it's the local government's opportunity to take the series of codes and make any local amendments that they deem necessary based on their own unique community needs. And once that's done, they would adopt that as a local ordinance, either through City Council Board of Supervisors or a fire district board. With that said, that's the California process. At the same time, we participate very heavily in the national code development process so we have the model code. We work on trying to help influence change nationally which helps California ultimately. And so we look at it from both the California perspective and nationally. I'll provide a quick overview of state law, mandates, inspection frequencies and the type of occupancies that those affect. In California there are basically four categories or four different occupancy types that have a mandated inspection frequency. Those are public and private schools kindergarten through 12th grade, multi-family dwellings, so, apartment houses, hotels, motels, lodging houses etc., high rise buildings. Which in California health and safety code defines as any building with the highest habitable floor 75 feet above ground level is a high rise. Those three categories are, it's incumbent upon and required in state law that the responsibility for inspections of those resides at the local level with the Fire Chief or his or her designee. And the frequency required for those is annually once a year. The fourth category is detention facilities, so, jails and prisons. Those are required to be inspected every two years. The inspection responsibility resides with my office, the office of State Fire Marshall with the exception that the law allows the local jurisdiction to perform those inspections if they opt to. So, we go through a process where they're given an opportunity to let us know if they're going to inspect them. If they are, we document that and make sure that that gets done. And if they don't provide that, then we perform those inspections. So, essentially, those are the four categories. All other occupancies above and beyond those are really done at the discretion of the local community. As was mentioned before I believe by Ms. Cabio, there's a process typically at the local community level, where you go through and you have to look at your risks, and you prioritize your fire prevention activities based on those risks and the resources that you have available. So again, anything beyond those four categories is identified as a target hazard or some other kind of life hazard prioritized and then performed at a frequency that's determined by the local jurisdiction.

And our ability to recover those costs is not good at this point, I would say they're certainly universal.

John Gioia: Good afternoon, Chair Skinner and members. I am John Gioia from the Contra Costa Board of Supervisors and I'm here to support this bill and tell you a little bit about why Contra Costa County ended the practice of collecting these fees last year. Last October, a bipartisan Board, we have three Democrats and two Republicans on our Board last year, unanimously voted to suspend collection of these fees after we conducted a thorough study of these fees at our Public Protection Committee, which I serve on. We concluded that these fees do not further public safety. They economically burden families and that they raise very small amounts of revenue. So we joined other counties, there are now six counties in California that do not collect this fee. And those six counties represent 40% of the population of this state, including Alameda, San Francisco, and Los Angeles are three of those counties, Alameda. We found that this is one of those high cost, low return fees. High cost to families. High cost to collect, and low return in terms of net revenue collected. Our experience, I think you'll find, reflects the experience of many other counties. And the hidden secret in this fee, one of the hidden secrets, it costs more to collect this fee than what it generates in net revenue. We spend around $300,000 to collect $500,000 which means we net $200,000. Not a very efficient way to spend taxpayer dollars. Same issue in Alameda County where they spend $250,000 to collect $420,000 or net $170,000. We net less than what it costs to collect this fee. Also, the net revenues received are an extremely small part of the cost of operating our juvenile detention facilities. It costs around $30 million to operate our two facilities. We net 200 to 250 thousand out of this fee. That is less than one-half percent of the cost of operating those facilities. This is not a fee that benefits victims. It supposedly, for the purpose of allowing counties to recoup their cost, it clearly doesn't serve that purpose, and its price on families far outweighs what small monetary benefit we get. In addition, in our review of our own fees, we found that these fees were assessed on many families in violation of state law. There were some statutory exemptions on collection of this fee. Our own chief probation officer was unaware that we were collecting fees that violated state law. In fact, we looked at cases over a three-year period, and found that of the 930 families that paid the fee, 130 of them were improperly assessed; that's about 15%. In addition, we're exploring refunding to those families. The majority of the fees assessed remain unpaid. We have $8,000,000 in unpaid fees. For those families, they have the potential to have their credit impacted, their financial lives impacted by failure to pay these fees. So, for families that are trying to improve their situation, provide stability, and support their children, they are being impacted. For all of those reasons, our bipartisan board voted unanimously to suspend collection of these fees and to explore how we provide refunds for those improperly assessed.

It was one of the worst experiences of my life. At 17, I was taken to the police station and put into a small room. There, I was interrogated for 25 hours. I don't remember them reading me my Miranda Rights. I'm not saying that they didn't. I think they probably did, but my teenaged self had no real understanding of what those constitutional rights meant or what it meant to give them up. During the first five hours of being questioned, I gave the investigating officers a detailed outline of my day's event up until the point I was placed in the backseat of the patrol car. I spoke the absolute truth, but they kept questioning me. By the tenth hour of the interrogation, the officer's attitude had changed. He moved from being comforting and engaging to provoking and authoritative. He told me that the truth, my truth, was a big lie and that I needed to stop playing games. By hour 15, I was drained, and I couldn't have told you if it was night or day. There, it was just a small window in the room, and that was taped with a folded piece of cardboard on the outside of the glass with a small peephole cut through it. At hour 21, the interrogating officer asked me to put myself into the scenario that they had displayed before me. In my 17 year old brain, all I wanted to do was go home. By the 25th hour of the interrogation, I would have told the interrogating officers anything. So, I confessed to the crime that I didn't commit. Maybe some of you listening right now can't really comprehend how a 17 year old can give up his rights without understanding them and then go on to confess to a crime he didn't commit. But I did not understand what it meant to give up my constitutional rights. And after the intense interrogation experience, I would have told the police officers anything. I was convicted based in part of that confession. Tried as an adult, I served 21 and a half years in prison for a crime I didn't commit. I never had not one disciplinary action throughout the whole years of my incarceration. In October of 2011, I was paroled. I support SB 395 because I think young people deserve to have an unbiased person explain their rights to them. It is the least we can do to protect youth. Please vote yes for SB 395, thank you.

Our overarching concern is that this bill goes far beyond what existing case law requires as it relates to juveniles and Miranda. For nearly 40 years, US Supreme Court case law has held that quote, the court must take into account, special concerns that are present when a young person is involved, including a child or youth with limited experience, education immature judgement. That's from the Fair Case in 1979. SB 395 and SB 1052 before it exceeds that standard bill, requires a minor to console with council prior to a custodial interrogation and prior to, before they waive rights under Miranda and that this consultation cannot be waived. This raises questions like who will provide the counsel? Who will pay for it? And why is it being mandated, even in cases before a person is arrested? Law enforcement may simply want to talk to a minor and even if the parent or guardian is present and notified in advance, this discussion would have to wait until a council could consult with minor if there was a chance the interrogation could fall under the undefined umbrella of a custodial interrogation. SB 395 will cast out on an otherwise truthful statement that is called into question, simply because a minor had not consulted with counsel before choosing to waive Miranda. For these reasons, we are opposed to the bill. Thank you.

[{'start': 60, 'end': 72, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Heidi Rummel: Members of the Committee, thank you. My name is Heidi Rummel, I'm a Professor of law at the University of Southern California Gould School of Law. I was a federal prosecutor for 12 years in both Washington DC and Los Angeles. I prosecuted violent crime, gang crime, rapes, murders, human trafficking in two of this country's most crime ridden cities. I know very well the impact of crime in our society. I support Senate Bill 394, because it brings California into conformity with the Eighth Amendment and the national trend to eliminate this sentence. Science, the courts and this legislature agree about the fundamental principle that underlies this bill. Children are different from adults. Their brains are not fully developed. They have a great capacity for growth and change. They outgrow the behaviors that lead to crime. Last year, the US Supreme Court clarified the constitutional limits on sentencing children in Montgomery. It is cruel and unusual, it violates the Eight Amendment to sentence a child who possess the potential for rehabilitation to life without parole. Only those rare few who are eruptively corrupt with no hope of redemption can be sentenced to die in prison. California courts are struggling with how to make that very difficult determination. These sentencing require many hundreds of attorney hours, costly mitigation investigations, experts, court time and many years of appeals. Senate Bill 394 provides the alternative suggested by our United States Supreme Court that will make sure California gets it right. On the front-end, no child will face an unconstitutional sentence. On the back-end, California's rigorous parole process ensures that those who do prove to be irreparably corrupt are never released. In 2012, California took the lead on this issue when it passed SB 9. Creating a statutory after the fact opportunity for re-sentencing for some, but the US Supreme Court has gone much further in Miller and Montgomery and California has fallen behind the curve. 24 jurisdictions in the United States do not use the sentence at all for youth under 18. Another 14 states have legislation in the works to remedy the issue. There is growing national bipartisan consensus of the 10 states that have banned the use of juvenile life without parole since Miller came was decided. Nine of those pieces of legislation were sponsored by Republicans and, or received more than 90% of the votes in both houses of the legislature. Texas, South Dakota, Utah, West Virginia, Wyoming and others. It's time for California to catch up. As a prosecutor, I advocated for prison sentences that would best protect the public and hold offenders accountable for their crimes. As co-director of USC's post conviction justice project, I have seen first hand that it is impossible to know how people will grow, mature and change in the course of 25 years. This bill makes sure that we always get it right. That those who change and rehabilitate can seek release on parole after 25 years. Those who do not will remain in prison. I strongly urge your support of Senate Bill 394. Thank you.

In other words, people who were convicted by a jury and found to be morally and actually culpable of the offense went to state prison, but can now apply for a reduction in sentence. Whereas people who were found not guilty of an offense by a jury because of their mental condition and confined to a state hospital cannot. We think this is fundamentally unfair and actually contrary to the intent of the voters in passing the initiative statues. The second two points Senator Beall has already made, but I think they're worth reiterating. One is is that these people are taking up bed space that might be used by people who are actually in need of acute psychiatric treatment and because the Prop Prop 47 and Prop 36 statutes require a court to evaluate that person's current dangerousness. This may free up bed space that's needed for people who are actually currently dangerous that are currently sitting in county jails. And the final point, of course is that because this bill would require courts to make an individualized determination as to dangerousness, none of the people who would be released by this, by extending this to the mentally ill, would actually be dangerous according, at least, to the trial judge who sentenced them.

This is the authors of Prop 36 and Prop 47. So whether it was an oversight or whether it was a purposeful ignoring of this particular thing, that's the reality of it. So for that reason, the material differences that exist between criminal sentences for the purposes of punishment and a term of committment designed to treat a mental condition. Stephen Manley: My name is Stephen Manley, I'm a Superior Court judge from Santa Clara County. I'm speaking for myself only and not in behalf of the courts. I have been working with mentally ill and substance abuse offenders for over 25 years. I supervise all the mental health and drug cases in our court and what I wanted to speak to is this. I believe that judges need to have more options in terms of disposing of cases and finding the right answer for those who are mentally ill. What we have seen in my county, and across the state, is a dramatic increase in the number of mentally ill offenders who are in custody. In our jails, since realignment, it has gone from 12%, we did a study last year, the county did it, not the court. 40% of the individuals in our county jail suffer from mental illness and are diagnosed as mentally ill. It's an incredible cost to the county. Our county is joined with the court in trying to find alternatives to move the mentally ill out of jail. I think SB 8 would give the court another option in working with these offenders and I want to point out the fact, as the previous witness noted, we have military diversion. The statute is based somewhat on military diversion and that model. It is a model that requires a standard of proof that is much less, much lower than SB 8. It only need be demonstrated that the individual served in the military, and as a result of service, I mean nothing to do with the crime, has mental illness or some other serious disability. What we have found is that those veterans coming back from Iraq and Afghanistan often commit serious misdemeanors. Domestic violence, battery. These offenders, if diverted, do very well and that is because the mental illness, the symptoms of the mental illness relate to the crimes and if you don't treat the symptoms, you do what we've done for years in the courts, which is sentence far too many mentally ill people to far too long in jail. They receive disproportionate sentencing in comparison to those who are not mentally ill and commit the same offenses. And I think what diversion allows to do, with a high standard of proof placed on the defense, and in the requirement of an adversarial hearing, is to move more mentally ill offenders who are appropriate into the community without the necessity of long periods of incarceration. Having watched cases over many years, and supervising over 2,300 mentally ill offenders, I can tell you what happens in the courts is they sit in jail, and in the end, the charges are dropped to a lower charge, they plead guilty, they're given credit for time served and put back into the community with no treatment, no intervention at all. Therefore, the criminality continues. If you do not treat the underlying basis of the criminal behavior, you get nowhere, in my view, and I have seen this over the years. And we've made real progress has been pointed out in San Diego, Orange County, Santa Clara, and many other counties, in military diversion. Showing that we can take offenders who do commit serious crimes as well as crimes that are not that serious, and through treatment, get them back in the community. The bottom line, to me as a judge, is no matter what the punishment is, no matter what the sentence is, all of these offenders come back to the community, and often, back to our courts and we start all over with the same process. We need to do something different, and I think this gives us an opportunity with a very high burden of proof, and the opportunity for an adversarial hearing. I'm often asked, do these programs require more judicial resources? We have not needed more judicial resources to handle military diversion where, I assure you, is an adversarial hearing. Because the prosecution, often, for very solid basis, opposes because wanting to protect victims and the seriousness of the offense. Not everyone is diverted, many are denied, but it is not a process that requires great resources from the court. Because in the end, the court has to deal with all of this anyway and therefore, I urge you to support this bill. Thank you.

Caitlin Bellis: Yes, I'm Caitlin Bellis of Public Counsel in Los Angeles. I'm here to provide technical assistance today. And also, Public Counsel is in support of this bill. So, first of all there is no right to appointed counsel for people who are in removal proceedings. So, you can be detained and you can be removed from this country without ever having the support of an attorney. Even though the government is represented in every proceeding, and even though it's a trial-like environment. And so, in fact, the vast majority of detained people who are in removal proceedings currently do not have counsel and never receive competent legal advice in their proceedings. This includes many people who have meritorious claims for relief and who would have a legal right to stay in the United States, and who fail to achieve that relief because they don't have counsel. I also would like to clarify that the bill would only provide funding to attorneys, that we are hopeful that the requirements would actually be quite stringent where removal defense is extremely complex. And immigration law is extremely complex. And we're hopeful that the eligibility requirements for grants would ensure that funding only goes to organizations that have sufficient expertise in the area. And so, not just attorneys but attorneys where their organizations have five years experience providing complex removal defense services or have already shown their competence by undertaking contract with the federal government through a couple of the programs that have provided counsel to unaccompanied minors or to mentally incompetent detainees. And then, there are a couple of other eligibility requirements. On the post-conviction relief point, oftentimes, a conviction will completely bar someone to immigration relief, even if that was convicted without the confident advice of a public defender as to the immigration consequences of the conviction. And so, people can sometimes accept pleas where, it reduces peas where they end up being automatically deportable. And they had no idea that that was the case when they would have otherwise fought the conviction. And also, under Prop 47, a lot of current felonies can be reduced to misdemeanors. And that can help provide people with immigration relief. Furthermore, immigration law is retroactive, so sometimes a person is convicted of something when it wasn't a deportable offense, and then, it becomes a deportable offense. So, in all of these scenarios, sometimes with decades old drug convictions or minor convictions that end up rendering someone automatically deportable, at post-conviction, relief is the best way to help that person stay in the country. So, it's not to, it's really to-

At the same time, California's poise to lead the country in fighting back against mass deportations because of ground work led my many years of state organizing by immigrant communities and immigrant rights organizations such as those who help pass the Trust Act and the Truth Act over the past few years, many of whom are in the room today in strong support of this bill. The California values act will keep our communities are being torn apart. It'll keep families, such as Pedro's, from being being torn apart. It'll protect due process rights, it'll reduce fear in our communities, and it also will make sure we don't use state and local resources to fuel mass deportations, and also to burden local resources. In particular, the bill contains the following key provisions. First, state and local law enforcement agencies along with school police would not be allowed to engage in immigration enforcement, with some exceptions. No state or local law enforcement will be allowed to detain or transfer any person for deportation without a warrant. There's also a federal case law that supports this since it's a due process constitutional violation to do these things. No state or local resource will be used to investigate, detain or detect, report or arrest a person purely for immigration purposes. Secondly, the bill will also create safe spaces. It will require that California school, hospitals, and court houses remain safe and accessible to all California residents regardless of immigration status. Each agency would be required to establish and make public policies, model policies, that limit immigration enforcement to the fullest extent possible under federal and state law. This bill would save us local and state resources, because it costs a lot of money to engaged in Trump's deportation machine. We'll fight, we'll resist and we'll protect our communities against mass deportation. We look forward to working with all of you here to protect California, to protect our residents and to make sure that our residents are not in fear because of a broken immigration system that does not allow many people in California who contribute immensely to this economy, and this large community, to remain here and to feel safe. California's ready to lead the charge, and we want to really encourage you and support you in voting yes for the California Values Act, SB 54, today, thank you.

[{'start': 25, 'end': 40, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Hailly Korman: Good morning Senators, my name is Hailly Korman. I'm a civil rights attorney at Bellwether Education Partners and I work with public education and justice agencies across the country to improve the ways that they meet the education needs of students involved in the justice system. I was a member of the state's education transitions work group, LA County's probation work group and the Camp Kilpatrick redesign team. I've worked with nearly 20 states and visited schools in secure facilities across the country. When I ask young people in those schools to share with me the last time they remember going to school every day, the answer is almost always fifth or sixth grade. Before being incarcerated, many of these students have not attended school regularly for three to five years. But reentry is an inflection point, and the better prepared they are when they leave a secure facility, the more likely they are to be accepted, welcomed and supported by a receiving school. For many of our students, their transition from a juvenile court school back to their community will be their last best chance to move forward on a trajectory towards productive civic, social, and workforce participation. Returning to a community based school with a full record of necessary basic educational information, as SB 304 would provide through the individualized transition plan, not only facilitates the correct placement in credit bearing coursework and the provision of all appropriate special education supports, but it also empowers that young person to begin to become an advocate for their own bright future. Researchers estimate that upwards of 60% of young people who are incarcerated will never successfully return to school. Reentry's a crucial moment in a young person's life when they're vulnerable to losing essential course credits or dropping out entirely. Despite that, we still see astonishing variance in policies and practices across the state. Some counties are making remarkable efforts to ensure continuity of care and warm hand-offs. However, the statutory clarity that SB 304 provides will support statewide progress and help to ensure that all students are prepared to return to their communities as full participants. Finally, please note that SB 304 is aligned with the new provisions of the SSA, our primary federal education statute, which now requires states to ensure records transfer, reentry planning, and credit transfer for students returning to their communities from juvenile court schools. Section C of the revised federal planning template requires states to, quote, "provide a plan for assisting in the transition of children and youth between correctional facilities and locally operated programs." Thank you.
