SB 233 helps the people caring for our state's foster children access the educational information they need, to both meet their legal mandates, and support our young people. You may be surprised to learn that many caregivers are afraid of engaging in their foster youth's education. Not all caregivers hold educational rights, so social workers and school districts aren't clear about the role that caregivers can play in their youth's education. SB 233 will clarify that caregivers, even if they aren't the educational rights holder are in fact supposed to have access to educational records. I remember when I scored the highest grade in my 8th grade Algebra exam. I was so proud and excited, but when I tried to show my test to my foster mother, she told me she wouldn't sign it. She didn't even want to look at it, the message I got was clear. I didn't matter. But the reality was, she was afraid she could lose her license for doing something she might not be allowed to do. When I became a foster parent school districts were inconsistent with me about what they would share, if anything. They were worried they might be violating privacy rights. Without sharing the information, I didn't always have what I needed to help my foster daughter.  Imagine how difficult it would be to help your foster child in school if you didn't know they were failing. Now over a decade after exiting foster care myself, I train other foster parents. This bill will help caregivers get the needed training and clarification. I ask for your support for SB 233, thank you.

Tam Ma: Good afternoon, Mr. Chair and members. My name is Tam Ma, and I am the Legal and Policy Director at Health Access California. We represented consumers when regulators consider health insurance mergers, including the four mergers that the state has seen in the last couple of years. And the key question that we always ask is, is bigger actually better for consumers? Health plans and insurers should not be allowed to get bigger unless they actually get better. And we are sponsoring this bill because we want the DMHC, our state regulator of health plans, to actually have the ability to protect consumers and reject mergers if they are bad. Generally speaking, we hear the same promises when insurance company executives when they seek to merge. They promise lower costs, better quality, higher stock prices. But we also know from history that having fewer insurers leads to higher premiums, both for large employers who buy coverage for their workers, and for consumers who buy their own coverage in the individual market. As we looked at the recent mergers, we were surprised to find that the Department of Managed Health Care, which regulates 95% of the market, doesn't have sufficient authority to make sure that bigger is actually better for consumers. As a result, DMHC can approve or approve a merger with limited conditions but they can't reject a merger. And they're not even required to hold a public hearing. We had to ask them to do that in the mergers that they've reviewed. AB 595 strengthens the DMHC's authority over these mergers, and makes it clear in statute that they can approve, approve with conditions or reject the mergers. And much of what the DMHC would be required to do is modeled after what the general attorney currently does, when it comes to mergers involving non-profit hospitals, and we want to make sure the process is public and transparent. Even though two of the major mergers, the Anthem Cigna merger and Aetna Humana mergers, were blocked in federal court for the time being, we expect health plans to continue merging in the future. And we know that premiums go up and not down when markets become more concentrated. That's why we think AB 595 is an important bill, and we respectfully ask for your aye vote.

Nick Louizos: Thank you, Mr. Chair and members. Nick Louizos on behalf of the California Association of Health Plans, regrettably in opposition to Assembly Bill 595. Let me start by saying that we do appreciate the sentiment that a healthy competition is good for consumers. California's market is both competitive and healthy. Our association for instance represents 49 health plans covering 28 million lives in all lines of business. With 23, excuse me, with 2.3 million enrollees including 1.4 million enrollees in Covered California, our state's individual market offers competition and choice. With 11 health plans participating in the exchange, consumers can easily shop for coverage and compare prices. Our issue with this bill isn't whether public authorities have some role in mergers and acquisitions. Indeed, they already have a role. In fact, in approving recent transactions, the DMHC has required extensive undertakings on the parties involved, including my member health plans. Our opposition then is based primarily on the vast scope of the bill and what we view as a vague and broad standards that plans and regulators would have to meet in order to obtain prior approval from a state regulator for transactions. As currently drafted, Assembly Bill 595 discourages reasonable new investments in health care that are intended to create efficiencies in economies of scale. From our read of the bill, even a relatively basic consolidation or transfer of assets within the same corporate family could trigger prior approval from state regulators and hold back innovative investments. We believe that this is an intensive amount of work for relatively little value. AB 595 also institutes unreasonably high hurdles for mergers and acquisitions. As only one example, the measure expressly requires that regulators find in fact, that a merger proposal itself will lower prices before the merger or acquisition can be approved. Which consumer prices? Prices that doctors charge health plans, prices that hospital systems charge health plans, prices that drug companies charge health plans, or are we talking about premiums? If we're talking about premiums or other prices, the language fails to take into account the reality of the health care market. It fails to take into account potential increases in utilization, provider rates, government mandates, rising drug costs. All of these things together impact consumer prices in a short and long-term. So we believe that codifying unreasonable standards will make conditional approvals under this bill inevitable, thus placing the plans that are contracted provider groups and consumers and limbo. And actually, the conditional approval provisions in this bill are treated in a somewhat interesting way in one section of the bill. The regulator must take, make a series of findings that, again, from our perspective, we view as unrealistic in order to approve or conditionally approve a transaction. And in another section of the bill, conditional approvals are only allowed if the parties of the transaction agreed to prevent, not mitigate, but prevent things from happening that may or may not happen. So we have a question of how that sequence would unfold. Okay, my time's almost up. I just want to say that we appreciate the author's amendments which resolve one issue, but again, the bill applies to vast, vast majority of the market. And if there is a demonstrated issue with the merger, we are willing to have a discussion. A version of this bill was purposed last year in the Senate when a series of planning, carry of mergers were being proposed. Some of those mergers were blessed by public authorities, other mergers were not. So I bring that up because we do have a process in place that allows some to go forward and some not to go forward. And unless, it's a demonstrated problem that we are missing, we relatively, respectfully, believe that no action is required at this time. No further action. Thank you.

They try to let go of these events but sometimes the events won't let go of them  and national studies indicate that one out of every five firefighters suffers from post traumatic stress disorder which is roughly the same rates that's seen in the military and firefighters are often four times as likely to take their own lives as they are to lose their life in a fire or other traumatic event. So, we strongly ask for an aye vote on AB 1116.

California TB case rates has steadily declined since 1992, however TB is not evenly spread across California. And many local health jurisdictions have few if any cases of tuberculosis each year. The declined in cases and case rates is not the direct result of mandated universal TB testing of low-risk populations. But, instead public health efforts in TB surveillance, screening treatment, contact investigation, and outbreak control. The public health infrastructure has weathered the recession and continues today to our TB elimination. AB 511 is aligned with the California Tuberculosis Elimination Plan of 2016 to 2020 which has seven key recommendations. Specifically recommendation number two is to apply focus and effective strategies for TB testing in California by reducing TB testing in low-risk populations. The groups targeted by AB 511 are TB low risk populations. Current laws regarding mandated TB examination of low risk persons are not evidence based, are not consistent with guidelines numerous to expert bodies, and are not cost-effective given diminishing resources. Healthcare providers can effectively assessed person's risk for TB using a risk assessment tool jointly developed by CDPH and CTCA. Yes response to any of the questions on the risk assessment would indicate that the respondent should be tested for TB. Robert Kim-Farley: Good afternoon, Chairman Wood and Assemblymembers.My name is Dr. Robert Kim-Farley. It's my pleasure to testify on behalf of the Health Officers Association of, California, or HOAC. I've extensive experience in managing communicable disease control programs, including programs to prevent and controlled tuberculosis. Having served with the California Conference of Local Health Officers as chair of the Communicable Disease Control and Prevention Committee. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and in my current capacity as Director of Communicable Disease Control and Prevention Division at the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health. However, today I'm speaking on behalf of HOAC. I urge your support of AB 511. The intent of this bill is to bring California's tuberculosis testing requirements into alignment with current evidence-based guidelines and recommendations from state and federal public health agencies. AB 511 would shift California's TB testing requirements away from universal testing to a targeted approach that focus on identifying individuals, who are at highest risk for tuberculosis infection. And is consistent with prior legislation. The bill removes specific testing requirements for schools and for a number of low risk populations, such as the blind and deaf. Current statute gives a local health officer the discretion to require TB testing for students entering K through 12 schools, but requires testing of students in special schools for the deaf and blind. Since 1995, the National TB Control Community has acknowledged generalized school screening as a public health measure is an ineffective method of detecting and preventing cases of childhood tuberculosis. For this reason many counties with the highest burdens of TB such as San Francisco, Santa Clara, Los Angeles, Alameda, and San Diego have moved to a risk-assessment process rather than universally screening and testing all K through 12 entrance. AB 511 will allowed health officers to determine the best approach for students at schools to the deaf or blind, whose risk for TB is considered to be similar to the risk face by K through 12 students. The bill does not address testing requirements for healthcare personnel, which were addressed under Cal OSHA standards. Again, I urge your aye vote on AB 511, as an important step that will align testing requirements with evidence-based guidelines, minimise unnecessary harm, and move us towards the goal of eliminating tuberculosis in California. I'd be pleased to answer any questions that you may have.

Elena Lopez-Gusman: Thank you, Mr. Chair and members, Elena Lopez-Gusman on behalf of the California Chapter of the American College of Emergency Physicians. Pleased to be sponsoring this piece of legislation. We have a fundamental principle in our healthcare delivery system and that is, is that if you are a patient facing an emergency condition or crisis, you go to the emergency department. And the emergency department has to treat you regardless of your ability to pay. That fundamental principle was enacted into federal law. We commonly call it EMTALA, several decades ago. And it was also in our California Health and Safety Code Section 1371. And that provides that protection to patients. That no matter what, even if they can't afford it, they can go to the ER and they will be treated. That requirement extends not just in the emergency department, but to other facilities where the patient might need to be transferred in order to stabilize their care. So for example, if you are a patient and you're experiencing excruciating back pain, you go to the. The ER doctor examines you and diagnoses that you have kidney stones. But there's no urologist at that facility, and so you need to be transferred to a hospital where there's a urologist. And so, the physician will get on the phone and start calling around. And say hey, do you have a urologist there? I need to transfer my patient to you. That hospital, because of EMTALA and our state law can say no, I can't take the patient because we don't have enough beds. No, I can't take the patient because we don't have a urologist. But they can't say does that person have insurance? Are they on Medi-Cal? Will they be able to pay the bill? They cannot ask that question. They have to take the transfer if they have the ability to provide care. And the same is mostly true for psychiatric care because we've tried to achieve parity in California to provide the same kind of care for psychiatric patients. Well, what this bill does is try to close a loophole where stand-alone psychiatric facilities are not accepting patients regardless of ability to pay. They're accepting transfer of paying patients. But they're financially screening other patients. And so we're trying to close that loophole here with this bill. And the other provision that is really important too is to protect someone's civil rights. We have a provision in the state law. It's called the 5150 that basically says, we can violate your constitutional right to liberty when we believe you need to be detained against your will because you're a danger to yourself or someone else and provide medical care. But if someone is voluntarily seeking care in the emergency department because they know they're sick and they're not a danger to others, we should not require them to have their constitutional rights be violated simply to get the care that they need. And so this bill also addresses that important issue. We urge your aye vote.

San Jose State University is among the handful of participating CSU campuses in the DNP pilot program. I want to assure you that we are ready and eager to continue. Let me very briefly explain what has been accomplished thus far during the pilot period established by the 2010 legislation. As you've heard, the CSU established two pilot consortia, one each in northern and Southern California. The Northern California Consortium is a partnership between my campus, San Jose State University, and Fresno State. The Southern California Consortium comprises CSU's Fullerton, Long Beach, and Los Angeles campuses. Once chosen for the pilot, our faculty develop curriculum that was specifically designed, both to develop future nursing faculty members by embedding teaching pedagogue and strategies within the program and to train advance practice clinicians. In other words, our faculty created a curriculum aligned with the statutory goals of the 2010 authorizing legislation. The first cohort of DNP students enrolled in Fall of 2012. By the end of that year, our program achieved national accreditation from both the Commission on Collegiate Nursing Education and the Western Association of Schools and Colleges. Three cohorts of students have since graduated, and are having a significant impact. both in our academic nursing programs, and in clinical healthcare positions throughout the State of California. I am pleased to report that this program is working just as it was intended. One third of CSU's DNP alumni have taken faculty positions in California, and nearly one in four are teaching at the CSU. In fact, CSU DNP graduates represented one in six nursing tenure track faculty hired through out the CSU in 2014. The importance of growing our nursing faculty ranks cannot be overstated. The CSU is facing an impending wave of faculty retirements. Two-thirds, two-thirds of our tenured nursing faculty members are age 55 or older. Only one in five, is younger than age 50. As these faculty members retire, CSU's nursing faculty shortage will be exacerbated. AB 422 is our best opportunity to address this impending nursing faculty short fall, thereby insuring that we can continue to educate and train the nurses we will need to serve the health needs of our citizens. Thus, on behalf of all of the CSU's 19 campuses offering nursing programs, and indeed, all Californians. I urge you to allow us to continue to offer the DNP degree by supporting Assembly Bill 422. Thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today.

Food insecurity impacts a striking number of students on college campuses, particularly in California. In the UC system alone, almost half or 48% of all undergraduate students and a quarter of all graduate students are food insecure. This means that one in every two undergraduate students eats a reduced quality of quantity diet mostly due to an inability to purchase foods. How can we expect a student who's constantly hungry to get good grades, balance a full course load, and work, pay rent, graduate, and be successful when they enter the workforce? There are many efforts on college campuses to address food insecurity Including food pantries and meal point donations. However these don't address the underlying root causes of food insecurity, such as the inability to select and purchase foods. Students who are feeling insecure talk about being negatively impacted, physically, emotionally, and academically. Those who do not receive CalFresh speak about the barriers to signing up, and those who do speak to its ability to lift them out of food insecurity, allowing them to flourish in school. He's beginning the process of applying for Cal Fresh but has struggled with the complicated nature of the application process. Making the application more accessible, and being able to buy food with Cal Fresh dollars on campus, would be hugely helpful for him and the other tens of thousands of students who are food insecure. The face of food insecurity is diverse and widespread. I consider myself to be a successful graduate student at a top University. And I attribute much of my success to the fact that I am on CalFresh. Without the extra $194 per month to spend on food, I would certainly struggle to pay my rent and make ends meet, while juggling a full course load, doing my research, and working two jobs. There's no question in my mind that continuing to find ways to simplify CalFresh is a necessary step towards supporting our students. At the federal level, again in 2011, then President Barack Obama embraced the look back mechanism in his Executive Order 13563, requiring federal agencies to conduct a retrospective review. Similar to what AB 12 would require, as part of his administration's commitment to improving regulation and regulatory review. And this is because good governance experts agree that one of the most effective ways to get effective regulation is to evaluate whether the rules we adopt are doing what we adopted them to do. There's no reason to be afraid to ask if what we are doing is working. By looking back, California is both able to identify successful programs as a model for new regulation, as well as identifying ineffective, inconsistent, contradictory, outmoded regulation. And alleviate the accumulation of regulation the burdens our businesses. Now, more than ever, California must be a leader in demonstrating how to govern well. AB 12 is a key step in assuring that California's regulatory framework secures our policy goals, ensures compliance, and encourages entrepreneurship and investment. And we respectfully request your support.

This has two benefits, the first is that can be used to cover the higher cost of major projects that can be difficult to pay for all at once and secondly because the projects themselves, have service over many years. Jarrell Cook: Jarrell Cook for the California Manufacturers & Technology Association, we are here in support of this bill because it meets our long-standing goal to improve California's regulatory climate and ensure good governance. This bill follows a recommendation in 2011 by the Little Hoover Commission, as well as a February 2017 recommendation by the Legislative Analyst's Office. And the reason why can be best summed up by the former Chief Economist to President Obama, Michael Greenstone, when he states that the single greatest problem with the current economic system, or with our current regulatory system, is that most regulations are subject to a cost benefit analysis only in advance of their implementation. This is the point when the least is known, and any analysis must rest on many unverifiable and potentially controversial assumptions. This bill cuts through our intuitions and beliefs about what works and gives us the foundation to regulate intelligently and with evidence based solutions, again, I want to emphasize that this is a non partisan, or bipartisan approach, it's not pro or anti regulation. If regulations are working, what this bill provides us is models to continue to regulate well, and if they are not working, it provides us the opportunity to fix them and meet our important public policy goals, that is how we govern well in California, so I respectfully request your aye vote.

In Colorado, 80% of the fatal crashes involving use of cannabis also involved alcohol. So you have that problem. Now, normally in drunk driving enforcement you have certain high intensity times. One of them is when the bars close at 2:00. Everybody's emptying from the bars, people are a little inebriated. They're not being responsible. What this bill will do, the unintended consequence, it will create two peak drunk driving risk times at night, at 2:00 and at 4:00. Not to mention the alcohol tourism you're going to get, where people go from one city to a city where the bars stay open until four. Now, this bill has also been framed in the context of urban nightlife, and those are serious issues, to be treated with respect. However, the law is so broad that, let me just give you an example. The City of Manteca could decide, three members of the City Council, hey, we're going to let our bar stay open till four in the morning. And then they're going to market that throughout the Central Valley, so think about people driving from Turlock or Stockton, after their bars close. And alcohol tourism is going to be a serious problem. You're going to see an increase in drunk driving. You're going to see two different times in the evening, where you're going to have a peek drunk driving risk time. And think about that four am closing time, people who leave at four are now going to be driving into very early commuter traffic as well. This is a bill that I think merits serious scrutiny. The nightlife issue is serious. However, it's premature and the submitting of the safeguards are illusory. If any of you have ever participated in an ABC protest hearing to protest a liquor or a bar in your community, you know that you're ability to protest that is largely illusory. And this measure builds on a flawed ABC protest system. So the safeguards talked about, although they exist on paper, are not safeguards in real life. We respectfully oppose.

But opposed to AB 1575 because it will not help salon workers, it will only lead to confusion and it's duplicative and I don't think many understand some of the issues related here today. So I want to take a moment to explain a few things to you, if I may. First, AB 1575 cites the Sherman Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Law, but it ignores the more applicable Federal OSHA workers right to know and understand regulations. In 2012, OSHA established a standard of right to understand. It outlined specific safety data sheets and information that needs to be on these as far as also training and employee requirements. Safety data sheets must include hazard identification, ingredients with specific hazards, first aid measures, applicable exposure limits, appropriate personal protective equipment, safe handling, storage, disposal guidelines as well as emergency contact information, relative exposure, expected symptoms if overexposure should occur. Secondly AB 1575 misrepresents the DTSC's safer cosmetic product list of candidate chemicals which is not intended to be a list of chemicals that are harmful to health as suggested. This is an attempt to turn the candidate chemicals list into something that is not. The DTSC clearly states and I quote, the DTSC publication of the candidate chemical list imposes no requirements on manufacturers of products that contain candidate chemicals. And they go on to say, again quoting, the candidate chemical list is not a list of chemicals of concern. This is the bill that's putting the cart in for the horse by categorizing ingredients in reality, that have not yet been categorized by the DTSC. Now perfect example is this titanium dioxide which is the most widely used commodity colored pigment on the planet. AB 1575 mischaracterizes titanium dioxide as a carcinogen in nail polish. Proposition 65 is one of the strictest standards in the world and it clearly states that titanium dioxide is a risk only when unbound, airborne, and respirable. This cannot occur with nail polishes since titanium dioxide is bound in a liquid suspension which quickly transforms into a solid film the titanium dioxide is bound not airborne and certainly not respire-able. So lastly imposing a state specific California only label requirement on global brands just doesn't make sense. So the PDA and myself we urge the Committee to reject this bill and I thank you very much for your time.

[{'start': 28, 'end': 38, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Janet Coffman: Thank you very much Mr. Chairman. It's a pleasure to be here with all of you today. I am Janet Coffman. I have a PhD in Health Services Research and a Master's in Public Policy from U.C. Berkley. I am on the faculty at the Phillip R. Lee Institute for health policy studies and the health force center at the University of California San Francisco and as was mentioned I serve as the lead investigator on the team that is evaluating the California community para medicine pilot projects and we issued our first report in January. First a little background on community para-medicine and this is also known as mobile integrated health and it is an innovative model of care that is being implemented and tested in most states across the United States. Utilizes the new week of the abilities of paramedics and emergency medical system as well as their availability 24 hours a day, seven days a week to provide alternatives to ambulance transport and ED visits that are tailored to meet the need of local communities, and to supplement other services available in the communities. Community paramedicine aligns with the aims of healthcare reform to improve patients experience, improve community health status and decrease the cost of care. Community Paramedics receives additional training beyond that required for paramedic licensure. And they provide care outside their traditional role which under California law is restricted to responding to 911 calls, transporting patients to an acute care hospital emergency department and performing inter facility transfers. And under the pilot project all of the community paramedics had to have first obtained their paramedic licensure. EMTs, advanced EMTs do not participate. And not only have obtained the paramedic licensure, but to have had approximately four years of experience in the field. So in the California project, all our experienced paramedics they all underwent a two-part training. One, a training in fundamentals of community paramedicine, and then a second set of training that was tailored to the community paramedicine concept being tested in their jurisdiction. In the current community para medicine projects are being conducted under a health workforce pilot project and this is a statutorially authorized program that's overseen by the office of statewide health planning and development. The project is sponsored by the California emergency medical services authority. And the evaluation includes 13 projects that are testing six community paramedicine concepts. Four of which are addressed in AB 1650. And the four concepts that AB 1650 addresses are short term home-based follow up care for persons recently discharged from a hospital due to a chronic condition such as heart failure or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. And the goal is to decrease their hospital re-admissions within 30 days and to generally improve their ability to manage their chronic illness. A second, and that's being tested in five sites. Two sites are testing frequent emergency medical services user concepts. And these projects provide case management services to persons who call 911 frequently, and frequent visitors to the ED. And the goal here is to reduce their use of EMS system by connecting them with primary care behavioral house, substance use disorder, social service, housing services. Services that more directly meet the needs that are driving them to call 911 or go to the ED. Third one site is testing directly observed therapy for tuberculosis. And this is a collaboration between the local EMS agency and the local public health department to provide directly observed therapy to people with Tuberculosis. And for those of you who may not familiar with tuberculosis, this involves dispensing medication. And observing patients taking their medication to ensure that the treatment is as effective as possible. And it involves taking treatment and a prescribed schedule over a period of multiple months. It's a complex treatment and the goal is to stop. You know, not only to cure the tuberculosis in that patient but also to stop the spread of tuberculosis. Which is a highly contagious disease. There's also one project that's testing a hospice concept. And in this case in response to 911 calls. In cases in which the patient, the family, if the person is in a residential facility, the residential facility has called 911. So 911 system has been activated, paramedics have been summoned. And the goal here is for the paramedics to collaborate with the hospice agency, nurses, the patients and family members to treat the patients in their home where that's possible. And to honor the patient's wishes and to avoid transporting to the ED unless that's what the patient wants. And unless the hospice nurse and the patient family have made a determination that that's in the patient's best interest. So it's really a collaboration. There are also several projects that are testing transport to alternate destination, to a mental health crisis center. And to urgent care centers. But I won't talk much about those because they are not addressed by AB 1650. I should mention, too, that there are 13 projects that were included the evaluation. A 14th project was approved and added in February 2017, that's in San Francisco. That's testing alternate transport directly sobering Center for chronic inebriates. And so we have results from the first 19 months of the projects. The first project started in June of 2015. And of the 13 included in the evaluation the last one got up and running in October 2015. And I'll need to move more quickly. So what did we find? We found from the post-discharge projects that hospital re-admissions within 30 days of discharge decreased significantly for all five projects. To somewhat lesser extent for one but, all five were successful. Both of the frequent EMS User Projects achieved a 50 percent reduction in numbers of 911 calls, ambulance transports and E.D. visits. That the tuberculosis project, the community paramedics works effectively with the Physician in charge of Public Health. The public health nurses in community health workers to administer treatment nearly 100% of the time. And that the community paramedics successfully work with hospice nurses to reduce the number of ambulance transports to ED's by approximately 50%. We estimate that the hospice frequent 911 caller and post-discharge projects achieve savings to health systems or hospitals by decreasing admissions or ED visits. The majority of these savings accrue to Medicare and MediCal. Because the majority of the folks enrolled in these projects either had Medicare or MediCal coverage. A couple other comments while I still have the floor. It's about how the projects are designed and implemented. They're designed to supplement existing services such as hospice and home health. And not to substitute with them. And as we've done our evaluation, and I think Jimmy and Brian can attest. As we've done our site visits that we've asked questions about this to see are you really doing this in a way that supplements and complements. And as far as we can tell, no personnel were displaced, that this really is a complement. That for example some of the post discharge projects are targeting people who do not have coverage for home health services. So as wonderful as home health is these are people for whom that's not an option. Or they're filling a gap. They're visiting people, say, within 72 hours of discharge, that's their protocol. To fill a gap and, for whatever reason, in the communities involved, home health is not able to respond that quickly. And so this is a gap filling service for those folks who are eligible for home health coverage. To have somebody out there in the home or on the phone checking with them to make sure they have their meds. Make sure they have their follow-up Doctor appointment scheduled. And so just I think in closing, since we're running low on time, to emphasize that. Two things that we feel is really reflected in these projects, the collaboration, the filling gaps in the community. And also that this really does I think improve outcomes for individuals and for society.

Heather Leutwyler: Thank you Mr Chair and members, and thank you Assemblywoman Waldron for your support of our bill. My name is Dr Heather Leutwyler, I am an assistant Professor of nursing at UCSF, and I come to you with more than a decade of experience caring for people with serious mental illness, and doing research with this population. I'd like to tell you the story of Earl, a gentleman with schizophrenia that I interviewed during my dissertation work. When I met Earl, he was 61 years old, and had been released from prison five months ago after serving an 18 year sentence. During our interview, he described how ultimately, his untreated mental illness led him to prison, and how effective case management and treatment while in prison was helping with the transition out of prison and back into the community. Prior to going prison, Earl made repeated failed attempts to receive consistent psychiatric care. He explains that he was basically on his own. He ran out of medication and began self medicating with alcohol, heroin, and cocaine. He became homeless, then he committed a crime that led him to prison. As he spent time in prison, his symptoms worsened until he was eventually transferred to a state psychiatric facility, where he began to receive consistent psychiatric care. And slowly began to feel better. He was eventually released from prison and was linked up with a case-management program, as well as a psychiatrist upon his release. Earl described how he felt living out in our community with these supports in place. He said, I'm in a beautiful spot, my case-management program helps get a little more structure in my life. It helps me cope with staying clean and sober, so I am not self-medicating. Earl went on to describe the role that case managers play in his life. He said, we talk once a week about anything I want to talk about. We meet every Friday at 11. She tells me what she thinks I should be doing or I shouldn't be doing. She asked me a lot of questions about how I feel. She's kind of like a psychiatrist. I missed a few days and she asked why, I said I feel depressed. She said, when you feel depressed, come here and we'll work through it. Earl ended our interview with an important insight that I think can be a guide for our care of people with serious mental illness. Every time I go out on the street, I see somebody talking to themselves. They need to reach out to someone, that's going to be understanding, that's going to help them feel real comfortable and cared for. There's an opening there to make a better person out of that person. Earl is a great example of some of the main points in our bill which are, jail based screening and diagnosis to identify population early in their involvement in the criminal justice system. Integrated mental health and substance use treatment that begins in jail and continues out in the community. Transitional case management that similarly extends from jail to the community. And a robust, data driven evaluation process to ensure that we're doing is effective, thank you.

Services at crisis stabilization units are provided to people in acute distress associated with mental health issues such as suicidal behavior, psychosis, and other mood disorders. They're unpredictable when they come in, and they receive a really full evaluation at that point of entry. They reduce unnecessary stays in psychiatric hospitals, reduce the number and expense to emergency rooms, and divert inappropriate incarcerations. Crisis stabilization teams work at these facilities to stabilize individuals. With specialists working to provide, either an appropriate outpatient or inpatient treatment referral, depending on the specific needs of individuals. These treatment teams work very closely with the consumers who are in crisis, who are built to rebuild their coping skills, reduce symptoms, and empower self-care. Statewide counties have faced delays, or lack of bed availability for different age groups, as well as both, in terms of age, and co-ocurring conditions that sometimes present themselves. This bill gives crisis stabilization units more flexibility in caring for individuals in a psychiatric crisis, by allowing them to continue to provide care and support beyond the current 23 hour and 59 minute limitation. The bill helps further these efforts by allowing a certified CSU, crisis stabilization unit to extend the time frame for providing the care on a case by case basis, and a pending a referral to another level of care. AB 1372 requires each county mental health plan that accesses this flexibility, created by this bill, to establish specific treatment protocols. Documentation standards, and administrative procedures, consistent with best practices and other evidence based medicine. To provide treatment to individuals who are provided this crisis stabilization service for more than 24 hours. And so these reasons that we are in support of AB 1372, thank you.

Tara Needham: Hi, my name is Tara Needham, I'm a clinical psychologist and assistant Professor at UC Davis Medical Center. I am also the Executive Director of the early psychosis programs there. I've had the pressure of working at the forefront of clinical service and research, related to early intervention and prevention for serious mental illness for about 17 years. Today I'm very happy to be here and talk about why this is so important. Many people say that the onset of psychosis is like falling off a cliff. An analogy that can phase a devastating outcome, we don't typically fall off cliffs and survive. I've heard this sort of analogy used many, many times. And if you think about the previous experiences that many people have had, you can understand why they think this way. Before the onset of the medications we have today, many individuals with psychotic symptoms experience significant side effects. And there was little focus on therapy to improve their functioning, or support their family to maintain important social connections. People were often institutionalized, and after the end of institutions, they ended up homeless, and we all know too well the devastating outcomes of homelessness. Our outpatients mental health system was not equiped to handle their long standing and pervasive needs. If these were the available treatments psychosis would seem like a cliff, like a deep dive from which thereis no return. In this day and age, research and common sense, allow us to change this narrative from failure, to one of recovery and fulfillment, when we think about prevention and early intervention. In Sacramento County alone, with our population, we would expect to see over 630 new cases of psychosis per year. With an average age of onset around 18, 19, 20 years old, that's 630 individuals who are facing a drastic change in their life. 630 families who are questioning what to do and how to help. Sacramento County is very lucky, we have the clinic at UC Davis. Whose mission it is to put these young people and their families back on the path to wellness and hope. Each year, we serve over 175 individuals in the early stages of psychosis. We provide accurate diagnoses, evidence-based treatment, support for work or school, and support for their families. We do not see psychosis as a cliff that you fall off of. It is a disease of the brain, and with good treatment you get back to living your life. Many of our clients are still in school and our goal is to keep them there. It may take some time, it will take hard work, but recovery is possible. And this is consistent with US and international research, that shows better outcomes and lower costs associated with this kind of care. We have clients attending University of California schools, working full time, completing graduate degrees, raising their children. Their family members have knowledge and know how to support their loved ones. The goal of this bill, AB 1315, is to find ways to bring these evidence-based practices to more youth, more families, and more communities in California. Out of 58 counties, only 24 have early psychosis programs. In Sacramento, we regularly get calls from counties without programs. This morning I walked into a phone call from Modesto, for a family who had no place to send their son. This is unacceptable, this is not fair. Why would we ask those families to struggle to find care if their children had cancer or diabetes? We would not ask that, why would we ask this for mental healthcare? Why do we ignore this problem? On average, individuals and families struggle with psychosis for one and a half years before they are diagnosed and treated. For optimal outcomes, research consistently shows that it should be less than three months. And AB 1315 will help California get closer to the sensible and necessary goal. We should strive in every way to make early psychosis care available across our state. No one should worry that the onset of psychosis is a cliff their child might fall off of. Thank you so much for your support.

Contrary to the experience noted earlier, our experience here in California is very clear that the majority of cases of food-borne illness are caused by home-prepared foods and a sizeable share of outbreaks are caused by home-prepared foods as well. The other issue to note with regard with local permitting is that there are several reasons why this is not a good idea, from our perspective. Food handling guidelines are national in scope. Home-cooked foods cross county lines, as do the illnesses caused by outbreaks, so that a locality that would not permit this would still suffer from a neighboring locality that does permit it and it legitimizes a dangerous practice. Individuals who perform this type of cooking in the home will assume that it's appropriate for them to do it. It's been noted that with this type of cooking already occurs, it's a source of a lot of illness. And the point I would try to make is that, unlike many small businesses, the preparation of food places the consumers of food at very specific risks and our job in public health is to protect people from those risks.

Daniel Mirda: So my name is Dr. Daniel Mirda. I have been a practicing oncologist and hematologist in Northern California for over 30 years, with training at Stanford and UCSF. Guidelines are agreed upon evidence-based treatment plans for a specific diagnosis that have been formulated by committees of experts from universities around the country. The preeminent set of guidelines in oncology have been published by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network or NCCN since 1996 for over 20 years. These guidelines are nationally and internationally respected and are highly trusted and recognized by physicians and many health plans. Because they are developed by national experts donating over 26,000 hours yearly of volunteer service. Their names, affiliations, potential conflicts of interest of these experts are disclosed publicly at the beginning of each guideline for each disease. NCCN does not accept pharmaceutical support in development of these guidelines. A pathway is a subset, occasionally a single choice from a guideline. Many practices, including my own review national guidelines for specific diagnoses. And select one or a smaller subset of the guideline recommended treatment plans for our patients with that diagnosis. For more than 20 years, pathways have been recognized as an important method by which the quality of care can be improved. By insuring evidence-based care, standardizing therapies and processes, and decreasing treatment errors. Practices including my own are able to select pathways from available guidelines, because we can consider the expertise of the Committee that developed those guidelines. And review the underlying rationale for their treatment recommendations. In other words, transparency of the guideline is essential to selection of the pathways. That is why AB 1107's requirements for pathway transparency is so important to physicians. As a physician, we are concerned by the recent foray of health plans as designers of treatment pathways. And not being transparent on how these pathways are decided and by who. We understand that they are voluntary. We are concerned about the payers of oncology care having undue influence over these treatment decisions. We are concerned how the pathways were chosen from among essentially equivalent treatments, but with varying costs and side effects. Currently, as a physician, we make choices based on what is best for our patients characteristics, understanding side effects, outcomes, affordability, etc. At our board meeting, a presentation by health plans for pathway programs was unwilling to share committee members' rationale for treatment decisions it called proprietary. So health plans are proposing pathways, and thereby limiting choices on a national level. And I would hope that California would be a leader, to ensure transparency of pathway programs by insurers. This bill allows doctors to have the information we need to provide the best care for our patients. It's important to physicians and our cancer patients, that you should support AB 1107.

John Winger: Thank you, Mr. Chair and members. John Winger on behalf of Anthem Blue Cross, respectfully here in opposition to AB 1107. As way of background for some of the new members of the Committee. Anthem began developing voluntary clinical care pathways for cancer treatment back in July, 2014. Due to medical innovation and the wide variety of cancer treatment options. Research shows that up to one in three people treated with chemotherapy do not receive a treatment plan that is consistent with current medical evidence and best practices. In order to address this disparity, Anthem has developed its Cancer Care Quality Program in collaboration with oncologists, pharmacists, and others. Anthem's voluntary pathways are based on medical evidence that analyzes outcomes related to clinical benefit. Both survival and quality of life, toxicity, and strength of national guideline recommendations. Costs are considered only when clinical outcomes among therapies are equivalent. These voluntary pathways are peer-reviewed by external advisors, that consist of roughly a dozen geographically-diverse physicians. Who are actively treating cancer patients, and work in academic and community oncology groups. Anthem evaluates clinical data, performance status and planned treatment pathways within the program. Those metrics, along with newly introduced treatments, are evaluated on a quarterly basis. To ensure these voluntary pathways are constantly up to date with the best, most effective clinical treatment guidelines. Anthem's pathways are value-based treatment options based on evidence, national clinical guidelines, and treatment outcomes. If any of our in-network doctors disagree, and choose not to follow our recommended pathway. Then they can continue to be fully reimbursed for the treatment pathway they decide to use. In regards to AB 1107, Anthem has two fundamental objections to the bill. First, AB 1107 singles out clinical care pathways developed by health plans as needing additional oversight standards. And ignores pathways that are developed by drug distributors, hospital systems and others. We have heard that health plan pathways need additional oversight, due to our unique relationship with the provider. And that a potential for undue influence is there. We would argue that the other entities that develop pathways have unique relationships that are equally as important. Hospital systems and medical centers develop pathways, that can be used as a direct performance matrix for their employed oncologists. They can also influence outside oncologists who seek admitting privileges to their facilities. Hospital system pathways themselves can be also influenced through their purchasing prices for distributors. Drug distributors develop pathways that have a unique relationship with drug manufacturers. In regards to purchasing price and reimbursements, which may also influence oncologists' decisions. Academic centers also create pathways. These pathways are influenced by the academic centers' unique relationships with pharmaceutical manufacturers in terms of their pipeline products. Which can create bias in their development as well. Given all the various relationships in the system, we strongly believe that if the Legislature feels compelled to add additional oversight to clinical care pathways. Then the oversight should apply to all pathways being developed by healthcare entities. Last year, the Committee recommended applying the provisions of this bill to all pathways. We would continue to support that approach. We also continue to object to the disclosing of names of our third-party independent panel of advisors. It is evident that when panelists' names are shared, they are lobbied by numerous entities. Including pharmaceutical manufacturers, which creates bias in the clinical evidence review process. Also, our advisors require that we keep their names confidential within their contracts. If we were required to disclose those names, even to contractor physicians, we would have to renegotiate those contracts. We are pretty confident that most of those advisers would choose not to participate. Which would diminish our ability to have the most qualified experts on our panel. For those reasons, we must respectfully oppose AB 1107. I have with me today Ann Nguyen who is Director of Oncology Solutions for Anthem, if you have any specific questions to our pathways. Thank you.

Current state law ensures access to free medical records in SSI and SSP cases on appeal. This is incredibly important for the lowest-income Californians that we serve. One of the most common reasons for denial in Social Security applications is insufficient medical evidence to establish disability under Social Security regulations. This often occurs because individuals are not able to provide documentation of their illnesses, because their healthcare providers require payment to copy and provide records up front. This places a huge hurdle in front of individuals applying for SSI benefits, who are often homeless or marginally housed, with no income or savings. One recent SSI client for Bay Legal met with us days before a scheduled hearing to appeal a denial. This client was homeless and not receiving any public benefits at all. We obtained their case file from Social Security to assess their case for representation. And the case file was thin, as no medical records were provided from either a large private or public healthcare organization that had provided healthcare treatment. This individual would almost certainly have been found not disabled under Social Security standards, because of the lack of medical evidence. We requested a postponement, and while our request was granted, the individual now must wait months more until their day in front of a judge and a decision in their case. Bay Legal attorneys were able to advocate continuously for the release of the individual's records from the provider, which the client has a right to under current state law, and we are now preparing the meritorious case for hearing. Were it not for state law requiring the free release of medical records for applications on appeal neither the individual nor Bay Legal would have been able to afford these records. And their case would likely have failed before even being presented in full. Current wait times from requests from an administrative hearing, to receive of a decision average 595 days nationally, which reflects our clients experience in the Bay Area, it is in an individual's best interest to obtain approval early on in the process. As SB 575 extends free access to medical records to the inital application in the Social Security disability process, it will increase the ability of applicants and organizations like ours to fully present their case earlier and help them receive life sustaining and stabilizing benefits earlier. These same issues with Social Security apply to the Veterans Administration, another federal administrative agency, where people are more likely to be unrepresented in their case, and cases often take even longer to reach a decision, thank you for the opportunity to speak on this important issue.

[{'start': 0, 'end': 15, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Joseph Morgan: Thank you Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee. My name is Joseph Morgan, I'm an Associate Professor of social work at the University of Minnesota. I'm here today as a researcher who has studied dialysis social worker caseloads for more than a decade. SB 349's proposal to establish minimum staffing requirements for social workers, nurses, and patient care technicians in chronic dialysis clinics, as well as minimum transition time between patients receiving dialysis. Services can help strengthen patient's safety reduce dialysis acquired infections, and contribute to overall positive health outcomes. My research has shown that California has had consistently high patient caseloads for social workers compared to many other states. Between 2007 and 2014, a full time Dialysis Social Worker in California, had an average case load ranging from 121 to 137 patients. With some social workers reporting individual case loads as high as 500 patients. Of all the states in the country, California Dialysis Social Workers had the highest patient case loads in 2007. The second highest case load in 2010, and the second highest case load in 2014, these findings illustrate a troubling trend. The staffing requirements proposed in SB 349 offer hope for dialysis patients being treated at more than 550 clinics in California. The National Kidney Foundation's Council of Nephrology Social Workers strongly recommends a maximum of 75 patients per full-time social worker. This ratio would allow practitioners to utilize their full range of training and expertise. To assist their patients with interventions such as depression screening and treatment, motivational support to promote medication adherence, and strategies to reduce missed or shortened treatments. Nurses and patient care technicians are also vital members of the care team because, they work collaboratively to ensure that patients are dialised safely and infection risks are reduced. Unfortunately, these professionals confront pressures similar to social workers, large case loads, and inadequate time to complete required tasks to ensure patient safety. In the absence of minimum staffing requirements that are grounded in the reality of everyday practice, we run a risk of diminishing patients' well being. Increasing their likelihood of being hospitalized due to infections, and adding to already high healthcare expenditures for dialysis care. I urge your support of SB 349, and I thank you for your consideration.

Brian Wong: Good afternoon Senators, my name is Dr. Brian Wong. I'm a board certified doctor specializing in kidney diseases and specifically helping to treat those patients needing dialysis to survive. I've been in practice over 30 years and am the past President of the California Dialysis Council. Over the years, I've treated thousands of patients with kidney failure that required dialysis and have spent a lot of time in outpatient dialysis clinics. I'm currently serving as a medical director for two clinics in the San Francisco Bay Area. I believe Senate Bill 349 is a solution in search of a problem. In fact, the bill creates a tremendous health care access problem for our dialysis patients. And like a hospital setting, a dialysis clinic typically runs an open floor plan, where the patients are treated around the perimeter of a large room. Caregivers are always having a direct line of sight to patients and are never more than a few feet away.  The staffing of a dialysis unit is based on the individual needs of the patients. SB 349's rigid staffing ratios do not allow for this personalized care and they will limit the number of appointments each dialysis center can accommodate in a given day. For example, SB 349 creates a dangerous situation whereby any sick call absence of the healthcare team will result in cancellation of an entire shift of patients. This same staffing ratio prevents acceptance of patients discharged from the hospital's emergency rooms for same-day dialysis. Studies have already shown that even missing a single dialysis treatment increases a dialysis patient's mortality for a staggering 30%. SB 349's mandatory 45-minute empty chair time would further limit the number of dialysis patients that can be treated. It practically eliminates the fourth shift of operation where working dialysis patients can count on getting the treatments after they get off from work. Nocturnal dialysis programs would, likewise, seize to operate. SB 349 would add hundreds of millions of dollars in new cost for care. Over 90% of dialysis patients depend on medical and Medicare for coverage so SB349 would exacerbate the current medical funding shortfall. As a doctor caring for this fragile and vulnerable population, two-thirds of whom is either black of Hispanic ethnicity in my clinic, I take issue with the assertion that current dialysis care is jeopardizing patient safety. Dialysis centers are already operating under very strict federal and state guidelines. Supporters have failed to make a credible argument that quality is suffering. In fact, according to data from California Department of Public Health, complaints in the last two and a half years represent less than one-tenth of 1% of the total treatments given across the state and there has been no evidence that states with staffing ratios have a better outcome. In fact, according to independent data from federal regulators, California dialysis clinics outperform other states, including those who stuff in ratio, in both patient's satisfaction, and quality measures. In conclusion SB 349 is not about improving patient care, it will hurt access to care and will unnecessarily disrupt the lives of thousands, and thousands of dialysis patients. And SB 49 will add hundreds of millions of dollars annually to the cost of state's MediCal. I urge you to oppose this misguided bill.

We do see big differentials in the cost of land, impermanent cost, in reserves that other financial entities require. So again, affordable housing finance is made up of multiple, multiple factors depending on where you are geographically. We're seeing these same issues all across the United States. And the biggest thing we can do to stop the need for more affordable housing is to pay people a living wage so they can live in these communities in which they work. To work with members of the community through apprenticeship programs in Salinas, 40% of the workers on site are now joining the union, having a good opportunity going forward. It's a great alternative to college for families that can't spend $100,000, $200,000, $300,000, on the cost of University. So we are very supportive of this bill. We believe it supports the development community by not overstepping on financing options that don't require prevailing wage. One of the biggest vehicles for financing affordable housing is low-income housing tax credit that's obviously not included here. And that remains the biggest subsidy for affordable housing and that, even though it's a federal program and a state program does not trigger prevailing wage. So we are in support of this bill, happy to answer any questions.

Erin Guerrero: Good afternoon, Mr. Chair and members, Erin Guerrero, on behalf of the California Building Industry Association. Members, we're in the middle of a housing crisis that is escalating to the level of an emergency. California ranks 49th in the nation in home-ownership rates. That's the lowest level since the 1940's. We're dead last in terms of first time home buyers. The average California home already costs two and a half times more than the national average. Only 41% of Californians can afford the state's median priced home California's average monthly rent is 50% higher than the rest of the country. We're producing less than half the number of homes needed to keep pace with the demand, and we need to build 3.5 million more by 2025. Now, enter AB 199. This bill will drive costs up even further during this emergency, resulting in almost no additional homes and making all homes even less affordable and further out of reach for the majority of Californians. This is not a narrowly crafted measure. AB 199 eliminates the private residential exemption from prevailing wage. The sponsors would have you believe that this bill is just about making sure subsidized housing projects pay prevailing wage, but it goes way beyond that. In fact, we can't come up with a project, a privately financed project that would not become a prevailing wage project under the terms of this bill. The reason for this can be boiled down to two issues, what a public fund is and the nature of the agreements referenced in the bill. The labor code contains a very broad definition of public funds, and it's not what the average person would think of. Most importantly, public funds as defined in a code are not the same as a subsidy as the sponsors would like you to think. Here are a couple of examples of what a public fund is in the code. If a developer pre-pays his processing fees, plan check and inspection fees, that money is received into the local government coffers and placed into its own account. When that money enters the account, it's considered public funds. If the developer overpaid and goes to receive a refund on the excess, those are public funds that he's just now received. Another example, if the developers is asked by local government to construct an improvement to accommodate another unrelated project. For example, if the city asks him to install a slightly larger trunk sewer line for the benefit of an adjacent property, legally, the city has to pay it's portion of that project. But once they do, those are public funds. Those are just two of many examples. It's because the definition of public funds is so convoluted that the residential exemption was included in SB 975 in 2001. That exemption created a firewall at the curb. Beyond the curb, improvements would be prevailing wage projects, but on the lot side of the curb, the bricks and mortar of the vertical building, those were to be exempted. The second issue is the nature of the agreements. Who is making what agreements? This bill expands the agencies making the agreements to political subdivisions, which include counties, cities, and districts. We cannot identify a single project that would not include an agreement with at least one of these entities. In fact, most have multiple agreements with several of them. For example, upon filing a development application, cities and counties require the applicant to agree to pay processing cost and sign an agreement to indemnify the city or county. And in the other example of the sewer trunk line, that would require a reimbursement agreement with the local government. There are many more examples. Members, this bill will have immediate and tangible impacts on the housing market. There are quite a few estimates out there on what prevailing wage does to the cost of a project. According to a 2016 Beacon Economics study, mandated prevailing wage would result in up to a 46% increase in the total cost of a new home. According to a study by UC Berkeley, it would drive up costs by 37%. According to early reports from our members, costs would increase by $46 to $77 per square foot. Pick any of those estimates. Suffice it to say, the impact will be significant, making housing even further beyond the reach of teachers, firefighters, police, grocery clerks, nurses, and the average Californian. According to the Eye on Housing report, for every $1,000 increase in the price of a home, over 15,000 California households are priced out of the market. Californians already can't afford to buy homes. The consumer certainly cannot sustain the increases this bill would bring about. However, neither can the builders absorb these cost increases. The industry average pretax profit margin hovers around 6.5%, regardless of which cost estimate you choose, under no circumstances can these increases be absorbed at today's housing cost. Our members simply will not build a product for which there is no market. This means housing production will be dramatically cut through out the state as a direct result of AB 199, and the housing crisis will only escalate further. Thank you, Mr. Chair.

Gayle Batiste: Thank you. Mr. Chairman and Committee, I'd like to thank you for allowing us to come here and speak today on this issue. My name is Gayle Batiste. I'm the President of SIEU 121 RN, and I represent nurses from Ventura County all the way down to Indio and other parts of Southern California also. I'm also an operating room nurse at North Ridge Hospital Medical Center and I became a nurse 34 years ago because I wanted to help people. Well, with the State of affairs as it is now, it's kind of hard to do that when we're being put out of ratio and we're asked to take on unsafe patient assignments. Current law, gives RNs protection if they file complaints with CDPH about unsafe and unlawful assignments. However, the law does not provide them from retaliation from the employer if they refuse those unsafe assignments that put patients at risk. In fact, since 2014, CDPH has received staffing complaints at 31% of all acute care hospitals in the state. That's a big one, that's a large amount. Nurses file complaints after complaint with the state to no avail. Knowing this, hospitals continue to violate the law and give unsafe assignments to RNs. That is why SEIU is sponsoring AB 1102 because as nurses, we need to know that fulfilling our legal and moral obligation to advocate on behalf of our patients will not cause us to be retaliated against by our employers. AB 1102 would extend existing healthcare worker whistle blower protection to nurses who are directed by their employers to take unsafe patient assignments that violate Title 22, California's code of regulations. In doing so, nurses will be empowered to stand up for the patients they already have in their care and won't be forced to choose between breaking the law, or putting patient's safety at risk. As President of my nurse's union, I come across members who have experienced retaliation. I'll tell you about a nurse that this happened to. An example is an RN at Monterrey Park Hospital was suspended for refusing an unsafe patient assignment. He's telemetry RN and was told he was going to floated to the Intensive Care Unit, that's a higher level of care. He refused because he knew he did not have the training or competency needed to properly care for patients in the ICU unit. He was concerned about providing sub-standard or dangerous care to those patients, but he also knew that his employer was asking him knowingly to break the law.  He asked if they could assign another nurse that was properly oriented and competent to provide care for the ICU patient. In response, the hospital suspended him for what they deemed insubordination. When nurses are not competent to care for certain types of patients or when they have more patients that allowed under the law, patients die, and a nurse is left with his or her conscience and legal liability. This is why we need AB 1102. AB 1102 would protect nurses from these types of retaliation, and it closely resembles a bill introduced last year at the federal level by CNA's national arm, the National Nurses United, which also provides that a nurse who refuses an assignment on the basis that it violates the nurse's staffing ratios will be granted whistle blower protection. AB 1102 would apply this thinking to strengthen our state's enforcement of our existing staffing ratios and bolster our nurse's ability to serve as patient advocates without having to choose between providing safe patient care or protecting their license. On behalf of the nurses in California, I respectfully urge you to pass AB 1102 for the protection of all patients we see at our hospital. Thank you.

[{'start': 9, 'end': 13, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 27, 'end': 38, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 212, 'end': 221, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Sharon Rapport: Good morning, Sharon Rapport with the Corporation for Supportive Housing. Data show homeless people, particularly chronically homeless people, are extremely expensive to MediCal. Generally, comprising over half of a hospital's frequent user population, people experiencing chronic homelessness incur between $30,000 and $75,000 per year in publicly funded healthcare cost. These individuals have poor health outcomes dying on average 30 years younger than their housed counterparts. Data also shows supportive housing affordable place to live with services promoting housing stability, works and homelessness among chronically homeless people, while also saving publicly funded healthcare dollars. We are excited that Medi-Cal is rolling out new programs, like the whole person care pilot and the health home program, to fund services that help get chronically homeless people connected to supportive housing, and help keep them sustainably housed. However, based on data, we also know that services alone no matter how good those services are or how intensive they are, do not allow someone experiencing chronic homelessness to get healthier or to stop using acute care services. To achieve any cost savings to our health care system, homeless people must get connected to housing first. AB 74 would create the Housing for a Healthy California Program. And I think Assembly Member Chiu talked about the essentials of that program. Counties would have to tie these rental subsidies funded under the program to services funding that will now become available under MediCal. The bill requires a rigorous evaluation, which HCD will spearhead in collaboration with the Department of Healthcare Services. While we know what Medicaid cost savings are in other states from moving people from homelessness to housing stability, we do not have good data here in California about MediCal savings. The evaluation findings would also help the Legislature decide whether to continue the program after five years.
