Dan Rinzler: Thank you. Is this mic close enough to me? Yeah? Okay. All right, so thank you so much to the Committee and to Senator Beall for inviting the California Housing Partnership to be part of the hearing today on the housing affordability crisis. My name is Dan Rinzler, and I am a senior policy analyst at CHPC. Which was created by the state in 1988 as a privately-funded non-profit to help lead around affordable housing preservation, finance, and policy. Since then, we have helped developers create and preserve more than 60,000 affordable homes for the state's lowest income residents through technical assistance, training, and policy leadership. So, my presentation will cover the magnitude of the need for affordable housing in the state and the inadequate resources we have to address that need. And I will also touch on the specific and critical role that the state plays in financing affordable housing, and I will offer a few ideas for how the state can help address this crisis by increasing its investment. So, first the need. There is a shortfall of 1.54 million affordable homes for low income renting households in the State of California. So, big picture the trend has been lands have increase while income have declined and as a result renter have lost an average of $6,000 in annual purchasing power of the last 15 years. The burden of the affordability crisis is almost entirely shouldered by the lowest income Californians. It's not on this slide but the overwhelming majority of extremely and very low income Californians spend more than 50% of their income on rent. This means that the poorest families and individuals are foregoing basic necessities like food Healthcare and transportation because the rent literally eats first. So, what do we have to address this problem? Since 2008, California has actually lost 66% of state and local funding for affordable housing development and preservation mostly due to the loss of redevelopment. And also exhaustion of Prop 1C and Prop 46 bond funds. So, we are actually in a weaker position today than we were several years ago to address a crisis that itself has gotten worse over that period of time. So I'm going to run through a quick primer on how affordable housing finance works. And this is important because I just want to point out the very specific and critical roles that the state plays in creating affordable housing in conjunction with other financing sources. So there are basically three types of sources that cover the cost of affordable housing development and keeps rents low over a period of multiple decades. So first, you need a loan from a bank. Just like any real estate investment. But if you're going to keep rents low you can not support very much debt. So you've got this gap, and you need to fill it with subsidy basically from the government. First, with housing tax credits which developers apply for and then sell to investors to raise equity for the project. And this fills some of the gap. To cover the rest of your costs you need a subsidy or gap financing from federal, state, and local sources. And this is the role that the state plays in financing affordable housing. as that gap subsidy piece. And anyone who has seen the kind of layer cake of financing and sources for an affordable housing development will know that developers typically draw on multiple state and local sources to really make the deal feasible and work at all. So just to further add context to the state's role, you really need to understand the low income housing tax credit program or LIHTC which is the largest federal subsidy for affordable housing production. It is run through state finance agencies. And it is really what drive affordable housing in The State of California. You are not going to have a new development that serves low income people that doesn't have tax credits in it. And one key point that I want to make here is that the price for tax cut, it says, actually dropped over the last few months. Because investors are anticipating a drop in the corporate tax rate under the new administration in Congress. And this means that developers need even more subsidy than they did ever a few months ago to fill that financing gap that I was talking about on the previous slide. To take an even closer look at the light tech program on, there are two types of Housing Credits, first. The 9% credits, which cover most of the causal development, but they are capped, so there are very competitive and over subscribed and it's a limited number of units you're going to get out of every year through that program. The 4% credits on the other hand are uncapped and not competitive but they don't generate as much equity as the 9% credits. So the only, really, way to make 4% deals work is with substantial gap subsidy provided by the state and other sources. So basically, we actually could be getting more affordable units out every year if we only had more state subsidy for affordable housing development. These states has successfully played this gap financing role to help leverage 4% credits before and continues to do so today. One very succesful example is the multi-family housing program or MHP which was created in 2003 Using bonds created through Prop 46 and 1C. From 2003 to 2015, California invested $1.5 billion through the MHP program to create around 25,000 affordable homes, at a cost of only $67,000 Per unit, and that actually comes down to around $425 per year to house a low income Californian, which is an incredible bargain considering the social benefits that have been very well documented through research health earnings, educational outcomes and so on. As I mentioned before, MHP funds are actually mostly exhausted at this point and we need something to replace them. A little bit of additional context. In the fall elections this year, voters in L.A. and in the Bay Area approved more than $3 billion in new funding for affordable housing production. They saw the effects of the crisis and they did something about it. With these new local funds available, if the state makes an investment of $1 billion, we estimate that we can increase production per year of 14,000 new affordable homes per year. This obviously would not meet all of the need. But a state investment of this skill would make a large dent in addressing the affordability crisis facing low income families in the state. So I just want to end with the few options, ideas for sources of finding to increase the sales commitment to portable housing production and preservation. First, a new state housing bond similar to proc 1c and 46. You've seen that work well in the past. Would be good idea moving forward. A documentary recording fee. Elimination of the mortgage interest reduction on second and vacation homes. Elimination of some 1031 exemptions for large corporations which basically encourages flipping. And finally, a tax on bank profits in California which has increased pretty dramatically just even over the last year or so. So, I will stop there and ask if there any questions.

Shamus Roller: Thank you Chairman Bell, Members of the Committee. Shamus Roller with the National Housing Law Project. We are a national support Center for legal services, attorneys, all around the country, and also do advocacy at the federal level around housing programs. I started my career running a street outreach program in Portland, Oregon, working with homeless youth and adults on the streets. And then I moved to San Francisco. And I remember very well that first day in San Francisco walking through the Tenderloin and realizing just that I was in a different place. That the homelessness that I saw in San Francisco, the degraded condition of many of the people there was just different that what I've experienced before. What I didn't understand then and that I do better now, is that many of the visual signs of homelessness, those things that we see walking down the street, tend to obscure some of the causes and the underlying conditions that cause people to become homeless. That being homeless itself degrades your physical and psychological condition faster than just about any other malady out there. And that if only we look at the people who we most know are homeless, sometimes what we think is wrong, is sort of like thinking that only people that have gray hair get old. When in fact, it is the process of aging which makes us look so distinguished. That we need to understand that moment people become homeless and what that means as far as what our public policy is. That summer and fall before I started working in homeless services, I worked with a guy, Alejandro, on a building project and we were remodeling a house. And he used to make fun of me because I would break for lunch and he would just work right through lunch. And when I started that spring I saw him in a line waiting to get into a men's shelter and he looked 10 years older than he had that summer. And that just being homeless and being on the streets just degrades people so rapidly in so many parts of their lives. Both on the social strains that they have and on their physical health. And we tend to want to think of people who become homeless as a population of people. But in reality, for every person that becomes homeless, there are many, many other people that are demographically exactly the same as those people who become homeless. That it's a bit of bad luck often times it lands people on the streets. Poverty is a risk factor. One in 10 people who are in poverty will become homeless at some point this year. Mental illness is a risk factor. But yet, many people with severe mental illness do not become homeless. Drug and alcohol addiction is a risk factor. And yet, many people with drug and alcohol addiction issues are very successful in their lives and do just fine. If people become homeless when they have a number of different risk factors on top of a little bit of bad luck, a bad landlord at the wrong time. A whole host of other issues and I think what this means from a policy level is that we think about trying stop people from becoming homeless, we have to also be able to tackle the issues that create housing instability. And as sometimes we view homeless people as being somehow other. We often view homelessness as being something intractable, something that can't be solved. But in reality, the modern homelessness situation comes from two issues. The significant defunding in the 70s of the Department of Housing and Urban Development. The dismantling of the mental health institutions without any community response to that. That there are two real big reasons why we ended up with a homelessness problem that we have in this country and that problem is not intractable. It is one that we can tackle. The success in our country over the last five years in ending veteran homelessness, I think the perfect example of how this problem can be solved. In 2010, they created a program opening doors at the federal level, combining VASH vouchers which are essentially Section 8 vouchers along with services from the Veteran's Administration. Between 2010 and the current time, we have decreased veteran's homelessness in this country by almost 50%, but there was a 17% reduction just between the years of 2015 and 2016. This isn't rocket science to fix this problem in many ways. But as we've seen the system of moving people out of homelessness and into housing become much, much better over the last decade, we've struggled in California, because our housing costs are just so high. As we move people more quickly into housing, we are seeing more and more people enter into homelessness, because of the housing situation we have in California. That high housing costs are making people homeless, they're also making it more expensive to move people out of homelessness. I was doing a tour here in Sacramento, I still serve as the chair of the Continuum of Care in Sacramento County and I toured a house for people that are being moved out of homelessness, they spent 30 days sort of intense. Getting all of their documents together. Getting ready to move in the housing. A house like that was renting for $1,200 a month, it's renting for $2,000. It's just become more expensive to move people out of homelessness. So, many people move themselves out that the average person only spends four months on the streets. Many people find their way out, but they are struggling to find their way out. Because if you're renting $1,000 studio and you've gotta come up with first month, last month and a deposit, that barrier is becoming so high in California. And in California, I think we tripped away so many of the tethers that can prevent someone from becoming homeless. For many years, we zoned out shared housing and boarding houses. We demolished single occupy hotel and other housing of last result. We eliminated redevelopment agencies and we've refused to invest general fund dollars into affordable development. We've also let wealthy enclaves be cartels to block any new housing from occurring in our state and creating that supply problem that we have, and we've left many vulnerable renters to be at the mercy of predatory landlords that can evict them at will. It used to be that you could rent a cheap apartment and feed yourself just on Social Security. It used to be that a general assistance check in LA can get a few weeks at a single occupancy hotel or a flop house. It used to be that you could find some level of assistance if you hit hard times and that's really no longer the case in California. The housing crisis that we have has become the driver of inequality in our state. Exposing a larger and larger part of the population to the risks of homelessness and this doesn't diminish, I think some of the great efforts over the last couple years of this Legislature to deal with homelessness, but you can't divorce homelessness from some of the broader housing issues that we have in our state. The basic level through public policy we've managed to expand the number of people who live in the river sticks. We're one mistake, one stroke of bad luck, on crappy landlord can put them on the streets. So to finish up, I got to spend a couple of hours with giving a tour to the guy. He used to run the Mayor's Office of Housing in London and I got to talk to him about some of the really innovative programs that we have in California to help families that have kids in foster care move back in to housing, and move families that are on CalWORKS move back into housing. And after talking to him for a little while, what I released is that in comparison to what they're doing in London like we have all of these innovative programs that are essentially a patchwork for the fact that we haven't developed any comprehensive system to help people who are dealing with housing instability and to have a general plan of how we're going to deal with housing crisis in the California and I think we've hit that point that that it's time to do that work.

Pete Parkinson: Good afternoon. Thank you, Chairman Beall. I'm Pete Parkinson, I'm the President of the California Chapter of the American Planning Association. And I also have the privilege serving as the Planning Director for two counties in California including a stint working for Senator Mcguire over there in Sonoma County. So really appreciate you inviting us here today. We've been working at APA California on housing issues, literally, for decades. But like everybody else that you've heard from today, we're frustrated with the State of housing in California. And so, last fall we convened a group of experienced professional planners, all of whom have grey hair like myself, to talk about solutions that we could come up with for actually increasing housing production and improving housing affordability in California. And one of the things that I'm excited about in hearing both from the panelists here today and from the Senators is that there is a lot of agreement already, it seems to me about what the nature of the problem is, and what the range of solutions are. So for example, we know that we spend a lot of money planning for housing in California, every city and county in the state has to do a housing element. They're expensive to do, they're time consuming to do, but we also know that we can't plan our way out of the housing affordability crisis in this state. Good long range planning is critical, but it's not enough and now we have to work on getting those planned units actually built. You've also heard that while increasing production is essential. We can't build our way out of the affordability crisis either. We've heard about the need for housing subsidies in a lot of different markets. But I think you've also heard this afternoon that there is no silver bullet for resolving our housing problems in the state. It's going to take a package deal that addresses a number of different points to increase housing productions in State of California. And it's going to have to focus more than just local governments, it's part of the point that I'd like to make to you this afternoons. Local governments are very important in this process but local governments don't build housing, nor do they control a lot of the factors that influence housing development. So this means that the solution has to include all of the actors in the housing picture. It has to include local governments, it has to include the state. Has to include builders, including nonprofit builders, laborer and environmental organizations and, of course, the communities themselves. And, so again, it needs to be a package solution so as planners want to do we've come up with a series of recommendations that address six different themes in that area. First one is providing adequate funding. Next is providing certainty in the development process. Third, reducing the cost to produce, especially affordable housing projects. Fourth, we have some ideas for some different things that HCD can be worked on. We think that housing element law can be streamlined and we think we can do a better job of enforcing existing housing statutes that we have. On the issue of providing adequate funding we've already heard about the need for subsidies and many markets in the states. And so, I'm not going to go into that further but we also have a need in our community for funds to do that good long range planning that helps communities prepare for the housing that they're going to need to accommodate And helps streamline the process for approving that housing later on. Those planning efforts specific plans and general plans are expensive and time consuming, and funding is needed to do that. But we also need funding and funding mechanisms to improve the community capacity, increase the community capacity, excuse me, for housing development. And in the world of housing, we also think about, we often think about capacity just in terms of land. Does your city have enough sites that are zoned forthe number of housing units that you need to provide? But really it's a much a bigger issue than that. We have to increase the capacity of our communities to accommodate additional growth, including the local infrastructure and services that are needed to support housing, including water, sewer, transportation, parks, schools, libraries, the whole range. So, this investment in increasing community capacity, we see as something that is critical to solving the problem In terms of creating certainty for housing approvals, I think you've also heard some about this today. Housing developers often face a lot of uncertainty as they go into the process, that adds not just to the time but to the cost of developing. Developing those projects. And I think you heard from Ms. Archuleta earlier that it often times affects even the willingness of developers to get into a project to begin with, if the process is too onerous. So, to address this APA California supports ministerial or by-right housing approvals, for most housing that is consistent with adopted plans. At the same time, we think we need to allow cities and counties to address project design in a review processes without triggering CEQA process on projects that would otherwise be exempt. So, let's include CEQA exemptions for design review for housing projects there otherwise allot by right. Along with reasonable time limits for completing the sign review process. We should also provide expedited CEQA litigation for housing projects much like the Legislature has done in the past for some stadium projects. And lastly, kind of at the very end of the process, let's talk about the building code revision process. Let's change that so that projects that have planning entitlements and have been through that process aren't saddled with an expensive and extensive redesign at the very end of the process due to building code requirements that changed while they were going through the planning process. We think that we could do more to reduce development costs especially for affordable housing. Affordable housing is very, very sensitive to cost issues and improving the certainty of those approvals is definitely going to help. But we can do some other things too. Smaller units are less costly to build, so let's eliminate to the extent that we have minimum size requirements on affordable affordable units. Let's reduce or eliminate those. Let's encourage zoning strategies like form-based codes, for example, that limit the height and bulk of projects rather than the number of units. And let's ensure the impact fees of very large component of the cost of developing projects are appropriately scaled to the size of the units. In terms of recommendations for some additional assistance that we think HCD can provide, being more proactive in developing some new strategies. We'd like to see HCD shift its focus a bit from focusing on more housing element requirements to doing things like working with private sector architects, engineers, and hosing developers and local planners, to develop prototypes for housing unit including accessory dwelling units that can then be use to facilitate and speed up the process for getting those permitted and built. We believe that the state should fund HDC to track affordable units that are at risk for loss due to loss of subsidies or expiration of restricted covenants. Affordability covenants and work with the owners of those units and the communities to help preserve those affordable units. And we think that we can improve local accountability around housing issues, and I want to spend just a second on this one. When planners and housing advocates and HCD staff often get together to talk about improving the housing situation in California, we hear a lot of anecdotal comments about good actor cities and bad actor cities and who's doing a good job and who's not doing such a good job. But we don't really have the data, in my view, that it takes to look at that problem from a statewide level. Everybody has to report, as part of their annual reports to the state, how many units got built and whether those units are affordable. But that's not quite enough. We think that there can be an objective accounting of the city or county's record on approving housing development projects. How many units were applied for? How many were built? How long did it take? What incentives did the city or county provide to get those built? And so we think that that's going to provide tremendously important information, if we can do that. And it's also going to improve accountability for housing production. We think this housing element law can be streamlined. It is a critical piece of the package for addressing our housing problems in this state. But let's eliminate some of the requirements in the state element housing law that don't directly result in housing production. So we've got requirements, for example, to analyze non-governmental constraints that local government can't control. We have a requirement in every single housing element to plan for farm worker housing, even in urban areas with little or no agriculture nearby. I think we can streamline the analysis that is needed for each housing site shown in the plan. I thought Ms. Feldman made some great points about what is really needed to look at the adequacy of those sites. But we think that that can be streamlined to some extent. And energy conservation. There's a requirement in housing element law that we address energy conservation. But we do that so thoroughly through the state's building codes and energy codes that we don't think we need to address it in the housing element. So instead, we can focus the housing element on making sure that we've got sites that are zoned for affordable housing and for homeless shelters. Ensuring conformance with state law requirements for transitional and supportive housing. And people with disabilities and farm worker housing. We think that there needs to be more analysis of affordable housing that may convert to market rate, and state funding to help preserve that. And encourage the regional and sub-regional analysis of housing issues instead of having separate analysis for each city or county. And then last but not least, there's enforcement of existing housing laws. Again, we do hear often about these bad actor cities and counties that aren't complying with housing element law. We believe that those cities and counties are the relatively small minority in this state. But there is no reason why any city or county in this state should get a pass on complying with State Housing Law. So let's fund the Attorney General's Office to proactively enforce housing laws, especially in communities that haven't adopted a housing element, haven't done the promised rezoning that they've committed to, or those that deny projects in violation of State Housing Law. So, again, thank you and I look forward to the opportunity to answer questions.

So consistent with years past, LCFF implementation is among the very highest priorities for the administration, and there's no change when it comes to this year's budget. Unfortunately, revenues have begun to lack expectations such that this year's budget proposes to maintain the progress that we've made in previous years towards fully implementing the LCFF. Specifically, the Governor's Budget proposes nearly $750 million in Proposition 98 general fund, towards closing the gap between current funding levels and the targeted funding levels for school districts and charter schools under the LCFF. This $750 million will close about a quarter of the remaining funding gap for each school district in charter school, and keep us at an overall implementation of the LCFF at 96%. I'd also note a related proposal to the LCFF. This was mentioned in last week's Subcommittee here as we talked about kind of the overall Proposition 98 package. And that is the deferral of $860 million of LCFF payments from June to July of 2017. So as we mentioned last week, the deferral is not an ideal fiscal situation for us. It's not where we'd like to find ourselves, but it's sort of the reality of the fiscal constraints. And as we looked at the other options when building this budget, it was sort of the least painful. Again, the size of the deferral would represent about a third of the payment that school districts and charter schools would otherwise receive in June of 2017. And unlike previous deferrals, this would be essentially a deferral of funding that would be repaid two weeks after it's made. So you could think of school districts and charter schools as receiving 11 and two-thirds LCFF payments in the 16-17 fiscal year, and then 12 and one-third LCFF payments in the 17-18 fiscal year. As part of the shift to Local Control Funding Formula in 2013-14, the state included 2 hold harmless provisions for COEs, which we describe on page 3 of your handout. The first hold harmless provision determined that each county office would continue to receive at least as much funding as it received the year before LCFF in 2012/13 even if that amount was above the target rate that was determined for a given county. Currently we estimate that 34 county offices benefit from this hold harmless provision. The second hold harmless provision determine that each county office would continue to receive as much state categorical funding as they received before LCFF, we estimate that 18 county offices benefit from this provision and that this provision is growing rather rapidly over time we also note the county offices that are not required to perform activities associated with these hold, harmless amounts they were typically tied to categorical programs that the state used to have prior to LCFF. The chart on page 4, shows proportionately how the three elements of county office LCFF interact. We can see here that the county office LCFF is made up of district services, the juvenile court schools and county community schools portion, and then about a quarter of the LCFF for counties is made up with these hold harmless provisions. This is at a statewide level but if we look more deeply at a county by county level we'll see that their funding rates are very different. The chart on page five shows this county by county analysis. And how many counties receive hold harmless funding as compared to their LCFF funding rate. You'll see that about 40% of counties are at their target funding level while the majority have hold harmless provisions in place with some receiving more than twice their LCFF target level.

On page one, so we start on page one, just providing you with some background on how the framework for the system was developed. This was all part of the 2013 Legislation that created the LCFF, it also created this framework for a new state accountability system. That system is built upon these eight state priority areas that you have heard folks mention already today. The idea is these are the key places the the state think are important and they want districts and schools to be paying attention to and focusing on these areas. the statute lists these priority areas and then also lists a number of associated performance measures for those priority areas to give you a sense of ways that we can measure how districts and schools are doing with regards to these priorities. So there are two main places where these priority areas manifest themselves. The first is in Local Control and Accountability Plans or LCAPs and districts now are, they already have now adopted three years of LCAPs. So they have now been getting more comfortable with that system and And doing the work required. Under law districts are required to work with their communities to get feedback in developing their LCAP and they need to have it approved by the County Office of Education. And in that LCAP they need to set goals based on these eight priority areas and specify the actions they're going to take to meet those goals. The second piece is something that hasn't really been implemented yet but, we're not getting into the place for the state is ready and that's what are called evaluation rubrics in the code and I think now, we'll be talked about as the school dashboard. The original legislation tasked the State Board of Education with adopting these evaluation rubrics. And the intent is that these rubrics would be used to determine whether districts needed additional support. And the law there were two different kind of levels of support. One level of support for districts who for one sub group for example was having trouble in a priority area, so a much more narrow kind of need for support and then a larger level of support for districts who maybe have more systemic problems that have been underperforming for many years. The board adopted the rubrics in September 2016 and I believe this month. At some point this month the dashboard will be made public and will be available for For youth. There are a variety of performance indicators in the dashboard. There are two different categories, and how the public can interact with them is a little bit different. There are the state performance indicators that are based on state-wide information, this is information the state already collects. We have consistent data across the state where you can compare how districts are doing across the state. For that you'll have more detailed information, districts will be classified into a number of color coded categories to give you a sense of how well they're doing. You'll also be able to look at data by school and by subgroup. Then you have these local performance indicators where there will be less information. These are areas like say for example in the priority of parent engagement we don't have any state wide or data metrics that we use so what the desk will ask districts to do is to develop a local local measure and then provide some information and a narrative form on how they're using that. How they are using that tool to identify whether there are some room for improvements in that area. Alan Roth: I will give my brief comments of our testimony for this morning. Good morning to Chairman Hill, Chairman Salas and Members of the Committee and staff. I am Alan Roth. I'm President of the Respiratory Care Board. I'm joined by Tom Wagner, my Vice President and Stephanie Nunez, our executive officer. I know you have a lot to cover today so I will provide you with a brief overview. The Respiratory Care Board was created by the Legislature in 1982 to protect the vulnerable population from the unqualified practice of respiratory care. The composition of the board consists of nine members. Four respiratory care practitioners, four public members and one physician/surgeon. Appointments to the board are made equally by the Governor, the Senate Rules Committee and the Speaker of the Assembly, each authority appointing three members to the Board. The Board is responsible for enforcing state laws pertaining to the practice of respiratory care, and regulates a single category of healthcare specialists, respiratory care practitioners. The RCPs are specialized healthcare practitioners who work under the supervision of medical directors and are involved in the prevention, diagnosis, treatment, management or re-rotation of problems affecting the heart and the lungs and other disorders as well as providing diagnostic, educational and rehabilitation services. PCP's provide care for those who are dependent upon life support and that cannot breathe on their own. RCP's treat patients with acute and chronic diseases including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, trauma victims and surgical patients. They are typically employed in hospitals, however, a growing number of RCP's work in alternate care settings like subacute facilities, home medical device retail facilities, hyperbaric oxygen facilities, and sleep laboratories along with transport. The law governing RCPs, the Respiratory Care Practice Act requires licensure for individuals performing respiratory care. In carrying out its mandate to ensure the protection of the public shall be the highest priority in exercising the licensing, regulatory and disciplinary functions of the Board. In that sense, we screen every applicant for licensure to ensure minimum education and competency standards are met and conduct a thorough criminal background check with each applicant. We investigate complaints against licensees including those generated from updated criminal history reports and mandatory reporting of violations by licensees and employers. We aggressively monitor our CPs placed on probation. We exercise the authority of the penalized or disciplined applicants and licensees including issuance of citations and fines while public reprimands ordering denial, probation, or revocation of a license. We address current issues related to the unlicensed and/or unqualified practice of respiratory care. We promote public awareness of the mandate and its function as well as current issues affecting respiratory care. Since 1985, when the first license was issued, the Board has licensed over 39,000 licensees, of which over 20,000 remain active. The Board has a $3.8 million budget to which it manages closely. The last renewal fee increase was made by statute in the 1999 and was not implemented until 2002, over 15 years ago. Since our last sunset review four years ago, the most significant changes have taken place include the establishment of two additional respiratory baccalaureate degree programs as a result of SB 850, one of which I am involved with, Raul Modesto Junior College and Skyline College. Improving respiratory care competency standards by requiring the passage of an advanced competency exam for licensure AB 1972. Successfully implementing BreEZe with our new database. Entering into a contract with UC San Francisco to delve further into the issues that the board believes may significantly improve consumer protection. That's the end of my remarks, I will pass it on to Stephanie Nunez to continue. Wait, I apologize. I have one more thing. The Board is proud to share its success in meeting the performance targets. In early 2016, they were developed as part of the Consumer Protection Enforcement Initiative. The Board's performance targets for its enforcement program are 7 days to complete the complaint intake cycle, 210 days for the investigative cycle and 540 days for the formal discipline cycle. For years, the Board has consistently met all of its performance measure targets, with the exception of the formal discipline cycle, which includes processing time by the Office of Attorney General and the Office of Administrative Hearings. However, in 2016, for the first time, the Board met its formal discipline target with an average of 538 days to process a case from beginning to end. The Board is working closely with the Office of the Attorney General to improve processes and communication so that this target can be met on a more consistent basis. The Board is committed to conducting business in an efficient and effective manner, and responding to practice in operational issues in a proactive, forward-thinking manner. Moreover, the Board is committed to ensuring that consumer protection is always its highest priority. Now, I'm going to turnover to Stephanie Nunez, our Executive Officer.

So that you are referring the appropriate compliant to inappropriate individuals to investigate those complaints. The next area to talk about ties to that. What we found, is we found incomplete investigations were causing delays in discipline or resolution of a complaint, and the reason these were incomplete investigations is because some of them were being assigned to an appropriate individual. That individual did not gather sufficient evidence. So when there was discussion with the Attorney General's Office or with Consumer Affairs to take disciplinary action against a nurse. So we found not only at the board but some at the division of investigations that required a supplemental investigation. Is it a training issue, is it an issue where it was assigned to the wrong unit? Whether it was at BRN and it should have been at Division of Investigations. Again this recommendation has been partially implemented. So then that took us to training. So we looked at the Board of Registered Nursing and did they have a formal training program? They do not. So they don't have that comprehensive program. What we saw that they are using is they have a checklist and if I'm a new investigator I'm using that checklist to learn how to conduct an investigation and then I'm shadowing someone. Now that's certainly an approach to use, but what we were looking and hoping to see is very formal training, specific courses, specific training programs. Now the Division of Investigations, again they're peace officers. So they have to go through post training, so they do receive some formal training, but the investigators at the board are not receiving that type of very specific and important training. Consumer Affairs also provides training resources to their boards and their enforcement academy. The concern we had here was not with the training program, but that the Board of Registered Nursing is not tracking who's taking the training. When are they taking it? So we minimize the number of supplemental investigations or subsequent investigations we have to do. The final two recommendation related to training is just develop a system by March. That allows them to track the internal and external trainings that their staff participate in. Seriously, yes, and thank you, Chairman, Senator Hill, as well, for the opportunity to address you this afternoon. I'm I'm Dr. Alison Grimes, I'm a dispensing audiologist and the board chair. Speech language pathology, audiology, and hearing aid dispensing are independent and rapidly expanding professions in both healthcare and educational systems. Professional in this three fields work with people of all ages,from newborns to geriatric,to address and rehabilitate communication impairments. Communication skills are essential for the well being and societal contribution of all Americans,affecting quality of life including psycho social,educational and occupational endeavors. Speech language pathologists provide assessment therapy and counseling for individuals and their family members. There is a wide range of disorders addressed by the speech pathologist including speech and language impairments, swallowing disorders or dispasia, strokes or other brain trauma, stuttering and voice and speech production. Audiologists provide diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation and counseling for individuals with hearing and or balance disorders and their family members. We work with patients of all ages. Audiologists provide diagnostic follow-up and treatment for infants who fail their newborn hearing screenings and subsequently fit hearing aids on infants found to have permanent hearing loss. We work closely with early intervention professionals and families to ensure the best speech language and psychosocial outcomes. In older children and adults, audiologists provide treatment and rehabilitative services, including communication counseling, provision of hearing aids, and assessment for cochlear implants, and post-implant management for infants and children and adults who receive cochlear implants. Audiologists work with other assistive technologies to address handicap imposed by hearing loss, and provide communication rehabilitation and ongoing patient and family management. We carrying out hearing conservation programs for individuals in industries where there's risk of noise-induced hearing loss. Hearing aid dispensers, test hearing in adults to select and fit hearing aids and provide post-fitting verification and validation of hearing aid amplification to ensure that the hearing aid is meeting the consumer specific hearing needs. Speech language pathologists, audiologists and hearing aid dispensers in California provide services to linguistically and culturally diverse populations representing all age groups and must continually adapt to new developments. Technologies and research findings, in all aspects of their respective professions. Services are provided in both public and private agencies, including schools, hospitals and private practice settings. For the history of our board, the demand for regulation of these three professions has existed since the early 1970s. Oversight of the professions of Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology has been governed by a combined board since it's inception in 1974. The regulation of hearing aid dispensing was enacted in 1970 originally under the jurisdiction of the medical board of California. But for the past 20 years has operated either as an independent board or a bureau under the department. On January 1st 2010, Assembly Bill 1535 created the speech language pathology, audiology and hearing aid dispensers board. This merged the hearing aid dispensers bureau into the Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology Board. The newly merged board regulates the professions of Speech-Language Pathology, Audiology and Hearing Aid dispensing. Each profession is separate and distinct. Each has its own scope of practice. Each has its own entry level requirements and professional settings with some overlap in groups and pathologies served. To balance the professional expertise and public input on the board, the government structure of the board consists of two speech language pathologists, two audiologists, one of whom must be a dispensing audiologist, two non-audiologist hearing aid dispensers, and a public member, who must be a licensed physician and surgeon board certified in otolaryngology. All of these members are appointed by the Governor. In addition, one public member seat is appointed by the Senate Rules Committee and one by the speaker of the Assembly. Members are appointed for four-year terms and no member may serve more than two consecutive terms. Our board serves to protect the public through licensing and regulation of speech language pathologists, audiologists, and hearing aid dispensers. Who provides speech and hearing services to California consumers. The boards sets entry level licensing standards which include examination requirements that measure the licensees' professional knowledge and clinical abilities. That are consistent with the demands of the current delivery systems. To ensure ongoing consumer protection, the board enforces standards of professional conduct by investigating applicant backgrounds. Investigating complaints against licensed and unlicensed practitioners, and taking disciplinary action whenever appropriate. The board jurisdiction encompasses the regulation of 11 license types including speech-language pathology, audiology, hearing aid dispensing, paraprofessionals, and education programs offering degrees in speech-language pathology assistance. Today the board licenses well over 25,000 individuals and has an operating budget of approximately $2.1 million. In the past four years, the board has face many challenges. Since the last sunset review, the boards licencee population has grown by 28%. Resulting an increase work load in all areas. Despite it's challenges, the board continuous to make great improvements in all of it's operations. This year the board has made significant improvement in meeting all of its enforcement performance measures, excuse me. Licensing cycle times have been very significantly reduced in the past two years from an estimated 8 to 12 week time frame previously. To approximately two weeks today. The board will continue to take steps to enhance this process to reduce application cycle times. Access to the hearing aid dispensing profession has improved greatly due to the increase in the practical examinations offered by the board. Prior to 2015-16, the board examined an average of 120 candidates annually. In 2015-16, the board examined 306 candidates for the hearing aid dispensing practical examination. There remain many initiatives and activities that the board plans to develop and accomplish to further support consumers. There is a growing demand for licensure and enforcement in our professions. Additionally, with the population of California aging, demand for services has increased. The board staff works overtime to provide timely management of services. In conducting our hands on hearing aid dispensing exam, we must literally borrow real estate for the exam site. Further, this examination program draws considerable resources in terms of staff preparation and time, pulling staff from other essential and time sensitive activities. The board deftly does more with the staff that is frankly, inadequate, given the desperate needs of regulating three separate professions and practices. I believe strongly that our board does an admirable job with limited staff and resources to protect the public as it accesses hearing and speech care.

Within our domain of practice, occupational therapists and occupational therapy assistants consider the repertoire of occupation in which the client engages, the performance, skills, and patterns the client uses, and the client's body functions and structures. It's a very complex issue. As Rose pointed out, 27 years ago, one of the primary factors of creating certification was with the intent of identifying interior designers with qualifications that would let building officials know that these people had an expertise in order to do this. We operate, as interior designers, under exemptions that are codified into the Architects Practice Act, specifically 5537 and 5538. This is a line, we look at it as a line. Everything above this line architects, that's architecture. And you don't go there unless you are a licensed architect. Everything below that line is an exemption. And, technically, that's really none of their business, because it's exempt. And so, really under the exemptions, and these exemptions have been in effect since 1939 and they've been updated a few times, these exemptions really allow the general public to operate without an architect or without an engineer. Now in 1990, when certification came into effect, the state set a standard for interior designers. Education, work experience, and an examination in order to raise that level to identify those people both to the public and to building officials. That these people were competent and qualified to do this kind of work. So, that's sort of how we operate. Now, with all good intentions what's happened over 27 years is there is no consistency with building departments. There's 450 building departments in the state. Probably 95% of them don't really have a problem with certified interior designers submitting commercial interior design work and residential interior design work. And we're talking significant projects. I mean, the projects involve laying out offices and office buildings, and exiting corridors, and reflected ceiling plans. A whole host of elements that go to the making up the interior of a vacant building. It's non-structural and it's non-seismic. And it falls under the exemptions of the Architects Practice Act. That's where we practice. And some building officials say, nope, we won't accept that, we need architects only. And that's probably about 5% of the building officials. Unfortunately, that 5% are in the major city centers: Los Angeles, San Francisco, and San Jose. There are some surrounding jurisdictions to them that also go along that way, but for the most part those are the three big ones. And we understand all of that. We understand that that's their prerogative under the law and under the California Building Code to do that. The acceptance of the stamp issue, and we tried to address this four or five years ago, at the last Sunset review hearing. And we were turned down at that point, or it wasn't put forward, shall I say, because there was a lot of opposition. It appears we're at the same impasse. We were at a meeting last Thursday with the Architect's Board. I was informed that CALBO, which is the organization of building officials, are somewhat opposed to us making these amendments that are in the background paper and in our Sunset Review report. The California Architects Board has also taken a position of opposition. And, not surprisingly, the American Institute of Architects California Council has also taken an opposition. So, the architects generally, and with the building officials, kind of following along, are all taking an opposition to the amendments that we have proposed to our statute to clarify what certified interior designers and all interior designers can do under the exemptions. So, in following all of this, what we raised the question of where is the evidence? Where is the proof? We've got 27 years of operating under these exemptions. We have been doing horizontal exiting for longer than that. We have been doing one hour corridors for longer than that. We've been doing reflected ceiling plans. We've been building out buildings, in major cities across this state, for over 27 years. There is not one instance of a safety violation. Not one instance of consumer harm, bodily harm, or a death. That's not what we do. We operate under the exemptions. If it's structural, if it's seismic, if it has a real safety issue, then it falls under architecture or engineering. If it doesn't, it falls under the exemptions. So, what we're here today is to, sort of, we want to keep pushing this forward. We've been here before. If we don't get it, we'll be back again. It is just part of what we do in order to continue our practice, and it's what we settled for, or negotiated for, 27 years ago, so that's where we're at, issue number 1.

Alan Roth: I will give my brief comments of our testimony for this morning. Good morning to Chairman Hill, Chairman Salas and Members of the Committee and staff. I am Alan Roth. I'm President of the Respiratory Care Board. I'm joined by Tom Wagner, my Vice President and Stephanie Nunez, our executive officer. I know you have a lot to cover today so I will provide you with a brief overview. The Respiratory Care Board was created by the Legislature in 1982 to protect the vulnerable population from the unqualified practice of respiratory care. The composition of the board consists of nine members. Four respiratory care practitioners, four public members and one physician/surgeon. Appointments to the board are made equally by the Governor, the Senate Rules Committee and the Speaker of the Assembly, each authority appointing three members to the Board. The Board is responsible for enforcing state laws pertaining to the practice of respiratory care, and regulates a single category of healthcare specialists, respiratory care practitioners. The RCPs are specialized healthcare practitioners who work under the supervision of medical directors and are involved in the prevention, diagnosis, treatment, management or re-rotation of problems affecting the heart and the lungs and other disorders as well as providing diagnostic, educational and rehabilitation services. PCP's provide care for those who are dependent upon life support and that cannot breathe on their own. RCP's treat patients with acute and chronic diseases including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, trauma victims and surgical patients. They are typically employed in hospitals, however, a growing number of RCP's work in alternate care settings like subacute facilities, home medical device retail facilities, hyperbaric oxygen facilities, and sleep laboratories along with transport. The law governing RCPs, the Respiratory Care Practice Act requires licensure for individuals performing respiratory care. In carrying out its mandate to ensure the protection of the public shall be the highest priority in exercising the licensing, regulatory and disciplinary functions of the Board. In that sense, we screen every applicant for licensure to ensure minimum education and competency standards are met and conduct a thorough criminal background check with each applicant. We investigate complaints against licensees including those generated from updated criminal history reports and mandatory reporting of violations by licensees and employers. We aggressively monitor our CPs placed on probation. We exercise the authority of the penalized or disciplined applicants and licensees including issuance of citations and fines while public reprimands ordering denial, probation, or revocation of a license. We address current issues related to the unlicensed and/or unqualified practice of respiratory care. We promote public awareness of the mandate and its function as well as current issues affecting respiratory care. Since 1985, when the first license was issued, the Board has licensed over 39,000 licensees, of which over 20,000 remain active. The Board has a $3.8 million budget to which it manages closely. The last renewal fee increase was made by statute in the 1999 and was not implemented until 2002, over 15 years ago. Since our last sunset review four years ago, the most significant changes have taken place include the establishment of two additional respiratory baccalaureate degree programs as a result of SB 850, one of which I am involved with, Raul Modesto Junior College and Skyline College. Improving respiratory care competency standards by requiring the passage of an advanced competency exam for licensure AB 1972. Successfully implementing BreEZe with our new database. Entering into a contract with UC San Francisco to delve further into the issues that the board believes may significantly improve consumer protection. That's the end of my remarks, I will pass it on to Stephanie Nunez to continue. Wait, I apologize. I have one more thing. The Board is proud to share its success in meeting the performance targets. In early 2016, they were developed as part of the Consumer Protection Enforcement Initiative. The Board's performance targets for its enforcement program are 7 days to complete the complaint intake cycle, 210 days for the investigative cycle and 540 days for the formal discipline cycle. For years, the Board has consistently met all of its performance measure targets, with the exception of the formal discipline cycle, which includes processing time by the Office of Attorney General and the Office of Administrative Hearings. However, in 2016, for the first time, the Board met its formal discipline target with an average of 538 days to process a case from beginning to end. The Board is working closely with the Office of the Attorney General to improve processes and communication so that this target can be met on a more consistent basis. The Board is committed to conducting business in an efficient and effective manner, and responding to practice in operational issues in a proactive, forward-thinking manner. Moreover, the Board is committed to ensuring that consumer protection is always its highest priority. Now, I'm going to turnover to Stephanie Nunez, our Executive Officer.

Speech language pathology, audiology, and hearing aid dispensing are independent and rapidly expanding professions in both healthcare and educational systems. Professional in this three fields work with people of all ages,from newborns to geriatric,to address and rehabilitate communication impairments. Communication skills are essential for the well being and societal contribution of all Americans,affecting quality of life including psycho social,educational and occupational endeavors. Speech language pathologists provide assessment therapy and counseling for individuals and their family members. There is a wide range of disorders addressed by the speech pathologist including speech and language impairments, swallowing disorders or dispasia, strokes or other brain trauma, stuttering and voice and speech production. Audiologists provide diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation and counseling for individuals with hearing and or balance disorders and their family members. We work with patients of all ages. Audiologists provide diagnostic follow-up and treatment for infants who fail their newborn hearing screenings and subsequently fit hearing aids on infants found to have permanent hearing loss. We work closely with early intervention professionals and families to ensure the best speech language and psychosocial outcomes. In older children and adults, audiologists provide treatment and rehabilitative services, including communication counseling, provision of hearing aids, and assessment for cochlear implants, and post-implant management for infants and children and adults who receive cochlear implants. Audiologists work with other assistive technologies to address handicap imposed by hearing loss, and provide communication rehabilitation and ongoing patient and family management. We carrying out hearing conservation programs for individuals in industries where there's risk of noise-induced hearing loss. Hearing aid dispensers, test hearing in adults to select and fit hearing aids and provide post-fitting verification and validation of hearing aid amplification to ensure that the hearing aid is meeting the consumer specific hearing needs. Speech language pathologists, audiologists and hearing aid dispensers in California provide services to linguistically and culturally diverse populations representing all age groups and must continually adapt to new developments. Technologies and research findings, in all aspects of their respective professions. Services are provided in both public and private agencies, including schools, hospitals and private practice settings. For the history of our board, the demand for regulation of these three professions has existed since the early 1970s. Oversight of the professions of Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology has been governed by a combined board since it's inception in 1974. The regulation of hearing aid dispensing was enacted in 1970 originally under the jurisdiction of the medical board of California. But for the past 20 years has operated either as an independent board or a bureau under the department. On January 1st 2010, Assembly Bill 1535 created the speech language pathology, audiology and hearing aid dispensers board. This merged the hearing aid dispensers bureau into the Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology Board. The newly merged board regulates the professions of Speech-Language Pathology, Audiology and Hearing Aid dispensing. Each profession is separate and distinct. Each has its own scope of practice. Each has its own entry level requirements and professional settings with some overlap in groups and pathologies served. To balance the professional expertise and public input on the board, the government structure of the board consists of two speech language pathologists, two audiologists, one of whom must be a dispensing audiologist, two non-audiologist hearing aid dispensers, and a public member, who must be a licensed physician and surgeon board certified in otolaryngology. All of these members are appointed by the Governor. In addition, one public member seat is appointed by the Senate Rules Committee and one by the speaker of the Assembly. Members are appointed for four-year terms and no member may serve more than two consecutive terms. Our board serves to protect the public through licensing and regulation of speech language pathologists, audiologists, and hearing aid dispensers. Who provides speech and hearing services to California consumers. The boards sets entry level licensing standards which include examination requirements that measure the licensees' professional knowledge and clinical abilities. That are consistent with the demands of the current delivery systems. To ensure ongoing consumer protection, the board enforces standards of professional conduct by investigating applicant backgrounds. Investigating complaints against licensed and unlicensed practitioners, and taking disciplinary action whenever appropriate. The board jurisdiction encompasses the regulation of 11 license types including speech-language pathology, audiology, hearing aid dispensing, paraprofessionals, and education programs offering degrees in speech-language pathology assistance. Licensing cycle times have been very significantly reduced in the past two years from an estimated 8 to 12 week time frame previously. To approximately two weeks today. The board will continue to take steps to enhance this process to reduce application cycle times. Access to the hearing aid dispensing profession has improved greatly due to the increase in the practical examinations offered by the board. Prior to 2015-16, the board examined an average of 120 candidates annually. In 2015-16, the board examined 306 candidates for the hearing aid dispensing practical examination. There remain many initiatives and activities that the board plans to develop and accomplish to further support consumers. There is a growing demand for licensure and enforcement in our professions. So, what I'll try to do, because of the time constraints, is be brief and try to give you issue number one, the acceptance of the stamp. And I'll try to, sort of, summarize that as best I can. It's a very complex issue. As Rose pointed out, 27 years ago, one of the primary factors of creating certification was with the intent of identifying interior designers with qualifications that would let building officials know that these people had an expertise in order to do this. We operate, as interior designers, under exemptions that are codified into the Architects Practice Act, specifically 5537 and 5538. This is a line, we look at it as a line. Everything above this line architects, that's architecture. And you don't go there unless you are a licensed architect. Everything below that line is an exemption. And, technically, that's really none of their business, because it's exempt. And so, really under the exemptions, and these exemptions have been in effect since 1939 and they've been updated a few times, these exemptions really allow the general public to operate without an architect or without an engineer. Now in 1990, when certification came into effect, the state set a standard for interior designers. Education, work experience, and an examination in order to raise that level to identify those people both to the public and to building officials. That these people were competent and qualified to do this kind of work. So, that's sort of how we operate. Now, with all good intentions what's happened over 27 years is there is no consistency with building departments. There's 450 building departments in the state. Probably 95% of them don't really have a problem with certified interior designers submitting commercial interior design work and residential interior design work. And we're talking significant projects. I mean, the projects involve laying out offices and office buildings, and exiting corridors, and reflected ceiling plans. A whole host of elements that go to the making up the interior of a vacant building. It's non-structural and it's non-seismic. And it falls under the exemptions of the Architects Practice Act. That's where we practice. And some building officials say, nope, we won't accept that, we need architects only. And that's probably about 5% of the building officials. Unfortunately, that 5% are in the major city centers: Los Angeles, San Francisco, and San Jose. There are some surrounding jurisdictions to them that also go along that way, but for the most part those are the three big ones. And we understand all of that. We understand that that's their prerogative under the law and under the California Building Code to do that. The acceptance of the stamp issue, and we tried to address this four or five years ago, at the last Sunset review hearing. And we were turned down at that point, or it wasn't put forward, shall I say, because there was a lot of opposition. It appears we're at the same impasse. We were at a meeting last Thursday with the Architect's Board. I was informed that CALBO, which is the organization of building officials, are somewhat opposed to us making these amendments that are in the background paper and in our Sunset Review report. The California Architects Board has also taken a position of opposition. And, not surprisingly, the American Institute of Architects California Council has also taken an opposition. So, the architects generally, and with the building officials, kind of following along, are all taking an opposition to the amendments that we have proposed to our statute to clarify what certified interior designers and all interior designers can do under the exemptions. So, in following all of this, what we raised the question of where is the evidence? Where is the proof? We've got 27 years of operating under these exemptions. We have been doing horizontal exiting for longer than that. We have been doing one hour corridors for longer than that. We've been doing reflected ceiling plans. We've been building out buildings, in major cities across this state, for over 27 years. There is not one instance of a safety violation. Not one instance of consumer harm, bodily harm, or a death. That's not what we do. We operate under the exemptions. If it's structural, if it's seismic, if it has a real safety issue, then it falls under architecture or engineering. If it doesn't, it falls under the exemptions. So, what we're here today is to, sort of, we want to keep pushing this forward. We've been here before. If we don't get it, we'll be back again. It is just part of what we do in order to continue our practice, and it's what we settled for, or negotiated for, 27 years ago, so that's where we're at, issue number 1.

The NCIDQ, is an optional three day exam containing a drawing practicum and is taken by a majority of interior designers working in the commercial environment. CID is appropriate for designers working in residential space and small commercial space. Within the profession, there are interior designers specialize in different areas. As an example, the kitchen and bath designers have developed their own certification and separate stamp. Although designers working on large commercial projects have passed the NCIDQ, no additional certification for these professionals currently exists. We believe another category and certification would be beneficial to these commercial designers and their clientele. Such a certification would require passage of NCIDQ and California codes-based test, education experience, qualifications and an ongoing education competency requirements. The certification could be one of many forms. Private certification through the CCIDC as part of an existing licensing board or perhaps other options. Carolyn Chu: Great, good afternoon, my name is Carolyn Chu from Legislative Analyst's Office. Hospital District Law in 1945. It was later renamed the Local Health Care District Law in the mid 90s. Health care districts are originally created in response to service shortages due to the population growth after World War II particularly in some cases in rural areas. The number of districts grew most substantially in the 1940s and 50s. Today, there are roughly 45 districts statewide, most other special districts, local voters created these local governments. Health care districts are governed by five-member boards, and are subject to state policies and regulations that other local governments are subject to including the Brown Act. Health care districts also are under the purview of LAFCO which will be spoken to next or Local Agency Formation Commissions. Health care districts have brought authority under current law for the activities they can do. They can operate health care facilities like hospitals, clinics, skilled nursing facilities, adult health centers, nurse training schools and child care facilities. They also can operate ambulance services within and outside of their districts. They also can support other types of social and health programs in their communities through grants or direct services. Health care districts carry out these activities through a variety of different structures. They can carry out their activities as corporations, joint ventures or partnerships. They can establish and participate in managed care plans. Or they can contract with other local providers in their communities and make grants to perform various activities. Today there are almost 40 districts still operating hospitals directly, most of these districts are in rural areas of the state. And more of our 20 of these hospitals are designated as critical access hospitals, the remaining district provider array of other services. About half of these other districts provide direct community services like ambulance services or skilled nursing. And the remaining districts provide grants to their local communities to support programs like health programs in schools or physical education. Many of the districts that no longer operate hospitals did have hospitals in the past, or have sold, or leased their hospital operations today. About 14 districts, however, closed their hospitals all together. Health care districts raise revenue through a variety of mechanisms. The vast majority of them receive property taxes through the 1% rate. They also can levy special taxes like parcel taxes which require two-thirds voter approval. They have service charges for the services like those provided in a clinic. They also can have revenue from leases and grants of their facilities. And they also can have debt financing, they can issue general obligation bonds with voter approval or issue revenue bonds based on the services they provide. Some districts in the last few decades, primarily those with hospitals, have faced financial challenges in the last few decades, 14 of those districts have declared bankruptcy, some more than once. One major challenge cited by the health care districts is the hospitals' inability to achieve a viable peer mix. That is, many of their clients either do not have robust health insurance or do not have health insurance at all. As a result of these challenges a few districts have been dissolved or reorganized through the LAFCO process. Moreover, number of grand jury inquiries have looked into some other district practices. In particular, these grand jury cases have looked up the use of public revenues by these districts, in some cases looking at the use of property tax revenues to support various community activities. One challenge that is not unique to health care districts, but perhaps more pronounced in these cases, is that residents and voters may not be aware of their existence. And moreover, voters cannot take steps to change the overall level of service for the health care districts. As you are aware, local government's taxes are locked in at their 1978 levels. As a result, not only do districts continue to receive property taxes, regardless of their change overall in the community but also residents and voters can neither increase nor decrease the level of service that they provide within their communities. This, however, is true for all types of local governments.

How does these districts relate to other governments? They are subject to the zoning power of the city or the county, depending on whether the territory their facilities are located in is incorporated or unincorporated. And their medical operations are subject to all the complex regulations that the state imposes and the federal government payers impose on participants in the medical industry. They have the power to change their name by resolution, as many special districts do, but that can be a little confusing at times. They are required to file a resolution with the county clerk when they do that. Other laws require them also to register with the Roster of Public Agencies maintained by the Secretary of State. Their financial powers are as broad as most local governments although this doesn't typically figure large in their lives. Where most of their money comes from if they're providing services is from their entrepreneurial activity, from their enterprise activity. But they're entitled to property taxes, some of them get a legacy share. They can pass special taxes with two-thirds voter approval, a few of them have. They are entitled to issue bonded debt and they commonly do. They do not seem to have the ability to assess real property with property owner approval as other governments do. Most of their money doesn't come in the transitional forms of government money. Formation and reorganization of a hospital district, creating one and changing one, is governed by the principal act. The statue says that and there's a bankruptcy case that says that. But the court says knocks Herzberg the Lafco law fills voids in the principal act and there are some. So the two laws both apply to creating and changing these districts. If Lafco receives an application to form or reorganize a healthcare district, they're required to give notice to the state health agencies. The solution requires voter approval, as does transfer of more than half of the healthcare district's assets. You can't close the hospital or sell it and go out of town without voter approval. The principle act for health care districts, refers to the district organization law, and the formation process requires a petition of voters or landowners to the Board of Supervisors of the county which has the larger amount of district territory, and the county board serves as the supervising authority not Lafco. It is clear that the Legislature intended healthcare districts to compete in the private marketplace for healthcare services. And they couldn't survive if they didn't. And the difficulty of maintaining a standalone hospital for anybody is one of the reasons you're seeing bankruptcies. Most hospitals have to affiliate with a larger network to capture more dollars in order to survive. These ones health care districts have been able to do that by joining power agreements and by contract. But not all of them have been nimble enough to do it quickly enough, particularly in rural areas and that has led to some of the bankruptcies that you have seen. A common strategy for a hospital that's not cutting it as a hospital is to become a skilled nursing facility which is why you see some districts providing that service because that's what the industry does when they get in a corner. How much power does Lafco have over a health care district? Some and some that's significant. They don't have quite as much power as they have over other special districts because the role given to the counties and the role given to voters. A sphere of influence every five years and reorganizations, which involve the elimination of merger of districts. The districts expect them to do it, but it's not quite clear what their authority to do it is, because 56133 is not a very good match for the problem we're trying to address. Some healthcare districts are attracting attention due to competition for scarce property tax dollars and are therefore vulnerable to criticism if Lafco, the grand jury or others conclude they are not serving the public interest.
