Health care districts can be square pegs in round holes and let me point out a couple of ways that that's so Most of their money comes from private sources. So, they can think like businesses. And they may need to think like a business to survive. But if you spend a lot of time thinking like a business, you may forget to think like a government. And we have different expectations of government, both legally and socially. You can think of them, at least the ones that are still providing a meaningful amount of services, as really a public private hybrid. And their talent pool comes largely from outside government circles. They're hiring hospital administrators from the labor pool of hospital administrators. And the hospital administrators aren't trained in the Brown Act, the Public Records Act, conflict of interest, 1090, etc. And, so there can be occasionally a sort of tone deafness about the expectations of government for some of these districts. And that can be very problematic. Like special districts generally, it's hard to generalize about healthcare districts. That label describes a motley crew of very different animals. Some of them are vital local governments well connected to their communities. And you're going to hear from some of them this afternoon. Some of them have very few resources, and barely show up on radar. You Chair can't find them on the Internet. Doesn't know who their officials are, who are they? Some of them no longer operate hospitals, and have yet to find a meaningful role for themselves. But still receiving property tax dollars, and that of course generates controversy particularly in the recession. My sense is that the LAFCO process may be better situated to sort out the wheat from the chaff in this area than any broad-based legislative fix. So, I would encourage your Committee to be careful about legislation. And especially be careful about legislation that makes exceptions to the LAFCO process. The closest was Reno, and this predates Interstate 80, so Highway 40 was a rather treacherous route and took time. Unfortunately, due to complications, his wife passed away giving childbirth. Rather than going to the dark side, Mr. Joseph banded together with community members, and successfully passed a local measure to create the Tahoe Forest Hospital District in 1949. He didn't stop there, he also donated all of the land that the hospital district campus is upon today. It is our legacy. In 1952 the hospital opened with a 10,000 square foot hospital with eight beds. And that served the entire area from Immigrant Gap all the way to the state line, of both eastern Placer County and Nevada County. The original structure was torn down earlier this year for reasons I'll share with you in just a moment. Tahoe Forest is governed, as you know, by an elected board staggered four year terms, always has been. And it had to grow with the region. In 1960, the Olympics were held at Squaw Valley, Tahoe was on the map and growth began. And the district had to move with that growth. Jumping ahead to today, Tahoe Forest Hospital District is a critical access hospital. It employs nearly 800 people. It is the largest employer in the region with the exception of ski resorts when there's a lot of snow. So right now we are not in the category. Our operating revenues are $133 million of which 5 million, or approximately 3.75%, we received from the property owners through property tax. It was interesting in 1966, I recently read the audited financials, I'm strange that way. And at that time the district received approximately two thirds of its funding from property taxes. That is a very different story today. Not only do we serve the 39,000 full-time residents that are in our district, but we have to be large and small at the same time. We have to flex. We have 39,000 full-time residents on Wednesday. But I can assure you that this Saturday, we will have 150,000 when the skiers come up to ski. We have to flex. That's a big challenge, and it makes us very unique compared to other hospitals. As far as services are concerned, I'll blow through some of the highlights. We do cardiac pulmonary, ER, Health clinics, hospice, in-home health, diagnostic imaging, med surge, long-term care, lab, occupational health, orthopedics. And Mr Colintuna was correct, our orthopedists see everything. It isn't just specializing in hands. But I can tell you it's shoulders, it's knees. We even perform anterior hip replacements, which is very rare, and a big investment in the equipment to do so. Your hip replacement one day, you're walking out the next, better pain management. We also have pharmacy, our brand new Joseph family Center for women and newborn care, our legacy service again, pharmacy. We have a research Institute, a wellness neighborhood which I'll speak to in just a moment briefly. And we also have the Gene Upshaw Memorial Tahoe Forest Cancer Center which opened in 2012. In 2006 Tahoe Forest Hospital District faced the challenging realities of compliance with SB 1953, Seismic Compliance. And at that same time, we utilized information gathered from our community health needs assessments, community working groups, leadership councils to determine the desired, needed elements of the hospital's future. Without the voters, passed what's known as Measure C in 2007 with a 73% yes vote. Approving $95.8 million General Obligation Bond consisting of 15 projects for compliance and others for enhanced services that the community desired. The Cancer Center is one of those. Today we serve not just our district patients, and cancer is a really good example of this. Our cancer program reaches far beyond our district boundaries. We have second-home owners who chose to receive cancer care in Truckee because they have a home there. There isnt traffic, parking is easy. They're a name and not a number. And also the care is exceptional. We have cancer patients that come from counties far away to the north and other rural environs. They may come for diagnostic purposes, but through a unique model of rural health care delivery, they can go home. They can receive treatment with their primary care physician, be with their family, not have to move in consultation with our cancer center. We are also the first rural hospital to receive Rural Prime Affiliation with UC Davis, which enables us to perform tumor boards with our Cancer Center. Every afternoon at lunch our cancer docs do Hollywood squares with cancer docs from UC Davis and UCLA discussing each and every case. We're very proud of our wellness neighborhood. And earlier I had mentioned that Tahoe Forest receives about 4% of its operating budget from the taxpayer. And we honor that, and we cherish it, and we try to shepherd those dollars very carefully. And the manner in which we do that is we support what we have coined the wellness neighborhood by pushing out into the community with many programs designed to promote community population health. These programs designed to aid disperate communities to promote access, navigation, and healthy living skills. So why a district? Well, in our case, as I said earlier, in 1952 there was not a hospital there. And if not for the enabling legislation there wouldn't be one there today. Tahoe Forest is there because the Legislature saw a need, particularly in the rural environments, and I would argue that that need exists today. Combined with the incredible philanthropic gift of land and the desire of our community, our district was created, still exist today. We enjoy great support from our community, and criticism from time to time. We are a community hospital and are constantly reminded of that proud fact. Much has changed in the last seven decades. There's no argument, I think, among many of us here today. Health care districts have adapted as we have to their unique communities and associated needs. In a world that's more complicated, regulated and advanced, my view is that healthcare districts are necessary entities that function closer to the people than a stand-alone private-sector hospital. They each evolve, and they each adapt to the communities in which they exist. A few comments as a former LAFCO Commissioner. Naturally when it came time for our municipal services review, it appeared in my inbox, all of the requests from Placer LAFCO. And it was interesting for me to be compiling the data as requested by LAFCO, rather than sitting on the other side of the dais analyzing the data as it's produced. And although it was accurate and the information was interesting, it was generalist in my view. What are your revenues? What are your boundaries? These types of things. But we are, as Mr. Cowentuna pointed out, a square peg in a round hole. We are different than a sewer district. We are different than a fire protection district or a city municipality. We're not reaching out, we have inmigration coming to us from other areas. We're out migration for different services. And therefore, we are unique in that regard. I do think that I would agree that the LAFCO process is probably the best process to satisfy the Legislature and the concern of oversight. Again for another reason, because LAFCOs are closer to the people and they're local. And we are all different. I would encourage exploration of how we can modify that with the LAFCO process so it better serves health care districts in the future and with that all I'll rest and answer any questions that you may have. Thank you.

Karen Hennings: Thank you very much, Chair Aguiar-Curry and members of the Committee, for inviting us here today. Good afternoon, my name is Karen Hennings and I'm the Administrative Director of the Del Puerto Health Care District. We thank you for the opportunity to share the story of our district's 71-year evolution. Del Puerto Health Care District is in the Northwestern Corridor of Stanislaus County. It borders San Joaquin County to the north, Santa Clara County to the west, the San Joaquin River to the east and the Newman/Gustine area to the south. Let me share a few more facts that'll help you better know our world. Stanislaus County has the fifth highest poverty rate in the State of California. 45% of our residents are MediCal eligible. The center of our district operations is the City of Patterson, where the economy in our region has always been based on agriculture and food processing. And our current unemployment rate hovers at around 9%. First, let's talk about our evolution of hospital to community clinic. The citizens of Patterson were early adopters of the California Hospital District Law. In 1946, our region voted for and established the Patterson Hospital District and by 1949 in partnership with the local rotary club, our hospital was built and serving the districts full time population of 1600. Our district provided more than just hospital services. In the old days, the local ambulance was one man, a station wagon, and a red light. But retirement came for the station wagon. And so, at that time in 1973, our district took over providing emergency medical technician level care and transportation. With the doing of business as Patterson District Ambulance, voters approved a special assessment of $27 per year per house. To support local medical transportation. By 1978, the ambulance care expanded to merit paramedic level advanced life support and emergency transportation. Most patients went to our local hospital. So one well-equipped ambulance met the needs of the then district population of 4,800. The district also worked within the community supporting educational programs in schools and community centers. The district worked to bring more medical providers into the community to meet primary and acute care needs. We encouraged and helped the development of local medical office space and sought partnerships with larger health systems rather than leasing our facilities, we thought more local providers would create more use of the local hospital. But as it turned out larger groups prefer to use their own acute care services. The district, however, was sensitive to the community and responded to the needs of the elderly by converting a section of our hospital into skilled nursing. When state law evolved, we changed our name from Patterson Hospital District to the Del Puerto Healthcare District, better representing the broad region we served. In 1996, we had a district population of 11,600. The ambulance transported about 200 patients per year. Skilled nursing was modestly used and the most frequent requested hospital room service was urgent but not acute care. As state regulations grew more complex, it was difficult to update the facilities and sustained the hospital with such a small population. In 1977, the Stanislaus County closed its county hospital and our in patient census dropped to about a quarter person of a day. Although the nearest hospital would be 26 miles and 40 minutes away, rather than bankrupt and dissolve the district the board closed the hospital in 1998 and looked to the future. This is one of the ways that we demonstrate how local government is best positioned to meet local needs. The district recognized in our rural area, basic health care access was the problem. Local doctors were retiring. Few new doctors entered into the community. Other provider options were impacted with waits up to three weeks. In Stanislaus County, 46% of patients use public transportation to and from their Doctor visit. And the closest county clinic was 16 miles away. District residents would forgo care care rather than spend an entire day on a Doctor visit or follow up. In response to the closing, the Board developed four post hospital goals. Portion off a section of the hospital land and build a modest building for ambulance operations and district administration. Unburden itself of an aged and costable building by selling the remaining property and building. Make good on $600,000 of residual hospital operation debt. And establish our next generation of district healthcare, that is a truly community-based clinic for primary and urgent care. Then, industry discovered Patterson's strategic location on the I-5 Corridor. There was cheap, non arable land to develop into distribution facilities and affordable housing. Patterson quickly grew into a bedroom community of the Bay Area and host to regional distribution centers such as Amazon, CVS, and Kohl's. This is the beauty field of local government. District residents on our board could work with district residents in the municipal government to foresee and respond to upcoming development. By the time the first distribution broke center broke ground, the Del Puerto1 Healthcare District was ready. In 2003, we opened a small downtown clinic. We immediately applied for and received rural health clinic status which under Californian federal law makes our clinic's operations eligible for full cost reimbursement for services provided to Medi-Cal and Medicare patients. We couldn't sustain a hospital in 1988 but, within 10 years, our district population had grown over 25,000 residents. Within a couple of years, the first rented space was outgrown and a short period later, so was the second rented space. Another important point is that healthcare districts can survive the ups and downs of local economy. The recession of 2008 had a huge hit on everyone's economy. Employer-based insurance fill and eventually the roles of public insurance greatly expanded. We were positioned to meet the changing local financial reality. With the USDA backed development loan, we built and moved into a modern facility in 2011. This, our current clinic location, has the capacity to double our current providers and patient visits in future years. The core of our practice is family medicine and pediatrics. We have two physicians and two mid-level providers, and we operate a lean medical assisting staff of 14. We also collaborate with cardiologist specialists who come to our clinic twice per month to see local patients. And we seek to add more services including dermatology, pediatric dentistry and mental health services. We developed a community partnership with the City of Patterson Fire Department who under our sponsorship and oversight now provides first responder medical services within the city limits. We recently purchased the building adjacent to ours and it is leased to a physical therapist, core fitness gym and orthodontist. In response to the exploding community population, the Del Puerto Health Center annually provides 15,000 visits to 6,600 patients. We now staff two full time ambulance who respond every year to 2,400, 911 dispatches and provide approximately 1,600 transports to 105 regional hospitals. We strive to meet the needs of the community, but service charges don't always equal self support. Healthcare districts like ours support vulnerable, under served populations but are also financially vulnerable themselves. In Stanislaus County there are three rural healthcare districts, ourselves, Oak Valley Hospital and Westside Community Health Care district. All three run ambulances and combined we serve 23% of the county population spread over 73% of the county's geography. We spend more time, drive further, and have a lower call volume than our municipal counterparts. Yet we have the same fixed costs for 24/7 365 staffing, vehicle maintenance and a base of operations. The point is, that it is inherently more expensive to provide ambulance cover in rural districts. You remember that economic picture I opened with? 9% unemployment, fifth highest poverty rate in the state and 45% of the population is MediCal eligible. Del Puerto does operate very lean, yet our net cost per ambulance transport is $1,130. Medi-Cal only pays us $115. WIth our high density of Medi-Cal patients, 45% of our transports account for 10% of our costs, of the income towards our cost, only 10% income. Even with tax subsidies, Patterson District Ambulance operates at a loss just to keep staffed for when that 911 call comes in. Healthcare districts providing rural ambulance and emergency medical transportation need the state to step up and reimburse at least the net cost of transporting rural health care district MediCal patients. Please consider a reimbursement model like rural health clinics who were made whole for the services they provide. In conclusion of my remarks today, I want to reiterate that recent district specific legislation and investigations have not told the whole story of healthcare districts. I was invited here to represent the rural healthcare districts that provide and care for their communities both with and without a hospital. Del Puerto healthcare district represents how local government has a definitive role in the historic immediate short term and long term solutions for healthcare access to California's rural populations. Healthcare districts must operate transparent, lean, pro community, pro quality, and pro local services that continually seek to meet the needs of growing communities in the changing world of healthcare economics. I thank you for the opportunity to testify today and happy for any questions.

The core of the IHHS program is the fact that it is 95% of what makes it possible for low income elderly and disabled Californians to remain at home. It is 95% of the home and community based services that California offers. And what California offers is by far the largest home community based service system in the country. We are one of very few states that spend more than half of our Medicaid long term support services funds on home based care rather than institutional care. The other key factor about our program that is essential I think to always emphasize is that it is also the most consumer centered and directed program of its kind. In almost every case, the consumer, the client of IHSS, the person living at home, is the employer of their provider. They select them, they supervise them, they determine how they serve them. And we consider that the most important feature of the entire program. Because nobody knows their needs better than the person who's living it. And throughout everything we have done over the years, the foremost issue has been to preserve that consumer centric view of the program. Everything else has been secondary. So what this will means is that in the budget year 2017-18, the overall budget for IHSS in California will be 10.6 billion of which we are assuming $5.7 billion as federal, but I just, again, note the possibility of reduction there. $3.1 billion is the state's share under the old sharing ratio and $1.8 billion will be paid by the counties, with the reversion to the old sharing ratios. The growth and cost of the program is driven by several factors. One of which has been the implementation of the Fair Labor Standards Act rule two years ago that requires home care workers with very few exceptions to be paid overtime, travel and wait time for medical accompaniment. And that has created a $900 million cost pressure in the current year. And then growth in the caseload as well as growth in the average hours per case have contributed almost $800 million to the growth of the program. To sort of get to the heart of what does the end of the Coordinated Care Initiative mean for the IHSS programme separate from the budgetary implications that many people are going to talk about today, it changes nothing for consumers. The consumers' care and services will continue. In those cases, where there have been enhanced care teams, starting to work between managed care plans and the IHSS program, we're going to be encouraging the continuation of those. Obviously more detail to come as to how that will be done. But literally, the consumers in the program, if they know anything about the end of the Coordinated Care Initiative, it will because they read it in the newspaper. It won't effect the hours of service, who is serving them or the circumstances. Two other features that are involved in the end of the Coordinated Care Initiative. The original legislation had called for development of a Universal Assessment Tool. So that in addition to the IHSS assessment tool that we have used, revised over the years, it would have been a common tool to assess on clients in IHSS. The big program as well as the much smaller MSSP program and the CBAS programs that are the, sort of, the day center programs, is what it used to be known as. We had, with very significant support from the Scan Foundation, we had contracted with UCLA to develop a tool that could be used between all programs, to inform a sense of what the consumer needs are. With the ending of CCI, the sort of the mandate for Universal Assessment Tool also ends. We have received from UCLA sort of their work, in terms of developing a series of possible approaches to interviews and assessments. Although it will not be continued in the form of the Universal Assessment Tool, we are certainly looking at it from the IHSS program perspective to see if there are tools or aspects that will be helpful for us. The final structural change that results from the end of Coordinated Care Initiative is the unwinding of what was called the Statewide Authority. As part of the Coordinated Care Initiative, it was determined that when enrollment in the Dual Status Program was complete in each of the seven counties sequentially, the Statewide Authority would undertake collective bargaining for the workers in those counties. At the time that CCI was determined to not be cost effective and therefore the unwind was to begin. The Statewide Authority had not entered into any contracts with any of the unions. They're still in the exploration, discussion, exchange of information stages. And so the original contracts, that had been previously negotiated by the seven counties, have been returned to those counties for them to resume their responsibility under the collective bargaining provisions of IHSS. And so, that has occurred and sort of Statewide Authority has been unwound and disbanded. So, I would like to stop with that part of the first part of the agenda to see if the Department of Finance, Leandra is going to add?

[{'start': 19, 'end': 27, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 58, 'end': 73, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Chris Schultz: Good afternoon, Chris Schultz, Deputy Commissioner with the Department of Insurance. Thank you to the chair, the Committee and the staff for inviting the department to participate. And compliments to the Committee staff on the excellent background paper. Appreciate excellent staff work. In 2012, the insurance Commissioner Dave Jones gave department staff a pretty clear directive, which is make sure there is insurance ready as soon as autonomous vehicles are ready to launch. We've taken our mission of consumer protection for all Californians pretty seriously. We've coordinated closely with our friends at DMV. We've reached out to stakeholders. And the Commissioner himself took a ride in one of these autonomous cars to see what it was like. In October 2014, the Commissioner held a public hearing in San Jose on these issues, where we invited insurers and academics and actuaries to kind of present on these issues. I think there are two big pieces of information. First, it's the Legislature sets the minimum financial responsibility limits. The bare bones insurance requirements for every car on the road. And these limits have not been increased in quite a while. And for some types of vehicles, like big trucks or vehicles that transport passengers for hire, the Legislature set higher limits. The second is that Proposition 103 approved by the voters is the controlling law in setting auto insurance rates. For commercial auto insurance rates, they fall under Prop 103, but there's considerable flexibility in how those rates are established. About 12% of the auto insurance market is commercial auto at this point. For private passenger auto insurance, that's 88% of the auto insurance market, the rates are governed by the mandatory and optional rating factors in Prop 103 and the optional rating factors adopted by regulation. And the three mandatory rating factors are the driver's safety record, the insured's miles driven annually, and the insured's years of driving experience. Those are the mandatory rating factors. We've been asking all the stakeholders whether there's an immediate need to change either the law or the regulations in order to insure autonomous vehicles. And the initial answer is, we do not think there's a need. If a manufacturer offers a vehicle for sale tomorrow, insurance will be available. For manufacturers who are testing AVs right now, commercial auto insurance is available. Once we get to a certain level of autonomy, as discussed in the staff background paper, insurers may well file for new rates. They might weight some of the optional factors like safety and protective devices or vehicle type more heavily. They might propose a separate class plan. We have these, for example, antique autos or motorcycles, they have a separate class plan. In order to do that, insurers would use estimates or projections based on the data that's available. We have some recent experience on this, as it relates to the personal auto endorsements approved for Uber and Lyft drivers. Some insurers treated a TNC mile like it was a personal mile. And some insurers filed rates that treated it more like a taxi mile, because they're making a projection on what these miles are going to look like. They don't really know yet. These projections are allowed to remain in effect for a few years, possibly three years for a smaller data set or two years for a larger data set. Until credibility is established. That's several quarters of data moving in the same direction. Is kind of credible data for insurance rating purposes, so it takes a while for the experience out there on the street to translate into data to translate into changing insurance rates. We'd expect the insurers would track autonomous vehicles separately and that would allow them to establish this credible data. There are a few quick issues I wanted to mention. The first is the Uber and Lyft example, in our view here is informed by Uber, a company who's changed the insurance situation for drivers, and pedestrians, and third parties when they put the cars on our streets. We think that with AVs, we might end up seeing a situation like Uber and Lyft where the insurance available in each collision could be the drivers, or the manufacturers, or a combination of both. That's a little bit complicated. The first time we really have seen that was with Uber and Lyft. And the statute calls for report on TNC insurance that's due this summer. And we hope that study will illuminate whether that kind of hybrid model is working for consumers. The second is that Proposition 103 is working. A recent study from the Federal Insurance Office, that's in US Treasury, found that while half of California zip codes meet their definition for low income zip codes, these are high poverty, high minority zip codes. Only six of those zip codes had insurance rates that were above their affordability index, that was 2% of the family's income. So compared to the rest of the nation, auto insurance in California is relatively affordable. The insurance Commissioner would caution that any rush to kind of amend Prop 103 risks harming Californians who benefit from Prop 103's protections right now. In many states, insurers use credit scores, or zip codes, or location tracking, or big data to, frankly, to try and cherry pick the best risks. And we think that's a risk in this conversation. I just mentioned data, and we're watching autonomous vehicles closely, because California has prohibitions on using data for certain types of purposes. Specifically, we allow tracking miles, but not the location of those miles. So when we think about autonomous vehicles or track Caltrans road charge pilot project, these are things that we're going to spinning off a lot of data about miles, but also the location of these miles. And we want to make sure there's a firewall between whatever purpose that might be used for, for autonomous vehicles or for the road charge. But a firewall for the insurance purposes, where we dont allow the use of that data. And the final issue is the determination of fault. The department has, principally, at-fault regulations that require insurers to look at each collision and determine whether the driver's at fault, that impacts the driver's driving safety record and the driver's eligibility for the good driver discount. These are provisions of Prop 103. We're planning to take a look at these principally at fault regulations to see if any updates are necessary based on further development with autonomous vehicles. Thank you for inviting us to be here, and I'll be here for the remainder of the hearing if the Committee has any questions.
[{'start': 16, 'end': 29, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 324, 'end': 334, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Brian Soublet: Good afternoon, I'm Brian Soublet, I'm the Deputy Director and Chief Counsel for the Department of Motor Vehicles, and been working on autonomous vehicle regulations for the past four plus years. And I'd like to thank the Committee for inviting the department to participate in the hearing this afternoon. I think one of the important things to talk about first is, what is an autonomous vehicle? And basically, under SB-1298, which was enacted in the 2012 legislative session. It created Vehicle Code Section 38750, and that's the section that required the Department of Motor Vehicles to come up with regulations for both the testing and eventual deployment of autonomous vehicles on public streets. And it defines an autonomous vehicle as a vehicle that has technology that makes it capable of operating without the actual physical control or monitoring of a human driver. So there are many vehicles on the street now that have driver assistance systems such as lane key, emergency pre-break, parking assist. Those things under the definition in the statute aren't autonomous vehicles, and so there is a distinction. The Nation Highway Traffic Safety Administration has adopted what are the levels of autonomy that were set forth by the Society of Automotive Engineers. And so those levels go from zero to five. The vehicles that we see on the road now are level two or below. So when we talk about autonomous vehicles, we're talking about vehicles that start at level three. Which is a vehicle that can operate for some time in an autonomous mode, but then require the driver as a, so to speak, a back up in case there is a need. Then you have a level four vehicle which doesn't require on the driver, but only can operate in specific domains. And a level five vehicle which can operate basically all the time without a driver monitoring it. So with that task in vehicle code Section 38750, back in 2013, we started working on regulations. One of the first things that we did was form a statewide steering committee, that included our sister agencies, the Department of Insurance, the Office of Traffic Safety, the Highway Patrol, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. And we started mapping out a course for, at first, testing regulations. With that process we availed ourselves of a technique under the Administrative Procedures Act which allowed us to hold workshops on drafts of the regulations. That's been a valuable tool for us. To date, we've held six workshops on both the testing, and what we would call our deployment regulations. Our testing regulations went into effect in September of 2014, and as of this morning, there are 26 companies that hold permits with the department to test vehicles on our streets. There are approximately 180 authorized vehicles that have autonomous technology that are testing right now. The law requires that the drivers of the vehicle be employees of the manufacturer. And so we added in our regulations a requirement that those drivers meet the definition of what is a good driver. So there's no violations in their record for the last three years, no DUIs. We also require that the drivers get enrolled in the DMV's Pull Notice Program. And that's a program where employers have to enroll their drivers so that they receive notifications when drivers have some form of a traffic violation. Those regulations have been in effect for two years. They seem to be working. We also require reports of accidents that the vehicles have been involved in. In the past two years, there have only been 25 reported accidents. They are all available on the DMV's website. The majority of those accidents that we've seen so far, are the result of someone actually crashing into the autonomous vehicle. They have a tendency to drive very conservatively. And so people don't know how to react to them. Accident reports are required to be submitted to the department within 10 days of their occurrence. And that's when we go ahead and post them on our website. So now we're at the phase where these have been in effect for two years. We're very shortly, pretty soon, going to roll out what we're calling our deployment regulations. And those will include testing for vehicles that do not necessarily require a driver in the seat of the vehicle. The current testing regime requires that there be an employee of the manufacturer in the seat of the vehicle. We're about to launch on regulations that would have requirements that would allow vehicles that don't necessarily have a person sitting inside the vehicle. We anticipate that with that rule making proceeding, we would probably have those regulations ready and in effect by the end of this year. So it is moving rapidly, and those regulations would allow the operation of basically all levels of autonomous vehicles. The issue becomes whether the vehicles are actually available. We don't have an estimate on that. I think the manufacturers would be better suited to speak on that issue. But in the very near future, we'll have our regulations ready to go. So, with that, I invite any questions.

Curt Augustine: Thank you Mr. Chair and Members, I am Curt Augustine I'm the Director of Policy for the Alliance of Automobile Manufacturers, and the Committee asked me today to put on my crystal ball a little bit to tell you essentially what the status of autonomous vehicles are, and what is literally coming down the road in the foreseeable future. The announced plans of some of our companies include that Tesla has announced fully autonomous vehicles in the next couple years, Volkswagen by 2019, Toyota by 2020. Ford has announced plans to quote, have a high volume, fully autonomous level four capable vehicle in commercial operation in 2011. And as I mentioned, they recently invested $1 billion in a new ride-sharing service. Volvo and BMW have announced that they will have vehicles in 2021. As of the end of last year, 33 companies around the world are working on some aspect of AV's. So what are the current A, B sales and travel projections? Well experts agree that it will likely be years before the level 4 and 5 AVs make up a substantial portion of our fleet. The consensus of all the research that we've seen that level fours and fives will not be ubiquitous on our roadways until the 2030s. And some examples, estimates obviously, but in the 20s, perhaps 2 to 5% of sales could be AVs. In 2030s, maybe 20% to 40%, which would then translate to 10% to 20% of the fleet. And then through the 50s, 80% to 100% of vehicles, and that would still only be 40% to 60% of the fleet. It's important to recognize that the longevity of vehicles and the condition that they are made, vehicles stay on the road. So drivers are going to have to learn how to interact with AB vehicles, and AB vehicles are going to have to learn how to interact with drivers. They're going to be on the road together for a very long time. In fact, the IIHS estimates that even if AVs were mandated today, it would take at least 25 years before 95% of the vehicles are AVs. So this is a very long process that we're looking for. Actually to mention, it wasn't in my remarks, but it was Senator Newman asked about trucks. But there's serious consideration on US Highway 83, in the middle part of our country running from Canada to Mexico, they're looking at devoted truck lanes solely for AV and commercial use. So what do we think will influence AV sales? Well, the public views AVs with both great interest and some skepticism. When we talk to consumers, three themes really jump out. First, cost is critical, these vehicles will cost more. They're extensive in their technology breakthroughs, and that's going to cost more. There's also uncertainty among the driving public about AV performance, and that really is much of the skepticism. So we believe that we will really only be overcome until AVs are able to demonstrate that they perform reliably and safety, and those potential purchasers will be able see that. And then finally, many drivers tell us that they would prefer to operate a vehicle both in the autonomous mode, but have the ability to be taken over by a human driver. Manufacturers understand that desire, and are building their plans accordingly. So, we do see several challenges to a successful implementation. One is the transition that I mentioned. AVs and traditional cars are going to be on the road together. Right now, the average fleet age of our cars is 11 and a half years. I mean, that's going to take many, many years to cycle that through. There are the laws, both nationally and in each state, that are going to provide challenges to that, and all the testing that goes along with that. I've mentioned cost is one, but there are also some other issues. We've had some questions about some of the accidents and potential failures. Does it hit the car or hit the dog? Those type of questions need to be answered. Liability, security for the vehicles, and the data privacy, much along the questions that Senator Gains answered. Auto makers are prepared to work with legislators, regulators, insurers, and other stakeholders to address these challenges. We don't have all the answers at this time. We believe there is time to do this, and forums like this are critical to begin that process. And so, this last set of remarks I'll make are both not only for insurance issues, but also for the actual implementation of the vehicles themselves. And the auto alliance that I represent, which I was remiss, I should have said, I represent 12 of the automakers, which is approximately 70% of the vehicles sold in the United States. So our policy is that we urge policymakers to proceed carefully in creating new and broad legal frameworks. The alliance cautions states against passing premature laws which would serve to inhibit vehicle innovation, and delay potential safety benefits. We encourage states to heed the NHTSA's advice about appropriate state action as expressed in the recently published document that Mr. Soublet mentioned. And this will thus avoid regulating vehicle safety performance design and certification. If states get involved in that we will have a patchwork of legislation that will be inoperable throughout our country. The alliance agrees with the United States Department of Transportation's assessment of the roles of federal and state authorities, with respect to regulating motor vehicles. As detailed in their document, the oversight of safety design, performance, and certification is best left to one unified federal standard. While traditional registration, licensing, law enforcement, and insurance issues are best left to the states. So in closing, the state chooses to take a legislative or regulatory action with respect to AVs. We recommend that such action be premised on removing impediments to safe testing or deployment of such vehicles. And we recommend that states concentrate on revisiting existing laws and regulations to accommodate the safe use of autonomous vehicles. And again, thank you for the opportunity.

Cliff Costa: Mr. Chair and Senators, Cliff Costa on behalf of the California New Car Dealers Association. I want to thank the Committee for including us in today's hearing. But as Mr. Augustine just said, the full potential will not be here for decades. We will continue to have these situations where we have human drivers on the road. It is our belief that regardless of vehicles being fully autonomous or not, there will still be some sort of need for insurance, like you presently have in your home for theft, fire, flood, and other potential damage. Ryan Gammelgard: My name is Ryan Gammelgard, counsel for State Farm, and I'll be talking about some background issues in terms of State Farm's involvement in autonomous vehicle technology. Give some current key issues from an insurance industry perspective and then also provide this Committee a broad overview of the current legislative regulatory landscape across the country, at the federal level, the state level. And also a little bit about international issues that are going on. And then Rex will be able to talk more about California specific issues. We thought it was important to provide that background to give this Committee a better context of some big picture issues that are going on. The mission of State Farm is to help people manage the risks of every day life and recover from the unexpected. State Farm and its affiliates are the largest providers of auto, home, and life insurance in the United States. It's 18 thousand agents and more than 65 thousand employees serve more than 83 million policies and accounts, with over 45 million auto polices, over 4 million here in California. Automated and connected vehicle technologies have the potential to significantly impact the manner in which insurance serves to protect individuals, families, and businesses from financial loss. In discussing the deployment and adoption of these technologies, we believe that property and casualty insurance industry Is a critical stakeholder in a conversation to consider a number of potential issues. Such as coverage and liability matters and the impact of automated technology to the general public. So as the nation's largest automobile and home insurer and an innovator in the field of automation and transportation. State Farm very much appreciates the opportunity to provide testimony to this insurance Committee on autonomous vehicles and auto insurance in California. In order to advance our understanding of the role of automation and transportation, State Farm has participated in a number of research opportunities around the country. State firm is a founding partner of the University of Michigan's mobility transformation center. Is a key partner in Stanford universities,center for automotive research. And most recently was appointed to the US Department of transportations,advisory Committee on automation and transportation that only ensured to be appointed to that advisory group. State Farm is also an active participant, at the federal and state level, in reviewing and commenting on proposed automated vehicle legislation, regulation, and guidance. State Farm also recently worked with Bloomburg Government to conduct research on the publics perception of automated vehicles. The timing for movement to the SAE level 4 and 5 environments is of obvious interest to the insurance industry. With many of the major manufacturers publicly promising the availability of level four technology by 2018, and a few manufacturers working toward level five by 2020. Historical experiences with other technological advancements such as airbags, automatic transmissions and navigation systems suggest that the time from availability to market saturation can be anywhere from 25 to 50 years. What sets this issue apart from others is the unusual collaboration that has occurred between competitors as well as the cross functional partnerships. Manufacturers are working together, seeking input from educators and others, and preparing for alternative adoptions the technology. For example a ride sharing fleet vs private ownership. One of the key issues for the insurance industry as it relates to automotive vehicles is data access. Data access is essential to developing proper pricing and underwriting of vehicles, critical for liability determinations. And, from the general public's perspective, important in determining the safety and reliability of the technology. In looking at data access, an existing corollary is what exists in current vehicles with their event data recorders. The ability to access data from EDRs is essential in helping insurers make liability determinations. Also of importance when discussing data, and looking to EDR scenarios for context, is that access to data does not default infringe on the proprietary nature of the data. In the contexts of underwriting in liability situations, the key is access to data, to certain data, that is relevant to those issues as opposed to wholesale collection of all data associated with the vehicle. For SAE level zero through three, there will likely be a continued reliance on the existing auto insurance products in existing liability systems. The question of the value of existing insurance products occurs in the SC level four to five range, when it is probable that the operating system is at fault. There will likely be considerable issues during the transition phase as instance occur between vehicles across the spectrum of all those levels. Due to costs associated with automated vehicles, there will possibly be increased repair and replacement costs, which may lead to reevaluating how insurers determine pricing associated with physical damage coverage. In addition, as new vehicles increasingly go into the SC levels four through five range. There will potentially be a reevaluation of coverage exclusions related to audio, visual, and electronic equipment as no policy on the market was drafted to cover those risks. Cybersecurity issues are also at play when surveying the liability landscape. There is growing concern about the ability for someone to hack in to automated vehicle operating systems, which could in term lead to auto accidents. To further complicate matters there are increasing risk associated with hacking by foreign countries. In such situations, we'll increase the complexity of under riding and adjusting cyber insurance products. Within this space however, there may be opportunities for new product developments. The move toward autonomous vehicles will have other impacts on the insurance industry, ranging from the need for a different skill set for its employees, new risk management considerations, and the development of new products and coverages. The changing liability landscape, where methods such as victim recovery funds, and no fault insurance models. Will also increasingly gain interest in public policy debates, and also could have a significant interest on the insurance industry. In the Fall of 2016 the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration or NHTSA. Issued its federal automated vehicle policy. It is important to note that the policy is guidance and not law. It was purposely crafted as such in order to provide the agency the flexibility to address rapidly changing technology without being burdened by the normal procedural issues associated with rule making. Also of note is that when NHTSA crafted the policy, it worked directly with a number of manufacturers and suppliers, but did not include the insurance industry in its initial discussion of the guidance. In its vehicle performance guidance section, NHTSA outlines 15 areas that any developer of an autonomous vehicle needs to address. These factors include data recording, sharing, privacy, system safety, cyber security, ethical considerations Minimal risk conditions and validation methods among others. For purposes of data recording, NIST states, manufacturers and other entities, should have a document process for testing, validation and collection of event, incident and crashed data for the purposes of recording the currencies and malfunction, degradations or failures in a way that can be used to establish the cause of any such issues. This data should be maintained and be available for retrieval by the entity developing the highly automated vehicle and also NHTSA. Of note is that NHTSA does not extend the ability to retrieve the data to any other agency at the federal or state level. In addition, the Department of Transportation recommends that manufacturers and other entities collect data associated with events involving fatalities, and damages to the extent that the vehicle can no longer be driven under its own power in a customary manner. It does not recommend the collection or retention of data associated with incidents outside of those two scenarios. For model state policy NITSA urges the states to focus on sufficient consistency of laws and policies with the goal of avoiding a patch work of inconsistent state laws. NITSA expects the states however to continue to retain control over the regulation of auto insurance liability issue. However, NITSA recommends creating a Commission on liability and insurance issues in order to make recommendations to the states. In commenting on NITSA's policy, the insurance industry has focused on the importance of data access, safety assurances, cybersecurity issues, and the continued need to explore insurance and liability issues. The data access issue in particular has been a focal point of insurance industry concern, as such information is vital to determining whether the technology is safe. How to underwrite and rate insurance products, and how to determine liability. These same concerns also apply at the state level as more states such as California start to incorporate NITSA's policy into their state laws. In addition to the Federal Automated Vehicle Policy, NITSA has also issued cyber security best practices in a proposed rule mandating vehicle to vehicle technology, or connected cars. All these actions implicate insurance whether it relates to the need for new products or determining liability issues. From A states perspective, since 2012 almost every state has considered or is considering an acting automated vehicle legislation. Initially as in California, such legislation focused on testing. Then last year starting in Michigan, there have been a number of comprehensive bills attempting to open the roads to all forms of automated vehicle use. A particular concern with these bills has been an increasing tendency to carve out liability exemptions for manufacturers in certain situations where a modification is made to the vehicle's operating system resulting in a safety-related defect. These type of exemptions, like seen in the Michigan bill, do not define what a modification is nor pay proper attention to the current work being done on cyber security issues at the NITSA or Society of Automotive Engineers' levels. It's also important to note how international law is addressing automatic vehicles. Germany is considering laws limiting recovery and accidents but also making data readily accessible to interested parties. The United Kingdom is considering a single-insurer model where an insurer covers both the driver's use of the vehicle and automated vehicle technology. An examination of all these developments show that the automated vehicle public policy issues are rapidly developing and increasingly complex. In conclusion, State Farm appreciates the opportunity to provide testimony on autonomous vehicles and insurance in California. The insurance industry's input on these issues is critical. And we look forward to continuing to be a part of the discussion and solution for protecting insurance consumers in the autonomous space. Thank you.

Rex Frazier: Mr. Chair and members, thank you for the opportunity to testify before you today. I'm obviously fighting a cold, so I'm sorry about that. My name's Rex Frazier. I'm the President of the Personal Insurance Federation of California. We represent seven of the nation's largest property casualty insurance companies that collectively write over half of the insurance premium on the personalized basis in California. And the membership has a long history of advocating for legal changes that improve safety on our roads and save lives. We strongly believe that autonomous vehicles have the potential to further both of these objectives but there are also many issues to consider. While Mr. Gammelgard from State Farm outlined the national perspective. I'd like to focus on California and offer three questions for the Committee to consider as we move forward with this conversation. First, how can the insurance industry recognize and encourage the safety benefits which autonomous vehicles have the potential to deliver for Californians? Second, what type of autonomous vehicle generated data is appropriate for insurers to access? And then lastly, what is an appropriate process for policy makers, the public and the industry to consider following today's meeting. So the first question, how can the insurance industry recognize and encourage the safety benefits which autonomous vehicles may provide. One of the biggest issues facing the insurance industry when it comes to autonomous vehicles is how do we properly insure them under our current legal framework California's laws are much more complicated than other states with much less flexibility and room for innovation. The current rules were conceived in a very different world 25 years ago and as noted by the Department of Insurance testimony they require auto insurance to use three driver centric factors. And to give them more rate impact than the other 16 optional factors which the insurance commissioners over time have permitted. The driver centric factors that are mandatory ,a driver safety record at the DMV, the number of miles driven annually, and the years of driving experience. And as one can immediately see, the most heavily weighted characteristics make no mention of the type of vehicle driven or, its safety features. For that, there are a few other rating factors, which the Commissioner has permitted carriers to use over time. The type of vehicle, for instance, is a rating factor, vehicle performance capabilities is another rating factor, and vehicle characteristics, which the rules indicate include safety and protective devices. While these latter rating factors could pick up the enhanced capabilities of autonomous vehicles. The current rules prohibit these vehicle factors from having a higher impact than the three mandatory driver-centric factors, which I mentioned earlier. So certainly a conversation has started within the insurance industry about how to recognize and encourage the safety benefits of autonomous vehicles when the current rules focus on the driver and not vehicle capabilities. So, imagine at level four or five of autonomy, the vehicles may not even have a steering wheel or pedals, but auto insurance rates will be based on factors such as the drivers DMV record, or their years of driving experience. Emphasizing these rating factors makes little sense when an autonomous vehicle is transporting a passenger who is reading or doing some other activity and not even looking at the road. At this point we certainly don't have the answers about how to proceed. But we know that at some point the current insurance rules will prevent insurers from providing the full amount of discounts which are justifiable for advanced vehicle technology. It's a public policy question for this body as to whether that State of affairs will be acceptable. But it's important to at least question whether insurers should be permitted at some point in the future to fully recognize and encourage in their auto insurance rates, the safety benefits which autonomous vehicles almost certainly will provide. The second question we're considering is what type of autonomous vehicle generated data is appropriate for insurers to access. The data created through the operation of self driving cars continues to be one of the most widely debated topics in this discussion. And the rapidly changing and innovative advancements that occur in this field only further complicate the issue. We believe access to the data is a critical component for all stakeholders, including car owners, manufacturers, law enforcement, and insurers. New rules should provide clear guidelines on the need for third parties to have reasonable access to autonomous vehicle data for legitimate purposes. While simultaneously respecting the privacy expectations of car owners and the economic secrets of manufacturers and component makers. For instance, at level three of autonomous operation, where a driver will control the vehicle part but not all of the time, we will certainly see crashes where the driver is not even looking at the road. And may not even understand how the crash occurred. In such claim situations, obtaining access to the vehicle data will be critical so that insurers can assess their driver liability, and fulfill their promises to your constituents. As the technology of self-driving cars progress. We ask that laws and regulations remain flexible enough to ensure that insurers can properly and responsibly undertake their operations. The final question we ask policy makers to consider is what is an appropriate process for policy makers, the public and industry to consider these questions following today's hearing? The PIP membership is certainly committed to new and innovative technologies. Even though for them they present significant business challenges and uncertainties for the future. But despite these challenges, the potential public safety benefits of autonomous vehicles simply cannot be ignored. As these issues develop and take shape we would welcome further opportunities to comment and participate in the dialogue. And we encourage this Committee to continue its investigations. Without a continuing discussion which examines the issues on a systematic basis, we certainly will end up addressing issues on an ad hoc basis. Much as we're currently struggling to address the many complicated issues with drone use on a bill by bill basis. In closing, autonomous vehicles can and should be a promising and life saving technology. However they also pose considerable and unique challenges. I want to commend the Chairman in this Committee for taking a leadership role on this issue. By bringing impacted parties together to work through these complex issues surrounding autonomous vehicles, thank you.

So and then finally, I think the other thing is one thing that is unstated here, but nobody and nobody really talks about it is, are we sure that every American is going to want to give up, surrender the ability to drive their own car? I spent a lot of time looking at the Society of Automotive Engineer's discussion of the different levels of automation. If you look closely at this thing, even level five which is considered to be the ultimate autonomous, fully driverless vehicle. This level five says that there could be a situation where the driver may request control of the vehicle. That presumes at least these people are presuming that these vehicles will be built with some kind of functionality the help that allows the driver to control the vehicle. Next thing, the other myth that I wanted to talk about is the suggestion that machines are infallible and that the safety that we can just kind of assume without any argument that these things will be perfectly safe, so that we won't even need insurance anymore, for example. Now take a look at a couple of the recent devastating airplane accidents that have occurred, exactly because of too much reliance on automation and these have been major crashes that caused many fatalities. It's obvious that machines are not infallible. Now let's look at the risks in the short term that are going to that consumers and insurance companies and manufacturers will confront in some of them have been mentioned, hacking. Both at the criminal level and potentially even at the level as the FBI has suggested a terrorist attempts to take over large numbers of vehicles. Software, this is something that none of us have really contended with and the companies, the software companies such as Google that are at the lead in programming these vehicles are going to be their engineers are going to be programming into these computers a substitute for the moral values and practical judgement of motorists and we don't know what rules they're going to use. But they're going to have to make a premeditated decision that when a car is faced with an unavoidable collision, it mean they're going to hit pedestrians or people in other cars or perhaps even the mom pushing the baby in the stroller on the sidewalk. That is a huge risk that nobody has really thought through and we don't know what the companies are doing when they're programming their computers this way. So what do these two myths or the explosion of these two myths mean for what I would call the personal responsibility system, which is what the Committee is discussing today? And that system is composed of a set of tort and insurance laws that have been around in the case of the civil justice system for hundreds of years that protect consumers against dangerous products, that protect consumers for the last 28 years against unfair and excessive insurance premiums and unfair underwriting practices. What the personal responsibility system that we have in California tells us is that people are going to be still at fault. Motorists are going to be still responsible for the actions that they take with respect to their vehicles. Let's start briefly with the Civil Justice System, I won't take that too much time, but the Civil Justice System is the technique is the set of tools that our nation uses to expose wrong doing. Determine responsibility. Make the wrongdoer pay for an accident. Pay to compensate for the harm done to victims and to force people to behave better, including manufacturers that may or may not produce a safe vehicle. And in the case of autonomous vehicles, because of manufacturers will bare some responsibility, they will be held accountable under the rules of strict liability. The question is will the manufacturers not contest liability? Nothing we've heard, nothing anybody has said, except with the CAVEAT of a Remarks by Volvo. Nobody has signed on the dotted line that if you buy one of our self-driving vehicles, we will cover you completely. For all of the harm that happens regardless of whether you, the motorist had something to do with it as opposed to us, the vehicle manufacturer. And until that happens and I would submit to you that it would never happen, that manufacturers will never agree to fully accept all responsibility without being able to contest it or blame the motorist or the owner that we have a personal responsibility system based on liability protections. As for Proposition 103, so long as consumers face liability, face the possibility that they're going to be blamed in some way for what their vehicle did whether it's a robot car or not. Consumers in California are still going to need Proposition 103 protections. Now I know the insurance industry hates Proposition 103 and they spent a fortune in 1988 trying to defeat it and they're constantly fighting it in the courts, and they've been up here a few times asking members of the Legislature to bail them out of something that voters passed. But the fact is that even in a driverless environment as long as motorists are responsible for anything Including, by the way, just having their vehicle in their driveway and making sure that they didn't ding one of those sensors. because if they ding a sensor, the results could be catastrophic. It's clear that motorists will have at least that responsibility to maintain their self-driving vehicle. As long as they have that responsibility and they face blame if they don't exercise that responsibility, they're going to need that system that protects them, that bases their premiums primarily upon factors within their own control such as what they do with their car? How they operate their car? How many miles they drive every year? How much experience they've had driving? Senator Newman, you raised a question about ZIP code, I believe. There's no problem with getting access to data about under Prop 103, about ZIP codes. That data is available, in fact, the Department of Insurance publishes quite a bit of data. But what Proposition 103 does not allow, what the voters got rid of when they passed Proposition 103 is the notoriously, the infamous practice of basing people's premiums primarily upon the ZIP code in which they lived rather than their driving record, because that was a form of pernicious redlining that discriminated against people that the insurance companies didn't want to sell to. So the system that the voters substituted is much fairer than a system that would be based on the location of your vehicle, the voters got rid of that system. You could still factor in the frequency and severity and there are ways that Proposition 103 through the optional factors permit some consideration of territory. But as the principal factor, it's been banned. So the second issue will be, well, how much will these cars cost? Nobody knows. Will they be more expensive to repair? Most people think yes. In those situations, will the insurance companies attempt to come in and say, we need to drastically raise our premiums? Because we're now insuring all of those greater risks. The answer is yes, they will come in and do that. But luckily here in California, a system that has already saved motorists $100 billion since it was passed in 1988. Makes sure that when they come in and request those rates, they are not approved, unless the insurance companies open their books and justify them. That's the critical savings of Proposition 103. That is what is responsible for the Consumer Federation of America's determination that California was the only state in the nation where the average auto insurance premium went down between the passage of Prop 103 in 1988 and 2010. Rates, average premiums were lower in California in 2010 than they were in 1988. And it's the Proposition 103 system that protects voters and consumers and motors and will even under the product liability rules, protect manufacturers and small businesses and purchasers to make sure that rates are fair. I want to conclude by saying, we've heard a little bit from the representative of the insurance lobby here in Sacramento about how we need to change Proposition 103 and there was a reference earlier to no fault insurance. The both of us here and the organizations that we represent over the last 30 years have really contended with the arguments brought by wrong doers, and the insurance industry that we have to restrict people's rights whether there is the right to go to court or the rights under Proposition 103. The voters rejected no fault at the ballot box twice. Once in 1988, once in 1996. The discussion here by the insurance industry with all due respect to them, really should be about loss prevention. The insurance companies are a cost plus system of insurance. They like to pass through the claims costs plus a little markup for their profit and overhead. So they don't have a huge incentive to crack down on accidents, to limit claims, because that reduces their revenue. Yet, now really is a perfect moment. I started to hear the gentleman from State Farm step up to this moment. Now this the moment for the insurance industry to focus its amazing resources and database on accidents to impress manufacturers to build safer autonomous technologies, and to advocate for stronger federal regulation of auto safety. Because you may not all realize this, but the NHTSA or the National Highway Transportation Safety Administration has recently done an about-face and now they are saying that they're going to let the auto industry regulate themselves. And in an era where the industry is evolving so rapidly and there are so many risks that are brand new to driverless vehicles, that is going in the wrong direction and the insurance industry should step up and insist that NHTSA do its job. Thank you.

Maritza Urquiza: Good morning, Maritza Urquiza with the Department of Finance. I will begin with a broad overview of the Governor's Budget for a higher education and highlight the new spending proposals for the community colleges, and my colleague will provide an overview of the Governor's Budget for the universities. Each year when we build the budgets, we begin by building in funding for community colleges based upon revised Proposition 98 guarantee. For the universities we build in the existing level of resources as well as growth pursuant to the administration's multi-year plan. Funding for the CalGrant program is then based on estimated participation pursuant to existing policies. Despite budget constraints due to lower than anticipated revenues, the Governor's Budget continues to increase funding for higher education. The budget proposal's total funding of 31.9 billion for higher education made up of 17.5 billion general fund and local property tax, and 14.4 billion of other funds. This total reflects both direct funding to colleges and the universities and the costs of financial aid that students may use at eligible institutions. The Governor's Budget continues the steady investments that the state has made since the passage of Proposition 30 in 2012. With the increases the administration proposes in 17, 18, funding for the University of California will have grown by 817.8 million since 2012. Funding for the California State University will have grown by about 1.1 billion. And Proposition 98 funding for the community colleges will have grown a total of 1.8 billion. The administration supports continued investment in higher education with the expectation that colleges and universities will work together and implement new and creative policies that consider the cost of instruction, better support student success and completion and expand access to higher education to more California students. The proposed investments in the Governor's Budget are also grounded in three efforts. First, to maintain affordability, second, to support success for all students including reducing the time it takes students to complete degrees, and third, to encourage greater alignment across entities to support students' transition from K-12 to higher education and into the workforce. These guiding principles are reflected in the Governor's Budget for the universities and for the community colleges. The Governor's Budget includes $8.8 billion in funding for community colleges and adult education when accounting for available Proposition 98 general fund, local revenues and fees. This funding supports apportionments and numerous student success programs including the student success and support program, the extended opportunity programs and services, and the disabled student programs and services. To further support student success, the Governor's Budget proposes several new investments for the community colleges. First, the budget includes a 150 million one-time Proposition 98 General Fund to support community colleges' effort to develop and implement guided pathways programs. A guided pathway program is an integrated institution-wide approach focused on improving student success. This one time investment will provide grants to community colleges to redesign academic pathways and organize student choices in a way that promotes better course taking decisions, and better integrate support services to make it easier for students to access the support that they need. The expectation is to improve completion rates, reduce time to degree, increase students' employment opportunities, and reduce student debt. The budget also includes ongoing increases of 94.1 million Proposition 98 general fund, reflecting a 1.48 cost of living adjustment, 23.6 million to support community colleges operating expenses, and 79.3 million to support a 1.34% enrollment growth, which would provide access to approximately an additional 11,500 full time equivalent students. To incent the development and implementation of innovative practices, the budget includes 20 million one-time Proposition 98 general fund to provide innovation grants to community colleges. This program will be administered by the community colleges' chancellor's office. Finally, the budget includes an increase of 10 million Proposition 98 general fund to provide system-wide access to the online education initiatives learning management system. And an increase of 6 million one-time Proposition 98 general fund to facilitate the development of an integrated library system for the community colleges. With that, I'll pass it on to my colleague.
