Christian Osmena: Thank you very much. Christian Osmena with Finance. I'll begin with the universities, and as Ms. Urquiza described, the Governor's Budget continues a multi-year funding plan for the UC and the CSU. The stability that comes with that plan has been a core component of the administration's approach to budgeting and higher education since the passage of Proposition 30. Our intent has been that predictable growth can allow the universities to engage in longer-range planning to manage costs within levels of resources that are sustainable for the state and for students. Specifically, general fund appropriations to the California State University are $3.3 billion in 16-17, the current year. The CSU reports enrolling about 400,000 students at its 23 campuses, with another 22,000 students seeking degrees and other credentials through continuing education. The budget proposes an additional $162 million general fund for the University. The 2016 budget called on the CSU to increase four year graduation rates and two year transfer graduation rates with specific emphasis on closing achievement gaps for low income students, first generation students, and students from underrepresented minority groups. The CSU graduation initiative 2025 adopted by the Board of Trustees in September commits the University to ambitious graduation goals, increasing the four year rate to at least 40%, increasing the transfer rate to at least 45%, and closing gaps and outcomes between the targeted students and their peers. Notably, in the current year, the state provided $35 million in one-time funding to jump-start those efforts, assisting campuses and making immediate changes, and helping to relieve some cost pressures over a longer term period. The budget highlights an existing structure, that is the methods used to place students in college-level courses, that warrants additional review. The budget argues that the graduation initiative can only be successful if education leaders across the system are clear about what a CSU education entails both upon entry and at graduation. More than 40% of CSU freshmen today are still identified as unprepared for college over courses based on their performances on a sequence of tests. Evidence from other contexts including California's community colleges suggests that many of these students actually are prepared for those college courses and that other measures like high school grades are better indicators of that preparation. There are notable opportunities for reform. As one example, a task force of the CSU Academic Senate released a set of recommendations that would define student proficiency before their entry at the CSU and at graduation. We'd be happy to discuss these issues further as the budget progresses. For the University of California, general fund appropriations are 3.5 billion in 2016-17. The 10 UC campuses enroll about 265,000 students with thousands more connected to its extension programs. The budget proposes an additional $131 million general fund for the University, which amounts to a 4% increase. The budget also includes $169 million general fund on a one-time basis as part of the agreement that funds some of the unfunded liabilities of the UC retirement plan, if the plan is structured consistent with one of the state's pension reforms. The administration continues to monitor progress on an agreement between the Governor and the UC President, aimed at making the UC's cost structure more sustainable. Their framework, which was also adopted by the Board of Regents, recognizes that lowering the cost structure, while maintaining quality, requires the University to reevaluate how students' prior academic experiences are recognized as part of UC degree programs, how academic programs are structured, and how instruction is delivered. The University has demonstrated progress in all of the areas of the agreement, but the work is still underway. I'll note two specific reforms that we are monitoring closely. First, the UC has begun pilots at three campus, Davis, Merced, and Riverside, on activity-based costing, something we've talked about in this Committee before. But it's a method of calculating the amount spent on individual courses based on the way those courses are delivered. These calculations would allow University leaders to better plan enrollment and determine which and how courses should be offered by understanding cost coupled with student outcomes. Second, the UC has made significant progress in improving access for students transferring from the community colleges and those students' experiences when they arrive at the UC. The agreement expects the UC to increase the number of transfer students its campuses enrolls so that by the upcoming academic year at least one new transfer student is enrolled for every two new freshmen. These reforms are important to the administration because their implementation would demonstrate the University's commitment to using resources in a cost-effective way and to aligning its own efforts with the state's broader higher education goals. Both segments have now considered tuition increases for next year. The budget reiterates that any tuition increases must be made only in the context of reducing the overall cost structure at UC and improving the graduation rates with the CSU. Tuition increases without these improvements would only burden families with the costs of an inefficient system. Any increases would also have impacts on the state budget, specifically the increases the governing boards have considered would grow Cal Grant costs for UC students by $18 million and for CSU students by $25 million in 17, 18, beyond those costs already reflected in the Governor's Budget. Finally, there are several additional issues related to financial aid that I know are of interest to members. We understand that these issues will be the subject of a future hearing, so we'll plan to present details then, but I'd quickly note that spending on financial aid is an important component of the administration's broader approach to higher education finance. The Cal Grant program, the state's primary financial aid program, is an entitlement for students who meet eligibility criteria, and students who do not qualify for the entitlement are able to compete for additional grants. Since 12/13 funding for the Cal Grant funding will have grown by $442 million, a 29% increase. In total, the budget includes $2 billion to award financial aid to about 382,000 students. With that I'll close, and we'd be happy to answer any questions.

Greg Oliva: Good afternoon Mr. Chair, members, and staff. Greg Oliva, assistant deputy directory, Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion. The writeup is excellent. I'll just take a little time in doing a high level discussion of the Prop 56, and the implications for the Department of Public Health. So on November 8, 2016, Californians passed the California Health Care Research and Prevention Tobacco Tax Act of 2016. And what it will do is raise the cigarette excise tax by $2, effective April 1st, 2017. And a commensurate tax on other tobacco products, such as smokeless, pipe tobacco, cigars, and also e-cigarettes. And those determinations will be determined by the Board of Equalization. So in the BCP, the Governor's Budget requests an increase of 57 positions and $223.5 million to help support the implementation of the three separate components that the department would be administering. So the first would be the Tobacco Prevention and Control programs that count, and that request is for 26 positions on $178.5 million. And that's to support prevention and reduction efforts using media, local programs, evaluation, and also some level of state administration. The second component is the tobacco law enforcement account and that request is for 20 positions and $7.5 million to increase Stop Tobacco access to kids enforcement, compliance checks, and to establish a local grant program that we would administer with local law enforcement to address tobacco enforcement activities. The final piece is the state dental program account, which the request is for 11 positions and $37.5 million. And that is to create a comprehensive public health infrastructure to support oral health education, prevention, surveillance and treatment activities. So just a little bit more about these three components. Two would be very mature efforts that already exist within the department. The first being our state's tobacco control program. So this program began as a result of the Tobacco Tax and Health Protection Act of 1988, which we call Prop 99. And we've been implementing this program for roughly 25 years. What Prop 56 would do is provide a lot more additional resources to do the same sorts of things that were required within Prop 99. So we would continue to do a media campaign, to conduct evaluation, to fund the local health departments, to fund a competitive grants program. And we think some reasonable resources to administer those separate programs. There's one difference between Prop 99 and Prop 56. And that is, which was identified in your write-up, is that Prop 56 does require that not less than 15% of health promotion, health communication activities, and evaluation. And tobacco use surveillance funds being awarded to accelerate and monitor the rate of decline in tobacco-related disparities with the goal of eliminating tobacco-related disparities. I'm confident to say that with our current appropriations from Prop 99, we're meeting that 15%. Most of our local, actually all of our local competitive grant awards are going to address health equity and tobacco control. And I'm confident with the Prop 56 resources we would meet that 15% very easily, it's a very important issue for us. So that's a very mature effort within the department. The other really mature effort in the department is our tobacco enforcement efforts. So, what Prop 56 will do is allow for more investigators to do more compliance checks. And also what is new for that is to issue some local grants to law enforcement to conduct their own activities at the local level, that's new for us. What's not a mature program is the oral health side. And that is, to date, it's our oral health efforts are primarily made up of relatively small categorical, federally funded programs, currently focusing on perinatal oral health, the virtual dental home, and water fluoridation. So, these funds will allow us to actually establish a comprehensive statewide program that we hope can be delivered to all counties within the state, so that's my overview.

[{'start': 4, 'end': 16, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Emma Jung-worth: Good afternoon everyone, I'm Emma Jung-worth, Department of Finance. So I'm here today to provide a brief overview of the State Penalty Fund proposal. The State Penalty fund was created as a depository for assessments on specified fines, penalties and forfeitures imposed and collected by the courts and counties for criminal offenses. State Penalty Fund revenues have decreased significantly over the past several years due largely to a decrease in traffic citations. Given that this decrease in revenue is projected to continue, the State Penalty Fund can no longer support all of the programs that receive this funding. In addition, the cost of these programs have increased. However, the statutory formula has not been updated to account for these increased costs. As a result, many funds currently have structural deficits and some have receive funding backfills to provide temporarily solvency. To recognize a decline in State Penalty Fund revenues, the budget proposes to amend the current process by which the state portion of the assessment is distributed and instead provide direct appropriations and transfers from the State Penalty Fund to the various programs. To ensure program expenditures remain within existing revenues, the budget proposes to reduce the number of programs supported by the fund. The existing programs were evaluated and funding from the State Penalty Fund was prioritized for law enforcement training, victims services programs, and driver training programs. With that, I'd be happy to answer any questions about the general State Penalty Fund proposal. We do understand that there will be additional hearings to discuss the specifics of program implementation. But again I'd be happy to answer any general questions about the proposal.

This table should look familiar to you as you saw it at our hearing two weeks ago. If you turn to page two of your handout, one of the numerous statutory distribution formulas requires that 70% of any payments that are used to address the state penalty assessment obligation be deposited into the State Penalty Fund, or SPF, with the remaining 30% going to county general funds. The flow chart in front of you then shows that additional state law requires that the state penalty revenues be redistributed to nine other state funds, to support 16 programs. The revenue that was deposited in the SPF peaked in 2008-9 at $170 million and has declined steadily since. If you turn to page 3 of your handout, I'm not going to going to go into detail, but we did provide an overview of each of the programs for your reference. If you turn to page four of your handout, we provide a table to summarize what expenditures would be for these programs under existing law absent any changes. If you look at the first three columns of the table, that shows 2016 -17 expenditures. Total expenditures are estimated to be 306 million with 97 million coming from the SPF and 209 million coming from other funds. This does include 24 million that was provided on a one time basis in 16-17 to address a decline in SPF revenue. The next three columns show 2017-18 expenditures. And so we estimate that 265 million in total expenditures would occur, with 90.4 coming from the SPF and 174 million coming from other funds. If you look at the last column in that table, you can see that it's a total decline of about $41 million from the 16-17 level and that the reductions are generally clustered around a few programs. If you turn to page 5 of your handout, we provide the same table then for the Governor's alternative expenditure plan. And the administration has discussed, they're eliminating the SPF formulas and allocating strictly to programs. And so, if you look in the 17-18 columns, you see that total expenditures are expected to be $269 million and that does include elimination of SPF support for four programs. Looking at the farthest column on the right, we see that this will be a decline of 36 million from 16-17 expenditure levels. We also see, in this column, that the reductions are generally distributed across many more programs and that programs that are deemed to be priorities by the Governor, such as training for state and local law enforcement, would receive smaller reductions than they otherwise would have under current law. If you turn to page 6 of your handout, we offer our assessment. So first, one of the key problems that we had previously identified with the state's existing fine and fee system is that the various statutory formulas made it really difficult for the Legislature to control the use of this type of revenue. The Governor's proposal to eliminate the SPF formulas will increase the Legislature's flexibility to reprioritize those revenues. However, because the administration doesn't specify how the reduction should be implemented, the potential impact on programs is unknown. Second, the amount of criminal fine and fee revenue that is deposited into the SPF can fluctuate from year to year. The administration's proposal does not include a plan for how to allocate additional reductions if SPF revenues in 17-18 are less than expected. Under existing law, the statutory formulas would have been responsible for allocating those additional reductions. And then, third, it is likely that the Legislature will likely have different priorities than the administration. The Legislature may want to eliminate different programs or provide a different expenditure level of reductions to programs or may want to direct programs to address the reductions in a particular manner to ensure that's consistent with legislative priorities. So if you turn to page 7 of your handout, the final page of your handout, in light of these concerns, we offer two alternative sets of recommendations. The first alternative is if the Legislature wants to focus specifically on the SPF. Under that scenario, we would recommend that the Legislature take three actions. One, modify the proposal to reflect its spending priorities. Two, to direct programs to take specific actions in implementing the reductions. And three, specify a plan to the extent that 2017-18 SPF revenues are less than expected. And to help the Legislature do that, we recommend that the Legislature direct each department to report in budget hearings on how it would implement those reductions. What impact those activities would have on programmatic operations, and then finally, whether or not there are additional funding sources that could be leveraged and used. Our second recommendation is if the Legislature chooses to take a broader approach to changing the overall distribution of criminal fine and fee revenue. We continue to think that this broader approach, namely removing nearly all statutory formulas, is preferable as it would maximize the state's ability to control use over this type of revenue. So as we mentioned two weeks ago, we do continue to recommend depositing nearly all criminal fine and fee revenue into the state general fund for subsequent appropriation by the Legislature. This would help ensure that funding was provided to programs based on workload need and legislative priorities, that programs are no longer disproportionately impacted by declines in criminal fine and fee revenue. And finally, it would eliminate the need for the Legislature to continuously identify and implement short term solutions to address structural shortfalls, or fund insolvencies, that are faced by other state funds, due to declines in criminal fine and fee revenue. So with that, we're happy to answer any questions.

[{'start': 4, 'end': 17, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Sarah Brooks: Hi. Good afternoon, Sarah Brooks, Deputy Director of Department of Health Care Services and appreciate the time to talk with you today. Excuse me. The Coordinated Care Initiative, which includes Cal MediConnect is focused on helping improve the lives of low income seniors and persons with disabilities in California. There are approximately 115,000 enrollees in Cal MediConnect today across seven counties, and hundreds of thousands additional beneficiaries who receive care through our Medi-Cal Managed Care Plans with respect to LTSS services. Early evaluation efforts show that Cal MediConnect is working. Participants report high satisfaction levels and are experiencing fewer hospitalizations and institutionalizations. The CCI itself consists of three different components. It integrates Medicare and medical services into one plan for beneficiaries who are eligible for both, otherwise known as Cal MediConnect. It integrates Medi-Cal funded long-term services and supports into managed care and requires mandatory enrollment for most other dual eligibles into Medi-Cal Managed Care. The implementing statute for CCI contained a provision requiring the Department of Finance, to determine if the entirety of CCI is cost-effective each January, and if not the entire program would be discontinued the following year. The Governor's proposed budget did estimate that CCI will not be cost-effective thereby triggering the poison pill, and ceasing CCI. Although CCI was found to not be cost-effective in it's entirety, the Duals Demonstration Program has shown the potential to improve the care and quality for those enrolled and help to keep individuals in their homes and community, thereby leading to likely long-term cost reductions and avoidance. The proposed trailer bill reflects this, striking a language authorizing CCI and replacing it with amended language that authorizes Cal MediConnect, MLTSS and Duals Demonstration, to continue with some modification. The administration proposes two key prorammatic modifications to the current programmatic structure. Those include the elimination of IHSS as a plan benefit, though beneficiaries will continue to receive those services as they did prior to CCI through fever service, and the delay of two years to January 2020 of the MSSP transition of the waiver to Medi-Cal Manage Care as a benefit as well. The DHCS will continue to work closely with our plans, our stakeholders, our advocates, as we continue to evolve and work to strengthen the program. You asked a couple of questions about passive enrollment. So, the Committee, our passive enrollment does continue to be a potential option to ensure sustainable enrollment in Cal MediConnect. We don't have a proposal on the table for Cal MediConnect today. Advocates themselves have preferred a voluntary enrollment strategy prior to passive enrollment. In 2016 we did work significantly with advocates to come up with a volunteer strategy and we continue to place our efforts today Into that strategy and move that forward. With respect to the recommendations of stakeholders, DHCS is committed to working with stakeholders on an ongoing basis as we continue to strengthen the CCI. The department does agree that continued coordination across systems of care is key, and we've taken a number of steps to strengthen both care coordination and referrals to long-term services and supports for this reason, including increased data reporting by health plans, as well as convening a work group with stakeholders on health risk assessments, which looks at standardizing questions across MLTSS and Cal MediConnect health plans. That will allow for better determinations when looking at care plans, in terms of overall care goals and needs. The plans and counties are still encouraged to collaborate on care and coordination and this is reflected in the revised trailer bill language proposed by the administration. Authorizing health plans and counties to continue sharing data and allowing beneficiaries to include both their IHHS providers and county social workers on their inter-disciplinary care team. And so with that I'm happy to answer any questions.

[{'start': 0, 'end': 14, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 79, 'end': 91, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 133, 'end': 142, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Amanda Mattson: Thank you, Chairman Salas for inviting me to testify today. My name is Amanda Mattson, I'm a Deputy Legislative Council at the Office of Legislative Council and I'm here to briefly go over the State of existing law with the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act and how it interacts with the licensing acts under the business and professions code. Under the general corporation law in California, any person is legally authorized to form a corporation for any legal purpose, unless otherwise prohibited. One such prohibition on this is what has been known at the common law as the Learned profession doctrine. This doctrine was created basically and it said, a certain learned professions and then beginning it was lawyers, doctors, and dentists and then the 80s optometrist were added as well are not authorized to practice in the corporate form in the state because that'll be against public policy. The courts were worried that due to the nature of these professions with the trust in the fiduciary type relationships they had with their clients and patients that it wouldn't be a good idea to have shareholders or the needs of the corporation basically being placed between the patient, and the practitioner of that profession. In 1968, the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act was enacted to statutorily authorize those professions that were prohibited from incorporating to incorporate at a professional corporation. the act itself did not authorize the existence of the corporations, but stated that if there is authorization in a licensing act of a profession, for a professional corporation to exist, then the provisions of the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation would apply. Those provisions generally deal with the origination and organization of a professional corporation. They specify who can and cannot be a shareholder of the corporation, who can. And cannot actually give professional services to the public, which employees can and cannot do these things. There are also statutory prohibitions on certain professions practicing in the corporate form and the licensing acts, and those prohibitions make these professions only be able to incorporate under the Professional Corporation Act. So in summary, the Moscone-Knox Act itself did not authorize or prohibit any profession or vocation to practice in a corporate form or not. It merely said if there's authorization in the licensing act for a professional corporation to exist then the provisions of the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act would apply. The act itself says that all other provisions of the general corporation act also apply unless there's conflict and this conflict is mostly seen in the provisions of who can and cannot be a shareholder, who can and cannot offer the professional services, and who can and cannot buy shares of the professional corporation. So in sum, under the General Incorporation Act, unless otherwise prohibited, whether a statutory prohibition, or a common law doctrine such as the Learned Profession Doctrine, a profession or vocation is authorized to form a corporation for any lawful purpose. If the licensing act authorizes the formation of a professional corporation. But does not expressly prohibit that profession from being able to only form in that way, that profession has the choices they can choose to form as a general corporation, or they have the option to choose to form as a professional corporation, and once they make that choice to form as a professional corporation, the provisions of the Moscone-Knox Act would then apply to that corporation. This is all I had to tell you today. If you have any questions please let me know.

Kimberly Kirchmeyer: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you Chairman Solace and members. My name is Kimberly Kirchmeyer and I am the Executive Director of the medical board of California. With me today is Carry Webb. Staff Counsel at the medical board. Thank you for asking the medical board to attend today's meeting and allowing us to provide the Committee with background information on the board's role with professional corporations. The medical board does not license any professional corporation and has a limited interaction with professional corporations. The board's main function is the licensure and registration of physicians and surgeons, and other allied health professionals. Including licensed midwives, research psychoanalysts, student research psychoanalysts, and Polysomnographic trainees, technicians and technologists. As you can see, this licensure and registration process involves sole individuals, not corporations. The board does approve accreditation agencies that accredit outpatient surgery settings, but the issue of being a corporation does not pertain to these entities. However pursuant to business and professions code section 2285, any physician who uses a name other than his or her own in any public communication, advertisement, sign, or announcement must hold a fictitious name permit. These fictitious name permits, or FNPs, can be obtained by a sole physician, a partnership or a corporation. Corporations applying for an FNP must comply with Corporations Code Section 13401.5. The corporation, this corporation section describes what types of corporations are allowed and who can be members of these corporations. For example, a medical corporation, in addition to a physician and surgeon, may have other members that are doctors of podiatric medicine, psychologists. Registered nurses, optometrists, marriage and family therapists, clinical social workers, physician assistants, chiropractors, acupuncturists, naturopathic doctors, professional clinical counselors, physical therapists or pharmacists. However, this code section also states that the sum of these shareholders cannot exceed 49%. Therefore, in a medical corporation, the physician shareholders must hold 51%. And the others can add up to 49%. The board requests a copy of the original articles of incorporation when a corporation applies for an FMP. These are reviewed to ensure they have an endorsement stamp and a corporation number. Staff also verifies information to ensure that the corporation has an active status via the Secretary of State's website. For the board's licencing unit this really is the interaction with corporations. The board's enforcement unit also may review articles of incorporation in additional corporation documents. Should the board get a complaint alleging a violation of the ban on the corporate practice of medicine. Or determined during an investigation that there be a violation on the ban on the corporate practice of medicine more information is then gathered. The board determines who the owner of the practice is by reviewing many documents, including the articles of Incorporation. The board may also review any management services agreement, and ownership documents. Should a violation of the ban on corporate practice be found, the board may take criminal or administrative action against the physician and laypersons involved. These are the areas where the medical board is involved with corporations. And Ms. Webb and I are here to answer any questions the Committee may have regarding the board's role with this issue.

Jessica Sieferman: Good morning, Chair Salas and Committee Members. My name is Jessica Sieferman, I'm the executive officer for the California State Board of Optometry. Since its inception in 1913, the board has been charged with protecting the health and safety of the public through its licensing, regulatory, and disciplinary functions. Today, the board regulates the largest population of optometrists and dispensers in the United States with roughly 12,000 active licensees and registrants. I thank you for the invitation and opportunity to participate in this hearing today. In your February 27th, 2017 letter, you requested hearing our organization's perspective on the role of regulating, both individual licensees and those professional corporation which are licensee owned, and are employed by corporations which are required to register with us or be licensed by our board. First I must state that the current board has neither discussed nor opined on the regulation of corporations and the impact on professional licensing, thus I cannot provide any formal perspective or opinion as it relates to this topic. If the Committee would like, I would be happy to add this as a topic of discussion for a future board meeting. Committee staff requested that I provided a brief history related to the board regulating corporations, insight as to why we stopped registering corporations, and the current role the board plays in professional corporations. From 1970 to 2007, Business and Professions Code 3160 through 3167 set forth registration and operation requirements for professional optometric corporations. Those corporations would need to register with the board by paying a $100 fee. And renew annually by paying $50 and submitting a renewal application. Optometric corporations were also regulated by the corporation code and still are. At that time, however, optometric corporations were the only healthcare corporations required to register with both the Secretary of State and the regulatory board. Under that structure, optometric corporations would apply with the Secretary of State's office. The Secretary of State's office would issue the registration and certify the articles of incorporation and by-laws. And then the optometric corporation would apply for a board registration and submit the articles of incorporation that the Secretary of State's office just verified. After a brief discussion in 2004, and more in-depth discussions in 2005, the Board believed existing requirements were duplicative and eliminating the registration for optometric corporations did not appear to pose any potential harm to the public. Rather, the Board believed removing the requirement would streamline government and improve services to the public. Omnibus Bill EB 2256, effective 2007, repealed the registration requirement, to ensure licensees were still held accountable, EB 2256 added Business and Professions Code 3111, which made any violation of the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporations Act on professional conduct, which is ground for disciplinary action. Post AB-2256, since 2007, the board has had minimal interactions with professional corporations. All the optimetric corporations practicing under a corporate name which were previously exempt from the FNP requirement are required to obtain an FNP from the board. As part of the application process, professional corporation provide a copy of the articles incorporation for preliminary compliance check with Business and Professions Code 3111 which looks at Moscone-Knox. Of those reviewed staff estimate, roughly 10 to 15% of the articles are incorrectly incorporated as general versus a professional corporation, and then applicant goes back to the Secretary of State's office to correct the articles and incorporation. Business and Professions Code section 3109 prohibits employment from any corporation or individual other than a licensed optometrist, a licensed ophthalmologist, or a healthcare service plan regulated by The Department of Managed Healthcare. Effective January 1, 2016, AB 684, a registered dispensing optician, which could be an individual, a corporation, or a firm may own a healthcare service plan if that healthcare service plan did not employ optometrists. AB 684, which moved the RDO program from the Medical Board of California to this board also allows a landlord tenant relationship between an RDO and an optometrist, provided specific additions are contained within a written agreement. In addition to other actions available to the board, Business and Professions Code 655, violations could result in administrative fine of up to $50,000, thank you.

No other state pays its workers on the last day of the pay period as California does. In fact California pays its workers five different ways. Monthly positive and negative, semi-monthly positive and negative, and bi-weekly. So right now, I am focused on two different elements on this front. First to say business process re-engineering effort. Secondly we have a pilot program that will do something I believe all of you have access to already here in the capital. And that is an employee self-service portal for everyone in state government. The first stage which I hope to make available later this year would let our own employees of the State Controller's Office view their pay stubs, their W2's, their leave balances, and their employment history in our existing legacy system. Stage two would give employees an edit function so they can change their mailing address or update their direct deposit account. Or alter the withholding on their W4. Once we have successfully tested the pilot within the state controller's office, my goal is to get your approval and likely, additional funding to roll the pilot out statewide. It is an initiative that I believe will save the state money immediately and in the long-run it will work with our existing system and whatever new payroll system is eventually deployed in the state. Ryan Miller: Ryan Miller, Legislative Analyst's Office, we have issued a couple of recommendations on this BCP. This is the second time you've reviewed the BCP, the first one came in 2014-15. And a substantial part of the work load associated with these security properties arise because of an 18 to 20 month waiting period in statute. A time that the State Controller's office is required to hold the properties before liquidating them into cash. Much of the workload, in our view, arises because of the waiting period and that's because, based on information we've received from the Controller's office, 99% of the properties have their corporate actions current, when they were made to the state. That is, that the mergers and other kinds of actions that make it difficult to liquidate the securities are current, and the state could sell them right away if we were to change the statute. Now some desire to keep the statute the way it is because there's value in being able to give the securities back to the owners in their current form. Some owners would prefer to get their securities back as a security rather than cash, of course. But the vast majority of people who do get their securities back in their security forms, get them back because of a different part of the program. Notices that we send them, that allow them to claim the properties before they even come to the state. Very few of them get them in their security form once they're with the state. So in other words, few owners are benefiting from the waiting period in our view and even of those that do get the securities in their original forms due to the waiting period, some are winners and some are losers. That is, some have their stocks increase in value while they're with the state, and others have stocks decrease in value while they're with the state. So because of the substantial workload that results from the waiting period and that few owners are benefiting from the waiting period, we recommend that the Legislature amend the statute to allow the controller's office to liquidate the securities immediately when they come to the state. Now, in cases where, say, an owner has initiated a claim process, has submitted a form and started that process, our recommendation will still allow the Controller's office to maintain them in security form for those owners. But we think that there would be a large workload savings that could either mean additional resources the Legislature commits to other purposes or could commit to other purposes within the unclaimed property program. And we think that that latter course actually could benefit more owners of unclaimed property than this BCP before you. So happy to answer other questions if you have them.

Greg Krotoll: Thank you, Mr. Chair and members. Greg Krotoll with the Department of Finance. So this language, we did bring the HDF on budget last year, part of trailer bill language. Part of the reason that we did that, it was kind of a two step approach. While we wanted to pursue combining all of the administrative expenses into one fund, we wanted to give CalPERS time to work through the technicals of combining the funds and that was ultimately our goal from day one. Moving forward, the reason we want to have one fund for all administrative expenses is currently, they're bifurcated between the CRF and HCF. Each one has a different cost recovery method. So the CRF is funded by an administrative rate that is assessed on all health plan premiums offered by CalPERS to state and locals. Whereas funding for the HCF is generated by a per-member, per-month fee that is built into the planned premiums for PPO and flex-funded plans. So utilizing a single cost-recovery method would simplify the process, and ensure that employers are not being charged twice for administrative costs. Also, this trailer bill language provides CalPERS with the flexibility to respond to changing employer needs to separate rates between the state and local agencies should the local agencies seek additional services that are above and beyond what the state is utilizing.

They can also use the consumers legal remedies act to bring actions if they are being harmed by a business as well. There's also, as you now know, the ability for DA's and attorney generals to utilize their power of pre-litigation subpoena under UCL actions. It would seem that these layers of options available in the courts have been sufficient in bringing justice for consumers under Section 17 200 of the Business and Professions code. We haven't seen a problem with it being enforced. We oppose the expansion of pre litigation subpoena to further government officials in these cases. We maintain that the power of issuing a subpoena before ever filing an actual action of alleged wrongdoing is of such intrusive magnitude that it should be maintained by those who are, as statute denotes, the chief law enforcement officials of the state. This view is not to disparage the role of a city attorney. That role includes among prosecuting issues, advising their cities on legal matters, financial matters, drafting ordinances, and arbitrating disputes regarding zoning ordinances. But the expansion of this power to a city attorney is unnecessary when that city attorney, should he or she feel it necessary, can simply work with his or her county District Attorney to issue one. We believe AB 814 adds yet another layer, under the UCL, by which we believe would further clog the court system, rather than relieve it. It should be noted that if a business does not respond to a pre-litigations subpoena the city attorney would then have to petition the Superior Court for an order compelling a business's response. While this might seem like an easy undertaking, it then places the burden on the business to prove why a subpoena has been issued when no actual allegation has been filed for wrongdoing. We believe that the burden to show that pre-litigation of subpoena is reasonable should be with the city attorney when he or she requests the subpoena from their District Attorney. The author and sponsor state the need for this bill because without pre-litigation subpoena power, the process of investigating claims of fraud against Wells Fargo, was quote on quote, more time consuming. That, again quote on quote, there will not always be a paper trail, or identifiable group of witnesses to help guide investigation, so the need for pre litigation subpoena is warranted. This seems to apply to any allegation of wrongdoing, even when there is no supporting documentation or known parties harmed will trigger the city attorneys to subpoena a business before ever claiming a filing of wrongdoing. We believe the current procedures protect the consumer. This current system provides a balance between government entities when enforcing the Unfair Competition Law. It took months to investigate Wells Fargo. Those months may have been stunted if Mr. Feurer had simply gone to his District Attorney to request a pre-litigation subpoena. In closing, members, there are a myriad of approaches to suing business for alleged wrongdoing under UCL. This additional power of collecting documentation from those business, again, before a claim is ever made of alleged wrongdoing against that business, should rest with those who, as stated in Government Code Section 26 500. In addition to bringing civil cases in their communities, rests with those whose most essential duty is investigating and prosecuting offenses on behalf of the people.

So what is it that these victims need? Well, clearly, they need counseling to address the immediate trauma. They need help developing safety plans, severing connections with perpetrators who may have access to their finances or personal information, they need support to resist the relentless pleas from perpetrators and often bullying. Financial counseling is also critical. And what I mean by that is to stop the hemorrhaging and get victims back on track financially. That may involve advocating with debt collectors Landlords or even the IRS when they stamps have tax implications. Some need hands on help to prevent foreclosure eviction, restructure budgets and debts, access to insurance and public assistance, subtle bankruptcy and banking issues. And some victims may need advocates to act on their own behalf, and in their interest.

Witness intimidation is of course a crime with significant sentencing enhancements applying if the intimidation is gang related. The court in the criminal case has broad discretion under penal code section 136.2 to issue protective orders to protect witnesses during dependency of the proceedings. If after the proceedings are concluded, a witness suffers harassment as required under AB 264 for the court to consider a no contact order, the witness can, under existing law, seek a civil protective order. That process differs from the process proposed, for the new contact orders under this bill in some significant ways. First, the order can last no longer than five years as supposed to the 10 years allowed under this bill. This will lead some defendants under the control of the criminal justice system for a period, far longer than their sentences, or terms of probation. Second, the terms of the restraining order allowed under AB 264 would bar all contact with the witness, while civil restraining orders can be crafted by the court may only restrain the respondent from harassment or from other specific behaviors. The end result will be more offenders who will remain subject to greater restrictions for a longer period of time. In many cases this will make it far more difficult for the offenders to reintegrate. A no contact order may in practice work as a bar to an offender returning to his former home or even neighborhood. If that would bring him into contact with the witnesses he is now barred from contact with. Sadly, the end result will be more offenders returned to prison for violations of the orders even when there was no harm to or harassment of the witness. We ask for your no vote on AB 264.

Doesn't make a ton of sense. Let me give you a couple of reasons why law enforcement agencies and officers may prefer short-barrel long guns. Particularly, in the context of a DA investigator's typical activities. Longer barrels hinder movement within structures, which is important when serving search or arrest warrants in buildings and houses or defending against active shooter scenarios in our offices. Similar to what we saw in San Bernardino, on December 2nd, 2015. That situation occurred just a couple of blocks from the San Bernardino District Attorney's Office, which was placed on lockdown. Longer barrels also restrict the ability to enter and exit cars rapidly, while protecting victims, witnesses, or deputy Das who are under protection. This is an important aspect of a DA Investigator's job. It's not unreasonable to imagine a scenario in which someone's trying to kill an important or high profile witness. He's wearing body armor. Handguns, while small and easily concealable are not particularly effective against body armor. And finally, smaller firearms are easier to conceal under clothing, while trying to remain discreet, while engaged in these assignments. Ultimately, the decision to use a particular type of weapon, rather than another, is going to be based on the circumstances of the assignment, the tactical expertise of the officer or investigator. So in other words, even though handguns are short barreled, fully-automatic rifles have short barrels and we can already use them. Their use may not be appropriate, based on the circumstance of a particular situation. We believe it's important that a DA investigator have the same flexibility and authority as other peace officers, to utilize the correct type of weapon based on the circumstances. We respectfully ask for your aye vote.

I've been working in Public Health and treating people living with HIV for over 20 years. I'm going to briefly review key scientific developments since the laws being discussed today were originally written. These developments require reassessment of the public health implications of HIV related criminal laws. I'd like to start by acknowledging that there is no evidence that the existing HIV related criminal laws have helped reduce HIV transmission. Multiple studies have found no association between HIV criminal laws and HIV disclosure, condom use, abstinence or numbers of sexual partners. ASA current forms, the laws have not work for their intended purposes. Since this laws were inactive, their have been extraordinary advances in the treatment of HIV. We've developed simple, potent HIV medication that is so effective that when taken regularly makes the virus completely undetectable in a person's blood. This allows that person to be healthy and live a normal life span, and also makes it impossible for them to transmit the virus to others. This fact has been confirmed by two very large international studies. From a public health perspective, to prevent new HIV infections at our communities, it is essential that we overcome any obstacle for people living with HIV to access and remain on treatment. We've also Learned that HIV related stigma which is the fear and the fear and isolation that it creates, makes it much harder and much less likely for people living with HIV to get tested, engage in care, and take the very medications that allow them to be healthy and uncontagious. In other words, the laws don't work for their intended purpose. And instead actually increase the risk of HIV infection in our communities. There are many reason for HIV related stigma, but state laws that criminal lies HIV are among the prime contributors. These laws, as they are currently written are not only outdated and ineffective but they are actually dangerous. Because they increase instead of decrease the risk of HIV infection. So this is not a partisan issue. It's not a political issue. It's not a matter of conflict in medical science. It's an issue that should be decided on the basic principles of public health, the proposed law presented today, bill presented today to modernize these laws is crucial to achieve our shared goals of reducing new HIV infections, and helping those living with the virus be safe, healthy, and empowered members of our community. Thank you very much for your consideration.

We've heard stories of transgender people in prison attempting to change their names and gender. The process is long, ultimately ending in many people being denied without explanation or response. As it currently stands, guards and other prisoners call transgender people by the name on their birth Identification documents. This constant use of the wrong gender and name has serious psychological, emotional, and spiritual impacts on a person, and is, itself, violence. Being identified constantly by the incorrect name and gender can cause people severe psychological discomfort and be an ongoing implication that transgender people are an other in society. This can lead to depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation. Not being well mentally translates into not being well physically, resulting in high blood pressure, self mutilation, and in some cases, suicide. This all from an ongoing assault on a transgender person's sense of self. For transgender people released from prison trying to find a job and housing is even more difficult when their name and gender presentation does not match the name and gender marker on their legal documents. One of our members told us recently that she did not apply for jobs because she was afraid employers would be less likely to hire her because of discrepancy between her appearance in her interview and the info on her ID documents. While trying to complete hours of programming as part of parole requirements, transgender people that have the added step of working to file a name and gender marker change with the courts, it would be much simpler and more empowering to leave prison with all this resolved. Prison conditions and the reentry process are challenging enough. This bill is a simple measure that would give incarcerated transgender people a moment of respite and dignity that would set them up for success in reentry to rebuild their lives. I am strongly in support of SB 310, the Name and Dignity Act. Please give incarcerated transgender people access to basic dignity and vote aye on this important bill.

This is most evident if the Postal Service is allowed to reduce delivery services to five days a week. Doing this would delay timely delivery of mail, including newspapers, newsletters, bill payments, letters, invitations, and even medicine. In addition, if these cutbacks are allowed to occur, it would seriously affect hundreds of postal employees in California alone. Over 22% of whom are United States military veterans, many with disabilities. These citizens rely upon the postal service to receive their mail delivery to their residence daily. According to the government accountability office cluster boxes are so unpopular compared with a door to door deliver of mail that less than 0.8% of business door delivery customers when given the voluntary choice opted to go to the cluster box deliver. And for residences just 0.1% agree to this change. How would the other 40 million USPS customers react if they were forced to convert to cluster box delivery. In some locations the Sostal Wervice has been soliciting customers to convert to a cluster box that could be placed anywhere, a sidewalk or a location at the end of a street. Meaning customers would have to retrieve mail from a cluster box. Security of this system has been an issue in some communities where these boxes have become easy targets for theft, vandalism, and tagged with graffiti. After bringing forth the issues just mentioned, along with many more, we believe that this resolution should be supported and passed by your Committee. Thank you very much.

But big problems started when my clinical hours begin. I had to quit my job because there wasn't enough time to do that and my internship hours. It was like having a full-time job that didn't pay. I've now been a pharmacy technician for 16 years. I love my job. But I wish the internship system hadn't made it so difficult for me to get here. People, especially single moms like me, shouldn't have to sacrifice so much just to get a good paying job in healthcare. That's why I'm sharing my story and working so hard to pass AB 387. Other moms like me must be able to have a medical career without seeing our families in our life suffer so much, thank you.

Michelle Cabrera: Thank you, Mr Chair and Members, Michelle Cabrera with the SEIU, California, we're the sponsors of this bill. On behalf of our 50,000 allied health professional members, and our 700,000 statewide, we'd like to thank the Chair for carrying this bill. AB 387 is based on extensive interviews with committed allied health professionals like Maita, who experienced being brought into hospital works that interns to the guys of clinical training. And who are then required to perform hundreds or even thousands of hours of work with little or no immediate supervision for paying patients. There is nothing wrong with the concept of works for extender in the health professions, as long as that individual is fairly compensated. We understand that this policy would bring about a major change in a culture of training an education for allied health professions and that's exactly what we are after. In this case, the employers have exploited a loophole to staff their radiology departments, pharmacies, and hospitals with free labor. The opposition have argued that these individuals are students who are covered by their educational loans or student financial aid to get by. But the clinical hours we're specifying here are separate and above classroom learning time. These are hours performed in real health facilities with real patients. Nevermind that most students can barely survive even with financial aid and students' loans. Researchers released a report earlier this month showing that one-third of community college students go hungry and 14% are homeless nationwide. The average community college student is barely getting by. And in most cases presented here, there's no option for a paid internship. The opposition argues that trainees are being supervised while they're working. In fact, this concept of supervision is built into the very structure of health professions. For example, scope of practice in the medical field dictates ongoing and continuous chain of delegation and supervision by those who have the highest levels of training and competency in a field, to those who support them all the way through to unlicensed aids and assistants. This is a field where health professionals are always providing some level of direct or indirect supervision and or delegation and yet, some of these individuals are compensated for their work and others are not. Traditionally, male dominated fields already meet this bar of fairly compensating individuals who are meeting training requirements. Whether it's a CPA, a construction worker, engineer, electrician or military allied health professional in training, many professions inside and out of the health arena compensate men for on the job work experience. By creating an industry standard in a series of female dominated professions where individuals contribute as many as 25 million hours of unpaid labor each year, the health industry has also created a serious barrier for low income individuals who wish to gain access to good paying middle class jobs. What good is a STEM education in elementary or high school if you literally can't afford to spend hundreds or thousands of hours each year paying someone else to work? And the trainee is paying, whether it's through their educational loans or foregoing other paid work, whether it's having to pay for childcare, parking, or transportation. It's the trainees who pay for the privilege of doing work in hospitals that are in turn, getting payment through their patient's insurance.

Our opposition basically comes from the fact that a lot of these are already covered in the Fair Employment and Housing Act with regards to the pregnancy disability, and any related conditions associated with pregnancy itself. The regulations that the Department of Fair Employment and Housing have adopted deal with perceived pregnancy, so even if you're not pregnant, but an employer perceives that you're pregnant, you can't be discriminated against that basis. Obviously, sex discrimination. There's cases out there that says, if you hire a woman and you expect that she's in her years that she may have a child, you can't discriminate against on that basis. Marital status is already a protected category, as well. So if you're not married and you show up to work and you're pregnant or you're perceived to be pregnant, an employer can't take action, retaliation, discrimination on that basis. And so our concern really is the fact that this should probably be in the government code under the Fair Employment and Housing Act, and not the labor code. When you put it in the labor code, then we have two different enforcement agencies, the Labor Commissioner's Office and the Department of Fair Employment and Housing enforcing the same basic protections. But they have different processes, they have different authority, different jurisdiction, different damages with regards to the labor code versus the Fair Employment and Housing Act. Then so basically, we don't want two conflicting agencies enforcing the same rights. So we'd like to see it moved to the Fair Employment and Housing Act. The second part is with regards to subdivision A2 of the bill dealing with a document or a waiver. We're not really sure what that's trying to get at, and so, it makes us very nervous when it's ambiguous as to the scope of what that is trying to protect. It talks about the fact an employer can't require you to sign a document or a waiver that impacts your reproductive health choices. One of our concerns was does this impact insurance coverage that we're offering to our employees that may not cover certain items, such as elective surgeries that have to do with reproduction and whether or not employers ultimately be reliable for that. It gets into the family leave laws that we have, if an employer may not allow leave beyond what's already covered. Is that impacting your reproductive choices? So we're kind of nervous on that ambiguity, but to the extent that can be clarified. Again, it's kind of like an opposed and less amended position. So, we just need some clarification and movement out of the labor code. Thank you.

Jeff Clayton: Madame Chair, Members of the Committee. My name is Jeff Clayton, I'm the Executive Director of the American Bail Coalition, which is a trade Association of national insurance companies that underwrite criminal bail bonds throughout the country, including the great State of California. Here today in opposition to this legislation. A couple of brief comments. I think the question of least restrictive conditions in this bill is problematic. I think it risks an as applied challenge. In this particular situation because all of the alternative restrictions on someone's liberty is free to the state. The last resort analysis risk and as-applied challenge because if somebody can post a bail which is typically a third-party benefit for a defendant. Which is denied in favor of correctional technology that can be more restrictive under the Eighth Amendment and risk as applied challenges. Certainly the Maryland Supreme Court rejected this methodology for that reason. Risk assessments mandatory on all defendants will slow down the process. Everybody who gets out of jail today, can't. The other thing is, if you don't have a bail schedule you can't schedule o.r. releases. Which means everybody is parked in jail at the front end of this process. And I think that's a problem. I do think risk assessments are good. Candidly, I commend the authors of this bill for the restrictions they placed on the risk assessments to make sure they're race and gender neutral. That's progressive. I think it's good policy. I'm not sure anyone could operate a risk assessment under it, today but I commend them for going in that direction. To answer the sort of statistic that 62% of people are unconvicted in the country, that's true. The question is what is keeping them in? And the vast majority of the reason they're in is non monetary holds which this bill does nothing to correct. Study the Los Angeles County Jail found that only 12% of defendants could theoretically post a bail. And of course some of them were getting advice of counsel not to. And so we think the numbers are probably a lot lower, particularly in California. Now in Harris County, Texas that's probably a whole different ballgame. Where you have whole classes of misdemeanants on low level bails which really doesn't happen as much in California. The missing component in this bill that's not part of the national movement is the expansion of preventative detention. And the previous witness talked about how a risk assessment can serve to keep the dangerous in jail. But this bill doesn't expand preventative detention. There is no basis to deny bail under this bill. The constitution of the State of California is not being changed under this legislation, which means that there is no greater avenue under this bill to keep the dangerous in. And I like to think that before the 1984 Bill Reform Act passed, that Tip O'Neill and Ronald Reagan were having a martini. And Tip said, Ronnie, we got all these people in here. They can't afford their bail. They're low level. Let's get some of these people out of here. And Reagan probably said, you know, Tip, we got these rich gangsters who are getting out because they have money and we need to do something about it. But that whole deal, that whole package, is missing from this legislation. The implementation cost of this would be huge. State of New Jersey is trying it. It took them three years to attempt to implement it. It started January 1st. Candidly I think, and I estimate, maybe $500 million at the low level to roll this out state wide, and I don't think you would be able to this January 1st, even if you'd want to. The saving certainly haven't materialized yet, at least in the amount of savings to offset the cost and so I think this is certainly a big shift. We have come to the table here, we have come to this capital with suggestions on how to improve the bail system in California. And we certainly look forward to continuing to work with the sponsors of this legislation to try to find a way to make California's bail system more fair. And certainly our ideas were to get at the bail schedules, lower the bail schedules, have more process and that sort of thing. But ultimately I think, it's not my job to come down here and protect every dollar of market share of the bail industry. What it is my job to do is to try to help to figure out where commercial bail bondsman work the best and it's typically in high risk felonies where the judges don't want to release them anyway. And so I think we can arrive at a more fair bail system in California. We are a partner in that and we want to continue to be a partner in that. So I thank you all for your time this morning. Thank you Madame Chair.

We know what she's trying to accomplish and we don't disagree with that, but the importance of the Incident Command System is to have scalability and flexibility, so that you can have an adequate response and a quick response to a potential spill if there is one. Of course, no one wants an oil spill to happen. No one actually wants that. We prepare for them, we prevent them, we train every three years with OSPR. We have a technical Advisory Committee that we participate with. There's federal, state, and local officials. They're all involved in these oil spill drills and we're graded every time we do a oil spill drill. You either get a passing grade or a failing grade. With respect to the spill management teams that the bill is trying to insert into the process, there are some companies that have spill management teams. Some contract with them, some are internal. We also use the OSRS, those are the actual equipment that actually go out and do the spill clean ups. So what we're trying to figure out, if this bill's not going to create any unnecessary duplications or conflicts between the roles, we don't know. The bill's granting a lot authority to OSPR to come up with regulations and we don't know if those regulations will spell out what criteria a spill management team will have to have. Will there be certain levels? Certain grades? Those are all things that need to be fleshed out as the bill moves forward and we're happy to work with OSPR in an offer on that. Again, we're not questioning the need for the bill, but it's important to recognize that some larger shippers actually have these internal strike teams too. So what they do is they actually go out, the spill management team will go out and do the initial assessment, then the internal companies will come in. The strike teams will come in and then take over and fill the role of the Incident Command System, depending on what that role might be. So, are the internal company strike teams going to be ready too? It's not clear in the bill, if that's going to be the case. Finally, we don't know what the criteria will be for the rating system and how many rating levels will be established and we're also not sure if the bill will require a certain size, SMT to respond to this bill. Planes that burn leaded aviation gas, or avgas as it's called, are the transportation sector's primary contributors to leaded air pollution. Avgas's lead not only pollutes the air, but it also pollutes all that it lands on. Lead does not break down but instead accumulates in soil and water, and can be absorbed by plants. As we know, lead is a neurotoxin. Exposure to large quantities of lead can cause kidney and brain damage. The University of North Carolina evaluated relationship between children's blood lead levels and their proximity to general aviation airports. The study found that children who lived within 500 meters of an airport had notably higher blood levels than children living farther away. AB 483's proposal to test the soil at General Aviation Airport is a good first step to identifying the presence of hazardous waste, such as lead at the airports, and then safeguarding the children and adults who lived in the surrounding communities. We do recognize that ingredient communication is valuable tool for consumers as well as the industry. And as it was also mentioned, there's a number of many factors in the industry that are already providing disclosure. We have also a voluntary program. And I just mentioned this to highlight that we're not starting from scratch today, that I think it's a good framework, and we'll be able to hopefully work something out this year with this vehicle. With that said, I do want to take the opportunity to just to highlight some of our main concerns which, again, we'll be working with the Senator on finding a workable path forward. As was mentioned, confidential business information, protecting that is critical in our view to encourage innovation. Companies make a very significant investment in research and development prior to bringing new products to market. So it's important that we find the balance that preserves the incentive to innovate. And also, again, gives consumers the information they need to inform their purchasing decisions. On fragrance, the SB 258 would require full fragrance disclosure, which does go further than any current regulatory labeling requirements. For example, under cosmetics, you are able to identify fragrance ingredient as a functional category that is, you can list on the label of ingredients that it contains fragrance. In food, you're able to provide, for example, lemon flavor but you don't list out the individual constituents of that lemon flavor. And again, I just used these as examples of where and currently labeling requirements, there are protections for proprietary information. And fragrance is one of the primary distinguishing factors in a number of these products that help stride purchasing decisions. For example, when we think about laundry detergent, most brands work about the same, but we tend to buy or make that purchase based on particular scent in the product. So again, it's just another thing that we think we can find balance to give consumers the information they find useful, but we're not providing the level of detail that only our competitors and our accounting vendors would find useful. And again, I'd be remised if I didn't mention that the market has responded in terms of fragrance as well. There are companies who are disclosing the fragrance ingredients, and then there are a number of variety of products that are fragrance free, so consumers do have a choice out there. And lastly, on finding a balance between providing information on the product label and on the product website, the way SB 258 is currently drafted, we could result in 50 to 100 different ingredients listed on a product label. For example, a typical laundry detergent, the fragrance ingredients are going to be about 50 ingredients alone. So as was mentioned, a lot of these ingredients are things that the typical consumer might need to seek out additional information about, in addition to what they might find on the label. So I won't list all of our other concerns, but I just mention that with some of the concerns more around implementation. There are significant cost impacts, that might be particularly hard on small and niche companies. But we do look forward to participating in the work group process, and hope to work these out.

Paul Towers: Great, thank you, Senator, and thank you, Chair Wieckowski and Members of the Committee. My name is Paul Towers, I'm with Pesticide Action Network and part of the Bee Smart California a coalition of conservation organizations of bee keepers, both hobbyist and commercial and farmers as well. We ask that you support SB 602, the Pollinator Protection Act in part because of the tremendous role that bees play in supporting our agricultural economy, our food and farming system. Everywhere from background gardens, where many of us grow tomatoes, to what we actually see in the almond orchards across the state. As you've already heard, bees are declining at an alarming rate across the state and across the entire country. We see neonicotinoids as a critical part of this equation as a class of insecticides. As the Senator described, these are particularly unusual, and I think important to understand, because of their long life in plants, and in the soil. So again, many of these, as the Chair described, are applied in various ways, but are taken up systematically, or systemically, rather, through the plants and persist for days, weeks, sometimes in the soil, years at a time. And so, this leads to not only ongoing exposures for target pests but also for beneficial insects like bees that visit these plants. So particularly effective at what they do. As we know that the science's growing incredibly strong in the case against this products and has been for years. The largest global body that looked it over 1,100 different studies concluded that they pose a serious threat to bees, aquatic organisms, birds, and other animals. But out of those recommendations, these 29 independent scientists, including those here in the US said, we must take immediate action to curb the use of these products. We know that they are a driving factor in the decline. We know they are not the only factor. And I think what's important to understand about these products, is that they can fundamentally disrupt communication, navigation, reproduction and so weaken immune systems of bees they leave them susceptible to other factors. Whether they be disease, other pests like Varroa mites, forage habitat, many other problems we see in agriculture. But the dramatic declines that we've seen in the past just less than 20 years have been coincided with the introduction of these products. So what's important about this bill is it does two things. One, it takes these product out of the hands of those that don't have training and background on using them. It puts them in the hands of certified applicators. We know that's particularly important for controlling the spread of diseases like huanglongbing that are a part of citrus greening rather. And it's important to find the best ways to control the spread of diseases like this. And so making sure that we have the best trained applicators with the tools to do that as effectively as possible is a critical piece of the first part of the bill. Secondly, as we look at what's happening with what people use in their own backyards when they purchase plants, they intend to be beneficial for bees and other species. Again, over 4,000 species of bees are native to California. Many of them don't realize they're causing harm to the entire colony. And what we have seen is that even when neonicotinoids have been studied for their impacts on honeybees, we see they can have dramatic declines in the cases of other native bees species that again are supportive of agriculture. We can see those effects are even more pronounced based on a growing body of research. So all this to say that we should and must take action on restricting harmful neonicotinoids. And then we should put tools in the hands of consumers to make accurate choices. None of this precludes farmers and state agencies from dealing with pest outbreaks as they happen. Again, certified applicators have the tools to deal with that. But this is a necessary step to curb unnecessary use, misuse, and overuse of products, and give the consumers the choice to make sure they are supporting pollinators as they can. Thank you.
