Shreyas Jutkar: Good morning, Chair Wieckowski and Vice Chair Stone, and Members of the Committee, Shreyas Jutkar with the Coalition for Clean Air, our group was heavily involved in the development of the Sustainable Freight Action Plan, and we remain involved now in the implementation of that action plan. We're also heavily involved at the California Transportation Commission, in a process that's somewhat parallel to this legislation to develop guidelines for California Freight Investment Program, which in some ways is sort of a new name for the Trade Quarter Improvement Fund, but those guidelines really will direct the federal funding from the FAST Act. We're here in support of SB 4, and we're working with the author on amendments to address issues on the infrastructure side of this funding measure. And before going into some of the details of the bill, I just wanted to sort of clarify, if I could, some of the funding issues here, because there were some comments that came up when this bill was heard in Senate transportation last week. And so I did want to try to address those questions about a lack of funding for infrastructure, and sort of a question from you, Chair, about what the specified projects and the funding allocated, what could you really get with the money called for. So, I just want to point out that funding for infrastructure in this bill is about $800 million in one time funding, but through SB 1, or whatever that turns out to be, there's hundreds of millions more in annual investments for trade corridor infrastructure improvements. By contrast, this bill calls for $400 million in one time funding for cleaner trucks and freight equipment. There is additional money for those types of projects through the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund. However, it's important to note that the revenues to the Greenhouse Gas Reduction fund are extremely volatile at the moment and so it's hard to sort of have clear forecast of the amount of funding available for cleaner trucks and freight equipment. So the point of all that is to say that there is more money for infrastructure than what it may seem here and also that there is more funding as a result of that, for projects like grade separations. Which I know you had asked about, Chair Wieckowski, last week. So, couple of points on the bill that I want to make. First of all, that there's a particular need for the funding for cleaner trucks and freight equipment in order to help mitigate the severe impacts from goods movement on the environmental and human health in California. Freight equipment accounts for about half of all emissions of cancer-causing diesel particulate matter and 45% of smog-forming nitrogen oxides. And this emissions profile gives a good illustration of how freight hubs and major freight facilities such as seaports, or warehousing and distribution centers are large stationary sources of air pollution in California, compared to what we may often think of as large stationary sources like factories or power plants. And just as one example, the Ports of LA and Long Beach emitted 14,000 tons of nitrogen oxide in 2013 compared to 68 tons from the Hanes power plant in Long Beach. So these ports are about 200 power plants worth of pollution. And so addressing the impacts of the freight sector is vital for air quality as well as public health. It's also an environmental justice issue. And just to your point earlier, Chair, we do all breathe air, but air quality is not the same in every part of the state. In the South Coast and San Joaquin Valley places that are near freight facilities and near freight corridors are disproportionately impacted by the pollution from this sector. And as a result, these communities that are predominantly low income, communities of color, experience increased illness and death, emergency room visits, doctor visits, hospital missions, and missed school days. And to go back just a little bit, ARB, between 2004 and 2008, conducted a series of health risk assessments to look at the risk levels in specific communities attributable to freight related diesel particulate matter emissions that are carcinogenic. And the researchers found maximum individual cancer risk ranging from 180 in 1 million to 1200 in 1 million, depending on the facility type and location. And so as a result ARB estimates that there's a healthy return on investments in cleaner freight vehicles and technology. For every $1 invested in reducing emissions ARB estimates about $3 to $8 in health benefits. So again, the funding for cleaner trucks and freight equipment are absolutely necessary. They're also really important pieces of how we're going to meet our 2030 climate change standard here in California, as well as the federal health based air quality standards for ozone and particulate matter. And the second point I want to make is that the funding particularly for cleaner trucks and equipment builds upon the successes we've had to date in California to improve the technology in the heavy duty sector. Which still lags far behind the light duty sector in terms of advanced technologies that reduce emissions through fuel efficiency and switching to cleaner transportation fuels. And that's starting to change thanks to tens and millions of dollars from the greenhouse gas reduction fund. Just a couple weeks ago we saw the first sort of handful of about 30 zero emission yard trucks that were delivered to a new freight transfer facility in Fontana. And those clean trucks are made here in California, and they're supported with greenhouse gas reduction fund money. Those money's are not enough and as I pointed out earlier the funding for those projects is very volatile at the moment.

Peter Calles: Peter Calles on behalf of the California Hospice and Palliative Care Association, Principal Co-Sponsor for the bill Briefly, Hospice and Palliative care are two different forms of treatment. Hospice is a mandated service, under California statute that is designed to provide palliative care, physical, spiritual, emotional, and social care at the end of an individual's life. In order to receive hospice care, one must give up curative treatment. The median length of stay in hospice is about 17 days. Palliative care is a permissive treatment. Palliative care is to provide comfort for suffering. It's referred to within the industry as pre-hospice if you will and it is until recently been linked to giving up curative treatment as well. So if you could imagine whether it be a child, a teen, an elderly person, a loved one, you'd have to give up cured of treatment in order to receive comfort care at the end of your life and you're given about 17 days roughly in order to reconcile all that needs to be reconciled as well as just be given comfort for your ending days. What this bill does is it follows up on legislation that was passed previously to enable contracts to be given for plans to cover palliative care should there be mutual agreement to do so beyond simple curative care. So you could receive palliative care while still receiving curative care. The statute was a little bit stale in order to conform what that intent is to provide palliative care treatment to individuals continuing to receive curative care. The statute needs to be modified to provide for ongoing treatment. So we're pleased to be a cosponsor of this, happy to answer any technical questions anybody might have, and ask for your support.

[{'start': 0, 'end': 10, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Toby Ewing: Mr. Chair and members my name is Toby Ewing. I'm the Executive Director of the Mental Health Services Oversight and Accountability Commission. Thank you for the opportunity to be here today. Although the Commission does not have a formal position on the bill, it's very consistent with the work that we've done. It'll be finalized at the end of this month. Earlier, actually last year, the Commission was very concerned about reversion and fiscal transparency, in part because of work that the press had done, because of work that the Little Hoover Commission had done and in part because of conversations we had with some of your offices about ensuring that these dollars were well spent and that there was a level of accountability and transparency that the public expected as part of the act and that you would have expected. So over the course of several months, the Commission started to try to unpack what's happening in terms of the country reporting, what's happening in terms of reversion and where this process that's outlined fairly clearly in the law has fallen short. Through that work, the Commission, through a Subcommittee, has adopted a set of recommendations. And in essence, what the Commission has found is that, primarily because of the transition of responsibilities from the Department of Mental Health to the Department of Health Care Services, around the same time that the Legislature change the way that MSH funds flow from a time when the state held on at the money, and then allocated to the counties through plant at the option and plant approval, to a system of almost direct deposit where the funds flow to the counties on a monthly basis based on revenues received. That the reversion policies that have been in place prior to that shift didn't apply to the financial arrangement after that shift. In response to that, the Commission Subcommittee has adopted a set of our recommendations that are very consistent with SB 192. In short, it calls for a resetting the rules around reversion to provide clarity to the counties. In our conversations with counties, they've highlighted that they have funds that they believe are subject to reversion, but they're not sure what to do with those dollars. And they can't spend them, but there's no provision for them to give them back. And so, what they're looking for clarity on the part of the rules that Department of Healthcare Service puts in place. We're working with the counties, we're talking with healthcare services to try to figure that out. We've also recognized as it's outlined in the bill that for very small counties, they've received so little money, that it often is difficult for them to actually spend those dollars within the three year time frame. It's a combination of how small they are, and how small their staff are and the difficulty for them to find contractors who can do this work. Plus the fact in some cases for innovation they might only receive $40,000 in a given year. And so, the Commission has identified the option of giving very small counties, because of the challenges and the service delivery side, not because of the risk of reversion, but because they just face exceptional difficulties standing up new programs, that they be given the option of some additional time to spend those dollars. We also recommend in there, consistent with the bill, that counties be able to adjust some of their reporting. There's disagreement between the counties and healthcare services over the extent that they're allowed to revise their annual revenue and expenditure reports. And so the Commission is suggesting that we need to clarify that, and the bill to do that. And lastly, the law says that unspent funds shall be made available to other counties in future years. That's what the law says, it's not clear how that is supposed to happen. The Commission has the recommendation before it to do exactly what SB 192 would do be to create a reversion fund for three specific reasons. One is to highlight transparency in terms of these dollars. The second is to create an additional incentive to spend. The reversion policy is an incentive to use the money. And if it's surplus, if you can't use it or you haven't used it to make it available for other high priority need. And so, pooling those dollars would actually enhance that incentive and allow that to occur more readily. The third issue, as Senator Beall pointed out, at the best calculations we have, it's somewhere between one quarter and one-half of 1% is the money that is unspent. But when you take even that small percentage of a fund that generates a couple of $1 billion a year and you look at that accumulation of that small amount. It can add up to a sizable amount of money. And so, the intent is to use that money to focus on unmet needs in ways that would be prioritized on an annual basis, and the reason we suggest that is because these are very volatile funds. These are not sustainable funds because they are in essence surplus from the county's annual expenditure over those three years. So because the bill is so consistent with the work that we're doing, although we have not finalized our position, I wanted to let you know that we're doing this work, we're very supportive of the leadership of Senator Beall on this issue. And we continue to work with him as the bill moves through the process. Thank you.

So, the bottom line is really, we believe a reversion policy does need to be finalized and implemented by the state and that existing law should be held in tact with respect to the use of those dollars, thank you.

Mark Jasper: Thank you, Madam Chair and members, for allowing me to tell my story today. I am Mark Jasper and I am the grandson of Sophia McAllister. Sophia was the absolute epitome of the sweet, little loving grandmother. She was barely five feet tall and that was in her heels. Everybody who knew her absolutely loved her and what was so adorable about her is that she couldn't tell you why, she didn't know why they loved her, they just did. But we knew why. We all tend to love those who love us first, and that was my grandmother in a nutshell. As kids, my brothers and I and my sister, we'd just light up when mom would tell us it's time to go to Nana McAllister's house. We just loved being there looking for the candy dish, finding the stale marshmallows and enjoying our time with her. In 1989, somebody broke into her home through the kitchen window, robbed her, raped her, and murdered her. She was 80 years old. She was a victim of a crime that was almost impossible to even comprehend how somebody could do something like that, but do it to someone like her. We all became victims that night, our grandkids, our parents, our extended family, her neighbors who loved her, the Lutheran church where she attended and went for two, three, four days a week, and the kind man from Meals on Wheels who used to bring her meals, who was the one who notified police that there might be a problem because she hadn't picked up her meals for a couple of nights. The police were looking at quite a few people but nothing ever materialized from that. And this incident, it changes the way you look at the world around you. You wake up the next day, and things just are never quite the same. All of that changed for us, or began to change in 2004, with Prop 69. I'll never forget the day that the cold case investigator called me and told me that, because of Prop 69, that there was at least hope. Law enforcement had never let my grandmother's case go. They talked about it in conventions, in law enforcement conventions, things like that, and they always kept it alive. We knew that they hadn't abandoned us but when we got that call, we had some hope. And it was five years but finally, we did get that call from that cold case investigator and he told us they believed that they had a hit on the DNA. It would take a couple more months, they sent that to an independent lab so it could be further verified and make sure, absolutely, that they had the right person. Finally, that day came as well and I was told that it was conclusive that Donald Carter was the perpetrator and that they had already picked him up and had him in custody. I can't even describe, even 20 years later, what my family went through and felt that day. It was like a warm sedative on a wound that had been opened for way too long. And while it would never get her back to us, at least it allowed us an opportunity and hope for closure; that we could finish the story, close the book, put it on the shelf and move on. Donald Carter was subsequently convicted and sentenced for that crime. And I know that we're running long today, but if I can detour just for a moment to make an analogy that came to me a couple of days ago. I write business software for a manufacturing company. When I design systems, I write in a concept called exception management. What it does is it allows you to evaluate your processes not from the point of view that what's working, but what's not working. So you could focus your resources and time on fixing the things that are broken. Proposition 69, to me, was an exception management tool for law enforcement. It allowed only DNA to be collected from a small group of the public who found themselves involved in a certain subset of offenses. And to me, it was a classic example of exception management. My family and I all support Proposition 69. I personally support Proposition 47 as well, what I thought it was. What I came to believe later, and as thus my family, that there were some unintended consequences in Proposition 47, and specifically, that was with the reclassification of certain felonies that are now misdemeanors, and no longer qualify for DNA collection. If Donald Carter were picked up today instead of in 2009, his drug crime would've been classified as a misdemeanor. The DNA would not have been collected and we would've never had any resolution for my grandmother's case. I remember all, when I came into her house afterwards, and I did want to touch on this. When I came to her house afterwards, there was dust everywhere. I remember seeing the fingerprints and the palmprints around the kitchen window, dust on every piece of furniture in the house. And of course, lots of fingerprinting dust in the bedroom, and with all of that, not one single usable fingerprint was extracted from her home. I saw prints with my own eyes. I know they were not hers, yet there was not one usable print to identify who this was. Law enforcement had done a sweep of the area, I know they were looking at dozens, and dozens of people. Mr. Carter was one of the people that they looked at, but nothing ever came of that either. The one thing that was in that house that identified who the perpetrator was, and the dozens and dozens of suspects that couldn't have been in that house, was the DNA. It troubles me terribly to think that we have technology that doesn't discriminate based on race, or religion or gender, or gender identity, or political affiliation or any other group classification. All it does is say that body created this substance and there's no question about it. It identifies who left that material. And that was the one thing that was missing that Proposition 69 gave us. Everything I can ask for from California and from law enforcement was given to me. We can't get my grandmother back, but we know all of the details and we were able to close that book and put it up. But even earlier today in SB 610, I was watching the parents talking about their children that they had lost. And they said something that every family member that has victimized members in it say the same thing. It's not about us, our fate's sealed. It's about the people who have not yet been victimized. We all share an urgency that we do whatever we can do to prevent people from becoming victims because that never goes away. My feeling of victimization for my grandmother will die about an hour before I do, and that goes for everybody in my family. We'll carry it forever, but we have grave concerns. I just, in closing, want to say that one more time, is that the reason I'm here today, you guys have done everything you need to be done for me. It's because I have concern for the people who are not victims yet and we have the tools in front of us to determine who has committed these higher level crimes and who may commit more and victimize other people. So in closing, me and my family support SB 781 completely, and it's our sincere hope that you will, too. Thank you.

Caliph Assagai: Hello again. Madame Chair, Members, Caliph Assagai on behalf of the California Public Defenders' Association, in respectful opposition to this measure. We've seen this bill three times now. And I think that it's informative that, or two times, I think that it is informative that both times this bill has failed passage because of the recent passage, still being recent passage, of Proposition 47 and the overwhelming support the public showed for that bill, I mean for that Proposition. Further this bill will add to the already disproportionate number of racial minorities whose DNA has been collected and added to the DNA database. Sure, while there is a color blind element to the idea of what DNA is, much more of it coming from low income communities of color is in the database, which leads disproportionate outcomes for those communities. As I believe you're aware, a number of studies have shown that despite the fact that people of color, and in particular African-Americans and Latinos do not commit crimes at any higher rate than white individuals, they are far more likely to be arrested and prosecuted for alleged criminal activity. Rates at which African-Americans were arrested for violent offenses and for drug offenses were each approximately 3.5 times the rate that whites were arrested for those categories of offenses. Latinos were incarcerated over 1.5 times the rate of whites. Because people of color are arrested and prosecuted at higher rates than whites, people of color are disproportionately included in the DNA database. Expanding the DNA database could likewise result in more communities of color being mistakenly identified as suspects of crime they did not commit, simply because they happened to leave their DNA at a place where a crime was committed, for instance on a cup or a napkin at a restaurant or neighborhood or at a bus stop. If this bill would place innocent undocumented individuals who are already concerned that they may deported from this country at an even greater risk. Also some believe if one is law abiding, there should be no real concern over having one's DNA in the DNA database. This is incorrect. Existing DNA technology permits laboratories to obtain DNA results from samples that contain as few as 10 cells and more importantly, from DNA that was left on items years before it was analyzed and collected. The type of crime in which DNA evidence is being collected is ever-expanding, and now includes property crimes such as auto burglaries, where DNA profile emanates from skin cells left on an item of evidence at an unknown point in time. In other words, DNA evidence is no longer collected only from items from which it can be clearly established that there is an association between the evidence and the crime being investigated. Increasingly, items of evidence are being collected and analyzed from property found at crime scenes, where the relationship between the evidence and the crime is not entirely clear. Additionally, it is no longer the case that only single sourced complete DNA profiles are uploaded and searched against the database. Today, law enforcement may request search of an inferred DNA profile which may be partially incomplete. Such a search may result in more than one hit or candidate which may potentially result in identification of an individual who is innocent of a crime being investigated or where a crime lab analyst may fill in gaps in evidence and submit for upload to the database. Consequently, when a DNA profile hits in the DNA database, it is far from certain that the DNA match will identify the perpetrator of the crime. Nevertheless, that person will come under the scrutiny of law enforcement, and will frequently be considered a suspect of a crime even when no crime has been committed. Because people of color are so disproportionately represented in the database, it is more often people of color who will be subjected to this type of criminal investigation whether or not they are responsible for having committed the crime being investigated. For those and other reasons, we are opposed to this measure.

Inclusion on the registry can make it more difficult for people to get a job, find housing, parent, and rehabilitate. It can also exacerbate existing mental health conditions and send people into depression. This does two things. One, it further disadvantages already disadvantaged communities. Communities of color are already facing barriers to employment and housing. And there are significant mental health issues in the low income community as well. This will further exacerbate that given the disproportionate inclusion. Second, to the extent that a person who has previously been convicted of a sex offense will recidivate. It is exactly this type of destabilization that will cause people to recidivate. So this inclusion on the sex offender registry will also make our communities less safe. Communities of color are already disproportionately represented in the DNA database as it is. And that means that all of the negative consequences that stem from the DNA database including familiar searching. Erroneous convictions will further impact those communities. And lastly, I would point out that penal code, 288.3 288 and attempted 288, are all already registrable offenses. And anybody who is required to register as a sex offender, also has to provide DNA to the database. So, this Bill is likewise unnecessary. For these reasons, we respectfully oppose the bill.

Tal Klement: Good morning, Chairperson Skinner, Members of the Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to testify on behalf of Senate Bill 180. My name's Tal Klement, I'm a deputy public defender in San Francisco. I've been a deputy public defender for 13 years. And I'm here to voice my strong support for Senate Bill 180, which would repeal an ineffective and highly punitive three-year prison enhancement for those with prior convictions for drug sales. Based on my time as a public defender representing thousands of people charged with crimes, I can tell you that I've personally observed how this enhanced punishment has negatively impacted the most marginalized members of our society. While television and movies often stereotypically depict drug dealers as violent, sophisticated criminals driving fancy cars, living in mansions, and rolling in cash, that's not who I see prosecuted and subject to this punitive enhancement. The people I see who are charged with these drug crimes and enhancements on a daily basis are poor, often people of color, usually homeless, living in shelters or on the street. Most struggle with their own addictions to heroine, crack, pills, or meth. Addiction issues that are usually compounded by untreated mental illness or PTSD related to the trauma of living on the street or former service in the military. The problem with punishing people with prior convictions by adding three years for every prior is that the line between drug dealer and drug user is blurry. And can change from day to day, even hour to hour. Many of the people I see charged with these prior convictions sell small amounts of their own drugs in order to buy more drugs to address their addiction. A recent client is a typical example, thrown out of her home because she was transgender, she lived in a cardboard box in the Tenderloin. She had PTSD from being sexually assaulted on the street and became addicted to crack and meth. She was arrested and charged because she sold 0.2 grams of crack to an undercover officer who offered her triple the street value, $30 for a $10 rock of crack cocaine. We call it rocks of crack cocaine, but my colleagues and I laugh because we're really talking about crumbs. A gram of crack cocaine is equivalent to a Sweet'N Low packet. This person was charged and facing eight years because she sold a fifth of a gram, a fifth of a Sweet'N Low packet to an undercover officer. Faced with that prospect, she took a lesser prison sentence, even though I believed that she had been entrapped. This is not isolated. Others similar public defendant clients have gone to trial and have been punished with lengthy prison sentences. Michael, a 44-year-old schizophrenic with a crack addiction, is serving a 14-year sentence when he was convicted after trial of selling less than a gram of crack. Kenneth, a 52-year-old heroin addict who became addicted to opiates after being shot outside a nightclub, received an 11-year sentence after trial because he had two prior convictions that were 10 years old. Albert received 9 years and 4 months after trial for selling a single rock of crack cocaine. And this is not just a problem in San Francisco. A colleague from Santa Barbara texted me yesterday and said he has a client who's serving 23 years for selling a small amount of narcotics and having prior convictions. I don't see these sentences imposed for other crimes for which the harms are more tangible and real, like DUIs causing injury, assault likely to cause great bodily injury. There are no three-year enhancements for those kind of crimes. There's no reason to single out drug sales for this hefty punishment. Finally, another problem with this three-year prior is that it makes no distinction based on weight. You can get this three-year prior for having a conviction where you sold a gram or less or whether or not you sold a kilogram. It's just not right, the punishment is disproportionate. The punishments don't deter people, I see how this causes a vicious cycle. People plead guilty to their first crime usually to get out. They don't have access to treatment because of the nature of their conviction. And the next time they're slammed, and the revolving door to prison opens and closes for the rest of their lives. SB 180 is not going to end all the injustices of the war on drugs or the war on crumbs, but it's the right direction to curtail that vicious cycle. On behalf of the San Francisco Public Defenders Office, on behalf of the clients who are addicted and sell drugs to support their addictions, people like Michael, Kenneth, and Albert, I urge you to end this unfair punishment and vote aye on SB 180, thank you.

[{'start': 0, 'end': 11, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Patrick Espinoza: Good morning, Madame Chair and Committee Members. My name is Patrick Espinoza, I'm the Deputy District Attorney in San Diego County District Attorney's Office, and have been a DA for 22 years, and our office is in support of SB 684. We've taken a number of significant amendments, and so it's the bill now is in a different form than what it was originally. And let me just start by explaining generally, what this measure is designed to do. It's designed to address the severely, mentally ill and most dangerous offenders in the criminal justice system. Those individuals who over a three year period have been mentally incompetent and cannot be restored to composite. So individuals who fall in that category have very limited options, they can not stay in custody, they can not stay in the state hospital. What this bill does is that it addresses a loop hole in the law, and the loop hole is this, is a Murphy conservatorship, is a conservatorship that is available for an individual who's charged with a felony offense, and a specific type of felony. A felony involving death, great bodily harm, or serious threat to others. That an individual to qualify for a Murphy conservatorship must not only be charged with that type of offense, but must also be deemed to be currently dangerous and must have been not been able to be restored to competency within three years. The quirk in the law, if you would call it that, the loophole, is that those individuals to be eligible for a Murphy Conservatorship have to have either been indicted by a grand jury, or have to have been already had a preliminary hearing, and been bound over, or are facing charges on a charging document called an information. An individual is not eligible for a Murphy Conservatorship if they were charged by those same crimes by felony complaint, but was declared incompetent early in the criminal proceedings before they went to a preliminary hearing and before that they could be bound over. What this legislation does, it closes that loophole, and identifies those offenders who are charged with the serious crimes, who are severely mentally ill and have not had a preliminary hearing. By allowing a judge to make a probable cause finding. And allow the prosecution and the court to order and place the individual on a Murphy Conservatorship. So long as there is a finding by a court, a probable cause, that's the fix in the law. There's a second thing that this legislation does as well. And the second thing that this does is it codifies. And puts into the statute the option of an LPS conservatorship, for this class of offenders. Previously, what we're seeing in practices that is done, if an individual otherwise qualifies, but what we're seeing is that oftentimes the LPS is currently not codified. And so this fixes that aspect of the law. There were other provisions in the initial legislation that are no longer in the bill. We've took substantial amendments and we've taken into account some of the concerns that the folks have. And so we're no longer seeking the codification of the credits that were in an original version of the bill. And we're not seeking the other issue which was what if an individual who can't be restored to mental competency and is not eligible for an LPS conservatorship nor a Murphy conservatorship. There was a provision previously to address the type of voluntary services that could be available for those individuals, that's no longer in the bill as well. And so our understanding currently is some of the folks that had opposed the bill for certain reasons, we've either addressed those concerns or we've focused the legislation to these two primary areas. And that is a probable cause hearing for folks to now be eligible for a Murphy Conservatorship and also to codify the LPS. And with that I'm happy to answer any questions the Committee may have. And in closing though I would ask the Committee to please, to vote aye in support of the now amended SB 684.

I want to thank Mr. Berman, the author of the bill for his leadership on this important issue. My name is Louis Blumberg. I'm the Director of the California Climate Change Program for the Nature Conservancy. The sea level rise database is an important tool in developing an effective response to the escalating impacts of climate change today as we have heard and will be so critical in the future, going forward. By eliminating the sunset clause through AB 184, the Legislature will ensure that decision makers, planners, and citizens, all have the latest information available to protect our coastal communities and the iconic natural shoreline that we all want to enjoy. Since the bill that established the database was passed in 2014, there have been several factors that have happened, changes and I just want to highlight a few developments in three key areas. The first is in science. First, 2015 and then 2016 were the hottest years on record. We've seen increased warming of the ocean, an accelerating ice melt at both poles, all of this contributing to sea level rise. Second, in the policy and planning arena, since this database was created, we've seen six bills passed by the Legislature addressing this topic in order to enhance the resilience of California to climate change. And they include sea level rise and other coastal hazards and many other provisions. And these bills are driving action right now by the Brown Administration and also by other state agencies, local government, and regional governments. And also the Coastal Commission has stepped in to continue to prioritize sea level rise as a serious threat with its new guidance on local coastal plans. And finally, I want to call attention to the federal threats that we're reading about in the paper this week. The federal administration in Washington, D.C. is proposing significant cuts to funding for climate change related scientific research, including sea level rising and cultural protection. These would be from the budgets from National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administrations and from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. So, maintaining California's climate data, including the sea level rise database, is more important today than ever given the current State of affairs at the federal level. So in conclusion, the sea level rise database is a critical component of the state's evolving and comprehensive response to climate change and it needs to be maintained. For these reasons, the Nature Conservancy supports 184 and urges your aye vote. Thank you for the opportunity.

Greg Stuber: Chairman, Committee Members. Thank you for the opportunity to speak. My name is Greg Stuber. I am the legislative Vice President of the State Coalition of Probation Organizations. We represent line staff probation officers up and down the state. Over the past several years, California has enacted a number of public safety and sentencing reforms. These reforms have created higher caseloads for probation officers throughout California. In addition, our caseloads are composed of more dangerous and often more criminally sophisticated individuals. In response to these impacts there are now significantly more probation officers actively supervising individuals in the community. In fact, on any given week day in Sacramento county, and many other counties, there are more probation officers on the streets than local police officers or deputy sheriffs. Because of this, by pure probability, when a call for mutual aid by another law enforcement agency is sent out, we are most likely the closest to the call and will be the first responders to the scene to provide assistance to that officer in distress, or to help control the emergency situation. As a matter of law under penal code 830.5, probation officers are required as a condition of employment to render mutual aid to other agencies. SB 587 would allow probation officers to display a blue warning light on our emergency vehicles in order to identify ourselves as law enforcement to the agencies we are responding to assist. And it will also identify ourselves as law enforcement to those agencies when they're responding to assist us. Even more important, the blue lights will also clearly identify us to the community when we are securing a law enforcement scene. To conclude, this bill does not expand our authority to drive emergency vehicles or to display red, white or amber lights. This bill simply adds blue lights in order for the public and other agencies to recognize us as law enforcement personnel. I ask for your aye vote.

Look up the words male and female in the dictionary, and all you'll find are physical descriptions. Our state driver's licenses have always recognized this truth. Pull out your driver's license and you will see, that all the identification characteristics listed are physical descriptions. Eye color, hair color, height, weight and sex. These are listed on the driver's license, because these physical characteristics can be independently verified by physical evidence, even if the person is unconscious. If you allow someone who is physically male, to list themselves on a government document as a female or vice versa, then the government will be legalizing a lie. That's assuming we're still using the dictionary to define what is male and female. As Senators, I know you think you are powerful, but you do not have the authority to simply change the meaning of words, just because you want to. If you are trying to resolve the identity document difficulties, that those who identify as transsexual. You would better off to remove sex as part of a person's physical description, on a driver's license or a birth certificate. Otherwise, you are knowingly letting citizens put false information on these documents. Senators, think about your own children. What did you tell them about their gender when they were born? Did you base what you told them on their physical characteristics? Or did you encourage your children to choose the gender, based on how they felt. Now this is a rhetorical question, because I know what most, if not all of you, did. You exclaimed to the whole world with joy the moment your child was born, that you had a boy or a girl. And you did this completely and without hesitation, based on the child's physical characteristics. In closing, the California Family Council believes government documents need to reflect biological facts, for identification and medical purposes. And secondly, we believe this bill advances a falsehood that being male or female, or no gender at all, is a choice that each person should make. Not a fact to celebrate or accept. Laws like this will simply erase any meaningful gender definitions. If being male or female is completely divorced, from biological facts. So we respectfully ask you to vote no on SB 179. Thank you.

[{'start': 22, 'end': 32, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Marc Joffe: Senator Beall, Members of the Committee, thank you for giving me the opportunity to address you today. My name is Marc Joffe and I am the Director of Policy Research at the California Policy Center. I'm speaking today in favor of Senate Bill 414, which would give California voters an opportunity to determine whether the California High-Speed Rail Project should continue. More than a decade ago, the High Speed Rail Authority officials compiled a cost benefit model that won the approval of the Bush administration, Governor Schwarzenegger and California voters. In the years that followed, we have learned several things that affect the calculations the Authority made back then. First, California's population is growing more slowly than previously expected. In fact, the Census Bureau recently reported that Marin County's population declined between July 1st, 2015 and July 1st, 2016, while both San Mateo County and Santa Clara County experienced net out migration. When it made its state population projections back in 2004, the Department of Finance predicted that California would have 55 million residents in 2050. Now, DOF only forecasts 49 million residents in 2050. The state's stagnating population casts further doubt on Authority ridership projections which have been disputed by independent researchers. Particularly striking to me, as an independent researcher, is the comparison between forecast high-speed rail ridership and actual ridership we see in Amtrak's Northeast Corridor, and as you can tell from my accent, I'm from the Northeast Corridor. HSR's median 2040 ridership projection of 40.7 million passengers per year is more than triple the current ridership of all Amtrak services between Boston, New York and Washington DC including both Acela and lower speed trains. The Northeast Corridor service area is more densely populated, has more overall population and has a century long tradition of inter-city train travel. It would thus appear that the Northeast Corridor ridership numbers are at best a ceiling rather than a floor for potential high speed rail ridership. Second, the system will not be able to transport passengers from San Francisco to Los Angeles in 2 hours and 40 minutes, as the Senator pointed out and as promised in the 2008 ballot language. By embracing the blended system and understandable cost saving measure, the Authority must accept maximum speeds well below the desired 220 miles per hour along existing rights of way. Third, hybrid and plug-in electric cars have become more popular than originally imagined. With California planning to migrate to a mostly zero-emission vehicle fleet by mid-century, the climate change benefits of high-speed rail will be much less than originally anticipated. Indeed, it may be many decades, if ever, before HSR emissions savings offset the greenhouse gasses being generated by the system's construction. Finally, estimated construction costs are now much higher than those provided to voters in the 2008 voter guide. Instead of $45 billion to create a truly statewide high-speed rail system, we are now looking at 64 billion just to build the segments connecting Los Angeles and San Francisco. I'm told additional billions would be needed to add service to Sacramento and San Diego. Aside from these changes and in part because of them, the financing picture for high-speed rail has become cloudy. The odds of the Trump administration providing more funding are close to zero. Private investors have not stepped up, and cap and trade revenues are coming in well below forecasts. If the state is serious about completing this project, it will need to issue tens of billions in additional bonds beyond those authorized in Proposition 1A. Recently, California Policy Center inventoried public agency obligations across our state, including bonds, pension obligations, and retiree medical care obligations, often called OPEC. We found that these debts amounted to $1.3 trillion, which is more than half of the state's gross state product. Layering additional bonds on top of this wall of debt can reasonably be regarded as unfair to our children and other future residents of this state. Given all that has changed since voters narrowly approved Proposition 1A in 2008, I believe that we need to revisit the cost benefit model on which HSR is based. By giving voters another chance to vote on high speed rail as provided for in SB 414, you can allow this necessary reevaluation to occur. Thank you for your time.

This is a good thing for California, but local government regulations governing the citing of wireless infrastructure have not kept pace with technology advancement. California needs a new regulatory framework for citing this modern wireless infrastructure in order to address consumer needs today and pave the way for 5G. We will continue to work in good faith as we have with the author and all stakeholders who are willing to work in good faith with us to achieve the share goal for California. There is an antenna at the top that is the small cell. This failure to keep pace with technology development inhibits the growth of wireless infrastructure and harms California, its consumers, and our customers, and public safety, all of which depend on this vital infrastructure. By doing the work together to modernize the regulatory framework for advanced wireless infrastructure deployment, the goal is to model the typical cases, and on that basis make a policy decision as a state to have those cases go through an administrative process focused on compliance with state and local codes. Cases that fall outside this framework will go through the existing process. It's that simple, it's more efficient, it's more cost effective and will streamline the deployment of this necessary infrastructure While allowing local governments to preserve their more time consuming discretionary review processes for those atypical cases that really should go through the full zoning process.

Some members of the community believe and some of the legislators believe and are concerned that we need to have the root cause analysis done. But the safety of the field and the results of the root cause are separate and independent. A federal agency task force has identified that the outer case of the well was the point of failure for the leaking well. As part of our safety enhancements what we have done, any well that will be used in operations, we've done a series of tests that were developed and in consultation with National Labs. To ensure that integrity of not only the outer casing of those wells, but also the inner tubing of those wells. As most of you are aware, there's two layers of piping that is used in each of these wells. So to take it even a step farther, the root cause analysis will determine that the mode and mechanism for the failure of that casing. But what we have done now on a going forward basis, we are not going to use the casing for any type of operation. It will only serve as a secondary barrier in case the brand new inner tubing that we have installed in any of these wells were to fail. We do not expect it, they have been tested, they have integrity, they are brand new pipes. We're being committed to safety and the integrity of the system in our activities. We now have multiple safety mechanisms in place. Not only the secondary barrier but we have you know, fence line monitoring. We do daily survey of each and every well with flare cameras, which are infrared cameras detecting the smallest amount of leaks on each of the wells. Throughout the entire facility, whether they'll be in operation or not. We also continue to have our daily inspections four times a day. People will basically view and see every site every day, four times a day, as we work through those. We also have continuous pressure monitoring on the wells, including that outer casing, which should not be used, which was formed a basis with 24/7 alert to the operations group in the field, if there is a potential problem that could be developing. Craig Lewis: Mr. Chair, members, thank you. My name is Craig Lewis, I'm the Executive Director of the Clean Coalition. And I'd like to establish eight very important facts with respect to transmission access charges. First, transmission access charges are defined as volumetric usage fees of the transmission grid for energy that flows over the transmission grid. Second, transmission access charges are paid by utilities not rate payers. But all rate payers will benefit when transmission investments are minimized. Third, SB 692 has no effect on net metering, whatsoever. Four, CAISO applies transmission access charges inconsistently. There's a correct way which applies in the majority of utility service territories in California. And there is an incorrect way that applies to the participating transmission owning utilities, which obviously include the big three investor owned utilities. The correct way meters transmission access charges at the substations, where energy is transferred from the transmission grid to the distribution grid. The incorrect way meters transmission access charges at the customer meter and charges exactly the same amount whether energy was generated in the neighborhood or whether it was generated a thousand miles away. Five, transmission access charges are massive, averaging about 2 cents per kilowatt hour in California today, and increasing to 5 cents per kilowatt-hour over the next 20 years. Transmission access charges are the fastest growing component of the energy, of the price of electricity. Six, the incorrect transmission access charge treatment represents an existing cost shift that is grossly distorting market outcomes and leading to overbuild of central generation and associated transmission infrastructure. Seven, participating transmission owner utilities receive 10.5% guaranteed return on equity. And I think it is fair to suspect that these utilities suffer from a conflict of interest in terms of whether to invest in more transmission infrastructure or not. Number eight, and lastly, local renewable energy is quickly becoming the cheapest form of renewable energy that can be procured in California. And local renewable energy also maximizes the community economic benefits of renewable energy and provides renewables driven resilience to communities. So, please, I ask you to support SB 692 so that all Californians can enjoy consistent and transparent structures resulting from more local renewables, and deliver the trifecta of unparalleled economic, environmental and resilience benefits.

Mr. Bloom talked about the court decision which was centered on the Costa-Hawkins Rent Control Act. Costa-Hawkins was never intended to apply to inclusionary zoning. There were an estimated 60 jurisdictions that had inclusionary policies on the books when Costa-Hawkins was enacted. And yet, in the reams of legislative history around the enactment of Costa-Hawkins, you will find not a single mention of inclusionary, as your analysis notes. You will find no mention of all these cities that had these policies on the books. It was strictly about strict rent control cities, and that's supported by the legislative history. And why would it mention inclusionary? If the Legislature's intent in adopting Costa-Hawkins was to examine whether and how local governments should apply inclusionary policies. Why would it only discuss, and why would it only aim itself at one aspect of inclusionary which is rental housing and not arguably the larger part of that policy which is its application to home ownership. It defines logic, and so we think the case was wrongly decided, it misapplied costs to Hawkins and this bill would fix that. Two other quick points. What is this bill not about, it's not about the validity of inclusionary. Let's be clear that the courts have been clear on this point, inclsuionary zoning is within the local control by a local legislative body. This has been the message consistently from the courts and as recently as two years ago from the California Supreme Court. This is well within your police powers to enact this and I know many of you are former local government officials. And this has always been understood to be a local decision. Now you may have different views about inclusionary, but I think you probably all share the notion that this is a local decision that should remain at the local level. And that's exactly what this bill does in my third and final point which is it takes the state back out of that question and leaves it with the locals. About 170 jurisdictions have adopted this policy, which means that the majority have not. And we want to continue to ensure that that is an option. Nothing in this bill changes any of that. It simply restores the status quo which takes the state out of that and leaves it to the locals to decide what is the right policy. And I'll pause in my comments there because we have one of our joint authors here we'd love to hear from him as well. Thank you.

And that is not something that can be facilitated if you're waiting a week to four weeks for your results. These are the laws that will provide the industry with an alternative to type A facilities for their production and internal quality controls. Helping to reduce the anticipated testing backlog that will likely occur when the mandatory type A testing requirement is triggered in January, 2018. Lastly, SB 311 will help incentivize testing throughout product development. Reducing the possibility of contamination and ensuring consistency before the product is sent to a Type A testing lab for final quality assurance and third-party verification. For these reasons, Sonoma Lab Works is pleased to support SB311 and respectfully ask for your support. And I'm available to answer any questions that you might have.

They did this not necessarily because they wanted to, but because they put the nation's interest before their own. It was about being honest with the American people. They help voters gain insight into a candidate's values by examining their finances and because presidents are exempt from conflict of interest laws, they ensure that voters would be able to check any candidate that might act from personal self-interest rather than national interest. This tradition, as we know, was broken by President Donald Trump. Today, our highest office is occupied by an individual who's finances we do not know. We do not know if tax code changes he's proposed to make would disproportionately benefit himself. [{'start': 151, 'end': 161, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 1342, 'end': 1354, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 2189, 'end': 2203, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 2205, 'end': 2215, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 2233, 'end': 2244, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 2322, 'end': 2334, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 2336, 'end': 2350, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 2352, 'end': 2364, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 2370, 'end': 2382, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Gowri Ramachandran: Sure, Madam Chairwoman, and members, thank you for having me here. I'm Gowri Ramachandran and I'm a Professor at Southwestern Law School. I'm not speaking on behalf of the law school though, just myself. I teach constitutional law and employment discrimination, and I supervise the Ninth Circuit Appellate Litigation Clinic. Thank you so much for the opportunity to testify today, as to the constitutionality of SB 149. I believe the bill is constitutional and would very likely withstand any legal challenge. States have brought authority to promulgate reasonable regulations of ballot access to candidates, but they may not add to the qualifications listed in the Constitution for federal office. First, the bill is a reasonable regulation of ballot access because it promotes a State and voter interest that is not only legitimate, but compelling. It does so without creating any onerous obligations for compliance. The interest, of course, is information for voters, and that is promoted without requiring candidates to file extremely early, gather large numbers of petition signatures, move their residence, or the like. It's very easy for candidates to comply with the bill. Second, the bill is, in fact, a ballot access provision rather than an added qualification for office because the underlying democratic principle behind that distinction is that voters must be free to choose the candidates of their choice. Unlike a law that imposes a term limit, which would prevent voters, for instance, from choosing an incumbent with a powerful Committee chair position, SB 149 does not restrict voter's choice. There's no person who cannot comply with the provision. While some voters may be uninterested in the tax return information, there's no legitimate voter interest in keeping that information from other voters who are interested. There's no voter interest in a candidate not disclosing, in the way that there is a voter interest in a powerful incumbent or someone who's a non-resident of the state at the time of filing. Finally, because the bill only applies to primary elections, there's no concern that California's ballot would undermine national popular vote counts, which may someday, if the national popular vote movement succeeds, determine who the majority of presidential electors select. For instance, if Mr. Trump fails to comply with SB 149 in 2020 and does not appear on the primary ballot in California, as long as the Republican party nominates him, he will appear on the ballot in California in the general election. So the national interest in being able to assess the popular vote and will of the people, consistency across the 50 states in the general election ballots, that's not undermined at all. So in some, I believe this bill would be very likely upheld in the courts because it promotes rather than undermining the constitutional interests of voters in our democratic system. Alex Alanis: Good afternoon, Madam Chair and members. Alex Alanis with the California Bankers Association. Just a few things to clarify. The private field loan market is actually a very small component of the overall student debt that's always discussed during these debates. Private students loans make up roughly about 6% of the student loan market or 94% is actually where the federal government does their lending through the direct lending program. The privacy to lenders, that should do a very good job of assessing borrowers prior to offering loans to students. They do an upfront assessment and an ability to pay standard. Unlike the federal government, they wanted to make sure that since the only collateral they have is the future earnings of the borrower. They want to make sure they actually get paid on a loan. The federal government does not do this up front assessment, which probably contributes to why private student lenders only have a 2%. Actually, it's less than 2% default rate on its loans. The federal government student loan program has over 11% default rate as part of its program. Now they're probably trying to do other attempts in order to reduce it, but everything they've done so far actually has not been all that successful, and so, Senator Wieckowski mentioned earlier about some of the additional programs that are used in order to at least keep the student up to date on their loans. The income program that they have actually has been somewhat of a problem. The Congressional Budget Office, I believe it was that did a report on this in showing that a lot of these loans are still, people are defaulting on them. So there's still a lot of work to be done in that area, but there is a big difference when it comes to collecting on these loans. As was mentioned earlier, our folks do actually do many attempts in order to keep the student up to date on their loans by offering different payment programs, but in the end, eventually you may have to go through a collection process. Private student lenders have to essentially file a lawsuit and accept a court order in order to do a wage garnishment and wage garnishments as we all know are actually court supervised programs. The federal government does not have that kind of restriction, whatsoever. It has a very heavy hand in how it does the collection for students. It can garnish their wages without a court order. It can seize your tax returns. They can take out some of your Social Security benefits and disability benefits and this is all without a court order. They can just go right in and take it. So, there are less restrictions for federal government on the collecting of their student loans. I think we do a very good job in borrowing to folks. As was mentioned earlier, a lot of these folks don't receive private student loans, because the program we have with respect to grants and the federal student loan market covers most of the tuition, but there are those instance in which you've got to fill the gap. With increasing tuition, there is probably going to be more and more need. We don't want to find ourselves in a situation where you make it more difficult for private student lenders to collect on loans. Because eventually the result is you're going to have less student loans or you'll have higher priced loans in this area, because the ability to collect is going to impact the price of the loan. So, we would hope that the bill would not move forward. With that, we oppose the measure.

Cliff Berg: Thank you, Madam Chair. Cliff Berg here on behalf of the California Association of Collectors. I would first start off by saying, we are sympathetic to the problem in America today of student loans. However, this bill is about wage garnishments and in effect this problem was solved last year in a bill that this Committee approved, which Mr. Wieckowski authored. SB 501, which was approved by the Legislature which was a negotiated agreement between the bankers, the collection industry and the author. Limited wage garnishments, California law up until SB 501 capped wage garnishments at 25%, under the provisions of SB 501, which applies to all consumer loans. We lowered the 25% cap and we lowered it below 15% for low income people. The major difference and the major thing that this bill accomplishes is it breaks the tie end between an income test and the garnishment. So by in essence, establishing a 15% cap across the board with no connection at all to income, you're in essence while trying to protect ex-students and let me mention the fact that again, wage garnishments are not brought against students. They are brought against people who have graduated and are in jobs and we'll talk about wage garnishments in a minute, but SB 501 was an agreement between industry and the author to cap wage garnishment on consumer debt including student loans tying it to income. This bill establishes a new cap for student loans only sets the precedent of starting to regulate wage garnishments by the type of debt not by the income of the debtor. That's why this bill is a problem. We have suggested to the author that he simply clarifying SB 501 that SB 501 apply to student debts, which we believe it is clear that it does. So why do we need this new bill other than because well the feds cap at 15%, so we ought to cap at 15%. 501 lowers the cap nearly to 8% for low income people, but 15% here applies to people who will make $1 million a year. There's no income limit or means test. That's why this is a bad public policy to both carve out wage garnishment laws on the type of debt creating problems for employers and sheriffs in servicing, and executing the wage garnishment. We're more than open to working with the author on a bill that limits wage garnishments based upon income, but you just create an arbitrary cap for people of any income level makes absolutely no sense. It's a bad public policy and for that reason, we are opposed to the bill.

[{'start': 23, 'end': 38, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Peter Treydte: Thank you, Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee. My name is Peter Treydte, and I am here on behalf of SEMA, the Specialty Equipment Market Association. Headquartered in Diamond Bar, California, we represent over 6600 member companies, some of whom manufacture performance parts for motor vehicles. Collectively, our member companies represent a $39.2 billion a year industry, with approximately 25% of their members calling California home. Emissions related performance parts are regulated by the California Air Resources Board. Parts and components that affect emissions of a motor vehicle require testing and approval by the agency to demonstrate that they do not increase emissions. Air intake systems, exhaust headers, superchargers, and tuning devices are examples of the types of parts that are regulated by the agency. Under section 27-156 of the Motor Vehicle Code, California requires an executive order exemption for any emissions related product sold into the state commonly referred to as a CARB EO. To obtain an EO, a company must submit an application and test data to prove these parts do not negatively impact emissions. Parts that are awarded an EO by CARB for legal sale and use in California are generally considered legal for sale and use in the other 49 states, as well. The testing done in support of the EO process is not done by CARB, but rather by independent laboratories recognized by CARB as being equipped to properly perform from the strict regulatory tests. Over the years SEMA has developed an excellent working relationship with CARB in its aftermarket parts division. As an industry group, we work to provide focused technical assistance to our member companies, which must have their parts approved through the agency. In 2014 SEMA opened an emissions testing facility of our own, the SEMA Emissions Compliance Center, which is one of about 40 labs nationwide that are recognized by CARB to run emissions tests on performance parts in preparation for the submission of an EO application. With the Emission Compliance Center operating at full capacity, and with an industry that continues to grow, we are sending more EO applications to CARB than in any time in our history. And to its credit, CARB has expended all existing resources to insure that parts needing an EO can move expeditiously through the process. However, the agency is simply understaffed, and with the growing demand from the automotive after market industry, substantial delays in the processing and issuing of EOs are not uncommon. This can be discouraging to the parts manufacturers when companies are unable to obtain EOs in a reasonable time frame. They may lose market share to companies that don't comply. This is bad for business, and it fosters a black market of products that are not legal. We are proposing through SB 660 to simply allow SEMA and other industry groups to reach an agreement with CARB to fund additional staff in the agency's after market parts division to process EO applications. If reached, our agreement would not provide preferential treatment to SEMA members, and we fully support the Committee's clarifying amendmen in that regard. I respectfully ask for your aye vote and am available to answer any questions, thank you.

According to election code 13119 B the measure required a ballot label for the proposed tax increase that included the amount of money to be raised annually, and the rate and duration of the text to be levied. Thus the City of Carson, along with the cities of Norwalk, Torrance, Santa Fe Springs, Signal Hill, Rancho Palos Verdes, and Commerce all filed suit seeking a court order to require the measure and ballot to provide the transparency described by law. Surprisingly, a Superior Court judge ruled that these transparency requirements only applied to tax measures proposed by citizens and not local agencies, which is why we are here before you today. AB 195 will clarify any ambiguities in the law, and ensure that citizens receive the information they're entitled to, regardless of who proposes a tax measure. Thank you for your time, and respectfully request your support today.

Nicholas Heidorn: Chair, members of the Committee Nicholas Heidorn with the California Common Cause in strong support of AB 1089 which helps secure the integrity of California elections down to the local level. Under current law the default, as the Assembly Member mentions, is that there are no contribution limits at the local level, unless the local government enacts it's own limits. This bill merely shifts that default role, so now there would be a default of $4,400 contribution limits, the same applicable to state officials, but again local governments which retain the local control to be able to opt out of the bill by enacting their own limits. Presently the vast majority of local jurisdictions have no contribution limits. Common Cause did a comprehensive survey had found that only 23% of cities and 28% counties have contribution limits. In jurisdictions without limits, we uncovered examples, numerous examples of candidates receiving five and even six figure contributions. Unlimited donations are a problem for our democracy, they open the door to corruption, pay to play, and undo influence.  They create the appearance of special interest control which demoralizes our democracy, and they help incumbents entrench themselves against competition. For example, in the City of Montebello the city sued one of its former Council Member alleging she voted for a $100 million plus trash hauling contract in exchange for a $45,000 campaign contribution. In Vallejo, a City Council candidate campaigned to build a port district on Mayor Island and received a $98,000 contribution, nearly all his money from the owner of the only rail line servicing that island. And in San Bernardino, County, one supervisor running for assessor received an astounding $242,000 direct contribution from a housing developer who had frequent business before the board. AB 1089 addresses the problems inherent in the system of unlimited contributions. by instead, placing a reasonable $4,400 default cap on local campaign contributions.  At the same time, I want to stress AB 1089 fully respects local autonomy. The bill establishes, again, only a default and locals can opt out of it. In closing, California is one of only four cities to have state contribution limits but no local contribution limits. We should not be an outlier when it comes to safeguarding the integrity of local elections where urge and aye vote.

I want to make sure that we get to the really important part today, is what's happening out there today. As Secretary Laird talked about, from the beginning of this when we first found out about this concern on the spillway. On February 7th, this is a game changer for the department. And many of the local agencies, but actually the region and California and now at the national and international level with respect to how we manage these kind of incidents. This is, we have a whole number of first times as we work through the response and recovery of this facility. So our department has focused on public safety and transparency throughout this entire process. Weve held 22 public briefings. Weve moved as fast as we can to address the comments and questions that come up. And we are focused on emergency response. But we are right now transitioning over to recovery as we're getting towards the kind of tail end of the spring run off period in the fed river basin. So what I want to do a little bit today, but I'm going to kind of go back to the Committee here to really focus on the interests. And making sure with the time that we have today to get to those points that you want to make sure that we talk a little bit about. But I do want to quickly highlight some of the response activities. And then really where we are transitioning to recovery today because there's a lot of steps, milestones that we've met here in the last couple weeks. First of all, again, this incident started on February 7th. This wasn't what we call a no notice event. This was not anticipated. This was not seen any threat, as a result of any inspections by multiple agencies and independent members in the past. But when this came to light the operators at Orville that were currently discharging flood waters over the spillway into the Feather River. Recognized they had a problem, had to shut the spillway down to start doing the assessments. So that led to a whole number of sequence of events, assessing the spillway. Assessing the weather monitoring the forecast a whole number of things started to happen. And we could not do this as Secretary Laird said with what we called the Unified Command Group and it included Army Core of Engineers, Bute County Sheriff Office. Sheriff Honey has being critical to addressing the public and security side of this. And they've been along with Calfire incident command team three. So as we brought those party together on almost a moments notice, again, there was lots of coordination, communication that needed to happen. Decisions need to be made, as we had an incoming extremely important weather event that posed a threat to the flood control facilities, with or without damaged spillway. Just to backtrack a little bit on Secretary Laird's comments, we again, thought unprecedented hydrology was a broken spillway. In 50 days of January and February of this year, 4.4 million acre feet of water went through the spillway and the powerhouse when it was operational. So this is is equal to average annual run-off, so that did not cause this spillway. But I think being able to manage this emergency response with incoming weather, with changing climatic conditions throughout this entire period. And the infrastructure that we still have on the mountain that's helping us manage this spring's run off with historic snow pack, it speaks to the engineering that's behind this facility. The dam is safe. The spillway is impaired. The emergency spillway worked. It does need some improvements and we're going to commit to make those improvements. So as we go through this, there's a whole number of, again, things with regard to emergency response happened. Again, our key unified command partners have been standing side by side with us throughout this entire process. We ask for funding from FEMA with regard to emergency response is $274 million, that's what we anticipate spending through May. We have an executive order from the Governor's office declaring an emergency that gave us the ability to do things that we would not normally be able to do. We have opened and closed this spillway a number of times to help manage this flood control system like we would normally would do. So the spillways that were generated from these hydraulic events and this runoff period up to date were managed through that spillway. And the power house in a way that did not threaten public safety. So taking water over the emergency spillway was a concern, and based on the latest information that we had at the time, with the changing hydraulic conditions We had to make a decision with regard to use of that emergency spillway, which was not by design. It was absolutely not part of the decision-making process. But it was there for the emergency, with the changing weather conditions over a period of about four to six hours. That in an effort to make sure that we had the spillway, itself, operational for the rest of this season. That we had to make sure that we kept it intact in a condition that we could use it throughout the rest of the season. But there is a point, through this whole period, that we needed to make sure that if we saw more degradation of the spillway to occur, there was a spot where, we call it a no-go point. In other words, the concrete on the spillway would degrade or fall away, because of the water we had to push over that spillway, to the point where we would have to stop using the spillway because of the threat to the radial arm gates. Which meant all of the water coming into the reservoir for the rest of the season would have to go over the emergency spillway. That's huge. That's a very tough decision to make when you try to use all your available flood storage, protect the infrastructure you have and the people downstream, not just in Oroville but all the way to the Delta, making sure that decisions that are being made are based on the latest information. And the impact of those decisions and unintended consequences are assessed as part of our contingency plan. So that was done throughout this entire process. Some of those decisions were really tough. But, again, I want to reiterate, we did not plan on taking water over the emergency spillway. But the spillway was used because of the change in hydrologic condition and that fact that we needed to better understand what the impact were with higher flows going over the spillway. Now, the good news is the spillway that we've been using, and is being used today, has been stable since February. So we have done some protective measures, rock bolting, grout, all of which is out there online, some of the protective measures. Some people have been out on the spillway deck and been able to see it firsthand. All of those protective measures have reinforced the integrity of the damage spill that we have, which allow us to pass the storm water that we receive in the snow melt here this spring. Lead is highly toxic to kids. Even small exposures to lead can cause irreversible damage to children's cognitive development and recent research shows that even at blood levels lower than five micrograms per deciliter, a level once thought to be safe, lead can still cause diminished intellectual and academic abilities, higher rates of neurobehavioral disorders like ADHD, and poor growth in children.
