However, we must acknowledge that the Ninth Circuit's decision was well reasoned as it applies to folding in air emissions into this complex statutory scheme. While it may be simple to add air as a medium to a statute it is not, because the change in the definition in this one area will have ripple effects throughout the statute and potentially other statutes, as well. We posit that the sponsor has identified an issue for the Legislature's consideration, but we do not believe that the solution has been found yet. The analysis identifies a couple of critical issues as Mr. Quark has identified the permitted versus unpermitted was one of them, so, I will not address that. It also identifies the question of joint and several liability which is a significant issue since there is no clarification under the HSAA at this point. I want to just raise four other concerns, just to explain how complex this issue is. Second, this would expand the statutory liability to everyone. As we mentioned, industry public entities and invaluable essential services.

In many cases, there doesn't seem to be any rhyme or reason for why these are so expensive or for why the prices are climbing so rapidly. And so we greatly agree that there needs to be more transparency as to the pricing of prescription drugs. To cite but a few examples Deflazacort is a steroid medication which is used to treat duchenne type muscular dystrophy. This is a medicine that's been available in Europe for sometime and sells there for about $1200 per year per patient. It recently gained FTA approval in the United States and now the plan is to price it at $89000 a year. For the same therapy. Just does not make sense. We often think of the high prices of health cares being driven by the new drugs but we are also seeing rapid price increases in drugs that have been around in some cases for decades. There's a medicine called nitropress which is used to treat high blood pressure and also congestive heart failure failure. It's been around since I was a medical student, which is a long time ago. But yet, we've seen the price of that drug go from $257 up to $805 recently a 212% increase. Doxycycline an antibiotic that's used to treat acne, bronchitis and other infectious diseases, has recently undergone an 1,000% increase in price. As much as I worry about the impact this is going to have on healthcare delivery systems, I'm also very concerned about how this impacts patients. As just referenced, we hear about patients whose insulin prices have increased 300%, and as a result, patients are having to use expired insulin, starve themselves, or do without insulin. And as a hospitalist physician, as someone who cares for patients in the hospital, I can tell you that when patients who are diabetic do without their insulin, it results in very, very serious illnesses that require very costly hospitalizations to remedy what is potentially an avoidable situation. So we wish to lend our support to SB17 and we thank Senator Hernandez for bringing forth this very, very important legislation. We think that it's going to provide transparency in pricing of prescription drugs, that is much needed. Thank you.

Sara Flocks: Madam Chair and members, Sara Flocks from the California Labor Federation. We are here today because our affiliates negotiate and purchase health benefits for 2 million members in California. And the skyrocketing price of prescription drugs is taking money out of our members pockets in the form of wages. And we find that SB 17 is important because it is an actual tool that purchasers can use in the face of skyrocketing drug prices. And I just wanted to touch very quickly on why the 90 day advanced notice of excessive price increases is so important to us. And why it is such a powerful tool. The first thing is it just allows us to manage our budgets. There's very limited amount of dollars that we have. It either comes out of wages or it comes out of employer's budgets. And so we want to know if there's a big price increase coming or even a smaller price increase for a high volume drug like insulin. We want to be able to prepare and to figure out how we can have the money to pay for it. The second is to be able to notify our members if there's going to be a change to the formulary. Pharmacy and therapeutics committees meet generally quarterly. And we want to have advanced notice before a drug is moved. We need to notify our members of this. And so, that 90 days gives a little bit of lead time, so we'll be able to get that notice out if there is a change. We also want to be able to avoid paying for unnecessary and expensive drugs. One example is Vemovo. It's an arthritis drug. And it went up 600% from 2013-2014. And we were paying for it. We never got a notice. We didn't know, except when we found out, we said Vemovo was actually just a combination of two over-the-counter drugs that cost $40 versus $1,600. So we would switch people but once people are taking a drug it's hard to reel them back and say, I know you had one drug now you gotta take two. We don't want to do that to our members, advance notice will help prevent that. And the last is just to be able to track these increases, there was public outcry over the increase in the price of the EpiPen, but that had been going up for years, it was a slow step increase. It got to the tipping point and there was people had outcry, but if we had known in advance that these increases were coming, we would've been able to try to do something about it. And so that is why the 90 days in this bill among the other parts are so important, thank you.

Kip Snyder: Thank you, Madame Chair, Members of the Committee. Kip Snyder, Vice President of State Policy at The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, or PhRMA, here in strong opposition of Senate Bill 17. Just to dig right into the bill, let me first address this concept of advanced notification of certain price increases. We're seeing a lot of pricing legislation in the states nationally. I have to say this one has us scratching our heads just a little bit as it's not really clear to us what sort of useable benefit is truly going to be derived from compelling manufacturers to wait 90 days before changing pricing, and on the flip side, on the risk side. We believe the bill's requirements could be highly disruptive and counterproductive within the pharmaceutical supply chain. In terms of supply of physical product, we're concerned that this could incentivize potential hoarding of product by distributors. A middle man in the period after the notification has occurred, but prior to the effective date of the increase, possibly resulting in lack of availability and access, as suppliers potentially try to game the system. We have no way of knowing, I don't think, how the marketplace would react to the provisions in the bill. We're not aware of any other industry where this sort of a mandated delay when physical product is involved. In addition to ramification with respect to supply we're concerned that this could actually disrupt competition across the industry. That's competition that has helped to keep prices down. I want to walk through specifically very quickly just a couple points with respect to how the bill would purport to work. The triggers in the bill are based on what's called wholesale acquisition cost, or WAC, which is essentially like a list or a sticker price. And like the sticker price for a car or the rate that you see on the back of your hotel room door, that's almost never the price that's actually paid. And that's because in the real world, we have these entities, pharmacy benefit managers, that negotiate very substantial discounts and the triggers, that are the backbone of this bill don't reflect those discounts. And keep in mind it's not manufacturers that are typically deciding and adjudicating what patients are going to pay at the pharmacy, it's the pharmacy benefit managers and the insurers who set up benefit design. We're also confident that the bill is structured could result in a voluminous amount of data and reporting. 10% over three year cumulative threshold is really roughly akin to CPI, so we believe there could be thousands of products in scope for the bill. Keep in mind again, based on list prices, and if you look at late available data on net prices produced by IMS, it shows that in 2015, on average, for branded pharmaceuticals, net prices only increased about 2.8%. Finally, the bill contains this requirement that manufacturers provide a host of proprietary information, which the state would then provide to the public. Our concern there, is that it will be disruptive to competition, again because the list price only tells part of the story. You might very well have a couple of companies in a commercial space that are in vigorous competition. And one company's commercial strategy may in fact be to discount heavily off the list price, in order to gain competitive advantage and formulary placement. And this bill would attempt to compel that manufacturer then to essentially disclose it's commercial strategy for all to see. We actually think it's a beneficial system when you have competitors that are offering rebates, and competing vigorously based on proprietary and confidential data. Similarly for new products, the bill would require companies to actually disclose their marketing and pricing plans. That's extremely proprietary information, so I certainly have a lot more to say. Want to be respectful of the time, but for those reasons as well as the overall way that pharmaceuticals fit into the health care system. We've got some, I think, pretty compelling data on that, I just want to close by saying there are some bad actors out there. We at PhRMA, we represent the research-based pharmaceutical industry. Our stomach turns sometimes with some of the things that we've seen by those bad actors as well. A lot of those egregious examples are what I've heard that's been highlighted. So I think that in a search for solutions, the focus should be potentially on those players. And I'll wrap up there, thanks.

PJ Barrilson: Good afternoon, PJ Barrilson from the California Hospital Association. And I just wanted to give you some additional statistics to some of the testimony earlier. Between 2011 and 2015 there were six closures of hospitals and emergency departments. In that same time, there were seven hospitals opened with emergency departments, and we had 710 emergency department bed spaces added to all of our 340 hospitals. So there is certainly a need for emergency services. And we are right there with the author, relative to the fact that emergency services and hospital care are vital to our communities. However, financially troubled hospitals may be unable to sustain continued emergency department losses. Hospitals that close are usually facing multi-million dollar losses before they close or reduce services. We have three issues with this bill. First, this bill adds AG approval to a process that already exists, whereby hospitals notify CDPH and LEMSA and EMSA relative to ED strategic closures. Adding an additional AG approval step could further jeopardize the financial stability of the hospital. Which further compromises access to care for the entire community. Our second issue was adding a retroactive clause to the bill that could significantly disrupt recent and finalized hospital transactions that have stabilized the hospital and services. Again could jeopardize community care. And finally, and oddly, while the state does not currently have a clear pathway to licence a free standing ED, there have been ongoing conversations about the advantages of this model in some communities with future changes in healthcare delivery. There are over 500 free standing emergency departments across the country that are serving under-served areas and seem to have a new focused way to deal with emergency care services. While the evidence and the objective information is yet to be collected we are looking at those models of care. And we're looking at those models to care to improve emergency services. This bill will strictly prohibit licensure of free standing EDs and impede the ability to explore this type of care delivery for our future. And it's for these reasons that Cha respectfully asks for your no vote on SB 687.

Dan Richard: My name is Dan Richard, I'm the chair of the High-Speed Rail Authority board. It's my pleasure and an honor to be here today. Mr. Chairman, as you said, this is a momentous project. And I appreciate the way you said we all have a stake in this. Part of our responsibility is not only to make sure that we are the effective stewards of public resources, but also to make sure that we are responsive to the oversight responsibilities of the Legislature. And so, we always appreciate the opportunity to come here and to answer your questions. I would note that I'm going to keep my opening remarks very short, there is a second panel on financing that will get in to more substantive matters. I also would like to keep my remarks short because, as I think the members know, we just delivered in the last few days, a project update report required by Senate Bill 1029 which the Legislature added to the appropriation bill for High-Speed Rail to assure ongoing oversight of the project. And I believe that this report, which is entitled in managing the nations largest infrastructural project, talks about where the project stands in terms of its costs and risk and so forth. I would just make a couple of quick points here. First of all, we are certainly not, we're not unaware of the controversial nature of much that surrounds this project. I think it probably goes with the territory these days of trying to do anything of this magnitude in America. But I would tell you that it's always important to come back to kind of a fundamental question, and often people ask me, well why does California need a high-speed rail system? And I respectfully always suggest that perhaps that's not the right starting place. The right starting place is to envision a state by mid-century that's going to have 50 million people. And the question for us as leaders, you as people's representatives in the Legislature, and those of us who are in the Executive Branch, is how we plan today to meet that challenge. We think that the data has shown that alternative investments to provide mobility for those 50 million people would cost two to three times what we're talking about here. And not provide the sustainability benefits that High-Speed Rail does provide. The authors of the High-Speed Rail bond act, had a vision that this transportation system would connect areas of California. And I think one of the things you are going to hear today, when you hear from the small businesses, is about the impact of high-speed rail on one of our most underinvested areas in California, in the Central Valley. The counties of Fresno and Merced have the two highest poverty rates in the state, in excess of 25%. And we are making a multi-billion dollar investment there to connect that economic, socioeconomic region with the rest of the state. Very quickly, in our 2016 business plan that we developed last spring, we indicated that the High-Speed Rail program has now moved from the planning stage to the project delivery stage. And as you mentioned Mr Chairman, construction is underway across the Central Valley, my colleague Mr Morales is going to update you on that. But we also articulated for the Legislature and the public in that business plan A real confidence that we have a path to getting the high speed rail program up and running, and it's really based on three legs of the stool. First, we envisioned the first operating segment that would connect the Central Valley to Silicon Valley. And this could have transformative effects on both regions. Central Valley needs the investment. Silicon Valley has no place to house people who are working in what is the engine of the California economy. Second, and we see that with the resources that we would have, particularly if cap and trade is extended, which we hope that issue is clarified by the Legislature, that under constrained budget scenario we have enough resources to make that connection between the Federal dollars, the bond dollars, and the cap and trade dollars. And that's a very significant determination we made. Second, we've been very proud of the fact, going back five years that we described the program as not a standalone transportation system but as an integral part of an integrated, rail modernization system in California. Becomes essential for us to work with local and regional transportation systems to connect to high speed rail. And we're the backbone of that but we're making parallel investments in Southern California and in the bookends with some very critical, timely investments that have immediate beneficial effects throughout the State. And third, we continue to do the work necessary to prepare for other legs of the project to be built when the funding becomes available. So we have a very clear sense of how we want to do this. And what I'm going to talk about in the next panel is how we're addressing and managing risks, financial and otherwise. But with that Mr. Chairman, I, again, want to thank you for the opportunity to appear here today.

But we're pleased that everyone has gathered here today to talk about this issue and how it impacts those served and supported by Regional Centers. What we see in other health and human services agencies' programs is that there is significant challenge in getting people in the front door. We see less of that in the Regional Center System, which means the outreach is working fairly well in those populations, but it's critical that we examine the issue of whether people's needs are being met through a combination of services available to them. The goal of Regional Centers is the service provision and meeting of people's need for individuals with developmental disabilities in their families. As the Chair mentioned, they were intentionally created to be non-profit agencies and the benefit of that is that they are responsive not just to the Department of Developmental Services, but also to their local communities. We know that there's certain things that drive disparity. We know that certain populations have a distrust of government and that people have a challenge in discriminating a Regional Center from a government agency. We know that that distrust of government has grown significantly in recent months because of issues at the federal level. We also know there are differing attitudes among various racial and ethnic groups about disability and also the private versus public role in meeting the needs associated with it. We also know that challenges associated, not with race and ethnicity, but with differing levels of socioeconomic status, also drive some of these differences. For instance, individuals who are facing housing or food insecurity oftentimes have difficulty prioritizing the developmental needs of their child over those concerns. We know that parents with difficult work schedules or who maybe are working multiple jobs also face similar challenges. As Dr. Level mentioned, the data that Regional Centers have been collecting tells a piece of the story, but there's other pieces that are missing and those are the things that we need to explore further. One pieces the data that's available tells only what Regional Centers are purchasing for individuals. Regional Centers are required to seek services from other generic agencies such as schools and Social Security and medic health and private insurance before they purchase services. The available data doesn't tell us the whole breadth of things that's being purchased for an individual, only those things that Regional Centers are funding when there is no other service available. The available data doesn't allow us to break out things that are purchased through a contract with a vendor, such as transportation and some supported employment services. So, even though an individual may be receiving those services, they won't appear in the data. We also are concerned and want to talk a little bit about individuals for whom the Regional Center isn't purchasing any services. It's important to note that the core mission of the Regional Center is service co-ordination, ensuring that an individual's needs are met across his or her lifespan. Individuals who have no services purchased from them through the Regional Center still receive the critical support of service coordination and they continue to rely on that service, and they continue to choose to have that person, their service coordinator, in their lives to help them to navigate other complex systems, such as Social Security and medical. Dr. Level did a fantastic job explaining the impact that living arrangements have on purchase of service utilization. And we know that individuals from diverse communities are much more likely to remain at home as adults than individuals who are Caucasian. There are some other things that we need to consider, such as systemic barriers, services to support families who are supporting individuals at home were cut in 2009, things like camp and social recreation opportunities, as well as, there was a cap put on respite. Additionally, in 2011, the federal government set, provided instructions that the state was no longer to pay families directly for services. And if they did, the federal government would no longer contribute to the cost of those services. Many of the families that were receiving respite services were doing it through an informal network that they had developed themselves and this change at the federal level required that this process become much more formalized and that the caregivers that they selected whom they chose and whom they trusted would go through formalized training, background checks, screenings, and it made the system much less nimble for them. A lot of work has been done in the last five years. As Director Bardsman noted, the promotora model out of Frank D. Lanterman Regional Center used two community members who were known entities in their communities. They spoke Spanish and they were trusted among the Spanish-speaking individuals who reside in that area. They each worked with 26 individuals and worked to meet them where they were, worked to help them to address things like housing and food insecurity, so that they could focus on their child's disability, help them to develop self advocacy skills so that they knew how to better access and navigate systems. This was a tremendously successful model, but there's been other good work done, as well. Both Golden Gate Regional Center and San Andreas Regional Center worked with Stanford University to explore different options for how to meet the needs of various communities. First, by identifying what are those barriers, what are their perceptions that may be blocking people before they access the services they need, and then coming up with creative solutions for addressing those. Regional Center of Orange County works with English, Spanish and Vietnamese language newspapers to make sure that they get the word out about meetings that they are having about important topics. There's been some good information that's come out of the annual meetings that each Regional Center holds as well. For example, San Gabriel Pomona Regional Center heard from their Spanish-speaking community that they were accessing less respite than they were authorized because they couldn't schedule respite providers with in a timely way and their monthly respite allocations would expire. So Pomona Regional Center changed their authorizations to quarterly to make those services more usable and more friendly to the intended audience. I could go on and on about various examples, but I did want to touch on the additional work that's being done as a result of the special session last year. Director Berg Smith spoke of the cultural specialist that Regional Center is in the process of hiring and there's many projects under way that are being tried to see what is it that will work because there is nothing like testing something in the field. For example, are there ways to address families maybe forgetting appointments, and so Frank D Lanterman Regional Center is working with other Regional Centers to develop an automated phone system that's multilingual to provide information for families. Another Regional Center, Inland Regional Center, is working to provide parent training specifically for people who aren't accessing Regional Center paid supports and they're using a known community entity to do that. So overall, I just wanted to share these things that have been done, and while recognizing that there's more work to be done, provide some assurance to the Committee that the Regional Center System takes these issues very seriously, and looks forward to continuing to address them. Thank you.

Ellen Peter: Thank you very much. Good morning Chairman Bloom, Members of the Committee. My name is Ellen Peter, I'm the Chief Counsel of the California Air Resources Board. Prior to joining ARB, I was at the California Attorney General's Office for over 20 years. There, I defended state agencies and also prosecuted their enforcement cases. Today, I'm going to talk about ARB's enforcement program. Of course, stop me at any time for questions. ARB's second witness today is Deputy Executive Officer Edie Chang. She will address the legislative mandates and also how ARB addresses them. As Edie will describe, a key approach of ARB is regulations, but without enforcement regulations are meaningless. Vigorous enforcement sets a level playing field and it also assures that companies that cheat do not benefit from this cheating. Regulations basically are setting out public health and air quality goals. Without enforcement, these aren't met. So, the case I want to highlight today is ARB versus Volkswagen, a diesel scandal case that broke in September, 2015. The reason I want to focus on this case is for two reasons. One, it's the biggest enforcement case that ARB has ever brought. And second, it really highlights the scientific and engineering abilities of the ARB staff. Frankly, I want to brag about them. They forced a confession with persistent questioning, innovative testing, an a refusal to back down. I'm still under the federal court's gag order in the civil case, but more information is now public because of the criminal indictments that were unsealed later this year, earlier this year, sorry. Last week, VW pled guilty in criminal court in Detroit and, also, there are seven individual VW employees that are now under indictment. So I'm going to rely on all of that public testimony that's out, available, for my testimony today. The conspiracy started a decade ago. Diesel vehicles are common in Europe, but they were not sold in California because of our tailpipe emission standards. However, over time, ARB cleaned up the fuel and then diesel vehicles became a possibility. VW jumped on this opportunity and was the first to announce a clean-diesel vehicle to be sold in model year 2009. The problem? Their marketing announcement was ahead of their engineering expertise. Instead of solving the engineering problem or waiting a year, VW decided to cheat and then to lie. In the criminal indictments and guilty pleas the facts are set out how a research project started by ARB and others, including the West Virginia University, blossomed into the discovery of this enormous emission scandal using a defeat device. So what's a defeat device? Essentially, it turns off your emissions control system in your car and, in some cases, the VW's system increased the emissions up to 40 times higher than was allowed. So cars are really complicated computer systems and they continually adjust the various systems. If your car has a problem, for example, a rock pierces the oil pan, and all your oil drains out, the car automatically goes into a protection mode and shuts down different systems including the emissions control device. That's totally okay, and a less dramatic example is if you're accelerating and passing another car, the engines are allowed to adjust the emissions control system, that's all okay. These are considered AECDs, auxiliary emissions control devices, and they're fine as long as they're listed in the company's certification application, they have to be disclosed. What's not okay is not telling ARB about these different devices. So for each year, for each engine type, for each manufacturer, both cars and trucks, ARB considers these certification applications. They must be submitted, and until approved, these cars cannot be sold in California. In VW's certification applications, instead of outlining the permitted AECD situations where the emissions control systems turns off, in fact, what they did was they had an emissions control device system that only turned on the emission control system in the lab, on the dyno, using the prescribed test cycles. So in our El Monte ARB lab we have these huge dynos where we put the cars on and run them on these cycles, they have certain cycles.

Edie Chang: Good morning. Good morning Chairman Bloom and Members of the Committee. My name is Edie Chang, I'm a deputy executive officer at the California Air Resources Board and today, I've been asked to talk about ARB's process in meeting our overall goals. The ARB is tasked with three main mandates. Achieving health based air quality standards for ozone, particulate matter, and other air pollutants that are regulated under the State and Federal Clean Air Acts. Second, reducing public exposure to toxic air contaminants, such as diesel particulate matter. And third, and most recently, is reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Thanks to the leadership of the Legislature and the administration, industry investment, and local and statewide policy, today cars, trucks, and other equipment in California are cleaner and more efficient than they ever have been. We've also seen significant reductions in emissions from stationary sources like factories and refineries. California has led the nation in developing innovative and technology advancing pollution control programs and over the last 50 years we've adopted regulations that set vehicle emissions standards, require cleaner fuels, and mandate cleaner consumer products. So a lot of our early programs focused on reducing smog-forming pollutants, but many of these programs have multiple benefits. As we've acquired these additional mandates we've been strengthening our efforts to develop programs that do all three. That reduce smog forming emissions, reduce toxic emissions and greenhouse gas emissions simultaneously through a coordinated planning effort. One example of this is the mobile source strategy that we released last year. So this strategy outlines a comprehensive set of actions to help the state simultaneously meet its air quality, climate change and toxics risk reduction goals over the next 15 years. In developing that strategy we did a coordinated assessment of how advanced technologies, cleaner renewable fuels, and efficiency improvements can all work together to meet our multiple goals. And then we identified a core set of measures that needed to be implemented to meet these goals. These include pushing new cleaner technology, cleaner fuels and also durability and inspection programs to make sure that in the field we actually continue to obtain those emission benefits. And that's a theme that you will hear from us over and over. Sort of this three prong strategy of having newer, cleaner equipment, having clean fuels to reduce emissions and help that clean equipment continue to run and then making sure that equipment stays clean. The light duty car sector is one example of that. So we set new standards and make sure that new cars are as clean as they possibly can be. We have fuel standards that require the use of cleaner fuels. Those cleaner fuels allow the technology in the cars to work and they also depending on the fuel formulation can reduce emissions of toxic air pollution. And then on the car side we have a smog check program and it makes sure that cars that are on the road stay as clean as they can be. On the light duty side we have an additional component sort of a fourth prong which is the zero emission vehicle program. So that electric car program is really designed to drive new technologies for the long term transformation that we need to meet our longer term air quality goals. So this integrated planning process is what helps ensure that our policies and programs are all working together. As we implement the specific programs that are described in these plans, we monitor the program effectiveness through reporting, certification, and enforcement programs, as you heard from our chief counsel. And through our public process, when something isn't working we hear about it from the public, and we work with the Legislature, the public, and the administration to develop a fix. These reductions translate into real world air quality benefits and the real world proof is in the air quality that we measure. We have over 250 air quality monitoring stations that measure the air in California every day. And what we see is that air quality is improving. I want to quickly walk through the progress that we've made in each of these areas starting with criteria pollutants. California has a long and successful history of meeting the health-based standards. If you look in the package of materials, there's a map of California and it shows the 19 areas of the state that once exceeded the federal ozone standards. Sometimes I'll use smog instead of ozone. So, the lighter grey areas are the only areas that are still non-attainment. That still have what the federal standard would be considered unhealthy air. Of these Southern California, we call it the South Coast, kind of in the air quality jargon and the San Joaquin Valley continue to face the most critical air quality challenges. The next map shows the progress that's occurred just in the south coast and that's the nation's smoggiest region. The map on the left, and if it was in color, you would see it's very, very dark red, it's very very dark black and gray in what you have, that shows ozone levels in 1990. In 1990, the entire region violated the ozone standard with peak levels, the highest levels that were measured twice as high as the standard. And I have to say I grew up in Riverside, and my family moved to Riverside in 1970 and I graduated from high school in 1986. So the whole time I was living in Riverside, it was much, much worse than the graph that you have right there. The map on the right shows peak concentrations today. They've declined 45% and 40% of the population lives in areas that meets the standard, because it's not in color you can't see, but the coastal areas are actually green, and so those areas are meeting the standard now. We still have work to do as we move to the eastern part of the air basin. Moving now to air toxics. Exposure to toxic air contaminants has decreased substantially since the 1990s when the Legislature passed the Tanner Bill and the Hot Spots Bill. The reduction in benzene is one of our biggest success stories. Benzene is known to cause cancer and can be found in gasoline. And as you can see in the chart that's in the materials, benzene levels have dropped nearly 90% since 1990. And 1990 was when we passed a package of regulations focused on cars, that required cleaner fuels, and cleaner emission standards for those cars. Benzene reduction and air toxics reduction was one of the points of those regulations. It included this cleaner-burning gasoline that I mentioned, cleaner air quality, cleaner emission standards for cars, and also better vapor recovery. So this is the gasoline that is emitted from your car when it gets hot and cold. Making sure that those vapors are captured, and also making sure that when you're fueling your car at a gas station, those vapors are captured and you're not breathing them in. In addition, in 1998, ARB identified diesel particulate as an air toxic and we embarked on an aggressive control program to reduce public exposure to diesel particulate. Since 1990, levels of diesel particulate have dropped nearly 70% with some of the most significant decreases in California's most disadvantaged communities. And then lastly, I want to talk about the greenhouse gas program. In AB32, ARB was given the responsibility for putting together the plan for how we will meet the state's targets. We work closely with our state agency partners develop and implement this plan. And together we're implementing the renewable portfolio standard, energy efficiency standards, the low carbon field standard, and the cap and trade program. As a result of these comprehensive actions, we're on track to meet the 2020 greenhouse gas target. More is needed to meet the 2030 target that the Legislature enacted last year in SB 32, and that's the subject of the draft scoping plan update which is currently out for public review, we've release the document in January. The scoping plan is our comprehensive planning document for climate change, and its development has been coordinated with a mobile source strategy and other work at the Air Resources Board. To get to 2030 on the climate perspective, we don't need new programs, we can depend on our existing and tested programs. The Draft Scoping Plan proposes increases to renewable energy, reductions in short live climate pollutants as called for by legislation in SB 605 and 1383. It incorporates the mobile source strategy that I discussed earlier, which also includes a sustainable freight strategy. And it proposes the continuation of the cap and trade program. The main goal of the cap and trade program is to cap greenhouse gas emissions and it is achieving that goal. One of the additional features of the cap and trade program is we auction allowances, these permit to emit, and the related investment of the proceeds to advance our climate program to provide multiple additional benefits especially in disadvantaged communities. Yesterday, we released the 2017 annual report for our climate change investments. It looks like this. A $3.4 billion has been appropriated to date by the Legislature and this report provides information about the projects that have been funded. We are always continuing to look for ways to improve our understanding and our methods. For example, in the scoping plan that I talked about we've begun to expand the types of analysis that we're doing partly as a result of direction from the Legislature. The scoping plan economic analysis looks at state level impacts which we've been doing for awhile. But it's also going to look at regional impacts to try to take those economic impacts and focus in, in different areas, which our particular concern as we start thinking about regional impacts in disadvantaged communities. We're also estimating the health benefits of the plan, and you're going to be incorporating that into our economic analysis. Having a better understanding of regional effects and health impacts is going to help us better design and implement our programs as we move forward. In response to feedback from stakeholders including our environmental justice Advisory Committee we have delayed the consideration of the scoping plan to June of 2017, to allow time to refine some of our analyses, and also allow time for additional public process, including community meetings in environmental justice communities. ARB and the administration as a whole is continuing to work to improve our outreach to environmental justice communities. Matt Almy: Thank you, good morning Matt Almy Department of Finance. The budget supports the state's ambitious climate change goals by proposing a $2.2 billion Cap and Trade Expenditure Plan to be allocated after a legislation confirming the Air Board's authority to administer the Cap and Trade Program beyond 2020 is acted through a two thirds vote. This proposal aligns with state wide climate change goals. In 2015, the Governor introduced the most ambitious 2030 climate target in North America, a reduction of greenhouse gas emissions to 40% below 1990 levels and the Legislature codified this target with the passage of SB 32. California also strengthened its global leadership role through its participation in the Paris Climate Agreement. Achieving these ambitious and necessary environmental goals while continuing to expand the state's strong economy requires implementing cost effective solutions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. As Ms. Chang discussed earlier, in January, the airboard released the draft scoping plan providing a blueprint for reaching 2030 climate targets. The scoping plan evaluates five scenarios for meeting the 2030 target which includes, sector specific emission reductions to traditional command and control regulations, a carbon tax and a continuation of the Cap and Trade Program. The draft's scoping plan explains that Cap and Trade represents the most flexible and cost effective approach to continue reducing GHG's to meet emission reduction requirements over the next 13 years. Furthermore consistent with the legislative directive and AB 197, to prioritize direct emission controls, the draft scoping plan calls for direct reductions at refineries. To complement these direct reductions an ongoing priority for the state will be to find ways to reduce toxic air contaminants and criteria pollutants from large emitters. In terms of the specific budget proposal and consistent with the proposed scoping plan, the Governor's Budget proposes trailer bill legislation to confirm the airboard's authority through a two thirds urgency vote to administer Cap and Trade auctions beyond 2020. Not only is the extension of Cap and Trade beyond 2020 necessary to meet the statewide climate goals, but to also address the significant volatility of Cap and Trade auctions over the past year. After several consecutive auctions that generated over 500 million in proceeds, the May and August auctions in 2016 generated only 10 million and 8 million respectively. The November 2016 auction generated 364 million, and then the most recent auction in February generated 8 million. One of the factors that may have contributed to this revenue volatility is the perceived legal uncertainty about Cap and Trade beyond 2020. The budget proposes a $2.2 billion Cap and Trade expenditure plan to be allocated after legislation confirming the Air Board's authority to administer Cap and Trade beyond 2020 is enacted through a two thirds vote. The budget builds upon the investment categories funded in the 2016 Cap and Trade agreement such as short lived climate pollutants, carbon sequestration, low carbon transportation and transformative climate communities. The Cap and Trade Plan also includes $500 million for the administration's proposed transportation package. Although the $2.2 billion budget proposal currently reflects broad program categories, it is the administration's intent to collaborate with the Legislature on the Cap and Trade package that supports specific programs. In closing and as Ms. Chang alluded to earlier, the administration has released the 2017 annual report on outcomes of Cap and Trade programs which will inform the budget discussions moving forward. Thank you.

In our view, the proposal raises kind of three broad critical questions that the Legislature will be wrestling with as they consider the proposal. First, should the cap and trade be authorized beyond 2020? Second, is the two-thirds vote needed to extend cap and trade and if so what are the merits of that? And third, how should the Legislature if it does approve cap and trade, how should it use the revenue? So in the first bundle of question, should the Legislature authorize a program beyond 2020, we are recommending that the Legislature extend the program. Either cap in trade, or a carbon tax, and I'm happy to get into a discussion of the tradeoffs associated with those two. But we do recommend the Legislature authorize some sort of market based mechanism to help achieve its 2030 goals. And I think some important context here is just the uncertainty around what it will take to meet those 2030 goals and the potential for actions needed to meet those 2030 goals being much more aggressive and potentially much more costly. And we think market-based approaches are much less costly approaches to meeting the 2030 goal. So that's our primary rational for recommending extension of either a cap and trade or a carbon tax. Along with that and related to kind of the uncertainty and the potential for significantly higher costs associated with meeting the aggressive goals, we make some more specific recommendations around the design of the program. We also make some recommendations related to just additional oversight, related to moving forward and analyzing the state's climate policies. If, I think technically, the cap and trade program could be extended with a two-thirds vote but we're recommending the Legislature to try to extend it with, excuse me, it could be extended with a majority vote. But we're recommending that the Legislature does extend it to try and do it with a two-thirds vote. That would provide some legal certainty around the ability auction off allowances which we think is an important part of the program and in sending the appropriate market signals. So there's the legal certainty around the two-thirds vote and the benefits there. Another key benefit we see with authorizing the program with the two-thirds vote is that it potentially gives the Legislature the flexibility to broaden the potential uses of the revenue that come in. Currently, the legal requirements on the funds are that they be used for greenhouse gas reduction activities only. And so, this gets to sort of our third set of recommendations on how the Legislature should use the money if the cap and trade program is reauthorized. And, we think broadening that allowable use is an important consideration for the Legislature generated revenue from the program isn't really a primary goal of the program. The goal is to use allowance prices and price signals to encourage those cost effective productions. And as sort of a result of implementing the program and auctioning the allowances, the state does generate revenue but that's not a primary goal. And so, we think sort of removing that requirement that the money only be spent on greenhouse gas reduction activities creates some additional flexibility for the Legislature to use that money on its highest priorities. In our view, one of those highest priorities that we think that the Legislature should be looking at when thinking about how to use the money is using that to provide rebates or offsetting tax reductions to help offset some of the costs to households and businesses that will be incurred if the program is extended. And, we think that's particularly important in light of some of the uncertainty around allowance prices. And if allowance prices do get significantly higher that means higher energy costs for households and consumers and using the money to offset some of those costs would be an important consideration. We make some other more specific recommendations related to the language that is actually proposed by the administration. For example, we recommend rejecting the language that makes the spending of the money contingent on authorizing the program with the two-thirds vote. Although we think the spending and the program itself are obviously very much related, we think that language unnecessarily ties the Legislature's hands on its authority to spend the money. And we also make some recommendations related to providing more specific program allocations rather than some of the broad categories that are in the current language that the administration has proposed. The administration has indicated that, that's just sort of its opening shot and is willing to engage in discussions with the Legislature around sort of specific program allocations but we just wanted to flag that for you. So I will end my comments there and I'm happy to answer any questions that you have.

[{'start': 19, 'end': 29, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Matt Almy: Actually Matt Almy, Department of Finance. Since this is kind of a multi-department package, I thought I would kind of give a little bit of an overview of how the different pieces interrelate. Just for context purposes, the state has experienced significant rainfall, as a result of several atmospheric river storms in January and February. As a result of these storms, the state's reservoirs are at capacity, and additional pressure has been placed upon flood control systems in the Central Valley. The significant amount of CRS snowpack, also makes it likely that rivers and streams will continue to experience high flows during the spring and early summer months. These significant weather events, as well as the spillway failure at Orville, illustrate the public safety importance of investing in the state's water infrastructure an emergency preparedness. Consequently, the administration is proposing to enhance dam safety and flood protection, through three specific measures. First, the administration's requesting the Legislature appropriate $387 million Proposition 1 Water Bond, for DWR to accelerate a balanced portfolio of flood-control projects over the next two fiscal years. These new funds provided from the flood-management allocation of Proposition 1 will complement existing Prop 1E and Prop 84 bond funds, that have already been appropriated. These funds will enhance flood production in the Central Valley, the Delta, and other areas of the state with significant flood risk. Consistent with the system wide approach identified in the Central Valley Flood Plan, these funds will help meet the urgent needs of urban, small community and rural areas throughout the Central Valley, Delta and beyond. Second, the administration is requesting the Legislature approve a comprehensive proposal to enhance dam safety, which includes the following elements. $3 million for DWR to conduct a more extensive evaluations of the appurtenant structures such as spill ways, gates, and outlets, than the current visual inspections. The inspections will include additional geological and hydrological evaluations, as well as updated design and construction standards. Also, Trailer Bill Language to require that dams have updated inundation maps and emergency action plans, that are updated every 10 years with limited exceptions for low-risk stamps. And finally $5.3 million for DWR and OES to review and approved, required inundation maps and related emergency response plans. And lastly, and this is under the Governor's emergency powers, and isn't requesting any legislative action, is the redirection of up to $50 million of DWR's existing deferred maintenance appropriation for emergency preparedness and response actions. Including pre-deployment of flood fight materials, flood fighting levy risk assessments, and increased coordination between state, local and federal agencies. Also, targeting flood control projects to be completed within the current flood season, which will address human health and safety issues, flood system convenes some limitations, and critical infrastructure needs in areas at risk of significant flooding. Thank you.

Dean Fujimoto: Good afternoon again. I'm Dean Fujimoto, Deputy Director with California Department of Aging. Let me first by start by giving a brief background of MSSP. Currently, we have 30 MSSP sites statewide that provide social and healthcare management to frail elderly individuals. On average, the average MSSP individual is about 85-years old. And these individuals are all certified for placement in nursing facilities, but wish to remain in the community. Services provided with MSSP funds include, but are not limited to, care management, adult social daycare, housing assistance, personal care services, respite, transportation, etc. Through an interagency agreement that our department has with the Department of Health Care Services, CDA oversees the operations of the MSSP program and contracts with local entities that directly provide MSSP services to up to 12,000 individuals annually. As it pertains to the community care initiative the budget proposal extends core elements of the CCI program for two additional years such as Cal Mediconnect, mandatory enrollment of dual eligible and integrating long term services and supports except for IHSS into managed care. With this in mind MSSP sites in the Cal Mediconnect counties will continue to contract with managed care and CDA and DHCS will work on the state transition plan to ensure a smooth transition of MSSP into managed care. This transition would occur no sooner than January of 2020.

Joe Rodriguez: Good afternoon again, Joe Rodriguez, California State Long Term Care Ombudsman. Authority for the Office of the State Long Term Care Ombudsman is found in the federal Older Americans Act, as well as our state's Older Californians Act. The office develops policy and provides oversight to 35 local long term care on ombudsman programs statewide. As independent advocates for residents of long term care facilities, ombudsman representatives promote residence rights and assure those rights are protected in federal and state law. As the California State Ombudsman, I analyze, comment on, and monitor the development and implementation of local laws, state laws, federal laws and regulations, and other governmental policies and actions that pertain to the health, safety, welfare, and rights of residence of long-term care facilities. I also recommend changes in such laws, regulations, policies, and actions as I determine to be appropriate. Approximately 740 certified ombudsmen volunteers and 150 part-time and full-time paid staff in local programs identify, investigate and resolve complaints and concerns on behalf of about 300,000 residents in about 1,250 skilled nursing facilities and about 7,500 residential care facilities for the elderly, assisted living, board and care type homes. Last year local Ombudsman programs investigated 41,788 complaints that affected the health, safety, welfare and rights of these residents. In fiscal year 2015 and 2016, 1.4 million in addition funds were allocated to provide increased support for the long-term care ombudsman program. This was part of a partial restoration that the Legislature made to restore funds that we lost in 2008. In 2008, we lost 3.8 million in general fund dollars. That was about half of the money we had in local assistance contracts. With that illumination of general fund dollars, we lost 76 of our 183 paid stuff, and that's have a riffle effect on the number of volunteers who work in the program. When I started as California State Ombudsman in 2002 we had close to 1,300 volunteers, we're now down to about 740. So the loss of staff has affected our ability to recruit, retain and keep volunteers. In addition to the 1.4 million in additional ongoing baseline funds for the program we've also received 1 million in one time only funds in 15-16 and 16-17 from the state health facility citation penalties account. With that additional one time only, we're at about the level of funding that we were in 2008 when we lost General Fund. So if that funding goes away at the end of this fiscal year, we'll be about a million below where we are now. This additional funding that we received has directly led to an increase in long term care ombudsman visit facilities to provide assistance to residents. Comparing fiscal year 15-16 to 14-15, we saw a 9% increase in the number of information and consultation sessions with individuals. During these sessions, ombudsman representatives provide information about long-term care and answer questions about residents' rights and other issues that residents, family members and friends may be concerned about. Those opportunities often empower residents, families, and friends to resolve issues on their own with the facility. We've seen an increase of 24% in the number of consultations to facilities. These consultations can resolve issues even before they become complaints. We've seen an 18% increase in the number of residential care facilities that were able to visit each quarter of the year, not in response to a complaint. Just to go in check on the condition of residents looks at what's going on, the facility, is there staff, is there food, is there supplies. Introduce ourselves to new residents and explain how our programs works and if they have problems, build relationship of trust with them so they know they can confide in us. We've seen a 10% increase also in the number of skilled nursing facilities that we're able to visit on a quarterly basis. We've seen a 3% increase in the number of complaints investigated by ombudsmen representatives in one year. And at 13% increase in the number of paid staff working in the program, boots on the ground, we can go into these facilities on a regular basis to resolve issues and problems for residents. We're fortunate in that we have the ability to get out there if we have the resources to fund the positions. We often prevent Complaints from going to the more costly regulatory systems to be investigated by the licensing agencies. We're able to keep those complaints, many of those complaints, out of public health and out of community care licensing and social services. You also asked, what we did with this one time only funding that we received. In fiscal year 1617, the most common use of one-time-only funding, was for temporary increasing staffing hours and to our limited term positions that we know will expire at the end of the fiscal year. The funding also supported volunteer coordinators, and paid ombudsman representatives. Local Ombudsman programs also uses funding for expenditures that are one time in nature, long delayed equipment purchases, reimbursement to volunteer mileage, volunteer recognition activities and infrastructure improvements such as increased Internet bandwidth for local ombudsmen program offices. Margot Kushel: Okay, Chair and Arambula and other members of the Budget Subcommittee. Thank you so much for inviting me to speak with you today. My name is Dr. Margot Kushel and I'm a Professor of medicine at the University of California San Francisco. I'm a practicing general internist at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital, which is the public hospital for the city and County of San Francisco. And I'm also an NIH funded researcher with substantial experience researching homelessness and health. The County Welfare Director's Association asked me to present on the issue of elder homelessness. To help explain the importance of the Home Safe Budget Proposal. I come to you today to share what I've Learned in my 20 years as a researcher and practicing clinician in a safety net hospital, about the toll of homelessness in older adults, and to speak about the urgent need to prevent homelessness among these vulnerable elders. In my research we've found that half of single adults who are homeless are over 50. Our work in Oakland has found that among those who are homeless and over 50, 44% had never experienced homelessness prior to the age of 50. Many of these individuals, left vulnerable by illness, job loss, or loss of a family member, became a victim of elder abuse. And it was that abuse, physical abuse, financial exploitation, that led directly to their becoming homeless. Being victimized either financially or physically. Either through overt action or through negligence can precipitate homelessness in these vulnerable elders. And as you know homelessness leads to devastating consequences for health and safety. Adult protective service workers interact with vulnerable elders at moments of crisis. These crisis if acted upon presented enormous opportunity to prevent homelessness. I have seen this in my research. One of our study participants whom I call Jay moved in with his daughter in Oakland when his kidneys began to fail. His daughter then took all of his money and told him he could not stay with her. So he became homeless three days a week he went to dialysis. Each night, he slept on the AC transit bus, carrying all of his belongings with him. After months of sleeping on the bus, he obtained temporary shelter in a winter shelter. And after months of that, he gained temporary housing, and transitional housing, but passed away before he could obtain permanent housing. Jay's situation unfortunately was not unique. There are well-known and severe consequences to homelessness among older adults. Our research found that homeless adults aged 50 and over had health indicators. Things like cognitive function and physical function, like the ability to walk across the room, that was worse than adults 20 years older than they, in the general population. Homelessness ages people. When older adults become homeless, they have difficulty accessing their primary care providers and their mental health providers and rely instead on expensive emergency care. In the prior six months, one half of the older homeless adults we studied have visited an emergency department. And 11% have been hospitalized for a physical health problem in the prior six months. Homelessness is catastrophic to both health and well-being. As a physician, I can say that the single most important step I can take for patients, is to retain their housing. There is simply no medicine in the world, as potent as housing. And no threat to health as significant as homelessness. Adult protective services workers come into contact with the older adults at a time when they're highly vulnerable to homelessness. A recent study in Chicago demonstrated that relatively modest assistance on the order of about $1,000 at a time of high risk for homelessness had lasting impacts on reductions on homelessness. They found with these small, one time payments, a 76% reduction in homelessness at six months. APS workers are well positioned to intervene to prevent the onset of homelessness and the devastating health consequences that follow. So I urge you to consider the enormous toll of homelessness on older adults, on their health and on societal cost.

We hope to demonstrate how intervening at the time of crisis can prevent homelessness among elder abuse victims. And save the horrifying effects on those individuals, but also save the state money from downstream costs associated with the homelessness of older folks. The proposal is modeled after the Coworks Housing Assistance Program that was conceived by in the Assembly. And enacted several years ago. And also modeled after the Bringing Families Home program, which was actually first adopted in the Assembly two years ago. It didn't make it into the final budget that year, but it was enacted, last year, into law. In this case, we've tailored the proposal toward particular population which are victims of elder abuse and neglect. So that people can stay safe or be safely rehoused. The program as we've envisioned it would require partnerships with local providers so that we're not reinventing the wheel. And we would envision a dollar for dollar local match. So, for the $10 million that we're requesting in state general funds, there would be a like amount of money in either cash or in-kind match provided by the demonstrating county, or cohortative counties. The baseline APS program never really grew into what the Legislature envisioned when the enacted it in the mid 90s. It provides Shorter term less intensive case management. We provide referrals to services. We don't have a lot of resources to provide the intensive services. And we do a great job in this program. But for people who are experiencing a crisis that's affecting them to the point of homelessness, there simply isn't a program as it's currently constructed that gives us the tools to provide the depth of intervention, the intensity of the case management, and the tangible support. Like short term rental assistance. Or assistance to get utilities turned back on, that we know from research are the things that help unhoused people become housed. To give you a sense, the APS program is about a $126 million program. It investigates 150,000 referrals, provides short term services to 25,000 clients per year. In contrast, the child welfare system serves a population four times larger than APS, and with funding that's about 40 times the APS program. And that's not to say child welfare is adequately or sufficiently funded. But it's to give you a sense of just how sort of bare bones that adult protective services programs are. And it's actually quite remarkable the return on the investment that we get from this very lean program. So with the home safe proposal that we'd urge you to adopt, we want to show the types of interventions that the state and the counties would partner in funding. And partner in developing can help people be house and avoid the horrors to human beings of homelessness. But also to save the state money because remember things like skilled nursing facilities stays or emergency room visits or in-patient stays. The state largely bears the cost of those. There are local cost certainly associated with homelessness. But we share those costs, the states and the counties. The effects of homelessness particularly on elder abused victims, we share. And we think that this proposal demonstrates a partnership for the state and the counties to develop evidence-tested models to be able to prevent the problem. And that's the federal measure that doesn't adjust for things that we're familiar with in California, like higher costs of living and those kinds of things. Another piece of information that we're always asked about, is the COLA history and the grant levels, and that's provided on page eight for individuals and page nine for couples. We broke in in these tables, the SSI piece from the SSP piece, and provided a total. And we show you at the federal level, and the state grant level, what happened on the COLAs in those years. And it goes back a little bit more than a decade on both tables. Page 10, I don't think I'm going to cover today, but it's also provided for the Committee's information. We're often asked about SSI/SSP and its relationship to the federal SNAP program, known as CalFresh in California, or colloquially known as food stamps. If you are receiving SSI/SSP, you don't receive food stamps in California. We're the last state in the country, and there's some description of that on page 10 for the Committee's information. Again, tried to be brief and happy to answer any questions. Thank you very much.

Frank Mecca: Thank you Mr. Chairman. Frank Mecca and the county welfare directors would like to add their support for the staff recommendation to restore funding for the HDAP program. Getting on SSI for people who are eligible is an arduous process, it's burdensome, it's difficult, and that's for people with needs and people with support. [{'start': 36, 'end': 49, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Nancy Bargman: Thank you Mr. Chair, this is Nancy Bargmann. As the agenda outlines for you, that we have a proposed trailer bill language regarding reporting employment outcomes in the performance contract for the Regional Centers. Just to provide you a little bit of a background into performance contracts. In 2002, the department began transitioning to an outcome based performance contract with Regional Centers, and it focused on public policies, compliance measures and then also afforded opportunities for Regional Centers to address local measures. Over the few years from 2012 until moving into the point when the original pilot project for the performance contracts was six Regional Centers and then the broadened effort to all Regional Centers was in 2006. When the transition to performance contracts and outcome measures occurred, it originally occurred with sitting down with Regional Centers, identifying what those measures were, and coming to an agreement as to how we're going to be able to move forward with these compliance measures. It hasn't been since 2002 when the original compliance measures had been identified, that changes were made in to those measures up until 2015. In 2015 we were including as an option for the Regional Centers to add a compliance measure for competitive integrated employment for employment measures, recognizing this is a priority to the department and certainly to our community as well. We also had in 2016 that moving forward with the performance contract needed to also have compliance measures related to disparity measures. As we move forward to the important policy measure for employment, and as I think it was, we've heard prior testimonial in other hearings, is that there's a competitive integrated employment priority. There's a blueprint as demonstrated by shared agencies agreements with Department of Rehab, Department of Education, and Department of Developmental Services, and we want to memorialize the efforts of competitive integrated employment, and by doing so, we can have it into the statute, and so every Regional Center can standardize measures and we have an area in which we can measure state wide that's consistent with the data that we need to collect. We certainly could move forward without statute, to be able to get to an agreement for the measures with the Regional Centers. Working with 21 Regional Centers, as wonderful as each one is, there's times when there's a challenge to be able to get a full agreement as to what those measures would be. In the spirit of time and also to really communicate to our community the importance of competitive integrated employment, we have elected to ask to have the statute modified and make this a requirement within the performance contract.

We took a look at the current statute. We also took a look at the current performance contract guidelines and we also talked with the department about the history of the performance contract development process. As Director Bargmann mentioned, the current guidelines have been in place with all 21 Regional Centers since 2006 and has been largely unmodified since that time. And those guidelines were developed in negotiation with the Regional Centers. So there is precedent for changing the performance contract outside of the statutory legislative process and we agree there's no real legal requirement that the department go through statute. Yet there is precedent for changing the performance contract through statute as Director Bargmann mentioned when it comes to disparities. So ultimately there are pros and cons to both methods. So I thought I'd just briefly describe the pros and cons of each method as we see it right now. So to change the performance contract outside of the legislative process, the pros would be that the department and Regional Centers have discretion over what's in the guidelines. The cons would be, so one, if the performance contracts are negotiated with the Regional Centers, the department risks not actually getting what they want from the employment measures, and they also potentially open up negotiations on all the other points in the performance contract guidelines and delaying the process as Director Bargmann noted. If the department simply issued a directive, it might risk sort of tarnishing the good faith that it's built up with the Regional Centers, on this issue since it developed those in concert with Regional Centers in the past. And the second option would be changing the performance contract through statue. So the pro on this would be that the department is assured of getting the information that they want. Out of the employment measures and this may be particularly important as the state moves forward with the employment blueprint and recent state and federal policy promote employment for people with developmental disabilities. The con would be In our mind that, by making a second change to the performance contract guidelines through statue, it could create a precedent, whereby it's difficult to make any changes to the performance contract guidelines without going through statute. So this remains an open question for further discussion.

[{'start': 14, 'end': 24, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Brian Winfield: Brian Winfield, Developmental Services. So you asked the Department to explain the difference between the health and safety exemption requests and the unanticipated rate adjustments. So health and safety exemption requests are a statutory provision for the Department to increase a rate for a service that a consumer is receiving if there are the potential for consumer health or safety risk. And the Department does receive requests from Regional Centers on a regular basis. The request must be consumer specific and they must justify why the rate is insufficient to meet the consumer's needs. So we received those and we provided you with that data to show you the volume at which we received those requests. The unanticipated rate adjustments, they are allowed for in state regulations. They are only applicable to community based day programs, and in-home respite agencies. And the regulations state that rate adjustments can be provided only when a change in law, or regulation, or a court order mandates an adjustment in services. Or also in an emergency relocation is needed to protect the health and safety of consumers. So the scope of the unanticipated rate adjustments is more limited, but it's specific to providers versus consumers.
