John Roth: Thank you Mr. Chairman, Members of the Committee. So I am John Roth, I'm the chief Executive Officer for the California Pharmacists Association. CPHA or the California Pharmacists Association represent pharmacists working in all practice setting throughout California. I appreciate the opportunity to be here at the hearing and I appreciate the invitation, particularly during the time when we are really talking about pricing and transparency throughout with respect to the entire healthcare delivery system. As Californians we wrestle with some of the new fundamental shifts perhaps in the State and Federal relationship. We support open and detailed discussion on the supply chain regarding consumer access to medicines that they desperately need. I was asked here today to talk about one specific aspect, the prescription drug benefit program. Ironically, as mentioned previously in this hearing, so far, many consumers know very little about, and yet has the single most influential role in the supply chain and that is a pharmacy benefit managers. PBM's largely operate in the background, as you've heard, out of sight from consumers, however, they play a crucial role in establishing the ultimate cost of a prescription paid by that consumer. As you've heard here today also, the role of PDM has evolved significantly over the years. Initially just being claim to adjudication companies between lays on, between the flow of dollars, between health plans and providers, for the benefit of the patient. However they've grown substantially, and are now ubiquitous role, involved in everything from price negotiation with pharmaceutical manufactures, to drug placement on the formularies, to contract with health plans for administering the prescription drug benefit, to directing consumers where, how and who they get their medicine from. Now the challenge in having a detailed discussion about the role PBM is that the relationship and business dealings had become very complex, and as I've mention are out of the sight of regulators, consumers on just about every aspect of the prescription drug process. It really creates a web of contracts, agreements and negotiations that are heavily intertwined. Add to this complexity the fact that PBM's largely operate in the shadows and are nearly unregulated and you can begin to see why hearings like this are so important when legislators, regulators, and the consumers begin to ask for transparency regarding the prescription drug system. Now unfortunately time doesn't allow us here today to unravel every aspect of this complicated system. However I would like to note that the background materials for this hearing, I think presented a detailed and compelling set of facts with regards to PBM industry, its relationship with other entities. And ultimately a call for the legislature to address potential market failure system that could harm consumers. I would also like to just make reference since Dr. Jones had made it part of his commentary to the Committee that CalPERS itself had these very questions back in 2011 when they dropped a multi-million dollar contract with the PBM for allegations of impropriety that involved the Securities and Exchange Commission and the California State Attorney General's Office. In any market, as Senator Pan was referencing, where a few companies control the majority of market share, as is the case with PBMs, where the three largest companies control 78%, or roughly 180 million lives, we're concerned about the potential negative impact on consumers. That concern and protection of consumers is magnified in health care of course, for regulators need to ensure that the care and fiduciary oversight of the market is the best interest of patients. Now, as the State Wide Association for Pharmacies, the number one complaint we received from our members is in regard to PBM practices and to be clear, our members routinely call and complain on behalf of their patients not on behalf of themselves. The typical scenario begins with the patient having received a communication from a PBM that has some adverse impact on their ability to get their medications. The community pharmacist is really on the front line of receiving these complaints and yet, has little ability to provide any advice or resolve of those concerns for the patient. In fact, if you were to look at many PMB contracts with pharmacies, they contain things such as confidentiality clauses and gag clauses, which bar the pharmacists from discussing certain aspects of the PMB agreement with that provider. This eliminates the pharmacist's ability to be the patient's advocate and render the patient simply frustrated. The problems that consumers bring to our members span a spectrum of concerns and while those concerns are broad in an array of subjects, have it suggested they're really true primary themes that emerge. One, either the patient is being told that they can no longer receive their medication that the Doctor has prescribed in the same manner for the same cost. Or two, the patient is being directed out of a relationship with their neighborhood pharmacist and forced into a PBM owned mail order or subsidiary controlled pharmacy. Now if I can get very practical for a moment, I'd like to share a story that demonstrates the types of consumer concerns that comes to our members. A case in point is an example that one of our members brought to my attention, and since then my staff validated with several other additional pharmacies as occurring, as well. The patient, we'll call him David, received a letter from the PBM and the header of the letter said, notice of denial for medical judgment. The letter goes on to state that the PBM had received a request from David's physician for coverage of a medication called Coreg CR. It's a drug used to treat high blood pressure and also to improve the chance of survival after a heart attack. In the letter, the PBM informed the patient that it was denying this medicine because, and I quote, you did not meet the established medication-specific criteria of guidelines for Coreg CR at this time. Coreg CR is denied for medical necessity. Now, understandably, there are times that a patient must meet certain medical thresholds for certain procedures and medications, that's how these utilization controls can help contain costs, but what is very concerning and candidly, quite suspicious, is what occurred next, and that is the patient handed the pharmacist the second letter, they had received just two days after the first. And it too was from the same PBM and in that letter, the PBM notified the patient it was quote, making it easy for you to get your maintenance medications by making the choice of filling 90 day supply through the PBM's mail order program or 90 day supply at a designated pharmacy chain which the PBM had a relationship and as you might guess, one of the medications approved through the PBMs program, was Coreg CR. I would ask, how can the patient be medically denied for the medication their physician prescribed in one letter, and just two days later, receive a letter from their PBM saying that it was approved if they use the PBM's wholly owned subsidiary operations. The patient, of course, was distraught and confused as you might imagine, and was not only sure whether they were going to even get their medication, but was completely flustered with the fact that they could no longer see the pharmacist that had cared for them for the past 10 years. Now perhaps for the benefit of argument, there was an error made in this case, and denial of medical necessity was incorrect, despite the fact that we validated this same tactic was used in other pharmacies with other patients around this time frame. But the point being is just that without over site, transparency and a regulatory framework to shed light on PBM practices. There's no method for determining and distinguishing between a legitimate processing error and an egregious policy that harms consumers. There are countless other stories where patients are disadvantaged by PBM practices. While, as Dr. Jones mentioned, PBMs will testify that they saved the health care system money. My own very simple personal litmus test is that my phone has never rang with the pharmacist telling me a heartwarming story about a PBM practice that made the patient life better. Because PBMs directly impact consumers, our Association believes that critical first step is bringing light to how they operate, and to do so is to create a regulatory framework in the State of California. We believe the most appropriate agency to oversee this regulatory process is the California State Board of Pharmacy. The Board of Pharmacy, by statutory definition, is a consumer protection agency, and as such currently regulates all aspects of the pharmacy supply chain and related activities in California, and this includes just much more than pharmacies and pharmacists. It includes organizations and companies such as wholesalers, third party logistics companies, reverse distributors, waste haulers, medical device companies, and even out of state companies that provide medication-related goods and services in this state. The entire supply chain, except PBMs are regulated by the Board of Pharmacy, when it comes to delivering pharmaceutical benefit to consumers. Given the direct relationship between PBMs and consumer access to coverage and medication benefits. It's not only appropriate, but a necessity for the Board of Pharmacy to regulate these entities. Mr Chairman, in lieu of time, I'd like to thank you again for inviting me to speak with you here today. Thank the Committee for their interest in the subject. Be happy to answer any questions.

Benjamin Frank: Thank you, sir, Chairman Hill. I will now summarize for you the results of my assessment to the board that I completed during the past year. I apologize in advance. My comments are a little lengthy. It will take me about 30 minutes to complete my testimony. As you are already aware from the legislative staff summaries, the Board's enforcement program was thrown in to disarray by the organizational and work flow changes that were implemented during 2011-12 and 2012-13. These changes included establishing a new non-sworn investigation section and assigning all licensee complaint cases to the new section, including cases involving serious criminal misconduct and significant patient harm that were previously referred to the department's Division of Investigation. As discussed by Miss Avella, members of the Board began developing an awareness of these problems and appointed the Enforcement Task Force to assess the Board's enforcement and discipline processes. Concurrently, reports surfaced during the Board's sunset review about these organizational and operational problems and the scope and magnitude of the problems became apparent to the Legislature. Subsequently, AB 179 was enacted requiring the department to appoint a monitor to assess the Board's enforcement program and specified administrative processes. On February 29th, 2016, DCA awarded a contract to Benjamin Frank LLC to provide the monitor services. Work on the project commenced almost immediately following contract award. During March and April of last year, I completed an initial assessment of the enforcement program. The initial report documenting results of the initial assessment was presented to the Board's governing board in June. The initial report provided a summary of historical information that I had collected, compiled, and analyzed and provided a foundation for completing additional reviews and analyses during phases 2 and 3 of the project. Additionally, in consultation with the department's Contract Manager and the Board's Executive Officer and Chief of Enforcement, I prepared a work plan to guide completion of phases 2 and 3 during the remainder of 2016. Additional interviews, research, and analyses of the enforcement program were completed during June, July and August. The second report highlighted the turnaround that had occurred during 2015-16 but also pointed out that there were continuing needs to further reduce legacy case backlogs, and the amount of time needed to complete investigations, and impose discipline. The second report also provided 29 recommendations to help address these and other improvement needs. The review of the draft's second report with the board's leadership team in late September was contentious. For example, the Executive Officer demanded that I delete some sections of the report and replace a summary of a confidential board member survey that I had previously completed with a subsequent non-confidential survey of board members, completed by the Executive Officer without my involvement. I was not agreeable to making these types of changes. Additionally, the Executive Officer expressed disagreement with nearly all of the recommendations for improvement. Also, during late September, the Executive Officer began limiting my access to the Chief of Enforcement, and a few weeks later the Chief of Enforcement began a leave of absence. The final second report documenting results of my phase two assessment efforts was presented to the Board's governing board on October 20th. At about that same time, I was directed to submit all request for information through the Executive Officer, which delayed and further restricted my ability to obtain information directly from subordinate managers and rank and file staff. Problems in this area later led to a meeting in mid-November with legislative staff to address these problems. During November and December, I completed an updated assessment of the enforcement program along with targeted assessments in several other areas. The third report documenting results of these efforts were submitted to the Board's governing board during February. The third report again highlighted the turnaround that had occurred during 2015-16, but pointed out that this turnaround appeared to have stalled. A number of changes became evident that supported this conclusion. Including one, reduced numbers of completed licensee arrest conviction report and non-sworn licensee complaint investigations. Two, unchanged numbers of pending licensee arrest conviction report and non-sworn licensee complaint investigations. Three, reduced numbers of completed discipline cases, and four, increased numbers of pending discipline cases. Additionally, the average elapsed times to complete investigations and impose discipline, while improved in comparison to earlier periods, remained quite long. For example, the one-year average elapsed time to complete non-sworn investigations and the two-and-a-half-year average elapsed time from case receipt to completion of discipline for processes referred for discipline were both still quite long. Additionally, the third report highlighted that staff turnover had increased and that, rather than continuing to decline, vacancy rates rose to about 17%. Some of these positions had been vacant for extended periods of time, including the Assistant Executive Officer position which, at that time, had already been vacant for 21 months. The Board's elevated number of enforcement division- vacant enforcement division positions, the extended absence of the Board's Chief of Enforcement, and turn over of experienced Enforcement Division staff appeared to be adversely impacting overall enforcement program performance. Additionally, based on interviews conducted during early December with about two-thirds of all the Enforcement Division's staff, the overall work environment and workforce morale appeared to have deteriorated markedly since March of 2016, at least within the enforcement division. I also pointed out that the Board's large number of vacant supervisory and management positions and the extent to which the Board was utilizing short term, out of class assignments to temporarily fill these positions, and noted that these temporary assignments were not a substitute for filling the positions on a permanent basis. The third report also spotlighted the dependency of the Board's governing board members on information provided to them by the Executive Officer for purposes of performing their oversight responsibilities. And noted that this dependency, while not unique to this board, can result in the Board being unaware of performance or other problems as occurred previously. I suggested that oversight of the Board's Executive Officer, and, by extension, the Board's programs and operations, could potentially benefit from utilization of a 360 degree, multi-rater assessment process, in which feedback regarding the Executive Officer's performance is solicited from a variety of points of view, and then I recommended establishing a work group, a multi-agency work group, to assess needs for development of a 360 degree Executive Officer feedback process. And, if needed, the best approach and time frame for developing and implementing the process. The third report also provided a summary of the status of the Board's implementation of the 29 recommendations for improvement provided in the second report. As of late December, the Board had implemented just four recommendations, had partially implemented eight others, and had not yet began implementing any of the remaining 17 recommendations for improvement. Finally, I disclosed in the third report a handful of potential problems that brought to my attention, that were brought to my attention, involving the Board's licensing and support service business processes. These potential problems were not assessed because they were not within the scope of the monitor assignment. Now, I would like to provide you with some additional updated information regarding the current status of the enforcement program and the overall health of the organization. What these updates show is that while the board's troubled history may not repeat itself, it does seem to rhyme. First, areas of improvement, some of these you've heard about. Areas that have improved significantly since the boards last sunset review include, one, the handling of license applicant cases. Two, the the handling of licensee subsequent arrest, conviction, report cases. And three, the referral of high priority licensee complaint cases to the department's Division of Investigation and the Division's of Investigation's handling of these cases. First, license applicant cases. The Board no longer unnecessarily opens several thousand license applicant cases involving minor offenses and offenses that occurred in the distant past that have no bearing on the Board's licensing decision. Currently, only about 600 to 700 license applicant cases are referred to enforcement, and the Enforcement Division's Complaint Section Analyst now consistently, promptly processed these cases. In most instances, the division authorizes issuance of the license, either without, or in conjunction with, a notice of warning. Denials of licensure are issued in the remaining cases. On an annual basis, a few dozen of the denials are appealed, which prompts referral of the case to the Attorney General's Office for hearing. Two, the licensee's subsequent arrest, conviction, report cases. The board continues to receive about 1500 licensee subsequent arrest, conviction, report cases per year, nearly all of which are now assigned to the Complaint Section Analyst for desk investigation. These cases consistently account for more than one-half of all the cases that the Board refers to the Attorney General's office for discipline. However, during 2015-16 the Complaint Section Analyst completed about 1,900 investigations of these cases, and a large number of cases closed during 2015-16 helped to reduce the number of pending cases. However, since that time, the pace of case closures has decreased and there has been no further reduction in the number of pending cases and little change in the average elapsed time to complete these investigations. Three, licensee complaint cases referred to the department's Division of Investigation. Following the Board's last sunset hearing, several hundred high priority licensee complaint cases that had been languishing in the Board's investigations section were transferred to the department's Division of Investigation. Concurrently, the Board began identifying high priority cases during intake and referring them to the Division of Investigation and, since that time, has been consistently referring about 180 to 200 cases per year to the division. Initially, during 2015, the transferred legacy cases, along with the newly received cases, created a large backlog of more than 360 pending cases at the Division and many of these cases were quite old. However, during 2016, the Division began consistently completing these investigations at a rate faster than new cases were being assigned, which enabled it to reduce this back log along with the average age of its remaining pending cases. Currently, the department's Division of Investigation has about 200 pending cases. About one-third of their investigations are referred for discipline, and these cases account for most of the licensee complaint cases that are referred for discipline. Non-sworn licensee complaint investigations. The area where this Board seems to continue to struggle most is with the handling of lower priority licensee complaint cases that are not referred to the department's Division of Investigation. As discussed in the third report, during the period from July to October 2016, the Board's non-sworn investigation section completed an average of about a dozen licensee complaint investigations per month and there was little change in the number of pending investigations. To keep case loads manageable for investigators, only about one-half of the more than 400 cases assigned to the section were assigned to specific investigators. The remaining, more recently received cases, were placed on a pending shelf. Subsequently, during November and December, the section continued to complete an average of about a dozen investigations per month which did not keep pace with the flow of newly assigned cases. As a result, the number of pending cases began to increase. As of late December, the section had more than 440 pending cases. For the 6 month period from July to December 2016, the Board's investigation section completed a total of about 75 investigations. Some of these cases were referred to discipline and about a dozen were closed with issuance of a citation. Only a handful of the cases were closed with issuance of a NOW, or a Notice Of Warning. Then, over a one month period extending from late December to late January, the Board abruptly reversed its process for completing non-sworn investigations of licensee complaint cases. The way that the investigation process usually works is that each case is assigned to an investigator to gather additional information about the case, including information to determine whether the alleged violation occurred, and to rule out other potential related violations. The results of the investigation are then reviewed by supervisory management personnel and discipline case analysts to determine whether the investigation was properly completed and whether the investigative findings support issuance of a NOW or a citation or referral of the case for discipline. The benefits of this process are that the investigation is not guided or conducted to achieve any predetermined outcome and blanket rules are not established regarding the type of discipline imposed for any broad category of cases. However, according to Board staff in late December, at the specific direction of the Executive Officer, investigation staff began a review of the sections pending cases, including the 200 or so cases that had not yet been assigned to an investigator. The review specifically targeted cases involving sleeping on the job and time sheet fraud, but also encompassed other types of cases. Following this review, and completion of some limited additional information gathering activities for some of the cases, 70 cases were abruptly closed with issuance of a notice of warning. Specifically, on January 11th, 27 non-sworn investigation cases were closed with issuances of a NOW. On the same day, a 45 minute teleconference meeting was held with the Board's Enforcement Committee, during which staff disclosed that they had initiated a review of the section's pending cases, and had identified 107 cases that could potentially be closed with a NOW. Contemporaneous minutes of this meeting were not kept, but it is our understanding there is only a brief discussion of this topic. Then on the next two days, January 12th and 13th, another 31 cases were closed with issuance of a NOW and over the next two weeks another 11 cases were closed with insurance of a NOW. During January, 24 other non-sworn investigations were also closed, but as of about two weeks ago, none of those other cases had resulted in either issuance of a citation, or referral of the case for discipline. In total, 94 non-sworn investigations were completed during January, equivalent to more than 20% of the sections 440 pending cases and about 75% of these cases we closed with issuance of a NOW. This compares to just 75 investigations completed during the entire preceding six month period with only a handful of NOWs issued for all of those cases. The abrupt closure of so many non sworn investigations in such a short period of time, and all with exactly the same outcome, which was issuance of a NOW, caught my immediate attention and prompted me to gather additional information about the surprising development. What I've since learned is encouraging in some respects and disconcerting in others. For example, it's encouraging that the Board finally began to implement my earlier recommendation to screen and triage lower priority licensee complaint cases not referred to the Division of Investigation, to identify those that could be handled as desk investigations and completed more quickly by gathering some additional records, making some phone calls to confirm or clarify the information provided with the complaint. However, I'm not comfortable with how this new process was implemented and I think my discomfort is shared by both the department's Division of Investigation, and staff within the non-sworn investigation section. Based on the information I've gathered to this point, it is self-evident from the large number of NOWs issued that the conventional investigatory process was reversed to instead search out cases where the currently available information could be used to support immediate closure of the cases with issuance of a NOW, rather than first investigating the cases and then determining what, if any, disciplinary outcome was supported by results of the investigation. I also believe that the section staff felt pressured to close cases with issuance of a NOW, in some cases without sufficiently investigating the cases. In summary, needs now exist to meet with the Board's non-sworn investigators and re-review all of these cases, to identify any cases that need to be reopened and further investigated. At this point, I expect the Board's investigators to be very forthcoming and helpful in identifying any such cases. Additionally, until this re-review is completed, caution should be exercised in interpreting any workload, backlog, or performance data provided by the Board concerning its recent handling of non-sworn investigation cases. Discipline case processing. The Board's discipline case processing, including the use of the Attorney General's fast track program, is continuing to improve marginally in some respects. Recently, however, there has been some additional accumulation of discipline cases. The recent increase in pending discipline cases appears to be the result of one, the increased number of discipline referrals to the AG, resulting from the larger number of investigations completed by the department's Division of Investigation. And two, larger numbers of subsequent discipline cases generated as a result of the large number of discipline case settlements reached during 2015-16, and related increases in the number of new probationers who are most likely to trigger subsequent discipline cases. Management and staff turnover and vacancies. As of early March, about 20% of the Board's positions were vacant. Additionally, excluding the Executive Officer, five of the Board's 10 supervisory and management positions were vacant. In my experience, I've never before seen such high levels of vacant positions, particularly at the supervisory and management levels. The Board's management structure has partially collapsed, particularly with respect to the enforcement program. One adverse consequence of the loss of key management personnel is that for the past seven weeks the Board has been unable to issue subpoenas for records that are needed to complete its enforcement investigations. Additionally, there are not currently any outside expert witnesses available to review cases involving psychiatric technicians. And there is only one outside expert witness available to review cases involving vocational nurses, and it is my understanding that outside expert witness recruitment activities have been stalled since the Executive Officer's leave began seven weeks ago. Also, probation reviews of new staff are no longer being consistently completed on a timely basis, as was previously the case. All of these circumstances increase the Board's vulnerability to various risk and should be a cause of considerable concern. My last topic is the Continuing Education Compliance Audit Project. The Continuing Education Compliance Audit Project, which has already been in the news, is illustrative of a broad range of problems that continue to be experienced by this Board. Despite obvious major problems with this project throughout the past four months, nothing has been done to restructure or abort this misguided, poorly conceived, runaway project. It is my understanding the CE Compliance Audit Project was initiated in late November during a meeting between the Executive Officer, the Acting Assistant Executive Officer, and two support staff. The project was launched shortly thereafter with the creation of a mass mailing list, the printing of about 57,000 dated audit letters, and the redirection of staff to stuff thousands of envelopes. Then, in early December, management apparently realized that they would be unable to complete the mailing. But rather than recognizing if Board staff were unable to even complete the mailing, then they certainly wouldn't be able to process the responses, management instead requested that the department's Office of Business Services complete the remaining mailings. Then, in early January, after requesting, expediting, receiving delivery of a large supply of window envelopes from the Office of State Printing, the Office of Business Services completed about 50,000 additional mailings. From this sequence of activities, it is evident that it was not the Board's intention to spread the mailings out in batches over a period of several months, as was suggested by the Board's Acting Assistant Executive Officer during the Board's February 10th meeting, or to send out 1,000 letter waves, spaced two weeks apart that was stated by the board in it's February 24th correspondence to Assembly staff. This latter report approach would have required more than two full years just to complete the mailings and would still have generated an overwhelming amount of work for Board staff. Had the Board utilized the 1,000 piece wave approach, it would have unleashed upon itself a 28-month-long flood of CE submittals, rather than the two month long tsunami of submittals that it instead experienced. Since completion of the mailings in early January, a group of two permanent full-time staff, two half-time retired annuitants, and one permanent full-time analyst on a half-time basis have been working on this project. This is equivalent to three and a half full-time positions. Additionally, other staff have been supporting the project on an intermittent basis and overtime was utilized during mid to late January to support the project and the use of overtime continued into February. Finally, at least two half-time AARP volunteers, equivalent to another full-time position, have been assigned to the project. To help handle deluge of submittals that were initially received, all of the Enforcement Division's managers, along with others, spent a full day together just opening mail. The Board's public phone lines have been continuously overflowing since early January, and during January the Board also received overflowing volumes of emails and faxes. The CE Compliance Audit has adversely impacted operations throughout much of the Board and has diverted staff, management, board member, and oversight agency attention from other more important business needs. Every passing day this project unnecessarily wastes more money and resources. The problems with this project will not somehow resolve themselves over the next several months as some seem to believe. Two weeks I visited the Board's offices and interviewed most of the staff that had been subsequently involved in supporting this project since its inception. I also requested access to a locked, vacant manager's office where I found more than 100 US postal service mail baskets filled with open but unprocessed CE submittals. In this same office there were just five baskets containing submittals that have been preliminary reviewed, but still needed to be re-reviewed and completed by the Board's CE Audit Specialist. Today, they have only about one basket of submittals has been fully processed by the CE Audit Specialist. Finally, there were a couple of trace that appear to contain about 800 pieces of unopened return mail but rubber banded stacks of unopened return mail were also present in many of the 100+ baskets of opened mail that had not yet been processed. These baskets may also contain license application fee remittances or other documents unrelated to CE that were not correctly separated from the CE documents. The Board does not track the CE submittals as they are received against the initial mailing list. Thus, there is absolutely no way that anybody can provide even a ballpark guesstimate as to how many of the 57,000 targeted licensees have actually responded to the mailing. Tracking against the initial mailing list is only completed by the Board CE Audit Specialist after completing a final review of the submittals and updating briefs. For various reasons, staff assigned to complete the preliminary review of the submittals sometimes experienced problems that prevent them from completing the reviews. The submittals with problems were set aside in separate stacks for subsequent review and handling by the Audit Specialist, who cannot possibly keep pace with the incoming flow of work generated by all the different staff involved in performing the preliminary case reviews. To date, the Audit Specialist has completed reviews and BreEZe updates for only about 1,000 CE audit cases. Based on actual performance, it clearly does not take an average of just 30 seconds to two minutes to review these submittals as has been stated by the Board. In fact, it probably took close to that amount of time per submittal just to open, date stamp and assemble the documents for subsequent processing. According to the Board's Acting Executive Officer, about 4,000 submitted packages have been preliminary reviewed today as evidenced by the Board's issuance of about 4,000 letters of compliance. However, in some cases, these letters were issued in error. In these cases, the CE Audit Specialist issues a letter of non-compliance to the licensee, after the licensee's already received a letter stating they were in compliance. So needless to say, this process necessarily creates a great deal of confusion among the affected licensees. Assuming that the Board continues to process an average of three baskets of submittals per month, using all the same staffing resources that have been allocated to the project since the start of the year, it will take two to three years just to do the preliminary reviews of the currently accumulated baskets of submittals. This does not account for any of the more time consuming work associated with completing the final reviews of the submittals and upgrading BreEZe, following up with licensees in cases where they're not in compliance with the CE requirements, following up with all the licensees that didn't even respond to the initial mailing and who are especially likely to have completed little or no CE, and tracking down thousands of licensees in cases where the initial mailings were returned to the Board because they were not deliverable to the address that the Board had on file. Additionally, most of more than 5,000 emails that the Board has received have not yet been processed at all. Finally, in those instances where the submittals do show compliance with the Board's CE requirements, the processes being used may not be producing documentation sufficient to support an actionable enforcement case. If enforcement actions are able to be initiated, then significant additional resources will be needed to perform citation preparation, issuance, fine collection and appeal handling services. This debacle needs to be stopped and it needs to be stopped now. There is no realistic path forward for this wasteful project. If the Board does not promptly abort this project, then legislation should be introduced to require such action. Hopefully, that would prompt the Board to terminate the project on its own accord. In conclusion, recent events and the Board's current circumstances may not repeat the specific events and circumstances that existed prior to the Board's previous sunset review. But they certainly have a familiar ring. In closing, I'd like to express my gratitude to the Department of Consumer Affairs leadership team, the Department's project manager, Bryan Clifford, and the Department's Division of Investigation, Office of Information Services, and Office of Human Resources for their cooperation and assistance throughout the past year and particularly during the past six months. Additionally, I would like to thank Board staff for their open and candid communication with me during my on site interviews, particularly, again, during the past six months. And I would especially like to thank those staff, who within, found ways to continuously relay additional information to me through various other communication channels. The information they provided was invaluable in enabling me to complete my assessments and helped immeasurably to keep me up-to-date regarding changes occurring at the Board. And that concludes my testimony and thank you.

Benjamin Frank: Good morning, Chairman Hill, Chairman Salas, and Committee Members and staff. And thank you for providing me with this opportunity to provide you with a brief summary of the work I've completed during the past year as the Administrative Enforcement Program Monitor for the Board of Vocational Nursing and Psychiatric Technicians. And by the way, I'm Ben Frank and I'm the chief Executive Officer of Benjamin Frank, LLC. By way of introduction, I began my professional career working for an accounting firm while completing my Master of Business Administration at Washington University in St. Louis. My management consulting career began with performing workload, staffing and business process re-engineering analyses for Fortune 200 manufacturing firms in high technology and other industries. I have come here at the request of the committees to provide my relevant experiences and perspectives with regard to the board's overall management and government process. And specifically, my experience in enforcement. I expect my testimony to last approximately 15 minutes. I was appointed by Governor Brown in September, 2013. And was reappointed in June of 2016, and regrettably resigned four months later in October. In the past few years, there certainly have been some board successes and I believe that the board was on positive path beginning in early to mid 2015. Benjamin Frank: Thank you, sir, Chairman Hill. I will now summarize for you the results of my assessment to the board that I completed during the past year. I apologize in advance. My comments are a little lengthy. It will take me about 30 minutes to complete my testimony. As you are already aware from the legislative staff summaries, the Board's enforcement program was thrown in to disarray by the organizational and work flow changes that were implemented during 2011-12 and 2012-13. These changes included establishing a new non-sworn investigation section and assigning all licensee complaint cases to the new section, including cases involving serious criminal misconduct and significant patient harm that were previously referred to the department's Division of Investigation. As discussed by Miss Avella, members of the Board began developing an awareness of these problems and appointed the Enforcement Task Force to assess the Board's enforcement and discipline processes. Concurrently, reports surfaced during the Board's sunset review about these organizational and operational problems and the scope and magnitude of the problems became apparent to the Legislature. Subsequently, AB 179 was enacted requiring the department to appoint a monitor to assess the Board's enforcement program and specified administrative processes. On February 29th, 2016, DCA awarded a contract to Benjamin Frank LLC to provide the monitor services. Work on the project commenced almost immediately following contract award. During March and April of last year, I completed an initial assessment of the enforcement program. The initial report documenting results of the initial assessment was presented to the Board's governing board in June. The initial report provided a summary of historical information that I had collected, compiled, and analyzed and provided a foundation for completing additional reviews and analyses during phases 2 and 3 of the project. Additionally, in consultation with the department's Contract Manager and the Board's Executive Officer and Chief of Enforcement, I prepared a work plan to guide completion of phases 2 and 3 during the remainder of 2016. Additional interviews, research, and analyses of the enforcement program were completed during June, July and August. The second report highlighted the turnaround that had occurred during 2015-16 but also pointed out that there were continuing needs to further reduce legacy case backlogs, and the amount of time needed to complete investigations, and impose discipline. The second report also provided 29 recommendations to help address these and other improvement needs. The review of the draft's second report with the board's leadership team in late September was contentious. For example, the Executive Officer demanded that I delete some sections of the report and replace a summary of a confidential board member survey that I had previously completed with a subsequent non-confidential survey of board members, completed by the Executive Officer without my involvement. I was not agreeable to making these types of changes. Additionally, the Executive Officer expressed disagreement with nearly all of the recommendations for improvement. Also, during late September, the Executive Officer began limiting my access to the Chief of Enforcement, and a few weeks later the Chief of Enforcement began a leave of absence. The final second report documenting results of my phase two assessment efforts was presented to the Board's governing board on October 20th. At about that same time, I was directed to submit all request for information through the Executive Officer, which delayed and further restricted my ability to obtain information directly from subordinate managers and rank and file staff. Problems in this area later led to a meeting in mid-November with legislative staff to address these problems. During November and December, I completed an updated assessment of the enforcement program along with targeted assessments in several other areas. The third report documenting results of these efforts were submitted to the Board's governing board during February. The third report again highlighted the turnaround that had occurred during 2015-16, but pointed out that this turnaround appeared to have stalled. A number of changes became evident that supported this conclusion. Including one, reduced numbers of completed licensee arrest conviction report and non-sworn licensee complaint investigations. Two, unchanged numbers of pending licensee arrest conviction report and non-sworn licensee complaint investigations. Three, reduced numbers of completed discipline cases, and four, increased numbers of pending discipline cases. Additionally, the average elapsed times to complete investigations and impose discipline, while improved in comparison to earlier periods, remained quite long. For example, the one-year average elapsed time to complete non-sworn investigations and the two-and-a-half-year average elapsed time from case receipt to completion of discipline for processes referred for discipline were both still quite long. Additionally, the third report highlighted that staff turnover had increased and that, rather than continuing to decline, vacancy rates rose to about 17%. Some of these positions had been vacant for extended periods of time, including the Assistant Executive Officer position which, at that time, had already been vacant for 21 months. The Board's elevated number of enforcement division- vacant enforcement division positions, the extended absence of the Board's Chief of Enforcement, and turn over of experienced Enforcement Division staff appeared to be adversely impacting overall enforcement program performance. Additionally, based on interviews conducted during early December with about two-thirds of all the Enforcement Division's staff, the overall work environment and workforce morale appeared to have deteriorated markedly since March of 2016, at least within the enforcement division. I also pointed out that the Board's large number of vacant supervisory and management positions and the extent to which the Board was utilizing short term, out of class assignments to temporarily fill these positions, and noted that these temporary assignments were not a substitute for filling the positions on a permanent basis. The third report also spotlighted the dependency of the Board's governing board members on information provided to them by the Executive Officer for purposes of performing their oversight responsibilities. And noted that this dependency, while not unique to this board, can result in the Board being unaware of performance or other problems as occurred previously. I suggested that oversight of the Board's Executive Officer, and, by extension, the Board's programs and operations, could potentially benefit from utilization of a 360 degree, multi-rater assessment process, in which feedback regarding the Executive Officer's performance is solicited from a variety of points of view, and then I recommended establishing a work group, a multi-agency work group, to assess needs for development of a 360 degree Executive Officer feedback process. And, if needed, the best approach and time frame for developing and implementing the process. The third report also provided a summary of the status of the Board's implementation of the 29 recommendations for improvement provided in the second report. As of late December, the Board had implemented just four recommendations, had partially implemented eight others, and had not yet began implementing any of the remaining 17 recommendations for improvement. Finally, I disclosed in the third report a handful of potential problems that brought to my attention, that were brought to my attention, involving the Board's licensing and support service business processes. These potential problems were not assessed because they were not within the scope of the monitor assignment. Now, I would like to provide you with some additional updated information regarding the current status of the enforcement program and the overall health of the organization. What these updates show is that while the board's troubled history may not repeat itself, it does seem to rhyme. First, areas of improvement, some of these you've heard about. Areas that have improved significantly since the boards last sunset review include, one, the handling of license applicant cases. Two, the the handling of licensee subsequent arrest, conviction, report cases. And three, the referral of high priority licensee complaint cases to the department's Division of Investigation and the Division's of Investigation's handling of these cases. First, license applicant cases. The Board no longer unnecessarily opens several thousand license applicant cases involving minor offenses and offenses that occurred in the distant past that have no bearing on the Board's licensing decision. Currently, only about 600 to 700 license applicant cases are referred to enforcement, and the Enforcement Division's Complaint Section Analyst now consistently, promptly processed these cases. In most instances, the division authorizes issuance of the license, either without, or in conjunction with, a notice of warning. Denials of licensure are issued in the remaining cases. On an annual basis, a few dozen of the denials are appealed, which prompts referral of the case to the Attorney General's Office for hearing. Two, the licensee's subsequent arrest, conviction, report cases. The board continues to receive about 1500 licensee subsequent arrest, conviction, report cases per year, nearly all of which are now assigned to the Complaint Section Analyst for desk investigation. These cases consistently account for more than one-half of all the cases that the Board refers to the Attorney General's office for discipline. However, during 2015-16 the Complaint Section Analyst completed about 1,900 investigations of these cases, and a large number of cases closed during 2015-16 helped to reduce the number of pending cases. However, since that time, the pace of case closures has decreased and there has been no further reduction in the number of pending cases and little change in the average elapsed time to complete these investigations. Three, licensee complaint cases referred to the department's Division of Investigation. Following the Board's last sunset hearing, several hundred high priority licensee complaint cases that had been languishing in the Board's investigations section were transferred to the department's Division of Investigation. Concurrently, the Board began identifying high priority cases during intake and referring them to the Division of Investigation and, since that time, has been consistently referring about 180 to 200 cases per year to the division. Initially, during 2015, the transferred legacy cases, along with the newly received cases, created a large backlog of more than 360 pending cases at the Division and many of these cases were quite old. However, during 2016, the Division began consistently completing these investigations at a rate faster than new cases were being assigned, which enabled it to reduce this back log along with the average age of its remaining pending cases. Currently, the department's Division of Investigation has about 200 pending cases. About one-third of their investigations are referred for discipline, and these cases account for most of the licensee complaint cases that are referred for discipline. Non-sworn licensee complaint investigations. The area where this Board seems to continue to struggle most is with the handling of lower priority licensee complaint cases that are not referred to the department's Division of Investigation. As discussed in the third report, during the period from July to October 2016, the Board's non-sworn investigation section completed an average of about a dozen licensee complaint investigations per month and there was little change in the number of pending investigations. To keep case loads manageable for investigators, only about one-half of the more than 400 cases assigned to the section were assigned to specific investigators. The remaining, more recently received cases, were placed on a pending shelf. Subsequently, during November and December, the section continued to complete an average of about a dozen investigations per month which did not keep pace with the flow of newly assigned cases. As a result, the number of pending cases began to increase. As of late December, the section had more than 440 pending cases. For the 6 month period from July to December 2016, the Board's investigation section completed a total of about 75 investigations. Some of these cases were referred to discipline and about a dozen were closed with issuance of a citation. Only a handful of the cases were closed with issuance of a NOW, or a Notice Of Warning. Then, over a one month period extending from late December to late January, the Board abruptly reversed its process for completing non-sworn investigations of licensee complaint cases. The way that the investigation process usually works is that each case is assigned to an investigator to gather additional information about the case, including information to determine whether the alleged violation occurred, and to rule out other potential related violations. The results of the investigation are then reviewed by supervisory management personnel and discipline case analysts to determine whether the investigation was properly completed and whether the investigative findings support issuance of a NOW or a citation or referral of the case for discipline. The benefits of this process are that the investigation is not guided or conducted to achieve any predetermined outcome and blanket rules are not established regarding the type of discipline imposed for any broad category of cases. However, according to Board staff in late December, at the specific direction of the Executive Officer, investigation staff began a review of the sections pending cases, including the 200 or so cases that had not yet been assigned to an investigator. The review specifically targeted cases involving sleeping on the job and time sheet fraud, but also encompassed other types of cases. Following this review, and completion of some limited additional information gathering activities for some of the cases, 70 cases were abruptly closed with issuance of a notice of warning. Specifically, on January 11th, 27 non-sworn investigation cases were closed with issuances of a NOW. On the same day, a 45 minute teleconference meeting was held with the Board's Enforcement Committee, during which staff disclosed that they had initiated a review of the section's pending cases, and had identified 107 cases that could potentially be closed with a NOW. Contemporaneous minutes of this meeting were not kept, but it is our understanding there is only a brief discussion of this topic. Then on the next two days, January 12th and 13th, another 31 cases were closed with issuance of a NOW and over the next two weeks another 11 cases were closed with insurance of a NOW. During January, 24 other non-sworn investigations were also closed, but as of about two weeks ago, none of those other cases had resulted in either issuance of a citation, or referral of the case for discipline. In total, 94 non-sworn investigations were completed during January, equivalent to more than 20% of the sections 440 pending cases and about 75% of these cases we closed with issuance of a NOW. This compares to just 75 investigations completed during the entire preceding six month period with only a handful of NOWs issued for all of those cases. The abrupt closure of so many non sworn investigations in such a short period of time, and all with exactly the same outcome, which was issuance of a NOW, caught my immediate attention and prompted me to gather additional information about the surprising development. What I've since learned is encouraging in some respects and disconcerting in others. For example, it's encouraging that the Board finally began to implement my earlier recommendation to screen and triage lower priority licensee complaint cases not referred to the Division of Investigation, to identify those that could be handled as desk investigations and completed more quickly by gathering some additional records, making some phone calls to confirm or clarify the information provided with the complaint. However, I'm not comfortable with how this new process was implemented and I think my discomfort is shared by both the department's Division of Investigation, and staff within the non-sworn investigation section. Based on the information I've gathered to this point, it is self-evident from the large number of NOWs issued that the conventional investigatory process was reversed to instead search out cases where the currently available information could be used to support immediate closure of the cases with issuance of a NOW, rather than first investigating the cases and then determining what, if any, disciplinary outcome was supported by results of the investigation. I also believe that the section staff felt pressured to close cases with issuance of a NOW, in some cases without sufficiently investigating the cases. In summary, needs now exist to meet with the Board's non-sworn investigators and re-review all of these cases, to identify any cases that need to be reopened and further investigated. At this point, I expect the Board's investigators to be very forthcoming and helpful in identifying any such cases. Additionally, until this re-review is completed, caution should be exercised in interpreting any workload, backlog, or performance data provided by the Board concerning its recent handling of non-sworn investigation cases. Discipline case processing. The Board's discipline case processing, including the use of the Attorney General's fast track program, is continuing to improve marginally in some respects. Recently, however, there has been some additional accumulation of discipline cases. The recent increase in pending discipline cases appears to be the result of one, the increased number of discipline referrals to the AG, resulting from the larger number of investigations completed by the department's Division of Investigation. And two, larger numbers of subsequent discipline cases generated as a result of the large number of discipline case settlements reached during 2015-16, and related increases in the number of new probationers who are most likely to trigger subsequent discipline cases. Management and staff turnover and vacancies. As of early March, about 20% of the Board's positions were vacant. Additionally, excluding the Executive Officer, five of the Board's 10 supervisory and management positions were vacant. In my experience, I've never before seen such high levels of vacant positions, particularly at the supervisory and management levels. The Board's management structure has partially collapsed, particularly with respect to the enforcement program. One adverse consequence of the loss of key management personnel is that for the past seven weeks the Board has been unable to issue subpoenas for records that are needed to complete its enforcement investigations. Additionally, there are not currently any outside expert witnesses available to review cases involving psychiatric technicians. And there is only one outside expert witness available to review cases involving vocational nurses, and it is my understanding that outside expert witness recruitment activities have been stalled since the Executive Officer's leave began seven weeks ago. Also, probation reviews of new staff are no longer being consistently completed on a timely basis, as was previously the case. All of these circumstances increase the Board's vulnerability to various risk and should be a cause of considerable concern. My last topic is the Continuing Education Compliance Audit Project. The Continuing Education Compliance Audit Project, which has already been in the news, is illustrative of a broad range of problems that continue to be experienced by this Board. Despite obvious major problems with this project throughout the past four months, nothing has been done to restructure or abort this misguided, poorly conceived, runaway project. It is my understanding the CE Compliance Audit Project was initiated in late November during a meeting between the Executive Officer, the Acting Assistant Executive Officer, and two support staff. The project was launched shortly thereafter with the creation of a mass mailing list, the printing of about 57,000 dated audit letters, and the redirection of staff to stuff thousands of envelopes. Then, in early December, management apparently realized that they would be unable to complete the mailing. But rather than recognizing if Board staff were unable to even complete the mailing, then they certainly wouldn't be able to process the responses, management instead requested that the department's Office of Business Services complete the remaining mailings. Then, in early January, after requesting, expediting, receiving delivery of a large supply of window envelopes from the Office of State Printing, the Office of Business Services completed about 50,000 additional mailings. From this sequence of activities, it is evident that it was not the Board's intention to spread the mailings out in batches over a period of several months, as was suggested by the Board's Acting Assistant Executive Officer during the Board's February 10th meeting, or to send out 1,000 letter waves, spaced two weeks apart that was stated by the board in it's February 24th correspondence to Assembly staff. This latter report approach would have required more than two full years just to complete the mailings and would still have generated an overwhelming amount of work for Board staff. Had the Board utilized the 1,000 piece wave approach, it would have unleashed upon itself a 28-month-long flood of CE submittals, rather than the two month long tsunami of submittals that it instead experienced. Since completion of the mailings in early January, a group of two permanent full-time staff, two half-time retired annuitants, and one permanent full-time analyst on a half-time basis have been working on this project. This is equivalent to three and a half full-time positions. Additionally, other staff have been supporting the project on an intermittent basis and overtime was utilized during mid to late January to support the project and the use of overtime continued into February. Finally, at least two half-time AARP volunteers, equivalent to another full-time position, have been assigned to the project. To help handle deluge of submittals that were initially received, all of the Enforcement Division's managers, along with others, spent a full day together just opening mail. The Board's public phone lines have been continuously overflowing since early January, and during January the Board also received overflowing volumes of emails and faxes. The CE Compliance Audit has adversely impacted operations throughout much of the Board and has diverted staff, management, board member, and oversight agency attention from other more important business needs. Every passing day this project unnecessarily wastes more money and resources. The problems with this project will not somehow resolve themselves over the next several months as some seem to believe. Two weeks I visited the Board's offices and interviewed most of the staff that had been subsequently involved in supporting this project since its inception. I also requested access to a locked, vacant manager's office where I found more than 100 US postal service mail baskets filled with open but unprocessed CE submittals. In this same office there were just five baskets containing submittals that have been preliminary reviewed, but still needed to be re-reviewed and completed by the Board's CE Audit Specialist. Today, they have only about one basket of submittals has been fully processed by the CE Audit Specialist. Finally, there were a couple of trace that appear to contain about 800 pieces of unopened return mail but rubber banded stacks of unopened return mail were also present in many of the 100+ baskets of opened mail that had not yet been processed. These baskets may also contain license application fee remittances or other documents unrelated to CE that were not correctly separated from the CE documents. The Board does not track the CE submittals as they are received against the initial mailing list. Thus, there is absolutely no way that anybody can provide even a ballpark guesstimate as to how many of the 57,000 targeted licensees have actually responded to the mailing. Tracking against the initial mailing list is only completed by the Board CE Audit Specialist after completing a final review of the submittals and updating briefs. For various reasons, staff assigned to complete the preliminary review of the submittals sometimes experienced problems that prevent them from completing the reviews. The submittals with problems were set aside in separate stacks for subsequent review and handling by the Audit Specialist, who cannot possibly keep pace with the incoming flow of work generated by all the different staff involved in performing the preliminary case reviews. To date, the Audit Specialist has completed reviews and BreEZe updates for only about 1,000 CE audit cases. Based on actual performance, it clearly does not take an average of just 30 seconds to two minutes to review these submittals as has been stated by the Board. In fact, it probably took close to that amount of time per submittal just to open, date stamp and assemble the documents for subsequent processing. According to the Board's Acting Executive Officer, about 4,000 submitted packages have been preliminary reviewed today as evidenced by the Board's issuance of about 4,000 letters of compliance. However, in some cases, these letters were issued in error. In these cases, the CE Audit Specialist issues a letter of non-compliance to the licensee, after the licensee's already received a letter stating they were in compliance. So needless to say, this process necessarily creates a great deal of confusion among the affected licensees. Assuming that the Board continues to process an average of three baskets of submittals per month, using all the same staffing resources that have been allocated to the project since the start of the year, it will take two to three years just to do the preliminary reviews of the currently accumulated baskets of submittals. This does not account for any of the more time consuming work associated with completing the final reviews of the submittals and upgrading BreEZe, following up with licensees in cases where they're not in compliance with the CE requirements, following up with all the licensees that didn't even respond to the initial mailing and who are especially likely to have completed little or no CE, and tracking down thousands of licensees in cases where the initial mailings were returned to the Board because they were not deliverable to the address that the Board had on file. Additionally, most of more than 5,000 emails that the Board has received have not yet been processed at all. Finally, in those instances where the submittals do show compliance with the Board's CE requirements, the processes being used may not be producing documentation sufficient to support an actionable enforcement case. If enforcement actions are able to be initiated, then significant additional resources will be needed to perform citation preparation, issuance, fine collection and appeal handling services. This debacle needs to be stopped and it needs to be stopped now. There is no realistic path forward for this wasteful project. If the Board does not promptly abort this project, then legislation should be introduced to require such action. Hopefully, that would prompt the Board to terminate the project on its own accord. In conclusion, recent events and the Board's current circumstances may not repeat the specific events and circumstances that existed prior to the Board's previous sunset review. But they certainly have a familiar ring. In closing, I'd like to express my gratitude to the Department of Consumer Affairs leadership team, the Department's project manager, Bryan Clifford, and the Department's Division of Investigation, Office of Information Services, and Office of Human Resources for their cooperation and assistance throughout the past year and particularly during the past six months. Additionally, I would like to thank Board staff for their open and candid communication with me during my on site interviews, particularly, again, during the past six months. And I would especially like to thank those staff, who within, found ways to continuously relay additional information to me through various other communication channels. The information they provided was invaluable in enabling me to complete my assessments and helped immeasurably to keep me up-to-date regarding changes occurring at the Board. And that concludes my testimony and thank you.

It is a home ownership loan program. We provide mortgages, we are like any other bank in providing those mortgages. We, like other banks, suffered through the great recession and did very little loans for that period of time. I'm happy to say that this year, we are very close, when we close this year, to being back to more of a normal operations in line with the rest of the industry.
