Ellen Peter: Good afternoon, Chairman Beall, Chairman Wieckowski, and Members of the Committee. As indicated, my name is Ellen Peter. I'm the Chief Council of the California Air Resources Board. And prior to taking that position at ARB, I worked for the California Attorney General's Office for over 20 years. So I defended state agencies and I also prosecuted their enforcement cases. So as this Committee is well aware, over 50 years ago car emissions were started to be regulated by the California Air Resources Board to reduce smog and also to protect public health. Each year, each manufacturer, both cars and trucks, for each engine family have to submit a certification application. Thousands of these cert apps come into ARB every year and they're reviewed. And there's follow up testing. And then once approved, an ARB executive order allows these cars to be legally sold in California. Today, as the chair has indicated I am going to discuss ARB versus Volkswagen. The diesel emissions cheating scandal that broke in September 2015. This case is the biggest enforcement case that ARB ever handled. And also, it highlights the skills and the talents of the ARB scientists and engineers that figured this out. Our staff forced a confession after persistent questioning, innovative testing, and just a refusal to give up. Volkswagen's confession was triggered to ARB not others, and it was triggered by the enormous amount of data that ARB had collected in the case. VW is left with no other option than to admit it's deceit. So, I'm still under the Federal Court civil gag order as to the negotiations but more information is now public because the criminal indictments are unsealed and Volkswagen entered a guilty plea in court. So currently seven individual VW employees are under indictment, one's in custody. VW filed a guilty plea last month in Detroit and this guilty plea and these indictments sent out some public information. And I'm going to on that public information, in terms of the history, for the Committee today. So this conspiracy started over a decade ago. Diesel vehicles are very common in Europe. But because of ARB's tail pipe emission standards, they were not sold in California. However, over time California cleaned up its fuels and made it the possibility of diesel vehicles in California. So in turn, with these diesel vehicles, clean diesel vehicles, we were told, where is the possibility. So VW jumped on this opportunity and it launched off, it was the first to announce its clean diesel vehicle, and was starting to be sold in model year 2009. But the problem was their marketing announcement was head of their engineering expertise. So instead of solving an engineering problem or delaying the release of the car to the next model year, VW decided to lie, and to cheat, and did so for years. In the criminal indictments and the guilty plea, the facts are set out how a research project with ARB and others, including West Virginia University. How it blossomed into the discovery of an enormous emission scandal for these diesel vehicles. What was used was a defeat device, as Chairman Bell indicated. A defeat device essentially turns off the emissions control system when the car is not being tested. In some VW cars, as was mentioned, the excess Nox emissions was up to 40 times the allowed limit. Now, cars contain very complicated computer systems, that are constantly adjusting various systems. If your car has a serious problem, a rock comes up, pierces your oil pan, and all the oil drains out. Your car automatically goes into a protection mode to protect the engine. So one thing that happens in that situation is your emissions control system turns off. So in a less dramatic example, it's fine if you're emissions control system is designed to temporarily switch off in certain situations. Such as, you're accelerating passing another car. These are considered AECD's, auxiliary emission control devices, and they're fine as long as they're listed in a certification application and use in very limited situations. What's not okay is not telling about these AECDs. So when Volkswagen diesel certification applications instead of outlining the permitted conditions were turned off VW lied. In fact, the emissions control system was on only when it was on the laboratory dyno being tested in the required cycles leading up to certification. So VW wrote and installed complicated computer code so the car knew when it was being tested. It turned of the emissions control device when it was not. So in ARBs El Monte lab, this is where the cars are tested.  They're attached to multi-million dollar, huge dynanometer called dynos. And then the cars run in place like they're on a treadmill while they're being tested. Another system captures the hard emissions and these are then tested in the adjacent chemistry laboratory. In fact, the emissions control system was on only when it was on the laboratory dyno being tested in the required cycles leading up to certification. So VW wrote and installed complicated computer code so the car knew when it was being tested. It turned of the emissions control device when it was not. So in ARBs El Monte lab, this is where the cars are tested.  They're attached to multi-million dollar, huge dynanometer called dynos. And then the cars run in place like they're on a treadmill while they're being tested. Another system captures the hard emissions and these are then tested in the adjacent chemistry laboratory. So the Dyno operator drives the vehicle through prescribed test cycles which replicate things like going up hills and so forth. Now these test procedures are set out both in federal and state regulations, because the regulatory agencies and the car manufacturers need to know what they test procedures and requirements are. So we know that on road, real, driving emissions are almost always higher then the lab results. Just like when you buy a new car, your fuel economy sticker, saying with your miles per gallon is typically a little higher than what you actually get when you drive. So when ARB's research study started, they were examining these questions about why these higher emissions on the road for these Volkswagen diesel cars. Is it the fuel? Something else going on?. So, now at this point we can look backwards and we know what happened. Because VW was required to produce documents in respond to the federal criminal discovery. So in those indictments it outlines publicly what was happening in the scandal. We also know more from these documents as to VW's motivation. For example, in VW's larger, three liter cars, a mixture of urea and water known as adblue is stored in a tank and injected into the exhaust system to reduce Nox emissions. However the adblue tank design was not viewed as marketable in the United States. The proposed tank Either reduce the rise on the trunk so you have less storage or the ad tank, the smaller ad blue tank had to be refilled for more frequently before you had to get your oil changed. So VW decided neither of these options were acceptable. Instead, the VW engineers changed the AdBlue injection levels to operate correctly only when they were tested on the dyno. AdBlue was not injected when it was on the road. So end result bigger trunk, but more emissions. We also know now that the VW engineers improved their defeat devices over time. Unbeknownst to the owners, software updates to make the defeat devices work better were added when you took your car in for routine service. What is also revealed in the indictment are emails sent by increasingly panicky VW employees. In one email, a VW German engineer worried about the upcoming ARB dyno testing. Another email discussed ARB's responses that they needed to make to ARB. The email suggested creativity would be helpful here. Another email also translated from German said quote ARB is still waiting for answers. We still have no good explanations, end of quote, followed by five exclamation points. So back in California, there was a breakthrough. One of the ARB engineers hooked up the ARB's emissions monitoring laptop To a VW Passat, embraced it on that, on the passenger seat, So, at this point, there was real-time emissions data being collected from the Passat on their monitoring laptop. Fortunately, he had a long commute, and so he saw, as he was driving, that the NOX emissions unexpectedly started going up. And while he was driving, he saw that the software turn off. So, we've got a piece of information. So then afterwards, the ARB engineers went back to the lab and figured out how to replicate those situations. And they designed an alternative set of tests that nobody else knew about to try to get this to happen on the dyno. So, what happened, is these new tests that our ARB engineers designed, tricked the car when it was on the dyno to think it was on the road and then turned off the emissions control device. So, then the emissions from the illegal defeat devices were recorded, and they could be analysed on the dyno. So, it was admitted later by Volkswagen, much later, if the steering wheel turned in a certain way after a certain length of time, the car thought it was on the road and turned off the emissions device. So, in addition to that example our engineers also figured out other triggers for these cheating defeat devices, plural defeat devices. So, at this point, ARB goes back to the company and says, okay, this doesn't make sense. What's going on here? But VW kept lying. So, in the summer of 2015, VW employees came from Germany and made personal pitches to the ARB management and they said we have new data to show your testing anomalies. It's your problem your engineers are wrong. However, ARB refused to certify the model year 2016 cars until these answers were provided. Then more importantly, later that summer, ARB provided to VW the data from our newly discovered testing. And these emissions traces proved the case. And shortly thereafter VW confessed. So, what VW admitted then that had built illegal defeat devices into it's cars, into it's diesel cars for years over many different models. Nationwide, the illegal cars number over a half a million. In California there were about 85,000 illegal VW cars on the road when the settlements were negotiated last year. And then the question is, what to do? So, in my view, the case revolved around several key concerns that needed to be addressed, the cars, the environment, the market, and then the penalties and the deterrents. So, as for the cars, the issue confronting ARB was what can the owners do with these cars? Can they be fixed to meet the original standards? If fixed will they work properly? Will they be durable? What about an extended warranty? So, all those questions were dealt with and addressed in our settlement agreement. Environment's another concern. How do you address these past and future excess NOx emissions? Then we have the market. Clean diesel advertising attracted purchasers and distorted the market since these people could have bought zero emissions cars instead. So, California's historically been pushing the adoption of zero emission vehicles through various regulations and programs funding by the Legislature. But VW's actions hindered this by diverting people to cars that weren't clean. So, final concern is penalties and deterrence. How do we ensure that VW does not cheat again? And how do we make sure that other manufacturers conclude it's not worth cheating? So, these settlements were crafted to make the consumers in California whole and our environment whole. I'll run through the agreements in reverse chronological order. Monetary relief is 153.8 million to the Air Pollution Control Fund, and the Legislature can decide how it wishes to appropriate that money. And this significant penalty should warn other manufactures of the risks of cheating. So, the next agreement from the bottom on the list is the California Only 3.0-Liter Agreement. Once it's approved by the court, it requires an additional 25 million payment to the Air Pollution Control Fund on July 1st of this year. This extra monetary relief for California is to provide additional monies for low income Californians to get ZEV cars or to have some other similar program. So, the Legislature could choose to supplement the EMP Plus-up program that was funded last year, or some other program of their choice. Each year, each manufacturer, both cars and trucks, for each engine family have to submit a certification application. Thousands of these cert apps come into ARB every year and they're reviewed. Today, as the chair has indicated I am going to discuss ARB versus Volkswagen. The diesel emissions cheating scandal that broke in September 2015. This case is the biggest enforcement case that ARB ever handled. And also, it highlights the skills and the talents of the ARB scientists and engineers that figured this out. Our staff forced a confession after persistent questioning, innovative testing, and just a refusal to give up. Volkswagen's confession was triggered to ARB not others, and it was triggered by the enormous amount of data that ARB had collected in the case. And I'm going to on that public information, in terms of the history, for the Committee today. So this conspiracy started over a decade ago. Diesel vehicles are very common in Europe. But because of ARB's tail pipe emission standards, they were not sold in California. However, over time California cleaned up its fuels and made it the possibility of diesel vehicles in California. So in turn, with these diesel vehicles, clean diesel vehicles, we were told, where is the possibility. So VW jumped on this opportunity and it launched off, it was the first to announce its clean diesel vehicle, and was starting to be sold in model year 2009. In the criminal indictments and the guilty plea, the facts are set out how a research project with ARB and others, including West Virginia University. How it blossomed into the discovery of an enormous emission scandal for these diesel vehicles. What was used was a defeat device, as Chairman Bell indicated. A defeat device essentially turns off the emissions control system when the car is not being tested. In some VW cars, as was mentioned, the excess Nox emissions was up to 40 times the allowed limit. Now, cars contain very complicated computer systems, that are constantly adjusting various systems. If your car has a serious problem, a rock comes up, pierces your oil pan, and all the oil drains out. Your car automatically goes into a protection mode to protect the engine. So one thing that happens in that situation is your emissions control system turns off. So in a less dramatic example, it's fine if you're emissions control system is designed to temporarily switch off in certain situations. Such as, you're accelerating passing another car. These are considered AECD's, auxiliary emission control devices, and they're fine as long as they're listed in a certification application and use in very limited situations. What's not okay is not telling about these AECDs. So when Volkswagen diesel certification applications instead of outlining the permitted conditions were turned off VW lied. In fact, the emissions control system was on only when it was on the laboratory dyno being tested in the required cycles leading up to certification. So VW wrote and installed complicated computer code so the car knew when it was being tested. It turned of the emissions control device when it was not. So in ARBs El Monte lab, this is where the cars are tested.  They're attached to multi-million dollar, huge dynanometer called dynos. And then the cars run in place like they're on a treadmill while they're being tested. Another system captures the hard emissions and these are then tested in the adjacent chemistry laboratory. So the Dyno operator drives the vehicle through prescribed test cycles which replicate things like going up hills and so forth. Now these test procedures are set out both in federal and state regulations, because the regulatory agencies and the car manufacturers need to know what they test procedures and requirements are. So we know that on road, real, driving emissions are almost always higher then the lab results. Just like when you buy a new car, your fuel economy sticker, saying with your miles per gallon is typically a little higher than what you actually get when you drive. So when ARB's research study started, they were examining these questions about why these higher emissions on the road for these Volkswagen diesel cars. Is it the fuel? Something else going on?. So, now at this point we can look backwards and we know what happened. Because VW was required to produce documents in respond to the federal criminal discovery. So in those indictments it outlines publicly what was happening in the scandal. We also know more from these documents as to VW's motivation. For example, in VW's larger, three liter cars, a mixture of urea and water known as adblue is stored in a tank and injected into the exhaust system to reduce Nox emissions. However the adblue tank design was not viewed as marketable in the United States. The proposed tank Either reduce the rise on the trunk so you have less storage or the ad tank, the smaller ad blue tank had to be refilled for more frequently before you had to get your oil changed. So VW decided neither of these options were acceptable. Instead, the VW engineers changed the AdBlue injection levels to operate correctly only when they were tested on the dyno. AdBlue was not injected when it was on the road. So end result bigger trunk, but more emissions. We also know now that the VW engineers improved their defeat devices over time. Unbeknownst to the owners, software updates to make the defeat devices work better were added when you took your car in for routine service. What is also revealed in the indictment are emails sent by increasingly panicky VW employees. In one email, a VW German engineer worried about the upcoming ARB dyno testing. Another email discussed ARB's responses that they needed to make to ARB. The email suggested creativity would be helpful here. Another email also translated from German said quote ARB is still waiting for answers. We still have no good explanations, end of quote, followed by five exclamation points. So back in California, there was a breakthrough. One of the ARB engineers hooked up the ARB's emissions monitoring laptop To a VW Passat, embraced it on that, on the passenger seat, So, at this point, there was real-time emissions data being collected from the Passat on their monitoring laptop. Fortunately, he had a long commute, and so he saw, as he was driving, that the NOX emissions unexpectedly started going up. And while he was driving, he saw that the software turn off. So, we've got a piece of information. So then afterwards, the ARB engineers went back to the lab and figured out how to replicate those situations. And they designed an alternative set of tests that nobody else knew about to try to get this to happen on the dyno. So, what happened, is these new tests that our ARB engineers designed, tricked the car when it was on the dyno to think it was on the road and then turned off the emissions control device. So, then the emissions from the illegal defeat devices were recorded, and they could be analysed on the dyno. So, it was admitted later by Volkswagen, much later, if the steering wheel turned in a certain way after a certain length of time, the car thought it was on the road and turned off the emissions device. So, in addition to that example our engineers also figured out other triggers for these cheating defeat devices, plural defeat devices. So, at this point, ARB goes back to the company and says, okay, this doesn't make sense. What's going on here? But VW kept lying. So, in the summer of 2015, VW employees came from Germany and made personal pitches to the ARB management and they said we have new data to show your testing anomalies. It's your problem your engineers are wrong. However, ARB refused to certify the model year 2016 cars until these answers were provided. Then more importantly, later that summer, ARB provided to VW the data from our newly discovered testing. And these emissions traces proved the case. And shortly thereafter VW confessed. So, what VW admitted then that had built illegal defeat devices into it's cars, into it's diesel cars for years over many different models. Nationwide, the illegal cars number over a half a million. In California there were about 85,000 illegal VW cars on the road when the settlements were negotiated last year. And then the question is, what to do? So, in my view, the case revolved around several key concerns that needed to be addressed, the cars, the environment, the market, and then the penalties and the deterrents. So, as for the cars, the issue confronting ARB was what can the owners do with these cars? Can they be fixed to meet the original standards? If fixed will they work properly? Will they be durable? What about an extended warranty? So, all those questions were dealt with and addressed in our settlement agreement. Environment's another concern. How do you address these past and future excess NOx emissions? Then we have the market. Clean diesel advertising attracted purchasers and distorted the market since these people could have bought zero emissions cars instead. So, California's historically been pushing the adoption of zero emission vehicles through various regulations and programs funding by the Legislature. But VW's actions hindered this by diverting people to cars that weren't clean. So, final concern is penalties and deterrence. How do we ensure that VW does not cheat again? And how do we make sure that other manufacturers conclude it's not worth cheating? So, these settlements were crafted to make the consumers in California whole and our environment whole. Seth Frotman: Thank you very much for having me. Chairman Dodd, Vice Chairman Vidak and Members of the Committee, thank you for the opportunity to be here today to discuss the magnitude of the student debt crisis that we're facing in this country. Its impact on the millions of student loan borrowers throughout the State of California, and the critical role that student loan servicing plays in their financial lives. My name is Seth Frotman and I service as the student loan ombudsman at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, where I lead the Bureau's office for students and young consumers. As I sit before you today, more than 44 million consumers across the country collectively owe $1.4 trillion in student loan debt, that's $1.4 trillion. Over the last decade the total volume of outstanding student loan debt has nearly tripled. Adding $900 billion on the back of student loan borrowers. This increase can translate into very real financial consequences. For example, a recent study found that today's average student loan payment for a millennial is $351 and amount more than 50% higher than it was a decade ago. Rising monthly payment burdens can further strain household balance sheets for young consumers, especially for those struggling to balance sluggish wage growth and increase in other expenses such as healthcare, housing, and child care. One study shows that here in California, the average student loan balance of college graduates has grown by nearly 30% over the last decade. In fact, over 50% of California students who enroll in a bachelors degree program now graduate with over $22,000 in student loan debt. Recent data further demonstrates that student loans borrowers in communities across the country are struggling under the weight of student loan debt. For example, despite the range of default prevention options available, over 8 million student loan borrowers are now in default, a number larger than the population of 38 states. And in the last year alone, nearly 1.2 million borrowers defaulted on a Federal Direct Student Loan. This translates to more than two per minute. Additionally, despite improvements in the labor market and the economy, the share of delinquent student loans remains stubbornly high. Over the last decade, the share of consumers with past due mortgages, credit cards and car loans are now at or below pre-recession levels. In contrast, the share of borrowers with delinquent student loans remains near its recession era peak. And while struggling student loan borrowers are widespread, data shows a strong relationship between the zip codes of minority population and its delinquency rate, at both the city and national level. Recent research shows that zip codes with higher shares of African-Americans and Latinos suffered disproportionately higher rates of student loan delinquency. However, some observers have questioned the negative impact of student debt, citing the widespread availability of affordable repayment options, like income-driven repayment plans. But these assertions only tell half of the story, while it is true that most borrowers with a federal student loan have a right to pay based on how much they earn. Borrowers report a wide range of industry practices and policy pitfalls that create unnecessary barriers to payment relief, contribute to borrowers financial distress in the short run, and extend borrowers debts by months or even years. Taken together, these observations paint a bleak picture, millions of student loan borrowers face severe, but avoidable consequences. Borrowers depend on private companies known as student loan servicers to help them manage this debt. High quality servicing can help borrowers enroll in affordable repayment plans, take advantage of forgiveness and other benefits, and avoid delinquencies and default. But for far too many borrowers, their student loan servicers fall short. A wealth of recent data from government agencies, researchers and regulators offer insights into the scale of this problem. For example, a 2015 government audit found that 70% of borrowers in default may be eligible for a substantially lower payment, some even as low as $0. And for borrowers who are actually able to enroll an alternative repayment plan, data shows that servicing challenges can still hinder their ability to maintain an affordable repayment with nearly 60% getting knocked off track. Servicing breakdowns can wreak havoc on service members, veterans, and military families. The bureau has released several reports documenting complaints from military borrowers who report being guided into more expensive options than their student loan servicers. The bureau has now heard from tens of thousands of borrowers every single year who are struggling to keep up with their payments because they are unable to access essential costumer protections. Clearly, the status quo is failing. But to understand why, it's important to understand how we got here. Conventional wisdom often points to the rise in college tuition as the sole driver of increased student indebtedness. We also know that increase enrollment at career, high cost career, and for profit schools has directly contributed to increased student borrowing. While there is no question that the rising costs of college contributes to the recent increases, this observation downplays the effect of a cost shift from parents to students. For much of our recent past, families have oftentimes shared the economic burden of paying for college. In part, because parents drew on a combination of income, savings, home equity, retirement savings, in order to contribute. The family contributions, when combined with the student's income from part time work and paired with a combination of loans and grants were usually sufficient to leave a typical borrower with a modest debt load. When the recession hit, millions of families, particularly middle class families, and those in African-American and Latino communities suffered an economic shock with many families seeing their net worth cut in half. While with household's balance sheets battered, particularly for middle class families and communities of color, many students faced the choice of taking on student debt or not going to college at all. For many families and for many borrowers carrying unprecedented debt loads, this is a hole that we have yet to dig out of. Researchers, policy makers, and advocates have cited the college wage premium to make a public case for why increasing levels of indebtedness shouldn't deter students from attending college. And college does pay off for many. However, observers too often confuse the soundness of the supposed investment in college with an assertion that increased student borrowing is not a problem that demands immediate attention. This misses the mark. Millions of borrowers are struggling under the strain of historic levels of student debt. And a growing body of evidence suggests that rising levels of student loan indebtedness are having a spillover effect on other segments of the economy. Potentially limiting borrowers access to credit, reducing home ownership, and threatening their retirement security. Student loan debt may also inhibit far worse from pursuing careers such as entrepreneurs or as health care providers and educators in underserved communities. The debt burden students are shouldering is increasingly a lifetime one. We should not be cavalier about the burden we're asking these students to shoulder. Notions like, other people may have it worse offers little solace when far too many of the borrowers who have done everything we have asked of them still struggle to afford a down payment, start a family, or save for retirement. Nor should we ignore the potential risk to society and the broader economy as rising student indebtedness influences changes in saving and spending by an entire generation of consumers, we must do better. And thus lending and burrowing has changed, so as the regulatory landscape. Today, the Department of Education owns over $1 trillion in outstanding student loans, and relies on a number of non-bank student loan services to manage this debt. These companies historically had been subject to limited oversight and regulation in their capacity as services providers to, or affiliates of, the banks and other lenders that made federally-guaranteed loans. When Congress eliminated the bank-based Federal Loan Program, this already limited-oversight regime, no longer covered servicing of the vast majority of new loans, exposing important gaps in the patchwork of federal and state oversight. In effect, because there was no formal role for regulated entities as lenders, the student loan servicers managing debt for tens of millions of Americans fell outside of the existing framework for oversight. However, the Bureau has brought to bear a unique set of oversight tools in order to change this, both strengthening supervision of student loan servicers, and increasing transparency in the student loan market. For more than five years, the Bureau has been building an examination program that focuses on compliance at both banks and the largest non-banks in the student loan market. And we have made it a priority to take action against companies that are engaging in illegal student loan servicing practices. In my written testimony, you will find a dozen examples of the bureau's findings of illegal practices in this market. Violations uncovered through our supervisory and enforcement actions, indicate there is much more work to be done to clean up and reform the student loan servicing. And to help fill this regulatory gap I discussed, state policy makers across the country have considered steps to expand their oversight and accountability tools. California has been a leader in this approach. Building on the foundation laid by this Legislature, and by Governor Brown and this Committee, the State of California has positioned itself to protect the over 3.7 million Californians that are burdened with student loan debt. With the passage of the Student Loan Servicing Act last year, they now have a strong ally in the State of California to ensure that student loan servicers comply with federal and state consumer laws. And I'm pleased to join Senior Deputy Commissioner Scott Cameron, who leads the Department of Business Oversights, Division of Financial Institutions. And we'll share a data-driven vision for how California can continue to lead on these critical issues. So I just want to highlight three key areas, where our continued federal and state partnership offer immediate benefits for consumers. First, by providing rigorous oversight in every corner of the student loan servicing market. Although expanded state oversight over the largest and complex companies, is welcome news for borrowers, states can also play a key role in overseeing the dozens of smaller companies that service loans made by private lenders, and by keeping an eye on new entrants in this market. This role maybe particularly important as private lending and refinance activities continue to grow, and if policy makers at the federal level consider new policies that may drive families to borrow more from private lenders outside the federal aid system. Because of steps taken by California, federal and state regulators can now cover the water front, ensuring Californians are treated fairly, regardless of the size or location of the companies managing their loans. Second, by driving better practices and demanding better data, both federal and state regulators depend on accurate and timely data to better examine how servicers operate, and identify practices that pose risks to consumers as well as inform additional law enforcement and oversight's work. As California continues to build out its oversight function and assess its own needs, data from student loan servicers can help inform oversight work across the country. I think the old cliche is particularly apt in this context, sunshine can be the best disinfectant. And lastly, by sharing knowledge and insights from state oversight to inform federal policymaking. California examiners and law enforcement officials have a unique ability to work on a granular level, while simultaneously spotting trends in systemic issues, at a state or regional one. Through close state and federal coordination on student loan servicing oversight, the bureau and other federal policy makers can have the benefit of unique insights, developed on the ground by states in a historically opaque market. So in closing, a series of economic and policy changes over the last two decades continue to drive historic levels of debt owned by students and their families. And we continue to see the consequences of these decisions. We have also seen student loan servicers engage in illegal practices, adding insult to injury for struggling student loan borrowers. If we ask our citizens to take on student debt to get the degree, we must also redouble our efforts to ensure a road to repayment that is free from harmful or illegal practices. When loan servicers can operate in the shadows, free from rigorous federal and state oversight, consumers too often pay the price. Policy makers and regulators at all levels, have made strides to improve oversight and halt illegal student loan servicing practices. And learning important lessons from the last crisis as we work to prevent the next one, we can't go back. Thank you again for the opportunity to address the Committee today and discuss this important topic. The bureau looks forward to continuing our important work together, and in particular, our work to increase accountability. Thank you. Thank you Mr. Frotman, appreciate that. Mr. Cameron.

Scott Cameron: Good afternoon, Chairman Dodd and Members of the Committee. I am Scott Cameron, I'm the Senior Deputy Commissioner of the Division of Financial Institutions for the California Department of Business Oversight. Commissioner Owens sends her regrets that she can't be here, but I would like to say on behalf of the department and the Commissioner, thank you for the opportunity to participate in this important informational hearing. Chairman Doug through his Committee staff has asked the department to answer seven questions, and I'd like to proceed with those questions. So question number one, what are the major requirements of and protections contained in the Student Loan Servicer Act? The law provides for the Department of Business Oversight to license, regulate and provide oversight to student loan servicers. In general, the act requires servicers to adhere to specific borrow protections, prohibits a person from acting as a student loans servicer without a license unless exempt. Specifically, with regard to protections. Servicers must notify borrowers 15 days prior to transferring the service of a loan to another provider. When the servicing is transferred, servicers must provide borrowers with the new servicer's contact information, effective date of transfer, the date when the current servicer will stop accepting payments and the date when the new servicer will begin accepting payments. Servicers must provide on their websites information about alternative repayment and loan forgiveness options. At least once a year, servicers must provide the information about repayment and loan forgiveness options through written correspondence and/or email. When a borrower sends written correspondence in which they either state they believe their account is an error, or request specific information about their account, servicers must acknowledge that correspondence within five days of receipt and respond within 30 days. Such correspondence is considered qualified written request, which is important. When an account is subject to a qualified written request, servicers cannot provide adverse information to any reporting agency regarding that account for 60 days after receipt of that request. Servicers must provide accurate information about borrowers payment histories to the National Credit Bureaus. With certain exceptions, servicers must ask borrowers how to apply excess loan repayments and follow those directions. In addition, the act prohibits servicers from misapplying payments. To a borrower's outstanding balance. Finally, the act contains other provisions that prohibit unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent practices by servicers. The act also includes provisions governing the licensing, examination of servicers, and enforcement of the law requirements. For example, licensees must file annual reports with the Commissioner. They must be audited annular by CPA. They must maintain a minimum net worth of at least $250,000 as well as a surety bond of at least $25,000. And licensees must undergo an examination by the department, at least once every three years. And with regards to the law itself, the department has the authority to issue administrative orders, impose civil money penalties, and suspend or revoke their license. At question two. What entities are required to obtain licences in California under the act? Basically it is any entity that services students loans in California or for Californians in any other state must be licensed with exceptions of course. This includes, for example, the nine large US Department of Education contract servicers plus other private loan servicers. Question three, approximately how many entities do you believe will be required to obtain student loan servicing licenses in California? Department estimates approximately 25 to 30 entities will be required to obtain licenses from DBO. Question four, how many staff has DBO requested to implement the act? The department is in the process of creating a new unit to handle the responsibilities of the act. Currently, we are considering a staff of five. That staff includes one attorney, one manager, one senior program analyst, and two senior examiners. Once established, the cost of administering the program will be covered by the licensing fees. No general funds will be used in handling this program. Question five, when does the department expect to release draft regulations implementing the act? The department plans to submit for publication the proposed rules and related documents by July 1st 2017. Once we publish the rule making package there will be a public comment period that will run a minimum of 45 days. Based on the comments received from the public, if we make substantial changes, the public will have an additional 15 days to comment on those proposed changes. The final rule will be submitted, of course, to the Office of Administrative Law for final review to determine whether it will be approved or not. And that will be done within a year of our publishing. Which I indicated we plan to publish July 1st 2017. Question 6, does the department anticipate, it won't occur any significant challenges implementing the act? The department does not foresee any challenges, that being said, it is a new industry that will be, the department will be a supervising. However, we have the expertise in regulating loan servicers. We currently supervise mortgage loan servicers. And we know how to protect consumers with regards to financial services. So we feel confident that we'll be ready to implement this new act. Finally, question seven, would the department like to share any additional thoughts regarding the Student Loan Servicer Act with the Committee? I'll be brief here. The student loan debt obviously is a major issue for the country. And the California Student Loan Servicing Act is an important financial services reform. We look forward to working with the policy makers and the stakeholders to make sure the act is implemented in the way that the Legislature intended. Thank you again, Mr. Chairman and members, for giving us the opportunity to testify.

As mentioned before, there a number of nonprofit state agencies that participate in the private student loan market. And so these are state agencies that have their own private student loan programs. There are about 20 states across the country that offer their own private student loan programs. A couple of the largest ones are in the states of Massachusetts and New Jersey. Community banks participate on a smaller scale and then finally, as many of you probably read there a good number of new student loan refinance players in the market led by Social Finance, also known as SoFi. Common Bond, DRB, and Earnest, and they have been extremely active since 2013 in refinancing both private and federal student loans. The size of the private student loan market is relatively small when compared to the federal student loan program. Based upon data that Measure One collects twice per year for the Federal Reserve we estimate the total outstanding private student loan balances to be about $102 billion. So that's a 102 billion, relative to the $1.4 trillion number that often read out there in the press. So that represents approximately 7.5% of the total student loan balances outstanding with the remaining 92.5% beyond the federal student load programs. In terms of loans originations, prior students lenders made approximately $10.5 billion of new loans in 2016 compared to approximately $125 billion in federal student aid dispersed over the same period. Next, I want to cover private student loan underwriting standards, there's a very big differentiator between the private market and the federal market. Private student lenders conservatively underwrite their loans and follow strict credit guidelines compared to federal student loans that are achieved purely based on a borrower's need, financial need. As mentioned before, private student loans are schools certified, meaning that lenders check with the school before this person funds to ensure that the student is not borrowing more than the cost of attendance. Private student loans also rely heavily on cosigners. Also previously mentioned, cosigners typically a parent and these cosigners have stronger credit scores than the student. This is especially true with the undergraduate loans where the primary borrower lacks a long credit history and in the undergraduate market we see a cosigner rate greater than 93%. So that is a big component of the under-writed standards in the private market and then finally, borrowers are urged to use all other forms of financial aid prior to taking out a private student loan. This really is a loan of last resort. Strong under rating principles and guidelines have resulted in loan repayment performance since the financial crisis, so we read a lot about defaults increasing in the student loan market, but in the private market, we actually see the opposite trend post financial crisis. Measure One has detailed the improve performance in our private student loan report that we published twice per year. This is the report, it's a little bit lengthy, but you can go to the Measure One website, measureone.com, and download the free report and again, it's there intended to inform the market of what's going on in the private marketplace. The performance information of the report is contributed by six of the largest holders of private student loans. Navient, Sallie Mae, Discover, Wells Fargo, Citizens, and PNC, all contribute data to the report that measure one's big goals in life, is to bring more clarity to the student loan market. That's something that even post-crisis when a lot of us realize, more transparency was necessary in the financial markets. The student loans base still struggles a little bit in terms of transparency, but a big part of this report and the contributions of the participants is to bring transparency to the private student loan market. I'll conclude by talking a little bit about the performance trends that we're seeing through the third quarter of 2016. That's the last time we published the report. 74, and these are stats in terms of outstanding loan balances. So 74% of loans are in active repayment, 18.2% of the loans are in deferment. That's typically while the borrower is in school. 5% of the private student loans are in their grace period. That's typically the six month post-graduation period before the repayment term starts. In terms of delinquencies, 2.9% of loans are 30 to 89 days delinquent. To give you some perspective on that, over the last five years, that delinquency rate has declined 71%. On the 90 plus days delinquent, also known as seriously delinquent, the 90 plus delinquency rate is 1.9%, that is a five year decline of 51%, and on an annualized basis, the charge off rate in the private student loan market and, to be clear, most of the lenders charge off at 120 days. That's what they're required by the regulators to do. One servicer charges off slightly later than 120 days, but for the most part it's 120 days when these loans are charged off, and that charge off rate is 1.9%, and that represents a 61% decline over the last five years. And then, finally 2.2% of the loans are in forbearance, and forbearance is typically offered in the private student loan market for those borrowers that are experienced in some sort of financial hardship. So in conclusion, the differences in repayment performance can be really attributed to two things. One, are the strong credit under rating criteria applied by the lenders, and two, generally improving economy especially in terms of decreasing unemployment rates. Thank you for your time and open to any questions.

Brian Metzker: Brian Metzker, LAO. We find that the Governor's Budget proposal could generate additional general fund savings from increased federal funding for the additional NQIs. And it is consistent with the concept driving the original 2013 legislation. We would note that the administration's rationale for the proposal to protect the additional NQI's from potential tax penalties under the ACA. It is uncertain, as it is unknown, whether or not NQIs are paying, or could in the future pay tax penalties because the coverage they received through the state only Medi-Cal program is not formally certified as minimum essential coverage. However, because of the potential general fund savings from the additional federal funding and the consistency with the prior legislation, the proposal warrants serious consideration by the Legislature and we would provide the Legislature some issues for legislative consideration, depending on the action that the Legislature would take. If the Legislature were to approve the proposal, it might consider expediting the development and approval of Covered California health plans for all NQIs, including those transitioning to Covered California under the 2013 legislation. The Legislature might also consider directing relevant agencies with input from insurers to regularly report on how they're addressing some of the administrative complexities of the transition, as well as how many NQIs have been or currently are subject to tax penalties under the ACA. The Legislature might also consider requesting DCHS to establish procedures for re-enrolling NQIs in the state-only Medi-Cal program should reductions on federal funding of state health benefit exchanges result in less general fund savings. If the Legislature chooses to reject the proposal, for example, because of legislative concerns around the federal uncertainty around the ACA. The Legislature might consider whether or not to continue the planned transition of NQIs under the 2013 legislation. This is because any concerns about the transition proposed under the Governor's Budget are likely also to apply to the planned transition under the 2013 legislation. If the Legislature decides to repeal the authorized transition under the 2013 legislation. The Legislature might also consider directing DHCS to apply for CMS to certify the state only Medi-Cal program for NQIs as minimum essential coverage. This action would protect NQIs enrolled in the state only Medi-Cal program from potential tax penalties and there would be, of course, a fiscal tradeoff to that decision as general fund costs could increase by an estimated 100 million annually, as NQIs would no longer qualify for federal funding through Covered California.

And that's when there were time elapse standards, like clear appointment wait times, where consumers have to have by law, access to a primary care provider within 10 business days. A specialist within 14 days. And so these are actually measurable standards that we can hold the plans accountable for. So in about three years ago, we sponsored SB 964 because we wanted to make sure the plans are held accountable for this time elapse standards. And so SB 964 required plans to essentially file reports based on the standardized methodology so we can do apples to apples comparison. What is anthem doing versus blueshield versus Kaiserr versus Healthnet versus Molina and so on. Tamara Armstrong: Hello, good afternoon, Chair, Vice Chair and Members. My name is Tamara Armstrong. I'm with the Office of Statewide Project Delivery within the Department of Technology as Director Tong mentioned. Well, I'm excited to be here to talk about a difficult subject but something that also has great rewards and that's our project delivery. It is a priority for our organization and our priority is to see IT projects be successful so that is the thing we're all working to. We have a couple of functions in order to enable that to happen. And I'll provide a little bit more detailing to those, but to just review them quickly. First of all, we have authority for a project approval and oversight. We also have approval and authority over state wide technology procurement. And lastly, we provide services in the area from our California management office and so let me touch on what those three items are. You have a handout in front of you that is titled California State White IT project delivery and that's what I will be using to briefly walk through how it is that we help projects and facilitate our project success. So that first bullet there where Independent Project Approval Life Cycle, that is the process that Department of Technology uses to ensure that projects are laying a solid foundation. And that is what our emphasis is. We know through both private an public sector on studies, that the probability of success for a project is highly correlated to the sufficiency of planning, sufficiency of thinking through challenging areas. And so our initial focus is to make sure that projects are getting off on the right foot. Thinking very deliberately about the business case. What are the business problems that we are attempting to solve? We want departments to spend time with their business areas. We don't want something that just has been thought of and brainstormed by IT. But really we want to, to see a partnership between the business areas and the IT folks to really satisfy the business problems or paying points or opportunities of an organization. So once we have ensured that they have those business problems articulated and they understand why they are doing it, then we move on to what is the best solution for your specific project, for that specific department? What are the characteristics of that project that would affect the different alternatives that are under available and the ones that they would choose? And then we look at are they ready, right? Given the projects that they're hoping to achieve. Given the outcomes that they're hoping to achieve. What is their readiness to take on that particular project? And how does that a line with the approach that they're looking at using? California has typically using a certain approach to developing IT projects. And we're even looking at partnering with departments for determine what is the right approach for a project. Instead of doing large, big, what we call big bang we've developed over many years and implemented all at once. We're encouraging projects to spend their time investing and understanding the customers of that system, and then absolutely breaking the products down into smaller pieces, right? Where we can approach those various iterations very deliberately. And that is one of the approaches that we're currently leveraging within department. One of the key of our, key success I think or key benefit of our project approval life cycle is that it is a partnership. We are working with departments very actively, working with their agencies in discussions. The prior FSR process had frequently had the departments working and someone in isolation preparing a feasibility study report, what we call an FSR. And then sending that over to CDT. And that really laid out what their plan was. But we, the Department of technology, has Learned a lot from interacting with other departments from providing oversight to projects. And so we have a lot of information that we can share and support departments as they're planning for projects. And so, we partner with the departments with their respective agencies and with our subject matter experts such as Peter, right? In terms of laying the foundation covering those key areas right up front rather than trying to bolt them on later when quite frankly it's more time consuming and more expensive. So once we go through, looking at those various alternative approaches and we select an approach, as the department selects an approach that they think is the right approach for their project. Then we go into our procurement phase. And we look at what is the best way to procure the solution for this specific project. And so CDT partners with the department again to really look at things from the perspective of those project requirements. Our team again is very experienced in this. And we again, work with the departments and with the agencies that the departments fall under to make sure that we are putting in the procurement strategy that makes sense for them. And lastly, we have the California project management office that is heavily focused on enabling projects to be successful. As Peter mentioned, you know to describe how to do something and then to provide examples and coaching is a different thing. So CDT is focused on not only providing oversight capacity of are you doing what you're supposed to be doing, but here are some examples of how to do that, here are some lessons Learned, here are the areas that we commonly find challenges. And we look at challenged projects and we like to make sure that you address those early. And here's a tool, here's a resource, here's someone that you can talk to that may be helpful. We use a four stage project approval process, where once they want to have a project, they go through these various gates, what we call gates. And it shows that each portion of their project plans, their project planning activities, have been sufficiently completed. Once they've moved through those four gates, that project is considered approved. Department of Technology will approve that project. And then the Department of Technology's responsibility transitions into monitoring the health of the project, monitoring the project to make sure that they are indeed on target to achieve those business outcomes that the project was intended to achieve. And we monitor that throughout the life of the project and that is what our oversight responsibilities are. We again, have an independent responsibility to monitor those projects but we also are well positioned to provide them with valuable insight and feedback to help them to be successful because in the end that is our mission. So in order to run this project, in order to run this organization, we are looking at how can we create the best business value for the departments. What do they need, and how are we providing it? And so in addition to revisiting the project approval life cycle, which we recently implemented in the last few years, and this new process, we're also looking at our procurement and saying how can we allow departments to get the solutions that they need in the most efficient and effective way possible. And we've leveraged that on several projects recently. We've established what we call our pre-qualified vendor pool for one of our projects so that they can get access to resources that have very specific knowledge in an efficient and effective way. And we're looking at working with the IT community in the state to be able to say what else do you need? And that is our mission, is to define what they need and then to be able to enable them and support them as much as we can. So this document that you have here provides a little bit more detail into that, but I'll try respect our time constraints here and allow you to move on.

Julie Su: Thank you, and good afternoon, Mr. Chairman and Committee Members. My name is Julie Su, and I am the California Labor Commissioner. And I'm here to talk about the strategic enforcement approach that we have utilized in order to improve our enforcement efforts, to make the best use of the resources that we have as well as to use the most cost effective and smart way to gain compliance throughout California. So by way of background just a few numbers, there are some studies about the Incidents of wage theft. There's a 2010 study by the UCLA Labor Center that talks about how much there is, but there's a 2014 US Department of Labor finding that the minimum wage is violated in California 372,000 times per week. So if you take a look at the enforcement resources for the division, there was a long period, a few decades, of declining staffing, at the same time that there was a growth in the number of employers and employees throughout California. To make it more concrete, if you take all of the investigative staff that I have right now we have one investigator for roughly 84,000 Californians in the workforce. That includes all of our investigative staff, meaning not just our field enforcement deputies, but those who adjudicate wage claims, those who investigate retaliation, and those who enforce judgments for wages. By comparison, in 1982 and 83, it was about one in 76,000, one investigator for 76,000 Californians in the labor market. So over the last 40 years, there has been evolution in the economy, there's been obviously growth both in terms of numbers but also complexity. There's been growth in the protections that working people in California people enjoy. I know we're all proud of that here in California. And there's been a growth in the underground economy. So arguably, the ratio should not be comparable, it should actually be lower in terms of investigators to workers. And if you just take out the field enforcement deputies, the disparity is even starker. So to be more specific about that, we essentially have two field investigators for all of Alameda and Contra Costa County. Three investigators for all of the area from Sutter and Yuba Counties down to Sacramento County. So we're talking about a dirth in the meets verses required to fault the underground economy, to fight wage theft and to make sure that the protection that working people are suppose to enjoy in California are real. So we have adopted strategic enforcement approach, which eliminates the random inspections. We no longer go out and do sweeps, where we just count up the number of inspections we've done and call it a day and say that we've been successful. This approach has been embraced by employers, who we now do not just again go out there and use our resources and often times don't find any violations, right. One oft he biggest improvements by strategic enforcement is that the ratio of citations to inspections has improved dramatically. So in 2010 it was about 46%, 46% means that it is less than half of inspections conducted by the Labor Commissioner's office resulted in a citation of some sort. So you can understand why employers would say we're being investigated and we're not doing anything wrong, that's not a good use of government resources, and it's not good for employers of California. In 2016, that number has risen to 85%, so we've steadily improved that. Now that means that almost 9 in 10 of our investigations result in a citation. So we're targeting better, we're using our resources smarter, and we're going after law breakers rather than compliant employers trying to make an honest living in California. We also find more violations per investigation, so we're really focusing on the biggest threat to working people in California, which is wage theft, the systematic denial of a worker's right to take home what he or she earned at the end of the day. So our strategic enforcement not only includes better targeting, it includes more in depth investigations. It's no longer good enough to go in and look for whether there's a posting on the wall, or whether there someone's licences are supposed to be, or even whether they have workers' compensation, all of which are important but don't get to the heart of why working people remain in poverty in California. So what we do is we actually interview workers, we need to gain their trust in order to find out what's going on, we get payroll records, we do compress wage audits and we cite for wages owed and penalties associated with wages, and that changed the way we operate. It also requires far more resources to do an in-depth investigation into wage theft than it does into a violation that can be determined just by looking at paper. So our strategic approach has also involved us working more closely with community partners on the ground, whether they be community's organizations or unions, or employer associations, or industry representatives to again, find the bad actors. And I will say that one of the biggest pushes for more investigations, more enforcement has come from employers in industry associations, who feel like the level playing field cannot prove reality without more enforcement and more of this type of strategic enforcement. So our request is to build on the success. We've started this enforcement, but in order to really gain an impact in order to attack the underground economy and stop the bad actors from continuing to operate, in order to put wages into working people's pockets, we would like to take the strategic enforcement approach, replicate it, use it throughout the division, and make sure that the promise of a just day's pay for a hard day's work is real in California.

Bonnie Holmes-Gen: Great. Mr. Chair and members, Bonnie Holmes-Gen with the American Lung Association in California. We strongly support this bill. Ari Freilich: Good morning. My name Ari Freilich, appearing on behalf of the Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence, and Americans For Responsible Solutions. I want to thank Chairman Jones-Sawyer for your leadership on this bill. Our state's gun safety laws are predicated on the basic consensus view that some individuals, due to their criminal, behavioral, or mental health history, pose a unique, an intolerable risk to public safety if armed with lethal weapons. Accordingly, under California law, the people convicted of any of roughly 40 separate misdemeanors are prohibited from owning or acquiring guns for a period of 10 years after conviction unless they successfully petition a court to demonstrate by preponderance of the evidence that they are not a threat to public safety. This list of prohibiting offenses, however, seemingly arbitrarily, does not currently include hate crimes. The large majority of which, according to DOJ records, are, in fact, violent or involving the use or threatened use of force. As the Chairman mentioned, this leads to sometimes absurd results. These individuals present a unique and growing threat to public safety and are not the law-abiding, responsible citizens that the Supreme Court has said are entitled to exercise a right to bear arms under the Second Amendment. This is especially true because violent extremists and hate groups so often use fire arms as tools of violence and intimidation. Recent mass murders targeting our nation's LGBT, African American, and religious minority communities. At a night club in Orlando, a church in Charleston, a Sikh temple in Oak Creek are among the deadliest hate crimes of committed on US soil and one of the deadliest mass shootings in American history. These are just some of the most visable examples of a larger, national trend. Between 2010 and 2014, roughly 43,000 hate crimes were committed in our nation involving the use or threatened use of a gun. And since 2014, hate crimes have become both more numerous and more vicious, with rising rates of hate crime driven primarily by rising rates of violent hate. Research has found that individuals who have committed hate crimes in the past tend to escalate their conduct and the level of damage or violence they inflict, making them an unique and intolerable risk to public safety with lethal weapons. These patterns underscore the need to ensure that individuals have already been dually convicted, for escalating bigotry and acts of criminal intimidation, are temporarily prevented from possessing or acquiring guns after conviction unless they successfully petition the court to demonstrate they are not a threat to public safety. Six other states prohibit at least some hate crime misdemeanants from accessing firearms. It's time that California joined them to make our state safer and freer for all who call it home. Thank you.

Yet immigration and custom enforcement's detainer requests violate this key principle. As the Committee analysis clearly states, ICE detainers do not require reasonable suspicion or probable cause, and do not require a warrant. And are not based on any of these basic tenets that we hold important in terms of when we must detain someone. California's Trust Act limited the circumstances under which a hold could be responded to but also cautioned That there is no requirement for a warrant and no established standard of proof, such as reasonable suspicion of probable cause, for issuing an ICE Detainer Request. Immigration detainers have erroneously been placed on the United States citizens, as well as immigrants who are not deportable. Just four months after California passed the Trust Act, a federal judge in Oregon confirmed or held that ICE detainers are unconstitutional, and violate the Fourth Amendment's protection against searches and seizures. In Miranda-Olivares versus Clackamas County, the court stated that detaining the woman beyond her release date was a clear violation of unreasonable searches and seizures, and ordered that damages be paid. Since then, hundreds of counties across the nation have adopted measures to stop submitting their local law enforcement to honoring these requests. Furthermore, mandating the continued detention under circumstances, absent a warrant, without reasonable suspicion or probable cause, violates well established constitutional principles. Just as recently as two weeks ago, a court in Florida also held that ICE detainers are unconstitutional, and the judge in that case ordered that ICE holds on county inmates violate the separation of powers between state and federal government, and the Constitution of the United States. The federal government is without power to compel state authorities to house federal prisoners. As stated previously in 2014, a Federal court already found Eskon to be unconstitutional, and in 2014 the Obama Administration acknowledged it's failures, and dropped the program all together. In January of this year, however, the Trump Administration reversed course and issued an executive order reinstituting Eskom, and we've already Learned these painful lessons in California. We had several cases of folks that had been, had no criminal history or had been convicted of low level offenses, who were detained for weeks, if not months, beyond what's permissible under the Constitution. California and local entities would subject themselves to continued liability, given that the case law has stated that these detainers are unconstitutional, and do violate the individuals Fourth Amendment rights. And just as recently as last week, LA Police Chief's Beck, already reported that given some of these policies by the Trump administration, we've already seen a decline in sexual assault cases and domestic violence cases. If we are really talking about enhancing public safety for all, we really need to ensure that immigrants can feel safe coming forward to work with law enforcement, and report crimes, service witnesses. This bill does nothing to enhance the public safety for anyone. And for these reasons I respectfully ask that you oppose. Thank you.

For those reasons, we must oppose AB 539.

The second is that the school systems, both at the local level and in the County Office, had to divert money from the classrooms to pay for these legal fees, and hopefully that won't be an issue in the future. And finally, it makes it more difficult for the CalPERS system to actually administer the Replacement Benefit Plan fund, and we hope that this bill will remedy that as well. Thank you.

Brandon Nichols: Great, good afternoon Chair and the members of the sub Committee. I appreciate you're taking the time on a very busy day to consider this issue. I am Brandon Nichols. I'm the acting Director of the Department of Children and Family Services in Los Angeles County, and I'm here on behalf of supervisor Sheila Kuehl and a broad coalition to talk about the child care bridge proposal. So I think that the presentation that you just had on CCR by Director Lightbourne, Sara Rodgers, Greg Rose, in Department of Mental Health, or Department of Health, it was a great intro to the issues that we're trying to address with the foster care bridge proposal. So as you hear, as we have had CCR come in our need for foster parent is going to be even greater, and that's happening at a time that we had been losing foster parents.  So in LA County in last 10 years we gone from 8,000 available foster parents to 4,000, and that's a trend that's been repeated across the state. As we moved out of congregate settings, we're going to need more foster parents to take care children. And we've also seen in that same time period an increase in young children coming into care. So our zero to five population since 2000 has gone from 28% of the population to almost 40% of the population. So we have young kids coming into care and those kids are kids that don't go to school, they're kids who need extra attention and extra resources. And this is a state-wide issue, it's not just an issue for LA. You heard testimony about the use of ... dollars. So when a proposal was put out from the department for our counties to submit recommendations on how to use ... dollars, I believe 58 counties responded. Out of those 58 counties, 28 counties included your request for child care. One of our local advocacy organizations did a survey of foster parents, to ask them what was one of the biggest barriers to being a foster parent in LA county, and they repeated the child care was a problem for them. So here's how it works. We take a child, now often under five years old. We knock on a door of somebody who maybe wasn't expecting to have a baby in their care, and say, please take care of this baby, sometimes it's a relative. In LA county, we do a good job placing with relatives. 52% of our children are placed with relatives. If that person works the next day, they have to miss work. And if they work the following week, they have to miss work that following week until they can get that baby into childcare, or they have to say, which is an untenable position to put them in, I just can't take care of my niece, or I just can't take care of my grandkid, and that's what this proposal would help address. I don't know how much further you want me to go until the speaker gets here, but families are an important resource for the kids. And if we don't support the families that take care of the kids, the kids are ultimately affected. So we as a system, we as a government, need to rally around those people who are willing to step up, open their heart and open their homes to take children in and this is a big way of doing that. It's a way to show that we as a community value the efforts they're putting forward. But it is also is a way for us to help them in a very tangible method. So there's three parts to the proposal. The first part is it provides a time limited voucher so that they can flexibly get kids into child care while we navigate the existing state system of child care provision.  It also provides navigators to help foster parents navigate that system. And the third part is it provide trauma informed training for people that actually provide child care. As you know removal of a child from a home is a traumatic event. Those kids express behaviors that are atypical sometimes and takes special skills to address and to stabilize. So that's the three primary parts of the bill.

Last year, the State Auditor released a report that found foster youth were being prescribed powerful psychotropic medications without adequate oversight. Often these youth were prescribed multiple medications, mixing classes of drugs in amounts exceeding recommended dosages. These practices were outside of the state guidelines for safe practice. The report also found that alternative therapeutic services were not being tried or made available. The Auditor's report really struck a chord with me, because it could have been describing my own experience. At age 14, the doctors gave me various powerful drugs. At one point, I was on four different medications at the same time. I was taking two antipsychotics, Abilify and Geodon, an antidepressant, Trazodone, a medication that's not approved for children, and a mood stabilizer called Lithium. This consisted of me taking six pills in the morning, and six pills at night for a total of 12 pills per day. These powerful and sedating psychotropic medications cause serious side effects like weight gain, tunnel vision, and gave me a zombified feeling. I couldn't stay awake in class, and failed classes because I could barely keep my head up to participate. I also developed an irregular heartbeat because one side of my heart was enlarged due to the weight I had gained from being on the medications, and I also suffer from ticks on my body that I continue to have to this day. What I actually needed was therapeutic behavioral services, not a cocktail sedating psychotropics, to help deal with my self-injurious behaviors. As well as, trauma-focused therapy for the sexual and physical abuse I had experienced. As well as grief counseling when my mother passed away while I was in care. A few weeks before aging out, I was finally set up with a trauma focused therapist. Nine years, after the initial abuse when I was eight years old. Those services were given to me too late, as I was already going to turn 18 and exit out of the system. And I needed that support earlier and for more time. I was exhibiting behaviors that doctors wanted to medicate me for. Instead of actually helping me deal with the trauma and cope without self harm. The foster care system neglected to take care of me and my needs from the trauma that I went through. And instead, the system over medicated me, and did not give me appropriate and effective treatment to help with my PTSD. Thank you.
