Pat Leary: We will do our very best to be mercifully brief. I'm Pat Leary, I'm the Chief Deputy Director of the Department of Social Services, and this is Pam Dickfoss who was our Deputy Director for Community Care Licensing. I think your agenda actually did a fantastic job of really laying out for you what the division is, who we are, what we do, and what we had gone through in the last years, and have a legislature who's played a really important role in supporting us in that. I think what we'd really sort of like to talk about is the programs that we have started are well under way. We were making up for a lot of deficit that got created during the recession where practice. And policies and documentation had sort of fallen away. The resources we've gotten have been well used and very strategically targeted to get us back. We have made I think excellent progress in trying to change the process and the practice. I think that the stakeholders that we work with would echo that, we're not late,  but I think that we still have a ways to go, and I think that the recent California State Auditor report pointed out that we do still have those deficiencies. We are aggressively addressing those right now, we agreed with all but one of the recommendations, and we are in the process of implementing those changes right now. We anticipate that at our six month response to the Auditor we won't have much at that work already completed. In terms of the things that we are looking at on our horizon right now, we are implementing the increased inspection frequency which was a huge sea change. Starting in January, we started inspecting all facilities once every three years instead of once every five years. That will continue for both adult and senior care and our children's' residential to go down to two years next year, and then one year the following year, which is really incredible. We have the staff on board. They are in the process of doing those inspections right now. And we do anticipate that we're going to be able to make those targets and stay on track. We also anticipate that as a result of those increased inspections over time, we expect to see fewer complaints as a result. One of the problems was once we went to every five years that's really what we became was a complaint based system of regulatory oversight where we were going into facilities after damage had already occurred, after something had already occurred. We are very much of the mind that once we start increasing the inspection frequency, we're out there more often. We're going to be able to spot things before they occur, help to address it with the licensee. Help to correct providing technical assistance to licensees, so that we can hopefully avoid harm. There will always be room for complaints. There will always be unforeseen events that occur, but to the extent we can move away from a complaint based system and more to a proactive forward looking system. We think that the public will be safer and the health and safety of the folks in these facilities is paramount. It's one of the foster parents was relating today. When the parent is standing there releasing their child, their baby into daycare, they want to have a reasonable belief that the regulatory system that's providing oversight is meaningful, and that is truly our intent as we do this. One other question, was just mentioned in the agenda was in term of what we're doing with our key indicator tool as well as our workload study. We did not get all the answers we hoped to out of that key indicator tool, but we have found it to be very useful. It allows us to do more inspections and we did get a lot of assistance from Sac State in honing the tool itself so that we were asking the right questions, which is more helpful in trying to determine which facilities need a closer look. Which facilities need further inspections and which, if they're performing well on the kit are more likely to not have any additional adverse events. So we intend to keep using that as we go forward, we hope to further refine it and further look at what we can do to make it a more useful and more targeted tool for different times of facilities. We're also looking one of the big things that we're in the process of doing, is creating some new information technology. Our systems are best to find as antiquated, there's someone above an IBM punch card but they are not what anyone would consider modern. As part of the child welfare system digital services project, the licensing functions are included within that for creating a new system and taking these old antiquated systems and moving them to the cloud and new technology. We think that's going to give us a lot of tools that we can implement in the future of using tools like business analytics. To try and help us even further define which facilities might need more attention, might need less attention, what types of things we should be focusing on. That's all information we kind of do by hand now. We have literally data miners who go in and pull out this information to try and assist us in looking at trends and what kinds of complaints we're seeing and what kind of violations we're seeing so that when we see those and in fact last year we did a survey on what were the most frequently cited complaints so that we could say to the field, to the providers. These are the things that you're getting citations for, here are the ways you can avoid these citations, and it was actually quite helpful and well-received by the provider community in order to do that, because they don't want to get the violation. We'd prefer that they don't have the violation, that they're in compliance. So it really does help us. So those are sort of the major things that we have on the horizon. There are lots of other process changes, practice changes, we're still implementing legislation on a regular basis. We get new legislation each year directing us to do things that we follow up on for example, the psychotropic medications. In addition, just this year we published for the first time. The information online about law enforcement contacts with youth in foster care and group homes specifically, group homes and shelters. Will Lightbourne: Great. Mr. Chair, Committee, thank you. We're moving now into the Continuum of Care Reform item of the CDSS budget. I'm Will Lightbourne. I'm joined by Sara Rogers, Greg Rose and Dina Kokkos-Gonzalez from our colleague agency at the Department of Healthcare Services. I'd like to sort of just frame and introduce the topic and then I will hand it on. Continuum of Care Reform is the initiative that was adopted by the Legislature in 2015 and signed by the Governor, which really represents probably the most significant change in 20 or 30 years in how we approach the foster care portion of the child welfare system in California. In some respect, it's probably one of the most far reaching initiatives in the country. Certainly, in any state, that it is, state administered county operated. The goal simply of the initiative was to say children should only be being cared for in an institutional setting to receive high level therapeutic services that can only be provide in that setting. But that the treatment services and the therapy services that they need should be well and safely cared for in home-like settings, should be provided wherever they are. So we should be moving the services to the children not the children to the services. This of course requires sort of a major integration across state level departments and systems, between counties and state, between local county agencies that are comparable to the state agencies, private providers, whether they are the managed care providers or the human service providers who either are licensed by the state or under contact to the counties. It requires a transformation of the residential services component of the system. It's in many respect a sort of a three dimensional process. The administration has been very strongly committed to this implementation. The budget year funding for CCR implementation is in excess $200 million above sort of the regular core realigned child welfare program. And the sort of artist of this three-dimensional process is Sara Rogers, who is chief of the CCR implementation branch, and so I'm going to turn it over to Sara.

I first entered the foster care system at age 4 and went in and out of the system from ages 8 to 12. Then I stayed in the foster care system until I turned 18 and emancipated. I went through many traumatic experiences in and out of the foster care system. I was physically, emotionally, sexually, and verbally abused. I survived it all and today I'm a senior student attending California State University East Bay, and an advocate with the National Center for Youth Law. Last year, the State Auditor released a report that found foster youth were being prescribed powerful psychotropic medications without adequate oversight. Often, these youth were prescribed multiple medications, mixing classes of drugs in amounts exceeding recommended dosages. And these practices were outside of the state guidelines for safe practice. The report also found that alternative therapeutic services were not being tried or made available. The auditors report really struck a chord with me because it could have been describing my own experience. At age 14, the doctors gave me various powerful drugs. At one point I was on four different medications at the same time. I was taking two antipsychotics, Abilify and Geodon, an antidepressant, Trazodone. A medication not approved for children, and a mood stabilizer called Lithium. This consisted of me taking six pills in the morning and six pills at night for a total of 12 pills per day. These powerful and sedating psychotropic medications caused serious side effects like weight gain, tunnel vision, and gave me a zombified feeling. I couldn't stay awake in class, and failed classes because I could barely keep my head up to participate. I also developed an irregular heartbeat, because one side of my heart was enlarged, due to the weight I had gained from being on the medications. I also suffer from ticks on my body that I continue to have to this day. What I actually needed was therapeutic behavioral services. Not a cocktail, sedating psychotropics to help deal with my self injurious behaviors. As well as trauma focused therapy for the sexual and physical abuse I had endured, as well as grief counseling when my mother passed away while I was in care at age 17. A few weeks before aging out, I was finally set up with a trauma focused therapist, nine years after an initial abuse when I was eight years old. Those services were given to me too late, I was already going to turn 18 and exile the system. And I needed that support earlier and for more time. I was exhibiting behaviors that doctors wanted to medicate me for instead of actually helping me deal with the trauma and cope without self harm. The foster care system neglected to take care of me and my needs from the trauma that I went through. And instead the system over medicated me and did not give me appropriate and effective treatment to help with my PTSD. Thank you.

For the success of the continuum of care reform, we must address the crisis shortage to poster parents. The number of poster parents in LA County has declined by over half of what it was a decade ago, decreasing from about 8,000 foster families to under 4,000 today. The landscape of our caregivers has changed from primarily retirees to working parents. At this time, LA's caseload of children ages zero to five has increased disproportionately from almost 28% in 2000 to 38% in 2016. One of the biggest barriers to recruiting foster parents is the lack of access to childcare at the moment of placement. It's a timing issue. They simply cannot wait until a spot becomes open on a waiting list. This is especially true for relative caregivers who answer the call to take in a child at a moment's notice without the opportunity to plan for who will care for the children while they are at work. By building an emergency care bridge between the child welfare and child care systems, we can recruit and retain families, stabilize children at a critical moment's notice, and help to ensure that they benefit from high quality ongoing trauma, inform child care development services Therefore, I urge your support.

Thomas Martin: Okay, great, so good afternoon. As Coby mentioned, my name is Thomas Martin. I'm the Assistant Deputy Secretary for Veteran's Homes. The proposal today combines a number of ideas that Cal Vet and the Legislature have been working on over the past few years. It also reflects a number of recommendations that were included in the Little Hoover Commission report from earlier this month. In a nutshell, the language addresses three key areas. First, there's a number of technical or structural changes to replace outdated language or update Department's authority and responsibilities. For example, we'd be eliminating a number of antiquated references to one veteran's home, as opposed to the eight veteran's home we have today. Also we're updating our regulatory authority and clarifying our building regulations. Second we're also proposing that the homes re-prioritze our veteran applicant population. Veterans with 70% or greater service-connected disability ratings, who, clearly in the service, left the most on the battlefield. They would be, they should be the first in line into our veteran homes. They should be right at the top of the list. Along those same lines, veterans who have the greatest need today, who need our services the most, they should also be at the top of our list. So, this is in line with the Department's overall mission. It's in line with our mission to make sure we serve those who need us the most and we think this is going to be a critical fix to make sure we can best serve the veteran community. Third, the proposal would also help reduce Cal Vet's impact on the General Fund. There's a number of changes, some of them large, some of them smaller. But overall, they make a significant impact on the, on our General Fund footprint.

Stacie Berumen: Good afternoon. Stacie Berumen. I'm an assistant executive officer for the Board of Registered Nursing and I will be speaking to this budget change proposal. The Board of Registered Nursing is requesting three nursing education consultant positions, beginning in fiscal year 2017-18 and ongoing. To ensure all approved nursing programs have a method to evaluate military education, experience, and training. May qualify to meet nursing education requirements, and evaluate military education experience and training at the time of application, to qualify to take the NCLEX-RN exam, and obtain licensure in California. The board understands that the LAO has concerns with the proposal, and as a result we thoughtfully considered what the statute states, in conjunction with the types of duties that could possibly benefit military applicants if they were to choose nursing as a career when they have completed their military service. We have determined there is additional workload in the following areas. In addition to evaluation of policies and procedures at all approved nursing programs, the NECs will work with licensing staff to review applications where the applicant graduated from California approved nursing program to determine whether nursing programs are indeed following their policies and procedures. The NECs will also gather data during the review of the applications for licensure to evaluate what type of training and experience was accepted for educational credits or challenge exams so a comparative analysis can be completed and disseminated to the board and the nursing programs as a means to identify best practices. The NECs will also monitor and collect exam scores for military applicants to determine whether the education, training and experience are sufficient to successfully pass the exam and obtain licensure. For those applicants who do not pass the exam, the NEC's will review exam information to develop a personalized didactic and clinical remediation plan with weekly follow up. The NECs will compile and distribute aggregate data related to areas of exam deficiencies in order to help them improve educational outcomes and improve exam pass rates. The NECs will be in contact with the various branches of the military, to stay up to date on the different types of positions where experience and training can be considered for possible credit, or challenge exam, when enrolling in a nursing program, and disseminate that information to the board and nursing programs. We have developed additional workload data that has been prepared, and is being vetted through the administration and this information can be provided for your consideration.

Senate Bill 1192 mandates the creation of a permanent Office of Student Assistance and Relief, or OSAR. This office is mandated to be staffed with individuals that have specific knowledge in student services as it relates to financial aid and advocating for students. As a priority, this office will assist students of the schools owned by Corinthian Colleges by providing individualized assistance in relieving or mitigating the economic and educational opportunity loss incurred by the closure of their educational institution, but the staff will be available to assist all students that are impacted by the closure of other eligible institutions. The bureau had 104 educational institution main and branch locations close in fiscal year 15/16 impacting approximately 5490 students. Juno Duenas: My name's Juno Duenas and I'm the Director of Support for Families. We coordinate Family Voices of California. I want to thank you, Senator Pan and Children Now, for inviting us to give input. I'll be talking about family services and family engagement. I'm a parent, it's my most important role. I have four children, one of whom has severe disabilities. My time is spent making sure she has the support she needs to have quality of life, reach her potential, and be a valued member of the community. She is not alone. One in five children has special needs in California, and that is a lot of California children, and all of those children use services. Services include therapies, medical care, educational support, transition, mental health services. These types of services for children and youth make a difference. Examples, a youth receives physical therapy that allows her to use a wheelchair and gain independence. A child who does not communicate well, because of his disability, learns to communicate through a computer, and eventually is able to support himself. A teenager who has mental health issues gets therapy and is able to learn to manage her inner resources and gains independence. This is the purpose of services, and this is the goal of the parents, to see our children independent, productive, and valued members of our community. Here's the challenge, not all services work. Services are not well coordinated, and not all services are delivered in a way that can be used. Honestly, California's not doing that well in comparison to other states, and I think you already know that. The California system needs to understand what works well and what does not work, and one of the best ways to learn how something is or is not working is to ask the person who uses it. Get the consumer input, in this case, the family input. Assuming you agree, how we assist families to give input is key. Just grabbing any family is not enough. Hand-picking families who will tell you what you want to hear, that doesn't work so well, either. Just getting one family to participate on a Committee will not get you the information you need to improve. Of course not. We want families who are supported to give us the best input possible. Best practice in engaging families requires supporting them by providing them ongoing information, training, and mentoring. That way, they understand the background, their role, how to give effective input, they have guidance in how to address challenges, they build confidence and are able to negotiate differences of opinions. This example of providing training, ongoing information, and mentoring to families, it's not a new concept. It's happening all over the country. New Jersey provides parent leadership development to verse parents to help them participate on groups, such as special ed, health related advisory, and even city councils. Rhode Island has more than 250 peer specialists. Rhode Island is this big. Rhode Island has 250 peer specialists who are trained and supported to improve quality and performance of their programs, as well as the entire system. West Virginia employs parents to hold public forums and participate in policy development. Idaho, Maryland, North Carolina, New Hampshire, Minnesota, Ohio, Wisconsin, New Mexico, Alabama, and I could go on. And you know who's paying? 90% of this is funded from government because this input is for government services. To some degree, it's happening here in California. We have an existing framework of parent centers. This includes family resource centers, parent training and information centers, as well as family empowerment centers, all who provide varying degrees of information, education, support and mentoring to families. In addition, we have a model of training, mentoring, and support. It's called Project Leadership, and has been funded over the years by Lucile Packard Foundation. The training includes the history of special needs, the systems, how to partner and give input effectively. Family Voices Project leadership has trained 145 families who are now represented on committees throughout California, including Department of Healthcare Services, technical work groups, California Pacific Medical Center, Kaiser, UCSF, and Oakland, as well as in San Francisco, as well as NAMI, the National Association on Mental Illness. Family engagement improves systems. A recent success was family input on SB 586, the whole child model. Families' voices were heard and that bill is better for their participation. If nothing else, think of it this way, consumer engagement is so important, even big business asks its consumers to give input and feedback. Appropriate, coordinated, efficient services make a difference. As parents, we're taxpayers and we recognize the resources it takes to provide the services our children receive. We know how precious these resources are and we all want to use California resources wisely. So here it is in the short, services are important, some services work well, some don't. We need family input to know what works. Families need to be trained and mentored. Parent centers are a great vehicle to make that happen. We have parent centers here in California. We have a model of training and mentoring. What's holding us back? Let's work together to create a service system that spends its money wisely, while also effectively supporting our children and youth to reach their potential. Thank you.

First, we'll be able to reduce the patient referral and transfer time frames. Thereby improving access to psychiatric outpatient programs. Currently, both CDCR and DSH are required to oversee and review each patient referral. Once that transfer occurs, we'll be directly responsible for the management of those beds. Including making local referrals and determination of appropriate levels of care as well as accountability. The bottom line is that patients will be able to be placed into beds more quickly. This can only be accomplished by creating a unified program structure under the control of one agency. Second, when CCHCS and CDCR is able to manage the complete continuum of care the communications between those levels of care can be smoother. Since the announcement of the proposal in the Governor's Budget, as Director Ahlin mentioned earlier, CDCR, CCHCS, and DSH have been working closely to develop the transaction or transition process, alignment of the policy approach, etc.  In fact we have folks working in real time on those policies right now. That work has been incredibly positive and productive between the agencies and the special master, in fact, some of his team also involved in some of that review process to ensure that it is consistent with overall process and philosophy. One issue that I think is important for you all to know is that CDCR and DSH share a common philosophy which is critical to the transition. And that has to do with putting patient care first, really ensuring that through this process of transition that we make sure we don't inadvertently harm the care to the patients. One way we do that is by trying to maintain the systems and structures in place to the extent possible so that we can make sure the continuum of care is managed well, and the patients are safe. So with that I think Dr. Burton might have some insight related to San Quentin program.

Paul Burton: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen of the Assembly. My name is Dr. Paul Burton. I'm the chief psychiatrist at San Quentin State Prison. Thank you for having me here today. Regardless of what treatment we provide as psychiatrists or psychologists or social workers to our patients, absent a court order, they're still going to be in prison. So if you have any questions, I'd be happy to answer them. But in brief, that's my experience with the San Quentin PIP.

Jonathan Peterson: Thank you, Madam Chair, Mr. Chair, and members. Jonathan Peterson with the Legislative Analysts Office. In our analysis of the proposed shift, we found that the shift could achieve notable outcomes but a subject to significant uncertainty. As a result, we recommended rejecting the Governor's proposal to shift these programs and instead shift a limited number of beds over a three year period. The Department already went over some of the positive outcomes, including reducing wait times for patients to get into appropriate care. We would also add the shift could generate additional savings from reducing the number of days patients spend in relatively more expensive mental health crisis beds and achieving economies of scale by not needing two different departments, having administrative staff to operate these programs. However, it's uncertain whether some of these outcomes will be achieved. There is significant uncertainty over how program costs will change, and in addition, how quality of care will be affected. This uncertainty stems from the fact that in the proposal, it indicates that the department plans to operate the current programs,as they exist now, for two years. After that period, they'll consider what changes need to be made for these programs to be operated by CDCR moving forward. We note that some of the smaller programs, like the San Quentin PIP are move expensive to operate than what it costs for DSH to operate these larger programs.  So that uncertainty in program costs, as well as what will happen to care as this transition occurs, is some of the uncertainty we were speaking of. This is why we are recommending the Legislature implement a pilot program in which CDCR would provide inpatient care to a portion of the inmates who would otherwise get their care from DSH. Such a pilot would allow the Legislature to determine whether wait times decrease as expected, what particular staffing changes need to be made and the cost of making those changes, and the effectiveness of the treatment that is provided. In addition we recommend approving the proposed beds at the California medical facility which we'll talk about in the next item on a limited term basis as one of the pilot sites that we're proposing. And finally, in order to ensure that the Legislature has adequate information to determine whether the shift will make sense moving forward,  we recommend that the Legislature require CDCR to contract with independent research experts such as a University, to measure key outcomes and to provide an evaluation to the Legislature so that it can determine whether the shift makes sense moving forward. Thank you.

So any changes that need to occur to address issues that come up could happen more expediently. In addition the review times will be decreased for the intermediate care facility. The referral review times will be decreased from 15 days to 9 days and in the acute care it would be from 6 days to 3 days. So you would have more of a patient turnover, which would allow CDCR to treat more inmates in the same amount of space which is important, because we've been seeing a growth in this area, and CDCR is experiencing running out of licensed space for mental health treatment.

Joel Anderson: We heard a lot of magical things already, with the presentation of the bill. What we didn't hear, is what it will do to dreamers. What we didn't hear, how this is the greatest threat that's ever been posed to dreamers. And let me tell you why. Actually, before I tell you why, let me just add this point. Every time we try to have an adult conversation about immigration, there are those that will immediately say you're a racist because we can't possibly have an adult conversation. Yet, on this floor, over the last four years, six years that I've been on this floor we have voted in a bipartisan manner. Sending a clear message to both the Obama administration and the Trump administration. Well, this year we didn't. It wasn't bipartisan. But we would have, had we've been allowed to participate. Send a clear message that immigration is broken. And we all get that. The question is how do we move forward and what is in the best interest? So if you're of the thought that if you have an adult conversation on immigration, that makes you a racist. They're not considering the 11,661 convicted felons serving in our prisons, who are undocumented, then you're a crime denier. And I think we have to not think about either one of those things. And we need to have an honest and earnest conversation. So let me explain to you why dreamers are so at risk by this bill. You see, this bill draws no distinction between people who come here to improve their life, to improve themselves, to lift themselves out of the poverty that perhaps they're in. And they come here and they want to work hard, they want to become US citizens. And maybe they didn't come through the front door but they still are here and they're still working towards that. Or maybe they came as a child and they had no choice. Their parents moved here and maybe they're two years old and all they ever did is speak English. And all the country they've ever known as home has been the United States. And I get those arguments but what I don't get is confusing them with felons and treating them the same as felons. Because on my opinion there is no good reason to shield felons from deportation. And yet that's precisely what SB 54 does. Now initially SB 54 shielded all felons and I want to thank the author because he's taken two amendments, initially took violent felons out, so that meant murderers weren't there. And later he took out serious, and that meant that child molesters and rapists were no longer there. But the bill isn't fully cooked. It still allows for human traffickers. If you're convicted and you're serving in our prison as a human trafficker, this bill shields you from deportation. If you have felony child abuse, this bill shields you. If you take hostages to prevent an arrest and you're serving in our prison, this bill shields you. If you are convicted of a felony and you had a hate crime enhancement, this bill shields you. Possession of restricted biological agents, and this bill shields you. If we were really serious about this, why won't we just say, no felons? You see, this bill continues to play hide the felon. It makes it difficult for ICE to identify these felons and deport them. It makes no distinction between people who come here to work hard, to become US citizens, from those who come here to prey on others. And what's most despicable is they come from undocumented communities. You see a lot of those criminals when you talk to the police and the sheriffs. They'll tell you it's so important that they don't do immigration work, because they need people in those undocumented communities to be able to feel safe enough to come forward and report the child molester in their neighborhood. To report the felony elder abuse in their neighborhood. And yet this bill draws no distinction between the two. It's very, very important that we maintain that relationship with those undocumented communities, because these felons first prey on the undocumented because they don't think they're going to get turned in. But they also prey on US citizens. Those felons are bad guys. They should not ever become US citizens, they deserve to be deported and yet this bill continues to shield them. Now I get what the author's trying to accomplish. We get that, but this bill's not fully cooked. The second issue in it, that to me is just so difficult, is that when we shield those felons, and those felons are guaranteed to return to those undocumented communities, ICE has but one choice. To show up at the schools, to show up in the neighborhoods, to knock on the doors, door by door, looking for those felons. And I'll give you a great example. In January in Los Angeles, 150 warrants were issued for felons in those communities. And along the way when they were looking for those felons, they picked up 19 people they didn't have felons for. Because when they showed up to the house and they knocked on the door. And the felon wasn't home they picked up, asked everybody in that house. Do you have papers? Do you have papers? And if they were undocumented, they got collected. If you want to see more of that, then you should support SB 54. But if you don't want to see more of that, you should oppose it like I am. When you look at that, the second thing is, everyone keeps talking about how Trump's going to take the money. The fact of the matter is much of the money, $117 million that goes to public safety. That money comes from grants that you have to apply for. When you shield felons from ICE agents, you lose the ability to apply for those grants. Now if you're thinking about your local police, if you're thinking, Kevin, I hate for you to miss this. I'm getting to the good part. So if you shield those felons and they return to the community. One, they're going to prey on their neighbors again like they did before. And two, it's going to force ICE into it but there's going to be fewer officers on the street, fewer deputies on the street to protect everyday Californians. Ordinary Californians will have to live in fear because we're going to lose them. Just think about it. If you lose 117 million, and by the way, AG Sessions, when he talked about it, it was 4.1 billion nationally. And we know the lion share of the money is spent here in California. Jennifer Barrera: Good morning, Mr. Chair and Members of the Committee. Jennifer Barrera on behalf of the California Chamber of Commerce, and we are opposed to AB 889. I want to start off by first thanking the author of the bill and his staff for working with us so far on the amendments that happened taken prior to hearing in the middle outlined. In the Committee analysis, we appreciate the work on refining this proposal and we look forward to continue working with him. Unfortunately, the bill is not in a position yet where we are comfortable with some of the standards that have been put into place. I want to say right now it's tragic the story you that you heard from the witness. Of course, it's horrible to hear of anybody being injured and much less a child, so I don't even want to take away for one second that that is not something that's tragic and certainly sympathetic. And we're not interested in maintaining the secrecy of public dangers that could harm the public, the health or safety dangers. What we concerned with is the interference that this bill and this current standards would create in civil litigation. I kind of just want to walk through that for a moment. We're not talking about the sealing of records at trial, that's a different standard altogether. There's a first amendment, constitutional right to access at trial. So when there's evidence submitted at trial, the court has to go through a balancing that's much higher to maintain public access to the trial and the evidence made at the trial. We're talking more about documents that are exchanged during the discovery process between parties, okay? So the discovery process is meant to be free flowing of information to get to the merits of the claim. It's broader than what the standard is for admissibility is at trial because you want parties to exchange that information to get to the merits, okay. So some of those discovery requests are very broad, and they can certainly ask for information that is confidential in nature. Yes, we've heard about trade secrets. It's a huge concern. Privacy with regards to financial information, medical information, personnel records, all of that information is presumed to be confidential and private. And right now, protective orders are utilized to maintain the confidentiality of that information. The court determines whether or not there is good cause, whether good cause exists, or whether protective order so that the parties can exchange that information, but the confidentiality of a trade secret is maintained. So the both parties have access to that information to determine whether it's relevant to the merits of the claim. But yet the public is not allowed to look at that information, because it's presumed to be confidential. That's what a protective order is utilized for, right now, not to hide any public danger, not to hide any danger to the safety to the public, but to maintain the confidentiality of information that, by law, has been deemed to be confidential. This bill would change that. From our perspective, it would essentially limit or ban the use of these protective orders, because the standard it proposed is so high, substantial overriding interest with regards to the confidentiality, that outweighs any right to the public for disclosure accessibility. That there's no other means alternative available that's less intrusive. That's a pretty high standard to satisfy and our concern is that you then jeopardize our ability to maintain the confidentiality of trade secrets based upon an allegation of a public danger, a safety. There hasn't been proven at this point that there's any danger. And it's based upon an allegation. So we're concerned about that imbalance that has been created right now where we don't believe that there's a harm that exists. Let's talk about the public danger and safety and notification to the public. One, the first document that's ever filed in court is the complaint. It's the charging document that identifies the parties, the name of the company or employer. Here, whoever has the alleged defective product, it sets forth all of the factual allegations supporting the allegations of a product defect or some harm to public safety and danger. That document in and of itself is never a subject to a protective order. It is never hidden from access by the public. It is always accessible. We have a changing dynamic in the world today with social media. I can tell you that I can look up on my Google or my phone. And I can find all of these alleged defects without having to go through a protective order, or undoing a settlement agreement. It's out there. The social media is out there. Volkswagen case, the Firestone case. All of those things we heard about well before, you ever saw anything with regards to a protective order or settlement agreement. So to say that there can't be any access to these allegations of public danger or safety without undoing protective orders or confidential settlement agreements, I think it doesn't take into account our changing dynamic in society, especially with regards to social media. The second part I want to get into is with regards to the settlement agreements. Settlement agreements, we want to encourage settlement agreements. We want to encourage parties to work things out amongst themselves without having to go to trial and utilize our judicial resources that are already overcrowded dockets that are already limited with regards to their resources. A settlement agreement is basically a contract. I have never seen a settlement agreement that actually outlines any facts with regards to the underlying claim. I've never seen a settlement agreement where anybody specifies, in that agreement, trade secret information, or confidential information that would be disclosed to the public. What's in a settlement agreement is the recitals of the claim from the lawsuit, reference to the case number, a waiver of the claims against them, confidential settlement amount, which I appreciate that the bill now allows for the confidentiality of the settlement amount. Usually, had no admission of liability by the business or the company. And then you have contractual terms, like severability, places where it's going to be litigated if there's a dispute over the contract. There's nothing in those settlement documents that disclose any public danger or safety. And yet, under this bill, because you would be opening up or limiting your right to utilize confidential agreements, you'll be interfering with our ability to settle cases and then forcing them to go to trial. So we're concerned with these standards that are being utilized, because we don't think it addresses the need with regards to making sure people are aware of a known public danger or safety. It's based only on an allegation, and for those reasons, we are opposed. But we, again, look forward to continuing to work with the author on these issues.

Virginia Early: Thank you, Mr. Chair and members. Virginia Early with the Legislative Analyst's Office. So today, I'm going to provide an overview of the state's child care and preschool system, some information on recent trends and a high level orientation to the budget. The sergeant is passing around a handout, so you can follow along with me as I go through it. On page 1 of the handout, we provide a chart that has brief descriptions of each of the child care and preschool programs as well as their estimated slots. As you can see from the chart, we attempt to categorize the programs in three ways. Child care programs for families participating in the states Welfare to Work Program, CalWORKS, child care for families that are not participating in CalWORKS, and preschool programs, and you can see a brief description of each. On page 2 of the handout, we walk you through some key components of the programs. All programs that we listed on page 1 have eligibility criteria, but the eligibility criteria vary. So in CalWORKS and most of the non-CalWORKs child care programs, families, to be eligible, have to have incomes below 70% of the 2007 state median income. That's about $42,000 for a family of three. Transitional kindergarten does not have any income requirements. Programs also set eligibility based on the age of the child. Most programs serve children ages birth through 12, but state preschool serves three and four-year-olds, and transitional kindergarten serves children born between September 2nd and December 2nd. The state also has what's called expanded transitional kindergarten, which allows school districts to serve children born between December 2nd and the end of the school year, but the state provides less funding for this particular program. Finally, eligibility varies. Most programs require parents to be working, in school, or in a training program. However, part-day state preschool and transitional kindergarten don't have these requirements. In terms of access, access to the programs also varies. So for the CalWORKS and transitional kindergarten programs, the state has traditionally allowed every single eligible child, who's interested in receiving the services, to be served, but for the other programs, the state has a certain number of slots, and those are prioritized based on family income. The state provides care in four types of settings. Licensed centers, which tend to be larger, more classroom type settings, licensed family child care homes, where the provider serves children in their own home, typically about 6 to 12 children. License-exempt homes, which tend to be family, friend, and neighbors just serving the children from one family, and license-exempt school classrooms that are similar to those in kindergarten. So in terms of programs, CalWORKS and the alternative payment program can access centers, family child care homes, and license-exempt providers, but the other child care programs can only access licensed centers and licensed family child care homes, and of course, transitional kindergarten uses school classrooms that are very similar to those used in kindergarten. Standards also vary across the programs. All programs have to meet certain health and safety standards as well as standards regarding staffing qualifications and staff-to-child ratios, but the specific ratios and standards vary across the programs. Some programs also require the inclusion of developmentally appropriate activities. So for example, in state preschool, programs are required to provide basic numeracy and literacy activities. On page 3 of the handout, we provide an overview of how the programs are funded. The funding model varies across the programs, with a combination of vouchers, direct contracts, and school district allocations. So for example, CalWORKS is funded primarily through vouchers, which means that families can choose the provider of their choice and the type of setting that they like, and then the state pays that provider on behalf of the family. This voucher value varies regionally across the state based on a survey the state conducts every couple of years and the state typically sets this regional market rate so that families can access a certain percentage of providers in their area. By contrast, for the other child care programs, such as state preschool and general child care, the state contracts directly with individual providers to provide the service to children. And pays a set standard reimbursement rate that's the same across the state. Finally, transitional kindergarten is funded based on average daily attendance through the Local Control Funding Formula, similar to kindergarten. On page 4, we summarize some trends over the last decade. So funding was cut during the recession and increased during the recovery. As you can see from this chart here on page 4, it decreased by about $1 billion between 2007-8 and 2013-14, and since 2013-14, the funding has increased by about $870 million. Rates were mostly held flat during the recession with some reductions to the license-exempt rate, and the amount the state provides for administrating voucher programs, but since 2014-15, the state has provided three consecutive rate increases to both the regional market rate and to the standard reimbursement rate, with expanding on rates in 16-17 about $400 million higher. Slots were what is responsible for the major funding reductions in the recession and when we talk about these reductions, we really have to talk about CalWORKS reductions. And non CalWORKS reductions separately because as I said before the state typically funds all eligible CalWORKS families and it does not fund all eligible non CalWORKS families. So between 2007, 2008 and 2013/14 on the CalWORKS side of the house slots decreased by 65,000. These reductions were primarily due to state actions that reduced the number of eligible families. So for example, in 2009, 10, the state exempted certain CalWORK families from the work requirement and allowed them to continue receiving cash aid while staying home with their children, to create the savings for child care. Since 2013/14, slots have increased due to the net effect of the state re-engaging this families on the workforce. And offsetting decrease in the overall CalWORK case load due to an improving the economy. On the non CalWORK side of the house slots again decreased during the recession by about 44000 slots due to cross the board funding reductions and since the recession has ended, the legislature has added funding that has resulted in there being about 25,000 more slots in 16/17, than there were in 13/14, and most of these additional slots have been for preschool. Page five of the handout has a sort of summary chart of the governors proposed budget for 17/18. As you can see, the governor's proposing $3.8 billion for these programs. This is a 2% increase, or $76 million increase from the current year, and that $76 million increase we break down in a little bit more detail on page six of our handout. As you all know, the Governor and the legislature had a multiyear budget agreement. The Governor is implementing certain parts of that agreement and choosing to pause other parts of that agreement. So the majority of the 76 million is due to annualizing certain rate and slot increases that were part of that agreement. So that's where we get that $91 million increase. However, the budget does not include funding to annualise the standard reimbursement rate initiated in the current year. Funding for new state preschool slots or funding for additional rate increases. In terms of our comments on the budge proposals we discussed on page seven, while the Governor has not added additional state preschool slots, we know that the legislature is interested in this because that was part of the deal, and so we wanted to share some comments with you. Based on a recent history, we've seen the state add a lot of full-day state preschool slots for local education agencies, particularly school districts in recent years and many of these have gone unused. So for example, in 15 the state funded almost 6,000 full day state preschool slots for LEA's, but LEA's were only issued about 1,600 of these due to a lack of applicants. So CDA had to issue the remaining funds to as full day slots for non LEA's and part day slots for a mix of LEAs and non LEAs. So we think, so why is this happening? We think the school districts likely have strong fiscal and programmatic incentives that prevent them from applying. So because they have the option of serving children in expanded transitional kindergarten who are the same age. And because the per day rate for transitional kindergarten is 21% higher than the average full day rate for state preschool and because transitional kindergarten requirements are significantly lower and less restrictive, allow for more local flexibility in state preschool. We think that school districts might be choosing to serve these children in expanded transitional kindergarten instead of state preschool. As a result, we would recommend that if the legislature is interested in adding additional full day state preschool slots that they allow all types of providers to apply for any newly funded slots so that the slots can be utilized as the legislature intends them to be utilized. Thank you and that concludes my presentation. Happy to answer any questions if you like.

Virginia Early: Hello Mr, Chair, members, again Virginia Early with the Legislative Analyst's office. I've been asked to provide a sort of background on the state's quality programs and discuss our assessment and recommendations on CD's plan and on the system as a whole. We're passing around a handout now. You got a lot of handouts from us today. And starting on page one we provide some background on the programs. So as Ms. Brown mentioned, the federal law requires us to spend a certain percentage of our federal funding and state match each year on activities to improve the quality of childcare. That was 78 million in 16, 17, because the percentage is going up, as was mentioned before, assuming federal funding remains flat, we'll be required to spend $95 million on quality improvement activities in 2021. Federal law allows us to spend this money for a wide range of activities, including licencing enforcement, developing early learning resources, doing trainings for childcare and preschool providers and so forth, and California currently supports about 30 different quality improvement programs. Some of these programs are specified in the budget act each year, such a resource and referral agencies and others are programs that C has developed over the years to respond to needs or things they've identified would be useful. But the majority of the funds in question, are funds that CD has discretion over. California counts--the programs are split into three categories. What we call state level activities, where the state has either developed some sort of training that is the same for everybody in the state or it does some sort of state level activity like licensing enforcement, then the state also funds core activities of certain local or county level support agencies that are involved in doing quality improvement work. So for example, the state funds resource and referral agencies, R and Rs, and local penning councils. R and Rs are responsible for collecting data on child care providers and helping parents find child care in their areas, while local planning councils are responsible for identifying areas in their county with the greatest unmet need for child care and helping other child care folks in their county coordinate child care services. Finally, the state also counts towards this quality spending requirement specific programs that are run by these county support entities in addition to their main key responsibilities. So for example, resource and referral agencies receive additional funding to conduct specific types of trainings while local planning counsels receive money as Ms. Brown mentioned for what's called the AB 212 program that provides stipends to providers taking child development courses. And community colleges also received some funds to support student's application fees as they apply for their child development teacher permit. On page three of the handout we give you an overview of the quality rating and improvement system, so of those 30 programs I mentioned, one of those programs provides $800,000 in 16-17, for QRIS consortia, up for child care programs serving migrant children. But outside of those 30 programs, and the funding that the state is required to spend, California also allocates 75 million to cure QRIS consortia. Of this 75 million, 50 million has provided annually in Proposition 98 funds for state preschool QRIS. And 25 million is provided by the first five California for QRIS all types of programs. In addition, you also heard CDE talk about how there had been a one time infant and toddler QRIS Block Grant in 2015-16, some QRIS consortiums still have funds from that block grant that they're using. These consortia have a small presence in many areas of the state, there are 48 consortia covering all 58 counties. And the consortia are comprised of various county level entities that are involved in improving the quality of childcare such as the R and R or such as the local planning council, but it also includes local education agencies. It includes the First Five Commission in the county, community colleges, and even potentially some child care providers. These consortia rate providers and offer resources to help them improve and maintain high quality ratings. So as I mentioned earlier, it's a five tier matrix with tier one being licensing standards. And tier five being the highest quality above licensing standards, and this matrix examines many aspects of providers, including child to teacher ratios, staff interactions, how child observations are used to inform curriculum planning, use of developmental screenings, classroom environment, and several other things. Consortia have flexibility once they've rated an individual provider, and how they choose to use their remaining resources to support the provider. So for example, consortium might choose to give a scholarship to teachers, to help them get more classes, if that's identified as the thing that will help that site progress. If the program is having trouble with their classroom environment, the consortium might choose to give some grant funding to help them purchase supplies. So consortia have a lot of flexibility to respond to the needs of providers. On page four of our handout we go through the revised quality improvement expenditure plan. I won't go into too much detail on this since CD has already covered it. But basically, as she mentioned, the 2016-17 budget directed CD to come up with a new plan for how to spend the quality funding, retaining funding for resource and referral agencies, licensing enforcement and local planning counsels but prioritizing the rest for QRIS. So the revised plan shifts funding from, shifts about 5.1 million in funding from nine other programs into a QRIS block grant for infants and toddlers. So while it's reducing funds for the AB 212 program that Ms. Brown mentioned, the consortia could continue to use these funds that their local planning council had already been getting for the same purpose. It's just now they have additional flexibility if they decide they want to do more of it, or they want to do less of it, they're able to make those decisions. In addition, CD is also proposing to add some rules to existing programs, requiring providers accessing some of the state level programs to be participating in QRIS. So on page five we share our assessment, as we looked at the system, we think some activities are really important to supporting the subsidized childcare and preschool system, including helping parents find child care, collecting data on child care providers, identifying areas in the state with the greatest unmet need. And these are activities that the R and Rs and LPCs are currently doing. But we also found that quality improvement spending at the county level can lack coordination and be difficult for these entities to direct to their highest priorities. Within each county these entities are not required to have an over arching quality improvement plan. That addresses both the folks in QRIS and not in QRIS. So, without a plan, there's no guarantee that the funding will be coordinated, that it will be efficient. There's no guarantee that training, for example, is not duplicative. So, in addition, the detailed requirements of having so many different training programs that these county level support entities are running means that they're unable to direct funding towards their highest priorities, that they hear from their child care providers in their area. Additionally, while there have been some evaluations of the state level programs, and there is some data available, we don't think these evaluations and this data is sufficient to enable the state to know whether the programs are cost-effective. On page six, we continue with our assessment. We also found that of the $28 million CD is proposing to allocate towards training activities, a large amount of it is being prioritized or restricted to contract-based providers. So specifically 28% is restricted to contract-based providers who are already required to meet higher standards than voucher providers. And under CD's revised program rules, another 37% would be prioritized for providers participating in QRIS. And these providers tend to be contract based, and so we're concerned about this focus on contract based providers because nearly three-quarters of the infant and toddler population and one-quarter of the preschool population in California of subsidized children are served by voucher-based providers. And so we'd like to see some spending on the quality where these children are being served, especially if they're in settings that don't have to meet as high standards. Finally, while we think that shifting funds to QRIS provides county-level support entities with more flexibility in terms of the types of activities they can offer, we also recognize that only a small percentage of providers statewide participate in QRIS. So restricting funds to QRIS consortia could limit the pool of entities that can benefit from the quality improvement funds. So on page seven of the handout, we summarize our recommendations. We recommend the Legislature retain funding for essential activities such as helping parents find child care, collecting data on providers, and identifying unmet need. And as I said, these are activities that are currently done by the R and R agencies and local planning councils. But moving forward, we would recommend the Legislature repackage other county level funding Into a block grant, so there are currently seven programs that are going to county level, sort of funding streams that are going to county level support entities. It's about $21 million, so we would recommend combining this into one consolidated block grant that all the entities currently receiving the funds would get together and collaboratively decide. They would have to agree on a plan for how to spend the funds, taking into account the subsidized population providers in their area. We recommend that the block grant be allocated across the state, based on each county's share of the subsidized childcare and preschool slots, and then collect data from each County on how the funds were used. We'd also like to recommend rejecting CD's proposal to limit access to certain state-level programs to QRIS participants, as it means that non QRIS providers wouldn't have access to some of the resources in the state. And finally, given that there are a number of state level programs, that there aren't good evaluations or data for, we recommend the Legislature and the state hire an independent evaluator to assess the effectiveness of these programs and make future funding decisions based on the results. And so the state could start with the largest programs and work its way down the list over a period of several years. Thank you so much. I'm happy to answer any questions you have.

David Newmark: Thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today about the EITC. My name is David Newmark. I'm chancellor's Professor of economics at UC Irvine and I direct the Economic Self-Sufficiency Policy Research Institute, or ESPRY. ESPRY receives foundation, University and donor support to see how to improve public policy and increase the ability of individuals and families. To become economically self-sufficient. I'm not here to advocate for or against a bill under consideration. Rather, I'm here to tell you what the research says about the effectiveness of the EITC. And what this might imply for the proposal in AB 225 to increase the number of California families eligible for the credit. And the amount of the credit available to those families. My research over many decades now has focused on the effectiveness of various anti-poverty policies. Most notably, the minimum wage and the Earned Income Tax Credit at both the federal and state levels. And a good deal of research by ESPRY affiliates, including other UC faculty, has documented positive effects of the EITC on other outcomes. Ranging from children's health to academic achievement. I will not have time to discuss these other findings today, but I urge you to look at our review of the research on the EITC on the ESPRY website. And I'm happy to share my statement, which has the URL listed. My research on the EITC leads to a few key conclusions I think you'll find interesting. On here I draw mainly on my worker with Bill Washer from the Federal Reserve Board. First, a more generous Earned Income Tax Credit boosts employment of lower-skilled adults who stand to benefit most from the policy, predominantly single mothers. Second, because female-headed households, i.e., single mothers, have very high poverty rates, the EITC reduces poverty. Third, a more generous EITC increases the number of families who earn their way out of poverty. For example, our evidence says that a 10 percentage point increase in a state's EITC supplement reduces the share of single mothers below one-half of the poverty line by about 3.3 percentage points. And reduces the share of single mothers below the poverty line by about 2.2 percentage points. Let me just elaborate on this last result, to make sure you know what it means. We can always reduce poverty by simply writing checks to poor families. But that's a very expensive Proposition and runs counter to our pre-disposition to alleviating poverty whenever possible through work. The magic of the EITC, if you will, is that it provides sufficiently strong work incentives. That it reduces poverty even before you take account of the EITC payment. And that's because of the strong employment effect it induces. In my view, the evidence at the EITC induces more families to earn their way out of poverty. That is its unique ability to alleviate poverty by encouraging work explains the historical bi-partisan support for more generous EITC at the federal and many state levels. I should also point out, these findings are driven, in large part, by variation in EITCs that other states have adopted. There are currently 27 states, including DC, that supplement the federal EITC. However, most of these other states simply add a percentage to the federal EITC, for which a family is eligible. And hence, the income range over which families are eligible is much wider than under California's EITC. This suggests that under AB 225 by moving California's EITC closer to the structure of other states, which see more of the employment increases and poverty reductions that have followed from other state EITCs.

Estella Cisneros: Good afternoon, Madam Chair and Committee Members. My name is Estella Cisneros. I'm the directing attorney of the Fresno Migrant Office of California Rural Legal Assistance, Inc. CRLA is a non-profit legal service program founded in 1966 to represent the low-income residents of California's rural communities. Although we have 19 offices throughout the state, 6 of these offices assist agricultural workers exclusively. As legal advocates, our attorneys and community workers are at the front lines of what has gone wrong and continues to go wrong in the agricultural workplace. Including the problem that SB 295 would help ameliorate, the pervasive and rampant workplace sexual harassment of both men and women by farm labor contractors. I have been asked by Senator Monning to give remarks on the need for SB 295 based on my experience as an attorney for farm workers. As their representative today, I will give voice to just two of their stories. A female client worked alone with one male supervisor in the shipping and maintenance area of a ranch from mid 2015 through mid 2016. The sexual harassment began during her first month at work, when her supervisor came up behind her and hugged her tightly. She pushed him away and realized there were other supervisors who had witnessed the harassment, but had done nothing. She complained to her ranch manager, who also did nothing. She endured cat calls, sexual comments, and various forms of grabbing and touching on an almost daily basis for over a year, mostly from her direct supervisor. Even after she complained to the Human Resources department and the harasser was fired, she continued to be treated the same way by other co-workers and supervisors because the tone had been set by that first supervisor and his superiors who did nothing for almost a year. The effect of the sexual harassment on our client is difficult to quantify. She no longer feels comfortable in her own skin. Even when she's not working in the fields she covers her face with handkerchiefs and wears two tight sports bras and loose clothing to hide her figure. She was suicidal, continues to see a psychologist, and has suffered setbacks in her romantic relationships. Her training on sexual harassment consisted of a single 15 minute meeting where she was handed a brochure with no explanation or discussion. In 2015 and 2016 a female client in a packing house was sexually harassed by two different foremen during two different seasons. The first foreman touched her leg and bottom with his leg. And asked her out multiple times, even though she kept telling him no. When she turned him down he would yell expletives at her and tell her to take off her top so he could see her body better. He would then put her to work by herself and was constantly changing her job tasks in retaliation. When she was working, he would sit in front of her and stare at her breasts. Other times, he would sit behind her, and when she bent down, her bottom would touch his knees. She would ask him to move but he wouldn't. He would also tell her coworkers this one isn't leaving here alive. The second foreman, who worked with the first foreman, told her that in order for her to be hired for the coming season she had to go out with him, she refused. When she started working he continued to ask her out and she continued to refuse him. While she was working, he would threaten to fire her, telling her he would only hire men for his crew because women were worthless. They only cause trouble, and he didn't want any women working for him. He would retaliate against her by giving her more difficult job duties. Although she complained to a supervisor and the Human Resources department after the foreman was disciplined she continued to be treated poorly by her coworkers, like our first client. One of her coworkers who was related to the second foreman threatened her, "you don't know what's going to happen to you". On another occasion another coworker yelled at her, "effing dog". She didn't receive any training on sexual harassment. In conclusion, SB 295 is needed because the problem of rampant and pervasive sexual harassment in the fields, various packing houses, and nurseries in California is alive and well. While SB 295's predecessor, SB 1087, was an incredibly important and critical first step in helping address this terrible problem, there remains much work to be done. And for these reasons I support SB 10, excuse me, SB 295. Thank you for your time and attention.

Jennifer Barrera: Good afternoon Mr. Chair and Members of the Committee. Jennifer Barrera on behalf of the California Chamber of Commerce, and we are opposed to SB 63. We've had this debate discussion for a couple years now, and I can reiterate that we are not opposed and do not disagree with the social benefits that come with providing a leave for families to bond with their new children. I don't anybody's going to disagree with the social impacts or the medical benefits that are associated with that. So we're totally in agreement with Senator Jackson on that issue. However, we disagree that there is no burden to a business to mandate the 12 week leave of absence on top of an existing, already four month protected leave of absence for employers with five or more employees under our pregnancy disability law. To suggest that this is not a burden and that there is no cost associated with that, I think fails to recognize the implications of actually running a business. This is applicable to any employer with 20 or more employees within a 75 mile radius. So it's not 20 employees at that same location. But yeah, you could have five employees in a separate location and that's the location that's going to be actually impacted by the leave. A mandated leave means that you don't get to take into consideration the fact that there are other employees out on one of our other cumulative list of leave of absences that we have specifically here in California. Our paid sick leave law, school activities leave, bone marrow organ donation transplant leave, kin care. I can continue to go on and on with the list of California specific leaves that we have, and yet, we don't get to take that into consideration when an employee comes in and says, I now want four months of leave under pregnancy disability and an additional 12 weeks of new parent leave with regards to that. That's equivalent to seven months, and yes I agree that not every pregnancy results in a four month disability but the potential is there to have a seven month protective leave of absence on an employer that may have limited employees at one particular location. That's a significant burden and what do you do with regards to an employee? You can't replace that job, you have to keep it open for the employee to return, because that's the nature of protected leave of absence. You have to hire somebody, usually at a higher price, because the time that they're going to be there is more limited. So the contract for their labor's higher. Or you have to pay overtime for employees to be pick up that work. Our overtime rate continues to go up as the minimum wage rate continues to go up year after year. So there is a cost associated with that as well. And then let's talk about the other piece that seems to be getting some attention now, which is a good thing from our perspective, the litigation aspect. This would be defined as an unfair or a fair labor employment practice under the Fair Employment and Housing Act. And that comes with it, the private right of action with damages for back pay, punitive damages, attorney's fees and costs. That's pretty significant. There was a study that came out two years ago that said just the cost of defense is $125,000 for a small employer just to defend themselves in one of these lawsuits regardless of whether there's any merit. There's already existing stats that show that employers, large employers who have a dedicated human resource department, who have a dedicated legal department already facing significant lawsuits under our California Family Rights Act. So we have sophisticated businesses who just can't seem to get it right. We disagree with that. There's abuses under that law. For example we have cases that we've represented in our letter where an employee was out on their 12 weeks of leave. An employer granted them additional time off and then when they failed to return after that additional time off the employer let them go, and they sued the employer under the California Family Rights Act for interfering with their rights to family leave. So, there are abuses that are going on. We are concerned that those same abuses for small employers who do not have a dedicated human resource staff, who do not have a dedicated legal department will be facing the complications of implementing this law and will face the cost of litigation. So last year when we we're at the table we discussed the possibility of developing a mediation program that's already in existence to the Department of fair employment and housing and have that to be a mandatory aspect, to have any lawsuit that is going to be filed under this new leave for the parties to be mandated to go to mediation before the Department of Fair Employment and Housing act. Why? To eliminate that cost and that risk to that employer. From our perspective, it's a good thing not only for the employer but also the employee if you can resolve the dispute at the beginning. The employee may be able to get back to work in time and not suffer any job loss as a result of this disagreement on their leave. That was not taken but yet, again the comment is we'll one I've heard that, well, that's unprecedented. We don't mandate that for any other existing leave, so why would we mandate it here? This new law is unprecedented. We don't have such an extensive amount of time for a small employer with 20 or more employees. And then the other comment was through the Department of Fair Employment and Housing there's already a voluntary option for mediation, or it's a mandatory. That's only if you go through the DFEH investigation process. What happens for the majority of these cases is the exhaustion of the administrative remedy. Which is you go online, you fill out a form, and you hit the button that says immediate right to sue letter, you're giving your immediate right to sue letter. That takes maybe a minute of your time to exhaust that administrative remedy. If you elect to go for the immediate right to sue, there is no voluntary or mandatory option for mediation through the Department of Fair Employment and Housing any more. So that is not necessarily applicable again to this new leave. And we're requesting that we mitigate that litigation aspect. If the true intent of this bill is to have family leave and the bonding time and the medical time is the important factor of this bill then why not address the litigation piece that the government recognized in it's veto message last year and that them employer community finds so objectionable for those reasons, we are opposed.

We're essentially asking victims to go on the Internet and pull these images, pull this content and then entrust the courts and entrust their counsel to make a case they can seek justice. I believe that the amendment that appears to be accepted by the author will actually ameliorate that concern. In terms of making sure they're not revictimizing themselves, republishing this content with the concerns the media and the public policy interest in general public interest in the media knowing about these types of actions, because often times the media is shedding light on these actions and making sure that further legislative measures can happen. That being said, I think there is a prevailing public policy interest here in ensuring that victims are often non-consensually being abused by this content. And if we are forcing them to have to go through the legal system and revictimize themselves, it is essentially a deterrent for these victims coming forth in the first place to seek justice. As an advocate, I can only tell my clients that I can, as much as possible through the current system, protect their interests. I'd like to 100% be able to tell my clients that I'm not going to harm them any further if I take them into a civil case. So I do ask this Committee to consider the fact that even though there are some First Amendment concerns, that the overriding privacy concerns the victims be taken into account here, so that victims can seek the justice they deserve. Title 8 at the Civil Rights Act of 1968 known as the Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in the rental, sale, or financing of housing on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, family status, or disability. In addition to prohibiting discrimination, the act includes a powerful affirmative mandate that federal agencies actively work to dismantle segregation and create equal housing opportunities. Known as the Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing or AFFH obligation. This obligation was flushed out by the Obama administration to make it explicit that states, local governments, and housing authorities must take meaningful action in addition to combating discrimination that overcomes patterns of segregation and fosters inclusive communities free from barriers that restrict access to opportunity.
