Republicans in Congress introduce HR 482 and S 103 in early January with the intention of gutting the AFFH rules. HUD Secretary Ben Carson has called the rules "government engineering" and doesn't appear to be inclined to protect them. California law does not explicitly include this obligation and it is our intention to remedy that with AB 686. The people of California are looking to our Legislature to reject the backward policies emanating from Washington, to protect the progress we've made, and to lead the fight to expand opportunity for all Californians. Students of history may remember that King led the fight for the Fair Housing Act. In fact, the last time Dr. King spoke in Sacramento, he spoke about fair housing. If AB 686 is passed and signed by the Governor, it will come into effect in 2018. It is our hope that we can celebrate the 50th birthday of the Fair Housing Act, and honor the memory of Dr. King by seeing this legislation enacted. Paul Soter: Thank you very much, Senator Dodd. My name is Paul Soter of The Law Offices of Paul Soter in San Francisco. I've specialized in financial services compliance law for 35 years. My clients include banks, finance lenders, lead generators, money transmitters and factoring companies. I'm honored to be able to assist Senator Dodd, as a technical consultant, with regard to the CFL law and the Law of Long Finders in California. And I appreciate his willingness to address an issue that's required attention for many years. The CFL Law is California's basic lending law and it governs all non-exempt lenders making installment loans in California. However, the CFL law has two key flaws in the area of lead generation. First, the law contains no workable definition of broker. Rather, the law defines a broker as one who engages in brokering activities and leaves and termed brokering activities undefined. Second, the CFL law fails to clearly and consistently regulate finders, that is persons who introduce prospective borrowers to prospective lenders without negotiating long terms or participating in credit decisions. Finding is recognized, under both California Supreme Court Case Law and in lending business practice, as separate from brokering. But it's not clearly addressed, in that way, under the CFL law. As Senator Dodd has just described, lead generators operate websites that ask for information from potential borrowers and pass that information on to potential lenders. The generators play no role in the credit decision but rather act as channels to introduce borrowers and lenders. In other words, lead generators act as loan finders, not as loan brokers. SB 297 updates the CFL by adding workable definitions for both brokering and finding and putting into effect the regulatory framework around current activity. The bill's definition of finder reflects the complexity of lead generation in today's marketplace. In a paper published last year the Federal Trade Commission discussed the any different business models used by lead generators to pair borrowers with lenders. The definition we chose in SB 297 encompasses those different models. Finally to be clear, SB 297 does not authorize nor incentivize new types of activities. It takes activity that is currently occurring and places a regulatory framework around that activity. By clearly stating the law as it applies to finders under the CFL, we are benefiting not only lenders and lead generators, but also the borrowers who use those businesses. Thank you very much Senators.

Suzanne Martindale: Mr. Chair, Mr. Vice Chair, Members of the Committee, my name is Suzanne Martindale, I'm here on behalf of Consumers Union. We appreciate the opportunity to testify today, with respect to SB 297. Although we very much appreciate the intent of the author to shine a light on online lead generation activities, we believe that this bill does something quite different, given the implications for deregulating and permitting unlicensed third parties to offer at a physical location, California Finance Lender loans. And for these reasons, we respectfully oppose the bill at this time. We submitted a letter, which at the time had 19 signers. I have an updated version, we have 22 signers now from a range of community legal services, small business organizations from across the state who share our concerns. Also notably, we are sitting here with Oportun, the largest lender of pilot loans as well as CFO loans of 2,500 and up, because we share concerns about this issue. So again, we agree that there are significant concerns with the proliferation of online lead generation activities, and where there are real questions as to what the ground rules should be. Online lead generation is prevalent not just in consumer lending and payday lending but also in promoting education services. I mean, you look at on Google and you're going to see an ad for University of Phoenix, right? There are a lot of industries that use online lead generation. However, we believe that the bill as drafted does something quite different than the stated intent. The finders and brokers have long been recognized at common law as two distinct categories. The distinction is essentially this, that a finder is like a middle man, someone who brings parties together, collects their finders fee, and then leaves it up to the parties to negotiate their agreement. But by contrast, a broker is really an agent of a particular business. A broker helps bring parties together but then remains involved and has an interest in seeing parties reach that agreement. The broker maybe handling customer information, sensitive information such as Social Security numbers, and may be making decisions as to whether a potential customer matches a business's preferences for who they want to, say in this case, lends to. So, as it stands, finders are really only explicitly referenced in our small dollar pilot program in the CFLL, which several of our groups have been involved in. And we've been very careful to ensure that finders, to the extent that they are engaging more actively in helping facilitate loans that we want to make sure that there are protections there. So we have asked that, certainly under the pilot, that those finders who are really helping facilitate, and even go so far as disburse loan proceeds for example, are actually required to have a license under a relevant license to ensure that we have people with the right oversight and expertise conducting those kinds of transactions. Meanwhile, brokers are regulated, as previously mentioned, in the CFLL. And so you have to obtain a license under existing law, if you want to be a broker. Now the Committee analysis for the bill states that this would, that SB 297 would help regulate finders by codifying their activities into law. However, we believe that as written the bill really changes the definition of finder to include and permit certain activities that would actually be considered brokering activities. And therefore would otherwise require the entity to obtain a license. because again, we're not talking just about online lead generation in terms of this legislation. This legislation would permit brick and mortar third-party origination of loans. Therefore, we believe that this effectively loosens the regulatory oversight that currently exists under the CFLL. Not to our knowledge, online lead generators are not expressly regulated by states, mentioned in name in statute. However, they are subject to DFTC Act and to state UDAP laws. So these are laws that prohibit businesses from engaging in unfair or deceptive practices. The analysis, in fact, notes that the FTC did a study on lead generation, mentioning that lead generators are used in the online context in payday, debt relief, mortgage lending, and so forth. And the takeaway from this report really is that online lead generation is a new version of a long standing practice using third parties to market products and services, but it has unique characteristics. And furthermore, it raises law enforcement concerns, not just policy concerns, given that there are probably activities that these companies are engaging in that are already illegal. So, again, we acknowledge the author's intent to better oversee lead generators, specifically online lead generators. However, we do not believe that this bill in fact advances that goal. And believe that a better approach would be to define the practices and characteristics unique to online lead generation to develop a regulatory framework that better takes that into account. Because at this point, what we see happening with this bill is the potential for unlicensed third parties to be acting as agents of lenders and originating loans with no limits on compensation. And that reminds us all too well of the previous decade when we saw similar activities in the subprime mortgage lending context, and we just don't want to go back there. So again, I'm happy to continue the conversation with the author and we'll continue to discuss in good faith how to find common ground on this really important issue. Thank you very much.

Eric Weaver: Thank you, Chairman Dodd and Members of the Committee and a particular thanks to Senator Hueso for authoring this important legislation. Opportunity Fund is honored to support Senate Bill 551 to increase the sustainability and integrity of California's Capital Access Program or CalCAP. My name's Eric Weaver, I'm the CEO of Opportunity Fund. I founded the organization more than 20 years ago to prove that small amounts of money and financial advice could help struggling entrepreneurs make permanent and lasting change to improve their own lives. Over those 20 years, Opportunity Fund has grown to become the nation's largest nonprofit small business micro lender. We supported more than 5,000 California business owners with over 164 million in new financing. These dollars are reaching underserved entrepreneurs. Our clients are 88% ethnic minorities and 39% women. This impact is statewide as we've reached over 80% of California's counties from rural Shasta County in the north down to Imperial County at the southern border. Every loan we make helps an entrepreneur support an average of three jobs and every $1 we invest generates $2 in additional economic activity. These investments help business owners, their families and their communities. These results would not have been possible CalCAP without the program. While the businesses we serve are credit worthy, lending to them involves greater risks than traditional financial institutions are willing to take. By providing a small, but meaningful match on each loan we enroll, CalCAP helps lenders like Opportunity Fund build up a loan loss Reserve pool to cover any potential losses. CalCAP provides tremendous leverage on state funds. Each dollar contributed by the state yields as much as $30 in loans to underserved communities. Robust ongoing participation from responsible small business lenders is integral to CalCAP's success and we believe that SB 551 will increase the sustainability, and integrity of the CalCAP program to ensure strong lender participation for decades to come. SB 551 would lower the required minimum match for both lenders and the state. By reducing the minimum amounts both parties can contribute to each covered loan from 2% to 1% in the loan amount. The bill ensures the public funds go further while still providing lenders needed coverage against risk. The bill also creates a formal mechanism for recycling funds within the CalCAP program that simultaneously supports multiple important goals. First, the bill improves program sustainability by allowing CPCFA to recapture any state contributions and any lender loan loss reserves that are above a predetermined threshold, just 20% of total loans outstanding for any individual lender. This allows CPCFA to utilize recycled funds to match new small business loans while also providing needed administrative funding. Secondly, by ensuring that lenders have meaningful and predictable coverage against losses, it maintains lender trust and participation in the program. This is particularly important given that lenders make underwriting decisions on enrolled loans with the confidence that they could rely on their loan loss reserves if individual loans and, or economic conditions deteriorate. Ultimately, both ongoing funding and strong lender participation are essential for the sustainability of the CalCAP Loan Loss Reserve programs. The CalCAP programs are national examples of how to cost effectively support access to capital for small businesses. SB 551 will increase CalCAP's sustainability and transparency, which will ultimately benefit borrowers across the state. Please vote aye on SB 551.

Parina Parikh: Good afternoon, Mr. Chair and Members of the Committee. My name is Parina Parikh and I'm the Regulatory and Legislative Policy Manager for Clean Transportation at San Diego Gas and Electric. I want to thank the Chair and Committee for the opportunity to speak on this important issue. SDG and E has long supported California's clean transportation goals and believes AB 1082 will help the state reach its goal of having sufficient infrastructure to support 1.5 million zero-emission vehicles on California roads by 2025. I will focus my comments on three reasons why SDG&E supports this bill. One, reducing emissions in the transportation sector is an absolute must if the state wants to meet its statewide GHG reduction goals. This is particularly acute in San Diego. While the transportation sector accounts for approximately 36% of GHG emissions on a statewide level, the transportation sector accounts for over 50% of GHG emissions in San Diego. AB 1082 will help with our GHG reduction goals by expanding access to ZEV charging in our schools. Two, we also need to help drivers get over the fear of range anxiety. In order to accelerate ZEV adoption, refueling or recharging should be as ubiquitous and convenient as with your traditional gasoline powered vehicles. According to the California Statewide Plug-In Vehicle assessment by National Renewable Energy Laboratory, California is only at 6% of the 2020 goal to have sufficient infrastructure to support 1 million ZEVs on California roads. Targeting schools presents and excellent opportunity to install EV charging infrastructure that can be fully utilized by a diverse set of drivers. During school hours, teachers, students and staff will be able to charge their EVs and outside of school hours community members such as parents, can use the EV charging infrastructure as well. In San Diego, there are 42 public school districts with over 780 schools. This illustrates the vast network of EV charging infrastructure that could be utilized by schools. Today, only a handful of K through 12 schools have any EV charging infrastructure in place. Charging infrastructure at schools can also facilitate visibility and understanding of electric vehicles to the younger generations. Education and outreach is important to accelerate EV adoption today and sustain it for the future. Lastly, we support AB 1082 because it requires use of a time-variant rate approved by the CPUC. SDG and E has proven through a multi-year plug-in EV pricing and technology study that customers can be incented to charge their EVs during off peak hours, 12 to 5 AM and daytime hours when there are abundant renewables on the grid. SDG and E is in the process of implementing power your drive. A CPUC approved pilot which will send drivers an hourly dynamic, day ahead price signal, that reflects circuit and system conditions. This rate is designed to encourage off peak charging and charging when renewables are plentiful on the grid. This not only maximized GHG in air emission reductions, It gives control to the customer, enabling them to reduce their own fuel costs. Ubiquitous and widespread access to charging and price signals to charge at the right time of day will play a critical role to achieving our GHG reduction goals. For these reasons, we urge your aye vote on 1082. I will be happy to answer any questions from the Chair and Members of the Committee, thank you.

Maybe now we're talking 10 to $15,000 a month again, out of pocket because unfortunately, this service isn't covered by healthcare. This bill is really just trying to find a happy medium to make sure that these home carried workers are able to provide a good living for themselves and their families. [{'start': 27, 'end': 40, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 116, 'end': 133, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Jeannette Zanipatin: Good morning Chair and Committee members, my name is Jeannette Zanipatin. I'm the attorney for MALDEF, the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund. I am here in strong support of Senate Bill 628. This bill, as Senator Lara mentioned, would delete the requirement that Los Angeles Community College District be elected at large, and instead would allow LACCD the option to be elected by trustee area. MALDEF is the nation's largest leading Latino legal civil rights organization, representing over 50 million Latinos living in the United States, which promotes social change through advocacy, communications, community education, and litigation. SB 628 is a simple straightforward bill that allows LACCD the option to switch its method of election from an at-large system to be elected by trustee area. The California Voting Rights Act of 2001 was designed to safeguard the right to vote in local, at-large elections, where racially polarized voting exists. The CVRA has played a critical and essential role in ensuring that local governments and local jurisdictions compliance with state voting right protections against unlawful voter dilution in these at-large systems. In the past 12 years, prior to this March 2017 election, 16 Latino candidates ran in 11 racially contested elections, yet only three Latinos were elected to the Board of Trustees. In the March primary that was held this year, seats numbers two, four, and six were up for election and three Latinos won the election to the LACCD Board. One election, however, does not validate the election system, that has usually and historically served to dilute the Latino vote, which is consistent with the US Supreme Court decision in Thornburg versus Gingles. In particular, the court in Gingles noted that the minority must be able to demonstrate that the majority votes sufficiently as a block to enable it, in absence of special circumstances, such as a minority candidate running unopposed, usually to defeat the minority's preferred candidate. The Gingles court went further to state that it is this usual predictability of the majority success that distinguishes structural dilution from the mere lost of an occasional election. LACCD is one of the most diverse community college districts in the state, if not the nation. Of its enrolled students population, over 58% of its students are Latino, 10.4% are African American, followed by Asian enrollment at about 7.1%. In addition, about 20% of its student population lives below the poverty line and about 20% of the student population are immigrants. Given that LACCD is at a critical juncture in examining student success rates and transfer rates, a growing and diverse student body, and the need to ensure that policies that LACCD adopt stand to protect its vulnerable population, the option to switch to an election by trustee area is an important tool at LACCD's disposal to address the growing, changing, and challenging needs of the needs of its students. The switch too election by trustee area would also ensure that LACCD is being responsive to the communities it serves. The Board plays a critical role in ensuring that community engagement at the local level, while at the same time ensuring that the Board is accountable to the trustee areas and the districts that it potentially serve. Furthermore, we cannot understate the critical role that community colleges play in California as a gateway to access not only higher education, but as a gateway to access the middle class through its degree programs, certification programs, and the ability to afford many students the ability to transfer to a four-year institution. SB 628 is a good government bill and for the many reasons cited above, we are in strong support and urge your aye vote, thank you.

[{'start': 14, 'end': 28, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 58, 'end': 68, 'label': 'PERSON'}, {'start': 854, 'end': 859, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Jennifer Whitaker: Thank you, good afternoon, Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee. My name is Jennifer Whitaker and I'm the Audit Chief of the Office of State Audits and Evaluations. We are the audit unit within the Department of Finance. As you know our report went final last Thursday afternoon, March 30th, and we're here to give a summary of the results of that audit and answer any questions that you may have. In accordance with the 2016-17 Budget Act, finance performed an evaluation of the Board of Equalization's sales and use tax, resource utilization, outreach activities and the supplemental annual report. This evaluation also included an evaluation of BOE's corrective actions taken to address the November 2015 state controller's, internal accounting and administrative controls review.  Our evaluation focused solely on findings one through six and included the proposed retail sales tax fund adjustment. During the course of the evaluation, we interviewed over 70 employees at the BOE Sacramento headquarters, 8 field offices, and 1 of their non-public offices. The interviews ranged from staff level to executive level management. We also, during the time period of our evaluation, were able to attend two BOE outreach events. At the conclusion of our field work, we met with all five board members individually to provide a summary of our evaluation, and obtain their perspective. Overall, our evaluation noted that BOE's operational culture impacted its ability to provide accurate and reliable information. BOE had a difficult time providing complete and accurate documentation and response to our inquiries, and in some instances, levels of management were not aware of and could not speak to certain district activities for which they held oversight responsibilities. We focused in on three main areas, one being resource utilization, and when we looked at resource utilization we found that revenue generating staff had been redirected to perform non-revenue generating activities, including outreach activities which directly violates provision one of the Budget Act. Additionally, BOE was unable to accurately reflect revenue and cost impacts in its accounting records and supplemental annual report. The second area that we looked at was outreach, and although the external affairs department coordinates the numerous aspects of the education and outreach program and the general policy is for the board members offices to request certain outreach activities through external affairs, this policy was not consistently followed. In addition, these outreach activities have a limited nexus on BOE's administrative tax programs and have increased in recent years. Additionally, BOE had not implemented budgets or cost tracking mechanisms to record outreach activities, when also the hired staff for these activities using practices that bypass budgetary and legislative processes. The third area that we reported on was the supplemental annual report and because of the information obtained regarding the staff utilization practices and also the outreach. The supplemental annual report submitted to the Legislature did not comply with the Budget Act requirements. Because of the redirections and the audit and collections, revenue and personnel costs are incorrect, it also skews the cost benefit ratio that are reported in the supplemental annual report. In addition, when we reviewed the processes for the supplemental annual report, we noted other areas of improvement that need to be addressed.  There was an absence of standardized written policies and procedures to prepare the report, and also to ensure that the accuracy and consistency of the information that was reported. Some of the examples include the methodologies and procedures used to compile the report were not documented and in some instances were unknown, and significant fluctuations and changes from methodology from prior years was not documented and cannot be clearly communicated. The second part of the evaluation also known as chapter two focused in on the corrective actions for findings one through six of the SEO report and also the proposed tax allocation adjustment. And we received 11 different versions of the proposed sales and use tax allocation during the time that we were there and with each version finance continue to find errors and omissions and the information that was provided. The last version was received in February 2017 and as indicated in our report, further review is needed to review that proposed tax allocation. We need to receive some additional information such as the methodologies and assumptions that were used to prepare that allocation. Those were not readily available during the time of our review. So in summary, those were the four main areas of our report. And I'll open up for questions.

Among the Board's duties under Government Code Section 15623, the four members elected to equalization districts are charged with investigating the administration, enforcement, and operation within their respective districts of all laws for which the four Board is vested with the responsibility to administer and enforce. BOE management is strengthening a number of other policies and controls. The Board approved the 2017 Annual Education and Outreach Plan, which identifies outreach activities scheduled for the remainder of fiscal year 2016-2017, and specifies an allocation of funds amounting to $200,000 for each equalization district to devote to outreach. BOE management will be examining each event to evaluate its cost versus benefit to the BOE tax payers. To ensure districts are staying within their budgets, the BOE is tracking outreach spending. The BOE is also updating the Board administrative manual to provide strict guidelines to managers and employees regarding attendance and participation at events and conferences and BOE has updated its facilities leasing policy also in the Board's administrative manual. In consideration of the LAO's and DOF's concerns about positions loaned to Board Member offices, the BOE has reduced its loaned positions and is developing a formal loan policy consistent with provision one. Although the BOE continues to encounter challenges to reducing its vacancy rate, we are proud to report that as of March 22nd, 2017, the BOE has reduced permanent positions in its temporary help blanket from 157, as of January 15th 2015, to eight today. BOE management continues to work toward reducing its overall vacancy rates and to that end has accomplished the following. The BOE has formed a vacancy work group that meets regularly to ensure the vacancy issue remains front and center as an agency priority and recognizing that we have aged vacancies. We are working with the Department of Finance to identify them and apply them against the requested PCPs. We estimate a total of 21 vacant PYs are available for this purpose, but we still need to work that out with the Department of Finance. The examination and certification online system recently was implemented and has also reduced the human resource division's processing time by 20 days. And that, of course, is the Brown Act, which is the Open Meetings Law, that allows the public to do what I'm doing now, to weigh in, to do so, in a publicly noticed hearing, also the Public Records Act, which says that the public can find out what's happening with their business. They're paying for these charter schools as well as traditional schools, they should be able to have access to records on how that money's being managed. The Political Reform Act as well, I mean all of you and many of your staff comply with the Political Reform Act, as well as many local school districts. And essentially, it protects public officials from having to influencing just some of the decisions they make and having a financial interest. It protects people from doing that, it holds them accountable. And also, Government Code 1090, it prohibits decision makers from being on both sides of a contract specifically. So essentially, you can't own a company, and then also approve a contract allowing for that company to get a benefit from the charter school. We think that's a very important accountability, and we think that this bill does put the public first. I know that the charter schools will say that they are also compelled by law to adhere to the conflict of interest of the Corporations Code. But the Corporations Code, the thing I would leave with you with, is the Corporation Code protects corporations, Government Code and the Political Reform Act protects the public. So we ask for your aye vote.

Rand Martin : Somebody else is pushing the button at the same time I'm trying to push it. Mr. Chair and members, Rand Martin on behalf of the California Charter Schools Association. So there are three points I'd like to make this, is it evening yet? Number one is there are four laws that we're talking about in this bill. Three of which the California Charter Schools Association supports. We support the Brown Act or Bagley-Keene, depending on your structure. We support the California Public Records Act, we support the California Political Reform Act and make no mistake that the Political Reform Act is the central conflict of interest law in this state. The other laws that we talk about are not the core conflict of interest laws the PRA is and we support it and we think it should apply to charter schools. The piece that we get stuck on is Government Code 1090. I want to point out something that the consultant wrote in the analysis today, which is really compelling, I think, to our argument. She talks about why Government Code 1090 was created. And says, mindful of the adage that no man can serve two masters. The section was enacted to ensure that public officials making official contracts not be distracted by personal financial gain from exercising absolute loyalty and undivided allegiance to the best interest of the entity which they serve. If you are a board member on a non-profit charter school board, and you're there to serve the best interests of that board. And part of serving that best interest is perhaps being able to arrange a low or no interest loan. Or being able to lease a facility that you own for a dollar a year. That's serving the best interest of that entity. And to take that right away from them by imposing Government Code 1090 is a direct contrast to what 1090 was intended to create in the first place. Yes, it works when you're talking about a City Council member or a school district board member. The person on a City Council should not be in any kind of financial relationship with a city on who's board they've been elected to. But when you're on a non-profit board, and many of you, I'm sure, have been on non-profit boards, you know what's required of you, expected of you. It's not just to go out and raise money, it's also to make sure that you do whatever you can as a board member to keep the doors of that facility open. When you, not you personally, but when the Legislature and the Governor deferred payments to schools and school districts during the worst of the recession. School districts were able to go out and get bridge loans at 2 and 3%. We were able to get bridge loans at 14 and 15 and 16%. If we were stuck with that as our only alternative, we would have been shutting doors right and left across the state. But we had board members who were willing to step up and do for that school what needed to be done. We should be applauding that. We should not be taking that right away from them. And that's exactly what 1090 does. The other three laws, absolutely let's put them in place, we agree, we like them we think they are appropriate. But let's not harm charter schools by taking away their ability of board members to do what they need to do. The last point I want to leave you with is a political one. As Mr. Jones-Sawyer indicated, the Governor has vetoed this bill. On three occasions, this bill has been vetoed, with 1090 in it. Now I'm not going to say the governor's going to veto it again, but if past is prologue, there's probably a good chance that he would veto this bill. If you and we, and Mr. Jones- Sawyer want to get this accomplished, let's get it accomplished with three of the laws that are the most important laws to protect the public interest, and the school's interest. So we encourage you to not move this bill forward with 1090. We do have another version, you'll hear, we expect eventually, coming from the Senate that deals with exactly these issues. But does not take away the ability of our board members to serve the best interests and their loyalties to the charter schools. We urge your opposition to this bill today, thank you.

It does not assess eye focusing, eye teaming, eye pressure, eye health, and so much more. To give you some more information, a landmark study funded by the National Institutes of Health determined the prevalence of vision disorders in children here in Californiao one of them being farsightedness, which means the child has difficulty with their near vision and they need extra focusing effort in order to try and see clearly at near. And what they found is preschool age children of Hispanic and African American decent had a 10 to 13% prevalence of moderate farsightedness, and this is something that's often difficult to detect in a vision screening. Another NIH study found that pre-school and kindergarten aged children with moderate, uncorrected farsightedness had a significantly worse performance.

According to most recent census data, California is home to more people of Native American, Alaskan Native heritage, than any other state in the country. At the time of our discovery by the Spanish, the Chumash had developed an advanced culture that included extensive trade networks, their own shell currency, and ocean-going paddle canoes called tomols. Few, if any, students learn about this Chumash history. Students instead learn about the Spanish missions. The missions and their accompanying presidio military garrisons were built to control Chumash lands and subjugate its Chumash people. After forcing the Chumash people to relocate to missions, the Spanish were forced to leave when Mexico declared its independence, which left my ancestors homeless when the missions were sold or cyclorized. The Santa Ynez Chumash were fortunate to find a sliver of open land on a river bed called Sandra Dakota Creek. Chumash settlement of the river bed can be documented back to before California statehood in 1835 but it took until 1906 for the Indian agent and the Catholic Church to finally deed the land to the United States to create the Santa Ynez Indian Reservation in what is now Santa Barbara county. The remnants of ancient civilizations are prominent throughout California. Today, Native Americans celebrate their heritage through language, customs and traditions. Every tribe has its own story and AB 738 creates the vehicle to expand the story of California Indians beyond just missions. We ask you for your support of AB 738. Thank you.

Eric Crane: Good afternoon, Members of the Committee on education. My name is Eric Crane. I'm a senior researcher at WestEd, a nonpartisan, nonprofit research development and service agency headquartered in California, and committed to promoting excellence, achieving equity and improving learning for children, youth and adults. In my 23 years in education research policy and practice work, I've written about student assessment and school performance, with a focus on making best use of assessment data and other information. Although it may be helpful to briefly discuss the different types of assessment practice, in the interest of time, I'll refer you to two pages that staff has included in your packet. These pages sketch out the difference among types of assessment. Now, it needs to be mentioned that those summaries are what's typical. Exceptions to these typical characteristics can be found. Without speaking to the specifics of the Smarter Balanced Assessment System, others on the agenda can do that more ably than I can, I will say that it was designed as a system with full awareness of how formative, interim and summative components work together to promote better teaching and learning. Generally, it is formative assessment practice that supports continuous feedback to adjust ongoing teaching and learning. There is interest, and not just in the Committee, in understanding the conditions under which interim assessment informs instruction, above and beyond the interim's primary function as student progress monitoring. Essentially, three conditions need to be met. Timing in receiving results, amount in grain size of information, and adequate teacher training, receiving results. Assessment results to the classroom teacher need to be timely enough that the teacher can adjust instruction, amount in grain size of information, the number of items in the typical interim assessment can't reliably determine whether a student has mastered a particular standard unless the entire assessment is built around one or two standards. There is a real risk of overleveraging interim assessment information, drawing incorrect conclusions about student mastery from just one or two items. Now, classroom summaries on a particular item can be informative and useful to the teacher. But that's a far cry from drawing a conclusion about a particular student's mastery of a particular standard. And that leads to the third condition, teacher training and assessment literacy. When teachers have been trained in assessment and understand how formative, interim and summative assessment activities can work together in a comprehensive system, they will be well positioned to draw defensible conclusions from assessment data. And that, in turn, will support world-class teaching and learning in California's schools. Thank you.

We eliminated many tests that were designed for accountability and the purpose to drive judgements at the end of the year. And moved us to a new era of designing assessments as AB 484 stated for the primary purpose of improving teaching and learning. We still use these assessments for accountability, but again its primary purpose is to improve teaching and learning. And that's why California elected to join Smarter Balance as its consortium, in order to have a comprehensive system of assessment. Which starts with formative tools, interim assessments, and ends with the summit of assessment. You've heard some criticism today, and I would say mostly fair criticism of our current interim assessments, and the reporting of those results. We knew when we implemented Smarter Balance, that the summit of assessment was going to be more advanced in readiness, than the interim assessments and the digital library. But it had to be that way. The initial priority had to be the successful implementation of the summit of assessment. We had to meet those federal obligations first, or we would lose the entire system. And we definitely were successful. California is now in its third year of testing 3.2 million students with computer adaptive tests. With embedded supports for all students, including our English learners, and our students with disabilities. Only 900 students out of 3.2 million have had to take the test on paper and pencil. Not all states had this type of success, and no one in the entire country has been as successful as we have here in California. So now we need to move to improve our formative tools and interim assessments, to match the success that we've had with the summit of assessments, and that's what our next step is. It's the states that establish the strategic plan, and it's the states that approve the budget for smarter balance. In addition to governments, Smarter is designed for teachers and by teachers. The sergeant just passed out a handout, and all of us will be starting on page 1. So on page 1 of this handout, we provide a brief description of California's child care and preschool programs. As you can see from the chart, we categorized these programs in three ways: childcare for families participating in the state's welfare to work program, CalWORKs, childcare for families not participating in CalWORKs and preschool programs, and the chart provides a brief description of each program as well as the number of slots associated with each program. And statewide, we have about 434,000 slots for childcare and preschool in 2016-17. Page 2 of the handout provides a brief overview of some key components of child care and preschool programs. All the programs on page 1 have eligibility criteria, but the criteria vary across the programs. So CalWORKs and most non-CalWORKs child care programs require families to have incomes below 70% of the state median income in 2007. This is about $42,000 for a family of 3. However, transitional kindergarten does not have an income requirement. Most programs also serve children based on their age. Most programs serve children birth to age 12, but state preschool serves 3 and 4-year-olds, and transitional kindergarten serves children based on their birth month, serving children born between September 2nd and December 2nd. Finally, the state has recently allowed school districts to serve children born outside of the transitional kindergarten birth window. Children between December 2nd and the end of the school year, if they turn five, but the school district doesn't received funding until they turn five. Finally, most programs require parents to be working or in school during the hours they receive care, but part-day state preschool and transitional kindergarten do not have work requirements. Access to the programs also varies; for CalWORKs and transitional kindergarten, the state typically funds care for all eligible and interested families. The other programs, the state budgets a certain number of slots, and families are prioritized based on income. The state provides care in four types of settings: licensed centers, which tend to be larger classroom-like settings; licensed family child care homes, where the child receives care in the provider's own home, and there're about 6 to 12 children total served; and license-exempt settings where families, friends, and neighbors care for children from one family at one time. And finally, school classrooms similar to those of kindergarten. CalWORKs and the alternative payment program can access care from both licensed centers, licensed family child care homes, and license-exempt providers. Other childcare programs and state preschool can only access care in licensed centers and licensed family childcare homes, and transitional kindergarten is served in school classrooms similar to that of kindergarten. The standards also very across programs. All programs have to meet certain health and safety standards, have to have certain staff qualifications and staff ratios, but specific standards vary across the programs. In addition, some programs are required to include developmentally appropriate activities. So for example, state preschool programs are required to include basic numeracy and literacy activities. On page 3 of the handout, we discussed program funding. The funding model varies across the programs. There are three main ways the state funds programs through child care vouchers, direct contracts, and school district allocations. In CalWORKs, for example, the families receive vouchers for childcare, which means families can choose a provider that meets their needs, and the state pays, reimburses the cost of that care. This reimbursement amount varies regionally based on regional market rate surveys the state conducts every couple of years. For other programs, the state contracts with specific providers for childcare and pays the same rate across the state. Finally, transitional kindergarten is funded through school district allocations through the Local Control Funding Formula. On page 4 of this handout, we cover some trends over the last decade. There's a chart you might be interested in. As you can see from this chart, a funding decrease by about $1 billion between 2007-8 and 2013-14 and has increased by 871 million since 13-14. During the recession, the Legislature held rates mostly flat but did reduce some rates for license-exempt care and for the amount the state provided to agencies administering the voucher programs. Starting in 2014-15, however, the state has provided three consecutive rate increases with spending on rates in 16-17 about 400 million higher than spending in 13-14. Slots were the main area where the cuts happened in the recession with substantial reductions and then increases during the recovery. But when we talk about slots, we really have to talk about CalWORKs slots and non-CalWORKs slots separately, because as I mentioned earlier, the state typically funds all eligible CalWORKs families and doesn't fund all eligible non-CalWORKs families. So between 2007-8 and 13-14, CalWORKS slots decreased by about 65,000. These reductions were primarily due to state actions that reduce the number of eligible families. So for example, during the recession, the state exempted certain families from the work requirement, allowing them to stay at home with their children while continuing to receive cash aid. Since 13-14, CalWORKs slots have increased by about $6,000 due to the net effect of re-engaging these families in the workforce and an overall decline in the caseload due to an improving economy. Between 2007-8 and 13-14 on the non-CalWORKs side of the house; state actions reduced these slots by about 44,000 slots due to across-the-board budget cuts. And since 13-14, increases in funding for slots have resulted in there being about 25,000 more slots available today than in 13-14. That concludes my overview presentation, I'm happy to answer any questions.

Virginia Early: Thank you, Mr. Chair. Virginia Early, again, with the Legislative Analyst's Office. So, we have a handout that's coming around right now on the quality improvement programs. I'll start on page one of the handout. So federal law requires the state to spend a certain amount of federal funds and the state matching funds that the state is required to spend, to improve the quality of childcare and preschool. So in 16-17 the state had to spend about 10% of these funds which equated to 78 million on these activities and this spending requirement will go up in the next few years, reaching 12% by 2021. If federal funding remains flat, we expect this to equate to about $95 million. So federal law allows us to count various types of activities towards meeting this requirement. For example, the state can develop early learning materials for childcare providers, use it to enforce licencing requirements and provide information about childcare options to parents. California currently uses these funds to support about 30 different quality improvement programs. We divide these program options into three categories. Programs that are operating at the state level including licensing enforcement, developing those early learning resources and developing say specific trainings that operate the same state wide, and that are available to everyone. The state also has funding going to certain county level agencies that are involved in quality improvement work. Resource and referral agencies are one of these and local planning councils are another. Resource and referral agencies are responsible for helping parents find childcare in their areas and collecting data on childcare providers, while local planning councils are responsible for identifying areas in their county with unserved eligible children, and helping generally in the county coordinate childcare services. And the last category of quality spending is when the state provides funds for certain activities to these county level support entities for activities. So, for example, R&R agencies get funding to run specific types of training on top of their main responsibilities, local planning councils get funding to provide stipends to early educators on top of their other responsibilities. And some community colleges get some funds to support students' application fees for the child development teacher permit. In general, these 30 programs, CD has broad descretion over what they fund. In some cases, the Legislature has a specific line item, for example R&R's in the state budget. On page three of the handout, we provide an overview of the quality rating and improvement system. As I mentioned earlier, this is a system that sort of rates the quality of childcare providers and provides resources to help these child care providers improve of those 30 programs I mentioned earlier the state counted $800,000 towards QRIS for migrant childcare programs but outside of that 30 programs, the state also provides an additional 75 million not counted toward the federal quality spending requirement. Of this amount 50 million is Proposition 98 funds for state preschool QRIS, and 25 million is provided by First Five California for all types of providers. Consortia have a small presence in many parts of this state. Currently there are 48 consortia operating in all 58 counties, and the consortia members include resource and referral agencies, local planning councils, First Five county commissions, community colleges as well as local educational agencies and childcare providers. These consortia rate providers based on the matrix I mentioned earlier, it includes things like child teacher interactions, staff standards, the use of certain development screenings, use of child assessments to inform curriculum and several other things. Consortia have flexibility in how they use their funds to help providers improve quality. For example if a program gets a low rating because their teacher needs more training they might provide financial aid to improve the education level of the teachers. If they get a low rating because of something going on in the classroom environment they might provide a grant to help purchase supplies, so it really varies. So on page four of the hand out, we discuss CDE's revised quality improvement expenditure plan. The 16-17 budget directed CDE to take a look at the quality improvement of those 30 programs that they have. And the provisional language requested them to retain funding for R and Rs, local planning councils, and licensing enforcement, while prioritizing the rest for this QRIS system I just mentioned. CDE submitted the plan to the Legislature in February. This plan shifts about 5.1 million from about nine programs, into one infant and toddler QRIS block grant. So under this, the QRIS members of the consortia could use the funds flexibly for the activities that they deem most important but the providers would be have to be those serving infants and toddlers. In addition CDE is proposing, changing some rules to existing programs for example, certain state level trainings that those members would now have to be participating in QRIS to receive the training. Our assessment is on page five of the handout. As we looked at the system, both broadly and CDE specific proposal, we found that there are some activities that were important to supporting the subsidized childcare and preschool system. For example, helping parents find childcare, identifying areas with unmet need and collecting data on childcare providers. But we also, as we look at the system and talked to folks it seemed that quality improvement funding at the county level can lack coordination and be difficult to target to highest priorities. So for example, within each county we have these multiple support entities all involved in the activity of improving quality. But there's no over arching plan that they have to have to improve quality. And so there's QRIS, but that just applies to the small number of providers that are participating in QRIS. So without having such a plan there's no guarantee that the trainings are duplicative and there's no guarantee that the training is directed to the folks that need it most. Additionally the detailed requirements of the various funding streams mean that these county level support entities have difficulty targeting funding to their highest priorities. Additionally, we found that there's little information on the effectiveness of the state level programs I mentioned earlier. We don't have data, we have some data but not enough to determine whether the state is serving the providers that we'd like to be serving. And while the state has conducted some evaluations on the programs, we don't have evaluations that these evaluations don't address whether the programs are actually improving the quality of childcare. We also found that the funding disproportionally serves providers that already meet higher standards and so of the 28 million in CDE's revised quality improvement budget for training activities, 28% is restricted to contract based providers and under their revised program rules, another 37% is restricted to providers participating in QRIS which tend to be again contract based providers. We're concerned about this focus on contract based providers because as I mentioned earlier nearly three quarters of the infant subsidized, infant toddler subsidized population is receiving care in these voucher settings that have lower standards. In terms of CDE's overall plan, with think that shifting funds to QRIS a limit, we like that it increases the flexibility of these county level support entities to conduct the types of activities that they think are the most beneficial. But we are concerned that restricting it to only QRIS types of providers limits the providers that can benefit because state wide a small share of subsided providers are participating in QRIS. So on page seven of our handout we go through our recommendations. We recommend the Legislature retain funding for essential activities like helping parents find childcare and collecting data on the childcare providers and identifying areas with unmet need. These activities are currently done by the resource and referral agencies and local planning councils. Then we would recommend the Legislator take the funding that's currently going to county level support entities for other activities and package it into one county level block grant of about $21 million distributed to counties based on each county's share of the subsidized population. We would recommend that the Legislator require all the entities currently receiving these funds to get together and agree on how they would spend the funds under the new block grant, taking into account the providers and the subsidized population in their area. So these providers could choose to do the same activities that they're currently doing. I'm sorry, these support entities could continue to do the same activities they're currently doing or if they have other ideas for how they can meet their local priorities, they could do those. Finally, we would recommend the state collect data from counties about how the funds are used. We'd also recommend that the state reject CDE's proposal to limit access to certain state level programs to QRIS participants as we want to ensure that all providers have access to these programs. And finally for the remaining state level programs, we recommend that the state hire an independent evaluator to assess each program and whether it improves the quality of childcare over the next several years, starting with the largest ones first. So those are our key recommendations and happy to answer questions whenever you think it's appropriate.

Beside the direct support for financial assistance for childcare services the block grant also requires states to spend a certain portion of funds along with matching funds on 10 quality improvement activities. And so those were discussed a little bit more. But training and professional development, supporting a quality rating improvement system, and improving the supply of quality programs for infants and toddlers. With the 2014 reauthorization of CCDBG, the quality set asides are increasing over the next few years. In the current year it's 7% increasing to 8% next year. For the 17-18 budget, there are currently no proposals to allocate new quality funds and so at this time our proposal provides just over $78 million, or proposes to provide just over $78 million which corresponds to the amount in the Governor's Budget proposal. In the development of the proposed plan, the department conducted stakeholder outreach last fall and so this was over two sessions last November. So the first session focused on the requirements of the of CCDBG act and the second session later in November focused on the QRIS and so as I was saying, commenters generally supported existing projects, many expressed the desire for additional funding to be used to make the sun setting infant toddler quality QRIS block grant ongoing, to maintain and build on the current investment for infants and toddlers. Others recommended support for workforce registry, coaching and mentoring, leadership training and services for a full range of providers. So based on the feedback we received, and building up the funding provided in the current year, so 16-17 we first removed the one-time funding that was provided in 15-16 and the draft quality improvement plan that we're presenting represents the department's efforts to balance the need to maintain the infrastructure of quality improvement activities with local flexibility. And so in most instances the CDE is proposing to keep the funding as established in the 16-17 plan, however again because some of the one-time funding went away, and there's no additional funding, the plan proposes reductions to 10 programs with additional funding for one program. So the two most significant changes in terms of dollar amounts are a proposed cut of almost $2.7 million to the childcare retention program, more commonly referred to as AB 212 and so this does represent one quarter of the reduction offset by child development contractors having access to the local QRIS block grants and then as was noted earlier we are proposing to provide $5.1 million for an infant toddler QRIS block grant which is about 40% of the current sun setting program. So a little bit more on those, so AB 212, the proposed reduction to this represents, again, a quarter of the reduction. This program provides funds to local planning councils to increase quality for programs serving infants and toddlers, through childcare staff retention activities, and is focused around retaining qualified staff who work directly with children in state-subsidized center based programs and promoting best practices that foster quality early education. And then we are planning on providing money to, essentially reestablish partially, an infant toddler block grant. So the $5.1 million proposed partially back fills 24 million that was provided over two years in one-time state funding. That goes away, so the local controller should use the infant toddler block grant to support local early learning programs to increase the number of low income children served in high quality programs by providing training, technical assistance, and other resources to the program. These are often the same recipients of the AB 212 funding, and both are focused on supporting providers meeting a higher tier of quality as determined by their local QRIS ratings system. And I would note in the future as federal quality percent spending increases, it would be our goal to increase the infant toddler QRIS block grant to restore the funding closer to the original amount provided. Another comment about the proposal is that 11% of the funding is restricted to state contract providers and the rest are open to all or are prioritized to those providers participating in the local QRIS and this was really around following budget language so, set to focus on QRIS. The evaluation of quality improvement activities so the budget proposes to maintain about $570,000 to evaluate quality improvement activities. And then we use the results of this reviews to make sure that there's alignment with the state's quality efforts and make funding adjustments. [{'start': 11, 'end': 22, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Virginia Early: Alright, good morning, Mr. Chairs, members. Virginia Early with the Legislative Analyst's Office. Today, on this item, I'll provide a brief overview of the state's child care and preschool system as well as some information on recent trends. The sergeant just passed out a handout, and all of us will be starting on page 1. So on page 1 of this handout, we provide a brief description of California's child care and preschool programs. As you can see from the chart, we categorized these programs in three ways: childcare for families participating in the state's welfare to work program, CalWORKs, childcare for families not participating in CalWORKs and preschool programs, and the chart provides a brief description of each program as well as the number of slots associated with each program. And statewide, we have about 434,000 slots for childcare and preschool in 2016-17. Page 2 of the handout provides a brief overview of some key components of child care and preschool programs. All the programs on page 1 have eligibility criteria, but the criteria vary across the programs. So CalWORKs and most non-CalWORKs child care programs require families to have incomes below 70% of the state median income in 2007. This is about $42,000 for a family of 3. However, transitional kindergarten does not have an income requirement. Most programs also serve children based on their age. Most programs serve children birth to age 12, but state preschool serves 3 and 4-year-olds, and transitional kindergarten serves children based on their birth month, serving children born between September 2nd and December 2nd. Finally, the state has recently allowed school districts to serve children born outside of the transitional kindergarten birth window. Children between December 2nd and the end of the school year, if they turn five, but the school district doesn't received funding until they turn five. Finally, most programs require parents to be working or in school during the hours they receive care, but part-day state preschool and transitional kindergarten do not have work requirements. Access to the programs also varies; for CalWORKs and transitional kindergarten, the state typically funds care for all eligible and interested families. The other programs, the state budgets a certain number of slots, and families are prioritized based on income. The state provides care in four types of settings: licensed centers, which tend to be larger classroom-like settings; licensed family child care homes, where the child receives care in the provider's own home, and there're about 6 to 12 children total served; and license-exempt settings where families, friends, and neighbors care for children from one family at one time. And finally, school classrooms similar to those of kindergarten. CalWORKs and the alternative payment program can access care from both licensed centers, licensed family child care homes, and license-exempt providers. Other childcare programs and state preschool can only access care in licensed centers and licensed family childcare homes, and transitional kindergarten is served in school classrooms similar to that of kindergarten. The standards also very across programs. All programs have to meet certain health and safety standards, have to have certain staff qualifications and staff ratios, but specific standards vary across the programs. In addition, some programs are required to include developmentally appropriate activities. So for example, state preschool programs are required to include basic numeracy and literacy activities. On page 3 of the handout, we discussed program funding. The funding model varies across the programs. There are three main ways the state funds programs through child care vouchers, direct contracts, and school district allocations. In CalWORKs, for example, the families receive vouchers for childcare, which means families can choose a provider that meets their needs, and the state pays, reimburses the cost of that care. This reimbursement amount varies regionally based on regional market rate surveys the state conducts every couple of years. For other programs, the state contracts with specific providers for childcare and pays the same rate across the state. Finally, transitional kindergarten is funded through school district allocations through the Local Control Funding Formula. On page 4 of this handout, we cover some trends over the last decade. There's a chart you might be interested in. As you can see from this chart, a funding decrease by about $1 billion between 2007-8 and 2013-14 and has increased by 871 million since 13-14. During the recession, the Legislature held rates mostly flat but did reduce some rates for license-exempt care and for the amount the state provided to agencies administering the voucher programs. Starting in 2014-15, however, the state has provided three consecutive rate increases with spending on rates in 16-17 about 400 million higher than spending in 13-14. Slots were the main area where the cuts happened in the recession with substantial reductions and then increases during the recovery. But when we talk about slots, we really have to talk about CalWORKs slots and non-CalWORKs slots separately, because as I mentioned earlier, the state typically funds all eligible CalWORKs families and doesn't fund all eligible non-CalWORKs families. So between 2007-8 and 13-14, CalWORKS slots decreased by about 65,000. These reductions were primarily due to state actions that reduce the number of eligible families. So for example, during the recession, the state exempted certain families from the work requirement, allowing them to stay at home with their children while continuing to receive cash aid. Since 13-14, CalWORKs slots have increased by about $6,000 due to the net effect of re-engaging these families in the workforce and an overall decline in the caseload due to an improving economy. Between 2007-8 and 13-14 on the non-CalWORKs side of the house; state actions reduced these slots by about 44,000 slots due to across-the-board budget cuts. And since 13-14, increases in funding for slots have resulted in there being about 25,000 more slots available today than in 13-14. That concludes my overview presentation, I'm happy to answer any questions.

I think the LAO and the Department of Finance did a good overview and discussion of the Governor's proposals. So I think I'll just provide a little bit more detail on some of the 2016-17 implementation issues that are referenced in your agenda. And so one of them, which the LAO mentioned, which was on the standard reimbursement rate, so that was increasing the rate that the Legislature approved a 10% increase midyear. So that was effective January 1st. And when we looked at implementing that, we ran into a few problems, namely that our system doesn't provide or doesn't allow us to do two rates within a single contract year. And so we looked at different options to doing that, including potentially having to do two contracts within a year, which we felt would be not only burdensome from the Department, but also from the provider side to have to do two contracts. Additionally, because of the way the earnings happen within contracts, it probably could have caused some more concerns in terms of when providers are earning most to their contracts, which varies from provider to provider. And so ultimately what we did in conversation with Department of Finance, LAO and legislative staff is we had a blended rate. And so what that blended rate was, was essentially a 5% increase over at the '15-'16. And so that provided providers with a $40.20 increase, rather than the 10% starting in January 1st. And so that took effect July 1st, 2016. And so the couple other notes on the, I would say we've done an updated survey on the regional market rate and so we will have those results soon and the new ceilings will be posted when the Legislature approves the increases to those ceiling rates. As Ms. Early mentioned, the preschool slots. So, as we've seen in the '15-'16 year, there were some challenges with uptakes, particularly on the LEA side, on the increased preschool slots, and so in the '16-'17 budget year, the slots were only for LEAs and so we've been now done a third round. So we're in the middle of a third round of seeking applications. So what we found is we did a first round and we filled about 1300 of those slots with 40% for full day and 60% for part day. We then did a second round, which closed recently, and in that round we were able to get to about not quite 1600 slots. And again, around the same ratio with sort of the 40/60 split between part day and full day. And because of those two rounds, while we have nearly 2,900 slots, which was the increase provided, there is funding leftover, about $11 million or $11.5 million because so many of those were part day. And so we put out another round of requests for applications to try to utilize all that money to increase the slot. So, that closes later this month and so we are hopeful that will get some increased interest in that so that we can fully utilize the slots in dollars that were provided in the budget. I would reiterate, I don't think that this means that there's a lack of need for preschool slots for four year olds. I think the challenge is that Ms. Early identified, when the money is primarily focused or limited to LEA's, becomes a little bit challenging because they're looking at different rules and requirements for state preschool versus TK. And so some of those issues are the reimbursement rate being lower as was mentioned. Also with TK, the eligibility is around birth dates versus income eligibility. And then also facilities and the ability to expand facilities on school campuses. And so we think those are some of the concerns or some of the trade offs that districts have to look at when they're deciding to apply for those. So I wouldn't want the implications that we're having trouble getting enough applicants for those slots to be an indication that there isn't need. I think there's probably a misalignment or a disconnect between need and how the slots are provided. One other issue that's noted in the agenda item was around the alternative payment program cost. What we found is we were alerted to some potential issues late last year around some over-enrollment issues within the AP programs, and so we started having conversations with those providers that we were hearing from, trying to assess what the situation was. So they were on track to base to essentially over earn their contract without changes to it. And one of the concerns that we had was not only the over-enrollment but, as the contractors were trying to manage that, not wanting to dis-enroll families. And so we began working with those providers and having conversations and really what we needed to do was get a assessment of how big the challenge was. Was this limited to a handful of contractors or was it larger than that? And so, in January, about the 20th, we received information from providers around their enrollment numbers through December 31st. And so, with that information, we were really able to determine that it was a significantly larger problem. And so we were looking at potentially just over $22 million in over-enrollment. And so we began having conversations with providers around what some of the rationale was for that. And also having conversations with Department of Finance, the LAO, and legislative staff. I think we all had a shared objective around not wanting to dis-enroll families. And so we initiated a process where we notified providers who were over-earning their contract to essentially let them know we were looking at solutions for this. We directed them not to dis-enroll families, but also not to enroll any more families with the idea being that we could look at potential savings to backfill some of that, and then also hopefully have, perhaps, attrition would help correct that over the year. We have a better sense of the problem with each month, so we also ask for APs to report their enrollments monthly; some do quarterly. So we're trying to track this on a much closer basis and also working with the, I think, it's around 34 contractors who are over earning that contracts right now. So working with them to get a sense of it, but we did submit a request to have to use some available money we had from general childcare and CalWORKs stage three that wasn't being utilized. And so we did submit a request to have that money transferred to fund this so, again, that these providers wouldn't have to dis-enroll families, if we could find a solution to that. And so that was approved on March 24th by the Legislature. And so, again, we're continuing to analyze the monthly reports, working with contractors and trying to get a sense of what the solution is. We don't think there'll be any additional over-enrollment this year, but in that analysis, we need to be sure that we understand what the problem is to make sure that it is limited to one time. And, again, with each month we'll have more information. So, later this month we'll have March's enrollment numbers. And then again in May we'll have April's numbers. And so we'll report back as those numbers come in so that we have a better sense of the scope of the problem, and if by maintaining enrollments and not dis-enrolling and not re-enrolling new families if that will change the size of the problem. And then the only other comment I would have is, as the Superintendent spoke at least to this Subcommittee number one, we do support the maintenance of the commitment to increase rates and slots again in the budget year and not to have the pause that the Governor's proposing. But as noted earlier, potentially looking at how do we make sure on the preschool slots that those are provided where there is need so potentially looking at beyond having that apply to LEA's. Thank you.
