Virginia Early: Thank you, Mr. Chair. Virginia Early, again, with the Legislative Analyst's Office. So, we have a handout that's coming around right now on the quality improvement programs. I'll start on page one of the handout. So federal law requires the state to spend a certain amount of federal funds and the state matching funds that the state is required to spend, to improve the quality of childcare and preschool. So in 16-17 the state had to spend about 10% of these funds which equated to 78 million on these activities and this spending requirement will go up in the next few years, reaching 12% by 2021. If federal funding remains flat, we expect this to equate to about $95 million. So federal law allows us to count various types of activities towards meeting this requirement. For example, the state can develop early learning materials for childcare providers, use it to enforce licencing requirements and provide information about childcare options to parents. California currently uses these funds to support about 30 different quality improvement programs. We divide these program options into three categories. Programs that are operating at the state level including licensing enforcement, developing those early learning resources and developing say specific trainings that operate the same state wide, and that are available to everyone. The state also has funding going to certain county level agencies that are involved in quality improvement work. Resource and referral agencies are one of these and local planning councils are another. Resource and referral agencies are responsible for helping parents find childcare in their areas and collecting data on childcare providers, while local planning councils are responsible for identifying areas in their county with unserved eligible children, and helping generally in the county coordinate childcare services. And the last category of quality spending is when the state provides funds for certain activities to these county level support entities for activities. So, for example, R&R agencies get funding to run specific types of training on top of their main responsibilities, local planning councils get funding to provide stipends to early educators on top of their other responsibilities. And some community colleges get some funds to support students' application fees for the child development teacher permit. In general, these 30 programs, CD has broad descretion over what they fund. In some cases, the Legislature has a specific line item, for example R&R's in the state budget. On page three of the handout, we provide an overview of the quality rating and improvement system. As I mentioned earlier, this is a system that sort of rates the quality of childcare providers and provides resources to help these child care providers improve of those 30 programs I mentioned earlier the state counted $800,000 towards QRIS for migrant childcare programs but outside of that 30 programs, the state also provides an additional 75 million not counted toward the federal quality spending requirement. Of this amount 50 million is Proposition 98 funds for state preschool QRIS, and 25 million is provided by First Five California for all types of providers. Consortia have a small presence in many parts of this state. Currently there are 48 consortia operating in all 58 counties, and the consortia members include resource and referral agencies, local planning councils, First Five county commissions, community colleges as well as local educational agencies and childcare providers. These consortia rate providers based on the matrix I mentioned earlier, it includes things like child teacher interactions, staff standards, the use of certain development screenings, use of child assessments to inform curriculum and several other things. Consortia have flexibility in how they use their funds to help providers improve quality. For example if a program gets a low rating because their teacher needs more training they might provide financial aid to improve the education level of the teachers. If they get a low rating because of something going on in the classroom environment they might provide a grant to help purchase supplies, so it really varies. So on page four of the hand out, we discuss CDE's revised quality improvement expenditure plan. The 16-17 budget directed CDE to take a look at the quality improvement of those 30 programs that they have. And the provisional language requested them to retain funding for R and Rs, local planning councils, and licensing enforcement, while prioritizing the rest for this QRIS system I just mentioned. CDE submitted the plan to the Legislature in February. This plan shifts about 5.1 million from about nine programs, into one infant and toddler QRIS block grant. So under this, the QRIS members of the consortia could use the funds flexibly for the activities that they deem most important but the providers would be have to be those serving infants and toddlers. In addition CDE is proposing, changing some rules to existing programs for example, certain state level trainings that those members would now have to be participating in QRIS to receive the training. Our assessment is on page five of the handout. As we looked at the system, both broadly and CDE specific proposal, we found that there are some activities that were important to supporting the subsidized childcare and preschool system. For example, helping parents find childcare, identifying areas with unmet need and collecting data on childcare providers. But we also, as we look at the system and talked to folks it seemed that quality improvement funding at the county level can lack coordination and be difficult to target to highest priorities. So for example, within each county we have these multiple support entities all involved in the activity of improving quality. But there's no over arching plan that they have to have to improve quality. And so there's QRIS, but that just applies to the small number of providers that are participating in QRIS. So without having such a plan there's no guarantee that the trainings are duplicative and there's no guarantee that the training is directed to the folks that need it most. Additionally the detailed requirements of the various funding streams mean that these county level support entities have difficulty targeting funding to their highest priorities. Additionally, we found that there's little information on the effectiveness of the state level programs I mentioned earlier. We don't have data, we have some data but not enough to determine whether the state is serving the providers that we'd like to be serving. And while the state has conducted some evaluations on the programs, we don't have evaluations that these evaluations don't address whether the programs are actually improving the quality of childcare. We also found that the funding disproportionally serves providers that already meet higher standards and so of the 28 million in CDE's revised quality improvement budget for training activities, 28% is restricted to contract based providers and under their revised program rules, another 37% is restricted to providers participating in QRIS which tend to be again contract based providers. We're concerned about this focus on contract based providers because as I mentioned earlier nearly three quarters of the infant subsidized, infant toddler subsidized population is receiving care in these voucher settings that have lower standards. In terms of CDE's overall plan, with think that shifting funds to QRIS a limit, we like that it increases the flexibility of these county level support entities to conduct the types of activities that they think are the most beneficial. But we are concerned that restricting it to only QRIS types of providers limits the providers that can benefit because state wide a small share of subsided providers are participating in QRIS. So on page seven of our handout we go through our recommendations. We recommend the Legislature retain funding for essential activities like helping parents find childcare and collecting data on the childcare providers and identifying areas with unmet need. These activities are currently done by the resource and referral agencies and local planning councils. Then we would recommend the Legislator take the funding that's currently going to county level support entities for other activities and package it into one county level block grant of about $21 million distributed to counties based on each county's share of the subsidized population. We would recommend that the Legislator require all the entities currently receiving these funds to get together and agree on how they would spend the funds under the new block grant, taking into account the providers and the subsidized population in their area. So these providers could choose to do the same activities that they're currently doing. I'm sorry, these support entities could continue to do the same activities they're currently doing or if they have other ideas for how they can meet their local priorities, they could do those. Finally, we would recommend the state collect data from counties about how the funds are used. We'd also recommend that the state reject CDE's proposal to limit access to certain state level programs to QRIS participants as we want to ensure that all providers have access to these programs. And finally for the remaining state level programs, we recommend that the state hire an independent evaluator to assess each program and whether it improves the quality of childcare over the next several years, starting with the largest ones first. So those are our key recommendations and happy to answer questions whenever you think it's appropriate.

Anara Guard: Good afternoon, my name is Anara Guard. And thank you for this opportunity. I've worked in suicide prevention since 1999, both here in California and at the national level when I worked for the National Suicide Prevention Resource Center. The staff requested that I appear today to help address the questions that were in the agenda. In the interest of time, I'm not going to give you my bio, you can get it, if you want it, later. I do have handouts for the Committee that I'll leave with you, so let's get to it. In terms of the first question, which had to do with the most common methods of suicide used in California, let's first step back and talk about data in general. In the US and in California, suicide has been on the rise in terms of both rates and numbers. And in California, it's been on an increase fairly steadily from 2005. Suicide is the leading cause of injury death in our state, which means there are more suicides than are motor vehicle deaths or fall deaths or homicide or unintentional poisoning. The populations at greatest risk include Native American youth, LGBT youth, at least four attempts, it's less clear on the death data, older adults, and by older I mean older than all of us, 65 and greater, veterans, men, who die at much greater rates than women. And in particular, I want to draw your attention to the latest very troubling trend in the US and in California. It used to be when we looked at charts of ages and suicide rates across ages, you would see a spike among youth and then a decline throughout the middle years, and then a spike again over age 65. But in recent years, the 45 to 64 year old age group is seeing huge increases in mortality from alcohol and drug poisoning, from suicide, from liver disease. These are called deaths of despair because they are primarily among white men, and increasingly, white women who have a high school education or less, health problems and very poor employment prospects. There's a real concern of what's going to happen with this group. Mortality in other groups has decreased, but this population is dying in terrible numbers. They're now the second highest age grade group in California dying from suicide. So the most common, the numbers, the numbers, of course, are highest in those areas with larger populations. But the rates are highest in rural counties, especially in the Superior region. This has been true for years. The most common method of suicide matches that of other states, most other states, which is firearms. About 41% of all suicide deaths in California are by firearms. And the rates of firearm suicide are highest in rural counties, basically those same counties, primarily in the more rural counties in Superior region. I want to say, too, that in an analysis of 18 states recently, California was not part of it, firearms accounted for 70% of all veteran suicides. Your second question had to do with the effectiveness of bridge nets, and I know that Dr. Bernert will speak more to that. I do want to point out there's not a lot of literature on this. Most bridges that have been modified to prevent suicides do not have nets. Instead, they have barriers added to them. And in general, reducing access to lethal means is a very effective strategy. Whether we're talking about locking doors to rooftops, packaging medications in smaller quantities, waiting periods for firearm purchases, our new gun violence restraining order law, which I have high hopes for, or the physical barriers on bridges. Your third question asked about evidence in supporting the effectiveness of hotlines. Crisis lines or hotlines are a vital component of the continuum of suicide response, offering trained counseling not only to those people who feel suicidal, but to us, their family and friends, who are worried about them. Most hotlines already offer multiple means of communication, including online chat and text, not just on the phone. A new study that just came out last month asked 550 callers who had called in to six different crisis lines, almost 80% said that call stopped me from killing myself and 90% said the intervention of the call kept them safe. I think that's highly persuasive. And finally, you asked how would I recommend that California invest in suicide prevention? There are a multitude of effective prevention strategies in this field that really need to be matched to the individuals. They might be individual interventions, they could be laws and policies, they could be training, there's many of them, but key to success in adopting any intervention is having a comprehensive approach to suicide prevention, combining multiple, ongoing efforts, rather than hoping that one single program or intervention Is going to be sufficient. Suicide is far too complex a problem for any simple solution to turn the tide. Without infrastructure and robust leadership, which unfortunately we lack, our investments lack context. They're not measured or evaluated by a central content-knowledgeable body. California lags behind other states. Our suicide prevention plan is woefully outdated and moribund, and we lack the infrastructure to do anything about it. We need a plan that is updated, leading edge, data driven, endorsed and adopted by multiple stakeholders not limited to state agencies or the public sector, broadly implemented and then evaluated. Our plan should focus both upstream and also on improving the systems that offer access to responsive care at the earliest signs of crisis. We need leadership at the state level with engagement by many sectors, public and private, and it's my sincere wish that today's hearing will be the first step toward a new, robust and coordinated approach to suicide prevention in California. Thank you.
[{'start': 27, 'end': 38, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 2966, 'end': 2973, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Rebecca Bernert: All right, hi, I'm Rebecca Bernert. Thank you so much for your flexibility and for our moving the time around. Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and Committee Members, for the opportunity to present. So I'm a suicidologist, I'm from Stanford, and I was asked to present on emerging best practices in suicide prevention or the field that is focused on the science of suicide prevention, suicidology. So as other speakers and Anara has emphasized, suicide is considered a preventable public health problem, accounting for nearly 1 million deaths annually or approximately one life lost every 40 seconds. In addition, the Institute of Medicine estimates that approximately 25 additional suicide attempts, or up to 204 youth, occur for every suicide death. So based on these numbers it is clear that everyone in this room, either directly or indirectly, has been touched by suicide, and often in profound ways. Suicide is considered a leading cause of death in California, as you heard, and was recently declared a public health emergency by the CDC among our youth in Santa Clara County here in California. The prevention of suicide has been named a global imperative by the World Health Organization, who have suggested the following public health model of suicide prevention, which starts with surveillance of the problem to identify risk and protective factors and to develop and test interventions for implementation, as well as the scaling up of those programs and policies. Unfortunately, there are inherent challenges, many of which are not necessarily obvious or intuitive, that really impede advancements across all four of these different areas. So this includes probability challenges first, insofar as suicide does occur rarely in the population to find prediction without large scale data capture. And this is really further challenged by increasing rates which vary, of course, significantly by age, gender, and other factors. Ethical issues including confidentiality and liability concerns limit disclosure and accurate detection and the lack of uniform nomenclature for the way that we talk, even, or define suicidal behaviors, reduce comparability across different studies and research. And this is despite emphasis by the CDC as well as an FDA mandate to assess suicide risk. Given distinct methodological challenges to surveillance demands and infrastructural need that are substantial and extremely cost prohibitive, be it for epidemiology or clinical trials. To this end, very few indicated treatment currently exist specifically for suicidal behaviors worldwide. Including not a single intervention to prevent repeat suicide attempts, for example, among our youth, despite over 20 years of intervention that's been committed to this cause. Global prevention strategies have prioritized the study of evidence-based risk factors, as well as interventions to advance what is known as the field. And factors that are visible proximal to risk, modifiable, and that really stand alone to predict risk, and what I mean there is above and beyond the influence of depression, which we know is present in upwards of 90% of cases. It takes obvious precedence here. Preventive frameworks, including primary interventions, secondary, selective, and universal frameworks, focused first on primary, generally focused on the prevention of suicide incidents that may increase risk for suicide, such as psychiatric or medical disorders, for example. Secondary frameworks, which may occur at really any stage of risk, generally focus on early detection to improve intervention. Examples here would be primary care based screenings for depression as well as gatekeeper training programs. Selective interventions test the use of new treatments among those that are already at elevated risk for suicide in what are called high risk clinical trials, whereas universal frameworks use population-based strategies to reduce risk universally by promoting health access to care as well as other factors. So the emerging state of the science in suicide prevention centers on addressing critical problems and gaps in our existing scientific literature. So I'm going to just focus on, or briefly review, three different examples that are currently in our state and underway that point to where I believe the science is going, and what it could achieve with adequate leadership to enhance intervention opportunity and reduce suicide mortality. This includes lethal means restriction with the suicide deterrent system on the Golden Gate Bridge, treatment innovation using novel treatment approaches such as sleep as a therapeutic target for suicide prevention, and cutting edge technologies that promise to meaningfully advance suicide prediction. So first for lethal means restriction. This is a universal strategy which limits access to lethal means for making a suicide attempt to prevent its occurrence in the general population. A large body of research indicates that this is among the most potent yet underutilized approaches in suicide prevention that also remains poorly understood as a public health strategy, excuse me. And it does encompass, really, a range of methods that include carbon monoxide emission control, automatic shut-offs, suicide barriers, as well as gun locks and safety protocols. So this research really comes from the observation of reduction to zero finding at numerous international suicide hotspots, particularly bridge sites, following implementation of a suicide deterrent system, whether its a net, more recently, or a suicide barrier of some kind. These effects are both large and immediate according to the research that exists, and in some cases at sites reporting as many as 95 suicides annually. Examples here include Memorial Bridge in Maine and the Muenster Terrace in Switzerland. Importantly, evidence does not support suicides occurring thereby at other locations, or something that's called method substitution or location substitution and a positive impact has been observed in overall suicides in some cases following lethal means restriction. But this is difficult research to do because it is oftentimes uncontrolled, for example. Likewise, there is research showing that suicides increase upon barrier removal temporarily, when that's done, for example, for reconstruction. An example there is the Grafton bridge in New Zealand, which then again reduced to zero following reinstallation. As I mentioned before, very few indicated interventions exist worldwide that investigate a new drug or treatment for suicidal behaviors specifically. Most concerning, we currently rely almost exclusively on what's called a treatment by proxy approach. So, in other words, we treat the depression or psychiatric disorder that's thought to underlie risk, and test whether it improives suicide risk downstream of the intervention. In addition, these treatments do remain alarmingly mismatched to the acute nature of a suicidal crisis, so taking weeks and months for therapeutic effect, and this is just by elevated need where half of those following a suicide attempt will refuse treatment, and of those who do pursue it, up to 75% will drop out within the year. So this really heightens the urgency to identify rapid action treatments for suicide indication using novel treatment approaches. I've included an example here from our program that involves two NIH and DOD-funded suicide prevention clinical trials testing the efficacy of a non-pharmacological insomnia treatment for suicidal behaviors among both high-risk civilians and military veterans. In this case, there is considerable rationale to test the use of a non-mental health intervention that's targeting a highly visible risk factor such as insomnia, for example, that's overrepresented among those at risk, based on the science that we have, yet highly treatable and non-stigmatizing by comparison to other risk factors. And this is based on the thinking that we all want to sleep well, and sleep better if we don't already sleep well, and we do know how to treat sleep disturbances and other factors similar to it very easily with large treatment effects observed in as few as one to four treatment sessions. Next, the final example just includes new technologies for suicide prevention and risk detection, with Facebook pioneering new ground here on a global scale. But just to step back for a moment, I thought it would be helpful to provide some context here. We do know that the majority of those who die by suicide do consult with their physician in the days and weeks prior to death, suggesting missed detection opportunities. And in the case of our young people, we also know that most confide in a friend or a trusted adult that they are thinking about suicide. Despite hundreds, I mean, hundreds of risk factors for suicide, our recent studies suggest that less than 5% of those studies evaluated the days and weeks directly preceding risk. So again, not seeing proximity to risk, which is hard because it affects precision, and those risk factors in general show poor sensitivity and prediction as as a result. So this has lead to the recent emergence or focus on artificial intelligence, or what's called machine learning algorithms. So this is a statistical method that basically enables the computer to learn patterns to evaluate or improve accuracy of risk prediction and which performs really optimally and best actually with hundreds and hundreds of variables to inform pattern recognition. And importantly, this is a theoretical, so, meaning that it does search, allows for the computer to search for patterns to reveal risk factors that we may expect or we also might not expect. And many have likely seen Facebook's press releases noting real time suicide prevention tools that are now available to all users. And this is world wide, as well as the use of AI to identify signs of risk with advanced options for connection to additional services. So here is an example in Facebook Live, as you can see in the upper right hand corner. So this enables the safe use of social media in suicide prevention, but also has the power to really critically impact prevention and risk prediction in particular. So a recent study shows using similar computer guided models that these models out performed clinical judgment in predicting a suicide attempt, for example, following ED admission when we know risk is highest and that was by three fold, in terms of an initial comparison. And this technology also recently revealed specific keywords in a crisis chatline that were more likely to be associated with emergency referral to law enforcement, so this is allowing kind of immediate use and prioritization of callers according to risk level, to then enhance and expedite triage. Finally, an Elegant study just recently reported in nature, showed that using only medical record information and medical tags alone across 76,000 patients, predicted new onset conditions of rare occurrence with relative or, excuse me, a remarkable accuracy in some cases over 90% accuracy of new onset occurrences. So this has really clear significance for the prediction of suicidal behaviors given their rare occurrence in our inability to predict suicide currently. So last, just to end, I believe these examples really show the way in which science could be combined with existing best practices to inform suicide prevention innovation in both risk prediction and, thus, prevention. Due to the inherent challenges that I mentioned within suicide prevention, really, as a field, multidisciplinary collaborations are required to advance. As an economy, a community, and as a leader in technology innovation, among others, California is uniquely positioned to pioneer and advance understanding of suicide in ways that are unparallel to those previously. We do know that any singular approach at this point will be insufficient and unlikely to change current suicide rates in our state, which have remained intractable and have increased in recent years. So this really speaks to the need for a state-driven suicide prevention strategy outlining an action plan that promises to impact suicide on a broad scale. Theresa Ly: Hi everyone, my name it Theresa Ly, I'm a program manager with the California Mental Health Services Authority, and thank you so much for allowing CalMHSA to come today and speak about its statewide suicide prevention initiatives and give you all some context as to what's already happened, and is currently happening, in California regarding statewide suicide prevention efforts. To give you a little bit of background, CalMHSA was created in 2009 as a joint powers authority, implementing programs on behalf of California County Behavioral Health Agencies. The first project, and the biggest project, that CalMHSA was task with launching was the statewide prevention and early intervention project that was funded by one-time set aside MHSA funds through the PEI, the Prevention and Early Intervention bucket. Under the statewide PEI project, there were three initiatives; a stigma reduction initiative, a suicide prevention initiative, and a student mental health initiative. The total budget for the suicide prevention initiative was $40 million initially. The stigma discrimination reduction initiative and the student mental health initiative both had budgets of $60 million, respectively. An evaluator was selected to evaluate the specific programs that were implemented under this larger project, as well as provide some surveillance and broad evaluation of how stigma was being reduced in California, as well as suicides. The primary goals of the statewide PEI project, which still are currently under way, are mental health promotion and mental illness prevention for all Californians. So, today I'm just going to be talking about the suicide prevention initiative that's implemented under the larger statewide PEI project. This initiative was built upon a comprehensive stakeholder project as well as recommendations from the 2008 California Strategic Plan for Suicide Prevention. Under this initiative, CalMHSA launched a public health population-based strategy to address suicide prevention through programs, a multitude of different programs that are multi-faceted, including social marketing efforts, trainings, technical assistance to counties and CPOs to improve their local capacity to respond to suicides, increasing regional and local networks for suicide prevention to get people talking about suicide, creating new best practices, and investing in the expanded reach and capacity of California's crisis hotlines, which Lyn will be talking a little bit more about later on. However, since fiscal year '15-'16, CalMHSA's statewide PEI project has not benefited from the one time set aside funds of those MHSA statewide funds. In fact, the current implementation of the statewide PEI project is implemented solely on the basis of voluntary county funds, so the funding for these projects has drastically increased since fiscal year '15-'16. Because of this reduction in funding, CalMHSA and its Board of Directors, which represent the California County Behavioral Health Agency directors, we were all required to make a very difficult decision, but strategic decisions on where to invest those limited funds so as to have the greatest statewide impact, while also not kind of treading on what counties are already doing to address suicide prevention, so we really wanted to be complementary to local efforts, not kind of supplant what they're already doing. So, given that, CalMHSA has only been able to continue implementing our statewide social marketing campaign called Know The Signs, as well as providing technical assistance and some other programs that I will mention later on. And just to let you know, there has also been a commensurate reduction in state wide activities with the stigma and discrimination reduction initiative as well as the student mental health initiative. So, since its inception six years ago, the Statewide Suicide Prevention Initiative has seen some positive results and I wanted to share some of those outcomes with you all. The statewide social marketing campaign, the suicide prevention social marketing campaign called Know the Signs, is projected to reach over 50% of California households. That was actually data from a few years ago, two years ago. So, I would imagine we have either reached that mark or have exceeded that exposure to California households. This campaign is unique in that it's engaging helpers of those at risk for suicide, so it's not speaking directly to the person who may be experiencing thoughts of suicide. It's really engaging helpers on how do you learn about the warning signs, what are the warning signs, how do you talk to someone effectively, if they are having thoughts of suicide? And then more importantly, how do you find local resources, local, regional, or national resources to help that person that you are concerned about or to help you along in your path of helping someone else? Studies have shown that people who are exposed to this Know the Signs campaign have increased levels of confidence to intervene with someone at risk for suicide. So, if you take that step a little further you can imagine that more Californians are actually equipped to support people at risk for suicide. Furthermore, a panel of suicide prevention messaging experts deemed the Know the Signs campaign to be one of the best suicide prevention campaigns that are currently available and largely adhered to best practices in messaging on suicide prevention. To address youth suicide prevention specifically, CalMHSA invested in the development of a novel program called Directing Change. You might be familiar with Directing Change. A few years ago, youth that participated in the Directing Change actually went around and did some Committee presentations, that was a few years ago. Directing Change engages high school and higher education students to learn about suicide prevention and stigma reductions through the unique lens of film making, and a recent evaluation, a case control evaluation of Directing Change, demonstrated that students who participated in Directing Change had significantly positive, and more importantly, sustained changes in attitudes, knowledge, and behavior compared to students who were not exposed or participated in the Directing Change program. In the area of suicide prevention gatekeeper training, CalMHSA investment in the growth of ASIST and safeTALK, which gatekeeper trainings are trainings for people who are not mental health professionals, your mailman, your teacher, people who are in a position to maybe notice warning signs or changes in behavior. So, ASIST and safeTALK are two large suicide prevention gatekeeper trainings that are available nationally, but the investment in the growth of ASIST and safeTALK trainings in California have catapulted California, actually, to become the number one state in the country with the most number of trainers, so we have a large capacity to address the need for trainings in California. A return on investment analysis demonstrated that the California State government will gain $50 for each $1 invested in ASIST trainings through averted MediCal healthcare costs and increased state tax revenue. And more importantly, from that human perspective, every one year invested in ASIST programs is projected to prevent at least 140 deaths and 3600 suicide attempts. And as a final example, CalMHSA's previous investment in crisis centers in the initial phase of the statewide suicide prevention initiative drastically increased knowledge and awareness of crisis services, as well as expanded the range of services that our crisis hotlines and crisis centers were able to provide. We actually also assisted some new centers and crisis services to become nationally certified and we also helped foster the coordination of activities across crisis lines, all of which resulted in increasing call volumes from all California counties. At the height of its funding and program implementation, CalMHSA was able to serve as a centralizing entity, coordinating statewide suicide preventions and ensuring collaboration and information sharing across a broad swath of agencies. So, as you imagine, from the state level, regional, local, everyone's trying to do something in suicide prevention and we were able to at least try to coordinate some of that. However, with reduced funding to the statewide efforts, CalMHSA has not been able to maintain the centralizing role and it's really had to scale back the scope of its activities and its reach. In the absence of an active statewide entity that also provides direction and leadership for statewide suicide prevention efforts, as well as the outdated, outmoded strategic plan that Anara and Dr. Bernert mentioned, CalMHSA, as well as other local agencies, really struggle to determine a collective and comprehensive path forward, one that is based on data, best practices, and the voices of stakeholders. So, based on this experience, CalMHSA recommends that there be, and I think this really echoes what we've already heard so far, a centralized statewide suicide prevention effort that really should be long term, as these public health efforts really do require a long term sustained investment in order to really see your ultimate outcomes, continued support for our network of suicide prevention crisis hotlines, a new investment in an updated strategic plan for suicide prevention that does include a stakeholder body and allows that stakeholder body to continue to advise on the implementation of statewide programs. And then ultimately, additional funding to implement the new state plan with provisions to evaluate those efforts to inform future efforts as we kind of evolve our statewide efforts for suicide prevention. So, thank you.

The National Suicide Prevention Lifeline is the equivalent of a 911 mental health line. Therefore, statewide suicide prevention funding is critical, since residents in every county in California call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline number. It was launched by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration in 2005, and then Lifeline expanded considerably over the years. It now receives over 1.5 million calls annually. It provides 24/7 Spanish coverage, a veteran's line, crisis chat, follow up services, and a disaster distress help line. All Lifeline members are accredited and adhere to standards and best practices that are based on current research and advances in the field, but the Lifeline is often thought to be funded federally. And it's not. All the lifeline member centers receive about $1,500 a year despite how many calls they receive on the crisis line. So, there is no stable suicide prevention funding that is statewide for California, yet there is widespread use and advertisement of the Lifeline, which really does attest to its importance, and up and down the state, you'll see insurance companies, universities, hospitals, media, social marketing, state and county agencies directing the public to call the Lifeline if they're in crisis. Even Siri, on your iPhone, if you talk to her and say, I think I want to jump off a bridge, she will say, it sounds like you're thinking about suicide, would you like to call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline and press a button to connect you? In California, the demand has increased dramatically, the call volume has tripled in the last eight years, reaching over 130,000 calls. Based on current trends, the Lifeline calls answered in California will increase to over 200,000 in the next five years. Our Spanish calls have increased five fold in the last several years, and these calls represent men and women of all ages and all ethnicities. Didi Hirsch Suicide Prevention Center answers approximately 50% of all the lifeline calls in California, and we're also the backup to the entire state, so when a call is directed to a crisis center, if they have too many calls coming in and they're not able to answer the call, it will roll over to us for us to answer so that those calls stay within California, and we're able to help our callers with local resources. Many of California's lifeline centers have been providing life saving services for decades with minimal funding, but between 2011 and 2015, a coalition of counties agreed to pull MHSA funding for three statewide initiatives, which Theresa spoke of, one of which was suicide prevention. Didi Hirsch was the lead on establishing California's statewide suicide prevention network, and with our crisis consortium, which includes all the other lifeline centers in California, we developed common metrics for collecting data on our callers, services in Korean and Vietnamese language, we increased our chat services, which reaches a high risk population, and we created five new programs that were accepted as best practices in suicide prevention. This doesn't even include all the other life saving work that crisis centers provide in regards to outreach, survivor's support groups, follow up and rescues. So since the funding for these statewide projects ended in 2015, our crisis center consortium of our lifeline centers has worked together to maintain their partnerships. However, services have been cut due to funding, and the suicide rate has not gone down, in fact, it's the highest it's been in 30 years, and we continue to try to work together to advocate for a stable statewide source of funding for suicide prevention. So on behalf of the 10 California lifeline crisis centers, we are respectfully asking for $4.3 million for the state budget fiscal year '17-'18. These grants were intended to increase the number of treatment facilities and diversion programs. And the funding would be used for facility acquisition or renovation, the purchase of land, equipment, and other program startup or expansion costs. Additional the Governor's Budget proposes to eliminate the authority to spend $17 million general fund for the Children's Mental Health Crisis Grant Program, intended to increase the number of facilities providing crisis services to children and youth under the age of 21. Approximately $11 million in Mental Health Services Act funding remains for this program. Additionally, the administration is proposing trailer bill language necessary to effectuate these changes. Given the lower than expected revenue picture, the Governor's Budget proposes to pull back one time spending commitments rather than make reductions to existing and ongoing programs to bring the state's finances back into balance. CHAFA was in the initial stages of program development for both of these grant programs, and the funding remains uncommitted. The Governor's Budget also assumes a $1 million forfeiture of grant funding from an SB 82 project. The 2016 Budget Act reappropriated the balances of the SB 82 appropriation for the purposes of Children's Crisis Services and extended the expenditure period until June 30, 2019. These forfeited funds would have been reappropriated per the 2016 Budget Act. Additionally, the administration does not have a position on the request to extend the encumbrance period for SB 82 funds at this time. However, the administration will evaluate this further, and we can provide technical assistance to your staff as necessary.

[{'start': 0, 'end': 16, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Toby Ewing: Hello, Mr. Chair and members, Toby Ewing with Executive Director of the Mental Health Services Oversight Accountability Commission. So as you saw in the earlier discussion, we are a state oversight agency. We are an independent entity within the executive branch. And do want to kind of want to respond to the general comment about providing an overview about the work that we do and then address the specific issues. So, the commission's a 16 member Commission, 12 appointees of the Governor, and then 4 sitting members, include a Senator, Assembly Member, two constitutional officers, the Attorney General, and the state Superintendent of construction. And we have a variety of roles, there are some broad general roles including research and evaluation work. And in that work we have two sides. One side is very traditional, almost academic data analysis and in that work what we're really trying to do is two fold. One is some classic evaluation work where we contract, usually with University researchers to look at specific aspects of mental health services act dollars and how they're funded. But more broadly, at how the counties are using the broad resources that are available to them to address outcomes. And so we have work underway to better understand what are called full service partnerships, which are our highest level of care that we provide in California, designed to be whatever it takes approaches, we don't have the tools yet, as sort of a community of practitioners to truly understand what those are. And so, the first stages of the work that we're doing now are really to understand how to define what a full service partnership, so we can compare across different approaches that counties are taking. The real challenge we have in California is that our mental health system is better described as a mosaic of services rather than a discrete system, right? No two counties are alike, no two strategies are alike. Our research budget is about $2.7 million, and so we make very high use of that. But it's not enough money to do this state level analysis of all services. So we really try to strategically allocate those dollars to really understand the foundational pieces like what is a full service partnership, so that we can move towards how effective are those services and for whom? There's other work that we're doing that is specific to what we call policy research projects. So, reversion is an example where the Commission identifies a challenge and directs the staff to roll up our sleeves and do the homework. And actually come up with an action agenda to try to improve that practice. We have work under way on what's called the issue resolution process, which is a grievance process that was established by the Department of Mental Health. We see some fundamental challenges there in terms of how that process is working. It's supposed to be designed as a strategy for a consumer or a family member to raise a concern about the quality of their care or the access to services that they have or have not received. And then use that process at the county level and then escalate it to the state level to try to find some relief. We've got a project on school mental health, so we're looking at strategies to improve educational outcomes. One of the explicit goals in Mental Health Services Act is to reduce school failure. We're trying to understand what does that mean? What does that look like? What are model programs? What's in place today? Where are their gaps? We have another project on reducing criminal justice involvement. That's actually an explicit goal in the act. And so we've spent the last year or so looking at strategies that are in place today in California, strategies around the country identifying gaps. When we do this work, we do Advisory Committee meetings, we do site visits, we do community forums, focus groups. For the criminal justice work, we co-hosted with the White House a forum on data driven justice. We led a delegation of California officials, counties, and state level officials to see model programs in other states. The feds funded our two state site visit for about 10 of us to go visit these model programs. All of that work is designed to come back to the Legislature and the Governor with a set of recommendations with the hope that it would result in change in policy or practice or budget or strategy, whatever the problem happens to be, right. I mentioned the school mental health and the criminal justice and mental health projects specifically because in addition to those issues, the act also identifies reducing unemployment, reducing homelessness, reducing out of home placements in foster care, a number of other explicit goals for mental health services dollars. We're working with our other state agencies to link data, mental health data and criminal justice data, for example, to see if we can map criminal justice involvement rates by county, so that we can begin to use that information to shape policy and programmatic decisions. We have legislation moving through the process right now to give us access to quarterly wage data for purposes of actually mapping unemployment rates. We're working with the Department of Education to look at school failure rates or what school success would look like. All of that is designed, part of our broad research strategy to understand what's in place, what's working, and how we can use information to guide decisions moving forward, mostly around what can we learn about what works and for whom? It's rare that an intervention always works for all people. It's more likely that we need to tailor our strategies around unique needs of individuals and their families. And what we really want is to build out the mental health system as a learning system, right, where there's the continuous improvement across the counties, among the counties with the state playing a facilitating role to support that learning over time. So in addition, that research takes up probably half of what we do. We have some other functions. We allocate grant dollars to counties through a program called triage that was created through SB 82 a few years ago. These are dollars that we allocate for reducing involvement with jails and emergency rooms. Quite often, what counties do with those funds is hire outreach workers or peer navigators who help people access services so they're not getting stuck in an emergency room or in a jail, rather than accessing services. We have stakeholder contracts. We provide funds through the budget process that you provide to us to make sure that consumers and family members and others, veterans, people working on disparities, the LGBTQ population, consumers, parents with children, parents of adults, have funds to be able to advocate effectively at the state level and locally. As somebody commented, the community consultation process is embedded in the act. And it's important that people with the experience can guide decisions, and so we provide resources to help them do that. Lastly, I would say that the next sort of largest program is innovation funds. There's about $100 million a year for innovation funds under the law as it's set up today. Counties have those funds in their bank account. They can't spend the dollars unless the Commission gives them authority, and so we review county plans. We're actually working with the counties, with the innovation sector in California to really think differently about innovation. What does it look like, what does it mean? How do we scale innovation back to that learning community strategy? The goal of these dollars is really promote transformational change. And we're just beginning to really engage our private sector partners about how to think about innovation. How can the public sector be more innovative and how do we do that in ways that shapes decisions over time? Kind of my broad overview with some discussion of the master plan. The master plan really was sort of a guide, as opposed to sort of explicit recipes of do this, do A, then B, then C, then D. It's more of a framework. We use that to sort of frame out the decisions that the Commission makes about how we allocate resource dollars. It was a five year master plan. We're starting to transition away from that broad framework, in part, because we're starting the link the data research with the policy research. In part, because we think it would be more productive to give you guidance not just on what's happening, but how to change the direction of those practices over time. And so, we want to link the analysis of the data with the policy and programmatic analysis. So we're just not telling you what's broken, but giving you a game plan for how to improve that. And so we actually think that we'll phase out some of the traditional master plan as we focus more on individual topics like crisis services and other parts I neglected to mention or reversion. And so that we can really use our ability to do the homework and put that before you and the administration but also the public to really shape the decisions that people are making around mental health. One last thing, I did mention the fiscal transparency tool. There are two other components to that that we're working on. The second one is to map services. And the third one is to map outcomes, and it's that data linking that allow us to map outcomes. And the goal is to actually empower the public to be informed about what's happening in California around mental health and to come to those community meetings and engage their county leaders with much more accessible information on what's in place today, what's working, what's not working, and to have the tools that they need to be effective advocates for transformational change. Happy to answer any questions you might have.

[{'start': 32, 'end': 44, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Stacie Walker: Good evening Chairman Arambula and Subcommittee Members. My name is Stacie Walker, I'm the Deputy Director of the Healthcare Workforce Development Division at the Office of Statewide Health Planning and Development. The Mental Health Services Act provided nearly $445 million over 10 years to support mental health workforce and education training programs, or WET programs. $210 million of those funds went directly to the counties for county-administered programs. OSHPD has no oversight over the county programs. The remaining $234.5 million went to support two state-administered WET five-year plans. The first five-year plan ran between 2008 and 2013. It received an allocation of $120 million and was administered through the Department of Mental Health Care. OSHPD was not involved in the administration of that program. The second five year plan is running between 2014 and will end in 2019. It received an allocation of $115 million and OSHPD is administering that five year plan. My comments today are limited to the state programs administered by OSHPD. The second five-year plan was developed through input from stakeholders as well as a comprehensive needs assessment of the public mental health system. The plan includes programs that incentivize recruitment and retention of mental healthcare workers into the public mental health system. It expands the training and education capacity within the public mental health system and it supports regional collaboration on strategies to address local issues. Funding for OSHPD WET programs will end in fiscal year 2017-18. However, our contracts will continue until the end of fiscal year '18-'19. Therefore, the outcome information I'm going to present you with today about our programs is incomplete. Thus far, our programs have encouraged individuals to pursue careers as mental health professionals, exposing more than 15,000 students to mental health careers and providing 90 students with internships in the public mental health system. We've supported more than 6,700 mental health professionals by providing up to $10,000 in loan repayment in exchange for working up to 12 months in the public mental health system. We've also provided more than 620 stipends of up to $21,000 to mental health professionals in exchange for working in the public health system for 12 months. OSHPD does not track the individuals past their 12 month service requirement. We've also increased the number of residency and training slots, providing rotations in the public mental health system, training at least an additional 64 clinical psychiatrists and 68 psychiatric nurse practitioners. Our programs have supported the training and job placement of more then 800 individuals with lived experienced in the public mental health system and we've supported regional coordination of strategic initiatives designed to increase the capacity of the public mental health system. OSHPD does not evaluate the mental health workforce in total. Therefore, we have no projections of what the future workforce might look like. We do, however, collect self-reported data about our programs. While we have data for the majority of our participants, about two-thirds of them, we do not have information for all of them. Of those who reported race or ethnicity, approximately 67% were from under-represented minority groups, and approximately 53% speak a language other than English. OSHPD will conduct a program review after all funds are expended and it should be available after July 2019. The review may prove valuable to future policy discussions about the public mental health workforce. Beyond the Mental Health Services Act funding for WET, OSHPD has several programs that provides support to mental health providers. However, they do not exclusively target providers in the public mental health system. So this concludes my overview of the state-administered WET programs.

Cardinal Health has long promoted the benefits of community pharmacy, remote dispensing pharmacies that we're talking about here today are one way which the pharmacist can further their reach to provide health care services in really medically under served areas. Remote dispensing pharmacies can improve patient's medication adherence, which reduces medical costs. It can provide local access to a pharmacist in communities that often lack any form of a healthcare provider. In order to further the goal of increasing access to both dispensing and pharmaceutical care services, AB 401 would allow the establishment of these remote dispensing site pharmacies in medically underserved areas. These remote dispensing site pharmacies would be licensed by the California board of Pharmacy. The remote dispensing pharmacies would be staffed as we said by one licensed and certified pharmacy technician under the supervision of a pharmacist at a remote location than electronically. Direct supervision does not require the physical presence of the pharmacist on site which is important in these remote areas because economically it is not feasible sometimes to place a pharmacist those areas. Access to prescription medications and pharmacist consultations in settings of a convenient to California citizens will improve health care for your constituents. We are committed to supporting the thoughtful and effective legislation that aligns with our mission of making healthcare accessible and more effective. We are in support of AB 401, thank you again for the opportunity and I can welcome any questions you might have.

Tom Jefferson: Good morning, everybody. My name is Tom Jefferson, and that is my real name. I'm a biologist who's been studying marine mammals for about 34 years, and I'm the Director of the nonprofit organization, Viva Vaquita. A little bit more background on the Vaquita, in addition to what you've already heard. It is one of only seven species of porpoises in the world, so it's not a very big family that it's a member of. And losing a species is a very, very big loss of biological diversity. The species was only scientifically discovered about 60 years ago, so we don't really know much about its biology. It's found only in a very small area of the Northern Gulf of California and Mexico. And it's sometimes called the Panda of the Sea, and that's in relation to both its appearance as well as its very endangered status. It is, without a doubt, the most endangered species of marine mammal in the world, quite by a long shot, actually. A little bit about the status of the population. The species has already thought to be rare when it was discovered back in 1958, and it was primarily due to entanglement in gill nets. For the last few decades, shrimp gill nets have been the major culprit. Currently, by-catch and gill nets set illegally for a large fish called the Totoaba are the main threat to the species. And Corvina fishing which uses gill nets, is also a threat. The Vaquita population declined from about 600 in 1997 down to about 30 in late 2016. And it's continued to decline, and we currently estimate numbers maybe as low as 25 or 26 individuals. And it's declining at about 50% per year, which means next year, there will probably only be 13 or so. A couple of recent developments. Mexico has established a two year ban on gill nets in 2015, but that has not been effectively enforced and it's set to expire later this month. There's currently massive illegal fishing going on in the Northern Gulf of California where the Vaquita lives. Recently, four or five Vaquitas have been found dead, including an aborted fetus. Enforcement appears to be minimal right now, giving poachers free reign. And finally, and I emphasize this, that situation for the Vaquita is currently very, very desperate, as desperate as it can be. And the species is on the very verge of extinction. Thank you.

Zak Smith: Thank you, Chair and Members of the Committee. My name is Zak Smith for the Natural Resources Defense Council. Getting the use of gillnets out of, from their habitat. The necessity of transitioning away from the use of all gill nets in the region by all fisheries, including the Corvina Fishery, which you may hear about today, is the reasoned conclusion of the International Committee for the Recovery of the Vaquita. This preeminent group of scientific experts, people at the top of their field in biology and fisheries management from the United States, the UK, Canada, and Mexico, including people from the Mexico's National Institute of Ecology and Climate Change, have concluded that gill nets must be banned entirely from this area. With respect to the Corvina Fishery, this is what SERVA said in its most recent report, that's the International Committee for Recovery. They state, they reiterated their recommendation that the gill net ban include the nets used in the Corvina Fishery. The existence of this fishery as an exception to the gill net ban reduces the efficiency of enforcement, and facilitates the illegal fishery for Totoaba during the Corvina season. I urge the members of this Committee to align themselves with the experts who have been working on Vaquita recovery for decades. AB 1151 reflects their conclusion that the time for half measures, incremental steps, carving out harmful exceptions has passed. If the Vaquita are going to be here in three years, comprehensive measures must be taken now. SERVA, the United States, Mexican officials, have dedicated time and substantial resources to the development of alternative gear and market development. And they will continue to do so, even this year, when the Upper Gulf Corvina Fishery was effectively canceled for not complying with Mexican environmental regulations. The Mexican government has offered compensation to fishermen at double the price that they were achieving on the market for the last two years. There is no silver bullet to save the Vaquita, I wish there was. People are working every angle, reducing Chinese demand for Totoaba, busting smugglers, tackling corruption, the live capture of Vaquita. They're using all of the laws that are available to them. And there's just a limit as to what these laws can do, such as the Endangered Species Act and others that can't reach as far into Mexico for good reason. But AB 1151 is part of this overall effort, and it supports Mexican initiatives to enforce its rules and realign the fisheries in the Upper Gulf. Doing, otherwise, will inadvertently support the status quo and doom the Vaquita. Thank you very much, and thank you to Assemblymember Gloria.

Over the past few decades, there's been a slow creep in a succession of authority from the Legislature to state agencies. And we've also seen, as a result, that sometimes agencies go beyond the authority that the Legislature has intended when they created the statute granting them their authority. As a result, this bill would correct that creep and restore the Legislature to its proper role in writing oversight for California. So we ask for your aye vote.

And it's been studied so many times, the security community of the United States is in, essentially, unanimous agreement that the transmission of voted ballots over the Internet is an extreme danger.  It's a national security issue and we really time and again have recommended against it. One of the problems with it is, of course, that when you transmit a ballot electronically, you don't have a hard copy record of the original voters intent, so there's no way to meaningfully audit ballots that are transmitted that way. But the thing that I'm even more concerned about is that of all of the forms of Internet voting, all of which are dangerous, email voting is I'm afraid the most dangerous.  Not all forms of Internet voting are created equal. I have provided for the Committee a letter from Verified Voting describing its position. I've also given the sergeant a letter from myself describing all of the technical concerns that we have, security concerns with Internet voting, and with email voting in particular, because email is not encrypted for transmission. It's transmitted essentially in the clear. Email is relayed from point to point several times between the voter and the county. There's no way to avoid that, it's transmitted in the clear. Anyone who controls one of those, any IT person who controls one of those intermediate points can read your ballot, can modify your ballot, can drop your ballot. Email is just extremely dangerous. Email is 40 years old. It was designed long before the technology, the security technologies that we have in other parts of the Internet today.  I'm especially concerned about email now because it's a national security issue. National enemies of the United States have demonstrated the capability and willingness to hack our email and in an election context, certainly the Russians in the current most recent election, but before that the North Koreans and basically every major power, foreign and domestic, have the capability to hack email. We just do not want ballots, I think, to be subject to that. We want to minimize, not encourage, the electronic transmission of ballots. [{'start': 25, 'end': 37, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Natalie Kofel: Thank you, good morning, my name is Natalie Kofel and I am here representing the State Building and Construction Trades Council. You've heard from Assembly Member Medina about what AB 890 does and why it is so vitally important. I would like to talk to you about what AB 890 does not do. It does not rewrite the California constitution. It does not violate the existing constitution. And it does not outlaw all initiatives. In fact, most initiatives would not actually be affected by AB 890 because they would not be considered projects under CEQA. The term project is well defined under existing law and the examples that opponents of this bill have put forward most certainly would not be considered projects under CEQA. While CEQA requires agencies to consider indirect environmental impact, those impacts must be reasonably forseeable, and they cannot be speculative. In addition, CEQA is only concerned with physical impacts to the environment, it is not concerned with economic or social impacts. That is why you would not see an environmental impact report for a minimum wage ordinance, for example. Additionally CEQA has numerous exceptions that would keep certain projects, or certain initiatives from being considered projects. That includes exemptions for government fiscal activities, and for environmentally beneficial projects. So you would not see a soda tax analyzed in a CEQA document. The Legislature has the constitutional authority to limit the initiative process when there's a matter of statewide concern. And the Legislature has already declared that the environment is a matter of statewide concern in Public Resources Code Section 21000. Accordingly because this is a matter of statewide concern, the Legislature could actually preempt all local legislation on this matter. Or it could exclusively delegate to local governments to legislate on this matter. AB 890 does neither, it actually preserves the local initiative process to the greatest extent possible, while delegating authority to local agencies when there is a potentially significant environmental impact. So those lead agencies can comply with their substantive mandate under CEQA and impose mitigation and consider feasible alternatives thank you.

Cassie Gilson: Good morning, Mr. Chair and members. Cassie Gilson on behalf of the California Building Industry Association, respectfully in opposition to the bill. As noted in the analysis, this bill is a significant departure from existing local initiative procedures developed by this Legislature, and it enacts a massive shift of power away from the local electorate to local elected officials. And it does this by barring virtually all local initiatives from going to the ballot. And instead, requires them to be reviewed under CEQA, and their fate determined by the elected officials at the local government level. It does this by amending the definition of project under CEQA. So it actually goes into the CEQA statute, takes the definition of project and adds initiative to that, and then bars any initiatives from going to the ballot that result in a direct physical change in the environment or a reasonably foreseeable indirect change in the environment. I'm a CEQA lawyer, not an elections person, but I suspect it would be quite difficult to find a local planning department that's willing to ensure that an initiative proposal will not result in a reasonably foreseeable indirect impact in the environment, given the way the CEQA law looks at indirect impacts today. The kinds of initiatives that we read this measure to bar include Ventura County's open space and Aglian preservation, measure E from last November, Richmond's measure L which would establish rent control. LA's measure JJJ, which imposed minimum affordable housing requirements, and the idea of being, we talked a little bit like would a minimum wage increase initiative, trigger this bill? If you raise the minimum wage in your community, then you have people coming to the community to get jobs, there's different traffic patterns. Under CEQA today, we look at all of those things. If these measures were done by legislation at the local level, you would do a CEQA initiative around them. And probably one of the clearest examples of this is the discussion we've been having statewide about plastic bag bans and whether you think well, that shouldn't trigger CEQA. But of course, there's been great debate about it, and it does. Even those initiatives where a planner's willing to say, this does not result in an indirect change in the environment are going to end up being held up by litigation because we're talking about this in the initiative context. People go to initiatives because proposals are controversial, and our experience and CEQA is that controversial projects get litigated. So, even a project that the planners say, okay, this can go to the ballot, the likelihood is that someone's going to sue at that time. So then that proposal is caught up in litigation for 6 months, 12 months, 18 months. I mean depending on the proposal, who knows whether it's right at that time when that litigation is concluded and it could actually go to the ballot. Fundamentally, AB 890 is also unconstitutional. So, not surprisingly, the Constitution really jealously guards a citizen's right to initiative. And, it says that there's a very narrow category of things in which this Legislature can designate local governments to be their sole agent, and those are on issues of statewide importance. Local land use is fundamentally not an issue of statewide importance. To speak to the concern that the author and the proponents raise, which i think is legitimate, which is that if you have, for the logistic center, that trucks are coming in. And obviously, those emissions don't end at the jurisdictional boundaries. I think a court would find that that's why the state has the Clean Air Act. And the purpose of California's suite of environmental laws, the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, other things, are to require analysis and mitigation and permits for projects regardless of how they're approved. That would certainly be the case here. Finally, the implication of 890 is that there would be no environmental mitigation required of projects that are approved by local initiative. And of course that's not the case again, because we have a suite of world renowned environmental laws. Endangered species, clean water, clean air hazards, all of those permits would need to be pulled, and all of their mitigation obligations would need to be complied with. So for those reasons, we respectfully oppose. Thank you.

As my colleague mentioned, AB 890 is a significant departure from current law, as it requires a legislative body to exercise authority to determine whether a proposed initiative is suitable for the ballot, and transfers power to the state over the local land use and initiative process. Moreover, our city clerks, city attorneys, and city planners all have expressed multiple concerns with this measure, such as ensuring elections are conducted in a timely manner, workload concerns around extensive and unnecessary CEQA reviews, as well as the cost and time associated with well documented and protracted CEQA litigation from stakeholders who either support or oppose a potential land use project. AB 890 fails to recognize that a stringent environmental review is a well established part of the local land use permitting process. If there are shortcomings in existing law, and practice relevant to environmental review. The permitting process should be the focus around this measure. And not a process that undermines local governments and public engagement. And finally, at the time, the Legislature and the administration publically advocates for and has placed a significant focus on addressing the states housing and homelessness crisis. AB 890 seems to run counterintuitive to this important policy objective with an unprecedented expansion of local elections duties, as well as increased workloads to every department that overseas land use planning and environmental reviews. Increasing staff costs and work time. For those reasons we oppose.

Sarah Newkirk: Chair Garcia and Members of the Committee my name is Sarah Newkirk. And I'm the Coastal Program Director with the Nature Conservancy. The Nature Conservancy's Coastal Program is committed to maintaining California's beaches and natural coastal habitat for wildlife. And people into the future, even in the face of sea level rise. These areas are important recreational and economic assets that belong to all Californians. Armoring including sea walls, threatens the long term existence of beaches by exasperating erosion. And preventing the beach from moving inland with sea level rise. Sea walls fix the shore in place leading to the loss of the public beach in front of the sea wall. We recognize that people need to protect their homes and property from coastal hazards. And although coastal armoring is not the only way to do this, it is clearly a part of the overall formula for protection of coastal communities. And is certainly appropriate in some places. For that reason this bill does not ban armoring. In fact, according to the Coastal Commission the bill largely codifies and clarifies existing permitting Permitting practice. A coastal property owner can still apply to install a sea wall. And assuming that he or she meets the Coastal Acts requirements relating to access and natural resource protection. He or she should expect to get the permit. We also recognize that emergencies arise unexpectedly. The call for the use of sea walls to protect property. And that their environmental review is not always possible under this circumstances. That's why the bill maintains the ability of property owner to apply for an emergency permit. It simply calls for environmental review to occur after the emergency is passed. As I said before, sea walls are not the only option for providing protection for coastal homes, although they tend to be the first and sometimes only option that people consider. We're learning more and more about using nature to protect people, and there's a whole category of coastal natural infrastructure that can be used in this way. For example in Ormond Beach where the Nature Conservancy owns a lot of wetland property we're learning how to use those wetlands to protect the Community of Oxnard nearby. Beach nourishment is another example of a non wall approach to coastal protection. In sum AB 1129 is an important tool that can help California prepare for sea level rise and climate change. It will also help to maintain our legacy of preserving beaches and coastal habitats for generations to come. I'm happy to answer any questions and we respectfully ask for your aye vote.

It receives less than 5% of the state's annual investment in state and customer funded energy efficiency programs every year. So AB 1088 takes the following steps to improve the accessibility of these available programs and to make sure that multi-family households are not left behind. It directs the Energy Commission to adopt regulations to streamline and coordinate the enrollment in these programs and to establish a statewide website and application for easy access to available programs.
