This bill builds upon last year's AB 2029 by Assembly members Daly and Gordon which made changes to the forest fire prevention pilot program. The pilot provides an exemption from the preparation of a timber harvesting plan only. The exemption acts as a ministerial permit whereby thinning can occur under specified and limited circumstances for the purpose of reducing fuels from the Forest. All the forest practice rules still apply and CALFIRE is still responsible for reviewing the work afterwards to ensure complete compliance. When AB 2029 came before this Committee last year it, extended the sunset date of its pilot until 2021, expanded the diameter of trees that can be removed from 20 to 26 inches and allow the construction of temporary roads up to 600 feet. The then chair of the Committee requested an additional amendment to limit the road construction to slopes of 40% or less. With that AB 2029 passed this community unanimously. The bill passed the Assembly floor in the Senate Natural Resources Committee with no no votes. However, by the time the bill got to Senate Appropriations Committee, CAL FIRE indicated they opposed the provision relating to the construction of roads. We offered to work to resolve their concerns with amendments but the roads provision was removed during Senate Appropriations Committee. Ultimately, AB 2029 passed without a single no vote and was signed by the Governor. We began conversations with CAL FIRE this year by expressing our members' concern that the inability to construct the roads was the single most constraining element to this exemption. CAL FIRE agreed to act as the arbitrator between us and the other departments impacted by this exemption. Before the bill was introduced, CAL FIRE gave us a list of concerns relative to the construction of temporary roads. As a result, we drafted a bill with additional protections from those in AB 2029. We met with CAL FIRE on a second occasion, where they expressed additional concerns. In response, we amended the bill on April 4th. In all, there are 17 additional protections in AB 425 that were not in AB 2029. While CalFire and the other departments do not have an official position yet on this bill, we remain committed to addressing any remaining concerns from any other departments weighing in on this bill. Our goal is not to have a bill passed by the Legislator only to have it vetoed by the Governor. Having the ability to construct these small spur roads and landings is critical to being able to thin our forests. And we also want to ensure that there are no negative impacts to wildlife, soil or water. The bill enjoys a broad range of support including local governments, insurance industry, firefighters, and the forestry sector. we ask for your aye vote.

This exemptions allows the thinning to reduce horizontal and vertical fuel continuity, both of which are significant factors in the intensity and rate of spread in a wildland fire. A temporary road is just that, temporary. Upon completion of use, temporary roads are required to be abandoned, meaning they be removed from the permanent roads network. In addition, maintenance-free drainages will be installed and often limbs and branches are placed on the road to help with additional stability. All of these measures, plus the numerous requirements within the forest practice rules reduce the potential for erosion and environmental impacts to levels of insignificance. Although this is a ministerial permit in a streamline process make no mistake, all activities comply with the stringent forest practice rules overseen by a state licensed forester like myself, and inspected by a Department of forestry and fire protection inspector, whom is also a state licensed forester to ensure that no negative impacts occur from these operations. The cost of not doing thinning projects is increased damage to cultural and natural resources, higher suppression costs, degraded air quality, lots of revenue to communities, destruction of homes, increase risk to firefighters and public safety. All of which are costs we cannot afford. The addition of temporary roads makes this exemption a much more effective tool for foresters to utilize, and enables us to create healthy forests, which are more resilient to drought, insects and disease, and catastrophic wildfire.

[{'start': 15, 'end': 25, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Kelly Browning: Good afternoon, Mr. Chair, Mr. Vice Chair and members. My name is Dr. Kelly Browning, I'm the Executive Director of Impact Teen Drivers, a nonprofit organization dedicated to stopping the number one killer of teens in America, which are preventable car crashes. In California alone we lose roughly eight school buses filled with teens every single year to preventable crashes. Across California and the nation, Impact Teen Drivers works with first responders, educators, and health professionals to provide education on how to stop this number one killer. Excuse me. We provide very specific strategies about the decisions and choices that both teens and their parents can make to help keep themselves safe behind the wheel, whether as a driver or as a passenger. An important part of our evidence-based curriculum is educating teens, parents and others about graduated driver licensing or GDL laws. GDL involves a three-tiered system of licensing in which novice drivers gain experience before being exposed to the highest risk situations of nighttime driving and driving with teen passengers. It's an evidence-based strategy that has proven to reduce teen driving fatalities by 40 to 60% across the US. The first chart in front of you that was provided shows a reduction in crash rates for California 18 year olds over a three year time period that went through the graduated driver's licensing system in California. That would be the red and the green lines, versus those who avoided the graduated California driver's licensing system, which is the blue line. This was a 10% sample of California licensed drivers of roughly 1.1 million people. California GDL laws clearly work. Teen drivers who successfully go through the graduated driver licensing programs are 45% less likely to cause a crash than older novice teen drivers who did not go through the GDL. AB 63 addresses a deficiency in California's otherwise successful GDL law. California's current GDL program ends at 18, leaving new teen drivers ages 18 to 20 without the benefits of the GDL program. The second chart that you see reinforces why it's so important to extend the current GDL program through the age of 20. California novice drivers ages 18 to 20 have higher fatality and serious injury rate than all other novice drivers, regardless of the age. GDL does not prevent teens from getting a driver's license. The three step program allows teen drivers to gain training and experience on the road, while minimizing those highest risk situations, before they can obtain an unrestricted license. Exemptions already exist in the current law to allow teens the flexibility to attend school functions, work, and help their families when no other options are available. I thank Assemblymember Frazier and his staff for their important and life saving work on the issue of extending graduated driver licensing for young novice drivers on our roadways, for my kids, for your kids, and for really all of us. I respectfully ask for an aye vote, thank you.

Wendy Reilly: Thank you. My name is Wendy Reilly I represent HID Global, manage government affairs at HID Global. HID Global manufactures secure identity credentials, including identity documents and digital credentials. He did a wonderful job laying out the bill, and I don't want to repeat what he said. But I think the most important thing that I would have to add is over the past couple years, HID's been working with stakeholders, privacy groups, citizens, law enforcement, federal authorities, and state licensing authorities. Citizens are concerned about the privacy of their personal information, they'll want to use your mobile drivers licenses for the same reason they use your physical drivers licenses. And it's important to mention that the physical driver's license will exist alongside a mobile driver's license for the foreseeable future. A driver's license built in a secure platform, will give citizens more control over their personal information, allowing them to choose when and with whom they share their information, and as importantly how much information they share. Law enforcement also has a compelling stake in the adoption of mobile driver's license. And we've Learned that police officers need to trust and authenticate an identity credential, in diverse and sometimes potentially dangerous situations. When appropriate, a secure mobile driver's license platform would allow the authentication of a person's ID from a safe distance by using Bluetooth technology, to give officers more time to determine if a traffic stop is routine, or if it's more complex. In our discussion with stakeholders four keys concerns surfaced, privacy, security, safety and compliance with the Real ID Act. Privacy emerged as the number one major consideration, citizens want to know that their personal information is safe, and state licensing authorities want to know that they're chosen mobile DL solution will protect a citizen's privacy. Such a solution must consider the Fair Information Practice Principles, which include transparency, individual participation, also know as Choice, purpose specification, data minimization, use limitation, data quality and integrity, security and accountability and auditing. Many of these principles must be implemented by the DL issuing authority, but that the underlying technology platform should enable those authorities to practice these principles. In conclusion, at the heart of our mobile driver's license solution concept, is the core value of freedom. That citizens have the choice to opt for a mobile driver's license, that citizens control who sees their information, and that citizens control what information is seen. And a citizen must not have to hand over their smartphone for a credential to be authenticated. Once again, I'd like to express my gratitude for the opportunity to testify, and thank you very much.

Only 5 to 12% of commuters will experience a travel time improvement of 2.5 minutes, that's after billions of dollars. The current EIR process asks the flawed question, how do we move more cars from point a to point b, from a southern stop to the northern stop? Caltrans has already acknowledged building more lanes is not the solution to traffic congestion. The tunnel alternative would create induced demand which would not reduce congestion, but simply shift congestion to other areas from one F fail-rated freeway to another, creating more tunnelling bottlenecks at off ramps and portals. Local voters have already demonstrated that there is no public support for the tunnel alternative when they passed the new sales tax measure Measure M, which included specific language to exclude funding for the 710 tunnel alternative. The San Gabriel Valley Council of Governments removed the project from their list of priorities for Measure M. The Southern California Association of Governments has called the tunnel alternative the worst case scenario in the 2016 Regional Transportation Plan. The tunnel alternative may have the largest construction cost, and therefore will generate temporary construction jobs. However, the alternative that provides the greatest number of long term jobs is the Light Rail alternative according to the EIR. I ask for your leadership and your support to help us move past, into the future, into 20th century solutions. And the reason for that was the court ultimately found that the State of California had to reduce their prison population by approximately 40,000 inmates, through the course of prison reforms and prison changes, and we were simply a part of that process, we were not the answer to that process by any means, we were part of that process, and we were proud of that fact. So in our practice what we've seen is that the petition process itself can actually serve as a motivation for people trying to get their life together. We counsel them that they may need to return and complete a class. They may need to enroll in school. Perhaps they need to excel at the workplace so they can provide certain letters to the court. The court will be looking at a series of letters to show that the individual has in fact achieved sufficient rehabilitation to have that criminal record removed. So again, this is a measure that will promote public safety in encouraging people to really get their lives together. It is something that an individual has to earn and we ask this Committee to provide this opportunity for people who are looking to change their life and also close a chapter of their prior history, thank you.

[{'start': 68, 'end': 84, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Jeff Rubin: Jeff Rubin on behalf of the California District Attorney Association, up until a few years ago, it was routine for warrantless blood draws to take place. Then, the United States Supreme Court in McNealy said you cannot justify a warrantless blood draw based solely on search circumstances. That was one of the exceptions to the normal requirement that we get a warrant to conduct any kind of search. Then last year, in Burchfield, the court said you couldn't justify a blood test under the Search Incident to Arrest exception which is another exception to the warrant requirement. And it also addressed the implied consent laws. Previously, we've been able to justify both a breath test as well as a blood test under the implied consent law. But Burchfield said look, we heartily approve of requiring breath tests to be taken under the implied consent law. And if someone refuses to do it, you can impose administrative penalties and you can also impose criminal penalties. What they said was, when it comes to blood, while you can potentially impose administrative penalties for someone who refuses to take a blood test, you cannot impose criminal penalties. Well right now, under our laws, as they're currently written, You can impose a penalty, either a criminal penalty or a fine for refusing to take a blood test. But that's not allowed anymore under Burchfield. So what this new law does is comports what we have to do, comports the statute, with the constitutional requirements. Now, Blood tests are better than breath tests. Blood tests are a direct evidence of the level of alcohol in the blood. And breath tests are a more indirect level. So because of this law, we are going to see fewer blood tests and that's not good because the more accurate the blood test, the better it is in terms of prosecuting individuals who are guilty and exonerating individuals who are not guilty. But what our bill does is, even though it follows what Burchfield requires, it also imposes an additional way of getting people to take breath tests. Now, breath tests are not going to show people who are driving under the influence of drugs. But at least now, under this new bill, someone will not benefit by refusing to take a breath test in juxtaposition to someone who agrees to take a breath test. So this is a reasonable and constitutional means of addressing the issue created by Burchfield and we would urge your support. Thank you.

Ignacio Hernandez: Good morning, Mr. Chair and members. Ignacio Hernandez on behalf of the California Attorneys for Criminal Justice, statewide Association for criminal defense attorneys. We are opposed to the measure. I want to thank the author of the bill for meeting with me and having a discussion. As always, it's always very beneficial. And I think, in many ways, we wholeheartedly agree with the testimony of the supporters of this bill. This is in response to the Supreme Court decision in Birchfield. You do have to eliminate the criminal penalties for refusal to take a blood test. And most importantly, the Birchfield court decided that law enforcement cannot draw blood, even after a lawful arrest, absent a warrant. You must have a warrant to draw blood. That was the fundamental anchor of the Birchfield decision, we agree. What this bill is doing is saying every individual who gets a license in California must waive that protection. Must waive the warrant requirement as a condition of having the privilege to have a driver's license in California. Now that, to be fair, up until Birchfield, we did require every driver to give permission to give a blood draw, breath or blood. I'm focusing on blood, that's the main issue. So, you did have to give permission. The difference being, as soon as the Birchfield decision came about, it's not permission anymore. It's waiving a constitutional protection under the Fourth Amendment, that is what this bill is doing. We do agree with the first part of it. But their resolution to getting blood, as they stated, they think blood is better, is to say, if you're going to drive in California with a license, you have to waive your right to a warrant. We don't ask a driver to waive Fourth Amendment protections to search a car. We don't ask drivers to waive the warrant requirement for cell phone, which I know all of you dealt with in the last couple of years. We don't ask for constitutional waivers to drive on our roads in California. We think the bill goes too far in that regard. Last thing, In Supreme Court decision, they took evidence that there are more refusals of blood when the penalties are only administrative. This bill, rightfully so, changes the penalties to administrative, which means we can expect more refusals of blood tests. Which means more situations where an officer wants a blood draw, and the driver does not want a blood draw. That is going to be a problem. Especially because in North Dakota, which is where this case originated, there is a law in that state that says there cannot be a forcible blood draw by a police officer unless it's a DUI with injury or death. We don't have that statute in California. We are concerned that individuals may not understand it. They waive their right to a warrant, the warrant requirement when they get the driver's license. And on the scene of the DUI they're going to say no, no, I don't want blood. And the officer's going to say, well, by having a driver's license you have waived that warrant requirement. You have waived your protection of the Fourth Amendment, and we're going to take blood from you. At that juncture, we're going to run into forcible blood draws, and we are extremely concerned about that. We think there are other ways to deal with this. We think breath is fine for DUI alcohol, and that should be the law in California. Not ask drivers to waive any constitutional rights simply for the right to drive on our roads. For those reason we are opposed, happy to try to fix the bill, and, like I said, I do appreciate the conversation with the author.

We don't ask for constitutional waivers to drive on our roads in California. We think the bill goes too far in that regard. Last thing, in the Supreme Court decision, they took evidence that there are more refusals of blood, when the penalties are only administrative. This bill, rightfully so changes the penalties to administrative which means we can expect more refusals of blood test. Which means more situations where an officer wants a blood draw and the driver does not want a blood draw. That is going to be our problem especially because in North Dakota, which is where this case originated. There is a law in that state that says, there cannot be a forcible blood draw by a police officer unless it's a DUI with injury or death. We don't have that statute in California. We are concerned that individuals may not understand it, they waive their right to a warrant, the warrant requirement, when they get their driver's license. And on the scene of a DUI, they're going to say, no, I don't want blood. And the officer is going to say, well, by having a driver's license, you have waived that warrant requirement. You have waived your protection of Fourth Amendment, and we're going to take blood from you. At that juncture, we're going to run into forcible blood draw, and we're extremely concerned about that. We think there are other ways to deal with this. We think breath is fine for DUI alcohol. And that should be the law in California. We should not ask drivers to waive any constitutional rights simply for the right to drive on our roads. For those reasons, we are opposed. Happy to try to fix the bill, and like I said, I do appreciate the conversation with the author. Thank you.

I think the key question before this Committee is whether it is in the public interest to have more loaded, hidden guns in public. This isn't about guns in the home. It's a person's choice whether they have a gun in the home or not, but once the gun is carried in public, that puts other people at risk. Consider law enforcement, and how much they are trained and repeatedly trained. And yet making that difficult decision assessing a situation, deciding whether to shoot or not. Whether they can possibly not hitting their target, or hitting bystanders. That's a very difficult situation for law enforcement. I have a hard time believing that the average citizen can handle that situation better than law enforcement. So again, I think this does put the public at risk. I understand the frustration of many people that the requirements vary from county to county. It does seem unfair, but rather lowering the requirement, I would support a stronger requirement, more strict requirement in all the counties in California. Consistency could be achieved that way. Again, we're opposed to the measure.

Though the gun lobbying has pushed many states to weaken these licensing requirements in recent years, California has thankfully not been among those states. Under California law, local law enforcement may issue CCW licenses to residents of their jurisdiction if they determine that the applicant is of good moral character and that good cause exists for the issuance of a license. This bill would effectively preempt those law enforcement decisions by requiring local police chiefs and sheriffs to accept applicants, quote, stated good cause without any additional inquiry. If they nearly state that they desire a CCW license for general self defense or crime prevention purposes. This would make the good call standard effectively meaningless, undermining law enforcement discretion and threatening our resident's right to safely and to peacefully enjoy public spaces. We urge you to oppose this bill.

 : These approaches in AB 1048 will help in addressing the opioid crisis.

Ruth Haskins: Thank you, Mr. Chair, good morning members. I'm Dr. Ruth Haskins, I'm President of CMA this year, and I practice OB and GYN right here near Sacramento. CMA is very pleased to sponsor AB 1048, and we thank Dr. Arembula for bringing this important measure forward. During the 1990s, there was a drive for improved pain treatment that resulted in various legislative and systems changes. As the science around one treatment modality, opioids, has evolved, there has been concern that some of the well-intentioned strategies have contributed to changes in prescribing that do not align with the current best practices in medicine. AB 1048 would allow for either a physician or the patient to initiate a partial fill of a prescription. This would allow for greater flexibility in providing care for acute pain. Data shows that most people who utilize prescription opioids, non medically, are getting these medications from friends or relatives. Unused medications that languish in the medicine cabinet can contribute to opioids diversion. Opioid prescribing guidelines recommend a limited quantity dispensed, based on the expected duration of severe pain. Viewing pain as part of the vital signs, or pain as the fifth vital sign, was one strategy that was codified for pain care provided in hospitals. Over time, this linking of pain assessment to vital signs has been called into question for its potential impact on increased opioid prescribing. AB 1048 would maintain a requirement that pain be assessed, but would not require that it be done in conjunction with the taking of all vital signs. Effective pain management is very complex, and individual variation in pain sensitivity can make that determination even more difficult. This bill ensures that the patient has access to appropriate care In a timely fashion, but reduces the potential risk associated with receiving more pills than the patient ultimately needs. For these reasons, we ask for your aye vote, and I'm very happy to answer additional questions you may have.

Beginning in the 1960s Pharmacy Benefit Manager served an important function as administrators of prescription drug benefits. Which health plans we're offering for the first time. But they have evolved from pape pushers to significant controllers of the drug pricing system, a black box understood by almost no one. And while PDMs were intended to reduce the prices Americans pay for medication, which are the highest in the world. In practice they have done little but exacerbate them. I see three major issues with PBM's, the first is the excessive sector wide concentration, three companies express scripts. CVS Caremark and Optum control between 75 and 80% of the market. Which translates into 180 million prescription drug customers. Furthermore, there are indications these major players divvy up the country, creating effective monopolies in most regions. Plan sponsors have little choice selecting a partner to manage their prescription drug benefits. And pharmacists must accept take it or leave it contracts with unfavorable terms. Second, PBMs operate with inherent conflicts of interest, the merger of CVS and Caremark in 2007 joined one of the biggest pharmacy chains with one of the biggest PBMs. Other PBMs establish mail order, and specialty pharmacies, so you have a PBM, which is a partner with pharmacies, and also a competitor to them using aggressive stealing of customers toward their own services. Leading in some cases to lower utilization rates and excessive waste while devastating local Independence pharmacies. And finally you have the extreme lack of transparency which is what this bill speaks to. The pharmaceutical supply chain involve drug manufacturers Wholesalers, health planes, and pharmacies. But only the PBM knows how much each component of this multi-sided market makes on every prescription drug purchase and they use that information advantage to capture profits on virtually every side of the deal. Whether it's capturing rebates negotiated with drug manufacturers employing spread pricing that charges health plans more than the PBM reimburses the pharmacy. Failing to update maximum allowable cost lists when drug prices spike or using fees to claw back reimbursement money. These schemes according to one report Express Scripts adjusted profit per prescription. Which is the money they take out of every drug purchase has increased 500% since 2003, and this types of practices contribute to that. PBM's exclusive control of the formulary which is the least of reimbursable drugs for their network. Also give them a crucial leverage point with their negotiations with drug manufacturers. And it artificially creates incentives for higher prices because higher cost drugs can yield more money in rebates. This has led, in many cases, to sort of hidden kickbacks between drug companies and PBMs where they keep the rebate themselves rather than passing it on to the health plan. Keeping formulary stock with high cost products. I believe states really must play a role to ensure a better functioning market and a better functioning drug supply chain. This can protect consumers, pharmacists and health plans from unnecessary charges. Prescription drug prices affect all of us. And there's simply too much information being hoarded by one obscure yet deceptively powerful player for the market to work effectively. Thank you.

Lizzie Buko: Good afternoon, Lizzie Buko with the ACLU California. Unfortunately, we are in opposition of AB 1298. We do think that this bill would impose a barrier to holding officers accountable for dishonesty. We acknowledge that the consequences for officers who have a sustained finding of dishonesty can be serious and they should be. The consequences for victims of officer dishonesty are far more severe. There are known incidents of innocent people who have been prosecuted, who have been convicted, who have been sentenced to prison and even death row based on testimony from an officer with a known history of dishonesty. There's no reason to believe that the current standard of preponderance to the evidence has resulted in any erroneous findings of officer dishonesty from an officer who is innocent. We do hear and know of many situations in which officers have repeatedly lied and not been held accountable for their actions. We have all, I imagine, seen videos that directly contradict officers' police reports, officers' testimonies and these are officers with a known history of lying, who have not been held accountable and certainly not accountable to the extent where they have not been able to continue making false statements that are endangering people's lives. And this is all with the current standard of preponderance of the evidence. This bill, by raising it to clear and convincing, would shield officers even further from accountability, raising the burden of proof far out of line with what is used in similar situations. Preponderance of the evidence is the standard burden of proof used in administrative hearings and disciplinary hearings and in court, in civil cases. There are very specific exceptions to that. Clear and convincing is really only used for situations where there are severe consequences for an individual's liberty. So examples are permanent termination of parental rights, involuntary commitment, really very specific and serious situations, not for administrative hearings, not for disciplinary hearings. Even disciplinary hearings that can ultimately result in termination. So again there's no demonstration that the current standard is not sufficient. But it is very likely that increasing the burden of proof would result in more guilty officers failing to be held accountable for dishonesty. As it is, the lack of accountability for officer dishonesty has resulted in severe damage to trust between communities and police and this bill would move in the opposite direction, so we are opposed, thank you. Thank you.

Lizzie Buko: Thank you, Lizzie Buko with the ACLU in California, we are also in strong support of AB 1448. The elderly parole program is a very common sense and humane program. That gives people who have grown old in prison an opportunity to go before the parole board to have an opportunity to be considered for release. This a population whose continued incarceration does not serve the goals of public safety. So a few points on that, age, I recognize that to a lot of people, 60 does not seem elderly or geriatric. But for the prison population, the correctional experts, health experts, academics all agree that people physiologically age much faster than they do in the general population. So that's why the National Institute of Corrections actually uses 50 as a threshold for elderly. The National Commission on Correctional Healthcare uses 55 as the threshold. This bill goes, and the current program goes beyond that using 60 as the age to be considered for parole. And so this is a population who physiologically is going to be more similar to someone who's 70 or 75 in the general population. So this is an elderly population that we're talking about. Second this release is conditional on the board of parole hearings. This is not a lenient body in any way. The current elderly parole program, 25% of the people who have gone before the board for elderly parole since 2014 have been found suitable. So the majority of the people who go before the parole board under this program are not found suitable. And then third, the 25 years is an extremely long period of time. It is far out of line with what people serve in other countries, regardless of the crime. Certainly other countries that we like to compare ourselves to, so that is an extremely long period of time. And this population as a whole, the data show they have a very low likelihood of recidivism. So people who are over 50 and leaving the prisons have the lowest recidivism rate of any other age group. People who have served longer than 15 years have the lowest recidivism rate of any other population. And people who are released by the board of parole hearings have a minuscule likelihood of recidivism. In the most recent data from the CDCR, the 400 people who have been released by the board of parole hearings, only 3 have been convicted of new crimes. So this is the population that accept the inner section of these three categories. And so they really, the likelihood of recidivism is practically nil. I also just want to bring up the enormous fiscal cost of this population. The LAO has found that people's medical costs for those who are elderly is two to three times greater than the regular population. And I also want to mention the human cost of the continued imprisonment of people who are geriatric in a place that is not designed to provide chronic care for people who are old and infirm. And, of course, people who are separated from their children, their grandchildren and their communities. I do want to acknowledge that many of the people who are eligible for this program have done things that have resulted in serious harm to other people. I acknowledge that that is true, but 25 years as I said, is a far more draconian punishment than what we see in other countries. And also, many of these offences are situational and they are singular events that are not representative of people's characters. So AB 1448, recognizes not only the lack of justification for continued incarceration of the geriatric prisoner population. And also the very circumspect parole board, but also people's capacity for change. So for these reasons we support, thank you.

We do think that this bill would indeed effective investigations and make it more difficult to hold officers accountable for misconduct under current law at a questioning officer. When they provide information on the nature of an offense prior to investigation, they can use their discretion to provide the information that they think would be helpful in providing a fair and effective investigation. There's nothing that precludes them from providing information that would be included in this bill. If they think that that would lead to a more effective investigation. This bill would undermine that process by requiring specific information to be presented before any questions are asked. This is not how one does investigations. In a criminal investigation, when an officer is questioning a person, they do not provide the facts of the case before they begin questioning. That actually helps with jail over crowding and helps assure the right to bail. Lillian Taiz: Thank you, Assembly Member Weber. Yes, my name is Lillian Taiz, and I'm a Professor emerita at Cal State Los Angeles. When I started at Cal State LA in 1992, 62% of the CSU faculty had full time, permanent jobs. Today only two in five faculty members have permanent positions. Over the years I have been both a lecturer, a part time faculty member, and a tenured faculty member in the CSU. As a lecturer in addition to preparing and teaching my courses, much of my time was spent traveling to other campuses to teach, or trying to figure out where I would be teaching next term. I taught at times at San Francisco State, CSU Hayward, Holy Names College, and UC Davis. Teaching under these circumstances made becoming part of the campus culture and developing strong mentoring relationships with my students extremely challenging. When I became a tenure-line faculty member at Cal State LA, the nature of my work changed radically. The long-term nature of my position allowed me to build ongoing relationships with my students. To be part of a larger teaching community developing curriculum and research projects for students. And to work on many projects that address student success and closing the achievement gap. Sadly, over the years, the University failed to replenish the ranks of tenured faculty. Relying instead on legions of talented, non-tenure track faculty. University work historically shared among 60 to 70% of us who are tenure line is now being carried by dwindling numbers of tenured faculty who are left. Faculty keep trying to do it all, but something has to give, none of us has superpowers. We knew back in 2001 and 2002 that our situation needed to change but over the last 15 years things have only gotten worse. This bill, AB 1464, will stop and reverse a trend that has resulted in more than 15,000 CSU faculty working on temporary, usually part time contracts. Thousands of these lecturer faculty are well qualified by education and experience for permanent tenure line positions, but they are hindered by virtue of their temporary appointments. Already a fair number of incumbent CSU lecturers apply for and are hired into tenure track positions. This bill would encourage the expansion of this practice by opening up more opportunities. It's really a no brainer for the University and for our students. Thank you for the opportunity today. I respectfully urge your aye vote on this important piece of legislation.

Unfortunately, what I have found is that due to my temporary status, I may never be considered for a tenure-track position. Because I have not held a full-time or a tenure track position previously. It is disheartening to know that although I play such an important role in providing my students with high quality educational experiences, both in and outside of the classroom, that this accounts for very little when seeking a more stable position. Every semester of my now four years of teaching in the CSU, I am fearful of the loss of my job due to budgetary cutbacks, and the vicarious nature of my employment status. Students' success outcomes are dependent on the consistent availability of faculty and the establishment of trusting relationships that are cultivated over time. A direct result of the inconsistency of employment for part time and temporary lecturers, such as myself, is that we are prevented from becoming vested in the long term growth of our respective campuses and in the CSU. The decline in tenure-track density is yet another example of the CSU's blatant disregard for its lecture faculty and students. As the decline in tenure-track faculty steadily reduces the CSU's capacity to effectively serve its students. Temporary lecturers have few opportunities to participate in program development, student advising, shared governance, and the implementation of University initiatives. As these opportunities and responsibilities are reserved for tenure line faculty. Several of my temporary lecturer peers have left the CSU for K-12 and other outside employment opportunities, seeking positional stability, wage increase, and greater opportunity for career advancement. AB 1464 is important because the CSU loses 10% of its part-time lecturer faculty annually. Over the course of a five year period, about half of the part-time temporary lecturers employed by the CSU will leave. For students, this means that 50% of the professors that they have during their freshman year are no longer on their campuses by the time that they graduate. And this is unfortunate. Building relationships with professors enriches students' educational experiences. For underserved students and students of color, these relationships are most often based on ethnicity and a cultural connection with their faculty and peers. These relationships are even more critical because they often mean the difference between a student dropping out of college and obtaining a degree. CSU part-time and temporary faculty are not just classroom teachers, we are mentors, we are trusted confidants, and we, as well as our students, deserve the opportunity to build and foster these relationships. More important, our students need and deserve the comfort of knowing that their teachers will be around for more than just one semester. This bill will not only increase the number of full time tenure track positions available to part time and temporary lecturers, it will reduce the cost of hiring, and afford greater parity in the recruitment and retention of underrepresented faculty and faculty of color such as myself in the CSU. AB 1464 is essential to me, as a temporary, part-time faculty lecturer. Because it will provide the opportunity for me to obtain the job that I have trained for, as I continue to teach the students that I love. Thank you for this opportunity.

At UCSF, we have four in-house languages, Spanish, Mandarin, Cantonese and Russian. And UC also contracts with several outside agencies for both in-house and other languages. Language Line is the agency use for phone and Video Remote Interpreting, VRI. In VRI, the patient and provider are at one location while the interpreter is at another, interpreting in front of a screen. When VRI was first rolled out at UCSF in 2013, UC stated that video remote interpreting and in-person were equal in quality, but that is not the case. They assured us that in-person interpreting would be the default and that vendor interpreters used would be nationally certified. Language Line is using interpreters from outside the US, from the Dominican Republic, Costa Rica, Peru, Panama, and the territories of Puerto Rico. The job requirement listed on their website is a high school diploma, not national certification. Local interpreters are familiar with the California patient population, both linguistically and culturally, and are exposed to issues that are relevant to the communities we serve. We have knowledge of the US medical system, which helps spot potential healthcare navigation problems. Communication mistakes cost money and lives. Interpreters from the US have training and a national certification that is vetted and verified. It includes privacy, ethics and protocol standards. There are two national certifications available to be considered competent to interpret in the medical field. UC prides itself on excellence, equity and diversity. Yet it has single out only the Spanish language, video remoting interpreting to offshore, the most common certification language among interpreters in the state. State and federal funds should not be used to offshore interpreting jobs, especially if it lowers the standard of care for our limited English proficient patients. Medical interpreters at UC are dedicated professionals who have a stake in upholding the reputation of UC as a place that provides equitable quality care and in maintaining the integrity of this prestigious medical institution. Please vote in favor of AB-848. Thank you very much.

My name is Laura Szabo-Kubitz and I'm here today on behalf of the Institute for College Access and Success, an independent non-profit organization based in Oakland that works to make higher education more available and affordable for people of all backgrounds. I'm here to voice our strong support for AB 1178 by Assemblymember Calderon which would require that colleges annually notify students about their student loan balances to help inform future borrowing choices. Students should always take advantage first of financial aid that does not need to be repaid before turning to student loans, however, when grants and scholarships do not fully cover their financial need, loans, and much safer federal loans in particular, can help ensure students stay enrolled and on track to graduation without working excessive hours that can harm academic success. While care must be taken to ensure that letters do not serve to deter students from re-enrolling or from borrowing what they need, research suggests that reminding students of their loan balances encourages them to seek more information or assistance from their college financial aid office and may influence some students borrowing decisions. And by deepening students engagement with their colleges students can learn more about the financial supports available to them including other scholarships and grants and the consumer protections like public service loan forgiveness unique to federal loans. For these reasons we strongly urge you to vote in support of AB 1178 to ensure that student loan borrowers receive key information to help them make wise borrowing decisions that keep them on their path to graduation. Thank you for your time.

Jesse Aguiar: Good afternoon Committee Chair and members. My name is Jesse Aguiar and I'm here representing Journey House as the proud sponsors of AB 1567. We have been working with current and former foster youth in the Pasadena community for the last 35 years. And as a former foster youth myself, I do understand, now navigating the professional work space, how critical and crucial the services that I received while in school were to my career advancement. So the mission of Journey House is to assist former foster youth Reach self-sufficiency, and we do this by supporting them through their educational journeys. We understand the impact that college or vocational degrees have on one's ability to obtain meaningful employment, so we focus our efforts to helping former foster youth enroll and graduate from colleges and universities. In California, less than half of former foster youth graduate high school compared to 79% of other students. By the age of 26, only 4% of former foster youth complete college compared to 36% of the 26 year olds in general student populations. AB 1567 to address this issue by providing former foster youth notification of on campus support programs on California community colleges and Cal State University's campuses. Programs such as the Extended Opportunities Programs and Services and the cooperating agencies for Foster Youth Educational Success, provides students with support, such as, books, supplies, transportation, counseling and tutoring.  These critical supports have a huge impact on a youth's ability to successfully complete college courses. We know that if a youth succeeds in college, they are more likely to find meaningful employment, contribute to the economy, be less likely to depend on government support, and ultimately break the cycles of poverty that lead children into the child welfare system. For these reasons, we request your support on AB 1567.

Jessie Ryan: Good afternoon, Chairman Medina and Committee Members. Jessie Ryan, Executive Vice President at the Campaign for College Opportunity, a state-wide nonprofit working to ensure that all Californians have an equal opportunity to attend and succeed in college, in order to build a vibrant workforce, economy, and democracy. We're here today as sponsors of AB 847, to promote transparency and accessibility of data on the representation of academic senates, in order to help foster a better understanding of faculty leadership at public colleges and universities. We know that the increasing diversity of students in higher education is a prevalent trend across the country. Such that, in certain states like California, the minority has now become the majority. Today students of colors are really the representative at 64% of all freshmen at the UC, 68% of all first-time freshmen at the CSU and 71% of first-time freshmen at the community college system. However, the proportion of faculty and leadership has not kept pace with the growing number of students of color enrolling in college and universities. With public colleges and universities averaging only 30% of its total leadership from people of color. We know diversity matters and that having diversity and leadership including academic senates has many benefits to students. Diverse leaders are well situated to make diversity integral to the mission of the college and into the fabric of their decision making, to ensure minority perspectives are incorporated into organizational decision making and they are creating opportunities where institutions are responsive to issues of diversity. We also know that the impact is profound for students, such that an intentional commitment to diversity will yield important improvements to campus climate. Furthermore, diversity in leadership is actively sought in corporate environments where increased leadership diversity is found to improve organizational outcomes. It's not enough to seek improvements in faculty diversity, we need to improve the diversity of the leadership, to change the institutional environments, such that it is more reflective and responsive to the students we serve. We strongly believe that as Assembly Member Bocanegra said, this is a pragmatic bill, and a simple matter of transparency. We collect student-level data as a tool for student-centered change. Similarly, we should make publicly available, upon request, data on the state's academic senates as a means of promoting equity and success. Lifting up culturally responsive teaching strategies and fostering a campus culture conducive to faculty diversity and student achievement. We believe that this bill is timely, as in the past faculty diversity has been made a priority of the chair and many in the legislature, thus we ask for your aye vote today.

In that report, we found that over a three year period the University had admitted 16,000 non-residents who's academic scores fell below the average scores of applicants who are California residents. This occurred in part because the University had changed its admission standard for non-residents, which it calls the Compare Favorably Standard. We recommended that the University replace its Compare Favorably Standard with a standard that reflects the intent of the master plan for higher education in California. The master plan states that the University should require non-resident applicants to stand in the upper half of those who are ordinarily eligible. More than a year has passed, however the University has not implemented our recommendation. Benjamin Palmer: All right, good afternoon. Benjamin Palmer, on behalf of the California Manufactured Housing Institute. Senator Leyva covered the issue well. These are houses built the same as regular stick-built homes. They cost under $100,000, they contain granite countertops, all the additional amenities you find in a regular house. So SB 329 seeks to ensure that state and local programs designed to facilitate homeownership or residence include manufactured housing. As a matter of policy, prospective homeowners and residents should be able to apply for the programs that facilitate homeownership or residence, regardless of the type of home that they're considering. Any categorical exclusion of today's lower cost, high quality manufactured homes creates additional barriers for those who are seeking to find affordable housing within the state. As Senator Leyva noted, the Department of HCD's housing report noted that today's homes are high quality, greater energy efficiency than prior generations, and cost 10 to 20% per square foot less than conventional homes. SB 329 seeks to ensure that state and local programs that facilitate home ownership or residence don't automatically exclude these affordable high quality manufacturered homes from their scope. For all of the above reasons we're pleased to sponsor SB 329 and respectfully ask for your aye vote.

Unfortunately, while we agree with the spirit of the bill, the bill seeks to take resources already dedicated to existing down payment assistance and home ownership programs and would reallocate those resources to chattel loans like those used to purchase a car. Loans for real property and personal property are vastly different. Personal property loans used to buy manufactured housing have different qualification criteria, reduced loan terms, and higher interest rates as pointed out by the Senator. While single-family homes are the predominant housing type serving 65% of California's families, they only receive about 20% of the affordable housing program dollars. With scarce resources, while well intended, SB 329 would jeopardize these existing programs. For example, California housing finance agencies programs facilitate the purchase of real property. It would prove costly to the agency and the state to force Cal FHA to begin making personal property loans, which is not within their scope of expertise, requires a significant rule making process, and staff would need training on a whole new lending product. Because California is amid an affordable housing crisis, it is vitally important that we not divert precious resources for real property home ownership opportunities to tangible personal property loans. We would respectfully suggest that the sponsor instead seek to create programs specifically designed to serve the community. We respectfully request your no vote on SB 329, and request that it be held in committee until we can find a resolution to this problem that works.
[{'start': 67, 'end': 81, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Alicia Sebastian: Hello, Alicia Sebastian, I'm the Director of Housing and Community Development Programs for the California Coalition for Rural Housing. Manufactured homes make up over 4% of all housing stock across the state. In California, at least 1 million people live in more than 5,000 registered manufactured housing communities or mobile home parks. They're in the rural Sierra Nevadas, the coast of Santa Monica and in the heart of Silicon Valley. While the price of homes, lots of land vary widely across communities, manufactured homes make up a significant portion of California's limited affordable housing stock. However, with the recovery of the housing market, these communities are being marked by owners and investors for acquisition and conversion to other uses. When this happens, residents cannot easily move to other parks, because affordable spaces are not available or the homes are too old to move, or because the cost of moving the home is too great an economic burden. In fact, over 81% of today's manufactured homes will never be relocated. As such, renters and homeowners alike lose their homes. CCRH has spent years exploring the challenges facing non-profit housing developers and resident groups who seek to preserve California's manufactured housing opportunities. Extensive stakeholder engagement helped identify this legislative opportunity. At this very moment, there are at least 10 potential parks our members are interested in, and many more of our partners would like to enter into park preservation. However, many organizations struggle to identify parks for sale. In some cases, a park may be on the market for over a year. Other times, sales move so quickly, developers are too late to the table. Every month, CCRH receives calls from organizations and residents and communities interested in park preservation. They can't figure out where to begin, they don't know what resources are available to them, and they don't understand what an acquisition will entail. Even expert organizations that exclusively operate park acquisitions are unfamiliar with MPROP or existing resources. Nonprofit acquisition of parks is a successful model, but it isn't widely recognized. People across the United States are looking at MPROP in California to see how this is done. We have an opportunity to lead across the nation, and facing California's housing crisis SB136 will allow the state to be nimble in meeting the needs of communities in order to make the most of existing resources to protect the housing we already have.
[{'start': 7, 'end': 23, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Paul Ainger: Paul Ainger, Development Solutions Manager for Rural Community Systems Corporation. As an affordable non-profit housing developer in California with Community Housing Opportunities Corporation, I used $1.5 million in MPROP funding as part of an overall $12 million package needed to acquire and rehabilitate the 153-unit Casa Del Sol mobile home park in Woodland, California. The project is now a vital improved development that provides long term affordable housing for farm workers and seniors in Woodland. The MPROP funding was pivotal in leveraging millions of dollars in additional funding for this mobile home park. This project, however, took eight years from start to finish. We began the effort in 2001 and completed it in 2008. One key reason for this long time period is the difficulty in securing financing for mobile home parks. Mobile home parks financing requires a mix of sources, and some of those sources have restricted uses. Further, there are issues related to loan values, subordination and the other issues that are substantially different from conventional affordable housing financing. One of the reasons for the current unspent balances and MPROP financing is not because there's a lack of demand for the financing, we get inquiries two, three times a month from different sellers and buyers. It's largely because of sellers aren't familiar with the program, and the buyers are really perplexed by the complex financing structuring required to purchase and rehabilitate the parks. So as a result, some of the sellers just take the cash, and sell the park and sometimes that park is no longer there because the buyer says, I'm not going to operate this as a park anymore. So some of these sellers may have preferred to sell to a nonprofit developer or to the residents, but they believe the alternative is too risky and uncertain. So what is the fix? Clearly there is a need for technical assistance to bridge the knowledge gap. This bill would add technical assistance as an allowable use of MPROP funds. By using this, the California Department of Housing and Community Development can set aside a modest amount of funding for the critical, technical assistance that is needed to make mobile home parks acquisition and rehabilitation deals happen. Thank you.

[{'start': 18, 'end': 31, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Anya Lawler: Good morning, Anya Lawler, on behalf of the Western Center on Law and Poverty, we're one of the co-sponsors on this measure. I probably don't need to go into a lot of detail about the depth of the housing crisis in California right now. I think you've all probably noticed by now, that it's pretty bad. How we got here is complicated, and fixing it is going to be even more complicated. But one thing is clear. California simply doesn't have enough housing units available to go around. And the shortage is most acute at the lower income level. A recent report by HCD, the state Department of Housing and Community Development, showed that the state is short nearly 3.5 million units affordable at the low, very low, and extremely low income levels. California law has long obligated citizen counties to plan to accommodate their fair share of housing at all income levels. The law recognizes that local governments aren't in the business of building, but they do have tremendous influence through their zoning powers, over what does and doesn't get built in our community. And the housing elements in cities and counties must show that they have enough adequately zoned land, to accommodate their share of the regional housing aid at all income levels. So, the market level, as well as the moderate, low, and very low income levels. To accommodate lower income housing, cities and counties have to have densely zoned land, that may be developed as multifamily housing. Many, many local governments take these planning obligations very seriously. Unfortunately, some do not and continue to skirt the requirements of the law, and include sites in their housing elements that are not truly buildable, which only serves to exacerbate the crisis. When a local law effectively makes it impossible for housing developers, particularly affordable housing developers to find a site on which to build, it's unfair to their neighboring jurisdictions that are welcoming housing development. Even though some cities are doing everything right, they still see their housing costs rise because of a regional shortage of units, exacerbated by neighbors who are not doing the right planning. It is also unfair to preschool teachers, restaurant workers, artists and other low wage earners, and increasingly to high wage earners like teachers and critical first responders, who are told that they're welcome to work in a community, but they can't live there. AB 1397 tightens the rules for what constitutes an adequate site under housing element law, to ensure all that local governments are providing real opportunities for developers to come in and build. It's the only way we're going to solve this crisis. We have to build. And with that, I will close.

[{'start': 25, 'end': 39, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Barry Jardini: Thank you. Good afternoon, Madam Chair and Members of the Committee. My name is Barry Jardini with the California Disability Services Association. And we are proud to sponsor 1607, which will help facilitate competitive integrated employment opportunities and outcomes for individuals with developmental disabilities. I want to thank Assemblymember Frazier for authoring this important bill. California's Employment First Policy prioritizes opportunities for integrated competitive employment for individuals with developmental disabilities, regardless of the severity of disability. However, we see significant unemployment in our population. In fact, according to 2015 EDD data, only 13.6% of working-age Regional Center consumers reported any income. And a national core indicators study of over 8,700 consumers indicated that fewer than 5% of those surveyed had a job in an integrated competitive setting. So AB 1607 seeks to address two issues that currently exist for providing requisite pre-vocational job discovery and skills training necessary to help consumers achieve competitive integrated employment. First, in 2014, the Legislature passed SB 577, which was intended to provide community-based vocational development services to consumers as a pilot program to increase employment in integrated settings. CBVD services are services designed to promote job discovery, employment exploration, skills training, volunteer opportunities, potentially educational opportunities as well. And we thought it would be a great program. But unfortunately, SB 577 has not been implemented because it required federal financial participation. And as a pilot program, it couldn't be included in the existing HCBS services waiver. In order to implement the program, DDS would have to write a separate, standalone waiver with CMS to put this into action and get federal financial participation. That process would take years and is not likely to happen. So what we're looking for today is to remove the pilot language on this, which would enable this service, which would, again, do the pre-vocational services to give people the skills required to achieve competitive integrated employment. And 1607 would make that happen by removing the pilot language, and thereby enabling participation in the HCBS waiver. And I also want to highlight that the recent California Competitive Integrated Employment Blueprint, which was put together by the Department of Developmental Services, Department of Rehab, and the Department of Education, specifically lists SB 577 as one of the tools to achieve competitive integrated employment. And this bill would actually make that possible. The second aim of the bill is to provide a means of transition for consumers who are currently working in supported employment group or work activity programs to transition into more competitive integrated employment if they choose to do so. Currently, there are over 15,000 consumers working in these settings that are earning wages. They're compliant with current rules. But they're at risk under new federal regulations that go into effect March of 2019. And those settings may no longer be eligible for federal financial participation. So what we want to do is start the transition process for those consumers to be able to move into more competitive integrated employment. And so as a second provision, this bill would allow individuals who are seeking competitive integrated employment. To apply for or to get tailored day services in addition to their existing work programs in order to start the process for them to do the skills training. And the job exploration and the different things to help them find a job in the community that they feel is appropriate for them. We believe that AB 1607 will increase opportunities for individuals with developmental disabilities to engage in that job discovery and job readiness training. That's necessary to assist their transition into competitive integrated employment and support their employment success. We believe this will start to build the self-sufficiency of adults with developmental disabilities. Which includes increased earning capacity and a reduced dependence on government support. By providing the necessary services to transition to those employment settings. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today, and I'm happy to answer any questions you might have.

George Kutnerian: Thank you Madam Chair and members. George Kutnerian here, on behalf of 6Beds Inc. Which represents more than 2000 small home residential care facilities. For the elderly and adult residential facilities serving six or fewer persons. I'd like to start by saying that 6Beds is very appreciative of Assembly Member Patterson for understanding this issue. And carrying this bill on our behalf. We'd also like to acknowledge our principle co-author, Senator Weiner. As well as the Committee staff for assisting us with this bill. The initial certification training program, known as the ICTP, requires a completion of 80 hours of initial course work and passing of the administrator's test. CCL's interpretation of current law, Requires a licensee to redo the ICTP if the licensee applies for a new facility at a date is later than five years since the license he last completed in ICTP. This requirement applies even to a licensing applicant who is a certified administrator, and has kept up with continuing education requirements, which consist of 40 hours of coursework, Every two years. Applying the requirement to redo the ICTP to licencing applicants who are also certified administrators is unnecessarily redundant and costly. This bill would acknowledge that licencing applicants who are also certified administrators should not have to undertake an entirely new ICTP. The bill will also address requirements pertaining the criminal background clearance transfer request. Current law requires a criminal background clearance for an employee to be transferred to a new facility before the Before the employee can work there. Even if the new facility is operated by the same licensee, 80% of California's RCFVs are six bed facilities. Many six bed licensees operate multiple facilities in the same geographic local. With such a license he has an employee who is cleared as associated to at least one of its facilities who is found to be working at another one of the same licensing facilities without being formally associated by CCL. Current statute and regulations treat that situation identically as a situation where licensing allowed a new employee to work without any criminal background clearing whatsoever, resulting in a subtle penalties of up to $500 However these two situations are not identical. AB 1437 would stop unfairly penalizing licensees who are simply trying to ensure adequate staffing, using their already cleared employees in response to situations such as when employees may go on family or medical leave. Or may abruptly quit their employment. AB 1437 will modernize statutes and regulations and better align them with the operational realities that RCFEs, particularly smaller RCFEs face on a regular basis. We also believe that AB 1437 will results in efficiencies that will reduce CCL's workload. We respectfully ask for your aye votes, thank you.

Tom Dominguez: Good morning, I'm Tom Dominguez. I'm President of the Association of Orange County Deputy Sheriffs. We're also a member of the Fraternal Order of Police, which is the second largest law enforcement Association in the State of California. Today on behalf of my Association and close to the 3,000 members that I represent, we are proud sponsors of AB 530. Law enforcement and my Association in particular for too long have seen labor disputes ranging from unfair labor practices, breaches of contracts, or bad faith bargaining sent to Superior Court. This is highly problematic for a couple of reasons. First, it can be too costly. A Superior Court filing for labor dispute can cost a peace officer thousands of dollars. It is not rare for these cases to incur cost upwards of $40,000 while a similar filing in PELRB would generally be well under $5,000. Most law enforcement associations in the state are relatively small with limited financial resources. When one of these Peace Officers Association are deciding whether to take contract dispute to court. The mere cost of this must be considered, and many times these claims were not taken to court solely because of the cost. This is creating a deterrent. By doing so, this gives local government and management an unfair advantage. Other public employee unions don't have this burden, because they are under the jurisdiction of PELRB, which in most cases is not cost prohibitive. Secondly, PELRB has the knowledge and expertise over unfair labor claims, because these are the only types of cases that they hear. In contrast in superior courts cover a multitude of subject matters including civil and criminal litigation.  This makes it more difficult for the courts to make consistent findings, on issues, such as bad faith bargaining. These cases are complex and unique to the labor management relationship. AB 530 will allow peace officers associations to draw from the expertise of PELRB, and give the smaller police Peace Officers Unions the ability to defend themselves against unfair labor practices, contract disputes, and bad faith bargaining, by removing the barrier of the excessive cost occurred by courts. Based on these reasons, we respectfully ask for your aye vote.

Dean Hutchings: Good morning, chair members. Dean Hutchings, with the League of California cities. First off, I want to be clear that this was a gut and amend measure. And I did reach out to the author's office the second I saw the language hit and was attempting to coordinate with the sponsors. I did not reach out to the sponsors directly, but I did reach out the author's office and attempt to set a meeting before this hearing. So I want to just put that on the record. AB 1250 eliminates local agency hiring discretion by limiting our local agencies' ability to utilize a contract for the sole purposes of savings through salaries and benefits. This creates a significant hurdle as agencies are now at a near breaking point in their unfunded accrued liability for normal pension and OPEC costs. Although touched on upon in the analysis, I would like to direct the Committee's attention to your page 12, lines 1 through 10, where it states that a measure that would require a state to perform a full economic impact analysis for environmental impact analysis, and a full annual audit, a performance audit for contracts $100,000 or more. These are significantly costly and time consuming requirements that would be placed upon a local government. Moreover, this measure would require that a city or county create a fully searchable database that must be posted on our websites. So the names, job titles, salaries of each non-city employee, and their subcontractors, which includes the service contract, the name of the agency, the department, so pretty significant information that we're going to be having to post. Non-city employees' personal information on our websites. So apart from the inherent cost drivers with this provision, our members do have privacy concerns about posting full names, job titles, and salaries for non-city employees. AB 1250 would also require that a city and a county staff provide prescriptive employee orientations for non-city employees. Additional orientations and non-city employees create significant cost and logistical concerns. Given that the language is so broad does not adequately define a contract for services. Cities that are built around the Lakewood plan who would identify as contract cities would be forced to comply with these provisions with virtually every contract they enter into. Cities such as Ontario and Pomona, Long Beach, Avalon, Signal Hill, Eastvale. These are all cities that are contract cities and by nature have that structure as their city was developed. The workload, privacy concerns, costs and litigation created by this measure places an overwhelmingly and significant burden on local agencies, and for those reasons we oppose.

Los Angeles County has safeguards and trainings in place for public employees such as myself. We attend monthly safety meetings, we have sexual harassment trainings. We are trained in the laws and rules regarding HIPAA regulations, to ensure that any medical documents as well are sacred. And protected from others as well as even ourselves knowing what to do with them. We do represent a well trained and qualified workforce. They may promise to save money, but it's not always clear the risks to the taxpayers are accounted for. For example, we've had outside contractors use our facilities and our vehicles and our equipment, but it's not clear that they have the same trainings or standards. When these companies bid on doing our work, the question that we ask is, are the tax payers still paying for the wear and tear on the equipment? That I cannot possibly answer for you, but it's a consideration. Another example, we had a contractor formerly, a former contractor, thank goodness, that provided fraudulent time cards. And what they claimed to the county was that they were using more staff than they actually were and that they were paying them in accordance with county regulations. Where in fact, they were not paying them the living wage that was required. There should be transparency on how public dollars are spent. Accountability is required if the public is misled on the savings. It can be disastrous to us all. It is the constituents that lose out on the quality of services if oversight is lacking. I am here supporting AB 1250 because the legislation would ensure that when services are outsourced, tax dollars are accounted for. And standards of service are in place. It simply says cities and counties must do the same due diligence that state agencies do when opting to outsource public services. AB 1250 is about protecting tax payers. [{'start': 0, 'end': 12, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
John Beyer: Thank you, Mr. Mccarty. Thank you, Mr Chair and members. My name is John Beyer, representing the State Auditor's office. With me is Heather Kendrick, our legal counsel. For the record the State Auditor does not take a position on any bills, but that said, Assembly Bill 581 does address certain recommendations from our November 2016 audit, that found problems with the oversight of apprenticeship programs by the Department of Industrial Relations. Specifically, our audit found that Industrial Relations was not verifying that apprenticeship programs were using grant funds only for training activities. We determined that Industrial Relations did have existing statutory authority to do this verification as part of an ongoing audit. However, outside of an audit we found that state law did not allow the industrial relations to do that verification. Therefore, to address the problem we found that the state law, we made two recommendations to the Legislator. One is that to provide industrial relations with authority to verify as a condition of receiving future grant funds that apprenticeship programs are using those funds for training apprentices. This verification would primarily consist of the apprenticeship program retaining and providing upon request invoices, receipts, and other accounting and records that would support that training was actually done. The second recommendation that we had to the Legislature was that it amend state law to provide industrialization see authority to deregister an apprenticeship program that either demonstrated that it wasn't using grant funds for training purposes, or that it had used grant funds for inappropriate purposes. A review of Assembly Bill 581 concludes that it does include both this recommendations within it and to address the issue that we identified. That concludes my testimony. Thank you. I can answer any questions.

Natasha Collins: Natasha Collins with the Legislative Analyst's Office, as you may know, it's our office's standard practice to neither oppose nor support bills. But we're here today to speak of a report that our office released last year that analyzed how the state collects and uses workforce education and training data about those programs that it funds. We found that although the state's workforce system is extensive, policy makers cannot answer basic questions about it. For example, even how many people participate, or how well these programs compare in getting people jobs and wage growth. One of the reasons we cannot answer basic questions like these is because historically, outcome measures have not been standardized across workforce programs. That is, state and federal laws have required service providers to report different types of outcome data even if the programs are quite similar and sometimes, this is even within a single agency. While there has been recent progress towards establishing and using common outcome measures at both the state and federal levels, some state workforce programs still require providers to track different performance measures, sometimes using different data definitions and different reporting schedules. This results in an inability to assess the system's performance at a state level, also, it's administratively burdensome as was mentioned to both providers and to state agencies themselves. To address this concern, our report recommended that the Legislature direct the California Workforce Development Board to lead a task force that would resolve some of these remaining inconsistencies. Specifically, the task force would work on the development of detailed data definitions, common performance measures, reporting schedules and other specifications to ensure a more efficient and consistent data collection and reporting system. We believe that this would be a step towards providing more useful information to help policy makers, the public, and providers make decisions about their programs and funding, which would ultimately result in better workforce outcomes. AB 849 would implement this recommendation. I'm happy to answer any technical questions as the Assembly Member mentioned, thank you.
