It is very important for the Committee to understand that when you look at suicide and mental health rates within our industry sector. Suicidal ideation is 13 times higher than the general population. Suicide attempts and completion, 10 times higher than the general population, and when you look at the progression from new career to severe mental health issues there is a clear, and very articulable pathway to that, and it starts with critical stress, whether it be accumulative or acute when that accumulative stress and critical stress is not relieved, at the 5 to 11 year mark depending on which report you look at creates career fatigue and burn out, which progresses to deep personalization, and we have a period in our careers where we no longer can empathize with the patients that we serve and we just flat out don't care. And when you get to that point it does not take much of a stimulus to move to severe mental health issues and so, our organization has looked at this and we have always supported back end mental health services, awareness, the check on your buddy and your partner programs, but we've also realized that if we don't do something about the front end critical stress, we're chasing our tail on the back end and we're never going to win when it comes to mental health issues. So what this bill does for us is provide some respite for the day to day, to reduce that opportunity for critical stress to rear it's ugly head and get us to walk down the path of significant mental health problems. And I'd like to introduce Lisa LaRusso. She's a paramedic and a colleague of mine, that can share a personal story of what happens when we do not manage this stress and the mental health issues that arise from them.

Measures that address the lack of transparency around pay are critical to addressing this complex economic issue, and one strategy alone is not enough to solve it. These measures that increase pay transparency are an important strategy because employers are often unaware that these gaps and disparities even exist in their own companies. Research has shown as the Assembly woman mentioned that when these pay and transparency initiatives are undertaken Begin businesses, and in this case, government civil service jobs find that these disparities exist, and are able to then rectify them. In California, companies in California recognize the need to take a proactive approach, and have conducted internal pay analyses, and have determined where paid disparities exist and where they have then taken action to close those gaps. These include Apple. Apple, Google, Salesforce, and SpaceX. The only other thought is that employers have already been gearing up for the EEO1 in federal revised form which will already require employers to do these types of internal pay data analysis, which would begin this year. Although that is at risk, employers already have been gearing up to do this and are ready to do this and these companies, private companies have done it, have shown that it is possible to do it. Jennifer Barron: Mr. Chair and Committee Members, Jennifer Barron on behalf to he California Chamber of Commerce and we are opposed to this measure. Obviously, we are supportive of equal pay, we supported SB 358 when Senator Jackson strengthened California's equal pay act, and we are still in support of that by working with the task force that has been implemented by the state. Make sure that it's clear and it's implemented and takes full effect in California. So we are in support of equal pay, but what we are concerned with the bill, of AB 1209 is it doesn't capture the balance that was captured in SB 358. Specifically, it says that we must compare the salaries, the mean and median salaries between men and women and I assure you that there is going to reflect wage disparity. There is going to be wage disparities between men and women captured in that data, but what it does not reflect is the bonafide factors listed in SB 358 upon which you can have a wage disparity for education, experience, training, merit systems, personal choices by the employees themselves. So it says compensation, we don't really know what the term compensation means. Is it adjusted gross income after you've had personal choices with regards to maxing out your 401k, medical deductions, etc. It doesn't capture any of those legitimate reasons as to why you're going to have a wage disparity and that's what we're concerned with, is that you aggregate this data, you force employers to put it on their public websites so they can be criticized and publicly shamed for having wage disparities, but yet it doesn't capture any of the justified reasons why you can have a wage disparity. So we don't think that this moves the equal pay forward. We think it is just a way in which to public shame companies who are already doing the right things. A lot of these companies are already conducting pay audits of their compensation structure to make sure that employees who are performing substantially similar duties are actually getting payed the same amount. This bill compares job descriptions and job titles which both the EEOC and California Courts have said that's not the proper analysis. You actually need to look at the duties of the employees and what they're doing to compare apples to apples and not apples to oranges. So for those reasons, we don't think it's going to provide any accurate data on what the wage disparity actually is in California, because it doesn't capture all of those personal choices, all of the bonafide factors upon which you can have a wage disparity legitimately. So for those reasons we are opposed.

We respectfully oppose Assemblymember Burke's bill and would like to make a few points to the Committee. I'm joined this morning by Tony Signorelli, deputy Commissioner for consumer services and market conduct, who was one of the architects of the regulation, in case there's additional questions that need to be answered. These are brand-new regulations, they just took effect. And generally speaking, the approach we think makes more sense for the Legislature and other interested parties is to wait and see what the impact of the regulations are. If there is a problem down the road, then the Legislature has the ability to revisit any issue that occurs. I will tell you that these regulations were developed over a period of years with dozens of meetings with all interested stakeholders. And so, the notion that this is some sort of hastily put together thing just is not accurate. And so, we would note that they're brand new, and literally a couple months old, and give them time to take effect first. I would note that on page three, lines five to ten of the Bill, it says that the intent of the Bill to quote supersede in their entirety, the amendments to subdivision E of section 2695.8 of title 10 of the California Court of Regulations adopted on November 9, 2016. And the supersede any provision of that regulation in effect prior to November 9 2016 that's in conflict with section 758.5 of the insurance code. So there is a wiping out, particularly in the area of anti steering of the regulations. And let's not pretend that that is not the case. We will also note that if these regulations were not lawful and appropriate with the statutory authority that exists with the department, the Office of Administrative Law would not have approved the regs. If there's an issue or a conflict, that is why the office of administrative law exists. Now, to pivot a little bit to more substantively, in terms of consumer impact we are concerned that the anti steering part. The new regs that clarified and enhanced consumer protections which allow consumers to not be steered by the insurance company to the repair shop of the insurer's choice, and allows the consumer to pick the shop of their choice, would be eroded. By eliminating new protections for consumers with significantly weaker provisions, some of these protections are wiped out. This means that, for example, to make it real, some consumers will have to wait a week or more, or will have to drive more than 15 miles in urban areas or 25 miles in other parts of the state to merely get an estimate or an inspection of their damaged vehicle. Pivoting to the labor rate survey provisions of the legislation, ultimately, the labor rate survey provisions are really about insurers not particularly wanting to pay the prevailing wage to a body shop. Despite their currently unfettered ability to negotiate any rate they wish with any shop that they wish in the State of California. They can do that right now under the regs, they can negotiate whatever rate they want with whatever shop they want on a bilateral basis or whatnot. They can do that right now. That's unfettered by the regs. The labor rate provisions also treat as trade secrets, some information that in fact is not a trade secret. And that would not only shield it from the public, but in some cases, shield it from the department. We don't see how that is in consumers' best interest. Finally, it grants the equivalent of a Good Housekeeping seal of approval, the rebuttal presumption, on virtually any survey methodology. Irrespective if it's statistically valid or logically sound or mathematically accurate, and that's obviously a concern. So we respectfully, we would welcome the opportunity to speak with the author and the sponsors in more detail about this bill, but we respectfully oppose this morning, thank you Mister Chairman.

Ray Britain: Good morning, and thank you for this opportunity to speak. My name is Ray Britain. On December 2nd, 2015, I was the Interim Division Chief for the Division of Environmental Health Services in San Bernardino. County. At approximately 10:50 AM that morning, my whole life changed forever. We were taking a break between presentations, staff were mingling at their tables, some were outside taking pictures and others were in the restroom. Suddenly, we heard five to six very loud popping sounds coming from the east glass conference room door. This got everyone's attention. We were trying to process what the noise was when suddenly the door flung open, a person dressed in black with a ski mask came into the room. As soon as they entered the room, they began to shoot my staff. I sat frozen in disbelief at the front of the room watching all my staff as they were hit. Some fell immediately, some were thrown out of their chairs. I could see their bodies contort in unnatural ways. At some point I took cover and there were two now in the room. Everyone was lying on the ground, the concrete was vibrating as they swept the room and shot everyone lying defenselessly on the ground. The feeling that we had in that room of helplessness consumed us all. Anyone that moaned got shot, anyone that moved was shot. There was nowhere to go, we were trapped, we were helpless, we were vulnerable. I will never forget the feeling of helplessness that consumed me that day. The things that I saw, smelled, will haunt me for the rest of my life. What I witnessed that day was inhumane. I didn't believe that a human being would be capable of such an act. The helplessness and vulnerability that I felt that day has never left me. In fact, it has been worsened by the helplessness and vulnerability that I'd made to feel at the hands of our employer and the workman comp system. Consistently since the day of the shooting, we'd have to fight with both our employer and their self-funded workers' compensation program just to receive the basic care that we need. What we have gone through is unconscionable and has directly had a negative effect on our healing. Our treating physicians, psychiatrists, and therapists have all stated that the continuous fight we have had to endure has been detrimental to our recovery and has delayed and/or prohibited our ability to return to work. I returned to work the day after the incident, and remained until mid-January. I was not physically injured, but the psychological impact of this incident has been tremendous. I have been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder by my personal physician, my workers' compensation psychiatrist, and a therapist who I had to seek out on my own. Despite these diagnosis, utilization review has denied psychotherapy appointments for me and counseling since day one. I was then required to undergo a qualified medical examination to validate my PTSD diagnosis. Not only did this QME validate, for the fourth time, my PTSD diagnosis, the QME psychiatrist also recommended psychotherapy, again, which I've been denied since day one. Is it really hard to believe that we are actually traumatized from what happened that day? Here we are 16 months after the incident, and still we're struggling for basic health care needs. I wonder if we received continuous treatment the entire time, without delays, without denials from utilization review, would I have been able to return to work? I believe I would. Other members of my staff, they still have shrapnel and significant scar tissue that remains in their bodies. They, too, are being denied psychotherapy and treatment as a result of utilization review. In closing, I would like to reiterate the fact that how the workers' compensation system has been applied on these cases, does not make any sense. The process is failing to treat PTSD and the complex and undeniable physical and psychological injuries that occurred that day. You would think that with all the information available regarding PTSD and trauma, that care would have been provided. Instead, there are still staff members of mine that have not received psychological treatment because they have been overwhelmed fighting for treatment of their physical injuries. On December 2nd 2015, the Division of Environmental Health operated with 114 full-time employees. Today, of those 114 full-time employees it is my understanding that only 10 to 15 people have returned to work full-time without work restrictions. This is less than 13%. If the purpose of workmen compensation is to treat uninjured employees and return them to work as soon as possible, then clearly you can see by the numbers the program has failed. I have been assigned a case manager, my staff who have been physically injured have had case managers from day one. The case managers become just as frustrated with the process. It's the process. This is why I support AB 44 and I thank you very much for your time and your consideration.

But that might be a very, very small price to pay for the vast, vast majority of these workers who are suffering, who are, essentially through no voluntary moment of their own, put on the front lines of a combat situation without any of the tools that soldiers have to defend themselves. Mike Egan: Mr. Chair and members, good afternoon. I'm Mike Egan from the California Teachers Association. Senate Bill 78 seeks to grow the after-school education and safety program grants to keep up pace with increases in the minimum wage. The current ASES program was created by the voters when they passed Proposition 49 in 2002. The California Teacher's Association supported Prop 49, both for the objectives of the program and because it was carefully crafted to not crowd out funding for public education guaranteed under Proposition 98. Prop 49 ballot materials made this clear. The official title and summary explained that the measure quote requires that new funding for before, after school programs not be taken from education funding guaranteed under Proposition 98. Likewise, legislative analysts stated that the annual grow funds appropriated would quote, depend on the growth in general funds spending outside of Prop 98. In reviewing the text to Prop 49, the findings and declarations state, quote, although new funding of after school programs is extremely important, revenues guaranteed by law for a public school system pursuant to Proposition 98 should first be fully appropriated, and therefore not be used to increase the funding of these after school programs. The new funding for after school programs will therefore be funded above the legally required educational funding. The stated purpose of Prop 49 was to fund programs only out of growth and state revenues, and only after state revenues that are otherwise legally guaranteed to fund education programs have already been fully appropriated. This intent was memorialized in California Education Code section 8483.6 which states that the additional money for after school programs shall not be appropriated until a Legislature has appropriated sums sufficient to fully fund the requirements of Prop 98. And to be appropriated in addition to the sums required by and shall not be considered toward fulfilling the funding requirements of Prop 98. SB 78 as currently drafted would automatically fund additional appropriations from within 98 adversely affecting funding for all California students in other critical public education programs. CTA believes this would both violate the intent and letter of Prop 49. The expansion of funding for ASES must come from the general fund outside of Prop 98. Considering the proposed Pre-K, 12 education budget, CTA believes Prop 98 funding must prioritize to local control funding formula and must oppose SB 78 as currently drafted. We would like to continue to work with the author, but at this point, must respectfully ask for your no vote.

As you heard during last months remediation hearing, California's community colleges identify hundreds of thousands of students as not ready for transferred courses in math and English. Because these courses are required to transfer to a four year college, students deemed underprepared are required to take basic skills or remedial courses in order to prepare for college course. These placement decisions have profound effects a sizeable proportion of students that go into these remedial courses never actually complete the college level courses and subsequently completed degree. Despite the critical role of assessment and placement for placement to math English and ESL there's actually little clarity like Senator said. To help address this gap, last Spring PPIC conducted a survey of assessment and placement policies across the 113 colleges. We had 86 of the two colleges participate in the survey, and they had their chance to report on the policies and practices in place in 2014, 15 academic year. And the prodigal of this survey was, to provide policy makers and practitioners with a landscape of this, has made a placement policies in place across the sea. Among some of the findings, I'll highlight some of the findings from our report. First we found that colleges vary widely on how they assess and place students. We found that 100% of the colleges base their placements on the assessment instruments. Which assessed students math, English, math, reading, and writing skills. However, there's a wide variation on how colleges use these tests. We find that even though over half of the colleges use the Accuplacer the way they use this instrument varies. For example, in math we found that colleges, the variation in the cut scores could range from 25 to 296 out of 120. When you have a median of 58, this means that half of the students with a score of 58 would be deemed college ready, at half of the institutions. But was needing remediation at the other half. Yeah, and I also wanted to mention that there's wide variation in the retesting policies, as was cited in the legislation. Some colleges allow students to come back and retest immediately, while other colleges require students to wait three years. We also found that the use of multiple measures continues to sparse and unsystematic. I can say more if you have questions about that. There's some positive movement in that area. We also found that assessment and placement for ESL students needs more attention. Every year about 30,000 new ESL students enroll in these courses. And we find that these students are particularly disadvantaged because they have fewer opportunities to be examined from assessment and placement. We also found that they have fewer test prep opportunities, for example when we look at test prep in terms of test prep test, 40% of students in ESL were offered these were over 70% for math and English were offered for test prep opportunities. We also want to note that there's a lot of exciting reforms however there's still some opportunity for more uniformity and consistency because we found that when we do have this wide a variation. Where students enroll largely determines whether they are going to get access to college level courses or not. So there is some equity implications here. Because students of colour we found enroll in higher shares in college set more strict policies for access to transfer courses. So I just want to summarize, that assessment and placement policies should help students reach their academic goals, not stand in the way of these goals. As colleges work to enhance the efficacy of developmental education, implementation of evidence-based practices are accurately assessed and place students into, assess students' college readiness will be critical. And a more equitable and efficient system for assessment and placement is a vital step in helping all students achieve their goals.

Joe Cohn: Hi. Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee, my name is Joe Cohn, I'm the legislative and policy director at FIRE, the Foundation for Individual Rights in Education. And the second most common form of censorship on college campuses in 2017 is the restriction of students to quarantined zones that are misleadingly titled free speech zones. And in fact one in 10 colleges across the country do that according to our most recent data. What that tells me is two things. It's a significant problem, but that 90% of schools managed to deal without them without the sky falling and without any of the kind of chaos that people claim sometimes would happen if you were to allow people, gosh forbid, to engage in leafleting about vegan diets in other places on campus. So, we're really proud to be sponsors of this bill. It doesn't change at all what is and isn't protected speech. It just says that if you're engaged in the kind of protected speech, you should be allowed to do it freely on campus. It allows schools to have significant and reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions, so long as they're in furtherance of significant interests that they have and their content and viewpoint neutral, and leave open ample alternative modes for communication. So what means is if the school has a reason to keep students from having a huge, loud event immediately outside of the library, courts are going to agree that's a significant interest. That makes sense, or right outside of classrooms. But they can't use that justification on a school of 1,400 acres to say you're only allowed to speak in one spot. So, we want to flip the mindset. We want schools to decide, where are the few places where we have to have narrowly tailored rules? And all of the other places people are allowed to engage in speech as long as it is protected. So, that's the genesis of the bill. And the only other thing I want to add to this, because I think it's important for you to know is, why there's a need for the bill. Courts routinely strike down these policies, but it's very hard for students to really get into court. And these policies easily evade judicial review because students graduate and that moves out court cases. So one of the key features of the bill is it improves the mechanism here, by saying that there's a $500 automatic penalty when it's used against a student or when it's challenged, so the court still has to issue an order. And they can't go back and forth and just constantly put them in place, take them out of place temporarily. So, that's one of the key and most important features of the bill. And I really appreciate your attention to it, and I'm here to answer any of the hard questions you might have about how the first amendment interacts in this area.

Rand Martin : Thank you, Mr. Chair and members, Rand Martin on behalf of the California Charter Schools Association. First, for those of you who haven't been around very long, a little history lesson. This issue has been with us for about a decade. We have been working, Roger is nodding his head up there. We have been negotiating this. Working through the various pieces of this since about 2009 and what you see today reflects a lot of that negotiation. The negotiation occurred with the California School Boards Association and the California's Teacher Association and others over the last decade. So we have made a lot of progress, to the point where CCSA actually agrees, as we have for a number of years. That the Political Reform Act, Public Records Act, and the Brown Act should apply to charter schools. That level of transparency is critical. Some of the other things that are new that Senator Glazer has outlined in the bill are new this year but we support those as well. What it leaves us with is the one issue that has caused some friction over the years as we've tried to get this issue resolved once and for all. And that's the issue of government code 1090. And I'm going to speak a little bit about that, but my colleague here, Marcia Aaron from KIPP LA will also speak to it, because she has personal experience with it. But the important thing about government code 1090 is that it bans absolutely a charter school board member, and some executive staff, from participating in financial actions that accrue to the benefit of the charter school. So if you have a board member who has taken out a second mortgage on his home, and to help keep the doors open, under government code 1090, that board member would be prohibitive from doing that. Or would not be able to serve on the board, or if he did, it would go to jail. A board member who has a facility that he could lease to the school for a dollar a year, would be prohibited under government code 1090 from doing that. Those are the kinds of people that we want to have on our boards of directors. Many of you have sat on nonprofit boards of directors. I certainly have over the years. And I know the demands on us, as board members, is to do everything we can to keep that entity alive. And sometimes that goes beyond just raising funds. It also goes to taking extraordinary actions to make sure that the doors were open. When the state was in the depths of the recession, and the Legislature and the Governor were seeking deferrals on payments to schools, including charter schools. School districts were able to go out and get bridge loans of 2 and 3%. Charter schools were able to go out and get bridge loans of 13, and 14, and 15%. So of course was not appropriate and not helpful. And so, we had board members who were willing to step up and keep charter school doors open until the recession ended and the money started flowing again. So it's critically important that we don't take what we know is a good government measure but in this context is an impediment and a harm to charter schools, and impose that on them. The last thing I want to point on the issue of for profit is that this is an issue we have long believed that charter schools should not be operated by for-profit entities. We are there for the kids. The money is there for the kids. The money is not there to make a profit off of. It's great to have for profit vendors who will work with our schools and we think those should be continued. But the operation of the school itself should be left to a nonprofit entity. We have created some firewalls though to ensure that a for profit contractor can not through backdoor means exert undue influence. And there are three firewalls in there, one that prohibits them through engaging in selecting or influencing who's on the board of directors. Selecting, or approving, or vetoing a budget. Or supervising more than, according to the amendments that Senator Glazer has accepted, more than 25% of the teachers on staff in that charter school. So we think that both those deal with some very, very important issues. I do want to raise one additional point because a question has been raised that I want to make sure is answered. There is language in the bill that occupies the field of conflict of interest language. In the print version it also occupies the field of open meetings and Public Records Act. In an agreement with the Chair last night we have decided to limit that occupy the field language to just conflict of interest. That means that the authority for a school district to impose additional requirements on open meeting or public records will be restored to the school district in the context of the amendments that Senator Glazer has just accepted. So it is broadening transparency back to where it was under current law, rather than restricting it on the open meetings and public records. And I will close with that and be available for any questions when appropriate.

Jessica Stender: Thank you Mr. Chair and Members of the Committee. My name is Jessica Stender. I'm an attorney at Equal Rights Advocates. We're a non-profit organization based in San Francisco. Our mission is to protect and expand economic and educational access for women and girls. We regularly serve women and girls who experience discrimination, including sexual violence and harassment on college campuses as well as in K through 12 schools. Today I'm going to discuss why SB 169 is so necessary to fill a gap in California, relating to protections against sex discrimination including sexual harassment and violence. And really why it's so critical now more than ever given the likely roll backs of protections and enforcement of these rights at the federal level.. While sex harassment has long been recognized as a form of prohibited sex discrimination under Title IX, sexual harassment and violence in schools and colleges is rampant. You've heard some of the statistics here. You read about it all the time. At least one in five young women will be subjected to an attempted or a completed rape during her college years. On large campuses, this translates to hundreds of attempted or completed rapes every year. While it is often less well-known, sexual harassment and sexual violence also plague K-12 schools. A survey of the American Association of University Women of over 1,000 K-12 students, in 2011, found that nearly half of the students from middle school through high school experienced some form of sexual harassment during their school year. According to a 2014 study by the University of Illinois, 21% of middle school students who were surveyed from the sample of nearly 1,400 students reported that they experienced unwanted physical touching on school grounds. We have a hotline, a nationwide hotline, but particularly focused in California, and we receive calls from students K through 12 and college level who have experienced horrific sexual harassment and sexual violence at their schools. And the calls really demonstrate the need for the kinds of guidance that this SB 169 would require schools to have. One California high school student we were contacted by was raped by a group of other students at a party. When another student reported to the school, a single school administrator was allowed to make a determination after engaging in informal interviews with the student who had been raped and the alleged perpetrators. Without conducting any formal investigation other than these informal conversations. The administrator determined that the victim should take time off from school while the rumors, quote, subsided and the students forgot about what had happened. She was provided with no accommodations to complete her school work during the time she was off, and when she returned to school she was placed in classes with her alleged assailants. Another call was from a California college student who was sexually assaulted by members of the school rugby team in her dorm room. When she reported it to her RA, the school disciplined her and expelled her for having violated their sexual conduct policy by inviting boys into her room. These stories indicate the types of guidance that are necessary for schools in terms of how to deal with sexual harassment and sexual violence. We also receive requests from Title IX administrators themselves, and coordinators themselves, of how to comply with Title IX requirements. Especially at the K through 12 level, Title IX coordinators are often full-time employees whose duties generally differ from Title IX enforcement. And in some cases they're provided little or no training. In a 2014 study and report that we conducted with the law firm of Morrison and Foerster, we surveyed all various school districts. And documented a startling unawareness, lack of awareness, among the area school administrators regarding the basic requirements of Title IX and their duties under Title IX. Some didn't even know that they needed a Title IX coordinator. And some Title IX coordinators didn't even know that they had been assigned this role. So why this guidance is so important, California has analogous laws to Title IX that prohibit discrimination in academic settings. However, California does not set forth how local schools and institutions can comply with these laws. This is why Title IX's implementing regulations and regulatory guidance provided by the Office for Civil Rights has been so critical, and is so critical that it is codified in California law. Title IX's implementing regulations require that schools take immediate steps to end harassment, prevent any discriminatory effects from the harassment, and prevent its recurrence. Thus, the regulations require schools not only to appropriately respond to allegations of sexual violence, but to also take action to address what is often a kind of broader culture of sexual violence in these schools. Finally, the regulations require, as Senator Jackson referenced, prompt and equitable investigation and grievance procedures for the resolution of students' sexual violence and harassment complaints. And this is an area in which schools really indicated the need for guidance. They know they're required under the law to have these prompt and equitable investigation agreements procedures, but they don't know how to do it. And so what the Dear Colleague Letter does, the 2011 Dear Colleague letter does, is set forth how schools can comply with these requirements under the law. It also addresses unique concerns that arise in sexual violence cases. Such as a school's independent responsibility to investigate. Allegations of sexual violence independent from any police investigation of such claims. It discusses proactive measures that schools can take to prevent sexual violence, and examples of remedies and enforcement strategies that schools may implement. And finally, it addresses that critical question of what a prompt and equitable grievance procedure might entail, and provides schools with this guidance that they need. So very quickly, these requirements provide this helpful guidance in saying notice to students of the grievance procedure, application of that procedure. Detailed explanation to students that both parties are allowed to present witnesses and testimony, prompt timelines, and notice of the outcome of any proceeding to all students. So this clear guidance has been critical for schools in knowing how to evaluate their own internal Title IX procedures. Finally, I'll just note that there's a very imminent rollback of these protections and the enforcement by OCR at the federal level. We know from what we've heard that OCR is critical to enforcing these laws. Theyve opened more than 340 investigations regarding mishandling of sexual violence complaints, and more than 200 of these investigations remain pending. Their intervention has been critical for victims to get some kind of relief under Title IX. However, were facing a very likely rollback of these protections. President Trump has said he would eliminate the Department of Education entirely, calling it, quote, massive and largely unnecessary. One of his advisors during the presidential campaign called the Office for Civil Rights unnecessary, and self-perpetuating absolute nonsense. Secretary of Education DeVos testified during her confirmation hearings that it was premature to say whether she would uphold the 2011 Dear Colleague guidance. And her first official policy as Secretary was to rescind federal guidelines related to transgender rights under Title IX. Finally, just last week, Secretary DeVos met with a Georgia State Representative who is suing the Department of Education over this very important guidance. So, all these indications show that this very critical guidance for schools, at the federal level, is likely to be rolled back. And really requires the implementation of SB 169 to guide schools in California as to their obligations under these laws, and to address this epidemic of sexual violence. So we therefore urge your aye vote, thank you.

Dan Roth: Good morning, Chairman Allen, Vice Chair Wilk, distinguished members. My name is Dan Roth. I am a criminal defense lawyer in Berkley. I applaud Senator Jackson and President Pro-tem De Leon for taking on the very serious issues of sexual harassment and sexual assault in our schools. Equal educational opportunity for people of all sexes and gender identities is a necessity. And harassment and assault can profoundly undermine and even destroy the student experience. Senate Bill 169 however is not the answer to these serious legal and cultural problems of sex, power, and violence that have challenged human beings since time memorial. I myself am a proud feminist and a fervent advocate for equality under the law for all. I am the immediate past chair of the Bay Area Lawyer Chapter of the American Constitution Society, a nationwide network of progressive lawyers and law students. And a racial justice advocate with Black Out for Human Rights and the Ella Baker Center for Human Rights. Today I speak only for myself, but my work with and for these organizations and the values they hold dear informs my testimony. Over the past three years, I have represented respondents in Title IX investigations at public and private universities around the Bay Area and beyond, from Sacramento to Silicon Valley. I have yet to see a Title IX investigation handled in a way that would make the people of the State of California either proud or satisfied that if their son or daughter was accused, they could get a fair shake. Instead, I have witnessed a system that lacks basic due process protections and that is driven by fear. Under the system created by the US Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights' 2011 Dear Colleague Letter, schools are terrified that they will lose funding if they are not perceived as cracking down on sexual harassment and sexual assault. And the schools act like it. Evidence is withheld and destroyed, conflicts of interest are bound, and justice is simply not achieved. The disciplinary system created by the Dear Colleague Letter is not the answer to the very real problems SB 169 seeks to address. Far from a federal regulation, the Dear Colleague Letter is an informal and vague set of policy instructions that has created a system lacking any of the checks that we as Americans normally require when we render potentially life changing discipline against our fellow citizens. The Dear Colleague Letter directs schools to conduct prompt and equitable investigations, but does not provide specific guidance as to how to carry out those investigations. It sets a preponderance of evidence standard, but does not instruct investigators how to weigh and evaluate evidence. There are no rules of evidence at all. Nothing to tell inexperienced, untrained investigators what is relevant, what is hearsay, or how to judge witness credibility. And it does not guarantee that respondents will ever have the opportunity to review the evidence used against them or to cross examine witnesses. The one very clear message sent by the Dear Colleague Letter to college campuses was, get tough or you will lose your federal funding. As heroes like Michelle Alexander and Ava Duverner have demonstrated in their masterful works, the new Jim Crow and 13th, getting tough in America always results in gravely disproportionate government enforcement against people of color. We in California have made mistakes, like three strikes, that we ought not repeat. A disciplinary system unmoored from our most basic due process protections and imbued with a clear monetary incentive toward findings of guilt will simply deepen the racial disparities in our educational and criminal justice systems. I, therefore, urge the members of this Committee to put a halt to this well-intentioned bill, the effect of which will be to simply strengthen the school to prison pipeline, which we ought to be dismantling root and branch. I urge the Committee to oppose SB 169 and would be happy to respond to any questions you may have. Thank you for your time and for your service to the people of the State of California.

Eric Wolf: Thank you. Thanks for the opportunity to address the Committee and respectfully request your support of SB 633. I'm Eric Wolf with the San Gabriel Valley Council of Governments. The current storm water permitting system for Los Angeles County highly encourages capture and infiltration as a means of limiting downstream pollution. An additional benefit of that system is that it augments local water supplies and both of these are noble goals, and we support them, but we want to find a manner that does this in a reasonable, practical, feasible, and affordable manner. The flood control system for LA County is an amalgamation of under-street storm drains, open channels, and riverbeds. Most segments of this system are regulated by water quality standards and pollutants are measured at downstream locations, receiving waters, as they're known. Any exceedance of a water body pollution standard constitutes a violation. For this reason, the LA Regional Water Board is driven towards disallowing the use of the existing flood control system to convey polluted water to sites that more economically capture and infiltrate. As you heard from Council Member Mahmud earlier, to recreate that system at local jurisdictions, county public works has projected that cost at over 20 billion. And just within San Gabriel Valley, it's estimate about $6 billion. So we worked with the Senator's office to draft the bill to continue to use the existing flood control system in order to accomplish our water quality goals in a far more cost effective manner. There's three good reasons to support centralized capture versus localized capture. The first is that we don't really need to rebuild what we already have. That would be redundant. In fact, the cost of capture at the local level is far higher on a per acre foot of water basis. Metropolitan Water District has calculated that an acre foot of water derived from a local source is 250% higher than water generated from a larger downstream project, a centralized collection. The next reason to support this is that we already have a system. It's been in use for over 50 years, and it's been effective and it continues to be what we use right now while we're sorting through how to create an additional way of capturing upstream at the local level and so before we get rid of that system, we should try and squeeze out every advantage that it gives us. And then finally, 633 is a tool for the Regional Board to use. They have to maintain water quality standards on one hand and at the same time, they want to enhance local water supplies through capture. 633 doesn't force the board to opt for moving storm water from one place to another. Instead, it recognizes and respects their judgement when considering the benefits derived from conveying water through this system in order to maintain water quality standards. If, in their determination, water can be moved and infiltrated at a downstream site with little to no ultimate detriment to water quality, then the board should have that flexibility to consider those proposals. So, Senators, thank you for your time, and I ask you for an aye vote.

Ben Eichenberg: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Chair and members. I would like to add my thanks to staff for your work on this bill. As the Senator said, my name is Ben Eichenberg, I'm with San Francisco Baykeeper. As it's been made clear, by the Senator, California needs additional protection in the event of a spill of tar sands, crude, and other non-floating oils. In response to concerns about the risks posed by tar sands spills, the National Academy of Sciences studied the environmental fate of spilled tar sands oil. It turns out, not all oil is the same. There are substantial differences in the chemical composition of tar sands and its behavior when released into the environment when compared to conventional crudes. Tar sands oil is often more dense than water. Its adhesion is up to 100 times greater than conventional oils. It creates sticky and easily submerged residues when burned and it does not quickly biodegrade. Tar sands will sink into the water column or to the bottom of water bodies as its lighter dilutents evaporate. Yet tankers entering California waters do not announce on their manifest what kind of crude they are carrying, so responders may not know what kind of oil they are cleaning up until hours into a response. The National Academy of Science has found that current emergency approaches are based on floating oil, so regulations and agency practices do not take the unique properties of tar sands into account, nor do they encourage effective planning for spills. Tar sands refining could increase drastically in California if existing pipeline and rail plans move forward, leading to an eight-fold increase in Canadian production. This increased production could mean more than 2,000 additional barges and tankers carrying tar sands crude to and from refineries on the West Coast in the coming decade. Each tanker trip carries an added risk of a spill. For reference, the tar sands spill the Senator referred to, the Kalamazoo, cost over $1 billion, still isn't cleaned up, with only 843,000 gallons. Even the smallest tar sands barge entering San Francisco Bay or the Port of Los Angeles would carry at least twice that amount. Ocean cleanup is far more difficult than a confined river bed. California's $46 billion coastal economy has a lot to lose to a spill. After the Costco Busan disaster spilled 53,000 gallons of oil into San Francisco Bay, the Governor closed the fishery and more than 50 public beaches. All told, that spill cost more than $73 million. Imagine that times 267, the amount of oil carried by a fully laden coastal tanker and instead of over a month to clean up, try five years. If we're going to ship this stuff through San Francisco Bay, we need to put our best scientists into imagining these scenarios and figuring out a plan to reduce the catastrophic damage that could result from an accident. By passing SB 709, the State of California will be taking a leadership role in addressing the regulatory gap identified by the National Academy of Scientists and ensuring that emergency responders have the tools that they need. I also respectfully ask for your aye vote.

Ellison Folk: Yes. Good morning. Ellison Folk, and I'm a partner at Chupmahaly and Wineburger. I represent both community groups and environmental groups and public agencies in the CEQA process. And I've been practicing CEQA law for over 25 years. And I will say that one of my eternal frustrations is when an agency uses illegal or unpermitted conditions as part of the baseline for evaluating the environmental impacts of a project. Now as a general rule, CEQA does normally require agencies to look at existing environmental conditions when evaluating the impacts of a project. However, the California Supreme Court has made very clear that existing conditions should not be used where they provide a misleading impression of a projects impacts. If your comparing project to illegal activities or unpermitted activities. You cannot provide an accurate view of the project's impacts or impose adequate mitigation measures. But not withstanding the Supreme Court's directive regarding the misleading use of the baseline, agencies repeatedly use illegal or un-permitted activities as the baseline. Or pressure put on them by applicants to do so. For example, in Napa County, where I do a lot of work, wineries routinely exceed the limits of their use permits, with respect to the number of events they can hold, or the amount of wine they can produce. And then, when they're caught, and they come in for a permit amendment the county uses the illegal or un-permitted activities such as the baseline, finds that there is no significant impact and no need for mitigation. And that system creates perverse incentives that reward people who violate the law and their permits, and it's inconsistent with the ultimate goal of CEQA which is to ensure informed decision making and mitigation of impacts. And I'd like to just briefly respond to the Cal Chambers comments that were submitted on this in opposition. Which focus on the alleged impact of this on development on brownfields or in fill development. Particularly Cal Chamber claims that SB 224 will interfere with existing laws that assign liability for the clean up of contaminated sites. But this is a total red herring. Nothing in SB 224 assigns liability to any parties with respect to the remediation of a site. In fact, under current law and as a practical matter, when someone is developing a contaminated site, they have to deal with the contamination issues. It maybe that a prior responsible party can be identified or not. But CEQA review is not going to change that relationship. And on the mitigation end If something's identified that is the responsibility of another party, and it can be shown that the mitigation would be unconstitutional, or that the agency does not or cannot require it to be implemented, CEQA itself does not provide the independent authority to impose mitigation. But again as a practical matter, if a developer wants to build a residential project on a contaminated site, that developer needs to deal with the problem under existing law. And there's nothing in SB224 that is going to change that reality. Finally, SB224 is a directive to OPR which is part of the resources agency to prepare guidelines to address this issue. This direction to the resources agency is a mechanism that CEQA often uses to address complicated issues like this. For example, section 21083 of the act Is a directive to the resources agency to adopt guidelines, SB 743 did a similar thing with EMT issues, and the resources agency in OPR is more than capable of drafting guidelines that strike the appropriate balance between. That reflect the consistent direction of the California Supreme Court to use an accurate and appropriate baseline while at the same time, recognizing the practical realities of environmental review. Thank you.

[{'start': 0, 'end': 11, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Diana Mahmud: Thank you Senator, Honorable Chair Committee Members, this is my second time up, Diana Mahmud, on behalf of the City of South Pasadena and San Gabriel Valley. Council of Governments, I speak in support of SB 589 sponsored by the LA County Division of the League of California Cities. This bill is intended to afford flexibility to extend the timeline for compliance with a storm water permit based upon a city's demonstrated financial need. Many LA County cities face extraordinary storm water compliance estimates exceeding several $100 million each. That's the capital cost alone. These high costs are especially challenging for disadvantaged communities who already struggle to provide basic municipal services. California cities, however, are not alone in facing extraordinary estimated costs in achieving clean water act compliance for storm water. This is a problem repeated in many areas of the country. In response, in November 2014, The US CPA released a financial capability assessment framework for municipal clean water act requirements. In a recent California presentation on funding storm water, region nine EPA staff described the FCA, the Financial Capability Assessment, as providing regulators with the flexibility to consider a municipal Committee's ability to pay for and deliver water services. It considers various measures of a household's ability to pay for services as well as the community's financial ability to deliver services, including the cost of achieving safe drinking water at compliance. The FDA does not, as asserted by some, weaken permit conditions. It only allows for an extended timeline for compliance based upon demonstrated financial need. I know an opposition letter critiques the FCA's affordability indicator based upon the argument that tenants do not pay water cost through the rental rates. This is fantasy. FCA methodology is sound and it should be applied here in California. SBA 589 was recently amended to provide for the state board's determination of financial capability assessment guidelines. And to establish a pilot project conducted by an educational entity to assess the LA regional board's use for the financial guidelines. The bill directs the State Board to make statewide recommendations regarding use of the financial guidelines upon completion of the financial capability analysis. This bill is focused on LA County since those cities face the strictest storm water standards in the nation. The State Board has importantly already signaled. It is considering statewide adoption of the same approach, storm water capture and infiltration, featured in the LA county permit as a means of achieving water quality compliance statewide. So this is of concern for everyone. The regions of the state will benefit, from the knowledge and experience gained through this pilot project. SB 589 offers a common sense approach to the high estimated cost to municipal storm water permanent compliance and will be particularly helpful to California's disadvantaged communities. It does not alter or waive water quality standards and its methodology is sound. South Pasadena and the San Gabriel Valley CoG, as well as a league of California cities, LA county division respectfully asks for your aye vote.

Scott Kernan: Thank you, Madame Chair and members. My name is Scott Kernan. I'm the secretary of the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation. And Madame Chair, I will attempt to address that issue. CDCR submitted emergency regs to the Office of Administrative Law about 20 days ago. It's really a monumental shift in how we are going to incarcerate in this state. We're creating a system of individual responsibility and expanding opportunity for parole suitability and early release by offenders. It requires, I mean it's requiring a sustained positive behavior on our offender population and requiring them to do something with their incarceration. I would not categorize it as soft on crime but smart on crime. The Governor has continued to emphasize throughout this process that public safety is a paramount responsibility. We have 160 days from just a couple of days ago, and the possibility of 2 90-day extensions to implement permanent regs. We will go through a process of public comment. We will have public hearings and we will accept information and suggestions from the variety of diverse stakeholders that we have in our state concerning corrections. I'd like to explain a little bit how we got to these emergency regs. Senior level executives from the administration and CDCR have met with the variety of stakeholders in a series of meetings. We explained how our credits, our complicated credit system is derived currently. We solicited ideas from a variety of stakeholders and we shared the regs, the emergency regs that we developed and submitted 20 days ago. While this is not a whole list, they included law enforcement, Das, public defenders, counties and cities, inmate advocates, victims, labor, legislatures, CDCR staff, and even inmates. We attempted to strike a balance while maintaining public safety. In a couple weeks, on May 1st, 80,000 inmates in our system's dates will change to the positive. I'm very proud of the really year-long effort to implement this historic reforms. And it really has been a Herculean effort, Madame Chair. We've had to develop these regulations through this collaborative process that I mentioned. We've had to completely rework our IT system and our sentencing calculation in really a period of 90 to 120 days. We've had to train thousands of staff. We've had to negotiate with our labor organizations to implement these reforms. The fact is we had to do something historic as a state. The old system wasn't working, overcrowding, violence. I think we were turning out a better criminal as a department. We were failing as a Department of Corrections in my mind. There was not a lot of hope in this system, we had punitive sentencing. And we got what we sowed, bad public policy, expensive correction system, and a failed system. One of the issues that I've been asked many times is, do we have enough rehabilitative programs? And I think including from this panel. And I think the short answer to that question is no. And the corresponding question is, why did we not have a budget request for Prop 57? When we met the first time in the scrutiny over our budget, I left that hearing thinking I made a pretty good decision. And that decision was based upon this body has given us a $100 million in current year and $8.5 million in budget year to implement rehabilitative programs in our system. We have been working diligently to implement academic vocational, substance abuse, cognitive behavior, arts programs, innovative grants, college, and many other programs throughout our system. Before we were going to ask for more money, we need to be able to spend the money that you gave us and to implement those programs. I feel as if there's a solid base of rehabilitative programs in our system, but I think much more can be done. Expanded technology, because of the space and time constraints in our prison, evaluate programs and evolve what works, continue improvements with our staff to accept rehabilitative programs as good prison business. We expect future requests in the future, but we're just not ready to make a budget request for additional rehabilitative programs at this point. I'd like to conclude by saying nowhere the nation has a system so significantly been changed so fast. I think that we have impacted hope into the inmate population. We incentivize participation in programs. We've required achievement to earn parole suitability or early release, and we have required disciplinary-free behavior of our prisons. As a result, I think we're going to have safer prisons for our staff and our inmates. I think we're putting discretion to our correctional professionals who are better positioned to make decisions. We found a durable solution and a path out of our costly court oversight. We've avoided indiscriminate release of offenders by the federal court. We have allowed the return of inmates from out of state, as was mentioned previously. I think that the cost to get to your central point in current year, those costs will be expanded. We expect 2,000 reduction of growing to 9,500 in 2021, but those were based on the Jan 10 budget. We've exceeded expectations in my mind of implementation. We are, again, two weeks from now, we'll implement good conduct credits. In July, the parole, non-violent parole process. And in August, milestones, enhanced milestones In rehabilitative achievement credits or self help credits. I think we told you at the last hearing that our projections were very preliminary, and that they will be modified as we go forward. And I believe that in the May revise you will see an update of those numbers that I just mentioned. And as we implement this going forward and we expand our rehabilitative programs, I think we're going to see a greater population reduction and greater cost reductions to your point. So with that, thank you very much, and I'd be happy to try to answer any questions you might have.

[{'start': 15, 'end': 26, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 431, 'end': 434, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Josh Garner: Josh Garner, Department of Finance, so we wanted to lay out a little bit of the technical details of the proposal. There certainly are quite a few technical details of it, and it's a quite complex pay differential, and some of the details are still being discussed and worked out with the CalPERS and CalHR. So there's understandably some differences in the understanding of exactly how the proposal would work. So I just wanted to take a couple of minutes to outline how we're currently envisioning the pay differential rolling out. And as the secretary mentioned, it would be four captains, three wardens, and includes additional headquarters positions that are in this chain of command. And it would be a 2% pay differential increase per year for three years. So the first year, an individual in these classifications would earn 2%, the second year would earn 4%, and the third year would earn 6%. But none of the pay differentials would be considered what we call PERSable or would count towards an individual's final calculation towards their retirement calculation until they have served 36 consecutive months in a classification. So that can be achieved a couple of ways. You could envision someone in a classification for only a single year before promoting to the next. And in that scenario, we would envision the pay differential going with them, and they would continue on their path to earning 6%. Meaning, they would earn 2% the first year, promote, move up to 4% the second year, and 6% in addition. However, in that scenario, again, until an individual serves 36 consecutive months in the classification, it would not be considered towards their final compensation. Alternatively, if an individual served 36 consecutive months in one of these classifications and then promoted, we would envision that the 6% that they had worked towards would continue with them on their promotions. So they would still earn 6% in the additional classification. However, the 6% at that new higher salary in the higher classification would not be, again, PERSable towards final compensation until the individual serves 36 months again in that classification. So we not only, as mentioned, the multiple challenges the department is facing, we not only thinking will help incentivize individuals to promote from the lieutenant to captain rank. But we also think it will incentivize individuals to stay and have the department benefit from their expertise and seniority once they have been in a position. So happy to answer any additional questions on the technical details of the proposal.

SB 131 would approve the memorandum of understanding that has been reached between the administration and the employees of bargaining unit 16, the Union of American Physicians and Dentists. To this end, the bill seeks to make the necessary statutory changes to implement these agreements. The MOU covers approximately 1,600 rank and file employees throughout the state. Over the course of this contract, the MOU will provide general salary increases ranging from 2% to 3% annually, as well as special salary adjustments to targeted groups of employees intended to address recruitment and retention issues. In addition to these economic provisions, the MOU includes agreements to participate in the administration strategy for addressing the state's $76 billion unfunded liability for post-employment benefits. The strategy for addressing this liability includes equal cost sharing between the employee and employer to prefund retiree health benefits, and for new employees extending the period to qualify for retiree health benefits as well as reducing the employer subsidy for retiree health benefits. The Bill also excludes new employees from receiving reimbursement of their Medicare part B premiums. With that, we're happy to answer any questions.
[{'start': 59, 'end': 68, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Greg Krotoll: Greg Krotoll with the Department of Finance. So, the calculation for OPEB contributions is based on looking at the employee group, and their overall normal costs, and the unfunded liability for that group of employees, and then, relative to that, the overall salaries for those employees as well. So, generally speaking, when you have a group of employees that have a larger salary, the contribution is less to pay down that unfunded liability versus those who make a smaller average salary. So that's why you see this group makes a particularly less contribution than others. As well as the fact that they began pre-funding OPEB contributions back in 2013. So this group of employees has been contributing 0.5% of their base pay since 2013. So, that's also included in there, and why you see their rate is lower than others.

Darren Bowden: Thank you, Chair, thank you, Committee. Darren Bowden with Southern California Edison. All due respect, no one is doubting energy storage is importance. No one is doubting the role that we all probably believe that energy storage needs to play in the future. But I think we also need to look at kind of where we are currently and where maybe we need to go. From our perspective, we're bullish on storage. I think our record of implementation of storage over the last couple of years shows that. We just don't think that SB 700 is currently necessary. We think the costs of storage are expected to decline by significant amounts within the next several years. There are efforts underway already to integrate storage at the PUC and Cal ISO. We don't think that California needs more storage mandates, at least at this time. At a minimum, SB 700 seems premature and should be deferred. Just to remind everybody, there have been at least three recent bills passed to foster increased energy storage adoption. Two passed just last year. Senator Skinner, when she was Assemblymember Skinner, had AB 2514 which created storage targets for the state. Subsequently, the PUC directed the IOUs to procure over 1300 megawatts by 2024. Edison's target is 580 megawatts. We've already contracted for over 400 megawatts and it's 2017, so we're very well ahead of schedule. AB 2868, Gatto last year required the PUC to direct utilities to propose programs and investments including customer side storage. And then just a reminder, SB 1637 was adapted last year which expanded rebates for SGIP through 2019. The other thing that I would like to add is that all three IOUs currently have applications pending before the CPUC that greatly improves the storage economics by shifting peak period pricing to later in the day. In terms of the cost of this program, we believe that it will potentially be costly for customers. Depending on the math, from the Committee analysis it looks like SB 7 would require somewhere between $660 million or to up of $1 plus billion over the next 10 years. It doesn't necessarily have provisions to ensure that the program meets GHG goals, supports grid needs, or is cost-effective. And on the SB 1637 implementation, just to note, less than 2 weeks ago the CPUC just adopted or authorized almost $200 million between 2017 and 2019 for battery storage in an SGIP decision. So I guess the question kind of becomes, why do we need to increase this now? Why do we need to create a 10-year program now? I don't even know if I want to spend a whole lot of time in suggesting that it's duplicative of the efforts in SB 350 because I think this Committee has probably heard that one a lot with the IRP. But we still do believe that that's the issue. And then last thing that I want to say is I don't disagree with anybody in this room that the California Solar Initiative was a successful program. However, was it the main thing that actually got more PV out there? And was it the main thing that drove that down costs? I would argue no. I would argue a 20% RPS, then a 33% RPS, then a 50% RPS had much more about trying to drop or affecting the cost of PV and dropping those costs. I would also suggest that from a customer-sided, solar perspective, the CSI was not the only driver. It was combined with NEM tax credits and time of use rates. So that industry was so heavily subsidized to drive down cost, it wasn't just because of the CSI. So I guess the question now is, do we need this program now or should we let the existing stuff run for a while and maybe target that as we go? Finally, I guess my question is just from our perspective, we're just kind of wondering when enough is enough. Thanks.

When I came to America in 1949 I didn't have $6 to get off the boat. My late husband was put in jail by the communists in Czechoslovakia because they confiscated a business and he didn't join. I'm a survivor and I don't say, why me, I say, what now. And so I packed up I knew I had to do something. I went to the jail. I took off my big diamond ring. I gave it to the warden. Laura Feinstein: I'm Doctor Laura Feinstein. I am a senior research associate with the Pacific Institute. We're a global water think tank. I was one of the lead authors of the SB for scientific assessment of well stimulation that was commissioned by the California Natural Resources Agency. At the time of the report, I was affiliated with California Council on Science and Technology. And they've asked me to speak about the report today. CCST does not endorse bills. I'm here to describe the findings and recommendations made in the report that are relevant to today's discussion. In SB 4 report, we were tasked with evaluating the impact to the environment and human health by well stimulation, specifically the practice of hydraulic fracturing or as people commonly refer to it, fracking. We found that we could not accurately assess the hazard of chemical releases to the environment because of the number of data gaps. One of these gaps was that we did not know the identity of all chemicals used in the oil and gas production process. As you may know, SB 4 requires disclosure for chemicals that are used specifically for well stimulation. SB 1281 requires reporting of the treatment and disposal of waste water from oil and gas production wells. However neither one of these bills requires that producers disclose the identity and quantity of chemicals used for purposes other than well stimulation. To remedy this data gap we made recommendation 4.2, which was that the state require reporting of all significant chemical use including acids for oil and gas development. Thank you very much.

[{'start': 49, 'end': 64, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Tanya Gulesserian: Good afternoon, Madam Chair, Members of the Committee. My name is Tanya Gulesserian, I'm here on behalf of the State Building & Construction Trades Council of California and the California Labor Federation. You've hard from Assemblymember Medina, Ms. Hasson about what AB 890 does and why it's so vitally important. I will be speaking what the bill does not do in response to the opposition. First, AB 890 does not outline all initiatives. In fact, most initiatives will not be affected by AB 890 since they do not constitute projects under CEQA. What constitutes a project is well defined, its impacts must be reasonably foreseeable. It's concerned with direct physical changes in the environment or indirect physical changes, not social and economic impacts. Finally, there are numerous exemptions from environmentally beneficial projects. It is certainly not the intent of the legislation to capture all initiatives and we, to the extent that there are more initiatives captured, then we intended, we are working with the environmental groups to determine a way to prevent this. Second, AB 890 would not lead to pre-election litigation, the CEQA Notice of Determination cannot be filed until after the initiative is directly adopted, or the election results are certified. Third, other environmental laws are not enough to protect public health and the environment. CEQA fills in the gaps where other environmental laws do not regulate, and not all initiatives will trigger Endangered Species Act or clean air act. Fourth, AB 890 does not violate the constitution. The Legislature has the constitutional authority to limit the initiative process because it has declared that environmental protection and public health is a matter of state wide concern. Finally, we understand the concern about not having some initiatives go to the voters. While the Legislature has the authority to restrict initiatives for projects with significant public health and environmental impacts, we are open to amendments to ensure that all initiatives go to the voters once the environment or review has occurred.

AB 36 would remedy a disparity by enabling products that have the same fuel input and meet the same strict emission standards to compete on an equal playing field. Furthermore, it would permit all California entities interested in on site generation to be environmental stewards. We respectfully request that you vote aye on AB 36.

[{'start': 0, 'end': 11, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Marc Joffe: Thank you, Mr. Chair. My name is Marc Joffe. I'm the Director of Policy Research for the California Policy Center, a non-partisan think tank. Before becoming a policy researcher, I was a senior director at Moody's Analytics. Given this background, I thought it would be most useful for me to address the financing cost reporting aspect of Assembly Member Patterson's bill. Last week's High-Speed Rail Bond issue is illustrative of the need for greater transparency around the project's financing plans. Although the Treasurer completed the sale of these bonds last week, we still do not know their total service and costs. The preliminary official statement included a blank debt service schedule and blank underwriter fee. Later this week, we should see an official statement with the blanks filled in. From the preliminary official statement, and information available from industry media, we know that the $1.248 billion offering had some unusual features. Most notable is the fact that the bonds are federally taxable even though the state had the option to issue tax-exempt securities, potentially at lower cost. That said, yields on the new bonds appear to be quite reasonable, perhaps because they were sold to yield-hungry overseas investors who cannot take advantage of the federal tax exemption. I estimate the lifetime interest costs on these bonds will be about $140 million, which seems relatively low. One way the state achieves such modest debt service costs is that it plans to retire much of the issue well before the 2047 final maturity date. In fact, $648 million of the bonds mature between 2018 and 2022, well before high-speed rail is expected to begin operations. Principal and interest payments on these shorter term bonds must come from General Fund tax revenues. Although $300 million of the bonds are variable rate securities paying 78 basis points above one month US LIBOR, currently this rate is just under 1%, making these securities a very good deal for the state, yielding only 1.77% to investors. However, a sudden rise in short-term rates could result in much higher costs for taxpayers. Going forward, the Authority has discussed the possibility of securitizing cap and trade revenues, and/or operating revenues. Relative to general obligation bonds, securitizations are more complex, require additional administrative effort, and pose greater risk for investors. As a result, securitization deals have higher financing costs. The gap in financing costs widens as securitized revenue streams become more uncertain. Recently, cap and trade revenues have proved quite uncertain. According to a recent LAO report, the last four cap and trade auctions earned the state $10, $8, $364, and $8 million, respectively. Barring miraculous results in the May auction, total cap and trade revenues for this fiscal year will come in well below budget. Investors will likely demand strong protections or higher interest rates to advance money against such a volatile revenue stream. Future high-speed rail business plans should address this concern. I just want to conclude by saying that I appreciate the motivations of some who wish to defend the high-speed rail project against the additional level of transparency and oversight in AB 66. Looking at such engineering marvels as the Golden Gate Bridge and the Los Angeles Aqueduct, it's reasonable to ask, what great public works can we leave for our children and grandchildren and to become frustrated with those who might impede the creation of this new legacy. But in the decades since the early 20th century, public policymakers have developed the discipline of cost benefit analysis. We owe it to future generations to conduct cost benefit analysis on major projects in a thorough and transparent manner. It is only by following this discipline that we can honestly say that the debts we leave our descendants were justified by the projects we created for them. Thank you very much.
