June Lopez: Thank you, there's a motion in the second. Good afternoon Mr. Chair and Members of the Committee. My name's June Lopez and I'm with Moulton Niguel Water District, and I thank you for this opportunity to spoke to speak in support of the long term efficiency framework. I'm not speaking in support or in opposition to any of the bills because I do realize that with all the discussion it might be helpful to have a little brief recap of how we got here and what the framework is trying to do. The last three years have been very challenging, but we did a lot and we Learned a lot from From that. And some of the lessons that we Learned, is that percentage reduction across the board is very challenging for water agencies. Because it doesn't recognize the past and present investment in water efficiency programs. We also heard from our stakeholders, our customers, the public, who really didn't understand how the percentages apply to them in terms of individual action in achieving efficiency. So we talked about this and variety of other elements during the urban advisory group, which was a cross section of stakeholders, which I and several people in the room have had the privilege of being members of. And we knew that the framework wasn't perfect. I'm not speaking in strong support because it's perfect, but it's a movement in the right direction. And we need to move now before we lose the momentum, the valuable momentum that we created with the public in the last three years because they get it. They know that the emergency is lifted, but we're not out of the woods yet and there are more conditions ahead, historic dry conditions, so we need to prepare now. So, we don't want to lose that drumbeat that we've built over the last three years, and that's what this efficiency standard does. And it's not that new, our agencies, as well as several other agencies in the room, have applied this methodology in achieving efficiency and we've had great success. Because it's not about using less, it's about wasting less. And the public understands that. And if you could identify in efficient use and you target those, and you recognize those who are efficient, then everyone benefits. And we also have gotten some very good data from this type of conjunctive level approach. The data that we could use not only to understand how water is being used, and how programs and projects to work, but also to balance. How much can you do with demand management strategy and how much infrastructure do you need to build to have supplies available when you need it? And having this data has allowed us in the last two years save $20 million because we're able to identify those opportunities where we didn't have to build expensive infrastructure. And we're able to leverage partnerships with agencies like Facebook and Netflix to really work together to have data drive decision for better and smart investment. And they're a lot of things that we need to work out and I'll look forward to being part of the dialog going forward and all the iteration talking to agencies across the state and learning and partnering together.

The Water Board is a regulatory agency and is set up to vet, issue, inforce and modify regulations in a timely manner, in a transparent manner. The Water Board already has a statutory mandate to set the water law standards, which is one of the three elements that make up the new water use standard in this bill. Data collection by the Water Board will directly support integrated water management. Through informing work by other Water Board divisions, such as drinking water, water rights and water quality. And finally, the Water Board has adapted balancing competing interests. And in fact, have a statutory mandate to balance those interests and to protect public interest. One of the main differences from this and 968 is that we're putting forth one standard by which would apply to all water suppliers. As you recall from my testimony on 968, when 20 by 2020 or SBX 77 was developed. They had multiple methods the water suppliers could use to calculate a target. And that was intended to address the fairness and equity concerns of applying one percentage reduction target to all water suppliers. Those fairness and equity concerns had to do with past investments in conservation, local climate and local land use. And the types of customers water suppliers were providing water to. This one approach setting an efficiency standard addresses all of those fairness and equity concerns. So there is no need for additional compliance methods. Additionally it results in targets that are customized based on local conditions. And provides flexibility and local control in how the targets are met. I would also like to mention that CII indoor water use would be proposed to be addressed through best management practices. As is reflected in the framework report. And not volumetric water use targets, as is the residential indoor water use or outdoor irrigation. For those reasons, we ask you to vote aye today and NRDC strongly supports this bill. Thank you.

Tracy Quinn: Mr. Chair, Members of the Committee. My name is Tracy Quinn, I'm a Policy Analyst with the Natural Resources Defense Council, speaking in support of AB 1668. Thank you for the opportunity to be here. California's recent drought was the most severe in modern history, and showed us that our previous drought planning efforts were not adequate for that drought or for the extreme weather we're likely to see in future droughts. The lack of consistency in current water shortage contingency plans made it difficult to understand what measures water suppliers were taking to meet water shortages, and how much water they intended to save with those measures. AB 1668 will require all water suppliers to prepare the same six levels of water shortage. This is the, I think primary difference between this bill and 1654. These shortage stages would represent the shortage or gap between the supplies available to a water supplier for the upcoming year or during a discrete emergency, and the projected demand for their service area. This could be determined during their annual water budget forecast which is an element of both this and 1654. Stage one of the of these uniform consistent shortest stage one would be a 10% shortage. Stage two is a 20% shortage up to stage five which would represent a 50% shortage. And finally, stage six would be a shortage of over 50%. Well, the shortage stages would be the same for every water supplier. A water supplier could use any mix of measures, programs, projects to reduce water demand or augment supplies that reflected the different circumstances in each community. For instance, for stage one, a water supplier could ask residents to reduce outer irrigation to twice a week, or they could pump ground water from an aquifer where they have stored water for emergency situations, or any combination of those types of measures. The benefits of consistent stages are that they're easy to understand by the public, they allow water suppliers to work better together in times of emergency because they're working within similar structures. And they allow water suppliers to share resources such as communication and outreach materials, and collective experience in approving plans going forward. For these reasons, and I already see strongly supports AB 1668, and we ask for your aye vote today. Thank you.

Ben Chou: Good afternoon chair Gracia and Members of the Committee, my name is Ben Chou on the policy of the Natural Resources Defence Council. Thank you for allowing me to testify today in support of this bill. California's most recent drought showed us that no one is immune from the impacts, urban and rural areas alike were affected by the drought. To preparing for future droughts requires a comprehensive approach that includes all of the ways that we use water, homes, businesses and farms taking steps to use water more efficiently. Improving water efficiency is generally the most cost effective environmentally sound and the most immediate way to meet our water needs. This bill ensures that more agricultural water suppliers, which supply water to the many farms in California that in turn feed families across the world, are better prepared for inevitable next drought. The bill also supports the adoption of water saving practices that benefit producers and growers. Enabling farmers to receive water delivery is nearly on demand, provides three key benefits. It eliminates water loss by leaking uncovered canals and ditches, it allows farmers to irrigate according to when their crops actually need water and it provide farmers the freedom to upgrade to more efficient drip irrigation systems. Which have also been shown to improve crop yields. Further, supporting on-farm practices like cover crops that build soil health will help farmers better prepare for future extreme weather. Healthier soil benefits our farmers and the environment by holding more water, improving crop yields and reducing water pollution. The water challenges that we have faced these past few years underscore the need to pursue a proactive and comprehensive approach to ensure safe, secure and sustainable water supplies for the future. For those reasons we respectively ask for AB 1667.

Even as we sit in this room this morning talking about the variety of bills related to making conservation a way of life. California's already had a long legacy in the area of water conservation. Many milestone water conservation measures have been signed into law over the last two and a half decades. Most of them have become second nature to us as we go about our day to day lives and our homes and businesses and farms, but they all demonstrate a strong and lasting water conservation ethic in our state. Beginning in 1991 with Senator Lucy Killea from San Diego authoring the first ultra low-flush toilet bill that ultimately became the water conservation standard in the world. To water efficient clothes washers and indoor plumbing fixtures, outdoor model water efficient landscaping. Water meters and submeters for conservation pricing signals, California has never shied away from being very aggressive on water conservation. Dr. Weber's measure, AB 1323, is intended to build upon that legacy of water conservation and water use efficiency. In 2004, the state was faced with a very similar situation, a variety of perspectives, multiple options relating to how to improve outdoor water use efficiency. Irrigation efficiencies a very highly complex issues, a variety of different perspectives and stakeholders. At the time a middle of the road compromise bill authored by then Assemblymember John Laird was introduced. That created a stakeholder workgroup with a process to develop a consensus base facilitated series of recommendations for addressing outdoor water efficient landscaping. And that report was ultimately submitted to the Legislature. Legislature had its oversight through the conventional legislative process and that process ultimately resulted in the successful model water efficient landscape ordinance that's in statute today. We think the time is ripe, the circumstances before the Legislature are ripe. And the issues and details relating to this policy area are exceedingly complex enough to give strong consideration to the common sense approach proposed by AB 1323. We strongly encourage you to take the time to allow a broad stakeholder group to collectively work through these issues, and we urge your aye vote on this measure.

Paul Cook: Good morning, Mr Chair, I'm Paul Cook. I'm the General Manager of Irvine Ranch Water District. It's a pleasure to be here. AB 968 and its companion bill, AB 1654, which we'll hear about next. They combine to implement the vision of the Governor's framework for making water use efficiency a way of life in California. Both bills are products of a three month process by the water community to develop a comprehensive, practical, consensus based proposal. To ensure that urban water suppliers improve water use efficiency over the long term. While simultaneously being prepared to reduce demands through water conservation measures during times of drought or other shortages. AB 968 was developed with input from dozens of water agencies who are committed to water use efficiency and conservation. Water banking, water reuse and other innovative ways of managing water resources. The water community supports the Governor's goal that California become more efficient in its water use. And proactively developed AB 968 in response to the Governor's call for action. So first, AB 968 will establish, strengthen water efficiency targets, as mentioned by the LAO's office, for water suppliers for 2025. It'll do this by providing three options to suppliers for the 2025 targets. Each agency would be permitted to set up their own targets. Based on daily per capita water use, retail level water budget, or a hydrologic regional target. It's inclusion of these three methods, AB-968 allows a water supplier to select a target setting method that is locally appropriate. And takes into account it's level of sophistication. While building upon and strengthening the existing requirements of 20% by 2020. Additionally, the bill requires each urban water supplier to meet its 2025 target. While preserving discretion as to how suppliers achieve their targets. The bill also extensively details how a supplier's compliance with the target is determined. It also recognizes large investments that many local agencies have made in water recycling. And incentivizes to continued local development of water recycling programs. It does this by applying it an evapo-transporation factor of 1.0 to parcels irrigated with recycled water. When calculating water use efficiency with a budget-based method of water use. Consistent with the approach of existing law, that we mentioned earlier, SBX 77, recycled water is given consideration in the calculation of gross water use. The bill's provisions recognize that the application of recycled water in landscape irrigation is already extensively regulated. Thereby ensuring its efficient use and encouraging the expansion of water recycling throughout California. And finally, the bill does provide that it does not alter any existing water rights laws. It does not authorize or enhance the authority of the state board to alter any water rights beyond its existing powers. We think that's an important feature as well, John?

Kim Thorner: Good morning, my name is Kim Thorner, I'm the General Manager of Olivenhain Water, I'm also the chair of the North San Diego Reuse Coalition, we are here in support of AB 869 on recycled water. Recycled water is the ultimate form of conservation, it starts as potable water subject to all water use efficiency regulations. Once it's salvaged as from waste water and turned into recycled water at great cost, it is all ready subject to the most restrictive regulations of any water source in the state. No other water supply in California is subject to the level of restrictions that mandate not only its efficient use, but also require annual inspections to verify that the water use is protective of public health, and that the water is used efficiently, such as note requirements for no over spray, no saturation of soils, and no leaks. Recycled water is more expensive to build as a supply source and it's more expensive to administer annually because of these inspections. If recycled water is restricted, two very negative consequences will result, water agencies will not build and finance these higher cost recycled water projects that we ultimately will be restricted from using, restrictions will be a disincentive to future development of this supply. Recycled water is salvaged waste water that is otherwise unusable, it is the ultimate form of conservation, and if it's not salvaged it goes out into the ocean and does not exist as a water source in California. Every drop of recycled water replaces a drop of potable water, reducing energy demands associated transporting water from the Delta and the Colorado. Excluding recycled water from reduction goals, by no means prohibits efficiency standards on potable water. Our motivation to develop recycled water is not guided to allow wasteful use of potable water. Recycled water is developed to increase local sustainable supply, and less Independence on imported water. Recycled water was not restricted under SB X7, it was not restricted under the drought emergency, and that promulgated its very development as a reliable supply. California cannot conserve its way out of the next drought, nor can we recycle our way out of the next drought. It is only through a combination of water use efficiency, water management, reuse, and new supply development combined, that we will address our future challenges. Therefore, we request your support of AB 869.

To deter behavior such as this, the critical issue is increasing the enforcement of the prohibition against taking water in these situations and so we would urge you to amend the bill to remove the criminal penalties, focus on increasing the civil penalties and increasing the enforcement measures, which is really what's needed here. Thank you.

Rachelle Ehlers: Good morning. Rachelle Ehlers with the LAO. The sergeant has passed out a handout from which I'll be speaking called overview of state's water conservation efforts because you have so many bills on this topic today and the Governor has some proposals, as well. Staff has asked me to give a brief overview for you just to provide some context for the discussion that's coming up. So I will give a very brief overview of some of the significant water conservation efforts in recent years. A very quick overview of the Governor's initiative and proposals and bills before you today and then provide some key policy questions to hopefully help provide some context for the discussion you're going to have today. So turning to page one there was very significant legislation in this area in 2009. That set a goal and requirement that the state reduce its urban per capita water use by 20% by the year 2020. So it's referred to as 20 by 2020 legislation. The legislation also set an interim goal of a 10% reduction. By a 2015 all compared to a 2009 baseline. So state agencies were under way implementing this plan. Local water agencies were underway working toward this goal as well. Even though it set a statewide reduction target, the legislation allowed for some flexibility at the local level for how to achieve that target. Four different methodologies that local water agencies could use and then the drought hit and that expedited things. So through his emergency powers declaring a State of emergency and executive orders. The Governor and his administration instituted some temporary requirements for water conservation. It began with a 20% voluntary reduction and then as the drought continued in 2015 moved to a statewide requirement of a 25% reduction across the state. The Water Board implemented that through emergency regulations. There were different targets set at different areas across the state. Depending on their previous water use that ranged from a 4% reduction to a 36% reduction with this goal of 25% across the state and we got pretty close through those emergency reductions. In 2016 as the hydrology improved somewhat the Water Board modified those requirements and allowed local agencies that could self certify that they had enough water supplies. To withstand three additional years of drought could then set their own requirements and targets for how much they wanted to reduce. So some moved away from the governor's requirements and some chose to keep them in place. You can see on the last bullet, there were also some emergency regulations beyond these reductions. Tony Thurmond: Thank you Mr. Chair, and Members of the Committee. It's my pleasure to be before you to present AB 224, a bill that we often refer to as Caleb's Law. First, let me start by thanking the Chair, who has been very diligent in trying to find amendments that will allow us to find a favorable outcome for this bill. I want to thank you for that Mr. Chair. While I think we've been close in the conversation about amendments, there are some aspects of the amendments that we feel is not consistent with the recommendations, that the California Dental Board has made. The chair has allowed me to offer a number of alternative amendments. I'd like to talk about some of those today, but I wanted to acknowledge the graciousness of the chair in his commitment to working to try and find a positive solution here today, thank you. Sadly, last year tragedy struck in my district when a six-year-old named Caleb Sears, who was an otherwise healthy boy, passed away in a dental chair. Ordinarily, healthy children do not die when they go to the dentist's office. And concern over his death led to legislative energy to look into the matter. We Learned that in all of medicine, oral surgeons are the only physicians who are able to both operate on a patient and administer anesthesia at the same time. Last year, this Legislature required the dental board to propose recommendations to improve the safety of pediatric dental anesthesia. Our bill today, codifies those recommendations. These are not recommendations that Tony Thurmond created, but the highest authority for dentistry in the State of California, has proposed the recommendations that are embodied in this bill. The dental board convened an initial Subcommittee of one attorney, and one oral surgeon. This Subcommittee proposed an initial recommendation. Later, the full board which is comprised of dentists, other oral surgeons and public members, amended the initial recommendations to include the recommendation, that we ban the operator anesthetist model in the interest of safety. My bill today proposes to implement the board's full recommendations. We've tried to be thoughtful, in working with stakeholders to carefully address cost and access issues. I want to also thank the California Dental Associations and the Oral Surgeons. Why they don't share all the views that we've had and held here today, they've taken many meetings with me and my stuff. And when I first decided to do this bill, the first person I called was CDA to say let us work together to figure out a way to keep children safe, and they committed to that. Obviously, we still have some work to do to find full agreement, but I want to acknowledge that we've met with countless stakeholders on this matter. We have removed one of the recommendations that there be an anesthesia assistant, in order to make the recommendations more in line with current practice. We have included nurse anesthetists, also in line with current practice. It's our belief that this inclusion addresses both cost and access concerns. Specifically, we believe that there are now 9,300 eligible providers in the state. We understand that the nurse anesthetists offer potential cost savings, compared to an oral surgeon. A nurse anesthetist can currently practice and act as the second provider with an oral surgeon, and a nurse anesthetist does not need a general anesthesia permit, to do so under current law. This will not change with AB 224. Nurse anesthetist, provide these services in all counties in California, and are widely available in rural communities. Further, in order to truly understand implications of this bill as it relates to cost and access, I'm willing to include a concurrent study of cost access concerns. I'll also commit today, to including a study on the safety of dental sedation assistance and a potential dental board training program, to further expand the group of eligible second providers. Since the Dental Board recommendations did not address these additional groups, I think it's important that we move the bill as is and Commission the concurrent studies to be finalized within a year. If after the study, the data that is produced and it's determined that dental sedation assistants and/or the new proposed training program is determined to be safe, in line with the Board's recommendations, I will happily champion their inclusion. I'm committed to addressing concerns, because this bill is about promoting patient safety and taking care of the most vulnerable. And I respectfully ask for your aye vote. With me today to testify is Dr. Jaques Corovo, a pediatrician, Dr. Karen Seibert, an anesthesiologist, Dr. Larry Trappe, a dental anesthesiologist. And to my right Tim Seers, who is the father of Caleb Seers, who requests to have a few words today.

So a physician, in setting up these types of agreements with a certified nurse midwife, by law, and it'll be in violation of their license. They have to understand, to have an intimate knowledge of the person's education, clinical training, capabilities, and abilities. And by law, they are required to be the first person that makes that patient assessment under the protocol. Thank you sir. So you're going to set up a situation because the CNMs in this bill say we don't want any supervision except when it comes to prescribing drugs and the law requires the physician to do the initial assessment. I think it's going to be very difficult to find a physician that will enter into that type of agreement because it's going to expose them to liability when they're not actually assessing and seeing this patient on a regular basis. What they're anticipating is a physician will develop this protocol or standard procedures and then walk away and not ever have any interaction with the patient. This is a situation that will not work in the marketplace. So there are other issues with the bill and I'll let people from ACOG and others have a talk.

Pest inspectors and roof contractors are licensed entities. The pest inspectors by the Structural Pest Board and the roofing contractors by the State Contractors Licensing Board. It also notifies the consumer that the repairs being offered are only for the roof and no repairs identified in the home inspection are allowed or authorized. Jeremy Pearson: Good afternoon, my name is Jeremy Pearson. I'm co-owner of Happy Bear Dental Surgery Center in Tulare, California. I would like to just take a couple minutes to untangle two issues that I believe are inappropriately tangled in this bill. First of all is the access to care issue, and second is the issue of needing two anesthesia permit holders to treat one patient. First of all, access to care. Access to care is a reimbursement issue, it always has been and it always will be. If you have private insurance, or if you are able to afford to pay cash, you can go to any dentist, any oral surgeon, and your good insurance and your cash will be accepted. The people who have a current access to care issue, a severe crisis right now, are the poor or the low income who have Denti-Cal. And there is no secret that Denti-Cal has a crisis access to care problem. There are many, many dentists who are registered with Denti-Cal, but do not take Denti-Cal because it's almost charity work. There are, and as far as oral surgeons, less than 10% of all oral surgeons in California are even registered with Denti-Cal, let alone taking new patients. Many dentists who are registered with Denti-Cal will not take new patients or maybe see one or two new patients per month. The fact of the matter is that Denti-Cal has not raised its rates in 20 years. Denti-Cal California rates 49th out of 50 states in the reimbursement, the lowest reimbursement for our Denti-Cal program. So access to care is a reimbursement issue. If you increase reimbursements, all dentists and oral surgeons would take the patients. Separate to that is the issue of having two people to treat one patient. This is a safety issue. It's not a reimbursement issue, it's a safety issue. The fact of the matter is, is that if you have a surgeon doing treatment on a patient, they should be concentrated on the surgery. Another professional should be concentrated on the airway and the anesthesia being provided to that patient under general anesthesia. It's the same thing as going, well, we need two people with a driver's license when you're driving a car. Well that doesn't make any sense until you add the extra information, that the person driving wants to text and drive. The moment you add that information, then it makes completely clear that one person should drive and concentrate on driving and the other person, even if they do have a driver's license, can sit in the passenger seat and text while they're driving, right? So the fact of the matter is that this is a safety issue and if we are not going to allow a person to text and drive, we shouldn't allow a surgeon to be responsible for the surgery and the anesthesia on the same patient.

So as you all know, SB 247 seeks to ease the burden of occupational licensing on various occupations that are attenuated to health or safety concerns. And for many occupations, sure, licensing can be intuitive, doctors and lawyers often come to mind for people. But for scores of others, licensing simply puts up an onerous and arbitrair barrier that deprives people of a way out of poverty. That deprives people of their right to earn a living for themselves and their families. Worse, while proponents claim that licensing laws are necessary to protect the public health and safety. In reality, there are plenty of studies that show that the these laws are often created and perpetuated by the people who are regulated themselves, as a means to protect themselves from competition. As the Senator noted, this is a bipartisan issue, largely because people recognize the disproportionate effect that licensing laws have on poor and minority groups. And also a very hot topic right now is how occupational licensing laws disproportionally affect people who have been convicted of crimes. Who turn to repeat offenses, rather then lifting themselves out of poverty and finding a job because they can't, because of these laws. So, when you try to do occupational licensing reform, which many states have, might I add. There are plenty of states, Wisconsin, Arizona, Florida, Minnesota, that are doing the same types of things, and picking off occupations that are attenuated to public safety. Like dietitians, arborists, funeral directors, talent agents, interior designers, photographers used to be licensed in Wisconsin in fact. Any how, when you try to do this stuff, you do have people come out and tell you, these people who are already licensed, why you need to perpetuate the licensing regime. But you don't hear from people who maybe operating illegally on the underground economy, and don't want to come out and say so, and talk about how these laws have harmed them. You don't hear from people who have been deprived of their ability to earn a living, and so they don't have the means to come out and represent themselves and to travel from afar. He tried to get a license and he was denied, simply because he could not afford an office in California. He could only afford actually to work from his home in his home state. And this is one of those scenarios where I don't think anybody can rationally say that having an office in California makes you a better private investigator. Where you have your office has nothing to do with your ability to perform. It's simply a way to keep out of state people from competing with California licensees. With regard to makeup artists, you have to have 140 days of educational experience, and pass two exams to do something that people do every day. And yet, this is a fun fact, in California it takes more educational experience and time to become a barber than it does to become an EMT. So there are all sorts of these irrational things going on because they've been lobbied for that way. Custom upholsters are something that the bill touches on, only seven states regulate custom upholsters. So it's difficult to argue that there's some nationwide crisis that requires licensing, when certainly in the majority of states see fit to do it without. And so, in sum, I just wanted to bring some facts to your attention, and tell you about things that are often not heard, and that is the way that these laws deprive Californians of economic opportunity.

Increases in housing and healthcare costs, combined with stagnant Social Security and SSI disbursements, are creating tremendous poverty among our older adult population. Starting in the late 1970s, Eskaton successfully developed 850 units of affordable apartments using primarily federal 202 funding. Amongst our 13 locations we have 1,600 names on waiting list with waits up to 3 years for an apartment to become available. For older adults, housing is healthcare. Non-profit affordable senior housing providers, such as Eskaton, have been providing service-enriched housing for decades. However, it is very difficult to create more such housing in California for a number of reasons. The biggest is that there is little funding to build affordable senior housing. There simply aren't enough affordable units being built to keep up with demand. If a project does receive funding and is built, it is extremely difficult to layer on coordinated social and health services because of strict regulatory and funding mechanisms. This incredibly important bill will bring together public and private stakeholders to help identify and solve barriers, as it seeks to encourage and grow the supply of service-enriched affordable housing in California. Lauren Treadwell: Good afternoon, I'd like to thank Assemblymember Rubio and the members of the Human Services Committee for holding a hearing on AB 480 and allowing me to testify. My name is Lauren Treadwell and I am the advocacy chair for Help a Mother Out, a non-profit based in the Bay Area working to increase access to diapers for families in need. Since its founding 2009, Help a Mother Out has distributed over 5 million free diapers to low income Californians. Not having enough diapers presents a substantial barrier to participation, and work, school, and job training programs for families who are struggling to make ends meet. Most child care centers require families to drop off a full day supply of diapers, and if they don't, they may not be allowed to drop off their child. And without child care, parents cannot go to work or school. We often hear inspiring stories from our partners about families who have received our diaper aid. One client was planning to attend GED classes, but no one was wiling to watch her child because she had no clean diapers. Being able to get free diapers made it possible for her to attend those GED classes. Another client was forced to use folded shirts to diaper her baby and she was embarrassed to leave the house. Once she received diaper assistance, she was no longer afraid to go out in public with her child.  As you can see, a small thing like a diaper can have a very big impact. In 2015, Help a Mother Out partnered with San Francisco Human Services Agency to launch the San Francisco Diaper Bank, which is the nation's first and only publicly funded diaper bank.  The San Francisco Diaper Bank is administered by Help a Mother Out and provides families receiving CalWORKS benefits with a full supply of diapers each month for children under the age of three. As of March 2017, The San Fransisco Diaper Bank has distributed over 1.1 million diapers to 1,500 children. This equates to a total program participation rate of 59% of eligible CalWORKS families within San Francisco. News of the diaper bank program is slowly spreading and participation is consistently increasing. Diaper assistance helps to remove a barrier to work, school and job training program for low income families, but nonprofits like Help a Mother Out cannot cover this gap with private support alone. Therefore, on behalf of the families we serve, we thank you, and thank you, Gonzalez-Fletcher, for your leadership of this important problem.

The registry was created as a way to ensure that home care clients were receiving quality licensed care. The registry was used so that an individual's can show that they've been trained, they passed TB test. They've passed a background check and so forth. So if I needed care for my mother, I could go on to the registry, say I was working with ABC Home Care. ABC Home Care is listed, Michael Smith, I can go to Michael Smith and say, Michael Smith has been trained, licensed. He's able to provide care in the home. This bill is looking to provide home care aides' name, home address, home phone number, and employment history as a public information's request. It's hard to justify that a public good for that kind of private information. There's countless California statutes that are looking to protect private information, and yet, we're making this information available via public information request. The proponents are saying that they want to do training with this, which is commendable. Although why is this information needed to provide training? You can advertise training online. You can advertise training in the newspaper. You can reach out to homecare organizations and say, hey, we'd be happy to work with you, homecare organization, to provide this training. Why do we need their personal information to offer training to these individuals? Additionally, the Department of Social Services has been talking with the Legislature about the need to increase licensure fees. They're looking to raise licensure fees for organizations by over $600 and double the cost for aides to be registered and the argument for this is because they don't have the resources on staff to meet current demands of the licensure process. The Department of Social Services is saying that they can't meet current demands. How are they going to meet the demands of this bill? How is the department going to justify who meets the requirements for this bill? They're going to need additional resources for that. They're already asking for additional resources to meet what they need now. We already work with a lot of organizations to provide training. All organizations as part of life insure are required to make sure that their aides are trained. At the end of the day, the aides need to make sure that they meet their training by their training requirements, but the organizations know that they cannot send an individual that does not meet the training requirements. Therefore, the organizations are already providing this training for them. One of the differences is we have home care aides that are associated with an organization, in which case, they have to be licensed. They have to be on the registry and then you have independent home care aides. Independent home care aides do not have to be on the registry. That's something that is completely different, two separate entities. Anybody that's working for an organization must be licensed, must be trained. The organizations already provide this training. If additional training is asked for, there's ways to do that. We shouldn't be giving anybody private home and phone numbers where their husbands, wives, and children live. We respectfully ask for your no vote, thank you.

Our mission is to assist former foster youth reach self-sufficiency, and we do this by supporting them through their educational journeys. We understand the impact that college and vocational degrees have on people's ability to gain meaningful employment. And so we focus our efforts to supporting youth through their journeys. California has the largest population of children and youth in foster care in the nation. Less than half of California foster youth graduate from high school compared to 79% of the general population. By age 26 only 6% of California foster youth complete college compared to 46% of the general population. As a former foster youth myself, I know first hand how important these supportive services are to helping not only navigate our education, but also to build our own personal lives. And so, AB 1567 seeks to address the issue of under utilization of on campus support program services by providing form of falsely used notification of on campus support Programs at the California community colleges and Cal State Universities. Programs such as Extended Opportunity Programs and Services, EOPNS, and the Cooperating Agencies of Foster Youth Educational Success, CAFYES, provides student support such as books, school supplies, transportation, educational counseling and tutoring. These critical supports have a huge impact on a foster youth's ability to successfully complete college. We know that if a youth succeeds in college they are more likely to find meaningful employment, contribute to the economy and less likely to depend on government support, and ultimately break the cycle of poverty that lead children into the child welfare system. For these reasons we urge your support on AB 1567.

So by way of very, very brief background, AB 32 and SB 32 are the economy-wide emission reduction goal legislation set up by the Legislature. And then SB 375 comes along and is the transportation, housing and land use component of that overall statewide plan and it's been a challenge for regions to be able to adopt their sustainable community strategies. The process that was set out by the Air Board was that they'd be aggressive but achievable. They're definitely aggressive, but one of the problems is that we don't have the tools that we had back when SB 375 was originally adopted. I refer to tax increment financing. We don't have the tools to be able to locate the housing in the areas and the density that we would like to see. But specifically, this bill has some additional provisions that are added and that direct CARB in the establishment of the targets. The bill says that CARB has to consider any other economy-wide greenhouse gas emission reduction targets in state law or executive order. So, I'm aware that AB 32 and SB 32 are the economy-wide greenhouse gas reduction laws. I'm not aware of any other statewide statute that fits this description. So I guess that really begs the question, what is it? What are we talking about here? And let's be specific. So, that's one of the fundamental questions we have. It's important that we have certainty in this process. The second part of it has to do with the executive orders and, again, this bill is pretty vague in its reference to executive orders. I think what they're getting at, is the 80 by 50 executive order that was first enacted by the Schwarzenegger administration and then carried forward with this current administration. So we, I think it's important that we be clear and define what both the state laws and the executive orders are, put them into statute so we can have a reasoned debate about whether those are appropriate or not, and then finally I would just note that with respect to the 80 by 50, this is exactly the issue that is in front of the California Supreme Court in the matter of the San Diego Association of Governments. Usha Mutschler: Good afternoon Mr. Chair, members, Senator Skinner, Usha Mutschler on behalf of the California State Sheriffs' Association in a respectful opposition to the bill. Specifically, crucial jail funding directed to counties results in appropriate facilities to provide education, rehabilitation, vocational programming, medical and mental health treatment that we desperately need at this time. These jail improvements are a direct benefit to the persons housed in these facilities, and they demonstrate the sheriff's commitment to providing appropriate services and treatment to our incarcerated populations. SB 630 will keep counties from applying for or receiving this crucial funding by tightening restrictions on leasing beds to other entities. We are concerned about this bill for a number of reasons, chief among them that it may keep counties in serious need of improving their jail facilities from accessing funds for which they are currently eligible. For example, SB 844 was negotiated as a part of last year's budget and received overwhelming bipartisan support in both houses. Counties are already limited to minimal increases in housing capacity and must focus on projects that replace compacted, outdated, or unsafe housing capacity and that add treatment space. While SB 844 contains a restriction on leasing beds, it only applies if the county is adding housing capacity. SB 630 expands this restriction to a county applying for SB 844 funding even if the project results in no new net beds or a decrease in housing capacity. These projects revolve around a desire and a need to replace outdated facilities. SB 630 attempts to change the rules late in the process after legislative and executive approval of the funding, submittal of county applications and the commencement of the review of submitted proposals have taken place. Counties have partnered with the state in good faith to address the shared challenges in our correctional systems, and SB 630 creates a serious impediment in the pathway to improved correctional facilities. For these reasons we respectfully oppose, thank you.

So we are step laddering into relief for this class of offenders. The record can be opened, as Senator Skinner mentioned, in a subsequent prosecution whether it's in juvenile or adult court. So we have taken a measured and balanced approach to remedying the situation that these young people face. So again, we're going to have further discussions with the district attorneys, who I think are interested in possibly looking at the bill again. That person would have had to have complied with the law, never committed another violent or serious offence, properly registered, and then would still have to petition to get off of the registry. Part of the other insurance policy that we put in place is that when someone wants to petition to get off the registry, they go into their local law enforcement agency. They have their record run, their registration run, the police actually have a say, and actually give input as to the person proceeding with their petition. Then there's another insurance policy. It goes to the District Attorney. They have the right to oppose anyone getting off the registry. People don't automatically get off when their tier expires, it must go through the District Attorney's office and law enforcement. The other measure which we have already in existence in the State of California is since 1996 we have had a sexually violent predator law. In 2006, it was even made stricter by Jessica's Law. Any person in the State of California who goes to prison on a predicate sex offense is evaluated when they are going to be released by the Department of Corrections and the California Department of State Hospitals. If they are still found to be a likely risk, then they are civilly committed in an indeterminate commitment to Coalinga State Hospital, and they are not released from custody. So we already have that insurance policy in place. When that person is released, that person's tier just then begins to run. One of the important aspects of the bill is, every single event which is now registrable, remains registrable. All of the serious offenders who have committed violent child molestation, who have committed murder, who have committed kidnap, they all remain in the lifetime tier. Absolutely nothing has changed as to that. We maintain that they are a risk and they remain lifetime. As District Attorney O'Malley stated, we have the Static-99R and it is highly predictable. Anyone, period, even on their first offense, if they are found to be one of the people to be high risk on that tool, it is lifetime registration. That is yet another insurance policy that we have put into place. It has become evident to us, those who are child sex crime prosecutors that the list has become meaningless. There is no way when a child is kidnapped or we have a stranger molestation to go to the registry and use it as an investigative tool, because everyone, including the 80 year old who committed an indecent exposure 60 years ago, is still on the list. We need to have the purpose of the list restored. It is for law enforcement to be able to go to the list, and see who are the risky offenders in their area? When a child is kidnapped to be able to look at it, and quickly find suspects and try to prevent that child from having any future harm or possibly death. The Los Angeles County District Attorney's office wanted to make sure that we had a common sense bill, which brought into the bill all the of the science that we have Learned in the last several decades. And, hopefully, prevent there from being future victims. Thank you.

Kim McGill: Good morning. Kim McGilligan from the Youth Justice Coalition. On behalf of our members and their families, we urge you to support Senate Bill 620, which would allow a court, at the time of sentencing, to strike a sentence enhancement for using or discharging a firearm. Currently, California law requires courts to extend the term of imprisonment when a person uses or discharges a firearm in the Commission of a felony. Unlike many other enhancements, these enhancements are mandatory in all cases. This bill is an historic effort to repair our overuse of enhancements, that have imposed mandatory minimums on tens of thousands of people. Most important, it is an important first step toward returning judicial discretion to judges. These justice coalitions work with families to understand and prepare for court. And we have seen directly the extreme impact that sentencing enhancements have on people's lives, overwhelmingly youth of color. While nearly all of these cases have been tragic, one case in particular stands out. Travis was 19 and had severe learning and developmental disabilities. He entered a game stop and asked for a $100 game while holding a BB gun. A month later he took that same game back to GameStop to turn it in for a new game not even understanding the consequences of his actions. The police were called and he was arrested. It was his first arrest. For his controlling offense robbery, Travis was facing up to five years in state prison and or a fine of up to $10,000. In many cases, robberies without a weapon result in probation. But with the gun enhancement, even with the BB gun that was never fired. Travis faced up to an additional 20 years. We met with the County Public Defender's Office, to change Travis' lawyer, because the first public defender was so over stretched, that he failed to challenge the gun enhancement, based on the fact that Travis had a bb gun and developmental disabilities. Even with our packing the court, and submitting several powerful testimonies at his sentencing hearing, Travis was sentenced to 17.5 years in state prison. The judge stated that under California law, he could not make any adjustments due to Travis' cognitive disabilities or his lack of a past criminal record. The term required by these enhancements are additional and consecutive and can be added for each potential victim if a group of people is present. Which is often the case. In Travis' case, the potential 20 year enhancement was based on there being two clerks in the store, even though one of the clerks wasn't involved in the transaction in any way. In addition to eliminating judicial discretion and imposing cruel sentencing on many of California's most vulnerable residents, sentence enhancements do more to erode our justice system, including these facts. Prosecutors use enhancements to force plea deals. People plead out their cases even when they are innocent of all charges, for fear that they will lose at trial and be subjected to extreme prison sentences. This undermines our public safety by greatly expanding wrongful convictions. Extreme sentences caused by enhancements decrease hope in the state prison system. And thus increase mental anxiety, suicide, and violence rates inside. Enhancements are not imposed equally across California's communities, overwhelmingly contributing to harsh sentencing for young people of color. And, finally, enhancements cost Californian's hundreds of millions of dollars a year in unnecessary prison costs. There are tens of thousands of Travis' in our state prison system. To ensure that California build a future for all its residents, we urge you to vote yes on Senate Bill 620.

Marty Veranacar: Madam Chair and members, Marty Veranacar on behalf of the California District Attorney's Association. Regret to inform you that we're strongly opposed to this measure, which would give courts the digression to strike the enhancement to felonies where firearm or an assault rifle was used in Commission of the offence. In the current environment where cities and communities are seeing increases in violent crime, it is inexplicable that this approach dealing with gun crime is what is necessary. In Los Angeles alone, last year, robberies were up 13%. Aggravated assaults were up 10%, homicides up 5% over 2015. Overall, as reported by the LA Times, violent crime was up 10% over 2015, and 38% over two years ago. Currently, under California's 10-20-life law, the personal use of a fire arm In the case of murder, kidnapping, robbery, or rape would result in the 10 year enhancement. If there is an intentional discharge of the gun, then the enhancement in those offenses is 20 years. And if the person causes death or great bodily injury, then the term is 25 to life. It is difficult to imagine that there would be circumstances in mitigation which will lead the court to strike the enhancement in those violent offenses. In addition, as stated by the Senator, because Prop 57 excludes violent felonies from early parole eligibility, ineligibility, striking the enhancement would also lead to early releases for some serious cases. And the example that the Senator indicated is correct. The additional term is imposed for assault on a police officer with a firearm under section 12022.53. Any violation of 12022.53 is then considered a violent felony, and ineligible for early patrol. Striking that term makes that primary offense only a serious felony and then as such, eligible for early parole. I think the core of the problem here is that gun crimes have the most serious impact on crime victims, both an emotional impact and if the firearm is used, physical consequences. The Legislature has consistently worked to tighten up gun laws, to keep them out of the hands of those who would misuse their power to damage or kill. Yet this measure sends those who would misuse these firearms, in the Commission of felonies, the wrong message. Use a gun, avoid the time. For these reasons, we remain opposed to this measure, thank you.

In reading the sheriff's opposition, it concerned me that they were thinking that we were trying to get information online that is not covered by CPRA. And the exemptions are very clear in 6254-F. So I just want to be clear that SB 345 doesn't change the substance of the California Public Records Act. In fact, as Senator Bradford mentioned, there are at least 20 that I could find in California, 20 law enforcement agencies. Berkeley Police Department, San Fransisco Police Department, San Diego Sheriffs' Department. Several of our law enforcement agencies across California are already doing it without concerns over these issues opening up. Things like tactical reviews or juvenile records, no one wants to see those things online. They're already covered under exemptions. So all we're trying to do is keep those exemptions where they are, but in the meantime provide access to information about policing. Including enhancing police community relations with easier communication, saving law enforcement agencies valuable time and resources. Making the criminal justice system more fair and efficient and effective by providing defense attorneys with easier access to what they need. And, finally, ensuring full statewide California Public Records Act compliance by law enforcement. So I'm happy to answer any questions you might have. And I respectively hope that you will vote aye on this bill.

[{'start': 14, 'end': 29, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Natasha Minsker: Good morning, Natasha Minsker on behalf of the ACLU of California. Regretfully, we do remain opposed to the bill. The rule against propensity evidence actually dates back more than 300 years in our legal tradition. It has deep roots, and any change to that rule raises serious due process concerns. The current exceptions to the rule against propensity evidence are narrowly drawn to crimes of sexual violence and intimate family violence. The United States' Supreme Court has not yet ruled on whether even the existing exemptions are constitutional. But the lower courts that have considered the issue have found these current exceptions to be constitutional, because the exceptions themselves have long roots in our historical legal tradition. In fact, courts for a very long time allowed propensity evidence in cases of sexual violence and intimate family violence. Based on what some courts called a lustful exception to the rule against propensity evidence. The theory behind this is that in these kinds of cases, sexual violence and intimate family violence, character evidence, propensity evidence is in fact more relevant, because it is believed that the underlying criminal behavior is driven by a deep propensity, by a compulsion to engage in the behavior. That is not true in the case of commercial sexual exploitation. The offenses that we're talking about here are driven by desire to make money. They are offenses that are largely engaged in by criminal legal, I'm sorry, criminal enterprises such as gangs that are engaging in human trafficking, in sexual commercial exploitation, along with other illegal criminal commercial enterprises, such as drug trafficking, and selling iPhones and identity theft. Their motivation continues to be financial even though the means by which they are caring out their offense is sexual exploitation. And so the theory behind allowing propensity evidence in sexual violence and intimate family violence, doesn't apply in these kinds of offenses. We understand that these are difficult cases to prove and we understand that they are horrible cases with significant impacts on people's lives. That is also true about homicide, and yet, we do not allow propensity evidence in homicide cases. We believe that extending the use of propensity evidence base on the theory that the case is difficult to prove, or that the case has harmful impacts is not a role that has boundaries to it. And it will lead to the expansion, and allowing propensity evidence, in pretty much any kind of case at all. And this gets back to our core concern that this simply goes too far in terms of the due process protections, that have been part of our historical legal tradition for more than 300 years. We appreciate the good intentions behind this bill, and we appreciate that there are existing  measures that allow character evidence for other purposes, besides proving propensity. And that there are existing provisions in law that allow, for example, cross jurisdictional prosecution in human trafficking cases, to address the concern of gangs and human traffickers moving across the state. We believe that this bill is simply not the right approach and goes too far in abridging fundamental due process protections. Thank you.

Rand Martin : Thank you Madam. Rand Martin on behalf of the California Charter Schools Association. Well, you've taken away the first part of my testimony so I won't repeat that. I do want to jump into this issue of whether we have settled law or not in this field. We would argue actually pretty strenuously and respectfully disagree with the analysis. We do not believe this is settled law. There is no case law on the issues of any of these transparency or conflict of interest laws. There is no statute on any of these laws. There is no regulation on any of these laws that indicate that charter schools are already covered by the Brown Act, Political Reform Act, Public Records Act, or even Government Code 1090. Without any of those three, it's hard to claim that this is settled law. I would also point out that there are a number of appellate decisions and one Supreme Court decision where there is some decisions relative to what the status of charter schools is. And in every single one of those cases, the status is that they are not public agencies. So there is a case called Knapp versus Pacific Palisades Charter School that had to do with the Tort Claims Act. In that decision, the appellate court concluded that charter schools are not public agencies. In Wells versus One to One, a Supreme Court decision, the Supreme Court concluded that charter schools are not public agencies. In Gateway versus, I can't remember who it was against, but Gateway, they decided that pertaining to certain labor codes, charter schools were not public agencies. So the question about whether there's any settlement of law, I mean the only indication so far is that the courts have been drifting towards charter schools not being public agencies when it comes to the application of a number of laws. There is again, as I say, no case law, no statute at all that deals with the laws that are before us currently in this bill. I would also point out, with all due respect to the chair and to this Committee, this Committee has passed virtually the same bill several times before. So our conclusion is that this Committee also doesn't believe that this is settled law, because they passed AB 709 last year. They passed AB 360 in 2011. They passed AB 572 in 2010. All of which did everything this bill did, plus 1090, but clearly there was an opinion by this Committee over the last seven years that these are laws that need to be clearly applied to charter schools. I'd also like to talk briefly about Government Code 1090 because that seems to be the one issue that we keep getting stuck on, and I'm talking about over the last five or six years. We all agree on Brown Act, we all agree on Bagley-Keene, the two PRAs. We totally believe that charter schools should have those laws apply to them. We disagree on Government Code 1090, and it's for a very practical reason. It's not because we're not supportive of conflict of interest laws or transparency or anything like that. Government code 1090 prohibits a City Council member or school board member from having any financial arrangement or relationship with the entity on whose board they sit. When you apply to that a non-profit charter school, you are talking about board members who actually are there to help keep the doors open. I know many of you have probably sat on non-profit boards. You know what it's like. The non-profit needs your help. They need you to raise money, but they sometimes also need you to step up and do extraordinary things. So a few years ago when the Legislature and the Governor deferred payment of Prop 98 dollars to all schools including charter schools. School districts were able to go out and get 2% and 3% interest bridge loans to get them through the hard times until the Legislature was able to send money again. Other schools were getting 13% and 14% and 15% and our board members were stepping up and making sure that they could get loans that they could actually afford. They would not be allowed to do that under government code 1090. They would not be allowed to lease a facility for a dollar a year under government code 1090. That only accrues to the benefit of the charter school, it does not accrue to the benefit of the person. And these are things that it's so important for a charter school to be able to do. Because we have one source of funding and that's our Prop 98 ADA. Everything has to come out of that. We can't rely on our charter school board members to step up and do the things that we need them to do to keep the school open.

As the analysis points out, legislative counsel explains that Government Code 1090 does apply at charter schools. The law subjects governing board members to criminal prosecution for self dealing in efforts to protect tax dollars. It makes clear that no member of a governing board may have a financial interest in decisions before the board. On the other hand the corporations code does allow half of the governing board members to be making a profit from the contracts they are approving. This is because the Corporations Code is meant to protect the corporation, the public record, I'm sorry, the Government Code 1090 is meant to protect the public. This bill that charter schools comply with Government Code 1090, why now? Amendments that were taken in Senate Education Committee allow a governing board member, at a charter school, to lease property Provided that it's below market rate. If one board member does own the property on which the school sits, the balance of power tilts. If it's my school, I'm calling the shots. As you consider this bill, I urge you to bear in mind why sexual violence is an educational civil rights issue. Sexual violence disproportionately affects women and LGBTQ and gender nonconforming people and especially women and girls of color. And it often has a devastating effect on students' abilities to succeed academically. In the absence of a fair and effective grievance procedure, students who are victims of sexual assault by classmates or by school personnel are left with the impossible challenge of attending school each day with the person who assaulted them. Combined with the normal effects of sexual assault, which include depression, nightmares, loss of self esteem, and difficulty concentrating. These students are faced with constant anxiety about encountering their assailant and often with further harassment from that person or their associates. Under these circumstances, students drop classes, their grades suffer, and many drop out of school. But the consequences go beyond the classroom. As one report on what has been called the sexual abuse to prison pipeline explained, when schools fail to support girls who are victimized by gender based violence and harassment on campus, girls no longer feel safe. And as a result may disengage, may become truant, or exhibit challenging behaviors that are rooted in the trauma they have experienced. Yet instead of being viewed as victims of sexual violence, these girls are often disciplined, including being suspended, expelled, or referred to law enforcement. The effect of sexual violence on women's access to education is a critical educational equity issue. Time and again, studies have confirmed the prevalence of sexual assault, both at the college level and in our middle schools and in our high schools. During the Obama administration, students benefitted from increased enforcement of Title IX and from guidance issued to schools to better equip them to respond to sexual violence fairly and compassionately.

Genevieve Casey: Got it. Okay, thank you My name is Genevieve Casey. I'm an attorney with the law firm, Feinberg, Jackson, Worthman & Wasow in Oakland. We focus on civil rights fiduciary duties, labor law, charitable trust law, and health care policy issues that affect workers and patients. The bill makes a limited but important clarification in the law regarding the Attorney General supervisory authority over nonprofit hospitals. Under the current law, the Attorney General already reviews proposed sales and transfers of non profit health facilities assets. These transactions cannot occur if the Attorney General does not consent. The Attorney General's authority to supervise these types of transactions is based on long standing legal principles. That charitable assets have to be used for the purposes for which they were contributed, and that the Attorney General stands in the public's shoes to oversee charities, making sure the assets they hold and trust are used to serve the public. The Attorney General's proposed review process is closely modeled on the process that exists, for when nonprofit hospitals seek to sell or transfer their assets. The Attorney General will hear public comment and can consider any factors he or she decides are relevant, including the impact on access to healthcare in the community. And whether or not the change is consistent with the nonprofit hospital's charitable purpose. The Attorney General has a great deal of expertise and experience in overseeing nonprofit hospital assets. So this is a flexible process that respects that expertise. The Attorney General has discretion in terms of what evidence to consider. We'll wait to give the evidence and what determination to make. For example, the AG could consent to a reduction in emergency services, but set forth certain conditions designed to ease the impact on patients. For that reason, my firm and I support the bill.

For the most part senior service providers and senior facilities want to provide a good care to the edgy clients but already disadvantage in knowing how to provide it. [{'start': 15, 'end': 26, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}, {'start': 108, 'end': 116, 'label': 'PERSON'}]
Ricardo Lara: Thank you. Mr. Chair and members, I really thank you for indulging me today. It seems like it's the Ricardo Lara Judiciary Committee hour. Mr. Chair, and members, I would like to start by accepting, and clarifying amendments included in the Committee analysis. To make it clear that a record of arrest can not be included in an investigative report unless an indictment, information, or a misdemeanor complaint results. SB 393 establishes a uniform legal process for sealing records of arrest that did not result in a conviction. Again, that did not result in a conviction. Arrest records that are not sealed can be costly and life-changing. Studies have found that 40% of men and 20% of women were likely to be arrested before the age of 23, yet 47% were never convicted. Law enforcement will continue to have access to the complete arrest records even if the cases did not lead in a conviction. Current law prohibits employers from asking an applicant about prior arrests that did not lead to a conviction. However consumer reporting agencies and major corporations routinely report arrest records and background checks and obviously can have a negative impact on job applicants for decades. The FBI reports that it has over 77 million individuals on file in their criminal master database, which translates to one in three adults. Many people find themselves trapped in a paper prison, in which they are denied employment and housing due to the arrest records that did not result in a conviction. With the rapid technological advances, government information is compiled in databases and utilized by consumer reporting agencies. This makes it easier for employers, landlords, and others to base decisions on the arrests, rather than on a conviction. Although California has a comprehensive statutory process to expunge convictions, it has an inconsistent standard for sealing arrest records for individuals not convicted. Many individuals who are arrested are never charged. Sometimes their cases are charged, but later dismissed or can be acquitted by a jury. People with public arrest records have substantially increased chances of living in poverty, earning lower wages with fewer educational opportunities. Current record sealing procedures are clearly ineffective and do not provide a mechanism to properly seal arrests for peoples' records. By removing the records of arrests for those who were never convicted of a crime we can remove barriers that are holding back Californians from employment, housing, and educational opportunities. I respectfully ask for your aye vote.

Jason Rhine: Good afternoon again, Mr. Chair and members, Jason Rhine, League of California Cities. We have concerns with the proposed to be amended version that is in mockup form in your analysis. We certainly acknowledge there's a housing crisis, there's no doubt about it. Two of our goals this year at the League of California Cities that were adapted by membership say that we need to do more on housing and we are making a very conscious effort to do that. However, the measure as it's going to be amended, we have two very significant concerns. The first deals with the burden of proof and it seems like it's easy to change substantial evidence to clear and convincing evidence, and that it would go on and be not that big of a deal. But it actually is a very fundamental and just a huge concern and problem because land use decisions at the local level are enshrined in the Constitution. And not only are local land use decisions in the Constitution, but the Legislature has taken it a step further and they have provided further limitations in the civil procedures code. So the whole underpinning to that process is that evidentiary standard of substantial evidence and if the Legislature were to do away with that and have a different standard of proof, it would just upend that entire process and what it would do is that there would be separation of powers issues between the judicial and the legislative branch, which essentially would be the city council at that time. And the reason for that is the city council is applying the law, which is the Housing Accountability Act or whatever the law, to a set of facts. It is not second-guessing whether the city is right or wrong in that decision, it is did they apply the laws that the Legislature has made appropriately? If they did not, it gets sent back to the city and you must fix it. You need to change your application of the law and redo it, basically. That can't possibly happen in a clear and convincing standard because it would allow the courts to say no, your conclusion is wrong, and essentially rewrite that law. So we believe it's unconstitutional and the measures, we'd oppose based on that alone. The second point, which is in our minds, equally as important, is the fine provisions. Not so much on the size of the fine, I mean $100,000 per unit fine is quite significant, but it's really the application of that fine and when that fine shall be applied to the local government. Under existing law now, if a city violates the law, the court sends it back to the local government and if they don't fix it and do it right and they act in bad faith, which is key, then the courts can fine you. Under the provisions of the bill now, it eliminates that bad faith provision, so the city would be faced with a fine if they just accidentally violated the law, not that they actually made bad faith. So with that, we ask for your opposition.

Erin Guerrero: Good morning, Mr. Chair and members, Erin Guerrero on behalf of the California Building Industry Association and the sponsors of AB 1515. The Housing Accountability Act or HAA is also known as California's Anti-Nimby Law. It has not been effective in preventing NIMBYs from blocking housing projects and perpetuating California's housing crisis. According to HCD, we need to build at least 180,000 homes annually to keep pace with the demand. Not accounting for the back log of 2 million homes that has accrued over the past several decades. Currently we're producing about half of the estimated need. Obviously, we're not on track to build an additional 3.5 million homes by 2025 to accommodate California's current and future housing needs, unless something changes. AB 1515 is intended to breathe new life into the HAA. It's been far too easy for project opponents, the NIMBYs that the HAA was originally addressing, to circumvent the HAA. They put pressure on a local government, which in turn can find that a project is inconsistent with any of a variety of local plans or ordinances. Once the local government makes a determination that a project is inconsistent, the project is no longer able to benefit from the protections of the HAA which basically said that housing projects can only be denied for health and safety reasons which cannot be remedied. Home builders are usually leery to sue over these matters. The courts show a tendency to find in favor of the local government and home builders are not in the practice of pursuing lawsuits that they feel they will lose, thats why theres not a breath of case law in this matter. AB 1515 levels the playing field, instead of NIMBYs having the advantage by their ability to point to a project being inconsistent, projects will now be deemed consistent if theres substantial evidence that would allow a reasonable person to conclude that the project is consistent. The reasonable person standard is a commonly applied standard in courts of law. By applying that standard to projects consistency with local plans and ordinances, more housing projects will fall under the HAA and will be less likely to be rejected out of hand base on NIMBY pressure. With me today is Paul Campos a lawyer with the Building Industry Association of the Bay Area, and a subject expert on the HAA, and we respectfully ask for your aye vote.
