[{'start': 0, 'end': 13, 'label': 'SPEAKER'}]
Sharon Rapport: Good morning, Sharon Rapport from the Corporation of Supportive Housing. One of the most disturbing trends that we see in homelessness in California is the increase in homelessness among unaccompanied children and youth. And as Assemblymember Gloria said, we have seen a 7% increase just between 2015 and 2016 and that makes California have the highest population of homeless youth in the country. We actually have almost a third of all homeless youth in the nation, 78% of whom are sleeping on the streets or in vehicles. Homeless youth are more likely to experience serious mental illness and substance use disorders. They are more likely to drop out of school. They are more socially isolated and they are far more likely to experience chronic homelessness and eventually die prematurely on our streets than their housed counterparts. 40% of young women experiencing homelessness and 56% of transgender youth experiencing homelessness are sex trafficked every year. And yet, despite this population's dramatic outcomes, they have very few resources to exit homelessness, far fewer resources than families and adults experiencing homelessness. They are typically excluded from programs that families and single adults can access. They're subject to barriers that communities have been working to eradicate for families and single adults for the last several years. Because of this, the US Interagency Council on Homelessness has urged communities to remove barriers to making housing and services available to any homeless youth who needs and wants it. They've urged communities to use a coordinated entry process to link youth to housing and services addressing their needs, to act with urgency to help youth be able to access non-time limited housing and to develop resources, plans and systems that address homelessness among youth. AB 1406 would allow California to make significant progress toward these goals. The bill would offer competitive funding to local jurisdictions to provide housing and services to young people experiencing homelessness. It would offer a flexible approach to address the specific needs of young adults, services tailored to support the youth transition to economic Independence and self-sufficiency, and support these communities to coordinate their systems and plan to ensure youth exit homelessness permanently. AB 1406 provides long-term solutions to stem the increases in youth homelessness while ensuring a more effective response to the crisis. I'd like to thank Assemblymember Gloria and the Chair for authoring this important legislation and I urge your aye vote.

So I went and told him I had to move and they told me how to go, and apply, and get it. So I was able to stay there and I have lived there for 29 years, 9 months and 5 days. We were the first complex that was sold in the State of California to a for-profit and they immediately wanted to evict all of that Section 8 tenants which was 100%, and go full market rent. We were able to go to Washington, DC and have a law written that grandfathered us in. So we were able to stay and then they tried again by raising the rent, and they raised the rent so high that the housing authority turned them down. So they sold and I was going to DC and the day before I left for DC, I got another notice that I had 30 days to vacate. So I had an appointment with HUD the next day and I went to DC, and went to HUD. And we made a conference call and they said, well, we're new owners, we don't want to accept this. And they said, when you bought the property, you bought the contract and they're grandfathered in. So they immediately started flipping the property and it was flipped I know at least 4 times, and it might have been 5 times in 1 year and we got another 30-day notice. But this time, the people had had died off or had moved away or had grown up were no longer there. And we went from 104 apartments down to 34 subsidized tenants and they gave all 34 of us a 30 day notice to move. Well, there was nothing here that could help. I couldn't get to DC and couldn't talk to anybody long enough to get something done. So consequently, I was evicted while I was giving shots to my neighbor for diabetes and they wouldn't even let me take my purse or my walker. And if it hadn't been a shift there, I told them, I can't walk without the walker and I have no ID. The sheriff actually went into the house and got those two items for me. I was locked out and no place to go. It was hard. I thought here, I came here to die. I am getting well and now then I am out on the streets, and thank God that there was an organization that took me out to a safe house, and took to me to a place that I could rent with my voucher. And I moved into Hansen Garden apartments and out of North in Hurley Avenue, and they had a very strong Tenants Association there which I was very thankful for. And I've been there since a year and a half, it'll be two years in August and they tell me now that they have said they've turned two people down and they said, we're no longer taking Section 8 vouchers. I don't know when they're going to give us a notice, if they're going to give us a notice, or if they're going to do what our other owners did, just kick us out. Because there has to be a way to notify tenants when they are struggling to keep a roof over their head. We're talking about veterans, women, children, the elderly, disabled, and the poorest of the poor. And they have no safe guards, they have no background. They don't even know it's happening to them until one neighbor says, they told they wasn't going to take my voucher, when I went to re-up. And then we're saying, what happened? Our manager is only there six hours a week, and this is an elderly complex. We need this bill for protection, we have already lost, you've heard the number here in California. But across the United States, we've lost over a million and a half units of subsidized housing. California leads the United States second behind New York State, of having the most subsidized housing. We need to protect them We need your help. Please see to the passage of this. Thank you for allowing me to speak.

Anya Lawler: Good morning, Mr.Chair and members. Anya Lawler with the Western Center on Law&Poverty, one of the sponsors of this bill. As Mr. Bloom said, AB 1505, restores the ability of local governments to apply inclusionary policies on a rental context of power that they had up until 2009. It's important to note that's what not an issue in this bill is for sale inclusionary which operates in California without restriction other than the usual constitutional limits that apply to similar land use controls. Inclusion policies have been in place in California since the early 70s and they've also been used successfully throughout the country to produce affordable rental homes and affordable for sale homes. Unfortunately, an erroneous court ruling in 2009 cut off the ability to apply these policies in a rental context. That case, Palmer versus City of LA, as Mr. Bloom said, said that rental inclusionary policies run afowl of the Costa-Hawkins act, which limits rent control ordinances. When House asked, if the Legislature in adopting Costa-Hawkins had truly intended it to impede rental inclusionary, why does the entire legislative history only mention the dozen or so cities that had rent control policies at the time Costa-Hawkins was adopted. And not the 70 jurisdictions that had inclusionary policies that applied to rental housing on the books at that time. Why would the Legislature, with absolutely no discussion whatsoever, decide somewhat arbitrarily, to cut off rental inclusionary and not for sale inclusionary? And why in the 14 years between the adoption of Costa-Hawkins and the Palmer decision, did nobody raise this issue when over 100 more cities and counties adopted inclusionary policies that applied to rental. It just doesn't make a lot of sense. AB 1505 restores a tool that local governments can use to address our state's deep affordable housing crisis. It's one tool, it's a tool that is designed locally, it's a local choice. And it has to be designed to work for the local market. We've worked hard to address concerns of the rental and for sale building industries, who no longer oppose the bill, once the amendments today are adopted. We think it's a fair policy. We think it's a critical tool, and we urge your aye vote.
